[828][Para 008] 
[829][Para 011] Fig. 5.2 Intraoral images of this patient, anterior and lateral occlusal views.
[830][Para 009]  
[831][Para 012] Social History
[832][Para 007] There is a history of bullying at school because of her dental appearance.
[833][Para 012] Medical History
[834][Para 007] The patient is medically fit and well.
[835][Para 014] Examination
[836][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[837][Para 007] On examination, the facial profile is essentially class I; the extraoral facial features of this patient are balanced; the chin does not protrude, and the maxilla does not appear retroclined clinically. A straightforward way to assess this is by drawing a tangent between the tip of the nose and chin. The vermillion borders of upper and lower lips should lie close to this line (E-line) ( Fig. 5.1 ). There are some signs of ectodermal dysplasia such as thin lips, sparse hair and fair skin.
[838][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[839][Para 001] There is a class III incisor relationship with a reverse overjet.
[840][Para 002] Teeth present:
[841][09 Block] 
[842][Para 002] Both maxillary permanent lateral incisors as well as both mandibular central incisors are absent clinically. Both lower deciduous central incisors are present and grade 2 mobile. There is an upper midline diastema and rotated upper canines (Fig. 5.2). It is important to assess if there is mandibular shift forwards on final closure; this is known as displacement. Clinically, the patient should be asked into go to maximum returned mandibular position: This can be done by asking the patient to roll the tongue to the back of the throat and close the mouth slowly. Manual manipulation can also be tried. Displacement is diagnosed if the incisors meet on closure and the patient has to protrude her mandible to achieve maximum intercuspation. Hallmarks for displacement are signs of attrition on the front teeth. In this patient, there were no signs of displacement.
[843][Para 002] In summary, the extraoral features (class I) and intraoral features (class III) do not match. Cephalometric analysis will be useful to assess the severity of the class III skeletal base.
[844][Para 024]  What are the Causes for Absent Lateral and Lower Central Incisors and the Class Iii Incisor Relationship? What Specific Questions Would You Ask the Patient/Parents?
[845][Para 020] Questions Regarding the Missing Teeth
[846][Para 001] It may be useful to ask if any teeth were missing in the deciduous dentition. This is unusual but not entirely implausible. It is extremely unlikely that permanent teeth are present if their deciduous predecessors were absent. Permanent teeth may be absent, however, when deciduous teeth are present, as shown in this case for the lower central incisors.
[847][Para 002] Hypodontia in the permanent dentition is quite common, the prevalence ranges between 0.15% and 16% of the population. It often runs in families, and the family history may reveal this. There are over 300 genes that are related to nonsyndromic hypodontia but AXIN2, MSX1, PAX9 and EDA are the ones most commonly mentioned in the literature.
[848][Para 002] Regarding the missing upper lateral incisors, trauma should be excluded.
[849][Para 020] Questions Regarding the Class Iii Incisor Relationship.
[850][Para 001] A class III incisor relationship can have a variety of causes, namely, unusual eruption path of the permanent teeth, missing teeth, poor growth of the maxilla and/or excessive growth of the mandible. Class III malocclusion may also run in families and are more common in the Far Eastern populations. The prevalence in Northern Europe is about 3% and is about 13% in the Far East. A positive family history needs careful evaluation and consent by the patient for further unfavourable growth, potentially requiring additional orthodontic or even surgical treatment at a later stage.
[851][Para 014] Investigations
[852][Para 001] Radiographs required for orthodontic purposes are a dental panoramic tomogram (DPT) and a lateral cephalometric view (see Fig. 5.1).
[853][Para 002] The radiographs show the developmental absence of both upper lateral incisors and both lower central incisors.
[854][Para 014] Diagnosis
[855][Para 001] The final diagnosis is a class III malocclusion on a class mild III skeletal base, with four missing permanent teeth: upper lateral and lower central incisors.
[856][Para 002] In the UK, the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN) is used to assess eligibility for treatment free of charge at the point of delivery (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/Orthodontics/).
[857][Para 099] The IOTN for this patient was 4 g. More detailed information on IOTN can be found at: https://www.bos.org.uk/Public-Patients/Orthodontics-for-Children-Teens/Fact-File-FAQ/What-Is-The-IOTN.
[858][Para 014] Care Planning/Treatment
[859][Para 001] Care planning requires interdisciplinary input with close collaboration between the specialist orthodontist and the general dental practitioner or specialist prosthodontist/restorative dentist.
[860][Heading 2]  What Other Diagnostic Tools Can Be Employed To Help Plan the Treatment for This Patient?
[861][Para 001] The following factors need to be considered before treatment commences:
[862][Para 016] 1. Can the class III incisor relationship be treated by orthodontic camouflage, or will this malocclusion need a surgical (comprehensive) approach?
[863][Para 016] 2. Will the spaces for the missing teeth be closed or opened for prosthodontic replacement of the missing teeth?
[864][Para 016] 3. What kind of prosthodontic replacement will be in the patient’s best interests?
[865][Para 016] 4. What will the retention regime be, particularly with a long-term view of the prosthodontic replacement of the missing teeth?
[866][Para 002] The above radiographs (see Fig. 5.1) can be used to decide question 1:
[867][Para 004] • The upper incisors are not proclined before start of treatment and the skeletal base is not excessively class III. An ANB difference on the lateral cephalometric radiograph of more than −4 degrees would be considered severe, most likely requiring jaw surgery for comprehensive correction. There is vertical overlap of the incisors, indicating a good prognosis for the orthodontic correction of the incisor relationship. Therefore, orthodontic camouflage can be attempted. There is a small but acceptable risk of unfavourable skeletal growth, which the patient needs to consent to.
[868][Para 002] To decide question 2, the following issues have to be considered:
[869][Para 004] • Closing spaces for the missing teeth has the obvious advantage that no prosthodontic replacement will be necessary for replacement in the long term. Modification of the shape and size of the upper canines using resin composite additions needs to be considered because better resemble lateral incisors.
[870][Para 004] • However, from an orthodontic point of view, biomechanical considerations speak against complete space closure. Space closure mechanics are likely to retrocline the incisors in both the upper and lower arches. This may have undesirable aesthetic consequences. In addition to that, in the lower arch, significant tipping of incisors lingually is associated with the risk of gingival recession. It is also unlikely that a class I incisor relationship can be achieved by retroclining the upper and lower labial segments. In orthodontics, a class III malocclusion can be camouflaged with three lower incisors, and this scenario might work well for the patient. Opening space for the missing upper lateral incisors makes sense because it will lead to proclination of the upper front teeth, thereby achieving a positive overjet and overbite.
[871][Para 114] Further Diagnostic Tools
[872][Para 001] A diagnostic set-up can be made to assess whether tooth movement can achieve a satisfactory occlusal outcome (Fig. 5.3).
[873][Para 002] In this case, the diagnostic set-up should be made in such a way that the position of the posterior dentition is not changed. This reflects the orthodontic anchorage balance; during fixed appliance therapy, the posterior dentition is unlikely to move significantly (the front teeth provide little anchorage and the back teeth provide significant anchorage).
[874][Para 002] The diagnostic set-up can also be used to answer question 3.
[875][Para 002] The set-up provided in Fig. 5.3 shows that two upper lateral incisors and one lower central incisor provide a satisfactory occlusal outcome, with a positive overjet and a positive overbite achieved. In other words, the two missing lower incisors will be replaced by one.
[876][Para 218] 
[877][Para 008] 
[878][Para 011] Fig. 5.3 Photographs of the diagnostic set-up. Please note that the posterior teeth were not moved; this allows better orthodontic anchorage assessment. The set-up shows that space requirements insufficient for replacing the lateral incisors with implant based restorations. Prosthodontic replacement of the missing teeth with a resin-bonded bridge should be sought. The set-up also demonstrates that space reduction for the two missing lower incisors to one lower incisor will give a satisfactory occlusal outcome.
[879][Para 009]  
[880][Para 002] It also shows that there will be no space for implants to replace the missing upper lateral incisors and the lower incisor. Resin-bonded minimal preparation bridges are the best option for replacing the missing teeth for this patient.
[881][Para 002] Dental implants, which can be an alternative to resin-bonded bridges, require a minimum amount of bone to be placed successfully. Currently, the smallest commercially available implants are about 3 mm wide. Additional space is needed for gingival margin, and this adds another 1 mm of space or more on either side of the implant at the gingival level. However, narrow implants may not be suitable for all situations, and more space will be required at crown level.
[882][Para 002] The considerations for question 4 are complex and require input from the general dental practitioner (GDP)/prosthodontist particularly for long-term planning.
[883][Para 002] The malocclusion was originally also characterized by an upper midline diastema and rotated upper canines. Orthodontic space closure of an upper midline diastema is usually easy to achieve but very difficult to maintain over the long term. Fixed retainers are recommended after space closure of diastemas to avoid relapse.
[884][Para 002] Resin-bonded bridges replacing upper lateral incisors often use the canines as abutment teeth. The advantage is that the upper canines are darker in appearance compared with the central incisors and are hence not as susceptible to further darkening by palatally bonded attachments of the cantilever abutment.
[885][Para 017] In this case, it was decided to provide a resin-bonded bridge attached to the central incisors and not the canines. Both upper permanent canines were rotated at the beginning of the orthodontic treatment, and this also is prone to relapse.  Fig. 5.4  shows a situation in a different case, where the canine position relapsed and subsequently led to poor alignment of the lateral incisor replacements.
[886][Para 002] During orthodontics, prosthodontic teeth can be added to the appliance to improve aesthetics (Fig. 5.5). Initial retention was by provided by Hawley retainers. It is important to note that the retainers had ‘stops’ added adjacent to the replaced teeth. This reduced the chances of relapse if the replacement teeth were to fail. The labial bow was acrylated, and this design was chosen to stop the anterior teeth from rotating and to support the prosthodontic teeth (Fig. 5.6).

[897][Para 002] The patient and her parents/guardian need to be consented by the different teams involved.
[898][Para 002] This is done in multiple stages. It is paramount to inform the patient that the two treatment phases are likely to take a comparatively long time to complete.

[906][Para 012] Orthodontic Consent
[907][Para 001] Consent in orthodontics is ideally a two-stage process:
[908][Para 002] At the first stage, the patient and their parents/legal guardian are handed the relevant written information (often at the stage of orthodontic records: impressions/scan, clinical photographs and radiographs).
[909][Para 002] Information leaflets for orthodontic treatment are available through the British Orthodontic Society at: https://www.bos.org.uk/Public-Patients/Patient-Information-Leaflets.
[910][Para 002] On return, the patient and parent/legal guardian sign the consent form. It is important to note that consent is an ongoing process and that changes in the treatment plan that may become necessary need to be documented.
[911][Para 002] In this particular patient, further unfavourable growth as well as unwanted tooth movement after completion of interceptive treatment should be explicitly mentioned.
[912][Para 002] It is important to emphasize that retention should ideally continue even after the prosthodontic replacement of the teeth has been undertaken. It should be made clear that aftercare is a shared responsibility of the orthodontist and the dentist. The patient’s responsibility in aftercare/maintenance compliance should be clearly discussed and noted.
[913][Para 002] Under current National Health Services (NHS) England commissioning guidelines, 1 year of retention is provided. Subsequent costs will have to be borne out with NHS agreements. Patients need to be made aware of this and any other such longer-term costs.
[914][Para 002] However, the patient needs to be informed that it is the responsibility of the dentist, not the orthodontist, to maintain the resin-bonded bridges.
[915][Para 012] Prosthodontic Consent
[916][Para 001] This needs to be undertaken separately by the GDP/prosthodontist/restorative dentist. It must be made clear that this is a separate process. Issues such as survival rate and long- term maintenance and costs arising from those issues need to be well documented.
[917][Para 014] Potential Legal Issues and Pitfalls
[918][Para 001] Unfavourable growth can be an issue, but a negative family history and a mild class III skeletal base with good vertical overlap will reduce this risk. Consent should be clear about the length of treatment time, as well as the commitments for maintenance and the costs thereof.
[919][Para 218] 
[920][Para 008] 
[921][Para 011] Fig. 5.8 Treatment outcome 15 years after debonding. The upper resin-bonded bridges had been replaced to improve aesthetics in the upper jaw. Both upper canines have relapsed and rotated mesio-palatally similar to the original occlusion. Cantilevering the lateral incisors off the canines would have led to compromised aesthetics of the upper labial segment.
[922][Para 009]  
[923][Para 014] Long-Term Outcome
[924][Para 007] See  Fig. 5.8  for the long-term outcome 15 years after debonding. The patient had been provided with a second set of resin-bonded bridges. The upper canines had moved significantly since completion of treatment, but because of the attachment of the cantilevers to the central incisors, this had not resulted in compromised aesthetics. The overjet and the overbite had reduced slightly but remained positive; there was little inadvertent growth. The patient had stopped wearing removable retainers at that stage.
[925][Para 014] Summary
[926][Para 001] The case presented was a reasonably complex malocclusion with multiple missing teeth that was resolved by collaboration, input by specialist orthodontist and restorative care. Care planning of cases such as the one presented is often a challenge, and good patient communication is key.
[927][Para 025] Case 6
[928][Heading 1] An Unsettled Patient
[929][Para 027] Yvonne M. Rooney
[930][Para 028] Summary
[931][Para 029] A 70-year-old man attends your dental practice for a routine dental check-up accompanied by his wife ( Fig. 6.1 ). He appears confused about why he is here; he had failed to attend his last three appointments.
[932][Para 218] 
[933][Para 008] 
[934][Para 011] Fig. 6.1 The patient and his wife.
[935][Para 009]  
[936][Para 014] History
[937][Para 019] Complaint
[938][Para 007] The patient has no dental complaints, but his wife tells you that he has a painful tooth on the top left.
[939][Para 012] History of Complaint
[940][Para 007] The patient tells you that he has not had toothache for several months, but his wife interjects to say that the patient complains of toothache every time he eats and is only able to eat on the right side of his mouth.
[941][Para 012] Medical History
[942][Para 007] The patient was diagnosed last year with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease, for which he is taking donepezil.
[943][Para 012] Dental History
[944][Para 007] The patient and his wife have been regular attenders at your practice for the past 20 years. You review his dental records and realize he was due to return for endodontic treatment of the upper left first premolar 1 year ago.
[945][Para 014] Examination
[946][Para 007] There is a heavily restored dentition with multiple crowns. The upper left first premolar has unrestorable caries and is tender to percussion. There is generalized periodontitis with moderate attachment loss.
[947][Para 017] You decide to take a periapical radiograph of the upper left first premolar. As you place the film in the patient’s mouth, he becomes restless and agitated. His wife tells you that he has been increasingly irritable in recent months and attributes this to his Alzheimer’s disease.
[948][Heading 2]  What is Alzheimer’s Disease?
[949][Para 001] Alzheimer’s disease is the most common reason for dementia, and its cause is dysfunctional synapses and death of neurones in the cerebral cortex. Its aetiology is protein deposition in the neurofibrillary tangles in the neurone cytoplasm and amyloid plaques between the cells. The key symptom is the inability to remember new information.
[950][Heading 2]  How is Dementia Different From Alzheimer’s Disease?
[951][Para 001] Dementia is more broadly defined as a clinical syndrome of progressive neurodegenerative changes characterized by deterioration in memory, learning ability, visuospatial orientation, language, comprehension and judgement.
[952][Para 002] Dementia affects one in every 14 people over age 65 years, with up to 10% of cases estimated to start at an earlier age. It is estimated that 850000 people in the UK have dementia, two-thirds of whom are female. Worldwide, it is estimated that 47 million people are living with dementia, with projections that this will almost triple by 2050. Common forms of dementia and their relative prevalence rates are listed in Table 6.1.
[953][Heading 2]  What are the Signs and Symptoms of Dementia?
[954][Para 001] Individual signs and symptoms vary among individuals. Progressive brain damage leads to social and occupational impairments, movement problems and difficulties performing daily activities. There is an increasing dependence on family or formal carers. Behavioural and psychological symptoms affect 90% of patients with dementia at some stage of their condition and include agitation, aggression, psychosis, depression and apathy.
[955][Para 018] Table 6.1
[956][Para 021] Common Forms of Dementia and Their Relative Prevalence Rates
[957][Heading 2]  What are the Stages of Dementia?
[958][Para 001] Dementia staging is based on its impact on the person’s daily living activities and detailed in Table 6.2. Patients progress through these stages at an unpredictable rate and with differing signs and symptoms.
[959][Heading 2]  How is Dementia Typically Managed?
[960][Para 001] Management of dementia mostly relates to control of symptoms and access to supportive services.
[961][Para 002] Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. donepezil, rivastigmine) are recommended for management of mild to moderate Alzheimer’s disease under certain conditions, but many patients are not taking any medications for dementia.
[962][Heading 2]  Are There Any Medical Conditions Associated with Dementia?
[963][Para 001] Conditions thought to be linked to the development of dementia include Down’s syndrome, Parkinson’s disease, type II diabetes mellitus and depression.

[979][Heading 2]  How Will You Determine Whether the Patient Can Consent To This Treatment?
[980][Para 001] Assessing capacity to consent is a two-stage process, as outlined in the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA). The MCA provides a statutory framework to empower and protect vulnerable people in England and Wales who are not able to make their own decisions about treatment. In Scotland, the equivalent legislation is the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000. Common law applies in Northern Ireland. These acts contain guidelines for carers and professionals on making decisions on behalf of people who lack capacity. The Act states that capacity must be assessed at each visit. All decisions should be in the patient’s best interests, and the least restrictive treatment option should be chosen. Table 6.3 describes how you can assess this patient’s capacity to consent.

[985][Para 002] The capacity of patients with dementia tends to fluctuate. There may be better times of the day or days of the week to organize their dental appointment. Compliance does not always decline rapidly with dementia progression. Some people with dementia, who attended the dentist regularly, appear to remember and cope with the normal routine of a dental visit. In the middle to late stages of dementia, patients gradually lose the ability to consent to dental treatment.

[987][Heading 2]  What is a Lasting Power of Attorney?
[988][Para 001] In the UK, a Lasting Power of Attorney is a legal document that gives another person authority to make decisions on a patients’ behalf when they lose mental capacity or if they no longer want to make decisions for themselves. There are two different types – one for financial decisions and one for health and social care decisions.

[991][Para 004] • Communication and reassurance using the approach given above
[992][Para 004] • Having a relative nearby for emotional support and hand-holding
[993][Para 004] • Giving the patient something to hold for sensory stimulation, such as a ‘sensory/fiddle cushion’ or stress ball
[994][Para 004] • Short appointments – but do not inadvertently put yourself under time pressure
[995][Para 004] • Remember that it is not what you say but how you make patients feel that affects how they respond

[997][Heading 2]  What are the Important Dental Considerations for Patients with Dementia?
[998][Para 001] The best time to achieve a stable and healthy mouth is during the early stage of dementia by instituting a preventive regimen, which should include the following:
[999][Para 004] • Consider verbal reminders about toothbrushing from his wife or a laminated oral health plan on the bathroom wall if forgetfulness is a problem.
[1000][Para 004] • Consider an electric toothbrush or handle adaptation if the patient is unable to perform adequate oral hygiene.
[1001][Para 004] • Consider at what point it would be useful to demonstrate assisted toothbrushing techniques that allow a carer to help.
[1002][Para 004] • Assess caries risk and consider prescription of sodium fluoride 1.1% (5000 parts per million [ppm]) toothpaste to be used twice daily and fluoride varnish applications every 6 months
[1003][Para 004] • Advise limiting sugary foods and drinks to mealtimes. Provide a list of safe snacks.
[1004][Para 004] • Encourage water between meals, and educate on hidden and natural sugars. Dehydration can worsen the symptoms of dementia.
[1005][Para 004] • Stress the importance of living well with dementia and of maintenance of good oral health.
[1006][Para 030]  What Additional Measures May Be Necessary in Later Stages?
[1007][Para 001] Depending on their ability to perform activities of daily living, some patients with dementia may not be able to be supported to live in their own home. They may move to residential care or a nursing home. In cases where it is too disruptive for patients to leave their normal environment, domiciliary dental care may be provided. For patients in late-stage dementia who become increasingly frail, management focuses on palliative care, preventing dental pain and oral discomfort. Atraumatic dental techniques are used (e.g. Carisolv for caries removal, glass ionomer restorations and applications of fluoride varnish).
[1008][Para 002] In late-stage dementia, patients become totally reliant on carers to provide their oral care. Toothbrushing may be forgotten amongst other time pressured daily routines. The results of poor oral care and a diet high in sugar can have disastrous consequences, even in as little as 3 months.
[1009][Heading 2]  How Can Pain of Dental Origin Be Identified in Late Dementia?
[1010][Para 001] In the absence of verbal communication, patients may display changes in behaviour indicating their dental pain, which may include the following:
[1011][Para 004] • Refusing oral care or becoming distressed when toothbrushing
[1012][Para 004] • Waking from sleep displaying pain-related behaviour
[1013][Para 004] • Refusing food, avoiding hard textures or cold foods, or eating on one side of the mouth
[1014][Para 004] • Refusing personal care involving the face (e.g. shaving)
[1015][Para 004] • Changes in normal behaviour (e.g. previously quiet but now distressed)
[1016][Para 030]  Do Dentists Have a Role in Recognizing the Signs and Symptoms of Dementia?
[1017][Para 001] Unlike many medical conditions, dementia may not be diagnosed until late in its course. There are multiple barriers to its diagnosis, including stigma and a belief that forgetfulness is a natural part of ageing. The dental team members are well placed to spot subtle changes in behaviour. The following are possible signs and symptoms of early dementia:
[1018][Para 004] • Missed appointments
[1019][Para 004] • Confusion about planned dental treatment
[1020][Para 004] • Difficulty recalling people’s names
[1021][Para 004] • Difficulty remembering and finding the right words to describe dental problems
[1022][Para 004] • Anxiety about normal routines such as travel to the practice
[1023][Para 002] If you have concerns, you can suggest patients visit their general medical practitioner (GMP) or, where you feel it may be beneficial, offer to contact their GMP for them.
[1024][Para 002] Also, remember that caring for a patient with dementia has a considerable effect on the carer’s health. Ensure the patient’s wife is also receiving dental care.
[1025][Heading 2]  When Might You Consider Referral To Your Local Special Care Dentistry Services?
[1026][Para 001] The role of the general dental practitioner cannot be underestimated. They can successfully support patients through the early stages of dementia by helping patients achieve a healthy, low-maintenance dentition and by implementing preventive advice. Referral should be considered for patients in middle-stage dementia who are finding communication more difficult or displaying more frequent changes in behaviour. The referral should enable effective transition to the next dental team and should include information on medical practitioners, family members/carers and any radiographs.
[1027][Para 014] Further Guidance
[1028][Para 001] Further guidance is available from the Faculty of General Dental Practice UK (https://www.fgdp.org.uk/ and search ‘dementia’), the British Society of Gerodontology https://www.gerodontology.com/ and the Alzheimer’s Society (https://www.alzheimers.org.uk and search ‘dental’).

[1030][Heading 1] A Dry Mouth
[1031][Para 027] Pepe Shirlaw, and Edward Odell
[1032][Para 028] Summary
[1033][Para 029] A 50-year-old woman presents in your hospital dental department with a complaint of dry mouth. Identify the cause, and plan the treatment.

[1038][Para 014] History
[1039][Para 019] Complaint
[1040][Para 001] The patient complains of dryness of mouth, which makes many aspects of her life a misery. The dryness is both uncomfortable and renders eating and speech difficult. She is forced to keep a bottle of water by her side at all times.
[1041][Para 012] History of Complaint
[1042][Para 001] The patient first noticed the dry mouth about 4 or 5 years ago, although it may have been present for longer. At first, it was only an intermittent problem, but over the last 3 years or so, the dryness has become constant. Recently, the mouth has become sore as well as dry.
[1043][Para 012] Medical History
[1044][Para 001] The patient describes herself as generally fit and well but has had to attend her medical practitioner for poor circulation in her fingers. They blanch rapidly in the cold and are painful on rewarming. She has also used artificial tears for dry eyes for the last 2 years but takes no other medication.
[1045][Para 014] Examination
[1046][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[1047][Para 001] The patient is a well-looking woman without detectable cervical lymphadenopathy. There is no facial asymmetry or enlargement of the parotid glands, and the submandibular glands appear normal on bimanual palpation. Her eyes and fingers appear normal.
[1048][Para 049] Intraoral Examination
[1049][Heading 2]  The Appearance of the Patient’s Mouth is Shown in Figs 7.1 and 7.2. What Do You See? How Do You Interpret the Findings?
[1050][Para 001] The alveolar mucosa appears ‘glazed’ and translucent or thin (atrophic), suggesting long-standing xerostomia. Some oral debris is seen adhering between teeth, again suggesting dryness, which causes plaque to be thicker and more tenacious. There are carious lesions and restorations at the cervical margins of the lower anterior teeth, indicating a high caries rate. The tongue is lobulated and fissured. Both features suggest a lack of saliva.
[1051][Para 002] If you were able to examine the patient, you would find that her mouth does feel dry. Gloved fingers and dental mirror stick to the mucosa, making examination uncomfortable for the patient. Parts of the mucosa, especially the palate and dorsal tongue, appear redder than normal. No saliva is pooling in the floor of the mouth, and what saliva can be identified is frothy and thick. Small amounts of clear but viscid saliva can be expressed from all four main salivary ducts.
[1052][Para 218] 
[1053][Para 008] 
[1054][Para 011] Fig. 7.2 Appearance of the patient’s tongue.
[1055][Para 009]  
[1056][Heading 2]  What are the Common and Important Causes of Xerostomia, and How are They Subdivided?
[1057][Para 001] In true xerostomia, the salivary flow is reduced. The term ‘false’ xerostomia or subjective xerostomia describe the sensation of dryness despite normal salivary output.
[1058][07 Block] 
[1059][Para 030]  On the Basis of the History and Examination, Which Cause is the Most Likely? Why?
[1060][Para 001] Sjögren’s syndrome is the most likely cause. It is the commonest single medical disorder causing xerostomia. It also causes dry eyes and predominantly affects female patients of middle age. Sjögren’s syndrome is sometimes defined by the presence of dry eyes and dry mouth, with or without an autoimmune/connective tissue disorder. This patient meets these criteria, although they are rather imprecise, and further investigations would be required to confirm the diagnosis.
[1061][Heading 2]  Which Causes Have You Excluded, and Why?
[1062][Para 001] Drugs are, by far, the commonest cause of true xerostomia, but this patient is not taking any medication.
[1063][Para 002] Dehydration is a common cause in older people who may have a habitual low fluid intake, especially when institutionalized. It also accompanies cardiac or renal failure or use of diuretic drugs. (The combination of drugs and disease probably explains the apparent association of xerostomia with age.) These are not factors in this case.
[1064][Para 002] False or subjective xerostomia is very common. Those who sleep with an open mouth will have xerostomia on waking, compounded by the normal reduction in salivary secretion at night. Diseases causing oral mucosal roughness, such as lichen planus or candidosis, may cause a sensation of dryness, but no such condition is present. False or subjective xerostomia, may be a feature, sometimes a central one, in psychiatric disorders. However, this patient’s mouth is genuinely dry; the mucosa is not lubricated, and there is no saliva pooling in the mouth. The history of prolonged and unremitting dryness over a period of years almost always indicates a salivary disorder, and the appearance of the mucosa and the high caries rate indicate true xerostomia.
[1065][Para 002] Neurological and developmental causes such as aplasia of gland or atresia of ducts are very rare and need not be considered further until common causes have been investigated. There is no history of irradiation of the head and neck.
[1066][Heading 2]  What is Sjögren’s Syndrome, and How May the Condition Be Subclassified?
[1067][Para 001] Sjögren’s syndrome is an autoimmune disorder in which exocrine glands are destroyed, causing salivary hypofunction. In primary Sjögren’s syndrome, the salivary and lacrimal glands are those most affected (although there are often nonspecific systemic signs of autoimmune disease such as Raynaud’s phenomenon), and sometimes, there is salivary gland swelling. Other exocrine glands and organs are also affected. In secondary Sjögren’s syndrome, there is an accompanying connective tissue disorder such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, primary biliary cirrhosis or mixed connective tissue disease. Other exocrine glands maybe less severely affected in the secondary form, and the mouth is usually less dry; however, the degree of salivary hypofunction can be quite variable in Sjögren’s syndrome.
[1068][Para 015] Investigations
[1069][Heading 2]  What Simple Test Differentiates False and True Xerostomia?
[1070][Para 001] Measuring the whole salivary flow rate. This may be done by asking the patient to tilt the head forward to allow all saliva to flow into a graduated specimen container for 10 minutes. Although this patient is strongly suspected to have true xerostomia, it would still be a useful test because it provides a baseline reading against which disease severity and progression may be judged.
[1071][Para 017] When you measure the flow, the patient has a whole salivary flow rate of less than 0.1 ml/min.
[1072][Heading 2]  What Salivary Flow/Objective Rate Would You Consider To Indicate Xerostomia?
[1073][Para 001] Approximately 500 ml of saliva is secreted daily, mostly during eating and drinking, and very little at night. Rates vary greatly among individuals, but less than 2 ml in 10 minutes (0.2 ml/min) unstimulated whole saliva flow is generally considered to indicate xerostomia.
[1074][Para 002] This patient has true xerostomia.
[1075][Heading 2]  What Further Investigations are Required, and Why is Each Performed?
[1076][Para 001] Although a number of investigations will be required to confirm the diagnosis, the immediate problem is one of soreness. A dry mouth is not usually sore unless there is superimposed candidal infection. A smear sample, a saliva sample or a therapeutic trial of antifungal agent is required to exclude this possibility.
[1077][Para 002] The diagnosis of Sjögren’s syndrome is straightforward when the clinical presentation is florid and may then be based on history and the results of physical examination alone. However, numerous investigations are required in most patients with suspected Sjögren’s syndrome, in whom there are just a few early signs (Table 7.1). Many investigations are possible, but only the minimum required to make the diagnosis needs to be performed. A selection is usually necessary because every test will be negative in a small proportion of patients, and none is completely specific.

[1100][Para 015] Diagnosis
[1101][Heading 2]  What is Your Final Diagnosis?
[1102][Para 001] The patient has primary Sjögren’s syndrome. The diagnosis was suspected on the basis of history and the results of physical examination and was confirmed by the characteristic findings on sialography and biopsy analysis. The primary form of Sjögren’s syndrome is indicated by the lack of autoimmune/connective tissue disease and the positivity for ssA and ssB autoantibodies. The presence of Raynaud’s phenomenon, the severity of the xerostomia and the dryness of the eyes are also more consistent with the primary form. In addition, the patient has candidosis, which is the probable cause of the soreness.
[1103][Para 015] Treatment
[1104][Heading 2]  How Could You Contribute To the Management of This Patient?
[1105][Para 001] Control of the underlying disease is not possible but the patient requires treatment for complications and continued follow-up:
[1106][Para 004] • Treat the candidosis, and follow up regularly for recurrence.
[1107][Para 004] • Help preserve what salivary secretion remains; saliva is more effective than saliva substitutes. Instruct the patient as follows:
[1108][Para 034] • Sip water rather than drinking it, so as to expand remaining saliva and not wash it from the mouth. At night, use simple oils such as coconut or olive oil to lubricate the mouth instead of water.
[1109][Para 034] • Whenever possible, avoid drugs that cause xerostomia.
[1110][Para 034] • Maintain fluid intake.
[1111][Para 034] • Stimulate residual salivary flow by using chewing gum (sugar-free).
[1112][Para 034] • Take pilocarpine if the condition is severe (although side effects and an appropriate dosing regimen can be problematic).
[1113][Para 004] • Prevent and treat dental caries.
[1114][Para 034] • Have the patient avoid sweets or overuse of citrus fruit to stimulate salivary flow.
[1115][Para 034] • Prescribe high-fluoride toothpaste (5000 parts per million [ppm]) for a period.
[1116][Para 034] • Provide appropriate dietary analysis and preventive advice.
[1117][Para 034] • Treat caries.
[1118][Para 004] • Consider prescribing saliva substitutes, although these are generally unsatisfactory and not liked by patients.
[1119][Para 034] • Carboxymethyl-cellulose and similar starch-based liquids may be prescribed.
[1120][Para 034] • Mucin-based preparations are more effective and generally better tolerated.
[1121][Para 004] • Warn the patient about, and follow up for, attacks of acute bacterial ascending sialadenitis in the major glands, which destroy residual gland function. Treat aggressively if it develops.
[1122][Para 004] • Warn the patient, and follow up for, development of persistent salivary gland swelling.
[1123][Para 004] • Provide continued reassurance and care to patients with this distressing condition.
[1124][Para 004] • Medications such as pilocarpine can be used to stimulate saliva production and to relieve the dry mouth symptoms. In some patients, the antirheumatic drug hydroxychloroquine has been beneficial in decreasing fatigue and joint pain.
[1125][Para 004] • Disease-modifying agents such as the tumour necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors infliximab and etanercept have been investigated, but neither has been found to improve disease outcomes. Rituximab, an anti-CD20 antibody that depletes B cells, has been evaluated in several trials with mixed results.
[1126][Para 004] • Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), a nonpharmacological technique, has shown encouraging results in increasing salivary secretion without side effects but is not widely available. Acupuncture has been tried in patients with Sjögren’s syndrome but has weak evidence, and further research is necessary.
[1127][Para 030]  What is the Significance of the Development of Salivary Gland Swelling?
[1128][Para 001] This is usually the first sign of lymphoma development; 10% or more of patients with primary Sjögren’s syndrome eventually develop lymphoma, and in some cases, gland swelling is the presenting sign. The lymphoma is usually a form of low grade B-cell lymphoma (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue [MALT] type), which has a slow indolent growth pattern, remains localized to the salivary glands for a long period and initially responds well to treatment. However, high-grade lymphoma may also develop. Persistent gland swelling would be an indication for biopsy.
[1129][Para 002] Less common complications might occur in various organs, causing pneumonia or bronchitis in the lungs and hepatitis or cirrhosis in the liver and might lead to problems in kidney function. In some patients, peripheral neuropathy develops, causing numbness, tingling and burning in the hands and feet.
[1130][Para 014] Further Guidance
[1131][Para 001] The Sjögren’s Syndrome Foundation clinical practice guidelines can be recommended to patients as a source for further information (https://www.sjogrens.org/home/research-programs/clinical-practice-guidelines).

[1133][Heading 1] Painful Trismus

[1158][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[1159][Heading 2]  The Patient Has Trismus. What is Trismus?
[1160][Para 001] True trismus is defined as reduced mouth opening caused by spasm of the muscles supplied by the trigeminal nerve. It was traditionally used to refer to the ‘lockjaw’ seen in tetanus, which is an infection with the toxin-producing anaerobe Clostridium tetani, but is more commonly used to refer to reduced mouth opening of any cause. Trismus can be permanent or temporary, but most causes of true trismus are temporary.
[1161][Para 018] Table 8.1
[1162][Para 040] Causes of Trismus
[1163][Para 044] 
[1164][Heading 2]  What are the Causes of Trismus?
[1165][Para 001] The causes of trismus are often divided into intra-articular causes and extra-articular causes, which are described in Table 8.1.
[1166][Heading 2]  What are the Common Causes of Pain in the Temporomandibular Joint?
[1167][Para 001] Pain in the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is a common complaint, but much of that pain is referred to the joint rather than originating in it. Many of the above causes of trismus are painful, but most disease of the joint is asymptomatic. The pathogenesis of painful TMJ disorders is poorly understood, and causes are notoriously hard to classify. Here are three common causes:
[1168][Para 002] Osteoarthrosis (noninflammatory degenerative changes) in the TMJ. These are similar to arthritic changes, but occur in the absence of severe inflammation. The cause has commonly been put down to ‘wear and tear’ but is probably multifactorial, with a genetic predisposition and abnormal cartilage repair. The severity of the process may be compounded by occlusal malalignment, ligament laxity and dysfunctional muscle contraction causing torsional loading. It is hypothesized that this causes mild trauma and persistent mild inflammation. Clinically, the disease is characterized by clicking, locking, chronic pain, stiffness, reduction in range of movement and crepitus. This is associated with anatomical and radiographic changes to the joint architecture, such as destruction of cartilage, resorption of subchondral bone, synovitis and osseous remodelling.
[1169][Para 002] Internal derangement of the TMJ is a description of a situation in which the biomechanics of the joint have become dysfunctional as a result of displacement of the articular disc on the mandibular condyle. Anterior displacement of the disc is most common, but it can occur laterally, medially or, rarely, posteriorly. Patients with internal derangement will often report an audible clicking or popping sound on opening the jaw. The condition is classified on the basis of the position of the disc, whether it returns to a normal position (is it reduced?) and whether there is associated reduction in mouth opening or locking.
[1170][Para 002] Temporomandibular joint disorder with myofascial pain is part of a group of TMJ disorders in which masticatory muscle pain predominates. The classification and nomenclature is contentious and complex, and the spectrum includes overlapping conditions from local to generalized myalgia. It is an extra-articular condition, and the joint is anatomically normal. This condition is often called temporomandibular joint pain–dysfunction syndrome, inappro priately suggesting that the condition is one of the joint. The patient reports a dull, heavy, diffuse ache over the side of the face, and the pain tends to vary in severity. Classically, one of two pain patterns is seen: pain being worst in the morning and slowly easing or pain that worsens progressively during the day. The masticatory muscles are often tense and tender to palpation, and joint movements are often painful. The causes are multifactorial and poorly understood. However, it seems that muscle tension/spasm, local and central pain processing and psychological response to stress all play a part.
[1171][Heading 2]  Why Do Temporomandibular Joints Click?
[1172][Para 001] The TMJ is a ginglymo arthroidal joint – that is, the condyle both slides and rotates. Anatomically, it is composed of the condylar head of the mandible, which articulates with the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone. Unlike most other joints of the body, these surfaces are lined with fibrous connective tissue rather than hyaline cartilage. In between, sits a biconcave fibrous disc held in place posteriorly by the superior and inferior retrodiscal laminae and anteriorly by collagenous fibres and the lateral pterygoid. The structure creates superior and inferior joint cavities filled by synovial fluid, allowing for both hinging and translational movement.
[1173][Para 002] In normal mouth opening, the initial opening results from a hinging movement that occurs predominantly in the lower compartment. As the mouth is opened further, translation occurs in the upper joint cavity and the disc, and the condyle slides forward. The thin part of the disc consistently lies in between the condyle and the temporal eminence. If the disc is anteriorly displaced, for example, because of laxity of the retrodiscal ligaments, then the thicker posterior part may restrict translation. When this is overcome, the disc snaps back with a click and mouth opening can continue – this is known as an ‘opening click’. On closing of the mouth, the condyle can be rapidly repositioned posteriorly, stretching the lax retrodiscal ligaments and forcing the disc anteriorly again. This creates an audible click or clunk and is known as the ‘closing click’. If opening and closing clicks occur in sequence, the patient is said to have reciprocal clicking. The mechanisms of clicks are shown in Fig. 8.2.
[1174][Heading 2]  Why Do Joints Lock in Internal Derangement?
[1175][Para 001] Inability to open the jaw indicates obstruction of the condyle during forward sliding/translational movement. The most common internal derangement to cause this is a grossly anteriorly displaced disc resulting from overstretched or ruptured posterior retrodiscal ligaments. The disc becomes fixed in the anterior fornix of the joint space and mechanically obstructs anterior translation of the condyle.
[1176][Para 002] Locking of the joint in internal derangement is rarely complete. It most often occurs after the initial hinge/rotational movement of the condyle. The patient will complain of being able to partly open the mouth but finds that it locks when the mouth is about half-open. This is called ‘closed lock’ despite the fact that the patient can usually open and close a little. It is uncommon for the patient to be completely unable to open the mouth. Closed lock can be acute but usually follows a long history of reciprocal clicking.
[1177][Para 002] ‘Open lock’ causes a TMJ to be ‘locked open’ and usually results from anterior subluxation or dislocation of the joint. The movements of the TMJ and the mechanisms of closed lock and open lock are shown in Fig. 8.2.
[1178][Heading 2]  Does This Patient Have an Intra-Articular or Extra-Articular Cause for the Locking? Explain Why
[1179][Para 001] The cause in this case is almost certainly intra-articular.
[1180][Para 002] In extra-articular causes, the joint itself is normal, and thus, although opening can be restricted, translation occurs, and the lateral and protrusive movements are usually unaffected.
[1181][Para 002] In intra-articular causes, the joint is abnormal and translation of the condyle is usually the movement initially affected. Translation occurs in the upper joint space, which is where opening, protrusion and lateral excursion take place. As a result, if the cause is intra-articular, then movement is restricted in all directions. Because there is both deviation on opening (indicating unilaterally reduced translation) and restricted lateral excursion in this case, the cause is more likely to be intra-articular. Movements possible in intra- and extra-articular trismus and locking are shown in Fig. 8.3.
[1182][Heading 2]  What is the Most Likely Cause?
[1183][Para 001] The patient is young, and both her social history and physical examination results indicate a degree of joint hypermobility. She reports no history of trauma or surgery and shows no signs indicative of septic arthritis, odontogenic infection or inflammatory arthritis. She gives a history of a chronic progression of painless clicking to rapid-onset intra-articular trismus, typical of internal derangement involving the articular disc and anterior displacement causing a closed lock. On examination, the mandible is found to be deviated to the right, indicating that condylar translation is intact on the left but restricted on the right. Lateral excursion is reduced on the right but unaffected on the left. The most likely cause is internal derangement with an anteriorly displaced disc in the right TMJ.
[1184][Para 002] Synovitis is an appropriate differential diagnosis but the history is usually of slowly progressive pain and all, rather than just some, joint movements are painful.
[1185][Para 015] Investigations
[1186][Para 024]  What Investigations May Help?
[1187][Para 038] Laboratory tests: In this case, it would be expected that all laboratory test results would be within the normal range. Blood tests such as a complete blood count, Cross-reactive protein level, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, anticyclical citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) and an autoantibody screen can help rule out other possible causes such as septic or rheumatoid arthritis.
[1188][Para 038] Plain radiography: The structure of the joint is unaffected in this condition so that, other than the abnormal po sition of the condyle, plain radiography is unlikely to show any abnormality. Plain radiography is useful if joint disease is suspected, and dental panoramic tomograms (DPTs) with specific TMJ projections (transpharyngeal or transcranial) are usually favoured initially. If further information is required, then spiral or cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), at higher radiation dose, provide additional information.

[1198][Para 038] Ultrasonography: Recently, the supplementary use of high-resolution static and dynamic ultrasonographic scanning of the TMJ has been highlighted as a noninvasive radiological adjunct used in clinical decision making. The position, size, shape and movements of the disc can be seen.
[1199][Para 038] Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is probably the most useful investigation for this case because it will show the position of the disc as well as the surrounding structures. Scanning can be performed with functional movement to produce a series of dynamic images. Common indications for MRI include severe pain or clinically abnormal locking, previous TMJ surgery or any anatomical abnormalities unclear on the DPT. Furthermore, extensive MRI scanning may be undertaken if other diseases are suspected. MRI images from this patient are shown in Fig. 8.4.
[1200][Para 038] Arthrography: A radiograph with contrast medium injected into the joint space. Once a commonly used technique, it has largely been replaced by noninvasive techniques such as MRI.
[1201][Para 038] Diagnostic aspiration: Unlikely to be used in this case, but would be necessary if septic arthritis were suspected. The resulting aspirate would be sent for microscopy, culture and sensitivity testing.
[1202][Para 015] Treatment
[1203][Heading 2]  How Should This Condition Be Managed?
[1204][Para 001] The majority of cases with closed lock related to internal derangement and an intact anteriorly displaced disc resolve spontaneously. It is generally accepted that a conservative approach with appropriate review for 3–6 months is appropriate. This should be combined with targeted education and counselling, if needed. Acute adjunctive management may involve simple oral analgesia (paracetamol or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs]), warm or cold compresses and gentle mobilization, as tolerated. The use of short courses of low-dose oral steroids and benzodiazepines is controversial but may have a place in select cases. Rehabilitation programs have been shown to reduce the time to resolution of symptoms and decrease the likelihood of recurrence. Programs often include targeted physiotherapy, joint mobilization, home exercise, use of passive joint-motion machines and the construction of an intraoral orthotic (splint). Current evidence indicates that forced manipulation or manipulation under anaesthesia provides no benefit over conservative management. There is a growing body of evidence suggesting that there is a complex interplay between the biomechanics of the TMJ and the surrounding musculature, with underlying mental illness or psychological impairment. A psychological component may be added to the rehabilitation, such as a formal psychological assessment, assessment of maladaptive oral habits and cognitive–behavioural therapy.
[1205][Heading 2]  Suppose There is No Improvement After 6 Months?
[1206][Para 001] In selected cases where mouth opening does not improve, patients may be considered for TMJ arthrocentesis or ‘lysis and lavage’. Under local or general anaesthesia, sterile saline or Hartman’s solution is injected into the joint, either blindly or under arthroscopic/fluoroscopic guidance, and the fluid allowed to exit through a second needle or port. The process is intended to flush the joint spaces, removing inflammatory mediators and toxins and breaking down adhesions. The inflation of the joint space can also encourage the disc to assume a more normal position. At the time of the procedure, additional medications such as sodium hyaluronate can be injected. When this procedure is not effective, the patient may be considered for arthroscopic or open joint surgery. Procedures generally aim to reposition the disc but may require meniscectomy, retrodiscal shortening or disc replacement.
[1207][Para 002] Long-term MRI studies have shown that an anteriorly positioned disc is compatible with normal function and that the condyle and disc can remodel. Therefore, these more invasive treatments, which have a weak evidence base, are restricted to carefully selected cases.
[1208][Heading 2]  Should Treatment Be Undertaken in Primary or Secondary Care?
[1209][Para 001] TMJ disorders can be challenging for both the patient and the clinician. Like other conditions with vague or poorly defined signs and symptoms, a multifactorial aetiology and a chronic course, explaining these factors to patients can be difficult. Treatment is commonly prolonged and can often have a less than satisfactory outcome. Sensitive communication, including a realistic and clear description of expectations, is essential for success.
[1210][Para 002] The complex aetiology and the need for investigations mean that TMJ disorders can be best treated in a specialist centre. Examples of criteria for immediate referral include limited or progressively limited mouth opening, inability to maintain a normal diet and associated joint disease such as rheumatoid arthritis. In primary care, assessment and diagnosis should be undertaken, and appropriate habit modification, simple analgesic advice and bite splints can be appropriate treatments. If the symptoms remain problematic after approximately 6 months, then referral to a specialist should be considered.
[1211][Para 099] Guidance on management in primary care can be found at https://www.rcseng.ac.uk/-/media/files/rcs/fds/publications/temporomandibular-disorders-2013.pdf.
[1212][Para 002] Evidence supporting TMJ treatments is of relatively low level, and following accepted guidelines is prudent because invasive treatment is a medico-legal minefield. Accurate and detailed clinical note taking is paramount.
[1213][Para 015] Another Possibility
[1214][Heading 2]  Is There Any Significance in the History of Joint Hypermobility?
[1215][Para 001] Possibly. Being genetically predisposed to generalized joint hypermobility or suffering from a disease such as Ehlers-Danlos or Marfan’s syndrome would make the patient much more likely to suffer from TMJ internal derangement. However, internal derangement is one of the most common TMJ disorders, and only a tiny fraction of patients have an underlying hypermobility disorder. Of note, joint hypermobility would not have been caused by this patient’s childhood involvement in gymnastics but likely indicates that she performed well in this field.

[1217][Heading 1] A Deep Carious Lesion
[1218][Para 027] Avijit Banerjee
[1219][Para 028] Summary
[1220][Para 029] How will you deal with a deep, cavitated carious lesion in a permanent maxillary molar tooth?

[1225][Para 014] History
[1226][Para 019] Complaint
[1227][Para 007] A 30-year-old patient complains of severe attacks of pain, each of a few seconds duration and fading slowly, but she cannot identify which tooth is responsible. Hot, cold or sweet foods and cold air on the upper right jaw make the pain worse.
[1228][Para 012] History of Complaint
[1229][Para 007] The pain has been present intermittently for several months but has only recently become severe. There is no pain on biting.
[1230][Para 012] Dental History
[1231][Para 007] The patient attends on a casual basis for dental treatment. Despite the fact that this carious lesion is very large, perhaps surprisingly, it is the only lesion in an otherwise intact arch, and there have been no other lesions noted in the last 3 years. The patient is, therefore, classified as having a low risk for dental caries.
[1232][Para 012] Medical History
[1233][Para 007] The patient is fit and well.
[1234][Para 014] Examination
[1235][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[1236][Para 007] The extraoral examination reveals no significant abnormality.
[1237][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[1238][Para 007] There is no tenderness or swelling over the buccal or palatal roots.
[1239][Heading 2]  The Maxillary Right Second Molar is Shown in Fig. 9.1. What Do You See and How Do You Assess the Problem So Far?
[1240][Para 001] The classic history of acute pulpitis and repeated attacks of pain – as opposed to continuous severe pain – probably indicates that the pulp can be preserved if the caries is treated. The fact that there is no pain on biting and no tenderness over the roots also suggests a reversible pulpitis and helps exclude periapical periodontitis.
[1241][Para 002] There is a deep, cavitated lesion on the occlusal surface, with extensive exposed carious dentine. Opaque white demineralization of the marginal, unsupported enamel indicates that it is demineralized despite not having fractured off during function. The slightly darker appearance of the tooth distally suggests that caries undermines enamel somewhat distally and that it possibly involves the dentine supporting the enamel of the mesial proximal surface.
[1242][Para 002] This is a relatively small upper second molar. Females have slightly smaller teeth, and when second molars are this small, the third molar may not have developed. This may influence the decision to restore or extract the tooth.
[1243][Para 015] Investigations
[1244][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Carry Out?
[1245][Para 001] A test of tooth sensibility (vitality) is required, even though the symptoms suggest a vital pulp. This is a large cavity in a molar, and partial pulp sensibility is a distinct possibility.
[1246][Para 002] Radiography is required for a variety of reasons. The proximity of the lesion to the pulp and its lateral extension, undermining cusps and the proximal enamel will all affect the overall restorability of the tooth. Pulp size reduction by tertiary, reactionary dentine will also be visible, depending on the chronic nature of the caries process in this tooth. It may also be possible to see evidence of periapical periodontitis, widening of the periodontal ligament and loss of the lamina dura. The ideal views would be a periapical or bitewings, depending on your suspicions about pulp sensibility or caries in other teeth. If symptoms were of an irreversible, chronic pulpitis, and there was potential indication for root canal therapy, cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) could also be considered. This imaging modality would give a much clearer indication of periapical pathological and anatomical changes with regard to radiolucencies, bone resorption, proximity to the sinus floor and the root canal apices that might be affected.
[1247][Para 218] 
[1248][Para 008] 
[1249][Para 011] Fig. 9.2 Radiograph of the tooth.
[1250][Para 009]  
[1251][Para 017] When you perform these investigations, the tooth responds quickly and strongly to ethyl chloride (cold), indicating a hypersensitive pulp, although the proximity of the pulp to the cavity may also contribute to this strong response.
[1252][Heading 2]  The Radiograph is Shown in Fig. 9.2. What Do You See?
[1253][Para 001] The coronal radiolucency indicates that the carious lesion is extensive. It reaches the inner third of the dentine close to the pulp. There appears to be a bridge of intact dentine between the lesion and the pulp chamber. Caries has undermined most of the occlusal enamel and also the distal enamel, but there are no separate proximal lesions or cavitation present. The coronal pulp chamber is rounded and reduced in size, with the pulp horns obliterated by reactionary (‘tertiary’) dentine.
[1254][Para 002] There is slight radicular cervical ‘burn-out’ of the dentine immediately above and below the mesial and distal amelo-dentinal junction. This could be mistaken for caries extending from the crown into the distal root, but the shape and site of the relative radiolucency do not suggest caries. If other radiographs are taken (e.g. bitewings), often the cervical burn-out can be observed on other teeth in a similar anatomical location. Of course, findings on radiography must be reconfirmed by further careful clinical examination of the particular area concerned.
[1255][Para 015] Diagnosis
[1256][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[1257][Para 001] Acute pulpitis in the maxillary second molar caused by extensive occlusal caries. The pulp appears vital, and there is no evidence of periapical periodontitis. The pulp does not appear exposed radiographically.
[1258][Para 015] Treatment
[1259][Heading 2]  Is This Tooth Restorable?
[1260][Para 001] Yes. The prognosis may be guarded because the pulp may still lose sensibility over time, as a result of either the caries process or restoration placement. There is no indication for immediate endodontic treatment. There is also sufficient supragingival tooth tissue available to support the restoration.
[1261][Heading 2]  What Will You Do First?
[1262][Para 001] The patient is in pain, and the immediate management response must be to relieve it. Pulpitis does not respond to analgesic drugs, and the appropriate treatment is suitable caries excavation and then restoration.
[1263][Para 002] If a definitive restoration cannot be placed immediately, a provisional dressing could be placed following the selective excavation of carious tissues. This would help relieve pain by removing the stimulus (bacterial products and acid penetrating dentine) and by insulating the inflamed pulp from any triggering stimuli. Eugenol-containing temporary restorative materials have an obtundent effect on the pulp, thus reducing pain. However, it must be noted that eugenol-containing materials must not be used if the definitive restoration to be placed is an adhesive resin composite as the eugenol affects adversely the bond/resin polymerization process. A second alternative might be to place a longer-term provisional restoration with indirect therapeutic pulp protection, as required, in an attempt to induce further reactionary dentine formation in the pulp. However, the carious lesion does not appear to be in imminent danger of breaching the pulp. Indeed, a growing body of evidence argues that indirect pulp protection is not necessary or beneficial because many of the modern adhesive biointeractive materials exhibit the desired properties of pulp protection materials (see later).
[1264][Para 002] Removal of caries will leave a weakened crown, more susceptible to fracture under normal occlusal loading. An immediate definitive restoration is the best course of action.
[1265][Para 002] Subsequently, the patient needs a full caries risk/susceptibility assessment and an intensive preventive regime that may include topical fluorides if other lesions are found or develop. Further details and discussion can be found in Case 1.
[1266][Heading 2]  Why Not Extract This Tooth?
[1267][Para 001] Such a large lesion in a casual dental patient might well lead to extraction if that were the patient’s wish. However, this is a young patient, and she may not have a third molar or, if present, it may not erupt spontaneously after extraction of the second molar. Even though the prognosis may be guarded, there is a good chance that this tooth could be retained for many years, with careful maintenance by the patient, aided by recall consultations with the oral healthcare team. This would be the better immediate option because the condition of the rest of the dentition has not yet been fully assessed.
[1268][Para 015] Minimally Invasive Operative Treatment
[1269][Heading 2]  How Will You Provide Analgesia?
[1270][Para 001] Buccal infiltration of a local anaesthetic, including a vasoconstrictor, should be sufficient. There is no continuous pulpal pain to suggest that obtaining analgesia will be a problem. If this fails, palatal infiltration or intraligamentary injection would be an appropriate next step.
[1271][Heading 2]  Is a Rubber Dam Essential for This Restoration?
[1272][Para 001] Yes, it is required. There is a risk of pulp exposure. Although the exposure is small, contamination of the cavity by oral bacteria could reduce the chances of success of subsequent endodontic treatment.
[1273][Para 002] The lesion is extensive, and some carious tissue will have to be retained (selective caries removal). The marginal seal of the restoration will be critical to its final success. An adhesive restoration will require a controllable, dry field to achieve the best seal. A rubber dam will also help by controlling soft tissues, thus improving visibility and access. The final quality of restorations placed under the rubber dam is considered to be higher than those placed without a rubber dam.
[1274][Heading 2]  How Do You Gain Access To the Lesion? How Much Enamel Will You Remove?
[1275][Para 001] The lesion is already open/cavitated, making access to dentine straightforward, but much of the peripheral occlusal enamel is demineralized, unsupported and weakened. Ideally, enamel at the cavity margins should be completely sound to ensure that etching and adhesion are most effective. Unfortunately, this is not always easy to assess clinically. All frosted, demineralized, unsupported and friable enamel must be removed. Pressure with a hand instrument (e.g. enamel chisel or excavator) will fracture off unsupported enamel, if the operator is unsure. Compromises might have to be made to conserve the cusp enamel. Once the enamel joining the cusps and marginal ridges, that form the thick outer perimeter of the occlusal surface, is lost, much of the intrinsic structural strength of the crown is lost. A tungsten carbide or diamond bur in an air-turbine handpiece or hand instruments may be used to remove the enamel and introduce a slight bevel, if required (Fig. 9.3).
[1276][Heading 2]  How Should You Remove the Carious Dentine?
[1277][Para 001] Conventionally, carious dentine is removed with large, slowly revolving, rose-head, carbon-steel burs and hand excavators. Possible alternative techniques are shown in Table 9.1.
