[1282][Para 018] Table 9.1
[1283][Para 021] Techniques for Excavation of Carious Dentine
[1284][Para 002] No method is completely guaranteed to remove only the necessary amount of carious dentine. The best methods are those that give the most tactile feedback to the operator because assessment of tissue softening and texture is critical to remove the optimal amount of dentine. These include the mechanical and chemomechanical methods.
[1285][Heading 2]  How Much Carious Dentine Needs To Be Removed?
[1286][Para 001] The ‘correct’ amount to remove is the minimum required to restore the tooth successfully, allow the dentine–pulp complex to stimulate healing and prevent further disease progression. To achieve this, it is necessary to understand the structure of different parts of a carious lesion.
[1287][Para 002] There is a continuous histological spectrum of degrees of dentine destruction in caries. At the advancing front (at the depth of the lesion closest to the pulp), there is demineralization (and remineralization during reversal). Behind that, the tubules are widened by demineralization and can be more easily penetrated by bacteria. Between this layer and the surface is progressive destruction of dentine by both demineralization and proteolysis induced by bacteria. The dentine structure is destroyed, and numerous bacteria live within it.
[1288][Para 018] Table 9.2
[1289][Para 040] Histological Layers of Carious Dentine
[1290][Para 044] 
[1291][Para 018] Table 9.3
[1292][Para 021] Pulp–Dentine Complex Responses to Dentine Caries
[1293][Para 002] This continuous spectrum of destruction is divided conventionally into zones to aid understanding, but it must be appreciated that this is an artificial concept and that the boundaries of the zones are based loosely on histological examination findings, not clinical appearance.
[1294][Para 002] Carious dentine can be divided into zones of destruction, bacterial penetration and demineralization, or caries-infected (bacterially contaminated) and affected (demineralized) zones. The features of the zones are shown in Table 9.2.
[1295][Para 002] In addition, there are changes in dentine caused by reactions of the pulp–dentine complex. These are not exclusive to the caries process (they may be induced by trauma, attrition or age, for example) but are present to some degree in carious but vital teeth and form an integral part of the overall picture. The pulp–dentine defence reactions are shown in Table 9.3.
[1296][Para 002] During carious tissue removal, the aim should be to remove all dentine that contains bacteria and where the collagen structure is denatured (contaminated/caries-infected dentine). Dentine that is only softened by acid can partially remineralize and be repaired and thus may be retained, especially when in close proximity to the pulp. Thus, it will be necessary to identify the layer or zone of the lesion that clinically corresponds to the level of the red line in Fig. 9.4.
[1297][Heading 2]  How Can You Recognize This Excavation Endpoint Clinically?
[1298][Para 001] This is difficult to do with clinical accuracy. The relatively smooth lines marking the edges of the zones in Fig. 9.4 do not reflect the irregularly shaped advancing front and the small tongues of bacteria that penetrate tubules in advance of the main lesion. Again, it must be emphasized that these zones are not histologically distinct but blend into each other with diffuse clinical boundaries.
[1299][Para 002] It is accepted universally that not all bacteria have to be removed during excavation. Those that are sealed from the oral environment, the primary source of their substrate, will either die or become dormant. Provided the restoration provides a good seal, the retained bacteria will not be sufficient to allow the caries process to progress below the restoration. Excavation of grossly contaminated/infected dentine is relatively straightforward. All superficial, very soft, wet (often more darkly stained) dentine is highly contaminated and is readily removed.
[1300][Para 218] 
[1301][Para 008] 
[1302][Para 011] Fig. 9.4 The zones of carious dentine and pulp–dentine defence reactions. Left panel, zones of caries: (A) Contaminated (infected) dentine (including the zones of dentine destruction and bacterial penetration along intact tubules); (B) affected, demineralized dentine. Right panel, pulp defence reactions: (C) translucent zone formed by peri-/intratubular sclerosis surrounds the lesion; (D) regular and/or irregular reactionary (‘tertiary’) dentine that has reduced the size of the pulp; (E) pulpitis, an immunological and inflammatory reaction triggered by odontoblast damage, but not helpful in resisting the advance of caries.
[1303][Para 009]  
[1304][Para 002] Whether the underlying demineralized caries-affected dentine, which can potentially be repaired by the dentine–pulp complex, may be spared is a decision that must be made on a case-by-case basis. It is usually preserved in the cavity depths to protect the pulp but cleared from around the enamel–dentine junction to ensure that the peripheral seal is most effective.
[1305][Para 002] Demineralized (caries-affected) dentine is often stained and is softer than the surrounding healthy dentine. A possible clinical indicator that the boundary zone between infected and affected dentine has been reached is that the cavity surface is both scratchy and sticky to a sharp dental probe (sometimes termed leathery). Unfortunately, this sensation cannot be appreciated in the words from a textbook and requires first-hand experience of the sensation!
[1306][Heading 2]  Can Caries Detector Dyes Help Identify the Zones in Carious Dentine?
[1307][Para 001] The original caries detector dyes, developed in the 1970s and based on propylene glycol solutions, were claimed to stain collagen that had become denatured by the caries process. However, they tended to penetrate too far into porous dentine and stain acid-denatured collagen, thus staining both infected and affected zones and even sound dentine. Removing all dye-stained dentine, therefore, risked excessive and unnecessary dentine removal.
[1308][Para 002] New caries indicators that are still being developed detect bacterial metabolism and have the potential to identify the contaminated/infected zone more accurately in future.
[1309][Heading 2]  The Appearance After Initial Caries Removal is Shown in Fig. 9.5. What Do You See?
[1310][Para 001] The dentine surface is still friable and flakes parallel with the surface, along clefts that are the result of bacteria breaking out of the tubules. The base of the cavity must still be in the contaminated/infected zone. It is just starting to feel scratchy with a probe. Further caries should be removed.
[1311][Para 218] 
[1312][Para 008] 
[1313][Para 011] Fig. 9.5 Initial removal of grossly infected dentine.
[1314][Para 009]  
[1315][Heading 2]  The Final Extent of Excavation is Shown in Fig. 9.6. What Do You See?
[1316][Para 001] Further dentine has been removed around the cavity periphery. Affected dentine over the pulp has been retained. It does not show the gross flaking seen in Fig. 9.5 but is still stained, but dry and appearing matt. It is still noticeably soft but distinctly scratchy with a sharp probe. Consideration must be given to the relative hardness of the dentine retained at the base of the final cavity. If it is too soft, there is a risk that cohesive failure could occur within the dentine itself on shrinkage of an adhesive restorative material. This decision must also take into account relative pulp proximity. Unnecessary exposure of a still vital pulp will significantly reduce the medium-/long-term success of maintaining pulp sensibility and should be avoided.
[1317][Para 218] 
[1318][Para 008] 
[1319][Para 011] Fig. 9.6 Final caries excavation.
[1320][Para 009]  
[1321][Heading 2]  Should This Restoration Have a Mesial Box?
[1322][Para 001] The amelo-dentinal junction is visible in Fig. 9.6, and both mesial and distal enamel have lost all, or most, of their support. There is an argument that the unsupported enamel will fracture, leading to failure of the restoration. If amalgam were being used, then both mesial and distal boxes would definitely be required.
[1323][Para 002] Conversely, removing the mesial or distal enamel would seriously compromise the strength of the remaining crown and predispose to cuspal fracture, particularly buccally. Modern adhesive materials have good compressive strength and adhesion to the whole of the dentine and enamel inner surface of the cavity and will provide some support for enamel. It must be accepted that leaving this enamel does incur a small risk of failure, but the potential benefit of a more conservative approach outweighs the risk. Proximal caries, adverse occlusion or the possibility that the patient might not return immediately if the tooth fractured would influence this decision.
[1324][Heading 2]  Surely Caries Has Been Left Under This Restoration, and It Will Fail?
[1325][Para 001] In the past, this cavity preparation would have been considered inadequate, with soft and stained dentine remaining on the cavity floor. There are certainly bacteria remaining in dentine. If this cavity were to be restored with a modern high-copper-alloy amalgam, with its inherently poor marginal seal, the restoration might fail fairly quickly. However, the principles of carious dentine removal have been revolutionized, partly by the advent of adhesive biointeractive restorations, which seal effectively, and partly by recognition that carious dentine can remineralize biologically and the caries process can arrest.
[1326][Para 002] There is a risk that this more conservative, minimally invasive (MI) approach will lead to failure if the quality of the overlying restoration is suboptimal. Leaving more carious tissue than was accepted in the past does carry a risk, but the affected dentine has been left behind for specific, justifiable reasons. This MI approach will require continued monitoring for success and, as with all operative dentistry, good patient behavioural adherence to oral hygiene regimens.
[1327][Para 002] Annual review will permit any visual changes to the restoration and its seal to be noticed. Early in its life, the restoration may develop some staining along sections of the margin but this does not constitute failure of the seal. However, if staining is accompanied by roughness/gap formation detectable with a ball-ended dental explorer (not accounted for by fracture of resin composite ‘flash’), this might indicate the seal has been breached and the restoration would require repair, depending on the extent of the breakdown (see Case 68). The ultimate success of the MI operative management protocol is dependent on case selection, appropriate selective (MI) caries removal protocol, appropriate handling/placement technique of the adhesive, biointeractive restorative material and patients’ ability to maintain adequate preventive care in the long term.
[1328][Heading 2]  What is Stepwise Excavation?
[1329][Para 001] A technique in which carious tissue is removed in increments to allow the dentine–pulp complex to heal the deeper layers of caries-affected dentine. Superficial infected dentine is removed and a provisional restoration placed to seal in the remaining tissue. Over a period of months, the deepest affected dentine remineralizes and develops an appearance similar to arrested carious dentine: darker, harder and drier than previously. Peritubular and reactionary dentine is also laid down around the lesion and at the pulp–dentine interface during this period.
[1330][Para 002] If this technique were to be followed, the restoration would be removed after approximately 6–9 months, further carious dentine excavated and a definitive restoration placed. Current evidence suggests that this second intervention is clinically unnecessary and can lead to cavity overpreparation. The peripheral seal of modern adhesive restorations is now good enough that lesion arrest and remineralization are predictable outcomes. Thus, the two-stage stepwise complete excavation protocol essentially becomes redundant.
[1331][Para 002] The notes might record that this tooth has been excavated conservatively and repeat restoration can be delayed until either the restoration peripheral seal fails or, perhaps, some unsupported enamel fractures off. At that stage a decision can be made about further excavation. After removal of the failed restoration, if the cavity floor is hard and dry, no further dentine removal may be necessary.
[1332][Heading 2]  Does the Cavity Require a ‘Lining’ for Pulp Protection?
[1333][Para 001] The purposes of cavity ‘linings’ are:
[1334][Para 016] 1. to protect the pulp from the bacterial infection and diffusion of bacterial acid and toxins
[1335][Para 016] 2. to seal, impregnate and mechanically reinforce any layer of caries-affected dentine that may have been retained
[1336][Para 016] 3. to stimulate the dentine–pulp complex to lay down tertiary dentine as a defence response, usually when using calcium hydroxide–based linings
[1337][Para 016] 4. to protect the pulp from thermal, electrical and mechanical stimuli transmitted through the overlying restoration.
[1338][Para 002] Many adhesive restorative materials and adhesives carry out all these functions and so the value of a separate ‘lining’ is nowadays debatable and, indeed, may compromise the final seal and adhesion of the material to the tooth structure.

[1340][Para 021] Potential Direct Restorative Materials for This Tooth
[1341][Heading 2]  What Materials Could You Use To Restore the Cavity?
[1342][Para 001] The choice of restorative material will be a balance between physicochemical properties, the skill of the dentist placing the restoration and the ability of the patient to maintain it. Choices for this cavity are shown in Table 9.4.
[1343][Heading 2]  Which is the Most Appropriate Choice for This Cavity?
[1344][Para 001] There is no absolutely correct answer. In this case, the decision was made to use resin composite. Resin composite would adhere well to the extensive supragingival enamel margins, supporting the surrounding tooth structure because of its adhesive and mechanical properties. One disadvantage of resin composite alone is the need to place the restoration in small increments to reduce shrinkage stress on the cavity margin. This is especially important in this case, where there is considerable poorly supported enamel, but can be overcome by using the latest low-shrink bulk-fill resin composite materials (for which less than 0.9% shrinkage by volume is claimed).
[1345][Para 017] The final restoration is shown in  Fig. 9.7 . It was finished using composite finishing burs and polishing discs and pastes to improve the final lustre of the restoration surface. This will improve the aesthetics.
[1346][Heading 2]  Are There Any Medico-Legal Considerations To Consider When Practising This MI Operative Approach?
[1347][Para 001] It is imperative that good-quality, contemporaneous notes are maintained. Patients should be included in the decision-making journey, with all options and material risks discussed. Intraoral photography is a sensible addition to the records that could be kept, showing the original situation along with a midtreatment and final outcome image. Suitable consent would be required for these. Medico-legally, there is significant clinical and scientific evidence that the MI approach is a valid alternative to the conventional complete excavation protocols. The onus is on the oral healthcare practitioner to offer this option as an alternative to the traditional approach. Ignorance and lack of clinical knowledge or skill is not a defence in a court of law. This MI approach is being taught and can be referenced in many textbooks.

[1354][Para 027] Anwar R. Tappuni
[1355][Para 028] Summary
[1356][Para 029] A 48-year-old man presents with a gingival swelling. What is the cause, and what would you do?
[1357][Para 218] 
[1358][Para 008]

[1360][Para 009]  
[1361][Para 014] History
[1362][Para 019] Complaint
[1363][Para 001] The patient complains of a lump on the gum at the front of his mouth on the left side. It bleeds sometimes, usually after brushing or eating hard food, but it is not painful.
[1364][Para 012] History of Complaint
[1365][Para 001] The swelling has been present for 4 months and has grown slowly during this period. It was never painful but now looks unsightly. The patient gives no history of other mucosal or skin lesions.
[1366][Para 012] Medical History
[1367][Para 001] The patient has hypertension, controlled with atenolol 50 mg daily.
[1368][Para 014] Examination
[1369][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[1370][Para 001] The patient is healthy looking but slightly overweight. There are no palpable cervical lymph nodes.

[1372][Para 001] The patient is partially dentate and has relatively few and extensively restored teeth. He wears an upper partial denture. The root of the upper lateral incisor is present, and its carious surface lies at the level of the alveolar ridge. The teeth on each side of the lesion are restored with metal–ceramic crowns.
[1373][Para 002] There is a mild degree of marginal gingivitis. Most of the interdental papillae are rounded and marginal inflammation is present around the crowns. Flecks of subgingival calculus are visible.
[1374][Para 024]  The Appearance of the Lesion is Shown in Fig. 10.1. Describe Its Features
[1375][09 Block] 
[1376][Para 002] If you were able to palpate the lesion, you would find that it is fleshy and soft and attached by a thin base to the gingival margin. It bleeds readily from the area between the tooth and the lesion when pressed with an instrument, but it is not tender.
[1377][Heading 2]  On the Basis of the Information From the History and Examination So Far, What is Your Differential Diagnosis?
[1378][Para 001] Likely:
[1379][Para 004] • Pyogenic granuloma (if the patient had been female, pregnancy epulis might have been considered)
[1380][Para 004] • Fibrous epulis
[1381][Para 002] Less likely:
[1382][Para 004] • Peripheral giant cell granuloma
[1383][Para 004] • Sinus papilla (parulis)
[1384][Para 002] Unlikely:
[1385][Para 004] • Papilloma
[1386][Para 004] • Benign hamartoma or neoplasm
[1387][Para 004] • Malignant neoplasm
[1388][Para 030]  Justify Your Differential Diagnosis
[1389][Para 001] A very wide range of lesions may affect the gingiva, and many possible causes cannot be excluded on the basis of the information given so far. However, the gingiva is the site of predilection for a number of inflammatory hyperplastic lesions comprising fibrous tissue and epithelium. All are associated with poor oral hygiene, and the lesion is almost certainly of this type on statistical grounds.
[1390][Para 002] Pyogenic granuloma is a localized proliferation of granulation tissue or very vascular fibrous tissue. It arises in association with local irritants such as poor oral hygiene, calculus or the margin of a restoration. The present lesion has many features of the pyogenic granuloma: it is asymptomatic, soft and vascular, bleeds readily, and has an ulcerated surface. If it were a female patient, a pregnancy epulis (a variant of pyogenic granuloma arising during pregnancy) would have been a possible diagnosis.
[1391][Para 002] Fibrous epulis (gingival fibroepithelial polyp/nodule) is a nodule of more fibrous hyperplastic tissue. It is not usually ulcerated, is firmer on palpation and does not bleed so readily. Some fibrous epulides develop from pyogenic granulomas through maturation of the fibrous tissue, and some arise de novo. They are usually associated with a local irritant in the same manner as pyogenic granulomas. The current lesion could well be a fibrous epulis, although its vascularity and red colour are more suggestive of pyogenic granuloma. These two terms are really no more than convenient labels for lesions at the opposite ends of a spectrum ranging from granulation tissue to dense fibrous tissue. All are hyperplastic.
[1392][Para 002] Peripheral giant cell granuloma is another hyperplastic lesion that seems to develop in response to a local irritant. Clinically, it may have a deep red, maroon or blue colour but is otherwise indistinguishable from pyogenic granuloma or fibrous epulis. However, histologically, it is distinctive, containing numerous multinucleate osteoclast-like giant cells lying in a very cellular vascular stroma. Giant cell epulis is commoner in children, although it can arise in an adult. Although it cannot be excluded, it is a less likely diagnosis for the present lesion.
[1393][Para 002] Sinus papilla (parulis) is essentially a pyogenic granuloma developing at the opening of a sinus. Infection and inflammation are the stimuli inducing hyperplasia. If the sinus heals, the sinus papilla may disappear, or it may mature and shrink into a small fibrous nodule. The usual site is on the alveolar mucosa and the lesion is usually no more than 4 or 5 mm across. This is an unlikely cause of the lesion in this case.
[1394][Para 002] Papillomas are lesions of proliferating epithelium. Their exact cause is not always clear although it is generally considered that most are caused by human papilloma virus infection. Others do not appear to contain the virus and may be benign neoplasms. Papillomas may arise at any site in the oral cavity but are often seen at the gingival margin and lips. Sometimes, patients have warts on their fingers as well. Papillomas usually have a white spiky or frond-covered surface or a smoother cauliflower-like surface, and neither is seen in the present lesion. Papillomas do not bleed easily, so this seems an unlikely diagnosis.
[1395][Para 002] It would not be useful to list the many other possible causes, but a few groups of lesions may also be considered.
[1396][Para 002] Hamartomas and benign neoplasms can arise at all sites. If this were such a lesion, a haemangioma would be likely in view of the vascularity. A haemangioma could appear very similar to a pyogenic granuloma.
[1397][Para 002] Odontogenic tumours can occasionally arise extraosseously in the gingiva but usually form uninflamed sessile nodules.
[1398][Para 002] Malignant neoplasms occasionally present in the gingiva. Metastatic deposits are commoner than primary lesions, and leukaemia is the most likely cause. Kaposi’s sarcoma might also be considered in an individual with human immunodeficiency virus infection. Both these lesions are vascular, may bleed on pressure and ulcerate.

[1420][Heading 2] Diagnosis
[1421][Para 001]  The Microscopic Appearances of the Biopsy Specimen are Shown in Figs 10.2 and 10.3. What Do You See, and How Do You Interpret Them?
[1422][Para 002] The surface is ulcerated and covered by a slough of fibrin containing nuclei of inflammatory cells. At higher power, you would be able to identify these as neutrophils. Below the surface is pale-stained tissue in which the endothelial lining of numerous small blood vessels stands out. The vessels have a radiating pattern and point towards the surface, reflecting a pattern of growth outwards from the centre. Between the vessels, there is a little fibrin, and the tissue is oedematous, myxoid or both. More deeply, there is a cluster of inflammatory cells, and collagen bundles are more prominent between the vessels.
[1423][Para 002] The lesion is a nodule of ulcerated maturing granulation and fibrous tissue.
[1424][Heading 2]  What is the Diagnosis?
[1425][Para 001] Pyogenic granuloma.
[1426][Para 015] Other Possibilities
[1427][Heading 2]  Is a More Conservative Approach To Treatment Ever Justified?
[1428][Para 001] Yes, elimination of the causative factors may induce considerable resolution. However, the degree of resolution varies; softer more vascular lesions shrink most and firmer more fibrous lesions hardly at all. Removal of calculus and improved oral hygiene may cause partial resolution and reduce the size of the lesion, which is then easier to excise and bleeds much less. Such a course of action is often appropriate for the treatment of pregnancy epulis, both because of the wish to avoid the procedure during pregnancy and because excision during pregnancy carries a risk of recurrence. Definitive excision may then be delayed until after parturition. Only very occasionally is resolution so complete that no further treatment is required.

[1436][Heading 2]  If, On Removing the Lesion, You Felt Bone Within It, What Would This Signify?
[1437][Para 001] Woven and lamellar bone, sometimes quite large pieces, can lie within fibrous epulides and pyogenic granulomas. Bone may be noted on excision or on histological examination. Sometimes, such lesions are referred to as mineralizing epulides (or peripheral ossifying fibroma in the USA). The presence of bone seems to be of no great significance, and it may indicate that such lesions arise by proliferation of the deep fibrous tissue of the periosteum. Some consider lesions that contain bone more likely to recur than those that do not, but there is no good evidence to support this belief.

[1439][Heading 1] Pain On Biting
[1440][Para 027] Francesco Mannocci
[1441][Para 028] Summary
[1442][Para 029] A 64-year-old man presents with intermittent pain on biting. Identify the cause, and discuss the treatment options.
[1443][Para 218] 
[1444][Para 008] 
[1445][Para 011] Fig. 11.1 A mirrored occlusal view of the teeth in the upper right and left quadrants; the upper right quadrant is the source of pain.
[1446][Para 009]  
[1447][Para 014] History
[1448][Para 019] Complaint
[1449][Para 007] The patient complains of pain on biting; the pain is unpredictable, extremely painful and sharp but poorly localized. It originates in the upper right quadrant and lasts a very short time, only as long as the teeth are in contact, and it is so painful that he has become accustomed to eating on the right side. The pain only arises on biting hard foods or deliberately clenching his teeth. Apart from this sharp electric shock–like pain, he has no other symptoms.
[1450][Para 012] History of Complaint
[1451][Para 007] The pain is a recent phenomenon, having been first noticed a month or two ago. At first, it was frequent, but it has become less of a problem now that he has learnt to avoid triggering the pain. He has not noticed the pain being provoked by hot or cold foods.
[1452][Para 012] Dental History
[1453][Para 007] The patient has been an irregular attender at another practice since childhood. At his last appointment, 2 years ago, the dentist had placed an amalgam restoration in the upper right first molar.
[1454][Heading 2]  On the Basis of What You Know Already, What are the Likely Causes? Explain Why
[1455][Para 001] Pulpal pain is the most likely cause because the pain appears to originate in a tooth and is poorly localized. Pain of periodontal ligament origin should be well localized. However, pulpitis does not appear to be present because there is no sensitivity to hot or cold foods. Pulpitis caused by placement of the recent amalgams, and pain caused by caries or exposed dentine can be excluded for the same reasons.
[1456][Para 002] A crack in the tooth and electro-galvanic pain are possible causes suggested by pain on biting. Both are triggered by tooth–tooth contact.
[1457][Para 002] Trigeminal neuralgia should be considered as an unlikely nondental cause. It causes paroxysmal stabbing or electric shock–like facial pain in distributions of the trigeminal nerve and may be initiated by touching or moving trigger zones. It usually affects middle-aged or older adults. Pain on biting almost certainly has a dental cause, but it can be difficult to exclude trigeminal neuralgia in some patients, particularly when trigger zones lie in the mouth or attacks are triggered by eating. If no dental cause is found, the possibility of trigeminal neuralgia may need further investigation.
[1458][Para 002] Acute periodontitis caused by an occlusal high spot on the recently placed amalgam needs to be considered. However, although this could cause significant tenderness on biting, it would be expected that the pain from the bruised periodontium would be present at other times as well. Also, such a periodontally triggered pain would be well localized to the specific tooth in most circumstances.
[1459][Heading 2]  What Additional Questions Would You Ask? Why?
[1460][Para 001] The patient should be asked about clenching, grinding or bruxing of teeth because the additional occlusal load can cause fracture, and this information will help determine treatment options.
[1461][Para 002] This patient describes a habit of nocturnal bruxism, with some tenderness of masticatory muscles at times of stress. Please note that partners can often be a source of useful diagnostic information because patients may not be aware of nocturnal parafunctional dental habits.
[1462][Para 014] Examination
[1463][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[1464][Para 007] There is a suspicion of hypertrophy/enlargement of the masseter muscles on clenching.
[1465][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[1466][Para 007] The incisal edges of the lower anterior teeth are worn, and dentine is exposed. The cusps of the posterior teeth are slightly flattened or rounded, consistent with mild attrition. There is no evidence of any loss of attachment or gingival recession.
[1467][Para 002] The appearance of the teeth in the upper right quadrant is shown in Fig. 11.1. The upper right first molar and premolar contain moderate-sized class II amalgam restorations.
[1468][Heading 2]  What Features of the Restorations Would You Note Particularly?
[1469][Para 001] The restorations should be inspected for occlusal high spots, indicated by a burnished mark on the occlusal surface. Premature occlusal contacts could be confirmed by using articulating paper, and relieving the area might cure the pain indicating the aetiology of the problem.
[1470][Para 002] Although they are unlikely causes for this particular pain, marginal caries, poor marginal adaptation or a cracked restoration should be investigated.
[1471][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[1472][Heading 2]  What is Your Differential Diagnosis? Why?
[1473][Para 001] The pain is almost certainly caused by a cracked cusp or crown. The presence of masseteric hypertrophy and attrition on the occlusal surfaces of the teeth would suggest a parafunctional habit that could predispose to cracked tooth syndrome.
[1474][Para 002] Galvanic pain may be excluded because there are no occluding restorations of dissimilar metals.
[1475][Heading 2]  Which Tooth Would You Suspect? Why?
[1476][Para 001] The upper first molar appears the most likely to be cracked. It should be investigated first because the pain seems to have started shortly after restoration. The risk of cracking is associated with the size of restorations. The upper teeth have restorations that are limited to fissures and mesial and distal surfaces. In the upper molar, the ridge of enamel joining the disto-buccal and mesio-palatal cusps is not intact, so the cusps may be undermined.
[1477][Para 002] Intact teeth can also crack, although usually only in association with an increased occlusal load. The most susceptible teeth are the premolars because moderately sized amalgams undermine the lingual and palatal cusps in the small crowns. Upper first molars are also prone to cracking because they tend to contain the largest restorations in the mouth.
[1478][Para 002] Root-filled teeth are prone to cracking but obviously could not cause pulpitic pain. Symptoms would then only be produced if the periodontal ligament were involved, and the pain would be well localized.
[1479][Para 015] Investigations
[1480][Heading 2]  What Tests and Further Examinations Would You Perform To Identify the Causative Tooth? What Do the Results Tell You?
[1481][Para 001] The investigations are described in Table 11.1.
[1482][Para 017] On performing these tests, you discover that all the teeth in the quadrant are vital. Biting on cotton wool on the upper first molar provokes pain that the patient identifies as the same as that on biting. No particular cusp can be identified, and no crack can be found.
[1483][Para 015] Treatment
[1484][Heading 2]  What Would You Do Next? Explain Why
[1485][Para 001] The path of the crack must be defined as far as possible because this will determine the treatment options. The restoration(s) in the tooth should be removed and a further attempt made to find the crack by using transillumination and dye as described in Table 11.1. If the crack appears to enter the pulp or is directed towards it, root treatment will be required.
[1486][Para 017] After investigation, the crack is found to run across the mesio-palatal cusp and disappear subgingivally. It does not appear to enter the pulp.
[1487][Heading 2]  What are the Treatment Options for Restoring Cracked Teeth? What are Their Advantages and Disadvantages?
[1488][Para 001] These are listed in Table 11.2.
[1489][Heading 2]  If, At Presentation, the Cracked Portion is Seen To Have Already Broken Off and the Pulp is Not Involved, What Restoration Options are Open To You?
[1490][Para 001] Assuming no second crack were present, this would present a simple choice. One of the methods described in Table 11.2 could be used, and this would have the advantage of preventing further cracks. In view of the history of bruxism, this may be an appropriate option.
[1491][Para 002] However, most cracks are single, and it would also be possible to adopt a more conservative approach and restore the tooth with a resin composite and a dentine bonding agent or a ‘sandwich’ restoration. The latter uses a high viscosity glass–ionomer cement to replace dentine and a resin composite to replace enamel. An amalgam restoration is also simple and highly effective, but with the shift to minimally invasive dentistry and the global phase-down of amalgam use in dentistry, it is less frequently indicated. Both approaches would require the cusp to be reduced in height to reduce the occlusal load.

[1496][Heading 2]  Suppose You Had Been Unable To Identify the Causative Tooth By Using the Methods Described Above. What Would You Try Next?
[1497][Para 001] Sometimes, it is difficult to identify a crack. The pain is poorly localized, and the first step would be to repeat the whole procedure on the upper molars and premolars in case the patient has incorrectly localized the pain.
[1498][Para 002] If no crack is identified, the restorations must be removed from other teeth that appear to be likely causes. Finally, the most suspect tooth may have a tight-fitting copper band or orthodontic band cemented around it. This can be left in situ for several weeks to see whether the pain is abolished and is a particularly useful test when the pain is felt infrequently. If the pain is persistent after 3–4 weeks, root canal treatment may be indicated, as suggested in the 2008 guidelines from the American Association of Endodontology; cuspal coverage with a cast restoration is then indicated, followed by a 1-year clinical and radiographic review (periapical radiography).
[1499][Para 025] Case 12
[1500][Heading 1] CAD/CAM Fixed Prosthodontics
[1501][Para 027] Rupert Austin, and Deborah Bomfim
[1502][Para 028] Summary
[1503][Para 029] A 38-year-old man presents with a missing anterior tooth. Discuss the fixed prosthodontic management options, including the role of CAD/CAM (computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing) in providing indirect restorative options in this case.
[1504][Para 014] Complaint
[1505][Para 007] The presenting patient complains of a missing front tooth, which he felt was impacting on his ability to smile and speak confidently.
[1506][Para 012] History of Complaint
[1507][Para 001] The patient reports having been punched in the face 6 months ago during a fight, resulting in the fracturing of the entire crown of his upper right central incisor. The patient attended a hospital’s accident and emergency department at the time, and there, it was confirmed that there were no head or maxillo-facial injuries. However, the patient also sustained injuries to his adjacent teeth and, therefore, underwent root canal treatment of the left maxillary central incisor in an emergency dental clinic. He was advised to follow up with a local dentist; however, as the affected teeth were asymptomatic, he did not seek treatment sooner.

[1509][Para 007] The patient was previously a regular attender before he moved to your area 2 years ago and has only recently managed to see a dentist. [1561][Heading 2]  What are the Definitive Replacement Options for the Missing UR1?
[1562][Para 001] A conventional cantilever bridge, with use of the central incisor as the abutment, is a possibility. Minimal preparation bridgework is not an option here because the central incisor is fractured (thus reducing the surface area of enamel for bonding), and both potential abutments are root filled. A minimal-preparation adhesive bridge, with use of the lateral incisor as the abutment, to replace the central incisor is generally contraindicated because of the reduced enamel surface area palatally for bonding, as well as the presence of generalized faceting and attritional wear, suggesting possible parafunctional bruxism.
[1563][Para 002] A conventional fixed–fixed bridge, with use of the upper left central incisor and the upper right lateral incisor, is a more predictable option. Clinical research evidence supports greater longevity for conventional fixed–fixed bridgework in comparison with conventional (or minimal-preparation) cantilever bridge work. Additionally, because the patient has a history of both repeated dental trauma and parafunctional activity, a fixed–fixed bridge design is likely to be more robust and provide a predictable and maintainable outcome. Using endodontically treated teeth as bridge abutments is less ideal. However, in this case, there was evidence that the endodontic treatment has been successful, and because the teeth were already restored, there would be less removal of natural sound tooth structure, justifying the more invasive restorative option in this case.

[1612][Para 002] An intraoral scanner is a device to acquire digital impressions of teeth, soft tissues and occlusion. Intraoral scanners utilize optical principles such as stereoscopic photogrammetry or laser scanning to acquire thousands of individual images, which are stitched together to generate a 3D model of the entire arch.
[1613][Heading 2]  What are the Key Features of Intraoral Scanners (Table 12.3)?
[1614][Para 001] All scanners comprise an acquisition device (scanner), hardware (laptop or tablet) and software (scanning only or scanning and chairside CAD-CAM). Some scanners are also linked to chairside CAD/CAM software or other software, including implant planning and surgical guide design, digital smile design, orthodontic planning software and removable partial denture design software. In addition, scanners can be linked to chairside mills for single-visit restorations, or scans can be sent to the laboratory for conventional indirect design and fabrication of restorations.
[1615][Para 002] All intraoral scanners apply an optical pattern to the tooth, so the scanner can trace its contours. There are two main ways to apply these patterns: video scanning technology and laser scanning technology. Video scanning requires a powder to apply a pattern to the tooth, whereas the laser scanning pattern originates from a laser beam projected on the tooth surface. By using a scanning powder spray, the pattern on the tooth is fixed, providing more consistently accurate scans compared with those from laser scanners. This technology is similar to that used by ‘motion capture’ movie effects; however, it does require application of an optically active powder to the teeth, and this is an additional process that affects the ability to overlay high-resolution true colour images for shade matching and improved margin marking detail.
[1616][Heading 2]  How Do Digital Intraoral Scans Compare with Conventional Impressions?
[1617][Para 001] Table 12.4 below lists the main applications of intraoral scanning in comparison with conventional impressions:
[1618][Para 002] The main advantages in comparison with conventional impressions include the following:
[1619][Para 004] • Ability to link to a chairside CAD/CAM system for single-visit restorations
[1620][Para 004] • Patient preference because of no taste, smell or gagging sensation
[1621][Para 004] • Ease of telemedicine by transferring the files to any laboratory worldwide instantaneously
[1622][Para 004] • Improved patient communication because patients can observe and appreciate the scan and design and manufacture of the restorations
[1623][Para 004] • In a model-free workflow, environmental benefits because there is no need for disposal of conventional impressions, chemical disinfectants, gypsum models and casting investment materials
[1624][Para 004] • Ability to save intraoral scans indefinitely, with no need for physical storage, thus assisting future recall and comparison.
[1625][Para 002] The main disadvantages in comparison with conventional impressions include the following:
[1626][Para 004] • Because of the optical stitching processes, artefacts can arise and can result in inferior full arch accuracy in comparison with a printed model of the intraoral scan.
[1627][Para 004] • Because of the limitations of the milling process, preparations may need to be reduced more than cast restorations, to compensate for the limitations of the dimensions of the burs needed to mill the restoration.
[1628][Para 004] • CAD/CAM materials are usually constructed from monochromatic blocks; therefore, the aesthetics of the milled CAD/CAM materials can be less than those of pressed or hand-layered ceramics.
[1629][Para 127] Table 12.4
[1630][Para 021] The Main Applications of Intraoral Scanning in Comparison with Conventional Impressions
[1631][Para 195] 
[1632][Para 196] 3D, three-dimensional; CAD/CAM, computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing.
[1633][Para 004] • As the scans can be retained indefinitely, clinicians may need to consider the possibility of future medico-legal claims; for example, claims regarding crown and bridgework may result in the preparations being analyzed for possible flaws or inadequacies in the tooth preparations, diagnosis and care planning.
[1634][Para 030]  Are There Any Medico-Legal Issues with Intraoral Scanning and Chairside CAD/CAM and Any Guidelines That Can Help Guide Their Adoption?
[1635][Para 001] As with adoption of all new technologies, detailed training, knowledge of the properties and safe handling and strict adherence to the manufacturer’s instructions are recommended. In addition, careful case selection is essential to ensure that the right treatment methodology is selected for the right patient. This is especially the case with technology with high capital costs, where clinicians may be tempted to prescribe more indirect restorations to amortize the cost of the equipment. Minimally invasive protocols must still be followed and direct restorations conserving tooth structure prescribed, where appropriate.
[1636][Para 002] In addition, the manufacturer’s instructions and guidelines need to be followed when preparing CAD/CAM restorations. All-ceramic restorations require specific preparation depths and cementation protocols, and not following them may lead to premature facture or decementation of the restoration. Intraoral scanning makes this medico-legally more difficult to defend because the intraoral scan can be analyzed precisely for the correct preparation features. This may result in more challenging medico-legal scenarios, especially because the cost of these types of restorations can be higher than that of conventional restorations.
[1637][Para 002] Intraoral scans can also be used diagnostically to analyze and record occlusion, aesthetics, restoration integrity and tooth wear. As with all diagnostic processes, medico-legal issues can be raised as a result of underdiagnosis, where issues apparent on scans were not picked up as soon as they should be, or because scans were used to overprescribe invasive treatments, for example, providing multiple indirect restorations in cases of minor nonprogressing tooth wear. Therefore, when adopting digital CAD/CAM technology, it is important to follow existing good practice guidance and, when in doubt, to seek second opinions and specialist expert advice to ensure that the technology is used optimally in the patient’s best interests.
[1638][Para 025] Case 13
[1639][Heading 1] Sudden Collapse
[1640][Para 027] Emily Sherwin
[1641][Para 028] Summary
[1642][Para 029] A 55-year-old male patient suddenly collapses in your general dental practice. What is the cause, and what would you do?
[1643][Para 014] History
[1644][Para 019] Complaint
[1645][Para 007] The patient has attended for a routine dental appointment to receive some simple restorative work under local anaesthesia. He is a regular attender but dislikes injections.
[1646][Para 017] Twenty minutes after injection of the local anaesthetic, he suddenly becomes anxious and complains of a pain in his chest. He is breathless. When your nurse asks the patient if he is all right, there is no response.
[1647][Para 012] Medical History
[1648][Para 007] Having checked the medical history before starting treatment, you are aware that the patient has well-controlled diabetes. He is overweight and suffers from hypertension, for which he takes enalapril (Innovace) 20 mg daily. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and describes himself as a ‘social drinker’, consuming 30 units of alcohol each week.
[1649][Heading 2]  What Would You Do Immediately?
[1650][Para 001] Check to see whether the patient is conscious. Make a determined effort to rouse him by shaking him and asking loudly, in both ears, whether he can hear you.
[1651][Heading 2]  The Patient Does Not Respond. What Causes of Sudden Loss of Consciousness Might Affect a Patient Undergoing Dental Treatment?
[1652][Para 001] The important causes of unexpected loss of consciousness are:
[1653][Para 004] • vasovagal attack (faint)
[1654][Para 004] • hypoglycaemia
[1655][Para 004] • cardiac arrest
[1656][Para 004] • steroid crisis.
[1657][Para 002] Loss of consciousness may also follow several other emergencies, including respiratory obstruction or respiratory failure, epilepsy, stroke or anaphylactic shock, in which the cause is likely to be evident.
[1658][Heading 2]  How May These Causes of Loss of Consciousness Be Differentiated?
[1659][Para 001] See Table 13.1 for common causes of loss of consciousness and the different associated signs and symptoms.
[1660][Heading 2]  Which is the Most Likely Cause in This Case? Why?
[1661][Para 001] In this case, the cause is very likely to be cardiac arrest. The symptom of pain in the chest radiating to the neck and arm is characteristic of myocardial infarction, the commonest cause of cardiac arrest, and is not seen in the other causes of collapse. Diabetes, hypertension and a high alcohol intake are all risk factors for atheromatous arterial disease and its complication myocardial infarction.
[1662][Heading 2]  Does Cardiac Arrest Always Follow Myocardial Infarction?
[1663][Para 001] No. The heart may continue to pump unless a large area of the myocardium or conducting tissue is damaged. Cardiac arrest may also follow hypoxia or respiratory obstruction.
[1664][Heading 2]  How Will You Confirm Your Provisional Diagnosis?
[1665][Para 001] For a diagnosis of cardiac arrest the patient must be:
[1666][Para 004] • unconscious
[1667][Para 004] • not breathing or have abnormal breathing (infrequent noisy gasps).
[1668][Para 014] Examination
[1669][Para 007] You place a hand on the patient’s forehead. His skin feels cold and clammy. Even though it is only half a minute since he lost consciousness, the patient already looks grey and he is beginning to look cyanosed. He is not breathing.
[1670][Heading 2]  What is the Current Protocol for Assessing and Managing Sudden Collapse?
[1671][Para 001] It is critically important to start Basic Life Support (BLS) procedures immediately without further consideration of possible causes. The current 2015 Resuscitation Council guidelines (Resuscitation Council (UK) (2015)) for adult basic life support (https://www.resus.org.uk/resuscitation-guidelines/adult-basic-life-support-and-automated-external-defibrillation/) for the management of respiratory and/or cardiac arrest in an adult are:
[1672][Para 018] Table 13.1
[1673][Para 021] Causes, Signs and Symptoms of Loss of Consciousness
[1674][Para 016] 1. Check the area for danger to yourself and victim
[1675][Para 016] 2. Assess responsiveness by shaking shoulders and shouting
[1676][Para 016] 3. Shout for help (do not call 999 (UK) yet)
[1677][Para 016] 4. Open the airway (tilt head and lift chin or jaw thrust)
[1678][Para 016] 5. Check mouth for vomit/debris, and remove with finger scoops
[1679][Para 016] 6. Assess breathing – listen and feel for breathing while observing chest movements. Take no more than 10 seconds
[1680][Para 016] 7. If breathing is abnormal (infrequent noisy gasps) or absent, call emergency service on 999; you may have to leave the patient to do this
[1681][Para 016] 8. Perform 30 chest compressions of 5–6 cm at 100–120 per minute; correct hand position is the middle of the lower half of the sternum
[1682][Para 016] 9. Give two ventilations with airway adjuncts such as a pocket mask
[1683][Para 101] 10. Send for an automated external defibrillator; as soon as it arrives, switch it on, and follow instructions
[1684][Para 101] 11. Continue compressions (30) and ventilations (2) until help arrives, the patient shows signs of life or until you are physically exhausted and unable to carry on.
[1685][Para 030]  What are Basic, Immediate and Advanced Life Support?
[1686][Para 001] Basic Life Support (BLS) is the diagnosis and immediate management of cardiac arrest (of whatever aetiology) with the use of basic equipment. Dental teams should have immediate access to airway adjuncts such as a pocket mask or two-person self-inflating bag-valve-mask, which avoids the need for mouth-to-mouth ventilation. BLS represents the minimum standard of resuscitation skills that all dentists, dental hygienists and dental nurses must acquire and maintain on a regular basis.
[1687][Para 002] Immediate Life Support (ILS) includes the recognition and treatment of an unwell patient by using the systematic approach of ABCDE (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability and Exposure) to prevent cardiac arrest along with immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation and defibrillation as required.
[1688][Para 002] Advanced Life Support (ALS) is concerned with the restoration of spontaneous circulation and stabilization of the cardiovascular system. Techniques include electrocardiography (ECG) assessment of shockable and nonshockable rhythms, administration of drugs, treatment of underlying causes and postresuscitation care.
[1689][Heading 2]  What is the Aim of Basic Life Support?
[1690][Para 001] To protect the brain from irreversible hypoxic damage. This develops within 3–4 minutes of cardiac arrest in a previously healthy and well-oxygenated individual, and BLS aims to delay the rate of deterioration of cerebral function. Effective and continuous chest compressions along with early defibrillation increase the chances of survival.
[1691][Heading 2]  Why Not Dial ‘999’ in the UK As Soon As the Patient Loses Consciousness?
[1692][Para 001] The most common cause of sudden loss of consciousness in the dental chair is a vasovagal attack (faint), which does not require attendance by the emergency services. The call for help in step 3 is intended to summon local helpers such as dental nurses or receptionist.
[1693][Heading 2]  What is the Most Common Cause of Failure or Difficulty with BLS?
[1694][Para 001] Airway obstruction in the unconscious patient is the commonest problem and is usually caused by the relaxed tongue falling back to obliterate the airway in the oropharynx. This may be overcome by measures that pull the tongue forward, such as head tilt, chin lift and jaw thrust. Blood, vomit or other foreign materials, including poorly fitting or broken dentures, may also obstruct the airway.
[1695][Heading 2]  Should Dentures Be Removed During BLS?
[1696][Para 001] Only if they are loose or broken. Well-fitting dentures usually facilitate a good oral seal during expired air ventilation.
[1697][Para 024]  Having Dialled 999, What Information Should Your Helper Give the Operator?
[1698][Para 004] • Your name
[1699][Para 004] • Address (with directions)
[1700][Para 004] • Your telephone number
[1701][Para 004] • That a patient has collapsed with a suspected cardiac arrest.
[1702][Para 002] Although this sounds simple, hurried calls may omit essential information. Response to cardiac arrest is usually provided at highest priority by a specialized team and is not a routine ambulance call. Failure to provide your telephone number leaves the emergency services unable to return your call.
[1703][Para 015] Prognosis
[1704][Heading 2]  Is It Likely That Your Patient Will Recover Spontaneously?
[1705][Para 001] Unfortunately, no. Even with prompt life support from a specialist team, the chances of survival are 50%. In this case, the patient recovered after ALS care provided by a specialist ambulance team that arrived at the practice 8 minutes after the 999 call was placed – a very rapid response.
[1706][Heading 2]  How Long Would You Continue To Provide BLS?
[1707][Para 001] Until help arrives, the patient shows signs of life or you are exhausted.
[1708][Heading 2]  How Can You Increase Your Chances of Providing Effective Basic Life Support?
[1709][Para 001] By regular practical instruction and testing the competence of yourself and your practice team. BLS cannot be learned from a book.
[1710][Heading 2]  What are the Medico-Legal Considerations After Providing BLS?
[1711][Para 001] Although the priority is to provide efficient life support and immediate care to the unconscious patient, it is also important to document the events that took place as soon as possible. This should include a timeline detailing observations and vital signs, treatment provided and any drugs administered. Having accurate records are important because further investigation into the incident may be carried out.
