[1728][Para 013] The child is fit and well.
[1729][Para 033]  This is Not Looking Hopeful. What Must You Do Before You Can Attempt To Examine the Child?
[1730][Para 013] You need to encourage the child to feel safe and engender feelings of trust. To do this, you must take the time to establish a rapport with the child. Without some form of rapport, little progress is possible.
[1731][Para 033]  The Child Appears Frightened. What Fears Would You Expect in a 4-Year-Old in a Dental Setting?
[1732][Para 013] A typical 4-year-old is usually scared of:
[1733][Para 013] • the unknown
[1734][Para 013] • pain
[1735][Para 013] • new environments
[1736][Para 013] • new people.
[1737][Para 090]  What Further Questions Would You Ask, and Why?
[1738][Para 128] Does the Child Attend a Nursery or Playgroup Full Time or Part Time? If So, for How Long Has She Attended?
[1739][Para 013] A child attending nursery should be more used to dealing with people outside her home and consequently have greater coping skills, be more socially developed and be used to being separated from the mother. The child should also understand the concept of rules that have to be followed. You can be more confident of successfully managing the behaviour of such a child.
[1740][Para 051] How Does the Mother Feel About Going To the Dentist?
[1741][Para 013] Maternal anxiety is a strong influence on the young child’s reaction to dentistry. If the mother is nervous at this appointment, the child will already have sensed this. Indeed, if the mother is severely anxious, it may be better to elect for another trusted adult to accompany the child. A mother who is herself very nervous may not be able to support you or her child later on if things get difficult.
[1742][Para 051] How is the Child’s Behaviour Away From the Dental Surgery?
[1743][Para 013] Here, you are trying to find out if the child is generally anxious or shy in other nondental situations such as going to see her medical practitioner or social situations. This would indicate a more generalized problem that will be more difficult for you to address.
[1744][Para 013] As there are different parenting styles, it important to identify which approach is used in the family. Some parents adopt an authoritarian approach and others a permissive approach, depending on social and cultural factors. Both approaches can be a challenge to the successful dental management of any child.
[1745][Para 013] The authoritative approach is the most desirable, in which the parent attempts to direct the child’s activities in a rational, issue-oriented manner. It is known that dental stress tolerance and coping skills of children are best when the home environment is structured, parents are responsive and self-assured and parents set limits, providing both ample rewards and appropriate punishments.
[1746][Para 013] Limit setting is considered good parenting practice. If the child is used to having limits set to her behaviour, she will be much easier to direct in the dental setting. In the case of an only child, the parents may lack experience. Others may lack role models or have their parenting strategies thwarted by relatives.
[1747][Para 051] Is the Child Genuinely Nervous or Just Playing Up?
[1748][Para 013] Your strategies for managing fear, shyness and naughtiness would be very different. However, this is difficult to assess without observing the child’s behaviour for some time and getting to know the child. You may not be able to make an immediate decision, and of course, it is quite possible that there are many contributing factors.
[1749][Para 013] You discover that the patient is an only child. She has just started part-time nursery and has settled well there. The child is generally good at home, and like most children, she likes to have her own way. However, she responds well to direction and is not allowed to have her own way all the time. Her mother attends the dentist but is rather nervous about her child’s treatment. From this, you can see that in addition to allaying the anxiety of both child and mother, you will also have to teach the child what behaviour is appropriate at the dentist’s clinic.
[1750][Para 033]  What Can the Average 4-Year-Old Child Be Expected To Do? How Does This Knowledge Help?
[1751][Para 013] Some of the developmental milestones for a 4-year-old child are shown below.
[1752][Para 197] Milestone
[1753][Para 013] • Usually separates well from mother
[1754][Para 013] • Names four primary colours
[1755][Para 013] • Can state own age and address
[1756][Para 013] • Listens intently to stories
[1757][Para 013] • Understands turn-taking
[1758][Para 013] • Starts to understand concept of obeying rules
[1759][Para 013] • Washes and dries own hands
[1760][Para 013] • Understands yesterday, today and tomorrow, simple past and future
[1761][Para 013] • Blows nose reliably
[1762][Para 013] Talking about these abilities with the mother allows you to develop a rapport with her and may alert you to any educational difficulties that the child may have. Not all parents are completely forthcoming about any problems with their child’s development. You need to know if there are issues because your approach will be slower and more considered if the child has learning difficulties. Some children may be small or tall for their age, and hence appear younger or older. This child is tall for her age, and so it is important not to overestimate her ability to cope with the experience.
[1763][Para 013] You discover that the child appears to have reached the normal developmental milestones for her age and is not usually anxious in other situations. You suspect, therefore, that shyness may be contributing to her behaviour, rather than fear.
[1764][Para 090]  Now That You Have a Better Appreciation of the Background, How Will You Develop a Rapport with the Child?
[1765][Para 128] Dispel Fear of the Unknown
[1766][Para 013] Tell the child that all you want to do today is talk to her and her mother, count her teeth and check that ‘mummy has brushed them properly’. Stress that you are going to do nothing else. Continually check back with the child to involve her, and ensure that she understands the limits of the planned dental experience.
[1767][Para 051] Use Nonverbal Communication
[1768][Para 013] Young children generally respond better to nonverbal communication, particularly touching and smiling. A pat or a stroke of the hand or hair is valued much more by a young child than a comment such as ‘good girl’ or ‘well done’.
[1769][Para 051] Be Aware of Body Language
[1770][Para 013] Children are very sensitive to nonverbal communication. Watch the child, and be aware of your own body language. Are you being defensive, or are you welcoming and friendly?
[1771][Para 051] Make Eye Contact
[1772][Para 013] You may catch the child’s attention while talking over the previous points with the parent and already be interacting with her in some way or other. If not, you must now direct all your attention to the child. Start with a compliment about the child’s clothes, toys, hair or a similar topic, and catch her eye.
[1773][Para 051] Talk To the Child in Appropriate Language
[1774][Para 013] You must be able to converse at the level of a 4-year-old, and this takes knowledge and practice. Always use the child’s first name and child-friendly language, and avoid potentially fear-promoting words. This is often called speaking ‘childrenese’, and examples are referring to your dental suction as a ‘hoover’ and the operating light as ‘sunshine’. Ask open-ended questions that cannot be answered with a simple yes or no to promote responses. Knowledge of some current children’s television characters is always useful and will provide plenty of topics of conversation.
[1775][Para 051] Consider Engaging Through Play
[1776][Para 013] Children learn through play, so consider the use of familiar toys or puppets. Perhaps she would like to show you how she brushes her teddy bear’s teeth? However, remember that toys and play alone are only a means to an end and are not a substitute for good behaviour management. The dental assistant may be able to help considerably with the use of this approach.
[1777][Para 013] With use of these strategies, you are able to open a conversation, although the child does not separate voluntarily from her mother. Ideally, you would examine the child at this visit to assess the treatment needs. As the child is not in pain, you could delay examination until the next visit, at which time you and the surgery will be more familiar to her. However, the mother is worried and would prefer that you would examine the child today.
[1778][Para 057] Examination
[1779][Para 033]  Would You Try To Use the Dental Chair for This First Examination?
[1780][Para 013] Not necessarily. The child may be examined initially on the mother’s lap, on an ordinary chair, or standing between the mother’s knees, all of which are more familiar to her than the dental chair. Place the mother where your dental light can be used if the child will tolerate it. If the child does not allow her teeth to be examined in these positions, then you must consider an examination under more controlled conditions.
[1781][Para 033]  How Could You Safely Examine the Child Without Frightening Her Further?
[1782][Para 013] If you decide to perform a full examination on a reluctant child, it must be done in a controlled, caring and confident manner, with experienced nursing support and with the consent and cooperation of the mother. You must explain to the mother exactly what you are going to do, seek verbal consent and repeat to the child that you are just going to count her teeth. It is often helpful to explain both approaches to the parent before he or she sits in the dental chair so that everyone is prepared and the transition to the second approach, if required, is seamless. Then:
[1783][Para 013] • Align the chair in a fairly upright position
[1784][Para 013] • Ask the mother to sit in the chair as if she is being examined – the child will probably come with her
[1785][Para 013] • Ask the child to sit on the mother’s lap with her back on her mother’s chest, facing away from the mother.
[1786][Para 013] Explain to the child what you are going to do possibly by using something familiar such as a toothbrush; you may be able to examine the child’s teeth in this position; if the child will not allow an examination in this position, it is time to adopt another approach.
[1787][Para 013] • Ask the mother to turn the child so that she is sitting across the mother’s lap, with her head at the 10 o’clock position
[1788][Para 013] • Ask the mother to control the child’s arms and hands
[1789][Para 013] • Have your nurse gently control the child’s feet
[1790][Para 013] • Slowly and calmly lower the child’s shoulders and head onto your lap, explaining what you are doing; it is helpful to have a pillow on your lap or a folded blanket on which to rest the child’s head (Fig. 14.2).
[1791][Para 013] This position is useful not only in uncooperative children but also in young disabled children. Understandably, the child sometimes cries, but not always. Although not ideal, crying often allows good access to the mouth. If the child will not open the mouth, having your nurse tickle the child’s stomach will usually have the required effect. Your nurse will need to position the operating light carefully because shining a light directly in the eyes often upsets children.
[1792][Para 009]  
[1793][Para 074] Fig. 14.2 Controlled examination technique.
[1794][Para 009]  
[1795][Para 198] Fig. 14.3 Appearances on examination.
[1796][Para 013] Keep the examination short, and immediately afterwards, whether the child is upset or not, reward her with words (a ‘soft’ reward) and a sticker or balloon (a ‘hard’ reward). This will encourage the child to allow examination at the next visit.
[1797][Para 013] It is important to explain the different approaches before the mother sits in the dental chair so that you can move, if necessary, from one technique to another quickly and confidently. This approach also ensures that everyone is aware of his or her respective role in the process.
[1798][Para 013] In your brief examination, you see the appearances shown in  Fig. 14.3 .
[1799][Para 090]  The Appearances On Examination are Shown in Fig. 14.3. What Do You See, and What Do the Appearances Indicate?
[1800][Para 013] • Caries in the occlusal pits and fissures of the second primary molar
[1801][Para 013] • Caries in the distal of the first primary molar, the marginal ridge has collapsed
[1802][Para 013] • Reasonable gingival condition with some interdental marginal inflammation.
[1803][Para 013] The management of caries in primary teeth should be approached in accordance with the relevant guidelines based on good clinical evidence on this subject.
[1804][Para 013] For this child, a key feature is the collapse of the marginal ridge of the first primary molar. However, you do not have any radiographs at this point, and so you are unable to assess the depth of the lesion and the likelihood of pulpal compromise. Depending on the radiographic appearance, this tooth may require pulp therapy and definitive restoration with a preformed metal crown restoration. However, provided the criteria governing their use are met, a Hall crown may be appropriate in this situation. Such a restoration has the advantage that local anaesthesia and tooth preparation are not required, which obviously is easier for all concerned and better tolerated by the child.
[1805][Para 013] It is also important to consider that for an anxious child and limited cooperation, it might be appropriate to stabilize the lesion with a temporary intracoronal restoration and delay the definitive restoration for a few months whilst the child’s confidence is increased.
[1806][Para 033]  What Would You Do Next At This Appointment?
[1807][Para 013] Nothing further is to be gained from this first visit. However, it is essential that you prepare the child for the next visit. Ask her to bring her toothbrush next time, and introduce the concept of future visits and a radiograph (‘photograph’). Perhaps tell her you are going to polish her teeth with a special electric toothbrush next time which is fun and tickles! Giving the child a plastic mirror to practise with at home may also be useful and will engage the parents.
[1808][Para 013] Discuss your findings and proposed approach, possible treatment needs and preventive advice with the mother, including use of a 3-day diet diary.
[1809][Para 013] During this period, your nurse should take the initiative to talk informally with the child, introduce the dental chair and equipment in a play-like manner and allow the child to take the lead in exploring the surgery. Some children respond very well to this indirect approach by a second person.
[1810][Para 033]  How Will You Plan Treatment Taking the Child’s Nervousness Into Account?
[1811][Para 013] The child may require treatments ranging from oral hygiene instruction to a pulpotomy and a preformed metal crown. You must teach the child to accept the more complex treatment by leading her along a graded pathway of increasing challenge.
[1812][Para 013] If treatments are listed in order of increasing difficulty for any child, the challenge scale would look something like Fig. 14.4.
[1813][Para 013] The speed at which you progress along the scale will depend on the individual child’s ability to cope with each procedure. You need to monitor the child’s reactions continually to check that you are not progressing too fast.
[1814][Para 013] Items in the treatment plan should be arranged as far as possible in order of increasing challenge. A child may accept a challenging treatment when in pain but subsequently might only accept a lower rated treatment.
[1815][Para 033]  What Behaviour Management Strategies, Tips and Tricks Might You Use During Examination and Treatment of Nervous Children?
[1816][Para 013] A range of methods are given in Table 14.1. All may be appropriate at various times.
[1817][Para 033]  Are There Strategies You Should Avoid?
[1818][Para 013] Yes, the following will almost certainly make the situation worse. Try not to:
[1819][Para 013] • use bribes or coercion – these do not work in the long term and reinforce bad behaviour rather than good behaviour.
[1820][Para 013] • use bland reassurance such as ‘Well done’ or ‘That’s fine’. Be more specific, tell the child what was helpful and she will usually try to help again in most instances.
[1821][Para 013] • belittle the child or tell her she is behaving like a baby. This lowers her self-esteem, and poor self-esteem is often linked to anxiety in children.
[1822][Para 125] 
[1823][Para 149] Fig. 14.4 Treatments in order of increasing difficulty.
[1824][Para 051] Table 14.1
[1825][Para 061] Behaviour Management Strategies
[1826][Para 013] • send the parent of a child this age outside. Removing the main source of security for a young child is counterproductive.
[1827][Para 013] • lose your cool or raise your voice. Treating anxious children can be stressful, and you need to recognize this.
[1828][Para 033]  If These Strategies Fail, What Other Options Might Be Open To You?
[1829][Para 013] With skilled behaviour management, many anxious children can accept restorative treatment. However, sometimes, when a child is too anxious and unable to cope, alternatives may need to be considered. If a child is not showing the desired behaviour by the second or third visit, you should consider referral to a specialist paediatric dentist or the use of nitrous oxide inhalation sedation.
[1830][Para 013] Inhalation sedation usually works best in children 5 years of age and older, although some younger children are receptive, depending on their emotional maturity and ability to cooperate. Intravenous sedation is unpredictable in children and not recommended. If all else fails, treatment under general anaesthesia is the last resort, but this must be carefully planned, definitive and completed in one visit to avoid the need for further episodes of general anaesthesia.
[1831][Para 013] If the child is older, the use of cognitive behavioural therapy can be considered to help address anxiety.
[1832][Para 033]  How Could You Have Made the First Appointment Easier?
[1833][Para 013] If you had known that the new patient was a nervous child, you could have used a preappointment questionnaire to obtain much useful information such as likes and fears, personality, previous experiences, nicknames, preventive habits and the names of favourite toys or pets. The form could also give information to the parent on your approach to children’s dental care and the concept of introducing the child to dentistry in a measured way through prevention. This allays maternal anxiety.
[1834][Para 013] Administering a questionnaire beforehand helps address unrealistic expectations in the parent, perhaps avoiding the situation where the mother asks why you are not going to do a filling at the first visit. It can also stress the need to manage the child through a preventive and measured approach.
[1835][Para 013] You would also have greeted the child and parent in the waiting room, reception area or office, rather than in the surgery, because this helps reduce anxiety in children. You also need to maintain a child-friendly environment with comics, computer games, toys or music and videos. These confirm to both the parent and the child that they are at a caring and understanding practice.
[1836][Para 033]  Are You At a Disadvantage Dealing with Nervous Children if You are Male?
[1837][Para 013] There is no good evidence that children prefer female dentists. However, many preschool or nursery children are more familiar with female carers and may take more time to settle with a male dentist. However, there is no need to refer small children to female dentists.
[1838][Para 013] Some male dentists feel uncomfortable about the use of touch as part of their nonverbal communication approach; indeed, some consider it culturally unacceptable. This could be a handicap in treating very young children. If you are male and are worried that touching children may be misconstrued by the parent, it is important to touch only the head and the hands and always in the presence of a chaperone.
[1839][Para 025] Case 15
[1840][Heading 1] Pain After Extraction
[1841][Para 027] Tara Renton
[1842][Para 028] Summary
[1843][Para 029] A 36-year-old lady presents with severe pain a few days after tooth extraction. What is the cause, and what can be done?
[1844][Para 218] 
[1845][Para 008] 
[1846][Para 011] Fig. 15.1 The appearance of the socket.
[1847][Para 009]  
[1848][Para 014] History
[1849][Para 019] Complaint
[1850][Para 007] The patient complains of a distressingly severe pain in an extraction socket on the left side of her mandible. The pain is localized to the extraction socket and is not sensitive to hot or cold. It is a constant, dull, boring pain, unrelieved by aspirin or paracetamol preparations. It prevents the patient from performing any normal activity, and it kept her awake last night.
[1851][Para 012] History of Complaint
[1852][Para 007] The patient underwent surgical removal of the lower left third molar tooth at her dentist 4 days ago. The extraction had proved more difficult than expected and involved repeated attempts at elevation and a small amount of bone removal with the use of a bur. After the extraction, bleeding had stopped normally. The extraction site had been tender but apparently was healing slowly until the pain started yesterday. Since then, the patient has also noticed halitosis and a bad taste in her mouth.
[1853][Para 012] Medical History
[1854][Para 007] The patient is otherwise fit and well. She is taking an oral contraceptive, and no other positive findings were revealed by the medical history.
[1855][Para 014] Examination
[1856][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[1857][Para 007] The patient has moderate extraoral swelling of the facial soft tissues overlying the extraction socket and some early discolouration of the skin as a result of ecchymosis. There is trismus, and she is able to open her mouth to only 22 mm interincisal clearance. There are no palpable lymph nodes in the deep cervical chain or submandibular triangle.
[1858][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[1859][Para 007] Halitosis is noticeable. The appearance of the socket is shown in  Fig. 15.1 . The lower left third molar socket contains no tissue, only food debris. The surrounding soft tissues are slightly swollen but not significantly inflamed as judged by the redness.
[1860][Para 015] Diagnosis
[1861][Heading 2]  On the Basis of What You Know Already, What is the Most Likely Diagnosis?
[1862][Para 001] The diagnosis is most likely to be dry socket (alveolar osteitis). The history of severe and persistent pain localized to the tooth socket appearing 3–5 days after extraction, particularly a traumatic one, is characteristic. The lack of local inflammation or enlarged lymph nodes is compatible with this diagnosis and argues against postextraction infection either in bone or soft tissue.
[1863][Para 002] The diagnosis is confirmed by the examination, which shows that the blood clot has disappeared from the socket. In severe cases, the bone of the socket may be exposed, and the bone of the distal lip of the socket can be seen (see Fig. 15.1).
[1864][Para 002] Halitosis is the result of food debris in the socket being degraded by partially anaerobic bacterial flora. The trismus is almost certainly related to the surgical trauma of extraction.
[1865][Heading 2]  What Other Causes of Postextraction Pain are There? Are They Likely in This Case?
[1866][Para 001] Pain from surgical trauma to tissues should be considered when extraction is difficult. However, pain starts immediately after sensation is regained in the area and responds to analgesics. Tenderness is characteristic, rather than spontaneous pain.
[1867][Para 002] Osteomyelitis is rare but should be considered because of its severity and difficulty of treatment, especially if diagnosed late. It causes a deep, boring pain, not dissimilar from dry socket, but is poorly localized. Osteomyelitis is almost exclusively seen in patients who are immunocompromised or have sclerosis of the jaw bones. It usually takes several weeks to become evident.
[1868][Para 002] Osteoradionecrosis is rare and only associated with previous radiotherapy in the field of surgery.
[1869][Para 002] Medication-related osteonecrosis (MRONJ) resulting in persistent symptoms should be considered if the patient has a history of osteoporosis treated with oral bisphosphonates or metastatic cancer treated with intravenous bisphosphonates or antiangiogenic agents (see Case 23, pages 127–134). However, this is not the case here.
[1870][Para 002] Fractured mandible is a very rare complication of extraction. It might be considered if swelling and bruising appeared out of proportion to dental extraction. Fracture is usually evident clinically if it is displaced.
[1871][Para 002] Retained root fragments are surprisingly rarely a cause of long-term pain, although the surgical trauma of the failed extraction may cause pain. Root fragments are almost never found in dry socket.
[1872][Para 017] None of these alternative causes matches the patient’s symptoms or signs as well as dry socket.
[1873][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Carry Out?
[1874][Para 001] At this stage, the history and examination are completely compatible with the diagnosis, and no investigations are indicated. If there were features of infection, culture of pus and antibiotic sensitivity would be necessary and the temperature would have to be taken. Radiographs are not useful unless a root fragment is suspected but cannot be seen or palpated. Even if osteomyelitis is suspected, radiographs would not provide useful information because there has been insufficient time for the characteristic radiographic changes to develop.
[1875][Heading 2]  What is Dry Socket?
[1876][Para 001] Dry socket results when blood clot in the socket is lost before it can become stabilized by ingrowth of granulation tissue. The exposed bone surface becomes colonized by anaerobic bacteria and spirochaetes and is partially and superficially devitalized. Loss of blood clot is thought to be the result of excessive fibrinolysis caused by bacterial, local tissue or salivary factors. In the absence of a blood clot, healing is delayed because soft tissue must grow from the gingival margin to cover bone and fill the socket.
[1877][Heading 2]  What Factors Predispose To Dry Socket?
[1878][Para 001] The risk factors associated with development of dry socket are given in Table 15.1.
[1879][Para 018] Table 15.1
[1880][Para 021] Risk Factors for Dry Socket
[1881][Heading 2]  How Would You Treat This Patient?
[1882][Para 001] Reassure the patient that although extremely painful, this condition does not signify any serious consequence of the extraction. Inform her that the socket will heal normally but more slowly than usual and that during the healing period, treatment can be provided to relieve the pain, although she may have to return for several sessions of treatment.
[1883][Para 002] Local treatment to the socket is the most effective measure. Irrigate the socket gently with warm saline. Place a dressing into the mouth of the socket to prevent further impaction of food. Many proprietary dressings are available, including resorbable materials, antiseptic preparations and analgesic formulations. In practice, almost all are satisfactory, provided they are used appropriately and replaced as required. Care should be taken not to pack the socket too much with the dressing because this would prevent it from filling up with granulation tissue as healing progresses.
[1884][Para 002] Effective socket cleansing and socket hygiene are more important than the type of dressing used, and the patient should come back every 2 days for retreatment, if necessary. In severe cases, a daily dressing may be appropriate initially, and as the socket heals and pain is reduce, the period between dressings may be extended. The trismus should be monitored and should reduce.
[1885][Heading 2]  What Drugs Might You Prescribe?
[1886][Para 001] Antibiotics should not be prescribed because they are ineffective. Analgesics are also largely ineffective in the absence of local measures. A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug should be adequate in most cases. The pain of dry socket is notorious for its severity, and in the past, controlled drugs have been prescribed. This is only occasionally justified but may need to be considered.
[1887][Heading 2]  How Quickly Will the Pain Be Relieved?
[1888][Para 001] Improvement of symptoms will usually be noted within minutes or in up to an hour and more quickly if the dressing contains a local anaesthetic agent. Pain may start again a day or two after dressing, gradually increasing in severity. After a few days, the pain will reduce and redressing may not be necessary. After about 10 days, the socket should be filled with tissue, and it will probably be asymptomatic for the last few days of healing.
[1889][Heading 2]  What if the Condition Persists for Longer Than This or Appears To Be Worsening?
[1890][Para 001] Failure to resolve in the longer term usually indicates the presence of small sequestra of devitalized lamina dura or root fragments. These are normal sequelae of extraction and are usually resorbed in the remodelling process during healing. Larger pieces may delay healing and sometimes sequestrate through the alveolar ridge mucosa many weeks after extraction, although they are not usually associated with significant pain. Occasionally, larger sequestra of lamina dura may be seen on periapical radiographs. If the sequestra are associated with symptoms and are not shed, surgical removal may become necessary. In practice, this intervention is extremely rarely required, and sequestra are usually small and lost without being noticed. The diagnosis will have to be reviewed, and radiographs are also useful to exclude other causes for the pain. The possibility of osteomyelitis should be considered and thoroughly investigated if the nature of the pain has changed or if the patient suffers any condition predisposing to this condition (local bone sclerosis, pathological or therapeutic immunosuppression, bisphosphonate drugs).
[1891][Para 025] Case 16
[1892][Heading 1] A Numb Lip
[1893][Para 027] Nicholas M. Goodger
[1894][Para 028] Summary
[1895][Para 029] A 68-year-old man presents to you at your general dental practice complaining that his lower lip has become numb. How would you investigate and manage this symptom?
[1896][Para 218] 
[1897][Para 008] 
[1898][Para 011] Fig. 16.1 The patient on presentation.

[1900][Para 014] History
[1901][Para 019] Complaint
[1902][Para 007] The patient complains of sudden onset of numbness of the lower right lip. It feels cold, as if he had had an injection for dental treatment ( Fig. 16.1 ).
[1903][Para 012] History of Complaint
[1904][Para 007] The patient noticed the numbness immediately after he woke up the previous morning. His jaw has been aching for some months, and he has noticed some tingling in the lip, which he ascribes to recent dental treatment.
[1905][Para 012] Dental History
[1906][Para 007] You are seeing the patient at an emergency appointment. He is normally under the care of one of your colleagues, and the patient’s records and radiographs are available.
[1907][Para 017] A series of appointments over the last few months have addressed pain in the lower right quadrant of the patient’s mouth. The tingling in the lip was noted 3 months ago. The lower right first molar had been considered as the cause. Your colleague had placed a root filling 4 months ago, but the pain did not resolve completely. Three weeks ago, the lower right second premolar was extracted as it was thought to be a likely cause of the pain. However, the patient’s discomfort continued.
[1908][Para 012] Medical History
[1909][Para 007] The patient reports that he is fit and well. He takes 50 mg atenolol daily for mild hypertension. In the past, he had suffered from depression and had been treated with antidepressants.
[1910][Heading 2]  What is the Sensory Nerve Supply To the Lip?
[1911][Para 001] The sensory nerve supply to the face is shown in Fig. 16.2. The three divisions of the trigeminal nerve supply most of the face. The greater auricular nerve is formed by the ventral rami of the cervical nerves C2 and C3.
[1912][Para 002] The lower lip is supplied by the mental nerve.
[1913][Heading 2]  What is the Course of the Nerve Supply?
[1914][Para 001] The trigeminal nerve starts in the pons, where its sensory and motor roots arise. The ophthalmic and maxillary branches leave the skull via the superior orbital fissure and the foramen rotundum, respectively. The mandibular branch leaves the skull at the foramen ovale to enter the infratemporal fossa, where it divides into an anterior group of mostly motor branches and a posterior group of sensory branches.
[1915][Para 002] The anterior group of branches includes the nerves to lateral pterygoid, deep temporal nerves to masseter and the sensory long buccal nerve. There are three posterior branches, including the auriculotemporal nerve, which is given off almost immediately. This passes backwards to innervate the side of the scalp and part of the ear. The main nerve then divides into the lingual nerve, which passes to the tongue along the lateral pterygoid, and the inferior alveolar nerve, which gives off the small motor branch to mylohyoid and then enters the mandibular foramen in the mandibular ramus. It emerges from the mental foramen to provide sensation to the lip.

[1929][Heading 2]  How Will You Test for Sensation? Why is This Necessary?
[1930][Para 001] A sensation of numbness may be central in origin, denote damage to the peripheral nerve or be psychosomatic. Only by testing sensation can the exact area affected be defined, and this will help define the cause.
[1931][Para 002] Tests of sensation may include light touch (with a wisp of cotton wool or a Von Frey hair – fine filaments of calibrated rigidity for testing touch), pain (with a sharp and blunt point), vibration, temperature and two-point discrimination. A cotton wool fibre and a sharp point such as a hypodermic needle are usually sufficient for a dental setting. Outline the area affected, making sure that hand movements cannot be seen by the patient so that the results are objective. Test and retest if the results are unclear.
[1932][Para 002] If the results are abnormal, it will be necessary to test the other cranial nerves because these may be affected if a lesion is present in the brain or along the common paths of the cranial nerves.

[1944][Heading 2]  How Should a Healing Socket Appear 3 Weeks After Extraction? Is This Socket Normal?
[1945][Para 001] The initial clot starts to be replaced by granulation tissue growing in from the periphery a few days after extraction. By 8–10 days, even a large molar socket should be filled with granulation tissue. At 2–3 weeks, there should be an intact layer of epithelium over the granulation tissue for a large socket. This socket is not epithelialized. The granulation tissue growing out from the socket indicates a process of hindered healing, which could have many causes. This socket has failed to heal.

[1976][Heading 2]  What is Your Differential Diagnosis? Justify Each Possible Diagnosis
[1977][Para 001] Chronic osteomyelitis. There is a history of dental infection, extraction with a nonhealing socket and tenderness at the site. Peripheral bone sclerosis and sequestra seen radiographically or in the socket would also be expected. The radiological features of osteomyelitis take several weeks to develop, but the symptoms started several months ago.

[2000][Para 002] All the primary neoplasms are relatively rare in the jaw.
[2001][Para 002] Metastasis the most likely malignant cause. Carcinoma of the breast would be very unlikely, although not impossible, in a male. All the other options need to be considered. Although those listed above are the commonest jaw metastases, almost any malignancy can spread to the jaws.
[2002][Para 002] Breast and prostate metastases are unusual in that they sometimes cause bone formation at the site, producing a sclerotic or mixed radiolucency rather than the more typical pure ‘moth-eaten’ poorly defined radiolucency. In this case, the lesion is purely destructive, and any of the common options could be the cause.
[2003][Heading 2]  What Further Investigation is Required?
[2004][Para 001] Biopsy of the socket is required to establish the diagnosis. This may be performed under local or general anaesthesia but must be representative of the lesion. It will, therefore, need to include tissue from the socket and the underlying radiolucency. Some of the sample must be fixed in formalin for histological examination, and a portion must be kept fresh to send for microbiological culture and sensitivity in case the diagnosis turns out to be osteomyelitis.
[2005][Para 002] This biopsy would be best performed in a specialist unit or local cancer centre, not in a general practice, because malignancy is strongly suspected.
[2006][Heading 2]  The Biopsy is Shown in Fig. 16.4. What Do You See?
[2007][Para 001] The left panel shows the bone curettings from the socket composed of normal lamellar bone (B) with several marrow spaces (M). These would normally be filled by fatty marrow in a patient of this age.
[2008][Para 002] However, they contain rings of epithelium (E), recognized by its darker staining pattern and the fact that it surrounds duct or gland-like spaces. The overall pattern is that of a glandular tissue. No glands are present in the normal mandibular marrow – this must be metastatic adenocarcinoma.
[2009][Para 002] Because the biopsy shows adenocarcinoma, lungs, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract and the prostate gland will be the most likely primary sites of carcinoma because these tissues give rise to adenocarcinomas.
[2010][Heading 2]  How Can the Primary Cancer Be Identified?
[2011][Para 001] Start again with a more detailed medical history, and refer the patient for medical examination. The diagnosis may already be known because metastasis to the jaw is usually a feature of late-stage disease. In other cases, jaw lesions may be the presenting sign.
[2012][Para 002] Some of the most likely primary sites can be investigated by relatively simple techniques such as physical examination, ultrasonography, chest radiography and blood tests for circulating prostate-specific antigen (PSA). If no primary cancer is suggested, imaging would be the next step.
[2013][Para 002] Often, it is possible to determine the primary site on the basis of the biopsy results. Cells in malignant neoplasms often retain some characteristics of their tissue of origin, and in this case, the glands have a resemblance to normal prostate gland, although metastatic adenocarcinoma from other sites would also be possible.
[2014][Para 002] It is often possible to detect specific marker proteins of the tissue of origin by using immunohistochemistry. The right-hand panel of Fig. 16.4 shows the biopsy specimen stained with antibodies to PSA. PSA is an enzyme secreted by prostate cells and expressed in their cytoplasm. Although not completely specific to the prostate gland, there are few other tissues that express high levels. The presence of PSA is indicated by positive staining (brown colour) around all the glands in bone marrow.
[2015][Para 017] Histopathology suggests strongly that this is metastasis of prostate carcinoma. A blood test reveals high levels of circulating PSA. No mass can be detected in the prostate gland on clinical examination, but prostate ultrasonography reveals a small nodule, and needle biopsy and histopathological analysis reveal prostate carcinoma.
[2016][Para 014] Diagnosis
[2017][Para 001] The diagnosis is metastatic prostate carcinoma.
[2018][Heading 2]  What is the Prognosis?
[2019][Para 001] In general, metastases to the jaws carry a poor prognosis because they indicate advanced disseminated malignancy, often malignant disease that has become refractory to treatment. In many cases, palliative care is all that can be offered, and patients with breast, colon or lung metastases are likely to die within a year. When bony metastases are in sites that risk significant morbidity, such as vertebrae, they may be treated surgically or with radiotherapy, but this is rarely indicated in the jaw unless there is severe pain.
[2020][Para 002] Some prostate carcinomas can respond to hormone treatment. Although the cancer remains sensitive to these treatments, it may progress only very slowly. This may be so even when there are widespread bone metastases and the course of disease may be significantly extended.
[2021][Heading 2]  Might There Be Implications for This Patient’s Future Dentistry?
[2022][Para 001] Yes, patients with multiple bone lesions of myeloma or metastatic breast or prostate carcinoma are often treated with intravenous bisphosphonates or denosumab (a monoclonal antibody that inhibits osteoclasts) to slow bone destruction and prevent spinal cord damage, pathological fracture and bone pain.
[2023][Para 002] Bisphosphonates such as zoledronic acid and monoclonal agents such as denosumab prevent bone turnover and reduce bone viability. There is a small but significant risk of developing the unusual pattern of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaws (MRONJ) associated with these drugs.

[2050][Para 001] Different patterns of dental trauma (e.g. crown fractures, crown and root fractures, root fractures, luxations, avulsion, etc.) have varying sequelae requiring a wide variety of management strategies. The history of the initial trauma suggests that the patient’s teeth suffered crown fractures only without any luxation injury or pulp/root involvement; however, the delayed provision of endodontic treatment suggests that possibly the root canal and/or the periodontal ligament may also have been affected by the trauma.

[2053][Heading 2]  How Would You Clinically Assess the Possibility of Root Fracture?
[2054][Para 001] By determining the axis of rotation of the mobile crown. Apply digital pressure forwards and backwards to identify how far down the root the axis of rotation appears to be. If when moving the crown bubbles of saliva are produced at the gingival margin, this would be an indicator of a root fracture communicating with a periodontal pocket or the gingival crevice.
[2055][Para 017] When you palpate the crown, you find that the crown appears to rotate bucco-cervically about a point 2–3 mm below the gingival margin. No such bubbles are seen at the crown margin.
[2056][Heading 2]  On the Basis of What You Know So Far, What are the Likely Causes?
[2057][Para 001] Having excluded mobility caused by periodontitis and coronal bone loss, the two possibilities that remain the most likely are resorption or root fracture. The mobile tooth is rotating about a point just below the gingival margin, so either process must affect the coronal part of the root.
[2058][Para 002] Resorption of the apical half of the root would move the axis of rotation of the remaining tooth coronally. There would have to be extensive resorption to cause this degree of mobility and raise the axis of rotation so far. Resorption is a recognized complication of trauma to teeth, and so this would be the most likely cause.
[2059][Para 002] Root fracture is possible. No fracture was noted but the marked mobility would be consistent with the root fracture of the coronal part of the root. If there is a root fracture it would appear to be independent of the original trauma. Teeth that suffer coronal fractures do not usually suffer root fractures as well because most of the energy is absorbed by fracturing the crown. However, if a root fracture had been present for the last 4 years, it might have triggered slow resorption, combining both possible causative factors.
[2060][Para 002] An unsuspected lesion may have destroyed the bone and/or the tooth root apically, leaving support only coronally. The tooth would then be mobile, whereas the periodontal ligament would remain intact in the mid- and coronal-third. The commonest lesion to do this would be a radicular cyst arising on a nonvital tooth.
[2061][Para 002] Finally, a neoplastic lesion remains a remote possibility. However, this seems most unlikely because there is no expansion and the adjacent teeth are not displaced or mobile.

[2079][Heading 2]  What Types of Dental Resorption are There? What are Their Characteristic Features?
[2080][Para 001] Resorption is the process of removal of dental hard tissues by osteoclasts. There is usually some form of repair by either reactionary dentine or bone. This repair may lead to ankylosis. All resorption is identical in its basic process, but it is convenient to subdivide resorption into clinically relevant types. Resorption may be classified by location (i.e. internal or external), as well as by aetiology (i.e. inflammatory or replacement). All types may be transient or progressive.
[2081][Para 002] Internal root resorption starts on the pulpal aspect of dentine. It typically affects the middle third of the root and forms a well-demarcated defect with a smooth symmetrical shape. Internal resorption indicates that the pulp is vital and that, provided the lesion has not perforated the root, the process will be halted by root canal treatment.
[2082][Para 002] External root resorption starts on the surface of the tooth, usually on the root but occasionally on the crown of unerupted teeth. A microscopic degree of superficial external root resorption can occur normally and is usually repaired by cementum. Greater apical root resorption may be seen radiographically, most commonly on teeth that have been moved orthodontically. Extensive apical resorption may accompany periapical inflammation or infection on nonvital teeth. A nonvital pulp may trigger external resorption of the middle or coronal one-third of the root by producing noxious byproducts, which diffuse outwards to the periodontal ligament along the dentine tubules. External cervical root resorption usually starts just below the gingival margin and may affect one or many teeth that may be otherwise healthy and vital. Radiographically, the early stages may mimic the appearance of an infra bony periodontal pocket. All types of external resorption are irregular in outline, and extensive lesions often spare a thin layer of dentine around the pulp so that the pulp can remain vital until a late stage, even if the defect communicates with a periodontal pocket.
[2083][Para 002] Inflammatory root resorption is associated with detectable inflammation and may be internal or external. This may be evident radiographically, as radiolucency in the adjacent bone, or clinically as redness. The inflammatory type of resorption has the positive aspect that removal of the cause of the inflammation (i.e. infected necrotic tissue) may halt the resorption.
[2084][Para 002] Unfortunately, this is not entirely predictable. Many cases of so-called inflammatory resorption, both internal and external, are not associated with significant inflammation clinically or histologically and are perhaps better regarded as idiopathic.
[2085][Para 002] Replacement root resorption is root resorption starting externally accompanied by progressive replacement of the tooth by bone. It is often associated with ankylosis and is a complication of luxation injuries, particularly intrusion and avulsion. Inflammation is absent; therefore, treatment must be directed at removing the resorptive tissue itself, which has a less predictable outcome. Internally, the pulp canal space may be filled with tertiary dentine, which is known as pulp canal obliteration, and is not a true form of resorption.
[2086][Heading 2]  What Causes Resorption?
[2087][Para 001] Resorption and repair may be physiological or pathological processes on both the external surface of the root and internally. Internally pulpal surface resorption is pathological; however, repair is one of the pulp’s natural responses to injury, as in the case of tertiary dentine formation. External resorption is known to follow damage to the cementum layer or loss of vitality of cementum, which triggers osteoclastic activity, which is why external resorption is very common after an avulsion injury. External cervical root resorption is assumed to be primarily inflammatory in aetiology, caused by the periodontal flora, though this does not explain cases where multiple lesions affect several otherwise healthy teeth.
[2088][Para 002] Internal resorption may follow loss of the predentine layer separating pulp from dentine, but the causes of this loss are unknown. A degree of pulp inflammation and increased pulp pressure are thought to be possible trigger factors.
[2089][Para 024]  What are the Features of Resorption?
[2090][Para 004] • Asymptomatic (unless an inflammatory cause is symptomatic)
[2091][Para 004] • Internal resorption occurs in vital or partially vital teeth
[2092][Para 004] • External resorption may develop on vital or nonvital teeth
[2093][Para 004] • Resorption itself does not compromise vitality until the pulp communicates with the oral environment
[2094][Para 004] • Usually slow and intermittent, occasionally very rapid
[2095][Para 004] • Mobility or pathological fracture
[2096][Para 004] • External cervical root resorption and extensive internal resorption appears as a ‘pink spot’, which is pulp/granulation tissue visible through the crown
[2097][Para 004] • Ankylosis (continuity of tooth and bone) is the sequelae of replacement resorption
[2098][Para 004] • Radiolucency and loss of tooth substance are the radiographic signs.
[2099][Para 080]  What are the Signs of Ankylosis?
[2100][Para 004] • Lack of normal mobility
[2101][Para 004] • High pitched metallic percussive sound
[2102][Para 004] • Infraocclusion (submerging tooth in the growing jaw)
[2103][Para 004] • Sometimes identifiable radiographically as a bridged periodontal ligament
[2104][Para 004] • Patchy ‘moth-eaten’ root surface/lamina dura.
[2105][Para 030]  What are Your Definitive Diagnoses in This Case?
[2106][Para 001] The maxillary lateral incisor has internal resorption, probably as a late sequela of the previous trauma or restoration of teeth. Resorption is advanced, and the root has suffered a pathological fracture making the coronal fragment mobile.
[2107][Para 002] The maxillary central incisor has a persistent periapical periodontitis despite root canal treatment, suggesting a lack of an efficient coronal seal. In addition, the restorative prognosis of the tooth is questionable, depending on whether a ferrule is present.
[2108][Para 002] There is a carious lesion present on the upper left canine.
[2109][Para 015] Treatment
[2110][Heading 2]  How Would You Manage the Lateral Incisor inthe Short Term and the Long Term?
[2111][Para 001] The prognosis for the lateral incisor is poor, and it requires extraction. It cannot be restored because the resorption has involved the periodontal ligament around much of the tooth circumference. A tooth with a more localized perforation might be repaired surgically. However, in combination with the necessary root canal treatment, this would be heroic treatment with an unpredictable chance of success at best. Surgical repair is more suitable for external cervical resorption, as opposed to middle third internal root resorption.
[2112][Para 002] Postextraction alveolar bone healing and remodelling will need to occur prior to definitive replacement; therefore, a provisional restoration will be required.
[2113][Para 024]  What are the Immediate Replacement Options for the Lateral Incisor?
[2114][Para 004] • A vacuum-formed clear Essix retainer with an acrylic tooth in the lateral incisor position
[2115][Para 004] • An acrylic removable partial denture, Every-type or spoon design major connector
[2116][Para 004] • A minimal preparation bridge of a cantilever design with a resin composite pontic for ease of adjustment after extraction
[2117][Para 004] • The existing crown could be splinted to the adjacent teeth using a fibre-reinforced resin composite splint.
[2118][Para 030]  What are the Definitive Replacement Options?
[2119][Para 001] Minimal preparation adhesive bridge replacing the lateral incisor, of a cantilever design with a retainer on the canine. This would require the carious lesion in the canine to be small and for there to be sufficient occlusal clearance for the retainer.
[2120][Para 002] A conventional cantilever bridge using the canine as the abutment, is a possibility; however, this is a more invasive option than a minimal preparation bridge. Either all-ceramic or metal-ceramic materials could potentially be used, each with advantages and disadvantages.
[2121][Para 002] A conventional cantilever bridge using the upper left central incisor as the abutment would be a less predictable option. The failed root filling in the central incisor would require retreatment, which would have a less certain outcome than de novo endodontics. Initially an investigation of the restorability of the tooth would involve removal of the pre-existing restoration and assessment of the amount of remaining tooth structure to ascertain if there was sufficient tooth tissue for at least a 2-mm ferrule. If there was less than 4 mm of coronal dentine, then a post would be required to provide additional retention for the crown retainer. This would require a parallel-sided, cast or preformed post and core to support a single cantilever pontic replacing the lateral incisor. Using a post crowned tooth as a bridge retainer has a relatively high failure rate; indeed, post retention is best avoided in all bridge designs. If an orthograde repeat root canal treatment is not successful in healing the periapical infection, then an apicectomy will have to be considered for this tooth; and if it is performed, the root length available for a post will be reduced. Therefore, considering these complicating factors together with the time necessary to ensure apical healing (up to 4 years), this suggests that the central incisor is probably not suitable as a bridge abutment in this scenario.
[2122][Para 002] A single tooth implant crown would be possible; however, the patient’s diabetes would ideally need to be well controlled to ensure a predictable outcome. Diabetes is not an absolute contraindication for implant provision, but the possibility of delayed healing in diabetes, in the maxillary site (where implants have a reduced survival rate), means that an implant might not be recommended. Further discussion of anterior single tooth implants will be found in Case 35.
[2123][Para 002] When managing trauma cases, comprehensive note keeping and documentation are essential to support optimal decision making and communication with the patient and clinical colleagues and also in the event of medico-legal scenarios. Depending on the nature and severity of the trauma, legal proceedings may be entered into, and clinical record keeping may form a part of the legal case. Therefore, the history of the trauma should be recorded as completely as possible. In addition, with regard to complex clinical scenarios such as this, effective liaison with specialist colleagues may be required, especially if three-dimensional (3D) cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) or endodontic surgery may be required. Adjunctive clinical photography with suitable consent forms signed would also be a sensible option in cases such as these.
[2124][Para 017] For this case, a specialist endodontic option was sought, and the outcome was that both the central and lateral incisors had a poor prognosis and were not amenable to endodontic treatment. Therefore, following discussion with the patient regarding the replacement options, the teeth were extracted and replaced with two separate cantilever-design minimal preparation bridges, by using the upper right central incisor as the abutment to replace the upper left central incisor and the upper left canine as the abutment to replace the upper left lateral incisor.
[2125][Para 025] Case 18
[2126][Heading 1] Oroantral Fistula
[2127][Para 027] Tara Renton
[2128][Para 028] Summary
[2129][Para 029] A 42-year-old man presents with pain following extraction of an upper first molar. What is the cause, and how will you treat him?
[2130][Para 014] History
[2131][Para 019] Complaint
[2132][Para 007] The patient is suffering dull throbbing pain in his upper jaw and face on the left side only. Pressure below his eye is painful, and all his upper teeth on the left are tender on biting. He has a nasal discharge and blocked nose on the left.
[2133][Para 012] History of Complaint
[2134][Para 007] The patient has had the pain for 2 weeks following extraction of the upper left first molar by his dentist. The extraction was difficult, and the roots required surgical removal. There was little pain immediately afterwards, but pain has slowly developed so that it is now preventing him from sleeping. The pain is constant.
[2135][Para 012] Medical History
[2136][Para 007] The patient gives a history of smoking 20 cigarettes a day for 18 years but considers himself fit and healthy.
[2137][Para 014] Examination
[2138][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[2139][Para 007] He is a healthy-looking man with no facial swelling or lymphadenopathy. There is a lightly blood-stained discharge from the left nares, and halitosis.
[2140][Para 049] Intraoral Examination
[2141][Heading 2]  The Appearances on Presentation are Shown in Fig. 18.1. What Do You See, and How Do You Interpret the Features?
[2142][Para 001] There is a large defect in the alveolus at the site of the first molar socket; the socket appears empty and the oral mucosa has grown to line the visible sides of the socket. After 2 weeks, the oral epithelium should have proliferated to cover the socket mouth, but there must have been a failure of clot formation and/or organization. One possibility is that the patient has dry socket (see Case 15). No bone is visible in the socket, but it could be exposed further apically. However, dry socket is rare in the maxilla, and it is more likely that the socket is communicating with the maxillary antrum.
[2143][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[2144][Para 024]  What Causes for This Pain are Possible, and Why?
[2145][Para 020] Sinusitis Secondary To Oroantral Fistula
[2146][Para 001] An oroantral communication itself causes little or no discomfort but usually induces a degree of sinusitis. The nature and distribution of pain and presence of nasal discharge are typical of sinusitis. This seems the most likely diagnosis. Fistula formation is most commonly associated with the extraction of maxillary first and second molars.
[2147][Para 020] Dental Pain
[2148][Para 001] Before jumping to conclusions, it is worth considering whether the wrong tooth may have been removed. If the extraction was performed for pulpitis (which is often poorly localized), it is possible that at least some of the symptoms may arise from the adjacent teeth. You will need to check whether additional symptoms suggest pain of dental origin.
[2149][Para 218] 
[2150][Para 008] 
[2151][Para 011] Fig. 18.1 The extraction socket on presentation.
[2152][Para 009]  
[2153][Heading 2]  What is an Oroantral Fistula?
[2154][Para 001] An oroantral fistula is a persistent epithelialized communication between the maxillary antrum and the mouth, present for more than 48 hours. The epithelial lining of the fistula grows from the gingival epithelium, periodontal pocket lining or the antral lining, and it may take up to 7 days for the epithelium to completely line the walls of the communication. If the tract is not lined by epithelium, it is known as an oroantral communication or perforation. Oroantral communications either close spontaneously or become epithelialized and persist as fistulae.
[2155][Heading 2]  What is the Aetiology of Oroantral Fistula?
[2156][Para 001] The vast majority of OAF result from dental extraction. Up to 10% of upper molar extractions may create oroantral communications, but very few, only 0.5%, persist to become fistulae. Other causes include malignant neoplasms arising in the oral cavity or in the antrum.
[2157][Para 024]  What Factors Predispose to Formation of Oroantral Fistulae After Extraction of Teeth?
[2158][Para 004] • Proximity of roots to maxillary antrum, large sinus
[2159][Para 004] • Difficult extraction, unfavourable root morphology
[2160][Para 004] • Periapical lesions such as apical granulomas or cysts
[2161][Para 004] • Bone loss caused by periodontitis or periodontal–endodontic lesion
[2162][Para 004] • Hypercementosis
[2163][Para 004] • Displaced root fragment
[2164][Para 004] • Local infection or sequestrum
[2165][Para 004] • Predisposition to infection (e.g. diabetes)
[2166][Para 004] • Dry socket or other poor healing
[2167][Para 004] • Advanced age
[2168][Para 004] • Pre-existing diseases in the sinus, although this is probably not a very significant factor.
[2169][Para 030]  What are the Signs and Symptoms of Oroantral Fistula?
[2170][Para 001] The symptoms depend on the size of the fistula. Initially, there may be persistent pain localized to the tooth socket but later, when inflammation has subsided, the fistula will be painless. If pain is a prominent symptom, some additional element such as infection must be suspected. The socket may present as an empty cavity or as a prolapse of antral lining through the socket into the mouth.
[2171][Para 002] The most characteristic symptoms are the escape of fluids from the mouth into the nose on eating, or air or fluid into the mouth on blowing the nose. Passage of saliva, food and bacteria into the antrum causes sinusitis and the symptoms experienced will depend on its severity. Unilateral nasal obstruction, a feeling of fullness, pain over the maxilla and tenderness on pressure are typical.
[2172][Para 015] Investigations
[2173][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Carry Out, How and Why?
[2174][Para 001] Investigations need to be performed to confirm the communication with the antrum, to check for associated complications and to exclude the possibility that a malignant neoplasm is the cause of either the antral communication itself or the failure of the socket to heal. Investigations are summarized in Table 18.1.

[2196][Para 001] Sinusitis secondary to oroantral fistula caused by extraction of the upper first molar. A root fragment has been displaced into the sinus. Apical periodontitis of the second molar may also contribute to the sinusitis, but this is a chronic problem and a lower priority for treatment.
[2197][Para 015] Treatment
[2198][Para 024]  How Would You Treat This Patient?
[2199][Para 004] • If pus is present in the fistula or if symptoms are severe, consider treating the sinusitis first and closing the fistula later after the sinusitis has partially resolved (it will not resolve completely until the fistula is closed). If there is long-standing infective sinusitis, this must be treated prior to surgical closure otherwise healing will be compromised.
[2200][Para 004] • Excise the fistula, otherwise remnants of the epithelial lining may proliferate to reform the tract.
[2201][Para 004] • Remove the root fragment from the sinus.
[2202][Para 004] • Close the oroantral communication surgically.
[2203][Para 222] 
[2204][Para 008] 
[2205][Para 011] Fig. 18.4 The buccal advancement flap. Note how the relieving incisions buccally flare widely, shallow incision of the periosteum, trimming of the flap apex to ensure a good fit palatally and the rim of palatal bone on which it lies.
[2206][Heading 2]  Would You Treat This Patient in General Practice?
[2207][Para 001] Provided you are confident of your ability to remove the root fragment, there is no reason why this cannot be dealt with in a general practice. However, if the root is mobile in the antrum, the patient should be referred to hospital.
[2208][Heading 2]  How Would You Excise the Fistula and Remove the Root?
[2209][Para 001] Under local anaesthesia, incise around the edge of the socket from gingiva right down into the antrum, removing all the soft tissue in the socket as a cylinder or cone-shaped piece, and draw it into the mouth. Depending on the size of the bony defect and the amount of bone resorption (usually greater in long-standing fistulae), this opens up a large hole into the sinus. With suction, good light and direct vision, try to identify the root fragment, and remove it with fine forceps, sucker tip or other instrument. Take care not to displace it into the sinus. If it becomes displaced, it may be possible to wash it out by flushing saline into the sinus. Alternatively, better surgical access to the sinus may be achieved by using the Caldwell—Luc approach under general anaesthesia. This is the main reason for referring patients with mobile fragments to hospital.
[2210][Para 002] Send the excised tract for histopathological examination in case of unexpected underlying lesions.
[2211][Heading 2]  How Will You Close the Defect?
[2212][Para 001] The buccal mucoperiosteal flap with advancement (buccal advancement flap) is the most commonly used technique, and it has more than a 90% success rate. The technique is shown in Fig. 18.4. After excising the fistula, as above, proceed as follows:
[2213][Para 002] Make two incisions buccally, anterior and posterior to the socket, passing parallel up the attached gingiva and then splaying to provide a wider base to ensure a good blood supply for the flap. The line of the incisions must be compatible with the flap sliding palatally to cover the defect in the alveolus.
[2214][Para 002] Elevate the mucoperiosteal flap you have outlined by lifting the soft tissues in the plane beneath the periosteum.
[2215][Para 002] Advance the flap. The flap cannot yet be pulled across the defect because the periosteum cannot be stretched. Fold the flap back to expose its periosteal surface and make several shallow parallel incisions across the flap that penetrate only the periosteum (about 0.25–0.5 mm in depth). This must be done very carefully with the flap under slight tension. As the periosteum is incised the flap will be felt to stretch. Do not perforate the flap, or it will either be cut off or have a compromised blood supply. Make sufficient incisions to lengthen the flap so that it can reach across to the palatal side of the defect with minimal tension.
[2216][Para 002] Prepare the palatal aspect of the alveolar defect. Refresh the margin of the palatal side to expose a narrow bony rim at least 1 mm wide, preferably 2 mm. The flap must be sutured into place at a site that has bony support.
[2217][Para 002] Suture the flap in place using slowly resorbable sutures (e.g. 3/0 vicryl) or nonresorbable sutures. Place several sutures around the apex of the flap (mesial, distal and central) and buccally. The flap must not be under tension, and sufficient sutures must be placed to ensure an airtight and watertight seal supported by underlying bone. Ensure haemostasis. The sutures must remain in place for 10–14 days.
[2218][Heading 2]  What Alternative Flap Designs are Possible?
[2219][Para 001] The buccal advancement flap may not be possible when the bony defect is very large or when a previous attempt at repair has failed.
[2220][Para 002] A number of other flaps are possible, including the palatal island flap, submucosal palatal island flap, combined buccal and palatal flaps and even pedicled grafts from the tongue. However, most of these techniques are complex and have been superseded by the buccal fat pad technique. The buccal fat pad technique, the second most commonly used method, is shown in Fig. 18.5. Alternative methods to close oroantral fistulae are noted in Table 18.2.
[2221][Heading 2]  What Postoperative Instructions are Required?
[2222][Para 001] In addition to the routine instructions given after extraction, the patient must be placed on an antral regime to reduce inflammation and prevent a rise in air pressure in the antrum. The upper first molar is situated in the lowest point of the maxillary sinus. Persistent infection or inflammation will induce exudates that will drain to this point and cause breakdown of the clot. Increased air pressure in the sinus, for instance, from sneezing or blowing the nose, will force air or exudate through the alveolar defect as well as physically disrupting the clot and flap. Decongestants maintain the patency of the opening of the sinus to favour drainage to the nose.

[2235][Para 015] Other Considerations
[2236][Heading 2]  How Might Formation of Oroantral Communication Be Prevented?
[2237][Para 001] The risk of oroantral communication should be assessed routinely on a radiograph before extraction of upper molars. If the risk is high, an experienced surgeon should remove the tooth. Surgical extraction, possibly with elective sectioning of the tooth, reduces the chances of disrupting the maxillary floor.
[2238][Heading 2]  The Preoperative Radiograph is Shown in Fig. 18.6. What Do You See?
[2239][Para 001] Several features in the list of risk factors above are evident. There is a low antral floor in contact with the roots, there is little alveolar bone height, and there is loss of lamina dura around the tooth root apices.
[2240][Para 218] 
[2241][Para 008] 
[2242][Para 011] Fig. 18.6 Preoperative radiograph.
[2243][Para 009]  
[2244][Heading 2]  How Could an Oroantral Communication Be Confirmed At the Time of Extraction? How Might This Help?
[2245][Para 001] If an antral communication is present, an echoing ‘wind tunnel sound’ will be heard if a small suction tip is held in the socket, the result of air being sucked from the antrum as well as the mouth. If the communication is large, you may be able to see into the antrum or identify nasal regurgitation of your irrigation fluids or blood from the extraction site. Do not ask patient to blow through their nose while holding it. The sinus lining may still be intact but would be burst by the pressure and a small communication might be enlarged.
[2246][Para 002] If a communication is suspected, stabilization of the clot, closure of the socket with resorbable sutures and appropriate warnings to the patient about blowing the nose should prevent a fistula developing. This is likely to be effective if the diameter of the communication is 4 mm or less. If it is larger, it should be repaired immediately using a suitable flap technique to avoid sinusitis and infection.

[2296][Para 015] Diagnosis
[2297][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis, and What Would You Do Next?
[2298][Para 001] The history and examination findings indicate recurrent aphthous stomatitis minor (RAS minor). However, it is necessary to consider whether there is an underlying predisposing condition that could account for the recent change in the pattern of ulceration.
[2299][Heading 2]  What Features of the Ulcers Might Indicate the Presence of an Underlying Predisposing Condition?
[2300][Para 001] Any feature in the history or examination that is atypical for RAS minor should raise suspicion of an underlying condition. In particular, the following should trigger a search for underlying predisposing causes:
[2301][Para 004] • Onset after the second decade
[2302][Para 004] • Significant increase in ulcer size, duration, symptoms or severity
[2303][Para 080]  Which Underlying Predisposing Conditions and Lifestyle Factors Should Be Considered for This Patient?
[2304][Para 004] • Haematinic (iron, vitamin B12, folate) deficiency
[2305][Para 004] • Gastrointestinal disease (e.g. coeliac disease, Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis)
[2306][Para 004] • Behçet’s disease
[2307][Para 004] • Smoking cessation
[2308][Para 004] • Medications
[2309][Para 030]  How Do You Assess and Investigate These Underlying Conditions?
[2310][Para 001] Iron deficiency is relatively common, particularly amongst females of child-bearing age. Check for a history of anaemia and its cause. Ask about common causes of iron deficiency anaemia include menorrhagia and upper or lower gastrointestinal bleeding (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug [NSAID] use, excessive alcohol use, peptic ulcer disease, inflammatory bowel disease, haemorrhoids and colorectal cancer). Dietary deficiency should be considered in patients who follow a restrictive diet. Coordination with the patient’s general medical practitioner is required. Patients should undergo blood tests for microcytic anaemia (reduced haemoglobin, reduced mean cell volume [MCV] and serum ferritin levels. Ulcers may be associated with minor degrees of iron deficiency insufficient to cause overt anaemia. Any evidence of iron deficiency anaemia should be followed by thorough investigation and treatment of the underlying cause.
[2311][Para 002] Other vitamin deficiencies associated with oral ulceration are typically folate or B12. Check whether the patient follows a restrictive diet, particularly a strict vegetarian diet, or has high levels of alcohol consumption. Both can result in vitamin B deficiency. Ask about any previous diagnosis of the autoimmune condition pernicious anaemia (B12 deficiency). Consider undiagnosed pernicious anaemia in patients who have a history of vitiligo, hypothyroidism or Addison’s disease, as these conditions are related. Consider the possibility of gastrointestinal disease (see below). Patients with suspected B12/folate deficiency should undergo blood tests (full blood count [FBC], folate, B12) with their general practitioner. These would show macrocytic anaemia (reduced haemoglobin levels and elevated MCV).
[2312][Para 002] Gastrointestinal disease can cause reduced absorption of iron, folate and B12, all of which cause recurrent oral ulceration. Ask about diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal cramps, weight loss and blood in the stools. Enquire about any family history of gastrointestinal disease. Patients with gastrointestinal disease may also experience recurrent oral ulceration in the absence of haematinic deficiency, reflecting their underlying inflammatory disease state. Pyostomatitis vegetans may occur in ulcerative colitis, linear ulcers of the buccal sulcus in Crohn’s disease and herpetiform-type ulcers in coeliac disease.
[2313][Para 002] Behçet’s disease is a rare autoinflammatory condition that can present with oral ulcers as the most significant problem. Patients may suffer from a broad spectrum of signs and symptoms and should be questioned about any history of genital ulcers, rashes including erythema nodosum or skin pustules, arthritis of large and small joints and history of venous thrombosis. Ocular signs including uveitis are found in a minority of patients, as well as central nervous system symptoms. There are no specific tests for Behçet’s disease (although human leucocyte antigen [HLA] typing may help identify those at risk from ocular disease). A biopsy of an oral ulcer may be helpful because it can demonstrate underlying vasculitis.
[2314][Para 002] Smoking cessation should be excluded by questioning. Ulceration related to smoking cessation can be difficult to manage, often not responding well to topical therapies, and may be sufficiently troublesome that the patient will recommence smoking. This does not usually induce remission of ulcers.
[2315][Para 002] Medications must be considered as a potential cause for oral ulceration. Review the medication history to ensure that nothing has been missed. Check for medication side effects in the British National Formulary (BNF) and assess whether the ulcer history coincides with recent prescription of a new medication, or a change in the dose of an existing medication. Medication causes of oral ulceration include nicorandil, used for management of angina, and methotrexate, which is used for such conditions as rheumatoid arthritis. However, these do not follow the pattern of typical recurrent oral ulcers seen in RAS.
[2316][Para 015] Treatment
[2317][Heading 2]  What Treatments are Available, and Which Would You Suggest?
[2318][Para 001] Many treatments are available, but none is highly effective in all patients and treatment must be selected to suit individual cases. Treatments may be topical or systemic, and sometimes both are used. Reassurance is an important part of treatment in RAS minor so that patient information leaflets can be provided. Specifically, inform the patient that:
[2319][Para 004] • RAS is very common and is a ‘nuisance’ condition rather than one that is harmful to health.
[2320][Para 004] • Although many treatments are available, none will ‘cure’ the ulcers. Rather, the goal of treatment is to reduce the duration and frequency of oral ulceration.
[2321][Para 002] Treatments available are shown in Table 19.2.
[2322][Para 002] For this patient, the most important initial step is to exclude an underlying cause, which may account for the recent change in the pattern of the oral ulceration. The overall history and examination findings are consistent with a diagnosis of RAS minor. The recent worsening ulceration is likely to represent a concurrent underlying problem, such as iron deficiency anaemia, and it would be advisable for this patient to see her general medical practitioner for blood tests. Treatment of the underlying cause of this exacerbation should reduce the ulcer severity to the previous pattern of occasional, solitary ulcers. In the meantime, a mouthwash such as benzydamine hydrochloride may improve the patient’s comfort. Prescription of hydrocortisone pellets could also be considered.
[2323][Heading 2]  The Patient Asks Whether the Buccal Ulcer Could Be Caused By the Temporary Restoration in the Adjacent Tooth. What is Your Opinion?
[2324][Para 001] No, this is very unlikely to be the primary cause. The history of RAS is so typical that the diagnosis is not in doubt. Reactions to dental materials are not associated with ulcers of this type. Remember that aphthae often develop at the sites of minor trauma. Mucosal trauma during restoration placement, from a sharp edge on the restoration, or from biting while the mucosa was anaesthetized might well explain the location of this particular ulcer.

[2328][Heading 1] A Lump in the Neck
[2329][Para 027] Nicholas m. Goodger, and Selvam Thavaraj
[2330][Para 028] Summary
[2331][Para 029] A 55-year-old man presents to your oral and maxillofacial surgery department clinic with a lump on the left side of the neck. You must make a diagnosis.
