[2336][Para 014] History
[2337][Para 019] Complaint
[2338][Para 007] The patient complains of the lump and has noticed some discomfort on swallowing, as if something is stuck in his throat. He assumes the lump is the cause.
[2339][Para 012] History of Present Complaint
[2340][Para 007] He thinks he first noticed the lump about 3 months ago. It has always been painless and is slowly enlarging. The discomfort on swallowing is of recent onset.
[2341][Para 012] Medical History
[2342][Para 007] The patient is otherwise fit and well. He has never smoked and drinks 10 units of alcohol (beer) each week.
[2343][Para 014] Examination
[2344][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[2345][Para 001] The appearance of the swelling is shown in Fig. 20.1.
[2346][Heading 2]  What Do You See? What is the Likely Origin of the Mass?
[2347][Para 001] There is a swelling just anterior to the anterior border of the sternomastoid muscle and below and behind the angle of the mandible. It is several centimetres in diameter and extends forwards below the angle of the mandible towards the submandibular region. The overlying skin does not appear to be inflamed.
[2348][Para 002] The swelling lies over the deep cervical lymph node chain and could well arise from a cervical lymph node. It is too low and too far posterior to be arising from the submandibular gland and too low to have arisen in the lower pole of the parotid gland. Other soft tissues of the neck could be the origin, but a lymph node is the most likely cause.
[2349][Para 017] If you could palpate the lesion, you would find that it is approximately 8 × 6 cm in size and feels very soft on palpation, making its edges difficult to localize. It is possibly fluctuant and seems cyst-like. It is mobile, not fixed to the overlying skin or deep structures. The patient has not noticed any tenderness on palpation. There are no other swellings or enlarged lymph nodes palpable on either side of the neck.
[2350][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[2351][Para 001] The submandibular glands are palpable bimanually and appear symmetrical. Both are mobile and clearly separate from the swelling, which lies posterior to the gland.
[2352][Para 002] The patient’s mouth has been well restored in the past but suffers from recent neglect, and several carious cavities are visible. There is no significant periodontal disease, with most probing depths less than 5 mm, and no mobile teeth. The lower left first permanent molar has lost a large restoration and has extensive caries. There is no soft tissue swelling, sinus or tenderness in the sulcus adjacent to the apices of the roots. The tooth is not tender to percussion. The oral mucosa appears normal, and the tonsils appear to be symmetrical.
[2353][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[2354][Heading 2]  What are the Most Likely Causes of the Lump, and Why?
[2355][Para 001] Metastatic malignancy appears likely, and this lesion is so typical of a cervical lymph node metastasis that it must be considered to be malignant until proven otherwise. The combination of features suggestive of metastasis is the patient’s age (should be considered a possible cause in any patient older than 45 years of age), the site (consistent with a cervical lymph node) and lack of tenderness. Fixation to the skin or other structures would be almost conclusive of malignancy but is a late sign. The one feature that seems to point away from a metastasis is the soft cystic consistency of the swelling. Metastases from oral, skin or salivary gland cancers, lymphoma or melanoma are typically firm or hard. However, some carcinomas such as those arising in the tonsil characteristically produce a cystic metastasis. Occasionally, a metastasis from carcinomas of the oral cavity, salivary glands or thyroid gland may be full of cystic spaces.
[2356][Para 002] Branchial or lymphoepithelial cysts develop at this site and, given the soft, fluctuant consistency, need to be considered. However, branchial cysts usually present in childhood or early adulthood. Lymphoepithelial cysts arise in developmental epithelial rests in upper cervical lymph nodes and present just like this in a middle-aged or older population. However, cystic metastatic carcinoma is such an important diagnosis that investigation must exclude this before considering these benign possibilities.
[2357][Para 002] Tuberculosis may present as a soft and painless neck lump and needs to be considered both as a possible diagnosis and as a factor affecting management. Most patients with cervical lymph node enlargement caused by tuberculosis have reactivation (‘secondary’ or postprimary) tuberculosis, in which a previous quiescent infection becomes reactivated. This localized infection may or may not be accompanied by pulmonary disease, although there may be radiological evidence of past tuberculosis on chest radiograph. Cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis is common in those from the Indian subcontinent.
[2358][Heading 2]  Which Additional, But Less Likely, Causes Need To Be Considered Whenever a Patient Complains of an Enlargement At This Site? Why are They Unlikely Causes in This Case?
[2359][Para 001] Numerous lesions could arise at this site, and it is not useful to list them all. A number of possible causes (Table 20.1) merit consideration because they are common, easily excluded or cause significant morbidity.
[2360][Para 015] Investigations
[2361][Heading 2]  What is the Most Important Investigation? Which Methods Might Be Used, and What are Their Advantages and Disadvantages?
[2362][Para 001] The critical requirement when malignancy is suspected is to obtain tissue speedily for microscopic diagnosis. All other investigations are less important at this stage. Three techniques are in common use; fine-needle aspiration biopsy, core biopsy and the surgical incisional biopsy (Table 20.2).
[2363][Heading 2]  What Other Investigations Might Be Performed, Either Now or At a Later Date? Why?
[2364][Para 032] See Table 20.3.
[2365][Para 002] In this case, a suitable combination of investigations would be fine-needle aspiration, dental radiography, vitality tests and possibly ultrasonography. Sialography would have been performed if a salivary origin remained a possibility after clinical examination.
[2366][Para 017] The lower first molar was nonvital and a periapical radiograph revealed apical radiolucency. Fine-needle aspiration of the mass was performed, but in this instance, there was insufficient cellular yield to reach a definitive diagnosis. A core biopsy was therefore performed under ultrasound guidance. The core biopsy specimen is shown in  Fig. 20.2 .
[2367][Heading 2]  What Does the Core Biopsy Show, and How Do You Interpret the Appearances?
[2368][Para 001] The image on the left is taken at low magnification. A cohesive sheet of epithelial cells is present on the left and these have a similar morphology to basal and lower prickle squamous epithelial cells. Occasional darkly stained (hyperchromatic) cells and variation in nuclear size (anisonucleosis) can be appreciated even at low magnification. Many normal lymphocytes are present towards the right of the image (around the yellow asterisk). There should be no epithelium in a lymph node; this indicates metastatic carcinoma to a lymph node. The image on the right is at higher magnification and highlights cells with pleomorphic nuclei (yellow arrow). An abnormal tripolar mitosis is indicated by the black arrow. These features also indicate malignancy. Although no keratinization is present, the basal and lower prickle morphology and cohesive sheets of epithelium suggest that this is squamous cell carcinoma, as opposed to adenocarcinoma or lymphoma.
[2369][Para 015] Diagnosis
[2370][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[2371][Para 001] The patient has metastatic squamous cell carcinoma in a cervical lymph node.
[2372][Para 015] Further Investigations
[2373][Heading 2]  What is the Next Step in Diagnosis? How Can This Be Achieved?
[2374][Para 001] To determine the primary site of this carcinoma. No oral carcinoma has been noted on examination. The primary carcinoma could be small or located in deep tissues. It might even be in the chest or abdomen, although this is unlikely, as discussed below.

[2384][Para 021] Other Investigations
[2385][Para 002] The primary site can be sought in several ways. The biopsy specimen already taken can be subjected to further laboratory tests that may indicate the site or, at least, narrow down the possibilities. Imaging of the head and neck with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may reveal the primary. A more complete examination of the upper aerodigestive tract can be undertaken with endoscopy, and any suspicious sites subjected to biopsy. If the primary is visible endoscopically, this is the definitive investigation. However, it will require general anaesthesia and is best deferred until the biopsy investigations and imaging have been completed, as these may provide additional useful information on where to look.
[2386][Heading 2]  What are the Likely Primary Sites for This Metastasis?
[2387][Para 001] The site must be in the drainage area of the lymph node, and it must contain epithelium, probably squamous cell epithelium. The likely sites, therefore, are:
[2388][Para 004] • Oral mucosa, particularly ventrolateral tongue, floor of mouth, soft palate or retromolar mucosa
[2389][Para 004] • Oropharynx (including tonsil and base of tongue) or nasopharynx
[2390][Para 004] • Maxillary sinus
[2391][Para 004] • Larynx
[2392][Para 004] • Facial skin and scalp.

[2400][Heading 2]  What Further Investigations On the Biopsy Specimen May Be Useful?
[2401][Para 001] It is possible to confirm the squamous differentiation of the carcinoma cells by immunohistochemistry. These stains detect cytoskeletal proteins or cell cycle control proteins that are normally only expressed in squamous epithelium, using antibodies that bind to them. In this case, the morphological appearances are typical of squamous cell carcinoma and immunohistochemical confirmation was not necessary.
[2402][Para 002] Once the squamous cell differentiation is confirmed, current guidelines recommend testing the tissue for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) if no primary is known. This is because HPV and EBV are the causes of many oropharyngeal and most nasopharyngeal carcinomas, respectively. These carcinomas often present with metastasis, and the primary tumour can be very small, so these tests are particularly helpful in directing imaging and further biopsy to either the oropharynx or nasopharynx.
[2403][Para 002] The biopsy was stained immunohistochemically for the p16 protein and by DNA in situ hybridization for HPV DNA of the high risk subtypes. The results are shown in Fig. 20.3.
[2404][Heading 2]  How Do You Interpret the Results of These Extra Investigations?
[2405][Para 001] When high-risk HPV infects a cell, one of the first proteins it synthesises, called E7, interferes with the cell cycle, putting the cell into continuous cell division to favour viral replication. The cell overexpresses the p16 cell cycle control protein as a result. In the left panel of Fig. 20.3, an antibody against p16 has been applied to the tissue where it has bound to the p16 protein. A brown reaction has then been produced to indicate the site of the p16 protein. The islands of carcinoma stain strongly and diffusely for p16. This makes it highly likely that they are infected with HPV and also shows that the virus has deregulated cell division. To prove the presence of the virus, DNA in situ hybridization must be undertaken. This uses DNA probes complementary to the viral DNA sequence and hybridization is shown by the blue staining. Note how the positive reaction stains only the carcinoma, in the same distribution as the p16 stain.
[2406][Para 002] Together these investigations demonstrate that the carcinoma is caused by HPV. There is a very strong likelihood that the primary carcinoma is located in the tonsil or base of tongue because HPV carcinomas start in tonsil crypt epithelium of the major or minor tonsils.
[2407][Para 002] The soft cystic nature of the mass and its site at level 2 or 3 in the neck are highly consistent with metastasis from an HPV associated carcinoma of the oropharynx. This presentation is unlike most other head and neck carcinomas because the primary carcinoma is usually very small, and the metastasis is often large and cystic. HPV associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma also more commonly arise in nonsmokers.
[2408][Heading 2]  What is the Next Step?
[2409][Para 001] Imaging and biopsy can now target the oropharynx and an endoscopy arranged. Co-localized positron emission tomography and CT (PET/CT) is the best imaging modality because it shows both anatomical alterations and the high metabolic rate of a cancer, improving the chances of finding even a very small primary carcinoma.
[2410][Heading 2]  What Would You Do if a Primary Carcinoma is Not Found?
[2411][Para 001] If no abnormal tissue is seen on endoscopy, bilateral tonsillectomy and a large mucosal excision (mucosectomy) of the base of tongue are performed because these are the most common sites for HPV associated squamous cell carcinoma. Very occasionally, no primary lesion is found, and the patient is said to have an ‘occult primary’. However, even if no primary were found, it would still be almost certain that it lay in the oropharynx, nasopharynx or other head and neck tonsil site because of the presence of HPV. It would simply be that the primary is too small to be found.
[2412][Para 017] In this case, a carcinoma 10 mm in diameter was found in the base of the tongue on biopsy during endoscopy. It was invisible on imaging.
[2413][Para 015] Treatment and Prognosis
[2414][Heading 2]  What are the Treatment Options, Assuming a Primary is Identified in the Oropharynx?
[2415][Para 001] Most patients with tonsillar, tongue base and pharyngeal tumours are offered radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy as primary treatment. Surgical options, including robotic resection of the primary tumour and neck dissection involving lymph nodes from the deep cervical chain, are also offered in some centres.
[2416][Heading 2]  What is This Patient’s Overall Prognosis?
[2417][Para 001] Patients with HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma have a significantly better overall survival compared with patients with HPV-negative head and neck cancers. The reasons for improved survival are complex but may be explained, in part, by increased sensitivity to radiotherapy.
[2418][Para 015] Another Possibility
[2419][Heading 2]  If the Fine-Needle Aspirate Had Shown Adenocarcinoma, Which Possible Primary Sites Would Then Have Required Investigation?
[2420][Para 001] Adenocarcinomas are carcinomas that show glandular differentiation and would have arisen in a gland or mucosa in the drainage area of the node. The thyroid, salivary glands and minor mucous glands in the upper aerodigestive tract would be the most likely primary sites.
[2421][Para 002] However, adenocarcinoma is much more common in the breast, lung or prostate gland. Although a solitary metastasis high in the neck would be unusual, it is not unknown, and these sites should be considered. A metastasis to the neck from these sites would be likely to be one of many disseminated metastases, although these might be as yet undiagnosed.
[2422][Para 002] The stomach and the oesophagus are further possible sources and a low (supraclavicular) cervical metastasis on the left side is a recognized presentation. However, in this case, the swelling is too high in the neck for the metastasis to have arisen from the stomach.
[2423][Heading 2]  Why Does a Gastrointestinal Carcinoma Sometimes Metastasize To the Left Side of the Neck?
[2424][Para 001] Lymph from the oesophagus and the upper part of the stomach drains upwards in the thoracic duct, which enters the lower end of the internal jugular vein. There is a rather variable anatomy at the site, and often the subclavian and internal jugular lymph trunks join the thoracic duct rather than the internal jugular vein. In this situation, malignant cells draining up the thoracic duct can be carried a short distance into the lymphatics of the neck by retrograde flow (because the lymphatics are at a low and fluctuating pressure). Such cells can seed metastases in the lymph nodes just above the clavicle, the presentation known as Virchow’s node.

[2433][Para 012] History of Complaint

[2435][Para 017] He did not lose consciousness and was taken to the local hospital Accident and Emergency (A&E) department, where a head injury was ruled out and a laceration below his lower lip was sutured. He was then advised to see a dentist to manage his upper left central incisor. He presented for management of his displaced tooth 5 days after the injury had occurred.
[2436][Para 017] No other injuries were sustained.
[2437][Para 012] Medical History
[2438][Para 007] The patient was medically fit and healthy, with no known allergies.

[2441][Para 024]  What Additional Questions Would You Ask the Patient, and Why?
[2442][Para 020] Have You Suffered Trauma Previously?
[2443][Para 130] Previous trauma to these teeth, depending on the age at which the trauma was sustained, could have resulted in arrested root development, disturbed crown formation, pulp necrosis or pulp canal obliteration.
[2444][Para 002] Such changes could affect treatment.
[2445][Para 017] In this case no previous trauma could be recalled.
[2446][Para 020] Can You Bring Your Back Teeth Together?
[2447][Para 001] If a patient is unable to bring the posterior teeth into maximum intercuspation, it may suggest displacement of a tooth.
[2448][Para 017] In this case, the patient had a class III incisor relationship, so the palatal displacement of the upper left central incisor resulted in a cross-bite, allowing him to bring his posterior teeth into maximum intercuspation ( Fig. 21.1 ).
[2449][Para 002] In patients with a class I or II incisor relationship, presenting with a palatally displaced tooth, an occlusal disturbance would be seen preventing the patient from bringing the posterior teeth into normal intercuspation.
[2450][Para 020] Do You Smoke?
[2451][Para 001] This may influence healing and the health of the dento-alveolar and periodontal supporting tissues.

[2453][Para 019] Extraoral Examination

[2474][Para 024]  What Investigations Would You Perform? Justify Each Option
[2475][Para 020] Percussion Sounds of Teeth
[2476][Para 001] Traumatized teeth should not be tapped to check the percussion sound because it is too distressing for patients and yields very little value at the acute stage of management.
[2477][Para 020] Sensibility Testing
[2478][Para 001] These may be thermal tests (e.g. cold test using Endo-Frost at −50 degrees) or electric pulp testing and are useful to help assess pulpal viability.
[2479][Para 002] These tests have been shown to give false-negative results for up to 3 months after acute trauma and so will not provide any useful information and can make patients more anxious.
[2480][Para 002] Radiography is required to visualize displaced teeth and the adjacent teeth.

A lateral luxation injury is often associated with a dento-alveolar fracture with the apex of the tooth being locked into the fracture line, resulting in the tooth being firm and immobile.

[2529][Heading 2]  What Follow-Up Should You Arrange?
[2530][Para 001] The patient should be seen after 4 weeks for splint removal when baseline sensibility testing should be recorded. The follow-up protocol is 3 months, 6 months and then annually.
[2531][Para 002] Each follow-up visit should include the following:
[2532][Para 004] • An enquiry into any symptoms experienced since the repositioning
[2533][Para 004] • A clinical examination to look for any discolouration, mobility, tenderness to percussion and palpation and the presence of a sinus
[2534][Para 004] • Periapical radiography to assess for any apical radiolucency or widening of the periodontal ligament space
[2535][Para 004] • Sensibility testing using cold and electric pulp testing.
[2536][Para 002] The aim of the follow-up assessment is to monitor for any signs or symptoms of pulp necrosis or root resorption.
[2537][Para 002] Root canal treatment should only be initiated if there are two or more signs and/or symptoms of pulp necrosis.
[2538][Para 002] Because of the severance of the neurovascular tissues at the apex resulting from the dento-alveolar fracture, there is a high chance that a laterally luxated tooth will become necrotic and require root canal treatment in the future (Fig. 21.7). This must be clearly explained to the patient and the patient’s expectations managed and documented in the notes. As for all cases, any investigations, including radiography, should be justified, graded and fully reported on, and this communicated to the patient. If a patient understands and appreciates the consequences of the treatment offered with a two-way open dialogue between the patient and the oral healthcare team, misunderstandings and eventual litigation risk can be minimized.

[2555][Para 025] Case 22
[2556][Heading 1] Hypoglycaemia
[2557][Para 027] Barbara Carey, and Michael Escudier
[2558][Para 028] Summary
[2559][Para 029] A 55-year-old man collapses in your general dental surgery. What is the cause, and how would you manage this patient?
[2560][Para 014] History
[2561][Para 019] Problem
[2562][Para 001] At the end of the treatment session, the patient becomes sweaty and has a slight tremor of the extremities. He is unable to respond rationally to questions.
[2563][Para 012] Medical History
[2564][Para 001] Having rechecked the medical history before commencing treatment, you are aware that he has insulin-dependent diabetes. He has had diabetes mellitus for 40 years and is currently taking long-acting insulin 20 IU in the morning and 15 IU at night. In addition, he has peripheral vascular disease, resulting in intermittent claudication and angina, for which he takes glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) spray, when necessary.
[2565][Para 012] Dental History
[2566][Para 001] The patient has been a regular attendee for a number of years. On this occasion, he has an appointment for endodontic treatment during his lunch hour.
[2567][Heading 2]  What is the Likely Diagnosis?
[2568][Para 001] Hypoglycaemia.
[2569][Heading 2]  Why Was This Particular Patient with Diabetes At Risk for Hypoglycaemia?
[2570][Para 001] The patient has insulin-dependent diabetes. This type, or class, of diabetes usually results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. The patient requires exogenous insulin to control his blood glucose. Hypoglycaemia results if insulin or oral hypoglycaemic drug levels exceed physiological needs. Thus, hypoglycaemia is a consequence of drug therapy for diabetes, not the underlying disease process.
[2571][Heading 2]  What are the Underlying Events Leading To the Clinical Presentation?
[2572][Para 001] The patient took his insulin as normal. This has mobilized glucose from blood into tissues, reducing the blood glucose level. The patient must eat to replenish his blood glucose; otherwise, the level will continue to fall. The brain relies almost exclusively on glucose as fuel, and hypoglycaemia starves the brain and causes abnormal brain activity. This may present as cognitive impairment, behavioural changes, psychomotor abnormalities, and, at very low plasma glucose concentrations, seizure and coma.
[2573][Para 024]  What Would You Do Immediately?
[2574][Para 004] • Reassure the patient
[2575][Para 004] • Assess vital signs, blood pressure, pulse and respiratory rate.
[2576][Para 014] Examination
[2577][Para 001] The patient is conscious. However, he is becoming increasingly confused and restless and has tachycardia.
[2578][Heading 2]  What Other Symptoms and Signs Might You Expect?
[2579][Para 001] Autonomic symptoms may accompany hypoglycaemia as the body tries to mobilize glucose. The symptoms include tremor, palpitations, anxiety, arousal, sweating, hunger and paraesthesias. The patient may be tachycardic.
[2580][Para 002] Neuropathy and vascular disease are common complications of diabetes and may prevent signs of sympathetic activation being apparent until at a late stage. It is important not to waste time looking for other signs to confirm your diagnosis for the following reasons:
[2581][Para 004] • the condition can worsen quickly
[2582][Para 004] • the history of diabetes and presentation are diagnostic
[2583][Para 004] • treatment cannot cause any significant adverse effects – raising blood glucose in the short term is safe.
[2584][Para 015] Treatment
[2585][Heading 2]  What Treatment Would You Provide?
[2586][Para 001] Give a glucose drink (20 g of glucose) quickly because otherwise the patient may become unconscious in minutes. Alternatively, the equivalent amount of glucose gel, sugar lumps or a proprietary glucose drink may be used. Measure blood glucose levels by using glucose monitors (glucometers) or finger stick testing. The patient should return to a normal state rapidly (within about 5–10 minutes). If necessary, a glucose drink may be repeated in 10–15 minutes. The patient should then be given long-acting carbohydrate, such as two biscuits, a slice of bread or 200–300 ml milk.
[2587][Para 018] Table 22.1
[2588][Para 021] Causes, Symptoms and Signs of Hypoglycaemia
[2589][Para 017] Unfortunately, there is a delay finding and dissolving the glucose, and the patient lapses into unconsciousness before he is able to drink it.
[2590][Heading 2]  How May This Cause of Loss of Consciousness Be Distinguished From Other Similar Causes?
[2591][Para 032] See Table 22.1.
[2592][Heading 2]  What Treatment Would You Now Commence?
[2593][Para 001] Hypoglycaemia which causes unconsciousness is an emergency. In this situation, there are three options:
[2594][Para 020] Give 1 mg of glucagon intramuscularly
[2595][Para 001] This will mobilize glucose from the remaining stores of glycogen in the patient’s liver, sufficient for him to regain consciousness. It is not a definitive treatment, but a way of producing a conscious patient who can swallow oral glucose. Glucagon works for about 15 minutes and is easy and safe to administer. As soon as the patient is alert and able to swallow, oral glucose should be given. Without this further treatment, the patient will lapse back into a hypoglycaemic coma, and a second dose of glucagon will be ineffective because all the liver glycogen will have been metabolized. Glucagon may take 15 minutes to work and may be ineffective in undernourished patients and in severe liver disease.
[2596][Para 020] Or give 100 ml of 20% glucose intravenously
[2597][Para 001] This requires venous access. Care is required because this concentration is an irritant, especially if extravasation occurs. Glucose 10% infusion may also be used but larger volumes are needed.
[2598][Para 020] Or give 50 ml of 50% glucose intravenously
[2599][Para 001] This treatment is not recommended. Glucose 50% infusion is like thick syrup and very difficult to inject. It is also a very strong irritant, will irreversibly damage the vein into which it is injected and is associated with higher risk of extravasation injury.
[2600][Para 002] The presentations of drugs useful in the treatment of hypoglycaemia are shown in Fig. 22.1.
[2601][Para 024]  How Would You Proceed Once the Patient Has Recovered?
[2602][Para 004] • Abandon dental treatment
[2603][Para 004] • Monitor blood glucose
[2604][Para 004] • Continue to monitor the vital signs
[2605][Para 004] • Arrange transfer of the patient to an appropriate secondary care facility
[2606][Para 004] • Advise the patient of the need for formal review of his diabetic control
[2607][Para 004] • Establish the cause of the episode (e.g. missed meal, dosage error, increased exercise, alcohol excess, deliberate overdose).
[2608][Para 015] Other Possibilities
[2609][Heading 2]  Can This Happen To a Patient with Non–Insulin-Dependent Diabetes Mellitus?
[2610][Para 001] Yes. Non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM) is managed by diet control, oral hypoglycaemic drugs, insulin or a combination of these. Both oral hypoglycaemic drugs and insulin could potentiate hypoglycaemia if there is a relative deficiency of glucose, for instance, if the patient does not eat despite having taken the normal dose of medication. Patients with hypoglycaemia caused by an oral hypoglycaemic drug should be transferred to hospital because the hypoglycaemic effects of these drugs may persist for many hours.
[2611][Heading 2]  What Could Have Been Done To Minimize the Risk of Such an Event?
[2612][Para 001] The scheduling of the appointment should have taken account of the patient’s need for avoiding disturbances in the normal daily routine. Routine treatment under local anaesthesia should be undertaken at a time that allows for completion of the procedure and recovery before the next food intake is due. In this way, the possibility of a hypoglycaemic episode can be minimized. It is also advisable to avoid appointment times at the end of the day when medical assistance may be less readily available in the event of a complication. In general, morning appointments are advisable because endogenous cortisol levels are higher at this time. Ensure that the patient has eaten and taken his medication as usual.

[2624][Para 015] Further Points
[2625][Heading 2]  What are the Oral Complications of Diabetes?
[2626][Para 001] Oral complications of diabetes include:
[2627][Para 004] • Reduced resistance to infection. Infection requires effective treatment early
[2628][Para 004] • Increased severity of periodontal disease and susceptibility to periodontal abscess
[2629][Para 004] • Xerostomia may also be a problem and may further predispose the patient to oral candidosis
[2630][Para 004] • Sialadenosis (asymptomatic salivary gland swelling for hormonal, metabolic or nutritional reasons)
[2631][Para 004] • Oral hypoglycaemics may be associated with the development of lichenoid reactions
[2632][Para 004] • Oral burning and taste disturbances
[2633][Para 004] • Peripheral mononeuropathy in the oropharyngeal area is a very rare effect.
[2634][Para 025] Case 23
[2635][Heading 1] A Tooth Lost At Teatime
[2636][Para 027] Vinod Patel, and Alexander Crighton
[2637][Para 028] Summary
[2638][Para 029] A 78-year-old female patient lost a tooth while eating. What is the cause, and what will you do?
[2639][Para 218] 
[2640][Para 008] 
[2641][Para 011] Fig. 23.1 The patient on presentation.
[2642][Para 009]  
[2643][Para 014] History
[2644][Para 019] Complaint
[2645][Para 007] The patient reports that one of her front lower teeth had become loose recently. The tooth simply fell out yesterday when she was eating a biscuit. There was no pain before, during or after losing the tooth.
[2646][Para 012] History of Complaint
[2647][Para 007] This woman has attended your practice for many years and has a well-cared-for mouth, a low caries rate and minimal periodontal disease. She is concerned that a healthy tooth has come out so easily and also that she has had no pain or bleeding from the area since.
[2648][Para 012] Medical History
[2649][Para 007] Five years ago, the patient fractured her arm in a fall, and a diagnosis of osteoporosis was made at that time. She takes calcium supplements daily and alendronate (Fosamax) weekly.
[2650][Para 014] Examination
[2651][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[2652][Para 007] Oddly, there is no lymphadenopathy, no tenderness to palpation over any area of the facial skeleton and no obvious halitosis.
[2653][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[2654][Para 007] The patient is partially dentate and wears dentures. Her mucosa is normal, the mouth is not dry, there is no active caries and no pocket depths exceed 3 mm.
[2655][Para 017] There is an area of exposed bone in the anterior mandibular alveolus and a socket from which a lower incisor has been lost, as shown in  Fig. 23.1 . The adjacent teeth in the exposed bone are mobile in their sockets and are also in danger of spontaneous exfoliation. The attached gingiva in the region is missing and the buccal soft tissue margin of the lesion is lax and can be lifted to allow a dental probe to be inserted down almost to the patient’s chin. No pus is present.
[2656][Heading 2]  How Do You Interpret the Findings So Far?
[2657][Para 001] The lack of bleeding and sensitivity suggest necrotic bone and nonvital teeth. Despite bacterial plaque and debris accumulating on the exposed bone, there seems to be no infection, even though there is a deep soft tissue pocket extending to the chin. The surrounding mucosa is hardly inflamed, suggesting that local trauma and infection are not responsible.
[2658][Para 002] The appearances are very characteristic, and it is possible to make a fairly confident diagnosis without any further investigations.
[2659][Para 015] Diagnosis
[2660][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[2661][Para 001] Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaws (MRONJ) is almost certainly the diagnosis on the basis of asymptomatic necrosis of bone without pain. The patient has taken alendronate, a bisphosphonate drug, for several years, and this is a recognized complication.
[2662][Heading 2]  What Alternative Diagnoses Have You Excluded, and Why?
[2663][Para 001] Chronic osteomyelitis would seem a possibility, but the presentation is not correct for this diagnosis. Relatively mild pain or discomfort would probably be present, as would bad taste, discharge of pus indicating infection and possibly sequestration of nonvital bone. There would also normally be both a cause and a predisposing factor. If dental infection were the cause, it would be evident clinically or radiographically, or there might be a history of trauma such as a fracture or dental extraction. Patients who develop osteomyelitis usually have some systemic predisposing condition such as diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression. It seems that this option is most unlikely, although a radiograph would help exclude or confirm it by the presence of periosteal reaction and new bone formation.
[2664][Para 002] Acute osteomyelitis is even less likely. Acute infection would be accompanied by the cardinal signs of inflammation, including pain, erythema and swelling. There is severe, deep, boring pain in acute osteomyelitis, with systemic signs of infection.
[2665][Para 002] Necrotizing periodontitis could cause necrosis of soft tissue and exposed bone but would be associated with other signs and symptoms. It is almost exclusively found in severe immunosuppression, usually in late or untreated human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Necrotizing periodontitis is usually painful and limited to the gingiva and alveolar margin. It would not cause extensive soft tissue separation from bone, as here.
[2666][Para 002] Cancrum oris (noma) is a necrotizing mixed bacterial infection that sometimes develops from acute ulcerative gingivitis. It causes tissue necrosis of large parts of the face or other tissues, including bone. The disease is almost confined to malnourished and debilitated children younger than 8 years of age in developing countries.
[2667][Heading 2]  What is the Difference Among Osteomyelitis, Osteitis and Osteonecrosis?
[2668][Para 001] Osteomyelitis is an infection in the medullary cavity of bone. It is usually bacterial. The resulting increased pressure in the medullary space and the inflammatory reaction devitalize bone marrow by compressing its blood supply and parts of the bone undergo necrosis. After an acute and intensely painful phase, pus drains, and osteoclasts separate the necrotic bone to form sequestra. If the sequestra can be shed, the bone may heal. If not, infection persists in the sequestrum and is difficult to treat, the disease becomes chronic and the surrounding bone becomes sclerotic.
[2669][Para 002] Osteitis is a superficial inflammation of bone, such as is seen in the exposed bone of dry socket (see Case 15). Small sequestra may form but infection does not penetrate into or spread within the medullary cavity.
[2670][Para 002] Osteonecrosis refers to death of bone. The cause is related to bone-modulating medications such as bisphosphonates or denosumab. The necrotic bone is sterile, at least initially, and only becomes colonized by bacteria once exposed to the exterior. Osteonecrosis can follow irradiation of bone because this induces endarteritis, which is narrowing of blood vessels with eventual necrosis. Osteonecrosis is increasingly recognized in patients taking bisphosphonate drugs for the prevention or treatment of osteoporosis, management of bone metastasis in cancer or treatment of metabolic bone diseases.
[2671][Heading 2]  What are Bisphosphonate Drugs, and Why are They Used?
[2672][Para 001] Bisphosphonate drugs reduce bone turnover. The drugs are adsorbed onto bone surfaces, where they remain bound for a prolonged period. They are taken up by osteoclasts at the sites of bone resorption and interfere with adenosine triphosphate (ATP) metabolism or membrane function. Osteoclasts either die or become unable to resorb bone. Bone formation then exceeds bone resorption, remodelling is slowed and bone density increases or stabilizes.
[2673][Para 002] These drugs have a variety of uses:
[2674][Para 004] • To prevent further bone loss in osteoporosis
[2675][Para 004] • To prevent malignant tumours in bone releasing excess calcium into the bloodstream
[2676][Para 004] • To prevent bony metastases from enlarging by inhibiting bone resorption around them
[2677][Para 004] • To reduce bone turnover in Paget’s disease of bone
[2678][Para 004] • To increase bone mass in osteogenesis imperfecta.
[2679][Para 030]  Are All Bones Affected Equally?
[2680][Para 001] No, the effects are systemic but the effects are much more pronounced in the mandible and the maxilla. The reasons for this are not clear, but these sites may be subjected to higher drug levels because of their good blood supply. They are also close to the surface such that the bone is readily exposed. Bisphosphonate-induced osteonecrosis affects the mandible twice as often as the maxilla but is almost never seen in other bones.
[2681][Heading 2]  Are There Other Prescribed Drugs Implicated in Osteonecrosis of the Jaw?
[2682][Para 001] Yes. Bisphosphonates were essentially the first group of drugs in which this complication was regularly seen. Since then, a host of novel drugs (Table 23.3) have been implicated in MRONJ. These medications are divided into two broad categories:
[2683][Para 004] • Bone-modulating drugs
[2684][Para 004] • Antiangiogenic drugs
[2685][Para 002] Bisphosphonates fall under the bone-modulating drug category, as does denosumab, a human monoclonal antibody. This novel drug is given subcutaneously for almost the same indications as those for bisphosphonates. The risk of osteonecrosis is the same as intravenous bisphosphonates when given on a monthly basis for treating malignant disease. For osteoporosis, the medication is prescribed as a 6-monthly dose; by 6 months, the drug effect is eliminated, allowing the bone physiology to return to its previous state, hence the need for repeat injections. This drug characteristically provides an ideal opportunity to provide any dental extractions required, await healing and then recommence the medication with little impact on the patient’s osteoporosis and very low risk of osteonecrosis. Such an approach would require communication and planning with the medical prescriber. Dental care remains the same after medication or if osteonecrosis develops, as discussed for bisphosphonates.
[2686][Para 002] A host of novel oncology medications termed ‘antiangiogenics’ has been introduced. The aim of these drugs is to starve solid tumours of blood supply, on which they are reliant for growth. Restricting the blood supply leads to either lack of further growth or even reduction in tumour size. Medications can be either oral or intravenous, and both types subsequently have a systemic effect, hence it’s antiangiogenic effect in the oral cavity can lead to MRONJ. When these drugs are taken solely, the risk of osteonecrosis is less than 1%; however, in metastatic malignant disease, they are often combined with either bisphosphonates or denosumab. This heightens the risk, with some reports showing an osteonecrosis risk as high as 14%. Dose and duration play a key role and need to be considered carefully to determine relevant risk.
[2687][Heading 2]  Why Does the Tissue Undergo Necrosis?
[2688][Para 001] The drugs interfere with inter- and intracellular signalling and inhibit the growth of new blood vessels. The tissue of bone marrow becomes avascular and dies. Bone also becomes depleted of both osteoclasts and osteoblasts because the two cell populations are interdependent. Osteocytes are not replaced by maturing osteoblasts and eventually die. Both bone and soft tissue undergo slow necrosis without symptoms.
[2689][Para 002] As the overlying mucosa partly relies on blood supply from bone and periosteum, it may also undergo necrosis. This is most commonly seen in areas where the mucosa is very thin, typically over the mandibular tori and on the posterior lingual aspect of the mandible where there are few muscle attachments.
[2690][Heading 2]  What is the Risk of Developing Osteonecrosis?
[2691][Para 001] The risk depends on the total dose of the drug administered, which is a function of it’s dose, frequency and duration of administration.
[2692][Para 002] The many different bisphosphonate drugs have varying potencies, as shown in Table 23.1. Non-nitrogenous drugs cause osteoclast death, and nitrogenous drugs inhibit osteoclast function. The more potent drugs are much more likely to cause MRONJ. This is especially so when the drug is given in high doses intravenously, as for metastatic malignancy.
[2693][Para 002] The proportion of patients who are taking bisphosphonates and are affected by osteonecrosis is estimated to be only 0.05%. However, the number of patients being prescribed these medications is increasing with an ageing population and improving survival rates in cancer. Oncology patients are often prescribed the more potent intravenous formulations and hence face a larger risk of osteonecrosis, whereas patients with osteoporosis are routinely prescribed the oral formulation. It is estimated that 4 years of oral administration is required before there is a significant risk of osteonecrosis, whereas the risk becomes significant after 4 months of intravenous administration. In clinical practice, the potency of the drug is not the overriding factor because lower-potency drugs may be administered in larger amounts over longer periods. The total dose administered is the key risk factor.

[2695][Para 021] Bisphosphonate Drugs and Their Relative Potency
[2696][Para 015] Investigations
[2697][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Perform?
[2698][Para 001] Investigations are not helpful in diagnosis but may provide useful information for treatment. The vitality of the teeth in and around the exposed area of bone must be determined.
[2699][Para 002] Obtaining radiographs of the area might seem the logical next step. However, you will find that on the radiographs, mandibular bone appears completely normal. This is because osteonecrosis is caused by loss of viable marrow. The disease does not alter the mineralized component that is responsible for the appearance of the radiographic image. This is very different from chronic osteomyelitis, in which there is patchy radiolucency and sclerosis, with separation of sequestra.
[2700][Para 002] There is no completely satisfactory method for showing the areas of bone that are dead in a patient with osteonecrosis. This is unfortunate because it would be useful to know the extent of necrosis in case extraction or surgery is required in other parts of the jaw.
[2701][Heading 2]  Can More Specialized Investigations Help?
[2702][Para 001] Radioisotope scanning measures bone turnover and should show lack of uptake in osteonecrotic bone, but image resolution is too poor to be useful.
[2703][Para 002] Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is probably the most useful modality, but it is expensive and only available in hospitals. Different types of MRI images define vascularity and fat content. MRI shows clearly the loss of bone marrow in affected areas, as shown in Fig. 23.2, where the normal marrow has a high signal (bright) and the affected marrow appears dark. This is currently the best method to identify the extent of osteonecrosis, but it is only useful in the mandible because the maxilla has little medullary space.
[2704][Para 002] It has been suggested that serum levels of C-terminal telopeptide of type 1 collagen (CTX-1), a bone turnover marker, reflect bone suppression by bisphosphonates. This small peptide is released into serum when collagen in bone is resorbed. It provides an indication of bone turnover in the body as a whole, but whether this is a useful reflection of the risk of osteonecrosis in the jaws remains unclear. The currently proposed risk values are shown in Table 23.2, but even a high value cannot guarantee that an extraction is completely without risk.

[2709][Para 017] You decide that no investigations are likely to be useful at this stage. You find that the teeth in the exposed bone do not respond to any tests of vitality. The adjacent teeth give an equivocal result.
[2710][Para 015] Treatment
[2711][Heading 2]  What Will You Do for the Teeth in the Exposed Bone?
[2712][Para 001] The teeth each side of the socket are pain free but mobile. They are best extracted before problems develop and for proper cleaning of the area. If the teeth were firm, they might be left in situ but would probably cause problems in the future. It is not clear whether the teeth in osteonecrotic bone retain their own independent blood supply. If they do not respond to any tests of vitality, the prognosis is likely to be poor.
[2713][Heading 2]  What Should Be Done for the Exposed Bone?
[2714][Para 001] Once the teeth are removed, the patient should be instructed to keep the mucosa and exposed bone as clean as possible by using simple oral hygiene measures and topical chlorhexidine, as needed. Any prominent bone or sharp edges can be trimmed and removed without local anaesthesia. This should prevent trauma to the oral soft tissues and make the area easier to clean (Fig. 23.3).
[2715][Para 002] The aim of treatment in MRONJ is very different from that in osteomyelitis or osteoradionecrosis. In these latter conditions, necrotic bone is limited in extent, and its removal exposes healthy, vital bone, which can heal well. In bisphosphonate osteonecrosis, the area of bone involved is very extensive, cannot be removed and is not surrounded by healthy bone. The MRI scan of this patient (see Fig. 23.2) suggests that the entire anterior area and one body of the mandible are involved. Trimming back bone and attempting closure of soft tissue surgically usually result in wound breakdown.
[2716][Para 218] 
[2717][Para 008] 
[2718][Para 011] Fig. 23.3 The patient after extractions and debridement.

[2723][Heading 2]  Will the Exposed Bone Get Infected?
[2724][Para 001] Infection can develop but is surprisingly infrequent. The bone will have been colonized by the oral flora as soon as it was exposed, but this is contamination rather than infection. Bone is not invaded by bacteria, and there is no host response in the avascular tissue, no inflammation and no immune response.
[2725][Para 002] Simple cleaning and topical antiseptics are the most effective methods of keeping the flora at bay. Antibiotics are ineffective. Drugs cannot enter bone because it lacks blood supply.
[2726][Para 002] Sometimes, a more aggressive infection will develop in the soft tissues at the margins of the wound, and this must be treated according to conventional principles. A microbiological sample should be taken for culture and sensitivity before commencing empirical antibiotic therapy. In most cases, metronidazole is an appropriate choice, but this can be supplemented by amoxicillin, if needed. In low-grade infection, doxycycline works well and can be used for a longer period compared with metronidazole and amoxicillin.
[2727][Para 002] Very rarely, there is extensive sequestration of bone and aggressive perilesional infection, as shown in Fig. 23.4. Open surgical debridement is then required, and antibiotics may need to be given intravenously. Debridement in such cases may aim to reduce the sharp and loose edges and bony sequestrum rather than achieving complete healing.
[2728][Heading 2]  What Would You Do if the Site Became Painful?
[2729][Para 001] Sensing pain requires an intact nerve and blood supply. Bone is insensitive, and any pain must arise from the mucosa. Significant infection must be suspected and excluded, but the cause is usually a local problem with tissue hygiene, and it can be managed with simple cleaning and application of topical antiseptics.
[2730][Para 218] 
[2731][Para 008] 
[2732][Para 011] Fig. 23.4 A different patient who has developed extensive infection in the soft tissues surrounding a zone of maxillary osteonecrosis.
[2733][Para 009]  
[2734][Heading 2]  Will the Bone Ever Heal? Should the Bisphosphonate Be Stopped?
[2735][Para 001] The continuation of the bisphosphonate drug must be reviewed with the patient’s medical practitioner or specialist clinician. When the drug is given for malignant disease, it may not be possible to stop it without risking major adverse effects.
[2736][Para 002] If the bisphosphonate can be withdrawn, the bone will gradually recover with no intervention other than cleaning. This recovery is very slow, and it may take many months to see an improvement. However in 1–2 years, most lesions will show significant improvement. Detached periosteum will reattach, and the mucosa will grow to cover the revascularizing bone. Fig. 23.5 shows regrowth of the mucosa to cover the exposed bone around a defect in the maxilla. An oroantral fistula remains, but the bone is now protected from infection.
[2737][Para 002] Those patients who continue to need medication may be switched to an alternative drug such as raloxifene or teriparatide, which do not seem to cause osteonecrosis. However, these medicines have potentially serious side effects and must only be prescribed by a medical specialist.
[2738][Heading 2]  Is Dental Treatment Safe in a Patient On a Bisphosphonate Drug?
[2739][Para 001] The risk is best avoided by instituting an effective preventive regimen for caries and periodontitis. An enhanced programme of oral hygiene improvement, dietary instruction and topical fluoride preparations would be appropriate for all patients on bisphosphonates.
[2740][Para 218] 
[2741][Para 008] 
[2742][Para 011] Fig. 23.5 A different patient with resolving osteonecrosis.
[2743][Para 009]  
[2744][Para 002] The safe period of 4 years after starting oral bisphosphonates and 4 months after starting an intravenous regimen gives a window of opportunity to deal with any sepsis or teeth with a dubious prognosis and to initiate prevention.
[2745][Para 002] Routine restorative dentistry can be performed without problems. It may be a sensible precaution to use a local anaesthetic without, or at a reduced amount of, a vasoconstrictor for infiltration anaesthesia, but this is not based on any sound evidence. Oral surgery and dental implants are best avoided if the patient has been taking bisphosphonates for a prolonged period.
[2746][Heading 2]  What Do You Do if a Tooth Needs Extraction in a Patient At Risk?
[2747][Para 001] Most patients will have no problems after an uncomplicated extraction. Complications are reported to develop in less than 1% of patients. It is important to discuss the risk with patients before starting treatment and give them a risk information leaflet (see further guidance at the end of this chapter). Extractions should be performed as atraumatically as possible and flap surgery avoided. No exposed bone should be seen at 8 weeks after the extraction. If bone is still visible at that time, the patient should be referred for assessment by a local dental specialist in osteonecrosis management.
[2748][Para 002] Every effort should be made to avoid extraction by root filling teeth and retaining decoronated roots in a similar fashion to overdenture abutments. Temporarily withdrawing bisphosphonate drugs for a period before and after the extraction (a ‘drug holiday’) is not thought to reduce the risk of bone necrosis because of their long activity. In contrast, in patients receiving denosumab, performing an elective extraction in the month prior to the next drug dose will likely reduce the risk of osteonecrosis because the drug’s activity will be at its lowest. All patients taking bisphosphonates should be expected to have slowly healing extraction sockets, even when no osteonecrosis develops.
[2749][Heading 2]  Could I Be Considered Negligent if Osteonecrosis Develops?
[2750][Para 001] No, provided the risk has been identified and managed appropriately and the patient has been informed of the risks and has given consent for the extraction. Good record keeping will provide evidence of this.
[2751][Para 002] Dental extractions or surgery appear to be a precipitating factor in one-third to one-half of cases. However, this is a complication of drug treatment, not of dental surgery. The bone may well have been necrotic without symptoms for some time; dental extraction simply unmasks the process by exposing the bone. Many patients develop spontaneous lesions without any dental interventions.
[2752][Heading 2]  Should Antibiotic Prophylaxis Be Given for Extractions in Patients Taking Bisphosphonates?
[2753][Para 001] No. The disease is not caused by bacteria, and drugs do not penetrate bone because it has no blood supply. Use of antibiotics risks adverse effects and microbial resistance for no benefit. Similarly, chlorhexidine mouthrinse will not prevent problems with the bone, although it may help keep the soft tissues disease-free during the healing process which may sometimes be slow. However, some patients taking bisphosphonates may also be taking other medications such as immunosuppressants (e.g. methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, corticosteroids). These medications place patients at a small increased risk of postsurgical infection. Hence, on the basis of individual clinical judgement, antibiotics may be prescribed, but this should not be done solely because patients are taking bisphosphonates. Furthermore, the addition of immunosuppressants for patients taking bisphosphonates increases the risk of osteonecrosis but for those taking oral bisphosphonates the risk still remains less than 1%. Both immunosuppressants and bisphosphonates will lead to slower healing, and this should be expected.

[2761][Para 025] Case 24
[2762][Heading 1] A Problem Overdenture
[2763][Para 027] Jonathan Turner, and David R. Radford
[2764][Para 028] Summary
[2765][Para 029] A 67-year-old lady is referred to your general dental practice with a complaint that her denture has never ‘seemed right’ from the day it was fitted.
[2766][Para 014] History
[2767][Para 019] Complaint
[2768][Para 007] The patient complains that a small filling has recently been lost from one of the upper canine roots below her overdenture. However, it quickly becomes clear that this has caused no symptoms (the tooth has been root treated) and that she is dissatisfied primarily with her upper complete overdenture. She can wear the denture in the morning, but by about 3 o’clock in the afternoon, it becomes too uncomfortable, and if she is at home, she likes to take it out.
[2769][Para 012] History of Complaint
[2770][Para 007] The patient successfully wore an acrylic upper partial denture until 6 months ago, but failure of restorations and root treatments led to loss of several upper teeth. She was provided with an upper overdenture on the two retained upper canine roots. The denture was fitted 3 months ago, reviewed on four occasions and minor adjustments made to the base extension. The patient is happy with the retention and fit of the denture. It does not move during eating. She reports no problems with her lower teeth.
[2771][Para 012] Medical History
[2772][Para 007] The patient is taking low-dose aspirin (75 mg/day) following a myocardial infarction and a statin for high serum cholesterol.
[2773][Para 014] Examination
[2774][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[2775][Para 007] There is no lymphadenopathy. The temporomandibular joint is free of crepitus and clicks, and no muscle tenderness can be elicited in the muscles of mastication. With the denture in place, there is no facial asymmetry. You notice that the patient has a slightly open lip posture when she is seated in the dental chair.
[2776][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[2777][Para 007] The patient has a well-developed upper alveolar ridge with limited resorption, consistent with the relatively recent loss of several upper teeth. There is slight redness of the palate under the denture-bearing area, but the ridge is not tender on palpation at any site, and there is no bleeding on probing around the canine roots and no detectable sinus. One of the root-treated canine teeth has lost a small restoration from the access cavity. The remainder of the oral mucosa is normal.
[2778][Para 017] There is an almost complete lower arch of natural teeth. These are adequately restored, many with large amalgam restorations, and there is no caries. The occlusal plane is relatively even. There has been slight mesial tipping of the lower second molars as a result of loss of both first molars.
[2779][Para 017] The denture appears clean and without obvious defects, and there is a definite post dam along its posterior margin.
[2780][Heading 2]  On the Basis of What You Know So Far, What are the Likely Diagnoses, and Why?
[2781][Para 001] The patient has successfully worn a denture and the transition to an overdenture from an upper acrylic partial denture should have been relatively straightforward. It might have been more difficult if the previous denture had been metal based. If the patient has persevered for 3 months without success, she almost certainly has a valid complaint.
[2782][Para 002] There appears to be no problem of displacement of the denture during eating, speaking or other facial movements. This makes it unlikely that the overdenture is poorly adapted or overextended or that the teeth lie outside the neutral zone. Occlusal discrepancies of some kind would appear to be the most likely cause, and the vagueness of the complaint – predominantly inability to tolerate the denture – is consistent with an occlusal problem. A further reason to suspect an occlusal problem is the difficulty arising from a complete upper denture occluding against a lower natural arch.
[2783][Para 002] It must also be borne in mind that some denture patients are particularly conscious of appearance and the construction of dentures that satisfy the expectations of such patients can be very challenging. Sometimes, a mismatch between the denture appearance and desired facial self-image may manifest as dislike of the denture or complaints about relatively minor features. There is always a potential cosmetic problem of an overcontoured labial flange when canine roots support an upper overdenture because the roots preserve the labial aspect of the alveolar bone.
[2784][Para 018] Table 24.1
[2785][Para 021] Examination of the Denture
[2786][Heading 2]  What Specific Features of the Dentures Would You Examine, and How?
[2787][Para 001] All features of the denture should be reviewed (Table 24.1). Denture complaints may have multifactorial causes, and only by examining all features can an accurate diagnosis be made.
[2788][Para 017] Having examined the patient, you find that the denture is correctly extended, stable and retentive. The denture was not displaced on lateral excursion. This leaves the vertical dimension as the most likely cause of an occlusal problem.
[2789][Heading 2]  What Methods Can Be Used To Assess Vertical Dimension? What are Their Problems?
[2790][Para 001] Initially, it is most straightforward to simply observe the vertical dimension with the denture removed (Fig. 24.1) and in place (Fig. 24.2).
[2791][Para 002] Note the open lip posture (see Fig. 24.2) when the denture is inserted. This is an important indicator that there may be an error in vertical height, and a more accurate assessment must be made.
[2792][Para 218] 
[2793][Para 008] 
[2794][Para 011] Fig. 24.1 Rest vertical dimension with the upper prosthesis removed.
[2795][Para 009]  
[2796][Para 008] 
[2797][Para 011] Fig. 24.2 Vertical dimension with the upper overdenture in place.
[2798][Para 009]  
[2799][Para 002] There are three common methods that might be used, the first two of which are essentially similar and have some of the same problems. These both measure the lower facial height at rest and with the dentures in occlusion. The rest value should be greater than the value with dentures in occlusion. The difference between these measurements, with the occlusal vertical dimension subtracted from rest vertical dimension, is the value of the freeway space. The head must be in a natural vertical position supported by the neck muscles. A fixed support such as a head rest can alter the freeway space. In most instances, these methods are satisfactory and readily applied, but sometimes, it may be appropriate to use all three methods to establish the correct vertical dimension.
[2800][Para 020] Dividers/Calipers Method
[2801][Para 001] Marks or adhesive markers are placed on the chin and nose and their distance apart is measured with calipers or dividers. One problem is that the markers are fixed to the skin and may move through muscle activity, particularly pursing of the lips. All suitable sites on the skin may move to some degree, so it is necessary to ensure that the patient remains relaxed during the procedure.
[2802][Para 002] This method is shown in Figs 24.1 and 24.2. The calipers are set to the resting face height (see Fig. 24.1). When the denture is inserted (see Fig. 24.2) the increase in vertical dimension is clearly seen and is about 3–4 mm. The patient, thus, has a negative value for freeway space.
[2803][Para 020] Willis Bite Gauge
[2804][Para 001] This measures lower face height from the lower border of the nose to the lower border of the mandible. It is important to use the same pressure when recording rest and occlusal height, otherwise compression of the tissues will affect the reading. More importantly, the instrument has to be used at a consistent angle at the base of the nose. This is particularly difficult when making complete dentures against lower standing teeth because removing the upper denture to record rest height removes the denture support of the upper lip, which is used as a landmark.
[2805][Para 020] Closest Speaking Space Method
[2806][Para 001] This method provides a rough estimate of the presence of a freeway space but does not involve direct measurement. The patient is asked to say words that include prominent ‘ss’ sounds, such as ‘Mississippi’ and ‘Tuesday’. These sounds are more difficult to make in the absence of freeway space. Unfortunately, patients adapt their speech to both increased and decreased occlusal heights, and this method can only be considered an adjunct to the more accurate methods above.
[2807][Heading 2]  How Large Should the Freeway Space Be?
[2808][Para 001] This depends on the patient. The average freeway space is 2–4 mm measured in the premolar region, and dentures may be constructed to this dimension for most patients. However, there are some circumstances in which this clearance needs to be increased. Some patients become habituated to an increased freeway space, either because of wearing of artificial teeth or because of faulty denture construction. In some cases, the freeway space may exceed 1 cm, and it would be unreasonable to expect such patients to accommodate rapidly to the normal freeway space. Provided the increased freeway space is not associated with any problems, a compromise increased freeway space is appropriate.
[2809][Para 015] Diagnosis
[2810][Para 024]  What is Your Diagnosis, and Why is This the Most Likely Possibility?
[2811][Para 020] Error in Occlusal Vertical Dimension
[2812][Para 001] There is clearly an increased occlusal vertical dimension, based on the measurements described above, and this is beyond the tolerance level of most patients. This fault is frequently associated with a history of being able to cope with the denture for a few hours and then having to remove the prosthesis. The open lip posture is also often associated with an increased occlusal vertical dimension. Some patients naturally have an open lip posture, so this sign is only an indication of potential problems. Until the fault is corrected, it is not really possible to consider any alternative explanation.
[2813][Para 024]  What Possible Diagnoses Have You Excluded? Explain Why for Each Possibility
[2814][Para 020] Error in Retruded Position
[2815][Para 001] Dentures with this fault produce pain on the ridge and pain on eating. If this were suspected, it would be necessary to take a precontact occlusal check record and to remount the dentures on an articulator to make a definitive diagnosis. Adjustment of the occlusion to the correct record should cure the symptoms, and this will confirm the cause. This possible error needs to be kept in mind in all such cases. If the occlusion is ignored and the denture base adjusted, the area of soreness will move to another area with each adjustment, progressively destroying the fit surface of the denture.
[2816][Para 020] Difficulty Becoming Accustomed To Acrylic Palatal Coverage
[2817][Para 001] Patients normally become accustomed to a new denture design in 3 months, even when there is a change to acrylic palatal coverage. In the very elderly or in those who have worn dentures for many years, this period may need to be extended, and a few patients need training bases or simple acrylic partial dentures before definitive complete dentures or overdentures. However, no patient should be expected to become accustomed to a denture with an increased vertical dimension.
[2818][Para 020] Denture-Related Stomatitis
[2819][Para 001] Redness of the denture-bearing area almost certainly indicates denture stomatitis (chronic atrophic candidosis). However, this condition is asymptomatic and not normally noticed by patients.
[2820][Para 020] Patient’s Expectation of Appearance Has Not Been Met
[2821][Para 001] Both men and women may be embarrassed to admit that their dentures do not fulfil their cosmetic expectations. This may not just be the fault of the denture but also result from patients seeking to recapture their youthful appear ance. Although this may not be unreasonable, it may be physically impossible. Sometimes, hurtful comments from relatives, friends or acquaintances may change the patient’s opinion about an otherwise satisfactory denture. This problem may be expressed as repeated minor complaints that do not make sense clinically or, as in this case, a dislike or complete rejection of the denture. This problem can only be diagnosed through careful and considerate questioning.
[2822][Para 002] In the present case, this possible diagnosis is unlikely, given that there is a fault in the vertical dimension and the patient appears happy with the appearance of the denture.
[2823][Para 020] Miscellaneous and Other Unusual Complaints
[2824][Para 001] These include complaints of irritation from a high residual monomer content in an incorrectly processed denture base or, very rarely, hypersensitivity to acrylic. In both cases, the denture-bearing area, and sometimes the whole mouth, would be sore. This patient has inflammation of the denture-bearing area, but this is much more likely to be related to denture plaque or perhaps candidal infection, and these should be excluded before considering the alternative causes. Another complaint, sometimes unfairly ascribed to dentures, is mucosal burning in an otherwise healthy mouth. This is usually psychogenic and associated with depression. Nothing in the history of this patient suggests this diagnosis.
[2825][Heading 2]  How Would You Manage the Case?
[2826][Para 001] Replace the missing restoration in the canine root to prevent caries.
[2827][Para 002] To solve the denture problem, the denture must be remade with an appropriate freeway space, but the denture stomatitis must first be treated to improve support for the new prosthesis. Treatment will involve improving denture hygiene, ceasing night wear, if appropriate. The possibility of an underlying condition predisposing to candidosis should be considered, especially if the infection involves other parts of the mouth or lips or if treatment fails despite good denture hygiene. In this case, referral to the patient’s general practitioner would be indicated for further investigations. Fortunately, denture provision is a less litigious situation; if the patient were unhappy with the denture, a wise practitioner would return the fee because the treatment is reversible, and the patient could find another practitioner or be referred to one who may be more successful.

[2872][Heading 2]  You Now Have Sufficient Information To Decide Whether or Not the Third Molars Should Be Removed. What are the Indications for Removal?
[2873][Para 001] There has been much debate about the indications for the removal of third molars, and those for the removal of asymptomatic third molars are particularly contentious. Mandibular impacted third molars (MITMs) are very common, affecting approximately 75% of 20- to 30-year-old patients. Surgery is unpleasant, carries risks and is expensive to the state and the patient; thus, following current UK guidance (National Institute of Clinical Excellence [NICE] 2000) is essential unless there is high risk of distal caries developing in the second mandibular molars. Current UK guidance is now somewhat dated and is being revised at the time of this writing.
[2874][Para 002] The suggested indications for removal are:
[2875][Para 004] • Recurrent pericoronitis and pericoronitis with acute spreading infection
[2876][Para 004] • Unrestorable caries of MITM or adjacent teeth
[2877][Para 004] • Untreatable periapical inflammation
[2878][Para 004] • Periodontal disease associated with the MITM or adjacent teeth
[2879][Para 004] • Internal or external resorption of MITM or adjacent teeth
[2880][Para 004] • MITM in fracture line
[2881][Para 004] • Associated cysts or neoplasm
[2882][Para 004] • For tooth reimplantation
[2883][Para 004] • For orthognathic surgery or restorative treatment
[2884][Para 004] • Prophylactic removal may be advised in specific medical conditions (before radiotherapy, cardiothoracic surgery or bisphosphonate treatment).
[2885][Para 030]  Should This Patient’s Teeth Be Removed, and Why?
[2886][Para 001] Yes, he has suffered two episodes of pericoronitis. There is increasing risk of future episodes as the number of episodes rises, and they are likely to become more frequent and more severe.
[2887][Heading 2]  How Will You Decide Whether Extraction of This Patient’s Third Molars is Within Your Ability?
[2888][Para 001] This is a matter of judgement. You must judge your own ability and experience against the likely difficulty and also consider your ability to manage any complications. In general, the following factors should be considered. The most important of these factors may be remembered by using the mnemonic WHARFE:
[2889][Para 038] W Angulation using Winter’s lines
[2890][Para 038] H Height of mandible
[2891][Para 038] A Angle of second molar
[2892][Para 038] R Root form and development
[2893][Para 038] F Size of Follicular sac
[2894][Para 038] E Exit path of tooth to be extracted
[2895][Para 002] Factors to be considered in assessing the difficulty of extraction are listed in Table 25.3.
[2896][Heading 2]  What are ‘Winter’s Lines’, and How Might They Help Assess Difficulty?
[2897][Para 001] To apply Winter’s lines, three imaginary lines are drawn on the radiographic image (Fig. 25.3). For descriptive purposes, the lines are assigned colours. The white line runs along the occlusal plane, and the amber line runs along the upper bone surface through the interdental bone crests and along the bone surface behind the third molar (not up the external oblique ridge). The red line passes vertically, at right angles to the white line, to the application point for an elevator. In mesio-angular impactions, the point of elevation lies at the mesial end of the amelo-cemental junction, and for disto-angular impactions, it lies at the distal end of the amelo-cemental junction.
[2898][Para 018] Table 25.3
[2899][Para 021] Factors Contributing To the Difficulty of Extraction
[2900][Para 218] 
[2901][Para 008] 
[2902][Para 011] Fig. 25.3 Example of the application of Winter’s lines.
[2903][Para 009]  
[2904][Para 002] The angle of impaction is judged against the white line. The amber line gives an indication of the amount of tooth that will be visible when the periosteal flap is raised and the amount of bone removal required over the crown. The red line gives an indication of the depth of bone removal required to gain a point of application for an elevator. If the red line is greater than 5 mm in length the extraction is likely to merit the use of general anaesthesia. If it is greater than 9 mm in length, it is likely that extensive bone removal will be required.
[2905][Heading 2]  What are the Deficiencies of the Winter’s Lines Technique?
[2906][Para 001] Winter’s lines are useful for mesio-angular impactions, but the length of the red line is almost meaningless in disto-angular impactions, which are always relatively difficult. The technique also ignores the possibility of sectioning the tooth which makes the extraction easier, changing the point of application of elevators and the path of removal. Winter’s lines should be applied to a periapical radiograph, preferably a geometrically accurate projection obtained by using a paralleling technique. The method can be used on oblique laterals or panoramic tomographs, but it provides a less accurate estimate of difficulty. In addition, a correction must be made for magnification in the panoral film, which ranges from ×1.2 to ×1.4, depending on the equipment used. Winter’s lines would not provide useful information in the present case, but they do provide a way of systematically examining a radiograph to ensure that no information is missed.
[2907][Heading 2]  How Difficult are This Patient’s Extractions Likely To Be?
[2908][Para 001] Both lower third molars are slightly disto-angularly inclined and the external oblique ridge overlies them. Although not very deeply placed, these are moderately difficult to extract. Extraction should not be attempted under local anaesthesia or sedation by anyone other than an experienced or specialized surgeon, regardless of the care setting.
[2909][Para 002] The majority of lower third molars which meet the criteria for extraction will be relatively difficult. This is because the commonest indication is pericoronitis, which affects mostly vertically and disto-angularly impacted teeth.
[2910][Para 002] Prior to surgery, you must warn the patient about the complications of removal. List the possible complications, and give an indication of their frequency.
[2911][Para 002] The complications are listed in Table 25.4. The top four are relatively common and should be discussed with patients as a matter of routine.
[2912][Heading 2]  What Warnings Would You Give To the Patient About Extraction?
[2913][Para 001] Deciding exactly which complications to warn patients about can be difficult. The decision must be made individually for each case. The patient must be provided with sufficient information to be able to give informed consent, and the clinician must answer all the patient’s questions correctly. It is generally considered mandatory to warn the patient about both the sequelae and the significant complications of extraction. Sequelae may be induced by surgery or anaesthesia and should be differentiated. Surgical sequelae include swelling (for 48 hours), pain (for approximately 48 hours), bleeding (for about 2 hours), sore temporomandibular joint and trismus, sensitivity of adjacent teeth, and remodelling of the sockets for approximately 10–12 weeks. Complications which must be described are the risk of dry socket (5%) and the risk of temporary (2%) and permanent (0.5%) damage to the lingual and inferior dental nerves. Warnings concerning damage to adjacent teeth or restorations, or displacement of teeth into the antrum, are usually reserved for patients who are at particular risk.
[2914][Heading 2]  Does the Patient Require Antibiotic Cover Before Surgery To Prevent Infection of the Bone Plate in His Arm?
[2915][Para 001] No, this is not necessary.
[2916][Heading 2]  Would You Prescribe Postoperative Antibiotics for These Extractions?
[2917][Para 001] Evidence does not support providing antibiotics perioperatively for dental extractions. Antibiotics do not significantly affect the incidence of dry socket and should not be given without a good reason. They would be indicated if there were an increased risk of infection, as in a patient with diabetes or immunosuppression, after radiotherapy, or if infection were present at the time of operation. However, in normal individuals, antibiotics are probably less important than local measures for preventing infection. A chlorhexidine mouthrinse before the operation and/or debridement of teeth and below the operculum are highly effective in reducing the incidence of postoperative infection and bacteraemia.
[2918][Para 002] In some centres, antibiotics are given routinely whenever bone removal is required, although the value is disputed. If antibiotics are provided, patients having extractions under local anaesthesia usually receive an oral course of amoxicillin or metronidazole. When general anaesthesia is used, a suitable regimen would be a single intravenous bolus dose of either co-amoxiclav or metronidazole.
[2919][Heading 2]  Is General Anaesthesia Required or Desirable?
[2920][Para 001] The choice of anaesthesia will depend on the indications for treatment, the assessment of difficulty and the anaesthesia risk assessment for the particular patient.
[2921][Para 002] This patient requires extraction of all four third molars. The indications for removal do not, in themselves, require general anaesthesia. However, the surgery is likely to take longer than 20 minutes on each side under local anaesthesia. Arguably, this procedure could be performed under local anaesthesia in two visits by an experienced clinician, but many patients find this unacceptable. The patient’s gag reflex is one factor suggesting that general anaesthesia or sedation would be appropriate, and the patient appears to have no medical contraindication. The patient must be fully informed of the risks of sedation or anaesthesia before making a decision. The risks of general anaesthesia are such that it is never the anaesthesia of choice for routine or straightforward extractions. The flow chart (Fig. 25.4) illustrates some factors in selecting a suitable type of anaesthesia.
