[2924][Heading 2]  What Surgical Technique Should Be Used To Remove the Lower Third Molars?
[2925][Para 001] There is much debate about the best method for removal of lower third molars. In the UK, the standard of care is usually removal via a buccal approach with a surgical hand piece if required for complete extraction. In this approach, no lingual flap is raised, and no lingual nerve retraction is performed, so this method carries minimal risk of permanent lingual nerve damage. This is the standard method used in Europe and the US and is increasingly used in the UK, replacing the traditional lingual and buccal flap methods.
[2926][Para 002] However, additional approaches are slowly increasing in popularity, often because of concerns regarding risk of inferior dental nerve injury. When CBCT is available to accurately identify a high risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury, coronectomy can be considered.
[2927][Heading 2]  What is Coronectomy, and When Can It Be Offered?
[2928][Para 001] Coronectomy is the elective removal of the crown of a tooth leaving the roots undisturbed in the socket. This is an alternative surgical approach for mandibular third molars close to the inferior dental nerve canal and is only considered after the risk has been assessed by using appropriate imaging, and there remains a genuine concern regarding nerve injury resulting from the extraction. The technique is not exclusive to third molars and can be used for any impacted mandibular teeth posing the same risk.
[2929][Para 002] Although the procedure of removing the crown appears simple, it can prove to be technically challenging, particularly in deeply impacted mandibular third molars. Amongst many factors, success is imperative on the removal of the crown at the cemento-enamel junction with no enamel retained on the residual roots.
[2930][Para 218] 
[2931][Para 008] 
[2932][Para 011] Fig. 25.4 Flow chart for selection of patients for general anaesthesia.
[2933][Para 009]  
[2934][Para 002] The principle of retaining the roots in situ requires that the tooth is healthy with no pulpal or periapical disease to allow the retained roots maintain their vitality. In the medium-term healing phase, an osteodentine bridge forms to seal off the pulp, maintaining the root in situ without symptoms. The result of a coronectomy in a different case is shown in Fig. 25.5.
[2935][Heading 2]  What are the Indications and Contraindications for Coronectomy?
[2936][Para 001] The only indication for coronectomy is to treat a mandibular tooth that merits removal on currently accepted guidelines, but that has roots close to the inferior dental canal risking nerve damage on complete removal. Pericoronitis and even a dentigerous cyst need not contraindicate coronectomy because these processes are associated with the crown. Contraindications for coronectomy are:
[2937][Para 004] • Caries involving the pulp
[2938][Para 004] • Apical periodontitis
[2939][Para 004] • Internal or external resorption
[2940][Para 004] • Mobile tooth
[2941][Para 004] • Periodontal involvement.
[2942][Para 030]  Are There Any Further Complications and Risks That Should Be Included When Obtaining Patients’ Consent for Coronectomy?
[2943][Para 001] Yes, in addition to the standard warnings for third molar surgery, there are a few specific issues that should be highlighted when discussing coronectomy as a treatment option with the patient. These are detailed in Table 25.5.

[2951][Para 025] Case 26
[2952][Heading 1] A Patient Presenting with an Avulsed Central Incisor
[2953][Para 027] Serpil Djemal, and Ravi Chauhan
[2954][Para 028] Summary
[2955][Para 029] A 26-year-old female presents with an avulsed upper right central incisor and brings with her the tooth wrapped in tissue paper. How will you manage this clinical scenario?
[2956][Para 014] History
[2957][Para 019] Complaint
[2958][Para 007] A 26-year-old female patient presents to your practice in the morning with her central incisor wrapped in tissue. The patient fell over in a nightclub in the early hours of the morning and knocked her upper central incisor out. She went to a hospital Accident and Emergency (A&E) department, where she was cleared of any other injuries and was asked to see her dentist as soon as possible about her tooth.  Fig. 26.1  shows the patient on presentation.
[2959][Para 024]  What Further Information Would You Want From the Patient?
[2960][Para 020] Are There Any Other Injuries?
[2961][Para 001] It should be established whether there has been any loss of consciousness or signs of concussion. Disorientation and impaired response to simple questions may indicate a brain injury that would require immediate hospital assessment. Dealing with these might be a higher priority than the avulsed tooth. In this case, the patient did not lose consciousness and was cleared of head injuries at her local A&E department.
[2962][Para 218] 
[2963][Para 008] 
[2964][Para 011] Fig. 26.1 An anterior view of the patient’s dentition in occlusion, on presentation. © Serpil Djemal.
[2965][Para 009]  
[2966][Para 020] Is There Any Relevant Medical History?
[2967][Para 001] Reimplantation of an avulsed tooth is contraindicated in a patient predisposed to infective endocarditis or is immunocompromised in any way. Any known clotting defect could result in problematic bleeding from a tooth socket. The patient was medically fit and well in this instance.
[2968][Para 020] Is the Patient Up To Date with Tetanus Immunization?
[2969][Para 001] The patient would require a booster if the injury involved soil contamination. Because the injury occurred in a nightclub, her tetanus status was not relevant, but it is good practice to check this for all patients. The patient was up to date her tetanus immunization.
[2970][Para 020] What is the Stage of Root Development?
[2971][Para 001] The management of a permanent tooth with an immature root is different from a permanent tooth with a fully developed root. An avulsed tooth with a fully developed root will always require root canal treatment within 7 days from the date of injury, regardless of the length of time the tooth was out of the socket. An avulsed tooth with an immature root should always be given an opportunity to revascularize if the extra oral dry time is less than 60 mins. In this case, the tooth had a fully developed root. A primary tooth should not be replanted because of the risk of damage to the permanent successor.
[2972][Para 020] When Did the Accident Happen?
[2973][Para 001] The length of time the tooth is out of the socket, the extraoral dry time (EODT), will influence the length of time the tooth is splinted and the overall prognosis. An avulsed tooth that has an extended EODT (>60 minutes) will need to be splinted for 4 weeks. An avulsed tooth that has a shorter EODT (<60 minutes) will need to be splinted for 2 weeks. The longer the EODT, the poorer the prognosis. In this case, the tooth had been wrapped in tissue for 5 hours.
[2974][Para 020] What Has the Tooth Been Stored in?
[2975][Para 001] A successful outcome requires a healthy viable periodontal ligament on the surface of the root, and in this case, because of the EODT of 5 hours, a significant inflammatory response is anticipated with resultant replacement resorption and ankylosis. An appropriate transport medium is essential, and the key parameter is its osmotic pressure. Hanks balanced salt solution is the best transport medium but is not readily available at scenes of trauma. It has been shown that the periodontal ligament cells can survive for up to 6 hours if placed in milk. The best outcome is seen if the tooth is reimplanted at the scene of the accident.
[2976][Para 015] Examination
[2977][Para 024]  What Will You Look for in the Clinical Examination?
[2978][Para 004] • Soft tissues. Check the soft tissues for any lacerations that may require the removal of foreign material and suturing.
[2979][Para 004] • The dentition. Check the adjacent teeth and those in the opposing arch for any other injuries such as fractures and other possible laxation/displacement injuries. A disturbance in the bite may indicate a displaced tooth. Also, check for the presence of periodontal disease and/or caries and the level of oral hygiene.
[2980][Para 004] • The avulsed tooth. The tooth should be examined and cleaned by rinsing with isotonic saline taking great care not to handle the root surface. Any soft tissues adhering to apex should be left, as they may contain Hertwig’s sheath remnants with potential for continued apical maturation.
[2981][Para 015] Special Investigations
[2982][Para 024]  What Additional Investigations Will You Undertake?
[2983][Para 004] • Sensibility testing. Cold testing or electric pulp testing of the avulsed tooth is not indicated.
[2984][Para 004] • Radiographs. A long cone periapical radiograph of the socket and adjacent teeth should be taken to detect any potential remaining root fragments, any associated dento-alveolar fracture and injuries to the adjacent teeth.
[2985][Para 004] • An upper standard occlusal radiograph is useful if a root fracture is suspected.
[2986][Para 002] Fig. 26.2 shows the long cone periapical radiograph of the upper incisor teeth, including the upper right central incisor socket.
[2987][Para 002] The periodontal ligament spaces around the upper incisor teeth are even with no obvious changes.
[2988][Para 015] Treatment
[2989][Heading 2]  How are You Going To Manage the Upper Right Central Incisor?
[2990][Para 001] Avulsed teeth with an EODT of less than 60 minutes should be rinsed and reimplanted under local anaesthesia.
[2991][Para 002] In this case, the EODT was 5 hours (>60 minutes), so root surface preparation is indicated to try to remove all the dead cells and reduce the risk of root resorption. Root surface preparation is as follows:
[2992][Para 004] • Soak the tooth in sodium hypochlorite for 5 minutes
[2993][Para 223] 
[2994][Para 008]

[2998][Para 052] Fig. 26.3 A radiograph of the upper right central incisor following extraoral root canal obturation. © Serpil Djemal.
[2999][Para 004] • Rinse the tooth with saline
[3000][Para 004] • Soak the tooth in 0.5% sodium fluoride for 20 minutes
[3001][Para 004] • Root canal treatment within 7–10 days, or if there is time, root canal treatment extra-orally before reimplantation.
[3002][Para 017] The upper right central incisor was root treated extraorally, and a radiograph of the completed root treatment can be seen in  Fig. 26.3 .

[3005][Para 011] Fig. 26.4 Periapical radiograph of the upper right central incisor after reimplantation. © Serpil Djemal.
[3006][Para 009]  
[3007][Para 002] The reimplantation protocol is as follows:
[3008][Para 004] • Anaesthetize the buccal and palatal tissues
[3009][Para 004] • Remove part of the blood clot in the socket by using a periodontal probe in the central portion rotating it to cause some bleeding
[3010][Para 004] • Digitally reimplant the tooth by holding the crown of the tooth and applying sufficient pressure in an apical direction to position the tooth as near to its original position as possible
[3011][Para 004] • Correct repositioning can be checked by asking the patient to bite together and observing if the patient can bring the teeth together into maximum intercuspation
[3012][Para 004] • Temporarily hold the tooth in position to the adjacent teeth using either a sausage of resin composite or a light cured acrylic material such as TRIADTM
[3013][Para 004] • Take a check periapical radiograph to ensure the tooth has been correctly positioned.
[3014][Para 002] Fig. 26.4 shows the upper right central incisor in the correct position with a relatively even periodontal ligament space.
[3015][Para 002] The splinting protocol is as follows:
[3016][Para 004] • Cut enough 018 stainless steel orthodontic wire to extend from the upper right lateral incisor to the upper left central incisor for flexible splinting
[3017][Para 004] • Prepare resin composite balls of 3 ×4 mm and 3 × 2 mm
[3018][Para 004] • Prepare the teeth by using acid etch and then fully cured unfilled resin on each tooth to be splinted
[3019][Para 004] • Place the 4mm balls onto each tooth, embed the wire into the resin composite and part cure them to secure the wire in position
[3020][Para 004] • Place the smaller 2mm balls on top of each of the 4mm balls encasing the wire and fully light cure each tooth
[3021][Para 002] Fig. 26.5 shows the splinted teeth.
[3022][Para 002] Postoperative instructions include the following:
[3023][Para 004] • Advise the patient not to bite anything with the front teeth and to cut up food and eat using the posterior teeth
[3024][Para 125] 
[3025][Para 008] 
[3026][Para 052] Fig. 26.5 Labial view showing the flexible splint on the teeth. © Serpil Djemal.
[3027][Para 004] • Advise the patient to brush teeth normally.
[3028][Para 030]  What Would You Do Next?
[3029][Para 001] Because of the extended EODT, the splint should be removed after 4 weeks.
[3030][Para 002] The patient will then need to be reviewed at 3 months, 6 months and then annually after the traumatic incident. Each follow-up visit should include the following:
[3031][Para 004] • A clinical examination that should include an assessment of mobility, tenderness to percussion and palpation and the possibility of a draining sinus of the avulsed tooth for any signs of inflammatory or replacement resorption
[3032][Para 004] • The adjacent teeth also need full assessment, as described above, including a note about any possible discoloration indicating loss of vitality
[3033][Para 004] • A periapical radiograph to detect any signs of inflammatory or replacement resorption of the avulsed tooth
[3034][Para 004] • Sensibility testing of the adjacent teeth should be carried out after splint removal.
[3035][Para 002] Throughout this period, the need for good oral hygiene should be reinforced.
[3036][Heading 2]  How Do I Manage a Tooth That Has an Extraoral Dry Time of Less Than 60 Minutes?
[3037][Para 001] The root does not need to be conditioned with sodium hypochlorite and sodium fluoride. The tooth should be replanted as soon as possible and splinted in the same manner for 2 weeks. Root canal treatment should be commenced within 7 days from the date of injury.
[3038][Para 002] The follow-up period for an avulsed tooth with an EODT less than 60 minutes is at 2 weeks for splint removal and then at 3 months, 6 months and then annually.
[3039][Para 002] In teeth with immature roots (open apices), revascularization should be attempted with continued root development.

[3044][Para 015] Long-Term Prognosis
[3045][Heading 2]  What are the Aims of Treatment and Chances of Success?
[3046][Para 001] The aim of reimplantation is to maintain the tooth, thus avoiding the need for prosthetic replacement for as long as possible.
[3047][Para 002] The periodontal ligament heals in 90% of cases if the tooth is replanted immediately but in only 25% of cases if the tooth is incorrectly stored or replantation is delayed.
[3048][Para 002] In one large prospective study of 400 replanted teeth followed up for 5 years, 30% were eventually lost. Immature teeth have a worse prognosis compared with mature teeth because the chances of successful revascularization of immature teeth are low (34%).
[3049][Para 015] Treatment Options if Reimplantation is Not Possible
[3050][Para 024]  Suppose Re-Implantation is Not Possible for Example, if the Tooth is Not Available, What Treatments are There?
[3051][Para 016] 1. Acrylic partial denture
[3052][Para 016] 2. Chrome partial denture
[3053][Para 016] 3. Resin-bonded bridge
[3054][Para 016] 4. Implant
[3055][Para 016] 5. ‘Mesialization’ of the lateral incisor – in the presence of a crowded malocclusion, orthodontic treatment to move the adjacent lateral incisor into the missing central incisor position, as well as to address the malocclusion, can be considered. The size of the lateral incisor will need to be checked carefully to ensure that the emergence profile of the tooth once recontoured to mimic the central incisor will be adequate from an aesthetic point of view. Similarly, the size and shade of the canine tooth must be assessed to ensure that it will be possible to adequately mimic the lateral incisor.
[3056][Para 016] 6. Autotransplantation – if a patient is going to undergo orthodontic extraction with one of the premolars being transplanted into the central incisor position.
[3057][Para 030]  How Would You Manage an Avulsed Tooth Primary Incisor?
[3058][Para 001] No attempt should be made to reimplant an avulsed primary incisor. Parents should be informed that any attempt to reimplant a primary tooth could result in damage to the permanent successor. A space maintainer with a prosthetic tooth would be advisable to allow for eruption of the permanent successor. If this is not provided, and space is lost, delayed eruption may result.

[3110][Heading 2]  What Further Investigations Would You Carry Out?
[3111][Para 001] The teeth should be examined, preferably with magnification, in a dry state and also in a wet state. By examining the teeth when dry, this allows observation of the surface texture and any porous defects. In addition, it becomes easier to observe banding or chronological defects.
[3112][Para 002] Photography is a valuable aid to record the appearance of these teeth to allow discussion with the patient and to record, in much greater detail, the appearance than with text alone. This is an important aspect of dental record keeping, and digital imaging is readily available. It is important to remember, however, that photographs constitute patient personal data and, therefore, must be considered in the same manner as written records as mandated by General Data Protection Regulation. In addition, examining the teeth in fluorescent or polarizing lighting conditions or obtaining fluorescent or polarized images may enhance your ability to observe changes within the tooth structure. This can be achieved by using filters on cameras or commercial devices such as DIAGNOCam (KaVo) (https://www.kavo.com/dental-instruments/diagnocam-small-devices-0#patient-cases) or D-Light Pro (GC) (Fig. 27.2).
[3113][Para 002] When taking intraoral images, it is advisable to use a standard colour scale to act as a visual reference to account for lighting/ambient conditions.
[3114][Para 002] It would be prudent to determine the pulp sensibility of any discoloured teeth.

[3122][Para 001] The diagnosis is enamel hypoplasia of unknown origin. The discolouration is not typical of developmental defects or of metabolic or drug-induced conditions such as tetracycline staining (although this is now so rarely encountered that the use of tetracycline medication during the period of tooth development is discouraged).
[3123][Para 002] Fluorosis would produce a similar appearance, but the lack of history of fluoride supplementation or living in an area with a high natural level of fluoride appears to preclude this.
[3124][Para 002] There is no definitive test for determining the causes of hypoplasia, but with the condition identified, management options can now be considered and discussed with the patient.
[3125][Heading 2]  What are the Management Options Available? What are Their Advantages and Disadvantages?
[3126][Para 032] See Table 27.5.
[3127][Heading 2]  How Would You Decide Which Management Approach To Use?
[3128][Para 001] The treatment and overall management of the case should involve the patient at every stage. This is the concept of shared decision making. The Montgomery ruling (Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board, 2015, UKSC 11) requires that clinicians translate their professional knowledge into something meaningful for the average patient as well as for the particular patient sitting in front of them. The beneficent aspect of care should be balanced against the nonmaleficent desire to avoid harm, where possible. Consent needs to remain valid through all stages of treatment.
[3129][Para 002] To obtain valid consent, the patient needs to be informed of:
[3130][Para 004] • The options for treatment, the risks and the potential benefits
[3131][Para 004] • Why you think a particular treatment is necessary and appropriate for them
[3132][Para 004] • The consequences, risks and benefits of the treatment you propose
[3133][Para 004] • The likely prognosis
[3134][Para 004] • Your recommended option
[3135][Para 004] • The cost of the proposed treatment
[3136][Para 004] • What might happen if the proposed treatment is not carried out
[3137][Para 004] • Whether the treatment is guaranteed, how long it is guaranteed for and any exclusions that apply.
[3138][Para 002] Leaflets, online material, discussion using visual aids such as photographs of the patients’ teeth and other resources may assist in obtaining informed consent. The discussions need to be documented, and it is good practice to allow a period of reflection so that the patient can consider the options before committing to treatment.

[3146][Heading 2]  What Would Be the Most Appropriate Treatment in This Case?
[3147][Para 007] The patient has advised that she is only concerned with the appearance of the two upper central incisor teeth and was not seeking a ‘perfect’ appearance because she was aware that this would make these teeth look different compared with her remaining dentition. On the basis of her friend’s experience, she was also aware of the effects of tooth preparation and the unpredictable results of using porcelain veneers.
[3148][Para 002] A minimally invasive conservative approach such as using a hydrogen or carbamide peroxide bleaching agent may result in an appearance that is satisfactory to the patient. This technique has the advantage that no tooth structure removal is required and the treatment may be repeated again in the future, if required. However, if this technique does not produce an outcome that is satisfactory for the patient, alternative techniques such as microabrasion to remove the areas of greatest discolouration, followed by surface application of flowable resin composite material, may be used. This was the completed treatment for the patient ( Fig. 27.3 ).
[3149][Para 014] Prognosis
[3150][Para 001] The appearance of the teeth after this treatment was not perfect, but there was a marked improvement from that at presentation, which allowed the patient to move to her new academic environment with increased confidence in her dental appearance. Importantly, the patient was satisfied with the outcome, and this was documented, along with the whole management process, contemporaneously in the dental notes.
[3151][Para 002] The prognosis for the teeth remains good. The resin composite will require repolishing to maintain the surface lustre and, in due course, will require repair and possible replacement. However, this can be carried out with a careful technique, preferably with magnification, to minimize the risk of tooth structure damage or removal of teeth. The patient has been informed of this.
[3152][Para 110] Case 28
[3153][Para 111] A Very Painful Mouth
[3154][Para 112] Pepe Shirlaw, and Sandeep Joshi
[3155][Para 113] Summary
[3156][Para 013] A 20-year-old man presents at your general dental practice, feeling ill and with a very sore mouth.
[3157][Para 009]  
[3158][Para 074] Fig. 28.1 Appearance of the patient’s mouth.
[3159][Para 057] History
[3160][Para 045] Complaint
[3161][Para 013] The patient complains of pain which is preventing eating and hampering drinking. He also feels unwell.
[3162][Para 045] History of Complaint
[3163][Para 013] He first noticed feeling unwell 4 days ago and thought he had the flu. He was slightly feverish and had a headache. His mouth was sore, but it was not until about 1 day later that it became very painful. Because he felt unable to take time off work, he took the remains of a course of an unknown oral antibiotic that had been prescribed for his brother who had an infected cut on his arm. This did not appear to have led to any improvement. He has had no similar attacks before.
[3164][Para 045] Medical History
[3165][Para 013] The patient is otherwise fit and well.
[3166][Para 057] Examination
[3167][Para 045] Extraoral Examination
[3168][Para 013] The patient has enlarged cervical lymph nodes that are slightly tender, mobile, soft and firm rather than hard. Apart from this finding, no abnormalities are found in a routine examination of the head, neck and hands.
[3169][Para 148] Intraoral Examination
[3170][Para 033]  What Do You See in Fig. 28.1?
[3171][Para 013] On the labial mucosa, there are numerous ulcers with the following characteristics:
[3172][Para 013] In addition, one large ulcer lies at the commissure, and there are small bloodstained crusts around the lips.
[3173][Para 013] If you were able to examine the patient, you would discover that more ulcers affect much of the oral mucosa, including the gingivae, palate and tongue, and that they extend back into the oropharynx.
[3174][Para 090]  Give a Differential Diagnosis On the Basis of the Information You Have So Far.
[3175][Para 013] • Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis
[3176][Para 013] • Erythema multiforme.
[3177][Para 033]  Justify This Differential Diagnosis.
[3178][Para 013] Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis and other oral viral infections typically cause multiple round, small ulcers of acute onset, sometimes coalescing, on a background of inflamed mucosa. The patient feels unwell and has enlarged tender lymph nodes, suggesting infection. Primary herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection usually affects much of the mucosa and has a predilection for the keratinized masticatory mucosa of the gingiva. The patient is older than is normally expected for a primary infection. However, the average age of patients with this infection has increased over the last few decades because improved living conditions have resulted in fewer individuals coming into contact with the virus during their childhood.
[3179][Para 013] Erythema multiforme (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) is possible. The acute onset and bloody crusts on the lips suggest this diagnosis, and the age of the patient is compatible. However, the distribution of ulcers is not particularly suggestive of this condition. Erythema multiforme affects primarily the lips and nonkeratinized lining mucosa of the anterior mouth, and the ulcers have ragged margins, whereas the irregular ulcers in the picture seem to be formed by coalescence of small, round ulcers. A trigger for erythema multiforme is sometimes identified, and antibiotics, particularly sulphonamides, are sometimes the cause. This patient has recently taken antibiotics, but only after the symptoms appeared. Erythema multiforme is typically recurrent, and a history of previous attacks and their periodicity is important in making the diagnosis. However, in a first attack, the features may be milder, and, as in this case, there is no history of similar attacks.
[3180][Para 033]  What Diagnoses Have You Discounted, and Why?
[3181][Para 013] Other oral viral infections do not produce a clinical picture of this severity. Herpangina and hand, foot and mouth disease are milder and usually affect the soft palate of children. Varicella zoster would be expected to cause chicken pox in this age group, although children are more typically affected; oral zoster usually affects older patients and is unilateral.
[3182][Para 013] Herpetiform aphthous stomatitis should be considered but is readily excluded. The ulcers may be numerous, small and coalescing and may have an erythematous background. However, they are usually limited to the anterior or posterior area of the mouth, do not affect keratinized mucosa and are not accompanied by systemic illness. Attacks are recurrent.
[3183][Para 013] In a mild primary attack of HSV infection in an adult, the ulcers may be limited to the gingiva, raising the possibility of acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis. However, in this case, the ulceration is too extensive for necrotizing gingivitis to be considered, and in any case, it is usually clinically characteristic.
[3184][Para 090]  What Further Questions Would You Ask, and What Further Examinations Would You Perform, and Why?
[3185][Para 128] Do You Suffer From ‘Cold Sores’?
[3186][Para 013] If the patient has had recurrent HSV infection, usually in the form of herpes labialis, then the present ulcers could not have been caused by a primary herpetic infection. Recurrent herpetic infection is sometimes a trigger for attacks of erythema multiforme and a cold sore 1–2 weeks before onset would raise this possibility. In answer to this question, the patient indicates that he does not suffer from cold sores.
[3187][Para 051] Have You Been in Contact with Anyone with Cold Sores?
[3188][Para 013] Identification of a possible source of HSV infection 1–2 weeks before the ulcers would give further credibility to this diagnosis. Contact with Herpes zoster is not significant in this case, but in less clear-cut cases, it would be prudent to ask about any exposure to chicken pox and shingles. The patient has no known exposure to any viral disease.
[3189][Para 051] Did You Notice Small Blisters in Your Mouth Before the Ulcers Appeared?
[3190][Para 013] This would suggest herpes virus infection, each ulcer being preceded by a small, round vesicle. Larger vesicles and blisters are also found in erythema multiforme, but these are irregular and usually limited to the vermilion border of the lips and the floor of mouth.
[3191][Para 051] Have You Taken Any Drugs or Medicines in the Last 3 Weeks?
[3192][Para 013] This will clarify the possibility that medication has triggered an attack of erythema multiforme. The patient has taken no medication apart from the antibiotic noted in the history.
[3193][Para 051] Have You Any Rash Anywhere On Your Body?
[3194][Para 013] Erythema multiforme is associated with a variety of rashes (hence its name), and the patient should have a skin examination. The presence of typical target lesions indicates erythema multiforme but other less characteristic rashes should also be noted, along with their time of onset. No rash is present.
[3195][Para 051] Take the Patient’s Temperature
[3196][Para 013] This simple investigation is easily forgotten, but often valuable. A raised temperature in the early stages indicates infection. The temperature is not raised in erythema multiforme even when severe (unless there is infection of skin lesions). The patient’s temperature is 38°C.
[3197][Para 102] Diagnosis
[3198][Para 013] Differential diagnosis in such cases sometimes poses problems. If the patient has erythema multiforme, he should be treated with a moderately high dose of systemic steroids, but this should be avoided if he has a viral infection. A certain amount of time must elapse before the results of investigations will be available.
[3199][Para 033]  Can You Make a Diagnosis and Commence Treatment?
[3200][Para 013] Yes. In this case, there is sufficient evidence to make a working diagnosis of primary HSV infection. Investigations should be performed to confirm the diagnosis but need not delay treatment. Investigations are probably only available to those in hospital practice. Practitioners confident in their diagnosis may well initiate treatment without confirmatory results from laboratory tests.
[3201][Para 057] Investigations
[3202][Para 033]  What Investigations Might You Consider, and What are Their Advantages and Disadvantages?
[3203][Para 161] See Table 28.1.
[3204][Para 013] In the current case, a viral swab was taken for PCR confirmation of HSV infection.
[3205][Para 057] Treatment
[3206][Para 033]  What Treatment Would You Provide?
[3207][Para 013] The patient should be reassured that he has a common viral infection, which, although unpleasant, has no significant implications. It will run its course for up to the next 10 days or so, but it is unlikely to worsen significantly now that it is in its fifth day. Some adult patients may confuse this condition with genital herpes and require some additional explanation.
[3208][Para 051] Table 28.1
[3209][Para 061] Investigations To Be Considered
[3210][Para 013] While he feels unwell, the patient should rest and maintain a good fluid intake. This is especially important in children who refuse fluids and become dehydrated rapidly. A sedative antihistamine such as promethazine is sometimes suggested for very small and fractious children who have difficulty sleeping during the acute phase. It also has the advantage of drying the reflex salivation.
[3211][Para 013] The patient should be warned about infectivity. The virus is transmitted only through close contact, but while there are vesicles or ulcers in the mouth, the saliva is infectious. Care should be taken to avoid close contact with other individuals, especially children. In the nonimmune patient (by definition, anyone with a primary infection), other sites may also become infected, and particular care should be taken to avoid saliva coming in contact with the eyes.
[3212][Para 013] Antiviral treatment with aciclovir should be considered. Aciclovir is only effective in the earliest stage of the infection when the virus is replicating. It must be taken in the first 48 hours for best effect while vesicles, rather than ulcers, are present. Aciclovir is not indicated in this case because of the delay in presentation (although it might be considered in an immunosuppressed patient). A dose of 200 mg five times daily is recommended for immunocompetent patients. Related drugs giving higher levels in blood such as valaciclovir, are usually reserved for varicella-zoster virus (VSV) infection.
[3213][Para 013] Preparations for symptomatic relief of the oral ulceration are indicated. Tetracycline mouthwash (250 mg capsule of a soluble preparation dissolved in water, used four times daily) or 100 mg doxycycline, also used topically, is very useful in reducing discomfort and would be an appropriate choice in this patient, who has presented too late to benefit from aciclovir. Antiseptic mouthwashes such as chlorhexidine are also effective. These presumably reduce oral discomfort by preventing bacterial infection of the ulcers. Chlorhexidine would also compensate for inability to carry out oral hygiene procedures. Analgesic mouthwashes such as benzydamine are an alternative.
[3214][Para 057] Prognosis
[3215][Para 033]  What is the Risk That This Patient Will Suffer From Cold Sores in the Future?
[3216][Para 013] Between 15 and 30% of individuals who come into contact with the virus develop recurrent infection. It is not clear whether those who suffer a symptomatic primary infection such as gingivostomatitis have an increased risk. Although this percentage seems high, many patients with recurrent herpes infection suffer only very occasional lesions.
[3217][Para 033]  What are the Mechanisms and Significance of Recurrent Infection?
[3218][Para 013] During infection, HSV is transported back along axons of sensory nerves to their nuclei. There, the neurones are infected but do not die, and the virus becomes latent – that is, virus persists but no infectious virions are produced.
[3219][Para 013] A viral latency gene and the cell-mediated immune response contribute to the balance between latency and reactivation. If infection is reactivated, the virus travels down the nerve to cause a localized recurrent infection of the mucosa or skin – a cold sore. Because the virus is intracellular for most of this life cycle, antibodies of the humoral immune response are not effective in preventing recurrences. Environmental triggers for cold sores include ultraviolet light, illness and stress.
[3220][Para 013] Latent infection has important consequences. Subclinical reactivation may result in the virus being shed from the mucosa without the individual realizing that he or she has an active infection. This may be one of the mechanisms of spread in the population. Latent infection in the geniculate ganglion is one cause of Bell’s palsy, and very occasionally, the virus may spread along the nerves to the brain, causing herpetic encephalitis.
[3221][Para 013] Labial recurrences are painful and unpleasant but relatively readily treated because there is often a characteristic prodromal sensation of burning or itching and the vesicles are easily seen. Early treatment is, therefore, possible, and antiviral drugs can be very effective. Topical preparations of 5% aciclovir are available without prescription.
[3222][Para 033]  When Would You Ask the Patient To Return?
[3223][Para 013] The patient should return in about 1 week to check that healing is progressing, but earlier if symptoms worsen or new signs develop.
[3224][Para 013] At some stage during treatment or follow-up, the patient should be warned about not taking medications that are prescribed for others. The antibiotic prescribed for the patient’s brother was apparently a harmless drug, but inappropriate for this patient. Those who take drugs prescribed for others run the risk of hypersensitivity, drug interaction or other unwanted reaction. The importance of completing the prescribed dose should be emphasized to all patients receiving antibiotics, to ensure effective treatment and because this is critically important in preventing the emergence of resistant strains in the community.
[3225][Para 102] Final Outcome
[3226][Para 013] The next day, the polymerase chain reaction report shows positivity for HSV type 1 DNA. The diagnosis of herpetic gingivostomatitis is confirmed.

[3239][Para 021] Radiographic Views Required for the Patient and the Clinical Justification
[3240][Para 002] The patient is concerned about radiation. Current regulations require you to have a meaningful discussion with the patient regarding the risks and benefits of the radiographic investigation, so you start to provide dose and risk information.
[3241][Para 024]  What Three General Guiding Principles Must You Follow in Deciding Whether or Not To Undertake Any Radiographic Examination?
[3242][Para 020] Justification
[3243][Para 001] Each radiation exposure must have a net positive benefit.
[3244][Para 020] Optimization
[3245][Para 001] The exposures must be at a dose that is As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP), taking social and economic factors into account.
[3246][Para 020] Limitation
[3247][Para 001] The dose to individuals must not exceed the recommended limits.
[3248][Para 002] The principles are set out by the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP), which also sets the recommended dose limits for staff.
[3249][Heading 2]  What is the Patient Dose Associated with Exposure of These Radiographs?
[3250][Para 001] Radiation dose measuring is complex. The effective dose (absorbed dose corrected to compensate for the type of radiation and susceptibility of different tissues) is usually quoted. The effective dose for an intraoral radiograph (periapical or bitewing) is in the range of 0.0003–0.022 millisieverts (mSv) and for a panoramic radiograph 0.0027–0.075 mSv, depending on the equipment used.
[3251][Heading 2]  Because These Technical Terms Do Not Mean Much To Most People, How Can You Reassure the Patient?
[3252][Para 001] The patient can be reassured that the doses are very small and equivalent to a tiny fraction of the natural background radiation (ubiquitous radiation) to which we are all exposed every day. If the patient wants to know actual figures, then she should be told that the annual dose from background radiation varies around the world, but, for example, the average is 2.3 mSv in the UK and is 3.1 mSv in the US. The dose for the radiographs required equates to approximately 8 hours of additional background radiation for an intraoral radiograph and 3 days for a panoramic radiograph.
[3253][Heading 2]  The Patient Accepts This But Points At the Hazard Warning Sticker On Your X-Ray Cubicle. What Exactly are the Risks?
[3254][Para 001] At these low absorbed doses, there is only one significant risk, that of cancer induction. This is a very low frequency and completely random (stochastic) effect induced by damage to DNA either directly or indirectly.
[3255][Para 002] The risk of developing a fatal malignancy as a result of taking a periapical radiograph varies, depending on the equipment used and dose delivered, but in ‘best practice’ radiography using modern equipment and techniques, it is estimated to be about 1 in 10 000 000.
[3256][Para 002] In panoramic radiography, the risk, again, varies, depending on the equipment used and the type and speed of the image receptor (film/screen combination or digital) but is estimated to be around 1 in 1 000 000.
[3257][Heading 2]  The Patient Wants To Know How You Ensure That She Will Receive the Minimum Dose of Radiation Necessary. What Methods are Used To Optimize Dose To Patients, and How Do They Work?
[3258][Para 001] After the radiographic image has been justified, the radiation doses can be optimised by using modern x-ray equipment and techniques, as shown in Table 29.2.

[3262][Para 040] Methods of Dose Optimization
[3263][Para 044] 
[3264][Para 002] You are planning to take the radiographs by using a photostimulable phosphor plate digital imaging system (PSP system). The benefit to the patient depends on the diagnostic information, or yield, provided, and this, in turn, is dependent on the quality of the radiographic images produced. To achieve this, a quality assurance (QA) programme in dental radiography is highly desirable and in some countries, including the UK, is a mandatory legal requirement. The World Health Organization (WHO) has defined QA in radiography as ‘an organized effort by the staff operating a facility to ensure that the diagnostic images produced by the facility are of sufficiently high quality so that they consistently provide adequate diagnostic information’.
[3265][Heading 2]  What are the Aims of a Quality Assurance Programme?
[3266][Para 001] The aims should include the following:
[3267][Para 004] • To produce diagnostic radiographs of a consistently high standard
[3268][Para 004] • To reduce the number of repeat radiographs
[3269][Para 004] • To determine all sources of error and allow for their correction
[3270][Para 004] • To increase efficiency
[3271][Para 004] • To reduce costs
[3272][Para 004] • To reduce the radiation dose to patients and staff.
[3273][Para 030]  What Areas or Topics Should a Digitally Based Quality Assurance Programme Address?
[3274][Para 001] There are five main areas or topics of concern that should form the basis of the QA programme. These include:
[3275][Para 004] • Personnel and training
[3276][Para 004] • Image quality
[3277][Para 004] • Working procedures
[3278][Para 004] • Patient dose and equipment, including the
[3279][Para 004] • X-ray set
[3280][Para 004] • Digital imaging receptor type (solid state detector/ PSP) and digital processing
[3281][Para 004] • Viewing screen (monitor)
[3282][Para 004] • Clinical audit.
[3283][Para 002] The essential procedures for each should be laid down in writing and should be the responsibility of a named person.
[3284][Heading 2]  How Can the Quality of Digitally Captured Images Be Assessed in General Dental Practice?
[3285][Para 001] One way to assess image quality is to visually compare every radiograph with a good quality standard reference image and to subjectively rate the quality using the 2-point scale as recommended by Public Health England/Faculty of General Dental Practitioners, shown in Table 29.3.
[3286][Heading 2]  What Should Be Done with the ‘Not Diagnostically Acceptable’ Category ‘N’ Images?
[3287][Para 001] They should be analyzed over a suitable period (e.g. a week or a month). This analysis is often referred to as image reject analysis. The category ‘N’ images are assessed as to why they have been rejected and to identify the causative error. Changes to practice can then be instituted to avoid the error being repeated. This process should be documented for best practice and for future reference.

[3290][Heading 2]  The Following Five Intraoral Digitally Captured Radiographs All Have Errors. What is Wrong with Each, and What are the Possible Explanations?
[3291][Para 130]   What is Wrong with the Image in Fig. 29.2 ?
[3292][Para 002] This is a periapical radiograph of the lower right first molar (grade ‘N’ quality rating). The image is ‘coned off’ – part of the image receptor has not been exposed. Typically, this happens when the spacer cone is not aligned correctly to the image receptor. In this case, the main reason for the ‘coning off’ is incorrect orientation of the rectangular collimator within the open-ended spacer cone. Note also that even if the rectangular collimator had been aligned properly, it is unlikely the apices of the teeth would be fully visualized because the incorrect photostimulable phosphor plate (PSP) size has also been selected.
[3293][Para 070]  What is Wrong with the Image in Fig. 29.3a?
[3294][Para 001] This is a periapical radiograph of the lower right first molar (grade ‘A’ quality rating). The image shows several white lines/marks on the image. These are artefactual due to scratching of the phosphor layer. A well-organized quality assurance (QA) programme should include visually inspecting the photostimulable phosphor plate (PSP) for scratches and checking for image uniformity by exposing the image receptor to radiation. Fig. 29.3b is a radiograph of the same PSP, which has been exposed to radiation as part of QA testing. This demonstrates the scratches and also shows areas of image nonuniformity along the long edges of the image receptor. Although in this case the radiographic image of the lower teeth is diagnostically acceptable, this PSP needs to be removed from clinical use.

[3315][Para 070]  What are the Advantages of Digital Radiography Over Film-Based Systems?
[3316][Para 001] The use of digital radiography has a number of advantages. One of the most important is that the image receptors are more sensitive than film, allowing a lower patient dose. In addition, image production is quicker allowing an almost immediate assessment of image quality. The images can be enhanced digitally to extract useful diagnostic information from underexposed or overexposed images and may be optimized to assess specific dental conditions such as dental caries or periodontal bone levels. Finally, electronic storage of data means that images can be accessed quickly. Digital radiography is, therefore, in the patient’s interests, with around 75% of dental practices in the UK now using digital systems.

[3321][Para 070]  What Regulations Must UK Dentists Comply with in Regard To Ionising Radiation?
[3322][Para 001] The regulations governing the use of ionising radiation in the UK are called the Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017 (IRR 2017) and the Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017 (IRMER 2017). Because the European Directive applies to all European Union (EU) countries, the regulations in the EU countries will have similar content to those of the UK. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the American Dental Association (ADA) provide guidance on dental radiography in the US.
[3323][Para 002] The UK regulations encompass the general principles of the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) – of Justification, Optimization and Limitation. After the introduction of IRMER 2017, there is now a requirement to provide the patient with risk and benefit information as part of the consent process prior to the radiographic exposure. This information should be provided in a qualitative rather than a quantitative manner.
[3324][Para 002] Both sets of UK legislation are criminal law; therefore, failure to comply with it could result in serious consequences, including, in extreme cases, a possible custodial sentence. As IRMER 2017 is designed to protect patients, failure to comply with it, potentially putting patients at risk, could also result in a practitioner’s ‘fitness to practise’ being investigated by professional regulatory bodies whose primary function is to protect patients.

[3344][Para 118] Complaint
[3345][Para 007] Your nurse takes the special trays out of the laboratory package for you to record secondary impressions of an edentulous patient. They are not as ‘special’ as you had intended.
[3346][Para 014] History of Complaint
[3347][Para 007] You are constructing new complete dentures for a patient who has been a poor complete denture wearer. She has lost her lower denture and does not like the upper, so you have decided to make a new set from first principles rather than use a copy denture technique.
[3348][Para 017] The upper primary impression was taken in alginate, and the lower was recorded in a stock tray adapted with silicone putty and covered with an alginate wash to record detail. This was because the upper edentulous stock tray conformed well the patient’s edentulous anatomy; however, the lower tray did not fit well. You were going to take both upper and lower secondary impressions in close-fitting trays by using a light-bodied silicone elastomeric material. Traditionally, close fitting impressions have been recorded in zinc oxide and eugenol (ZoE); however, although more expensive, elastomeric materials are increasingly being used because they are easier to handle. They have the disadvantage of tending to be hydrophobic, as opposed to ZoE, which is hydrophilic, so good moisture control is important.
[3349][Para 015] Diagnosis
[3350][Heading 2]  The Lower Special Trays are Shown in Figs 30.1 and 30.2. What is Wrong?
[3351][Para 001] The lower tray is asymmetrical: The extension on the patient’s left is considerably shorter than that on the right. However, when you look at the cast, you see that your impression was short in that area and that the laboratory has extended the tray as much as possible. The laboratory was correct not to have extended the tray over the land area on the stone cast (the ‘land area’ is that peripheral part of the model not recorded in the impression that the technician creates to preserve the rolled borders of an impression). The result is that the tray is underextended on the left buccal shelf. This is important because the lower denture will need to be extended here to gain good support.
[3352][Para 218] 
[3353][Para 008] 
[3354][Para 011] Fig. 30.2 The lower tray.
[3355][Para 009]  
[3356][Para 002] Conversely, the tray has been overextended onto the land area in the floor of the mouth, and this will need to be altered prior to recording a secondary impression.
[3357][Heading 2]  The Upper Special Tray is Shown in Fig. 30.3. What is Wrong?
[3358][Para 001] This shows a well-constructed upper special tray, but it has been perforated and spaced for an alginate secondary impression. The tray is properly extended, but spaced trays always look slightly overextended on a primary model because it sits lower after the spacer has been removed. Your heart sinks.
[3359][Para 017] You look at the laboratory request sheet to see what you prescribed and read: ‘Please cast upper and lower primary impressions. Construct upper and lower special trays. N.B.: Lower close fitting for silicone.’
[3360][Para 017] Your error is lack of suitable detail in your communication. Many dentists and clinical dental technicians (CDTs) use alginate in a spaced tray for upper impressions. You had expected that the laboratory would assume that if one tray was close fitting, then the other one would be, too. You make a note to be more careful in the future.

[3375][Heading 2]  What You Can Do About the Lower Tray?
[3376][Para 001] This has one laboratory fault (overextension) and one fault resulting from your original impression (underextension). Again, you could take a new primary impression and request new special trays, but the lower tray is more easily dealt with. The best solution is to extend your tray over the buccal shelf by using a material such as green or pink stick composition (pink is much easier to use because it flows at mouth temperature). The lingual overextension can be trimmed back with a bur to the correct extension, which is marked as a black line on the undersurface in the upper panel of Fig. 30.2.
[3377][Heading 2]  What Else Should You Check Before Trying To Adapt the Trays?
[3378][Para 001] The extension should be checked in the patient’s mouth to ensure that the other areas are correct. Other common errors in tray construction relate to handle design. You need to check the handles to ensure that they are properly constructed. Prosthodontists can become excited about tray handles, but there are no absolute rules regarding what can and cannot be used. However, some tray handle designs could cause you and your patient problems.
[3379][Heading 2]  Are These Handles Suitable?
[3380][Para 001] As indicated by the appearances in Figs 30.1–30.3, the laboratory has provided well-made and well-designed handles. Faults to look for are shown in Fig. 30.4. Can you identify them and the reasons for the deficiencies?
[3381][Para 002] The left and central images in Fig. 30.4 show the same tray that has been poorly constructed. The handle will almost certainly get in the way of the lower lip, risking displacement during use and distortion of the sulcus. As you are aware, complete dentures develop retention from a correct border seal, and this might be more difficult to achieve in the master impression if the tray handle distorts the lips. This fault usually arises because the tray is left sitting on the bench before light curing, during which time the handle sags under the influence of gravity. A stub handle would be better, as seen in Fig. 30.1.
[3382][Para 002] The handle also deviates from the midline, so it will be very difficult for the user to centre and seat the tray without the handle as a guide. This would certainly be the case with a spaced perforated upper special tray for use with alginate.
[3383][Para 002] The image on the right shows that the handle has fallen off. This is because the light-cured materials were not processed in the light box at the same time. With use of this type of material, a handle cannot be added at a later stage without using a special adhesive because the material has a high filler content. It is unlikely that you would have this adhesive in your surgery. This problem may only come to light when removing the impression. A well-recorded impression is normally very retentive and can be difficult to remove. The clinician has to first release the border seal in the buccal aspect of the premolar region and then remove the impression using the handle. It is a bit embarrassing if the handle falls off!
[3384][Para 002] Also, the technician has placed posterior stub handles. These are not normally used on maxillary trays and have no advantage there. Their sole advantage is to help prevent the clinician’s fingers from distorting the buccal sulcus when taking impressions of an edentulous lower ridge.

[3387][Para 007] You are constructing a new upper complete denture over a lower metal-based partial denture for a 52-year-old male when things start to go wrong. How will you rectify the mistakes?

[3391][Para 012] History of Complaint
[3392][Para 007] The patient lost all his upper teeth because of decay in his late 20s and early 30s despite extensive dental care. He has had five dentures over a 20-year period and managed with them fairly well. The current lower metal-based partial denture was his first partial denture. He dislikes the back of the denture lifting up during function but copes with this reluctantly.
[3393][Para 014] Examination
[3394][Para 007] The upper complete denture lacks retention, and no peripheral seal is evident when seated. There is some wear of the anterior teeth.
[3395][Para 017] The lower partial denture has wear on the prosthetic teeth, and they are no longer in occlusal contact. The patient has an inadequate posterior occlusion (posterior support).
[3396][Para 015] Solution
[3397][Heading 2]  What Will You Prescribe?
[3398][Para 001] Both dentures must be replaced. Relining the upper denture is pointless if the teeth are worn. The lower partial denture needs replacing because it is not retentive and is worn out. The posterior occlusion will have to be reconstructed with two new dentures because neither is currently correct.
[3399][Para 002] Replacing the upper denture alone might cure the aesthetic problem. However, lower natural teeth occluding against a complete denture with no lower partial teeth or with worn teeth will accelerate alveolar bone loss and risk formation of a fibrous ridge (‘flabby ridge’).
[3400][Para 017] You decide to construct a new metal-based partial denture for the lower arch and a new complete upper denture by using a copy denture technique.
[3401][Heading 2]  In What Order Do You Plan To Provide This Dental Care? Why?
[3402][Para 001] It would be best to start with the metal-based partial denture first. If the copy technique for the upper denture goes to plan, four visits will be required without reviews. If the metal-based partial denture goes to plan, even ignoring the altered cast technique, it will require six visits without reviews. Some laboratories prefer 3 weeks to make a metal framework, and you do not want to be recording the definitive upper impression too early in the treatment schedule.

[3404][Para 002] The metal framework is shown in Fig. 30.5. It looks beautiful and fits the model well. Everything seems to be going to plan until you notice that the laboratory seems to have omitted the cingulum rest and minor connector for the lower left canine.
[3405][Para 017] Before reaching for the phone to call the laboratory and complain, you look at the design that you sketched on the prescription card, shown in  Fig. 30.5 .

[3414][Heading 2]  Will These Design Faults Cause Problems? Why?
[3415][Para 001] Yes, probably. The patient is not keen on wearing a lower partial denture and complains of lifting of the free end (distal extension) saddle. A cingulum rest on the lower left canine would provide indirect retention (see Case 54) against this movement. This would cause soreness under the major connector.
[3416][Heading 2]  What Can You Do To Rectify These Errors?
[3417][Para 001] There are four options:
[3418][Para 016] 1. Ignore the indirect retention on the basis that there is good direct retention with three clasps. If the framework fits, it might be possible to take a chance and go ahead. If this works, you will owe the laboratory thanks for remembering to add the reciprocal arm to the premolar because this contributes significantly to the overall retention by ensuring that the clasp is guided, reciprocated and engaged.
[3419][Para 016] 2. Have a separate rest and connector cast, and ask the laboratory to try to laser weld that on. This is difficult, carries a cost implication and the fit might not be very satisfactory. It carries a risk of failure.

[3423][Para 016] 3. Make a new framework either on the existing master cast, if it has not yet been disposed of or damaged in any way, or record a new secondary impression and make a new framework – the optimal clinical solution, but with cost and time implications.
[3424][Para 017] As the patient is already waiting, you decide at least to try-in the framework. If it does not fit, the option of adding an indirect retainer is not practical.
[3425][Heading 2]  How Do You Decide Whether the Framework Fits?
[3426][Para 001] Check systematically that:
[3427][Para 016] 1. the rest seats are fully seated
[3428][Para 016] 2. there are no gaps between the soft tissues and the major connector
[3429][Para 016] 3. there is not an anterior–posterior or lateral rock
[3430][Para 016] 4. clasps and reciprocals are in close contact with the teeth
[3431][Para 016] 5. guide planes provide a clear single path of insertion
[3432][Para 016] 6. clasp tips engage in undercuts.
[3433][Para 002] Bear in mind that the saddle is not supported with acrylic resin under the mesh and that if you place vertical force on the saddle at this stage the framework will lift anteriorly, even if it fits well.
[3434][Para 017] When you seat the framework, it seems to fit well, and it appears that you may be able to adapt it. Confidently, you ask the patient how the framework feels. Unfortunately, he says it is lifting at the back and on both sides, not just the side with the distal extension saddle. Closer inspection reveals that the clasp on the lower left second molar is not providing any retention.
[3435][Heading 2]  A Close-Up of the Clasp is Shown in Fig. 30.6. What is Wrong?
[3436][Para 001] Lack of retention indicates that the clasp tip is not in an undercut relative to the path of insertion. The fault could lie with the construction of the clasp or the lack of undercut relative to the path of insertion.
[3437][Para 002] There is a design fault in the molar clasp. The clasp arm starts below the survey line and is, therefore, in the undercut relative to the path of insertion. The clasp tip is in contact with the tooth but above the survey line, which lies at the level of the gingival margin. In such situations, the clasp is usually so inflexible in the first third that it is impossible to seat the framework in that area.

[3443][Heading 2]  How Will You Take This Up with the Laboratory?
[3444][Para 001] If you have a good dental laboratory, you cannot afford to lose its confidence or support. You will be aware that metal-based dentures have to be designed using a team approach, especially if you are not an expert (see Case 54).
[3445][Para 002] You are responsible for the several prescription errors, which significantly contribute to the failure of the framework. Conversely, if the laboratory had phoned to query the design faults, they might have been rectified.
[3446][Para 002] You should already have a service level agreement with the laboratory, specifying what each party expects and provides. The laboratory will expect you to provide:
[3447][Para 004] • patient identification
[3448][Para 004] • an accurate legible prescription
[3449][Para 004] • identification of teeth with poor short- and long-term prognosis
[3450][Para 004] • dates that stages are required back in the surgery
[3451][Para 004] • accurate and correctly extended impressions
[3452][Para 004] • adherence to accepted infection control procedures.
[3453][Para 002] In return, you will expect the laboratory to contact you if it has any advice about your design or consider that it could be improved. You would expect it to contact you before changing your design, and you must be willing to take calls as often as necessary for minor queries.
[3454][Para 002] The agreement should include what should be done in the event of errors and provides a basis for negotiating a fair solution. Errors will arise, but often, both parties will need to take some responsibility for them.
[3455][Para 002] Unless you have a surveyor in your practice, you would not have been able to identify that there is no undercut on the distal aspect of the tooth. The dental technician should have pointed out that a better solution would be a circumferential ring clasp, engaging the mesio-lingual undercut from the distal aspect. This is exactly the sort of potential problem that is easily solved through good communication.

[3466][Para 025] Case 31
[3467][Heading 1] Ouch!
[3468][Para 027] Chris Dickinson
[3469][Para 028] Summary
[3470][Para 029] You sustain a substantial percutaneous injury to your foot. What should you do?
[3471][Para 218] 
[3472][Para 008] 
[3473][Para 011] Fig. 31.1 Murphy’s law in action. (Nice shoes – fine for a sunny summers day out, but not appropriate for clinical wear!)
[3474][Para 009]  
[3475][Para 014] History
[3476][Para 007] You are extracting a difficult tooth and have used a luxator to loosen the tooth prior to elevation. While transferring the luxator to the bracket table, you drop it ( Fig. 31.1 ). The luxator impales itself in your foot.
[3477][Heading 2]  What Diseases of Significance May Be Transferred By the Injury?
[3478][Para 001] Most infectious diseases can be transmitted by a percutaneous (sharps) injury, but the main concerns are hepatitis B, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.
[3479][Heading 2]  What Would You Do Immediately?
[3480][Para 001] Encourage bleeding at the injury site, and wash it with soap and water, but without scrubbing the wound. Antiseptics should not be used because their effects on the local defence mechanisms are unknown. Free bleeding should be initially encouraged.
[3481][Heading 2]  What is the Most Urgent Priority and Why?
[3482][Para 001] The most urgent priority is to assess whether there is a significant risk of transmission of blood-borne virus (BBV) infection. Postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) with antiretroviral drugs can significantly reduce the chance of transmission of HIV, but for maximum effectiveness, it is recommended that it be administered within 1–2 hours. The reduction in risk of HIV transmission may be as high as 81%. There is some evidence that some protection of transmission is still possible, even if the administration of the PEP is delayed, even by as much as 48–72 hours.
[3483][Heading 2]  How Could You Obtain Postexposure Prophylaxis, if Required?
[3484][Para 001] The Health Act 2006 requires every National Health Service (NHS) employer to have a policy on the management of exposure to high-risk body fluids such as blood. ‘Saliva associated with dental treatment’ is also classified as high risk because of its likelihood of being contaminated with blood during treatment. Saliva alone is classified as low risk. The policy must ensure that advice is available 24 hours a day and where to obtain that advice and any recommended treatment.
[3485][Para 002] PEP is only available following a formal risk assessment for each individual injury. This involves determining the severity of the injury and the risk that the patient is carrying HIV infection.
[3486][Para 002] The procedure for obtaining a formal risk assessment varies with local circumstances. In hospitals, the infection control consultant(s), hospital casualty or occupational health department will perform the risk assessment and provide the appropriate medication. Those in general practice must contact their local hospital casualty department, which will follow its local guidelines. Each dental practitioner should know the contact number and name/position of the appropriate local department or the nominated person.
[3487][Para 002] When you telephone, you will be asked for details of the injury and of the patient. You will then be told whether or not the injury carries a risk of transmission. To provide this information, you or a member of your team will need to carry out a risk assessment on the patient.
[3488][Heading 2]  What is the Risk of Developing HIV Infection After a Sharps Injury?
[3489][Para 001] The average risk for transmission of HIV is estimated at 3 infections per 1000 injuries. Comparatively, the risk of contracting hepatitis C is 10 times greater, and for hepatitis B, it is 10 times greater (if the recipient is not protected by vaccination).
[3490][Heading 2]  What Factors Affect the Risk of Transmission?
[3491][Para 001] An increased risk of occupationally acquired HIV infection is associated with:
[3492][Para 004] • a deep injury
[3493][Para 004] • visible blood on the device that caused the injury
[3494][Para 004] • injury with a needle that has been in a blood vessel
[3495][Para 004] • a high viral load in the source patient.
[3496][Para 002] The viral load is a measure of the concentration of the virus in blood. It is higher during the primary infection (the so-called window period), reduces with early infection but then rises with symptomatic and late-stage infection (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome [AIDS]). It is reduced with effective treatment.
[3497][Para 002] The risk from a needlestick injury, where the needle has been used to administer a local analgesic, is therefore lower because the needle would not be expected to have been placed in a blood vessel (if an aspirating technique) was used. PEP is therefore often unnecessary for a needlestick injury from a dental anaesthetic needle.
[3498][Para 002] Splashes of infected blood carry a low risk. Splashes on to broken skin or mucous membranes, including the eye, carry a risk of transmission estimated as being less than 0.1%. It is considered that there is no risk of transmission from a splash of blood on to intact skin.
[3499][Para 002] Your injury is a deep injury caused by a sharp instrument covered with blood, and therefore there is a risk of transmission of HIV.
[3500][Heading 2]  The Patient Has Returned To the Waiting Room with Your Nurse. What Will You Say and Do?
[3501][Para 001] In a private area, you should explain to the patient exactly what has happened and that there has been an accident involving a surgical instrument. Inform the patient that there is a practice policy, which is derived from national policy that should be carried out when this happens. Introducing the HIV assessment of the patient in this way depersonalizes the incident and avoids making difficult judgements and discriminating against perceived ‘high-risk’ groups for HIV infection.
[3502][Para 002] The patient should be asked to give informed consent for blood to be taken and tested for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C and for storage of serum. If infection has been transmitted, it will be necessary to compare the patient’s sample and the sample of your blood for industrial injury benefit or insurance purposes.
[3503][Para 002] Lengthy pretest counselling is now no longer a requirement prior to testing for HIV. It is only necessary to provide it if the patient requests it or needs it. The benefits of testing to both the dentist and the patient should be stressed. If the patient has an undiagnosed HIV infection or hepatitis, then an earlier diagnosis is more likely to lead to effective treatment, and the dentist can have the most effective prophylaxis to prevent infection. Most patients will be happy to give a sample of their blood under these circumstances. If not, then the reason for the refusal should be explored as sensitively as possible. It may be that patients have an impression that they have, in some way, done something illegal or hold a false belief about the virus itself.
[3504][Para 002] The general population has little knowledge of hepatitis, but many understand that it is a serious disease and may be aware that it can be transmitted sexually. At a minimum, blood should be obtained to store serum in case testing is required at a later date.
[3505][Para 002] The dentist will most likely not have the facilities to take blood, and the patient can be asked to go to his or her general medical practitioner with a request or to attend the local Accident and Emergency (A&E) department. If the dentist does carry out the test, then the patient should collect the results from his or her general medical practitioner.
[3506][Para 002] The possibility that the patient might be HIV positive will have to be addressed to assess the risk of transmission. This must be done in a sensitive manner, preferably in a private room and with reassurance about the confidentiality of any answers given. These questions should not be asked by the recipient of the needlestick injury because it is difficult to be objective if you are feeling anxious or distressed. However, in dental practice, there may be no other person suitable to handle this issue, and you may have to ask the questions yourself. As an alternative, you could consider asking the patient to speak on the phone to the local casualty officer responsible for the PEP, sexual health clinic medical staff, a sexual health counsellor or other suitably experienced person.
[3507][Para 002] You should remember that it is not the risk factor that denotes the risk of transmission but how the activity that dictates the relative risk takes place (Table 31.1).
[3508][Para 024]  What Questions Would You Ask?
[3509][Para 004] • Are you a regular blood donor in the UK?
[3510][Para 038] (Blood donations are screened for hepatitis B and C, and HIV).
[3511][Para 004] • Have you ever had a blood donation refused?
[3512][Para 004] • Have you ever been diagnosed with hepatitis B or C, or HIV?
[3513][Para 004] • Have you ever lived in HIV high-prevalence areas such as Africa or Asia?
[3514][Para 004] • Have you ever had a blood transfusion or surgery abroad?
[3515][Para 004] • Have you ever had an injury when you have been exposed to someone else’s blood?
[3516][Para 004] • Have you ever injected drugs into a vein?
[3517][Para 004] • Have you ever been imprisoned?
[3518][Para 004] • Do you have sex without using a condom?
[3519][Para 002] A positive answer to any of these questions requires further questioning to understand the degree of risk of acquiring hepatitis B or C or HIV through the activity. In practice, asking these questions does not usually constitute a problem because, in almost all cases, there will be either no risk or a very low risk. Similarly, most HIV-positive individuals will readily disclose the information in this situation.

[3523][Heading 2]  What are the Risk Factors for Contracting HIV infection?
[3524][Para 001] In the UK, in 2016, an estimated 54% of new diagnosis of HIV infection acquired it through men who have sex with men (MSM). In contrast, the numbers of new infections acquired through heterosexual sex were 19% for men and 22% for women.
[3525][Heading 2]  If the Patient Discloses That He or She is HIV Positive, What Information Would You Like To Know? What is the Significance of the Answers (Fig. 31.2)?
[3526][Para 001] Answers and significance are shown in Table 31.2. The answers to these questions would be invaluable to the person making the risk assessment.
[3527][Heading 2]  If the Patient Indicates That He or She is Not HIV Positive But Agrees To an HIV Test, Can You Carry It Out?
[3528][Para 001] Yes, UK National Guidelines for HIV Testing say that it should be within the competence of any trained healthcare worker to obtain consent and conduct an HIV test.
[3529][Para 218] 
[3530][Para 008] 
[3531][Para 011] Fig. 31.2 A ‘safety’ local anaesthetic needle system. Note the retractable sheath over the needle tip.
[3532][Para 009]  
[3533][Para 002] If you do not have the facilities to perform the test, then you can ask the patient’s general medical practitioner to carry out risk assessments, advise, test and provide PEP, if indicated. Your local A&E centre may also have facilities for the urgent, out of hours, assessment and treatment of body fluid exposures in healthcare workers. The result of the test should be given back to the patient by a person qualified to answer any initial questions that the patient may have and who has knowledge of the local specialist services for a prompt referral. This is often the patient’s general medical practitioner.

[3536][Heading 2]  What is PEP? Why Not Simply Take the Drugs Regardless of the Relative Risk?
[3537][Para 001] PEP is preventive treatment started immediately after exposure to an agent that causes infection. The regimes for PEP after exposure to HIV are complex. New drugs are being developed, and knowledge is continually acquired about HIV and the emergence of drug-resistant strains. This, along with the desire to reduce the side effects of PEP to increase compliance, means that the regime for PEP is constantly under review. At the time of writing (2008), the regimen includes a combination of tenofovir, emtricitabine, lopinavir and ritonavir. This is continued for 4 weeks.
[3538][Para 002] The side effects of these drugs include nausea, diarrhoea, dizziness, headache, muscle weakness and skin rash. These effects can be debilitating, and automatic prophylaxis for every sharps injury cannot be advocated. Pregnancy is not a contraindication for PEP, but the evidence for its safe use in pregnancy is limited.
[3539][Heading 2]  What if the Patient Indicates a Risk of HIV Infection To You But You Cannot Obtain a Formal Risk Assessment Within 1 Hour?
[3540][Para 001] You should not delay starting PEP while awaiting either a formal risk assessment or the testing of the patient’s sample of blood. PEP is at its most effective within the first few hours, and preferably the first hour.
[3541][Heading 2]  Do I Have To Give a Blood Sample for Testing?
[3542][Para 001] You will be asked to give a blood sample for storage of serum. This is because you may need to prove that infection was not present at the time of the injury. If the patient is subsequently shown to have an infection, you will be asked to provide a sample for testing 12 weeks (at a minimum) after the injury, or cessation of PEP if it was prescribed.
[3543][Heading 2]  What is the Risk of Transmission of Hepatitis B Through This Injury?
[3544][Para 001] This should be minimal. All members of the dental team should be vaccinated against hepatitis B. Once they have achieved a satisfactory antibody response of 100 mIU/ml to the vaccine, a single booster may be given after an inoculation injury. Nonresponders will receive anti–hepatitis B immunoglobulin on an occupational exposure. If recent evidence of the effectiveness of the recipient’s vaccination is not available, the recipient should have his or her antibody titre checked.
[3545][Para 002] If the recipient is not immune, the risk of transmission has been estimated as high as 30%, especially if the patient is e-antigen positive. Infection can follow transmission of as little as 0.1 ml of blood. Hepatitis B is so infectious that the degree of injury is almost immaterial. In the unlikely event that a nonimmunized individual receives a sharps injury, specific hepatitis B immunoglobulin provides passive immunity and can give immediate but temporary protection after accidental inoculation or contamination with hepatitis B–infected blood.
[3546][Heading 2]  Does This Mean I Have To Give Blood Even if I Know That My Hepatitis B Vaccination is Successful?
[3547][Para 001] You must also ensure that your serum is stored because you may need to show that hepatitis infection was not present at the time of injury.
[3548][Heading 2]  How Can You Determine Whether the Patient is Infectious for Hepatitis B?
[3549][Para 001] Blood must be screened for hepatitis B antigens and antibodies (Table 31.3).
[3550][Heading 2]  What is the Risk of Contracting Hepatitis C?
[3551][Para 001] The risk of contracting hepatitis C through a needlestick injury is 3% if the donor is infected. This risk is therefore higher than for HIV infection but, as for HIV infection, is dependent on the amount of virus present in blood. The consequences can be severe. As many as 75% of individuals who become infected will become chronic carriers. Of these, 20% will go on to develop serious sequelae, for example, cirrhosis, liver cancer or liver failure.
[3552][Para 002] It is estimated that 4 in 1000 individuals in England in the 15–59-years age group is infected with hepatitis C. The majority remains undiagnosed. The prevalence of hepatitis C in intravenous drug users has been estimated to be between 3% and 42%.
[3553][Heading 2]  Is Prophylaxis Against Hepatitis C Available?
[3554][Para 001] No PEP is available. However, early treatment of acute hepatitis C infection may prevent chronic hepatitis C infection.
