[3557][Heading 2]  How Can the Risk of Needlestick or Sharps Injury in the Dental Setting Be Minimized?
[3558][Para 001] Sharps injuries do not always result from needles. Burs, hand instruments (as you have just found out) and other contaminated sharps all constitute a risk. You should:
[3559][Para 004] • utilize ‘sharps-safe’ devices such as safety needle and scalpel systems, that have in-built covers that protect the needle point or blade after use. This is now law under the European Safer Sharps legislation of 2013. This legislation requires clinicians to risk assess the nonsafety sharps used in their practice and replace with safer sharps alternatives, if available, as long as procedural outcome quality can be maintained
[3560][Para 004] • ensure that the entire dental team is trained in the disposal of sharps
[3561][Para 004] • Identify and dispose of needles and other sharps immediately after use in the appropriate sharps container
[3562][Para 004] • always pass instruments with the sharp end pointing away from any person
[3563][Para 004] • remove burs and ultrasonic tips from handpieces immediately after use
[3564][Para 004] • pick up instruments individually
[3565][Para 004] • retract the patient’s cheek with a mirror while administering local analgesia
[3566][Para 004] • never resheath a needle holding the sheath in a hand: If a sharps-safe device is not available, then use a one-handed technique (Fig. 31.3), or dispose of the needle immediately
[3567][Para 004] • never place your finger or your assistant’s finger in front of a sharp instrument such as a scalpel or luxator
[3568][Para 004] • always use a firm finger rest while scaling
[3569][Para 224] 
[3570][Para 092] 
[3571][Para 093] Fig. 31.3 A simple needle sheath holder. The holder is not intended to hold the syringe upright, only to hold the sheath during resheathing.
[3572][Para 004] • dispose of sharps into a solid container (approved to BS 7320)
[3573][Para 004] • ensure that sharps are disposed of by incineration and by an authorized person registered to collect such waste
[3574][Para 004] • use heavy-duty gloves when cleaning instruments prior to autoclaving
[3575][Para 004] • keep your working area well organized and uncluttered with sharps in a separate area. Do not place waste material such as swabs or tissues, over instruments
[3576][Para 004] • always wear appropriate masks, visors or protective eye protection. Modern minimalist designer glasses offer little protection
[3577][Para 004] • footwear should cover the top of the foot. You would not have a problem today if you had worn footwear appropriate for the dental surgery.
[3578][Para 030]  What is Your Last Duty Before You Can Turn Your Back On This Unfortunate Episode?
[3579][Para 001] You must remember to fill in an incident report as required by law (the Reporting of Injuries, Disease and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 1995) and submit it to your employer. If seroconversion occurs, you will need to inform the Health and Safety Executive and the General Dental Council. This will be important evidence for industrial injury benefit or insurance purposes, together with the records in your notes.
[3580][Heading 2]  This Injury Has Ruined Your Day. This Has All Proved So Complex That Next Time You Might Just Wash the Injury and Ignore It. Why Not?
[3581][Para 001] The main reason is the worry that you might contract a blood-borne virus infection from an unsuspected carrier. The effectiveness of PEP – reducing the risk of transmission by greater than 80% – cannot be ignored. Also, it would be unethical for a dentist not to follow up the possibility of developing an infection that could jeopardize the wellbeing of his or her patients. There would also be a risk of transmission to the dentist’s sexual partner(s).

[3587][Para 025] Case 32
[3588][Heading 1] A Swollen Face and Pericoronitis
[3589][Para 027] Tara Renton
[3590][Para 028] Summary
[3591][Para 029] A 23-year-old woman presents in your hospital Accident & Emergency department with a painful swelling of the right side of the face and neck. What is the cause, and what treatment would you provide?
[3592][Para 218] 
[3593][Para 008] 
[3594][Para 011] Fig. 32.1 The patient on presentation.
[3595][Para 009]  
[3596][Para 002] Further information on the diagnosis of soft tissue infection will be found in Case 49.
[3597][Para 014] History
[3598][Para 019] History of Complaint
[3599][Para 007] The patient has suffered worsening pain ‘from her wisdom tooth’ on the lower right side for 5 days. There has been some swelling of the gingiva around the tooth, and she has been unable to bite her teeth together for a few days. Yesterday, she noticed pain in the floor of her mouth and found that moving her tongue was painful. Today, she awoke to find the facial swelling; she feels unwell and has difficulty eating, swallowing and opening her mouth. ( see Fig. 32.1 )
[3600][Para 017] She had an episode of pericoronitis a few months ago and is on her local hospital waiting list to have all third molars extracted. Until the swelling developed, she thought this was just another attack of pain from her wisdom teeth. She has not had facial swelling before and has come straight to hospital.
[3601][Para 012] Medical History
[3602][Para 007] The patient is otherwise fit and well.
[3603][Para 014] Examination
[3604][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[3605][Para 007] There are palpable tender lymph nodes in the upper deep cervical chain and submandibular triangle. Opening is limited to 15 mm interincisal distance.
[3606][Para 017] There is swelling below and around the lower border and angle of the mandible and extending back towards the neck. The swelling is hot, tender, very firm and a dusky red colour centrally. The swelling is not pointing to the skin. There is a marked halitosis.
[3607][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[3608][Para 007] Trismus hampers examination. The lower right third molar can be seen to be partially erupted, the operculum is swollen and pus exudes from below it on gentle probing. The second and third molars appear caries free.
[3609][Para 017] The floor of the mouth is very tender and firm on the right side.
[3610][Heading 2]  What Additional Examinations or Investigations Would You Perform? Explain Why.
[3611][Para 001] It is extremely important to take the patient’s temperature to determine whether the infection is exerting systemic effects.
[3612][Para 002] She has a temperature of 37.8°C (normal temperature 36.8°C) and is therefore pyrexic.
[3613][Para 002] There is a need to confirm that pericoronitis is the cause. It would be prudent to exclude the possibility that this is infection from a nonvital molar, and tests of vitality should be performed. If there were a suggestion from the examination that a lower molar was nonvital, a radiograph might be indicated; otherwise, radiographs would provide little useful information for diagnosis unless another lesion were present.
[3614][Para 015] Diagnosis
[3615][Heading 2]  What Do These Findings Tell You?
[3616][Para 001] The combination of inflammation (swelling, pain, redness and heat), together with local lymphadenitis and pus seen intraorally, indicates an infection. Pericoronitis is present, and this appears to be the primary source of the infection. Trismus is an important sign, indicating that the infection or inflammation has spread to involve the muscles of mastication.
[3617][Para 002] The patient is pyrexic and feels unwell. These features indicate that the infection is exerting a systemic effect. Infection appears to be spreading relatively fast because the swelling has appeared overnight, and there are already systemic signs.
[3618][Heading 2]  Which Type of Infection is This?
[3619][Para 001] It is difficult to tell because the tissues involved are deeply sited. Pus is draining from under the operculum, indicating abscess formation, but this might extend into a soft tissue space or be limited to the tissues around the unerupted tooth. The rapid spread, firmness and tenderness of the tissues (‘brawny’ swelling) indicate cellulitis. This might continue to spread or develop into an abscess. There is probably a mixed infection with a local pericoronal abscess and a spreading cellulitis.
[3620][Heading 2]  To Which Tissue Spaces May Infection Spread From a Lower Third Molar? What are the Boundaries of These Spaces?
[3621][Para 001] Pus from lower third molars may track to many spaces, and spread is unpredictable, depending on many factors including the angulation of the tooth, the size of the follicle, relationship to the second molar, degree of bone loss around both teeth and the anatomical relationships between teeth, bone and muscle attachments in the region. Pus may drain into the mouth from under an operculum, into the buccal or lingual sulcus or into one or more tissue spaces. The routes of spread to tissue spaces are shown in Fig. 32.2 and are described in Table 32.1.
[3622][Heading 2]  In What Tissue Spaces is the Present Infection Tracking, and Why?
[3623][Para 001] This swelling appears to be in the submandibular space. The main infected tissue is not visible and lies around the submandibular gland deep to the body of the mandible. The swelling just spreads round the lower border of the mandible onto the face. Moderate trismus is typical. It is relatively common for this tissue space to be involved in pericoronitis.
[3624][Para 002] There may well be early sublingual space involvement. Infection readily tracks between the submandibular and sublingual spaces around the submandibular gland and the posterior edge of the mylohyoid muscle. In addition, infection may spread through the mylohyoid muscle, which is thin, perforated by blood vessels, and a poor barrier to spread of infection. There is not yet an established sublingual space infection because this would cause extensive swelling of the floor of the mouth and deflect and limit any movement of the tongue. Swelling from sublingual space infection would be readily visible in the lingual sulcus and causes considerable oedema in the loose tissues rather than the firmness and tenderness seen in this patient.
[3625][Para 218] 
[3626][Para 008] 
[3627][Para 011] Fig. 32.2 Paths of spread of infection into tissue spaces from third molars: A, into the sublingual and submandibular space; B, into the parapharyngeal space; C, into the pterygo-mandibular space leading to the infratemporal fossa; D, into the submasseteric space; E, into the buccal space.
[3628][Para 009]  
[3629][Para 002] Pus from lower third molars tends to perforate the lingual plate, which is closer and thinner than the buccal plate. Infection is deflected to either the sublingual or submandibular space by the attachment of the mylohyoid muscle.
[3630][Heading 2]  Is This a Potentially Life-Threatening Infection?
[3631][Para 001] No, but it is serious. The patient’s airway will be at risk if the infection continues to spread posteriorly. This would be potentially fatal, and dyspnoea may develop unexpectedly and with great rapidity. Vigorous treatment of the infection must be commenced immediately.
[3632][Heading 2]  What is Ludwig’s Angina? Is This a Risk?
[3633][Para 001] Ludwig’s angina is a bilateral infection involving the submandibular and sublingual spaces. It is frequently caused by cellulitis when the classic ‘brawny’ (board-like) induration of the neck is seen. Spread of infection involves the epiglottis or parapharyngeal spaces rapidly and causes airway obstruction. Death may also result from septicaemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, or spread in the fascial planes of the neck to the mediastinum. Early diagnosis and prompt surgical intervention combined with definitive airway management are necessary to prevent serious morbidity or mortality.
[3634][Heading 2]  Is There a Risk That the Patient Might Develop This Condition?
[3635][Para 001] It would be possible for this patient’s condition to progress to Ludwig’s angina, but this is not likely to be imminent and treatment will prevent this complication. However, she could also develop airway problems from spread via other routes.
[3636][Para 018] Table 32.1
[3637][Para 021] Paths of Spread of Infection From Lower Third Molars
[3638][Para 014] Treatment
[3639][Para 001] The principles of treatment of odontogenic soft tissue infection are described in Case 49. It is necessary to drain pus, remove the cause of the infection, if possible, and provide antibiotics in selected cases.
[3640][Heading 2]  Where Should This Patient Be Treated?
[3641][Para 001] Admission to hospital will be necessary for this patient because she has systemic effects of infection and there is a risk that infection might impinge on the airway.
[3642][Heading 2]  Is Pus Present? If So, How Will You Drain It?
[3643][Para 001] It is unclear at this early stage of infection whether an accumulation of pus, as well as cellulitis, is present in the submandibular space. Incision may not be helpful. Infection at less important sites might be treated with vigorous antibiotic therapy and removal of the cause, followed by drainage, if required, 1–2 days later. However, because of the proximity of the airway, incision must be performed if there is suspicion of abscess formation. Even within cellulitis, there will be small collections of pus or necrotic tissue. Drainage is the safer option in this case.
[3644][Para 002] The submandibular space must be drained through an extraoral incision, ideally 2 cm below the lower border of the mandible (to avoid damage to the mandibular branch of the facial nerve). In practice, this may not be the appropriate site and a soft spot centrally in the hard swelling is the best place to incise. Distortion of soft tissues makes the position of the mandibular branch difficult to predict. Forceps use or an incision must extend up medially to the mandible to drain the submandibular space. A drain will be required.
[3645][Para 002] Drainage of the sublingual space is not indicated in this case and is rarely necessary. It could be achieved via an incision in the floor of the mouth (taking care to avoid damage to the lingual nerve).
[3646][Para 002] Pus should be released from the pericoronal tissue through either an intraoral incision or extraction of the tooth.
[3647][Heading 2]  How Will You Remove the Cause?
[3648][Para 001] General anaesthesia will be required to drain the swelling. Fibreoptic-guided intubation may be necessary because of trismus and infection around the airway. In a more advanced case with airway oedema or infection, intubation of a conscious patient may be required because paralysis for intubation prevents the patient from keeping the airway open voluntarily. Perforation of the pharynx during intubation is possible if it is oedematous or displaced, and this might drain pus into the upper airway. Forcing the mouth open under anaesthetic may have the same effect.
[3649][Para 002] It may well be possible to remove the third molar at the same time despite the poor access. This breaches the general surgical principle that surgery is best avoided in an infected field, but with effective antibiotic treatment, postoperative complications are rare. Obviously, the decision will depend on the difficulty of the extraction. Removal of the opposing third molar could also speed recovery and reduce the chances of another episode of pericoronitis. Removal of the lower third molar may have to await resolution of the infection.
[3650][Heading 2]  Would You Provide Antibiotics? If So, Which?
[3651][Para 001] Yes, prescription of antibiotics is required in such a case. An initial bolus of intravenous metronidazole would be appropriate, with an oral regimen for a few days afterwards. There is further discussion of antibiotics for odontogenic infections in Case 49.

[3655][Para 025] Case 33
[3656][Heading 1] First Permanent Molars
[3657][Para 027] Mike Harrison
[3658][Para 028] Summary
[3659][Para 029] A 7-year-old girl has pain from a first permanent molar. What is the cause, and how might it affect her dental development?
[3660][Para 218] 
[3661][Para 008] 
[3662][Para 011] Fig. 33.1 The occlusal view on presentation of the upper left quadrant.
[3663][Para 009]  
[3664][Para 014] History
[3665][Para 019] Complaint
[3666][Para 007] The patient’s mother reports that the child suffers intermittent spontaneous discomfort from the upper left teeth.
[3667][Para 012] History of Complaint
[3668][Para 007] The symptoms have been vague, no sleep has been lost and there has been no facial swelling. The patient has complained of the pain three or four times over the last month.
[3669][Para 012] Medical History
[3670][Para 007] The child is fit and well.
[3671][Para 012] Dental History
[3672][Para 007] The child has been a regular patient since the age of 3 years. She has required restorations in four primary molars, with one requiring local analgesia. You have identified a high caries risk in her. Despite intensive preventive advice and diet analysis, new carious lesions have been present at each recall visit.
[3673][Para 014] Examination
[3674][Para 007] You ask the child to point to the painful tooth, and she points to an apparently sound upper left primary canine.
[3675][Para 024]  The Appearance of the Upper Left Quadrant is Shown in Fig. 33.1. What Do You See?
[3676][Para 004] • An amalgam restoration with ditched or raised, defective margins on the palatal aspect of the first primary molar
[3677][Para 004] • An apparently sound amalgam restoration in the second primary molar
[3678][Para 004] • Possible caries in an occlusal pit on the second primary molar
[3679][Para 004] • An erupting first permanent molar with the occlusal surface not fully through the mucosa
[3680][Para 004] • An occlusal cavity in the confluence of the mesial fissures of the permanent molar
[3681][Para 004] • Plaque or food debris in the fissures.
[3682][Para 030]  How Do You Interpret the Information So Far, and What are the Likely Diagnoses?
[3683][Para 001] The child is probably pointing at the wrong tooth; the canine appears intact. Children are often poor historians, and they often have difficulty localizing the source of pain if the pain is not present at the time of examination.
[3684][Para 002] Pulpitis appears likely because the pain appears poorly localized and is relatively intermittent. A history of hot or cold or sweet exacerbating factors would point to this diagnosis. The likely causes are caries beneath a restoration or carious or traumatic pulpal exposure in one of the primary molars. Any primary molar with an unrestored carious cavity or even a clinically sound restoration should be examined closely for signs of pulp necrosis.
[3685][Para 024]  What Features Might Suggest a Necrotic Pulp?
[3686][Para 004] • Extension of caries or fracture into the pulp
[3687][Para 004] • Discoloration of the crown
[3688][Para 004] • Swelling or tenderness in the buccal sulcus adjacent to the tooth
[3689][Para 221] 
[3690][Para 092] 
[3691][Para 093] Fig. 33.2 The left bitewing radiograph.
[3692][Para 004] • Pus draining from a sinus in the mucosa, usually buccally, but occasionally lingually or palatally
[3693][Para 004] • Pus draining from the gingival margin
[3694][Para 004] • Facial swelling
[3695][Para 004] • Well-localized pain.
[3696][Para 002] None of these symptoms and signs is present. Therefore pulpitis seems likely.
[3697][Para 015] Investigations
[3698][Para 024]  What Investigations are Indicated? Why?
[3699][Para 004] • Bitewing radiographs to check the proximity of restorations to the pulp, the extent of the occlusal caries in the permanent molar and to detect small proximal surface carious lesions
[3700][Para 004] • Clinical examination of the other permanent molars for caries
[3701][Para 004] • Tests of sensibility of primary and permanent molars are unlikely to help because the results of such tests are often unreliably reported in children.
[3702][Para 030]  The Left Bitewing Radiograph is Shown in Fig. 33.2. What Do You See?
[3703][Para 099] See Table 33.1.
[3704][Para 015] Diagnosis
[3705][Heading 2]  What is Your Final Diagnosis?
[3706][Para 001] Pulpitis in the upper left first permanent molar in response to a deep occlusal carious lesion. On the basis of the report that pain has been intermittent, the pulpitis is probably reversible, but the rapid progression of the caries and proximity to the pulp may herald involvement of the pulp. Caries must be excavated to discover the true extent of the caries.
[3707][Heading 2]  How Can Caries Be So Extensive Beneath Such a Small Enamel Cavity?
[3708][Para 001] This pattern of caries is sometimes referred to as occult or hidden occlusal caries. This presentation was much less common prior to the 1970s, when caries was more prevalent, lesions larger and fluoride products less available. It has been speculated that the widespread use of fluoride toothpaste has resulted in enamel that is more resistant to smooth-surface caries. Fluoride in toothpaste has little effect on the progression of dentine caries and is less effective against fissure caries. Carious lesions in fissures that progress to dentine might well be able to enlarge greatly before the occlusal enamel cavitates significantly. In a partly erupted tooth such as this, there is no significant occlusal force to fracture away any unsupported enamel. This ‘traditional’ hypothesis seems feasible, but there is currently no evidence that the prevalence of such occult lesions is actually affected by exposure to fluoride. An alternative hypothesis is that there was a developmental defect of dentine mineralization in this tooth. After tooth eruption, cariogenic bacteria at the depths of the fissures could penetrate a more porous enamel–dentine junction and spread rapidly through the defective dentine. This is considered unusual, but it is difficult to prove that it was not present after caries supervenes without pre-eruption radiographs. Radiographs are required to diagnose occult lesions.
[3709][Para 018] Table 33.1
[3710][Para 021] Features Seen in Fig. 33.2
[3711][Heading 2]  Does This Discovery Have Significance for Other Teeth?
[3712][Para 001] Yes, it will be necessary to examine all the other permanent molars clinically again. Carious lesions may have been missed. The discovery of this large lesion should make you more suspicious, and you should consider exploration of any other suspicious fissures as well as obtaining a right-side bitewing radiograph.
[3713][Para 014] Further Investigation
[3714][Para 007] The child has been cooperative for restorative care under local analgesia in the past, so you make an appointment to investigate and, hopefully, restore this tooth. When you open the small occlusal cavity, you discover that the underlying coronal dentine has been almost completely destroyed by caries. Caries extends into the pulp.
[3715][Heading 2]  Why Did the Child Not Experience the Severe Symptoms of Irreversible Pulpitis?
[3716][Para 001] There is no clear correlation between symptoms and pulp vitality or histological evidence of inflammation in mature or immature teeth. The concept of irreversible pulpitis is a useful one for making treatment decisions, but it is only an average reflection of symptoms. It is not unusual for teeth to become nonvital through caries without any significant symptoms. This is even more likely in multirooted teeth or teeth with open apices in which the pulp has a better blood supply.
[3717][Heading 2]  Can the Tooth Be Saved with Root Canal Treatment?
[3718][Para 001] Root canal treatment in immature permanent molars is difficult and the outcome is unpredictable. The canals are wider and generally more accessible than in older patients, but it is virtually impossible to create an effective apical seal with gutta percha in the open apices. If endodontic treatment were necessary and the child could cooperate for the several long sessions of treatment required, nonsetting calcium hydroxide dressings could be placed to induce calcific barrier formation apically. This would require changing every 4–6 months until an apical barrier is felt on gentle instrumentation and a longer-term filling of calcium hydroxide powder or mineral trioxide aggregate could be placed. However, the chances of success are reduced because of the multiple canals. The tooth would remain compromised for future use, for instance, as orthodontic anchorage. The tooth is almost certainly better extracted.
[3719][Heading 2]  If the Pulp Reacted Positively To Sensibility Testing Under a Similar Deep Carious Lesion, What Would You Do?
[3720][Para 001] The guiding principles for the minimally invasive, selective removal of carious tissue are as follows:
[3721][Para 004] • Preserve nondemineralized and remineralizable tissues
[3722][Para 004] • Achieve an adequate seal by placing the peripheral restoration onto sound dentine and/or enamel, thus controlling the lesion and inactivating remaining retained bacteria
[3723][Para 004] • Avoid discomfort/pain and dental anxiety, as both significantly influence treatment/care planning and outcomes (operative methods that are less likely to lead to dental anxiety are preferable)
[3724][Para 004] • Maintain pulp health by preserving residual dentine (avoiding unnecessary pulpal irritation/insult) and preventing pulp exposure (i.e. leave softer, contaminated dentine in close proximity to the pulp, if required).
[3725][Para 002] To adopt a ‘minimally invasive’ approach to carious tissue removal, selective removal to soft dentine should be performed and pulp exposure avoided, where possible.
[3726][Para 015] Care Planning
[3727][Para 024]  What are the Effects of Extraction of a First Permanent Molar On the Developing Permanent Dentition?
[3728][Para 004] • The spaces created close more by mesial movement of posterior teeth than by distal movement of anterior teeth.
[3729][Para 004] • There would be only a small effect on any anterior crowding and minimal effect on the position of the midline.
[3730][Para 004] • Spaces close more rapidly in the upper arch than in the lower. Space closure in the lower arch is frequently incomplete, unless much of the space can be occupied by distal movement of a crowded second premolar.
[3731][Para 004] • Lower second molars tend to tip mesially and roll lingually, producing poor proximal contacts that are prone to food packing and periodontitis in the long term. Upper second molars rotate mesio-palatally as they drift mesially but produce much better proximal contacts than in the lower arch.
[3732][Para 004] • More satisfactory space closure and proximal contacts are produced in the lower arch if the first molar is extracted before eruption of the second molar (see below).
[3733][Para 030]  Do You Require an Orthodontic Opinion?
[3734][Para 001] Yes. If at all possible, an orthodontic opinion should be sought prior to the extraction of any permanent tooth in a child. In this particular case, the patient may well benefit from compensating or balancing extractions. This is a complex area and will require an orthodontic examination to assess crowding, the occlusion of the buccal segments, overbite and overjet.
[3735][Heading 2]  What are Compensating and Balancing Extractions, and What are Their Benefits?
[3736][Para 001] Compensating extractions are those of the opposing molar; balancing extractions are extractions of the contralateral tooth.
[3737][Para 002] Compensating extractions prevent overeruption of the opposing molar to maintain the correct occlusal level. Balancing extractions maintain the symmetry of the arch.
[3738][Heading 2]  How Will the Orthodontist Decide Whether To Perform Compensating or Balancing Extractions?
[3739][Para 001] The decision depends on weighing several factors:
[3740][Para 004] • The presence of the other permanent teeth, including third molars
[3741][Para 004] • The condition of the other permanent molars – whether they are already compromised by caries or large restorations
[3742][Para 004] • The presence of crowding in the buccal and labial segments
[3743][Para 004] • The acceptability of overbite and overjet
[3744][Para 004] • The stage of dental development
[3745][Para 004] • The patient’s likely future need and wish for orthodontic treatment and their likely compliance.
[3746][Para 222] 
[3747][Para 008] 
[3748][Para 011] Fig. 33.3 The extracted tooth.
[3749][Heading 2]  What is the Ideal Age To Extract First Permanent Molars?
[3750][Para 001] Extraction must be performed at the ideal time to minimize the adverse effects of extraction listed above. The stage of dental development, rather than the chronological age, is important. The crucial factor is the stage of development of the lower second molar because this determines how satisfactorily the space in the lower arch will close. The range of acceptable development is from crown completion to mineralization of one-third of the root, but primarily before it has erupted into the mouth. A frequently held opinion is that the appearance of an interradicular crescent of bone in the second molar indicates the optimal stage for first molar extraction (at approximately 9.5 years of age). More recent evidence suggests that other factors may be involved in favourable eruption of the second molar and that early extraction is not problematic. Radiography is required to confirm the stage of development and to ensure that the third molars and the second premolars are present and normal.
[3751][Para 002] Late extraction of poor-quality first molars is to be avoided, wherever possible, specifically when the unerupted second molar is no longer completely encased within bone, as seen radiographically.
[3752][Heading 2]  Does Extraction of First Permanent Molars Complicate Orthodontic Treatment?
[3753][Para 001] It used to be said that extraction of all four first permanent molars doubled orthodontic treatment time and worsened the prognosis. This held good only for removable appliance treatment and does not apply to fixed appliance treatment. However, closure of residual lower first molar spaces does pose complex anchorage problems, and it will sometimes be preferable to delay the extraction of compromised but symptom-free first molars until the second permanent molars have erupted. This is a further reason why a full orthodontic assessment is required.
[3754][Heading 2]  How Can You Change the High Caries Risk?
[3755][Para 001] Providing dietary advice to prevent dental caries, use of age-appropriate fluoride toothpastes and topical application of high-concentration fluoride varnishes are important tools to address an identified high caries risk. Bonded resin sealants on vulnerable pits and fissures must be carried out carefully to ensure a good seal, and if moisture control is difficult when molars are partially erupted, blocking out fissures with provisional glass-ionomer cement sealants is to be encouraged.
[3756][Para 002] Children can be members of a family with a high caries risk, possibly with low expectations of dental health, and changing family behaviours can be challenging. You should aim to work with the family to identify achievable goals. Contemporaneous notes of all discussions with the patient and the carer must be recorded.
[3757][Para 015] Further Information
[3758][Heading 2]  The Extracted Tooth is Shown in Fig. 33.3. What Do You See?
[3759][Para 001] Part of the crown has been removed to expose the carious cavity. On the left, you can see a small periapical granuloma at the apex of the palatal root. The pulp was therefore nonvital despite the lack of symptoms. On the right, you can see a large defect extending from the enamel to the pulp. The central occlusal enamel is completely unsupported but has not fractured. The carious dentine is hardly discoloured because it is progressing rapidly.

[3761][Heading 1] A Sore Mouth
[3762][Para 027] Davinder Bains, and Helen McParland
[3763][Para 028] Summary
[3764][Para 029] A 55-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman presents to you with a complaint of a sore mouth. You must make a diagnosis and institute treatment.
[3765][Para 218] 
[3766][Para 008]

[3768][Para 009]  
[3769][Para 014] History
[3770][Para 019] Complaint
[3771][Para 007] The patient complains of occasional soreness on the inside of her cheeks and white patches on the inside of her lips.
[3772][Para 012] History of Complaint
[3773][Para 007] The patient first noticed a burning sensation 3 months ago. She notes that the soreness is brought on particularly when she eats sour and mildly spicy foods. She had noticed that the white patches on her lips started around the same time, and she thinks these patches are spreading.
[3774][Para 012] Medical History
[3775][Para 007] The patient is generally fit and well. She is not on any current or recent medication. She has never smoked and consumes less than 5 units of alcohol a week.
[3776][Para 014] Examination
[3777][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[3778][Para 007] The patient appears fit and well. There are no rashes on her face, and no cervical lymph nodes are palpable. White patches were visible on the upper lip.
[3779][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[3780][Para 001] The mouth is well lubricated with saliva, and the patient has good oral hygiene. There is discolouration of the occlusal surface of the lower posterior molars and only minimal occlusal amalgam restorations. The appearance of the left and right buccal mucosa are shown in Fig. 34.1 and of the palate in Fig. 34.2.
[3781][Heading 2]  Describe What You See On the Buccal and Palatal Mucosa.
[3782][Para 001] The buccal mucosa is affected bilaterally by reticular white striae and associated poorly defined diffuse brown pigmentation found mostly at the periphery of the striae. The white striae extend from the posterior buccal mucosa to the commissural region. In the left buccal mucosa (see Fig. 34.1a), there is a central solid patch of white mucosa. Poorly defined striae are seen in the right soft palate. In the right buccal mucosa, the white appearance of the buccal mucosa is most prominent in the occlusal plane (see Fig. 34.1b). There are no obvious red patches and no ulceration.

[3786][Para 009]  
[3787][Para 024]  What is Your Differential Diagnosis?
[3788][Para 016] 1. Lichen planus
[3789][Para 016] 2. Lupus erythematosus (systemic [SLE] or discoid [DLE])
[3790][Para 016] 3. Lichenoid drug reaction.
[3791][Para 030]  Justify This Differential Diagnosis.
[3792][Para 001] The combination of reticular and diffuse white areas on a background of slight redness almost certainly indicates one of these three conditions. The lesions cannot always be diagnosed by their clinical appearance alone, although there can be some differentiating features to each condition.
[3793][Para 020] Lichen Planus.
[3794][Para 001] This condition is the commonest of the three possible diagnoses and most prevalent in women in their 5th and 6th decades of life. The striae and lacy patterns on the buccal mucosa are distinctive of lichen planus and are typically bilateral. Lichen planus can also cause white patches on the lip and palate as in this patient, although this is less common.
[3795][Para 020] Lupus Erythematosus (LE).
[3796][Para 001] The mouth may be involved in lupus erythematosus, either as part of SLE or in DLE. In both conditions, clinical features of oral mucosa resemble those of lichen planus and lichenoid reactions, but some findings may help in the diagnosis. LE is more frequent in females, and there is a higher prevalence in patients of Afro-Caribbean ethnicity. Lesions in LE often have a central ulcer or erythematous area around which the striae tend to radiate, rather than follow the random pattern of lichen planus. Lesions are also typically asymmetrical and affect the hard and soft palates, which are less frequently involved by lichen planus or lichenoid reactions. LE is much rarer than either of the other two possibilities but unilateral involvement of the palate and lip involvement, as well as the patient’s ethnic background, indicates that LE should remain a consideration in this case.
[3797][Para 020] Lichenoid Reaction.
[3798][Para 001] Oral lichenoid reactions may be localized (in response to topical triggers such as restorations) or more widespread, in which case they are usually caused by medication. Some features that point to a lichenoid drug reaction rather than lichen planus include acute onset, extensive ulceration, asymmetrical distribution and severe involvement of the dorsum of the tongue. Lesions may also affect sites that are less commonly affected by lichen planus such as the floor of the mouth. Lichenoid reactions may be clinically indistinguishable from lichen planus. In this case, a lichenoid drug reaction can probably be ruled out because the patient is not on any medication, although double-checking recently discontinued prescriptions and over-the-counter drugs is necessary to be certain. The location and distribution of the lesion do not correspond to any dental restorations so a topical lichenoid reaction can be ruled out.
[3799][Heading 2]  How Do You Explain the Darker Pigmented Areas?
[3800][Para 001] The combination of white patches and striae with pigmentation is potentially confusing, but the pigmentation is almost certainly a secondary effect called inflammatory or postinflammatory pigmentation. In diseases where the epithelium is damaged or becomes inflamed, melanin pigment formed by melanocytes in the epithelium fails to transfer into the epithelial cells and ‘drops out’ into the underlying connective tissue. Here, it is recognized as a foreign material and phagocytosed by macrophages and only slowly degraded, producing patchy brown discolouration. Inflammatory pigmentation is usually seen in dark-skinned individuals.
[3801][Heading 2]  What Further Questions and Examinations are Appropriate? Explain Why.
[3802][Para 032] See Table 34.1.
[3803][Para 017] On further questioning, the patient reports an itchy rash on the flexor surface of her forearms ( Fig. 34.3 ) and shins which developed around the same time as her oral white patches.
[3804][Para 002] Her rash is consistent with cutaneous lichen planus, which typically presents as raised itchy red/purple lesions. She has never had a facial rash, and she reports no other symptoms. Rashes in lupus typically affect the head and neck and sun-exposed skin.
[3805][Para 015] Investigations
[3806][Heading 2]  Is a Biopsy Indicated? Why?
[3807][Para 001] Yes. Ideally, biopsy should be performed in the majority of white lesions in the mouth, especially if the patient reports high alcohol or any tobacco consumption. When there is extensive mucosal involvement, ulceration or atrophy, or when the clinical presentation is not typical, other conditions need to be excluded through biopsy for example in this case, lichenoid reactions and LE. It is not always possible to distinguish between these three diseases histologically but microscopic characteristics may help favour one of these three entities. Histological features always need to be interpreted within the context of the clinical presentation and the results of other tests. A biopsy is also useful to exclude unexpected diseases, particularly dysplasia. Proliferative verrucous leucoplakia and other potentially malignant disorders can be misdiagnosed as lichen planus, particularly when the lichen planus forms plaques rather than striae. A further reason for biopsy is that lichen planus itself is considered to have a very low risk of malignant transformation.
[3808][Para 002] For this patient, incisional biopsy is indicated.

[3816][Heading 2]  Which Part of the Lesion Would You Remove for Biopsy?
[3817][Para 001] The biopsy specimen should be taken from the most clinically representative area, including both red and white areas, if present. If there is ulceration, it should be avoided because the epithelium is required for diagnosis, and there will be florid inflammation masking the histological features. The specimen should be elliptical, about 8–10 mm long, 5–6 mm wide and an even 3–4 mm deep. In this case, a biopsy specimen was removed from the left buccal mucosa, as shown later in Fig. 34.4.
[3818][Para 024]  What Other Investigations Would You Perform?
[3819][Para 020] Autoantibody Screen.
[3820][Para 001] If SLE is a possibility, an autoantibody screen may provide evidence to support the diagnosis. A serum sample should be sent for antinuclear antibody (ANA) extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) and double-standed DNA (dsDNA) assessment. Four-fifths of patients with systemic disease are ANA positive, often having high titres. A high titre of anti-dsDNA antibody is almost exclusive to SLE but is positive in only 50% of cases. Autoantibodies against Smith (Sm) antigen (part of the ENA screen) is also highly specific for SLE. In DLE blood tests are less helpful for diagnosis because few patients have a positive ENA or ANA. Individuals with lichen planus or lichenoid reaction are likely to have a negative autoantibody screen.
[3821][Para 020] Microbiological Tests.
[3822][Para 001] When lichen planus or a lichenoid reaction is widespread or becomes symptomatic, the possibility of superimposed candidal infection should be considered. The thick keratotic epithelium is more prone to infection compared with normal epithelium. A smear from the surface of the lesions on each side is an ideal investigation. Saliva sampling for candidal counts may also be helpful. This has the advantage that the organism is cultured for complete identification and sensitivity testing to antifungal agents. The disadvantage is that it cannot distinguish candidal infection from candidal carriage. In this case, saliva sampling was done.
[3823][Para 020] Other Tests.
[3824][Para 001] Because the patient has oral mucosal and cutaneous involvement, she may be a candidate for systemic medical management. Therefore baseline renal and liver function screens may be useful for monitoring any adverse drug effects. Furthermore, renal function tests may be useful in eliminating possible kidney involvement in LE.

[3828][Para 009]  
[3829][Heading 2]  In the Biopsy Specimen Shown in Fig. 34.4, What Do You See?
[3830][Para 001] The left image (a) at low power shows mucosa with underlying fat. The surface epithelium is slightly thinner than normal buccal epithelium and has a red layer of keratin just visible at the surface. There is a well-demarcated inflammatory cell infiltrate in a band immediately below the epithelium within the superficial connective tissue. The band is denser towards each side of the picture. At this magnification, the cells cannot be definitely identified as inflammatory cells, but this is the most likely explanation for the very cellular zone. There are also several foci of inflammatory cells in the deeper tissues, one particularly large one associated with a vessel near the bottom of the picture. The basement membrane is prominent.
[3831][Para 002] The middle image (b) is a higher-power view and shows the interface between the epithelium and connective tissue. The very cellular layer seen in (a) is composed of lymphocytes. Lymphocytes have infiltrated into the basal and suprabasal layers of the epithelium and caused the basal epithelial cells to undergo apoptosis. Apoptotic cells are visible as shrunken, very pink cells with nuclear remnants (black arrows). There is no remaining clearly defined basal layer of epithelial cells, and the cells lying at the basement membrane have the appearance of prickle cells. The surface is parakeratinized. Buccal epithelium is normally nonkeratinized, except along the occlusal line as a result of friction.
[3832][Para 002] The image on the right (c) is from an area adjacent to (b) at similar magnification. The surface here is orthokeratinized, a feature that is abnormal for the buccal mucosa. As in (b), cells in the basal layer have the appearance of prickle cells. The basement membrane is thickened. Within the lamina propria, there are macrophages containing melanin pigment (yellow arrows), which has ‘dropped out’ of the overlying epithelium. This explains the pigmentation seen clinically.
[3833][Heading 2]  How Do You Interpret the Histological Findings?
[3834][Para 001] The dense band-like infiltrate of lymphocytes and lymphocytic infiltration of the basal cells with focal basal cell degeneration, apoptosis, loss of basal cells and a thickened basement membrane are typical of lichen planus. There are no histological features to allow definitive diagnosis of LE over lichen planus, although the perivascular infiltrate seen in Fig. 34.4a may be suggestive of the fomer. For this reason, the biopsy diagnosis is ‘consistent with lichen planus or a lichenoid reaction or LE’. The histological findings should be correlated with clinical features before finalising a diagnosis.
[3835][Para 014] Other Results
[3836][Para 007] In this case, the autoantibody screen result was negative, and no Candida was found in the saliva or biopsy sample. The full blood count, as well as the haematinic, renal and liver function screen results were normal.
[3837][Para 015] Diagnosis
[3838][Heading 2]  What is Your Final Diagnosis? Explain Why.
[3839][Para 001] The final diagnosis in this case is lichen planus with oral and cutaneous involvement. Lichenoid reaction has been excluded because the patient is not on any medication, and the distribution of the lesions do not correspond to any dental restorations. The cutaneous findings are not typical of LE and the autoantibody screen was negative. With these other options excluded, the diagnosis of lichen planus is made despite the unusual distribution of disease in the mouth.

[3841][Para 021] Treatment Options
[3842][Para 015] Treatment
[3843][Heading 2]  How Would You Manage This Patient’s Oral Symptoms?
[3844][Para 001] The aim of management of lichen planus is to relieve symptoms because the underlying disease process is not easily influenced without the use of drugs that have significant adverse effects. Many patients with lichen planus have no symptoms andtherefore do not require any active treatment. Several options are listed in Table 34.2, and choice of treatment largely depends on severity of symptoms. Gingival lichen planus is aggravated by plaque, and in some patients, maintaining optimal oral hygiene can be difficult because of pain. Patients should be helped to maintain a high standard of oral hygiene. Some patients also find the detergent sodium lauryl sulphate (SLS) in certain toothpastes an irritant, and they should switch to an SLS-free toothpaste. Highly flavoured toothpastes should also be avoided.
[3845][Para 017] In this case, the oral symptoms were managed with 0.5 mg betamethasone dissolved in 5–10 ml water as a mouthwash for 2–3 minutes up to three times daily. The patient was referred to her general medical practitioner for the management of her skin lesions. At the review appointment, the patient reported that she was much more comfortable and that her oral symptoms were under control.
[3846][Heading 2]  What Considerations Would You Take Into Account When Determining the Frequency of Follow-Up Appointments?
[3847][Para 001] The frequency of review appointments depends on whether or not systemic medication has been prescribed, because this may require monitoring for adverse effects and the clinical appearance. There is also a very low risk of malignant transformation in oral lichen planus. There is controversy surrounding the exact rate of malignant transformation, but it is likely to be less than 0.1%. Some authorities suggest that malignant change is more common in nonreticular forms of oral lichen planus. Lesions in high-risk sites such as the floor of the mouth, should be monitored. Patients should be instructed to look out for changes in the clinical appearance of the lesions.

[3850][Para 025] Case 35
[3851][Heading 1] A Failed Bridge
[3852][Para 027] Sophie Watkins
[3853][Para 028] Summary
[3854][Para 029] A 40-year-old man has had a missing upper incisor replaced by a spring cantilever bridge. This has become decemented, and you must assess the options for replacement.
[3855][Para 218] 
[3856][Para 008] 
[3857][Para 011] Fig. 35.1 Anterior view of the patient at presentation with the bridge which replaced the upper left central incisor reinserted.
[3858][Para 009]  
[3859][Para 014] History
[3860][Para 019] Complaint
[3861][Para 007] The patient complains that his anterior bridge has become detached. He would like it recemented or replaced.
[3862][Para 012] History of Complaint
[3863][Para 007] The bridge had been satisfactory for many years but became detached about 2 years ago. It was recemented and had been firm until yesterday when it fell off the teeth without warning.
[3864][Para 012] Dental History
[3865][Para 007] The upper left central incisor was lost as a result of a bicycle accident when the patient was 16 years of age. The tooth was completely avulsed, and the adjacent upper right central incisor was fractured. The missing central incisor was initially replaced by a simple spoon denture and a few years later by a spring cantilever bridge attached to full-coverage crowns on the left first and second premolars. The other upper central incisor was root treated and a post crown fitted. The present bridge is a replacement made about 8 years ago after the cantilever spring fractured. The patient has never had an upper left lateral incisor.
[3866][Para 014] Examination
[3867][Para 019] Intraoral Examination
[3868][Para 007] The patient’s dentition is in good condition, with a few carious lesions and a small number of restorations. The upper left premolars are the abutment teeth and have conservative crown preparations. There is superficial caries over much of the surface of the first premolar crown preparation and a larger cavity at the distal gingival margin. The mesial surface of the second premolar is also carious. Both abutment teeth are vital. The gingival condition is good except for bleeding on probing between the abutment premolars. Here, the probing depth is 4 mm. The bridge can be replaced, and the appearance with it fully seated is shown in Fig. 35.1. The caries in the first premolar is exposed below the crown margin.
[3869][Heading 2]  What is the Prognosis for This Bridge? Why?
[3870][Para 001] Hopeless. Fig. 35.1 shows that the aesthetic result is not good. The bridge pontic has moved buccally and upwards, probably a combined result of alveolar ridge resorption and distortion of the spring cantilever. It also appears to have moved distally, increasing the median diastema. The abutment teeth will both require re-restoration, and the first premolar appears to be very carious. In the long term, both abutment teeth are likely to be compromised because of the risk of further caries and periodontitis.
[3871][Heading 2]  Why Was This Method of Replacing the Central Incisor Chosen Originally?
[3872][Para 001] Although a well-designed partial denture should not compromise the health of the remaining dentition, most patients prefer a fixed prosthesis without palatal coverage for a single tooth replacement.
[3873][Para 002] The spring cantilever design was considered suitable in this case for the following reasons:
[3874][Para 004] • It allows spacing (diastemas) between adjacent crowns. The spaces would have been present because the lateral incisor on that side was developmentally absent. A fixed-fixed bridge restoring the space, utilizing adjacent teeth as abutments, would not allow spacing to be maintained, resulting in a pontic that was either too wide, or with uneven, asymmetrical spacing between the anterior teeth on the other side.
[3875][Para 004] • The upper right central incisor was not a suitable abutment tooth for conventional fixed bridgework, having been traumatized, root filled and crowned with the use of a prefabricated post.
[3876][Para 080]  What Replacement Restorations Would You Consider? Explain Your Choices.
[3877][Para 020] A new spring cantilever bridge
[3878][Para 001] For the reasons noted above, the spring cantilever design remains a good choice, and it has served this patient fairly well. However, the abutment teeth will require restoration and may no longer be suitable abutments. The initial design in this case utilized linked abutment teeth (a ‘double-abutted’ design), which is no longer considered appropriate because forces placed on the bridge tend to result in the loss of cementation of one of the retainers; this is difficult to identify on clinical examination and results in caries in the associated abutment tooth, as occurred here. In addition, double abutting also hampers oral hygiene measures, and this may predispose the patient to periodontal involvement and marginal caries, as may also have occurred in this case. Therefore if a new spring cantilever were to be constructed, it would be advisable to modify the design to incorporate a single abutment tooth. This, as with all abutments, would need to be sufficiently robust to support a spring cantilever design with sufficient coronal tooth structure, clinical crown height for retention and resistance form and periodontally sound.
[3879][Para 002] An adhesive bridge could be supported on the upper left canine, with the central incisor replaced by a cantilevered pontic. This would be possible because the lateral incisor is missing but would not normally be practical in this situation. This alternative has the advantage of minimal/no tooth preparation and allows maintenance of the median diastema. Success is dependent on the area of enamel available for adhesive bonding on the palatal aspect of the canine, and the occlusal relationship. This is a realistic option because canines typically make good abutment teeth for adhesive bridgework because of their large crown offering a larger surface area of enamel for adhesion and a robust supportive root form. This also has the advantage that the existing abutment teeth could be restored independently, reinstating their embrasures to help prevent further caries and periodontitis.
[3880][Para 002] A single tooth implant would allow a restoration independent of the adjacent and abutment teeth. It would permit both mesial and distal spacing and would therefore provide an aesthetically acceptable restoration, comparable with the appearance achieved by the spring cantilever bridge. However, an implant would entail surgery, more protracted treatment and higher patient costs. A provisional restoration would be required until the definitive coronal restoration is placed. An implant should provide a successful long-term restoration, provided the patient is motivated and does not have any active periodontal disease. As with the adhesive bridge, the original abutment teeth would no longer be involved in the restoration of the anterior segment and can be restored independently, which may enhance their long-term prognosis.
[3881][Para 002] The above options should be presented to patients in a way that allows them to make an informed decision with regard to which one they prefer. It is essential that the advantages and disadvantages are explained in a way patients can understand and that discussions relating to this are carefully and clearly documented in the contemporaneous clinical record, with written information given to patients in the form of a letter outlining the options to allow them time to make their decision away from the clinical environment. In this case, discussion regarding the upper right central incisor will also be relevant because this tooth is somewhat aesthetically compromised and may also have a guarded long-term prognosis. It is not suitable as a bridge abutment for the reasons described above and may be a candidate for replacement at some stage. This may influence the patient’s decision-making process.
[3882][Para 017] After discussing the options, the patient opted to have the bridge replaced by a single tooth implant, thus maintaining the upper right central incisor for the time being because it is still functioning well.
[3883][Para 024]  What are the Components of a Typical Single Tooth Implant?
[3884][Para 016] 1. The implant or fixture that is osseointegrated to the surrounding bone. Anterior single tooth implants are normally between 10 and 13 mm in length and approximately 4–5 mm in diameter.
[3885][Para 016] 2. An abutment that is attached to the implant by an abutment screw. Abutments are provided in various designs (according to use) and lengths. For single tooth restorations, it is important to have an antirotational lock which prevents rotation between implant and abutment and crown.
[3886][Para 016] 3. The crown, which can be made of porcelain or porcelain bonded to metal. This is made on a prefabricated component that fits the abutment precisely. Single tooth implant crowns can either be screw retained as an integral part of the abutment or cemented onto the abutment, depending on the orientation of the implant and whether the screw access hole, which will be in the long axis of the implant, emerges on the palatal or labial aspect of the crown. If labially/palatally placed, a cemented crown would be required to conceal it. From a maintenance perspective, a screw-retained crown may be considered preferable because this is more easily removed to allow access to the implant. This option may not always be possible because of factors affecting the positioning of the implant itself, including the available bone quantity, quality, position, or how this affects the emergence profile of the final restoration.
[3887][Para 015] Investigations
[3888][Heading 2]  What Further Features Require Examination or Investigation To Assess Suitability for an Implant? How Would You Assess Them, and Why Need They Be Considered?
[3889][Para 032] See Table 35.1.
[3890][Para 015] Treatment
[3891][Heading 2]  What Precautions Must Be Taken When Inserting an Implant?
[3892][Para 001] The implant is inserted into a hole which must be made with a drill matched to the implant. A surgical stent (see Table 35.1) is used to ensure that the implant is placed at the correct angulation and depth so that the implant does not perforate the cortical bone and allows the final restoration to be constructed with a suitable emergence profile. Careful sterile technique is essential, and particular care must be taken to ensure that the bone is not damaged by overheating. Copious irrigation and slow drill speeds are required. The exact method of insertion and subsequent restoration depends on the type of implant and the manufacturer. The implant is normally left in place for 3–6 months to allow osseointegration before loading. A partial denture would provide a satisfactory temporary replacement during this period.

[3900][Para 001] Osseointegration is the direct structural and functional connection between living bone and the surface of a load-bearing implant. This implant was firm and symptomless and appears successful radiographically. There is bone in close apposition to the implant surface along its whole length. The head of the implant is level with, or only just above, the surrounding bone. Failure would be indicated by mobility, signs of infection, peri-implant radiolucency or progressive marginal bone loss.

[3907][Para 024]  At Each Review, How Would You Determine Whether the Implant is Successful?
[3908][Para 004] • The implant is immobile when tested clinically.
[3909][Para 004] • A periapical radiograph does not reveal any peri-implant radiolucency.
[3910][Para 004] • Radiographs taken at annual visits should reveal stable crestal bone levels after the first year of loading. This can be assessed with periapical radiography using the paralleling technique, to allow reliable comparison between successive radiographs. Ideally, the threads of the implant should be clearly defined to allow accurate assessment of crestal bone levels.
[3911][Para 004] • Vertical bone loss, assessed radiographically, should be less than 0.2 mm per year in subsequent years.
[3912][Para 004] • There is absence of signs and symptoms such as pain, infections, elevated probing, or, for mandibular implants, neuropathies, paraesthesia or a violation of the mandibular canal.

[3919][Heading 1] Skateboarding Accident?
[3920][Para 027] Jennifer C. Harris
[3921][Para 028] Summary
[3922][Para 029] A 6-year-old boy with a facial injury attends late one afternoon without an appointment. Assess the child, and decide what treatment he needs.
[3923][Para 014] History
[3924][Para 019] Complaint
[3925][Para 007] The child complains of loose front teeth and that his mouth is sore and it hurts to eat.

[3927][Para 007] The child’s mother says that he fell off his skateboard and banged his teeth. The injury occurred the previous evening when he was playing at a friend’s house.

When asked if he has injuries elsewhere, he does not respond at first and then shows abrasions on his knees and elbows.

No other injuries are visible on those parts of his arms and legs that are not covered by clothing.

[3972][Para 015] Diagnosis
[3973][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[3974][Para 001] Facial abrasions, intraoral soft tissue injuries, subluxation of the upper right primary central incisor and lateral luxation of the upper left primary central incisor.
[3975][Para 002] The findings are consistent with the history of an accidental fall from a skateboard but are accompanied by bruises on the neck and ear, which give cause for concerns about possible physical abuse.
[3976][Para 024]  What Factors in the History Make You Concerned That This May Be Child Abuse or Neglect?
[3977][Para 004] • The history is vague and does not fully explain the injuries observed.
[3978][Para 004] • There was some delay in seeking dental care, without satisfactory explanation.
[3979][Para 004] • There was possibly a lack of adult supervision to ensure his safety.
[3980][Para 080]  Why Does the History Not Explain the Injuries?
[3981][Para 004] • There are injuries to soft tissues not overlying bony prominences: in this case, the neck and ear.
[3982][Para 004] • There are injuries to both sides of the body: the left side of the neck and right ear.
[3983][Para 004] • The pattern of bruising on his neck is suggestive of a slap mark. There are parallel lines of petechial haemorrhages between the fingers, where blood was forced out of capillaries by the force of the slap.
[3984][Para 004] • Bruising on both inner and outer aspects of the pinna of the ear suggests injury from pinching or pulling.
[3985][Para 004] • The neck and ear are rarely injured in accidental falls because they lie in a ‘triangle of safety’, protected by the shoulder and the parietal area of the skull.
[3986][Para 002] You might also have a sense of unease about the boy’s behaviour and interaction with his mother. The patient seems unwilling to talk about the cause of the injury.
[3987][Heading 2]  How Certain Can You Be That Injuries are Not Accidental?
[3988][Para 001] Care must always be exercised when interpreting injuries. It is important to realize that there are no specific injuries that are diagnostic of abuse, even though some patterns of injury are highly suggestive of it. There will almost always be a degree of uncertainty, especially with the type of injuries seen in a dental setting. In all such cases, you are likely to be weighing evidence from a variety of sources and must come to a judgement yourself. There are no easy answers.
[3989][Para 002] A torn labial frenum used to be considered diagnostic of abuse, but it is now recognized that it may also result from an accident. In this case, accompanied by other intraoral injuries, it would not, in itself, cause you to suspect abuse. However, if seen in a young child who is not yet walking and is, therefore, unlikely to have fallen, it is a sign that should always be taken seriously and discussed with an experienced colleague.
[3990][Heading 2]  What General Risk Factors for Child Abuse are Recognized?
[3991][Para 001] Recognized risk factors are shown in Table 36.1. Such features may be noted during the appointment, be identified from previous knowledge of the family or be present in your dental records. They may be helpful when deciding how to interpret your findings and in deciding what to do.
[3992][Para 015] Treatment
[3993][Heading 2]  What Dental Treatment is Necessary?
[3994][Para 001] Advise analgesia, as required; the drug of choice in this age group is paracetamol suspension. Recommend a soft diet. Give instruction in oral hygiene, including use of chlorhexidine gel applied twice daily for a week. Advise the mother and patient to return if there is increasing pain or swelling.
[3995][Para 002] Inform the parent of the possibility of damage to developing permanent teeth and the need for follow-up. Make the first follow-up appointment after 1 week.

[3997][Para 021] Risk Factors for Child Abuse and Neglect
[3998][Para 002] Splinting the teeth is unnecessary and would hinder the recommended oral hygiene procedures.
[3999][Heading 2]  What Else Should You Do?
[4000][Para 001] The injuries to the mouth were probably caused in a skateboard accident. They are consistent with this explanation and accompanied by injury on the elbows and knees. However, there are unexplained injuries on the neck and ear. You need to decide what must be done about these additional injuries.
[4001][Para 002] It is often helpful to discuss the case with a suitably experienced colleague or advisor such as a nurse or social worker from the local safeguarding children advisory service. Telephone numbers for advice and referral should be available in the practice. A flowchart to guide your actions is shown in Fig. 36.6.
[4002][Para 002] In this case, it is likely that you would be advised to make an immediate referral to children’s services (alternatively known as ‘social services’). A full assessment of the child is needed to determine whether the unexplained injuries have occurred as part of a pattern of sustained and deliberate child abuse or may be the result of momentary loss of control by a frustrated parent (or other individual inside or outside the family). This child may urgently need protection, or the family may need advice and support.
[4003][Heading 2]  What Do You Say To the Child and the Parent?
[4004][Para 001] Explain that you are concerned about the marks on his neck and ear and that you need to arrange for someone else to look at him. Ask for consent to phone children’s services to share this information. If the parent questions whether this is really necessary, you will need to stand your ground and give further explanation. You should explain that your responsibility is not simply the health of the boy’s teeth but also his general welfare and safety and that you recognize that his mother will want that too. Research shows that being open and honest from the start results in better outcomes for children.
[4005][Heading 2]  Are There Any Circumstances in Which You Would Not Discuss Child Protection Concerns with the Parents?
[4006][Para 001] Although it is generally considered good practice to explain your concerns to the child and his or her parents, there are certain exceptions:
[4007][Para 004] • Where discussion might put the child at greater risk
[4008][Para 004] • Where discussion would impede a police investigation or social work inquiry
[4009][Para 004] • Where sexual abuse by a family member or organized/multiple abuse is suspected
[4010][Para 004] • Where fabricated or induced illness (formerly known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy) is suspected
[4011][Para 004] • Where parents or carers are being violent or abusive, and discussion would place you or your staff at risk
[4012][Para 004] • When parents or carers are not present and it is not possible to contact them without causing undue delay in making the referral.
[4013][Para 002] In these circumstances, first seek advice from your dental defence organization or from senior child protection professionals. Reasonable judgement must be made in each case.
[4014][Heading 2]  What Do You Do Next?
[4015][Para 001] Phone children’s services to make a child protection referral. You will be asked to give the full name of the child, date of birth, address, gender, school and the name of the person(s) with parental responsibility. Discuss your concerns, and agree on what will happen next. Agree with the social worker what you will tell the parent and child and what will happen next.
[4016][Heading 2]  Anything Else To Remember?
[4017][Para 001] You need to keep comprehensive contemporaneous clinical records, including any explanation given by the parent and the child in their own words. You should include both a written description and a diagram of the injuries. Differences between fact and your opinion should be clearly stated. You should include a summary of the discussions with the child and the parent.
[4018][Para 002] If other members of the dental team have been involved, they also should record their observations.
[4019][Heading 2]  What Action is Required Later?
[4020][Para 001] The telephone referral must be followed up in writing within 48 hours. Children’s services should confirm receipt of the referral, decide on the next course of action and give feedback to you.
[4021][Para 218] 
[4022][Para 008]
