[4024][Para 009]  
[4025][Para 002] If you hear nothing, you should telephone again to confirm that your referral has been received and acted on. You should be prepared to write a report for a child protection case conference, if requested to do so. You will also need to ensure that the child receives a follow-up dental appointment.
[4026][Para 002] It is important to acknowledge that involvement in child protection cases can be distressing. If necessary, take time to talk through your experiences with a trusted colleague, or seek further advice from the safeguarding advisory service.
[4027][Para 002] Research shows that dentists do not always respond effectively when they recognize signs of child abuse and neglect. This is a serious matter: It may be some years before another opportunity arises for someone to take action to protect the child from the misery of ongoing maltreatment. Furthermore, to ignore suspicions about abuse could result in a complaint against you and may put your registration at risk or lead to a professional negligence claim. The General Dental Council’s ethical standards guidance makes it clear that all members of the dental team must ‘follow local child protection procedures if you suspect that a child might be at risk because of abuse or neglect’.
[4028][Para 002] When dentists are asked why they do not follow child protection procedures correctly, they often say that they want to be really certain before taking action. You can be reassured that the responsibility for making a diagnosis of abuse is not something you have to shoulder alone but is always shared by a multiagency team. Discuss your concerns with the experts and refer early.
[4029][Para 002] Do not fear that the family will suffer drastic action. Children are only removed from their families when there is no safe alternative. Emphasis is usually given to supporting the family to protect their own children.
[4030][Para 002] You may be concerned about possible litigation if you get it wrong, yet the law places the child’s welfare as paramount and protects healthcare professionals who make child protection referrals in good faith. This is a challenging area of practice, but expert help is available.
[4031][Heading 2]  Is Dental Neglect Abuse?
[4032][Para 001] Child abuse is defined in four categories: physical abuse, emotional abuse, sexual abuse and neglect. Abuse or neglect may be by inflicting harm or by failing to prevent harm. Recently, there has been increased agreement that severe untreated dental disease can indicate neglect and should prompt a child protection referral.
[4033][Para 002] Under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child 1989, children have a right to ‘the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health and to facilities for the treatment of illness and rehabilitation of health’. To enjoy optimal oral health, children need their parents to provide a suitable diet, facilities for and help with oral hygiene and access to dental treatment when needed. There is no doubt that oral disease can have a significant impact on a child’s general health and can cause pain, loss of sleep and even poor growth and quality of life. Once dental problems have been explained to parents or carers, and appropriate and acceptable dental treatment has been offered to restore oral health, the following would be of concern:
[4034][Para 004] • Repeated missed appointments
[4035][Para 004] • Failure to complete planned treatment
[4036][Para 004] • Repeatedly returning in pain
[4037][Para 004] • Requiring repeated general anaesthesia for dental extractions.
[4038][Para 002] Preschool children are particularly vulnerable, and in such cases, it is recommended that you contact the child’s health visitor to discuss how you might work together to support the family to ensure that the child’s needs are met. This contributes to ‘safeguarding’ children, namely, not only protecting children from abuse and neglect but also taking a wider range of measures to promote their health and development and to minimize risks of harm. In many cases, lack of knowledge and difficulty accessing care account for the apparent neglect. However, if a child is suffering significant harm from untreated dental disease, it will be necessary to make a child protection referral without delay.
[4039][Para 025] Case 37
[4040][Heading 1] An Adverse Reaction
[4041][Para 027] Chris Dickinson
[4042][Para 028] Summary
[4043][Para 029] A 38-year-old woman becomes unwell during routine dental treatment at your general dental practice. What would you do? What is the cause?
[4044][Para 014] History
[4045][Para 019] Complaint
[4046][Para 007] The patient is to have a crown preparation performed on her lower second molar and a very small amalgam placed in an upper premolar on the same side. You have given an infiltration of 1.0 ml lidocaine (lignocaine) 2% with adrenaline (epinephrine) 1:80 000 (12.5 μg/ml) and used a further 2-ml cartridge to give an inferior dental and lingual nerve block. Having finished injecting, you turn away to prepare some instruments. Almost immediately the patient says she feels ill. She is clearly apprehensive and is holding her chest complaining of palpitations.
[4047][Para 012] Dental Treatment History
[4048][Para 007] The patient is in the middle of her first course of treatment in many years. She has been scared about visiting a dentist for some years. You have started a course of treatment and carried out several simple restorative procedures. You had seen her only 2 days ago to place several direct restorations, using three cartridges of a local anaesthetic. These restorations and one extraction have all been carried out under local anaesthesia using lidocaine (lignocaine) 2% with adrenaline (epinephrine) 1:80 000.
[4049][Para 012] Medical History
[4050][Para 007] The patient is apparently fit and well. The medical history indicates no allergies.
[4051][Para 024]  What Would You Do?
[4052][Para 004] • Reassure the patient; encourage regular breathing.
[4053][Para 004] • Have her lie down supine or with her head slightly down.
[4054][Para 004] • Feel the skin and take her pulse.
[4055][Para 004] • Prepare oxygen in case it is needed.
[4056][Para 002] This approach applies unless the patient were pregnant or obese, in which case having her lie flat on her side would be more appropriate.
[4057][Para 024]  One Minute Later, the Patient Feels No Improvement. What Would You Do?
[4058][Para 004] • Take the blood pressure, and monitor her pulse.
[4059][Para 004] • Check for pallor.
[4060][Para 004] • Check for rash or urticaria.
[4061][Para 004] • Wait and observe for dyspnoea while considering possible causes.
[4062][Para 030]  What Causes Would You Consider?
[4063][Para 001] Intravascular injection of the local anaesthetic appears to be the most likely cause of her symptoms because they started immediately after the inferior dental block. However, vasovagal attacks are common, and an acute medical or mental health problem unrelated to dentistry should not be excluded. Thus, possible causes include:
[4064][Para 004] • vasovagal attack
[4065][Para 004] • adverse reaction to the local anaesthetic
[4066][Para 004] • hypersensitivity reaction
[4067][Para 004] • myocardial infarction or angina attack
[4068][Para 004] • acute anxiety (panic) attack.
[4069][Para 030]  Is This a Vasovagal Attack? Explain Why.
[4070][Para 001] The features of a vasovagal attack are pallor, apprehension, restlessness, nausea, bradycardia, weak slow pulse and loss of consciousness (fainting). The loss of consciousness may be immediate. In more severe attacks, there may be clonic muscle contractions or rigidity as a result of cerebral hypoxia. None of these symptoms is seen in this patient. In addition, vasovagal attacks are usually caused by fear or anxiety and so may precede the injection. Patients will usually be able to explain that they feel faint either before or after the attack.
[4071][Heading 2]  Is This is Myocardial Infarction?
[4072][Para 001] No. The symptoms and signs of myocardial infarction are crushing central chest pain, sometimes radiating to the arm or the neck, dyspnoea and possibly vomiting, which may be followed by cardiac arrest. There is usually, although not always, an individual or family history of angina, coronary artery disease or hypertension.
[4073][Para 018] Table 37.1
[4074][Para 021] Unwanted Effects of Local Anaesthesia
[4075][Heading 2]  What are the Unwanted Effects of Local Anaesthesia with Lidocaine (Lignocaine) and Adrenaline (Epinephrine)? What are Their Causes and Signs and Symptoms?
[4076][Para 032] See Table 37.1.
[4077][Para 017] While these possibilities run through your mind, the patient remains conscious but nervous and agitated. She gradually calms down and says that the palpitations are reducing. She takes a few breaths of oxygen but refuses more after a few minutes and says that she feels better. Her pulse is 105 beats/min and her blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg.
[4078][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[4079][Heading 2]  What is Your Differential Diagnosis, and Why?
[4080][Para 001] Intravascular injection is the most likely diagnosis, the patient’s symptoms being caused by the vasoconstrictor component of the local anaesthetic. The solution contains 1:80 000 adrenaline (epinephrine), which causes tachycardia felt by the patient as palpitations. Intravascular injection is most common after inferior dental blocks and posterior superior dental blocks because of the high vascularity of the injection site.
[4081][Para 002] Anxiety can itself produce a significant level of adrenaline, but levels rise more slowly; and the patient would have to be very nervous, positively phobic, to generate endogenous adrenaline to the levels found in intravascular injection of the local anaesthetic. This patient is nervous but has recently accepted routine dental treatment without problems. A vasovagal attack would be a much more likely effect of marked anxiety, but a panic attack brought on by the emotional response to the tachycardia will need to be managed.
[4082][Heading 2]  Could the Local Anaesthetic Given 2 Days Ago Contribute To This Reaction?
[4083][Para 001] No, the adrenaline (epinephrine) will have been rapidly moved into the circulation from the site of injection in spite of its intrinsic vasoconstrictor effect. Its action is then terminated quickly by reuptake into the noradrenergic fibres and other cells and tissues. Metabolism takes place within these at various sites throughout the body by the action of the enzyme catechol-O-methyl transferase and to a much lesser degree by monoamine oxidase in the liver before undergoing renal excretion.
[4084][Para 002] As far as the local anaesthetic component is concerned, the symptoms experienced by this patient are not typical of an overdose, and in any event, the half-life of lidocaine (lignocaine) is only of the order of 90 minutes. Therefore, this event being related to either the local anaesthetic or the vasoconstrictor given at the previous appointment can be safely ruled out.
[4085][Para 018] Table 37.2
[4086][Para 021] Maximum Recommended Doses
[4087][Heading 2]  Is an Overdose Possible? What are the Maximum Recommended Doses of Local Anaesthetic Solutions Used in Dentistry?
[4088][Para 001] Although theoretically possible, it is actually quite difficult to administer an overdose of a local anaesthetic in dentistry. Because of the nature of the cartridge syringe and needle system used, doses are accurately counted and monitored, and the need to change a cartridge affords ‘thinking time’ for the operator. This is in contrast to the use of a local anaesthetic in the other areas of the body where large volumes of drug can be administered into body spaces more easily.
[4089][Para 002] However, one cannot be complacent. In recent years, the recommendations for maximum safe doses of local anaesthetics in the head and neck area have been reviewed. Because of the vascularity of the region and the recognition that vasoconstrictors do not hold the drug in place for as long as was previously thought, the recommendations have been rationalized and the maximum recommended doses reduced.
[4090][Para 002] It is important to realize that advice based on a recommended number of cartridges or fixed dose does not take into account different formulations. Some cartridges contain only 1.8 ml of solution, whereas others contain 2.2 ml and, therefore, 22% more drug. Thus, four cartridges of the larger volume will contain almost the same dose of the local anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor as five of the 1.8-ml cartridges. The concentration of drug also varies from preparation to preparation. Importantly, patients come in different shapes and sizes, and fixed dose recommendations are based on the safety limit for the elusive ‘fit 70-kg man’!
[4091][Para 002] Another way to consider the safe total dose is to relate it to body weight and the amount in a dental local anaesthetic cartridge (which varies among drugs).
[4092][Para 002] Thus, 2% lidocaine in a 2.2-ml cartridge is equivalent to 44 mg of drug. With a maximum safe dose of 4.4 mg/kg, a single cartridge could be administered for every 10 kg of body weight. For a 70-kg male, the maximum safe dose would be seven cartridges, and for a 20-kg child, the maximum safe dose would be two cartridges.
[4093][Para 002] Current recommendations are expressed in the form of the maximum safe dose per kilogram of body weight given over a period of treatment of 1 hour. The maximum recommended doses are shown in Table 37.2.
[4094][Para 002] These limits apply to all preparations of local anaesthetics irrespective of the presence of or type of vasoconstrictor. It is no longer considered that larger doses are safe to be given in one treatment session if the preparation contains vasoconstrictor.
[4095][Heading 2]  Immediately After Calming Down, the Patient Claims That She Must Be Allergic To the Local Anaesthetic. Is This Possible?
[4096][Para 001] It is possible but is extremely rare. Only a handful of cases of genuine lidocaine (lignocaine) hypersensitivity have been recorded. Very few older patients have given a convincing history of allergy to local anaesthetics, in some cases backed up by hospital investigations. This is because older preparations contained preservatives such as benzoates to which hypersensitivity was possible. The worst offending preservatives are no longer used, although a reaction to sodium metabisulphite preservative has been reported on rare occasions. Patients can be tested for hypersensitivity to anaesthetic agents, but this is only worthwhile when a typical allergic reaction is suspected.
[4097][Para 002] Hypersensitivity is unlikely to follow repeat administration of lidocaine (lignocaine) for dental anaesthesia. A much more potent cause is repeat application of lidocaine (lignocaine) creams to the skin. Local anaesthetic pastes and solutions should be handled with care; the dentist is more at risk compared with the patient.
[4098][Heading 2]  Would a Switch To Prilocaine with Felypressin in the Future Be Prudent?
[4099][Para 001] No, lidocaine (lignocaine) with adrenaline (epinephrine) has been used successfully in the past for this patient, and there is no evidence of an idiosyncratic or allergic response to the preparation itself. Prilocaine produces a shorter period of analgesia, and the patient should not be subjected to suboptimal pain relief because of the remote possibility of another intravascular injection. There is no evidence that prilocaine, with or without felypressin, is safer.
[4100][Para 002] Such a switch would reinforce the patient’s perception that she is allergic to local anaesthetics. A spurious history of allergy might compromise the patient’s general health. Lidocaine (lignocaine) is used in the emergency treatment of myocardial infarction and in many other medical situations.
[4101][Heading 2]  How Can the Risk of Intravascular Injection Be Minimized?
[4102][Para 001] Good injection technique is the key to reducing the risks associated with intravascular injection because it ensures that the minimum amount of anaesthetic solution is used. The solution should be injected slowly, thus reducing the risk of injecting a bolus into a vessel. An aspirating technique should always be used, even though it does not always guarantee success; because of the narrow needle diameters used in dentistry, aspiration is relatively poor.
[4103][Para 002] It is impossible to completely avoid the tip of the needle entering a vessel. Indeed, in some very vascular areas, penetration of a vessel is not the cause because the solution can be absorbed into blood almost as rapidly as it can be injected. Nothing can guarantee the prevention of complications of intravascular injection.
[4104][Para 015] Another Possibility
[4105][Heading 2]  If the Patient Had Genuine Anaphylaxis, What Causative Agents Would You Consider?
[4106][Para 001] Anaphylaxis to other agents is considerably commoner than hypersensitivity to local anaesthetics. A number of other agents used in dental surgery should be considered before the local anaesthetic is suspected.
[4107][Para 002] Latex hypersensitivity is increasing in prevalence and is commoner in patients with atopia and those who have come into contact with latex repeatedly such as healthcare workers, those with spina bifida or those who are subjected to multiple surgical procedures. Rubber dam, gloves and even traces of rubber from local anaesthetic cartridges or drug vials can trigger reactions. Other less obvious items that may contain latex are face masks with elastic components, amalgam carriers, plastic syringes, aspirator tubes, orthodontic elastics and emergency equipment such as ventilating bags and sphygmomanometer cuffs.
[4108][Para 002] Although some items containing natural rubber latex may still exist, most are being phased out now and are being replaced by silicone or the synthetic ‘nitrile’ rubber (acrylonitrile butadiene rubber, Buna-N, NBR), which is a copolymer. However, allergies to nitrile products have been reported, albeit extremely rarely.
[4109][Para 002] These usually cause type 1 reactions such as urticaria, asthma or anaphylactic shock. Glove powder is a particularly potent vehicle for dissemination of the latex allergen into the atmosphere; therefore, to reduce the risk of allergy developing among the dental team, use of powdered gloves should be avoided. In addition to allergy to latex, staff and, more rarely, patients may develop hypersensitivity to acrylics, composite resins, dentine bonding agents, eugenol, cleaning and disinfection solutions and metal alloys. Almost all materials may be allergenic to some individuals. The formulations of the worst offending agents have been changed, and the most notorious ones, particularly some synthetic impression materials and self-curing acrylics, are no longer available in their original forms. It is worth remembering that many of these agents are irritant as well as allergenic and that rashes may not be true hypersensitivity reactions.

She also recalls having gum abscesses on at least two occasions in the past and being prescribed antibiotics.

[4122][Para 007] The patient reports being fit and well, takes no medications, and has no allergies, as revealed by her medical history questionnaire.
[4123][Para 024]  What Additional Specific Questions Will You Ask the Patient? Explain Why
[4124][Para 020] Oral Hygiene Regimen
[4125][Para 001] The patient tells you that she cleans her teeth twice daily with an electric toothbrush. She uses floss on her anterior teeth every day and only occasionally on her molars and premolars, where access is more difficult.

[4129][Para 001] Poorly controlled diabetes has a strong association with periodontitis. This is relatively severe periodontitis, and there is a history of multiple abscesses. These features do not necessarily indicate an underlying condition, but it would be worthwhile to exclude diabetes and ask the patient to see her doctor to be tested. Another feature that might suggest diabetes is rapid attachment loss within a short period in middle age, suggesting type 2 diabetes.
[4130][Para 020] Family History of Premature Tooth Loss
[4131][Para 001] A positive family history can be associated with development of periodontitis at a younger age.
[4132][Para 020] Stressful Life
[4133][Para 001] Patients who cope poorly with stress are more likely to develop periodontitis.

[4136][Para 001] No cervical lymphadenopathy is present. The temporomandibular joint and mandibular movements appear normal.
[4137][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[4138][Para 007] The other mucosa and soft tissues of the mouth are normal except for a buccal sinus just anterior to the upper right first premolar. All teeth, with the exception of the third molars, are present. All remaining molars and two premolars contain small- to medium-sized amalgam restorations. No caries is detected.
[4139][Heading 2]  How Will You Assess the Patient’s Periodontal Health and Oral Hygiene?
[4140][Para 001] On examination of the mouth, the inflammatory status of the gingival tissues should be assessed visually, noting any redness, swelling and increased inflammatory exudate. The presence, location and extent of any visible plaque or calculus should also be noted, and can be recorded by using various indices. A common index used is the Plaque Control Record (Fig. 38.1), where a disclosing solution is painted on all exposed tooth surfaces. After the patient has rinsed her mouth, using a probe, the operator examines each stained surface for plaque at the gingival margin. If plaque is found, the information is recorded on the form in the appropriate spaces. After all the teeth are examined and scored, the index is calculated by dividing the number of plaque-containing surfaces by the total number of available surfaces.
[4141][Para 218] 
[4142][Para 008] 
[4143][Para 011] Fig. 38.1 An example of a plaque control record. Plaque was detected on 67 of the 112 surfaces, giving a score of 60%.
[4144][Para 009]  
[4145][Para 002] In this case, previous clinical records have documented pre-existing periodontitis, and this should trigger a full periodontal assessment immediately. In the case of a patient who has not previously been encountered and does not present with historical periodontitis ascertained through history and examination (interproximal recession), the health of the periodontal tissues should be screened by performing the Basic Periodontal Examination (BPE) with a World Health Organization (WHO) probe.
[4146][Para 002] The measurements that form a full periodontal assessment are:
[4147][Para 004] • probing depths with bleeding on probing
[4148][Para 004] • recession
[4149][Para 004] • mobility
[4150][Para 004] • furcation involvement
[4151][Para 002] Probing depth and recession and measurements are made at six points around the circumference of a tooth: mesially, at the midpoint and distally on the buccal and palatal surfaces. Probing depths are measured from the gingival margin to the base of the periodontal pocket. Presence or absence of bleeding on probing should always be recorded in conjunction with a six-point pocket chart. The presence and extent of palpable subgingival calculus should also be briefly noted. The distance from the cemento-enamel junction to the gingival margin indicates the amount of recession. The sum of recession and probing depth gives the extent of clinical attachment loss (CAL).
[4152][Para 002] Measurements are described in Table 38.1.
[4153][Para 002] Clinical photographs and results of these examinations are shown in Figs 38.2 and 38.3, respectively. The patient’s clinical appearance is not immediately suggestive of severe periodontal problems, and the relatively minor amount of clearly visible plaque and gingival inflammation appear disproportionate to the extensive CAL. This highlights the patient’s susceptibility to periodontitis and the importance of periodontal screening and subsequent comprehensive clinical assessment.
[4154][Para 017] On closer inspection, gingival inflammation is more noticeable palatally, and suppuration can be seen to be associated with the upper left lateral incisor distally, upper right first molar and upper left first premolar teeth. Furthermore, loss of the papilla between the upper central incisors could be indicative of previously treated periodontitis.

[4166][Para 015] Diagnosis
[4167][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[4168][Para 001] Under the previous periodontal disease classification system (1999), this case would have been diagnosed as generalized severe chronic periodontitis. Additional diagnoses include endodontic–periodontal lesions of the upper right first molar, upper left first premolar and lower left second molar.
[4169][Para 002] The periodontal disease classification system has since been revised (2017), and staging and grading of periodontitis is now similar to staging and grading in oncology. The system has been simplified by the British Society of Periodontology to make it workable for clinicians (see References). Staging of periodontitis reflects the severity and extent of the disease and is based on radiographic bone loss (Table 38.3). Periodontitis should also now be graded to estimate future risk of disease progression and responsiveness to standard management. If previous radiographs are not available to assess the rapidity of bony destruction, grading is calculated using the ratio of percentage bone loss adjusting for age (see Tables 38.3 and 38.4). In this case, because previous radiographs were available (see Fig. 38.5) clearly showing evidence of rapid destruction, calculating the ratio was not necessary. When known risk factors are also present (e.g. smoking and diabetes), they are now highlighted to support the diagnosis.

[4201][Para 021] Assessment of Stability of Treated Periodontitis
[4202][Para 094] It is important to note that a higher probing depth of 5 mm or 6 mm in the absence of bleeding may not necessarily represent active disease, in particular soon after periodontal treatment.
[4203][Para 124] ∗  A patient with successfully treated periodontitis, with sites of gingival bleeding, remains at high risk of disease recurrence at those sites and of progressive attachment loss. Therefore, gingival inflammation is defined as bleeding at a shallow site of 3 mm or less rather than 4 mm or less, as is the case in gingival health. Where the probing depth is 4 mm with bleeding, or higher, this is no longer a ‘closed pocket’ and is assumed to be unstable periodontitis.
[4204][Para 002] This case would, therefore, be classified as ‘generalized periodontitis; stage IV; grade C; currently unstable (pockets >4 mm with bleeding on probing)’. Parameters to assess stability after treatment are shown in Table 38.5.
[4205][Para 024]  This Patient Has Many Teeth with Furcation Involvement. What are the Possible Sequelae?
[4206][Para 004] • Further and more rapid periodontal destruction
[4207][Para 004] • Devitalization of the tooth
[4208][Para 004] • Periodontal abscess
[4209][Para 004] • Root caries.
[4210][Para 030]  This Patient Has Already Had Nonsurgical Periodontal Treatment. Why Has the Disease Progressed?
[4211][Para 001] Although her oral hygiene was fair, because of her susceptibility to periodontitis, further improvement is necessary to achieve an excellent standard (ideally, a full-mouth plaque score <10%) and to ensure that this is maintained meticulously. Interdental spaces are more effectively cleaned with interdental brushes, and floss should only be used in spaces where they do not fit. Resolution of pocketing where an angular pattern of bone loss with nonsurgical treatment is also more challenging, and multirooted teeth also may present inaccessible furcations. With improvement of oral hygiene, surgical intervention is a management option to reduce probing depths.
[4212][Para 002] The patient is also an irregular attender, and the importance of her role in controlling the condition must be clearly communicated. Because there is no cure for periodontitis (other than extraction!), the patient should be advised that at the outset, she will need to commit to maintaining excellent oral hygiene and attending the clinic regularly for necessary active and supportive periodontal therapy for an indefinite period. The patient’s responsibility in the long-term management of this condition should be clearly discussed prior to undertaking any treatment, and should be documented carefully in the patient’s records.
[4213][Para 014] Management
[4214][Para 001] Extraction of the teeth with a hopeless prognosis should be advised.
[4215][Heading 2]  Which Teeth Would You Advise To Be Extracted?
[4216][Para 001] The teeth with endodontic–periodontal lesions require extraction. Because devitalization has occurred as a result of progression of periodontitis rather than endodontic failure, further restorative treatment is highly unpredictable and likely to fail.
[4217][Para 002] The upper second molars have minimal bone support, and unfavourable root morphology will make treatment difficult; therefore, extraction must be considered.
[4218][Para 002] Extensive bone loss around the distal root involving the interradicular region is compromising the lower left first molar. The lower right first and second molars also have severe angular bone loss distally, a poor prognosis and may require extraction in the long term.
[4219][Para 002] However, all molars are in occlusion and functional. With the exception of the upper right first molar, the molars could be preserved in the short or medium term. A definitive decision on extraction could be delayed until an attempt has been made to improve the periodontal condition of these teeth. If these extractions are carried out, the patient may have to accept a premolar-to-premolar occlusion or a prosthesis.
[4220][Para 002] The patient did not wish to have any teeth extracted and accepted a plan to help retain a completely natural dentition for as long as possible. All molars will be retained for the time being. The risk of further bone loss potentially affecting adjacent teeth and of development of pain and abscesses should be clearly communicated to the patient and documented.
[4221][Para 024]  At This Stage, What are the Treatment Goals?
[4222][Para 016] 1. Improvement of the periodontal condition of the teeth that do not have a hopeless prognosis
[4223][Para 072] a. Elimination of suppuration and reduction of bleeding on probing
[4224][Para 072] b. Reduction of pockets depths to below 5 mm
[4225][Para 072] c. Establishing and facilitating maintenance of periodontal health with the aim of preserving as many teeth as possible in the long term, especially premolar-to-premolar
[4226][Para 016] 2. Removal of the teeth with a hopeless prognosis and any necessary replacement if the patient agrees.
[4227][Para 002] A premolar-to-premolar occlusion provides acceptable function, although the appearance may be unacceptable, depending on the visibility of the molar spaces. The upper second molars provide useful occlusion, and, although compromised, may last for many years with conservative treatment.
[4228][Heading 2]  What Treatment Should Be Provided Initially?
[4229][Para 001] Because of the presence of plaque, palpable subgingival calculus and inflammation, further nonsurgical periodontal treatment was provided, as described below. Prior to provision of the treatment, the benefits and potential side effects were clearly communicated to the patient and documented in the notes – in particular, the possibility of dentine sensitivity, recession affecting appearance and increased food trapping.
[4230][Para 016] 1. Oral hygiene advice: The patient was disclosed, and a suboptimal plaque score was revealed – 35%. Toothbrushing technique was checked and modified to ensure that the gingivae adjacent to palatal aspects of the upper teeth and the lingual aspects of the molar were covered. Interdental brushing technique was also checked and modified so that larger sizes were used in the upper interproximal areas, and the importance of daily use was reinforced.
[4231][Para 016] 2. Oral hygiene was reviewed and was found to have improved, with the full mouth plaque score dropping to 15%. Supragingival instrumentation and root surface debridement of all quadrants were carried out using ultrasonic and hand instruments under local anaesthesia over two visits. Oral hygiene instructions were reinforced at every visit.
[4232][Para 016] 3. Reassessment was performed, with full 6 point pocket charting 2–3 months after completion of root surface debridement.
[4233][Para 002] The patient maintained a more effective cleaning regimen, and over a period of 3 months, the suppuration was eliminated. However, residual pocketing with bleeding was still present, especially in the regions with angular defects. Conservative management was successful in limited areas; because the patient’s oral hygiene was good, more complex treatment options and specialist referral were considered. There can be a cost implication to specialist treatment, with potential discomfort from surgery and subsequent follow-up treatment. It is advisable to forewarn the patient of this prior to referral.
[4234][Para 002] The patient opted for specialist referral and had successful regenerative periodontal surgery carried out in the upper anterior and lower right molar regions. She also returned for extraction of the upper right first molar and the upper left first premolar, and an immediate partial denture was fitted (Fig. 38.6).

[4255][Heading 2]  Do Hemisected or Root-Resected Teeth Require Restoration?
[4256][Para 001] Ideally, yes. The large area of exposed dentine and risk of fracture of the overhanging crown after root resection do demand full coverage restorations. However, complex and expensive treatment is often avoided because hemisected and root-resected teeth are compromised.
[4257][Para 002] Hemisected or root-resected teeth that have proved themselves stable over a period of months or years are best restored. The tooth remains in function and is an excellent semipermanent solution to this patient’s problem.
[4258][Para 002] Root treatment, surgery, restoration and maintenance add up to a huge investment in time and money spent on just one very compromised tooth root, and the option of extraction and potential prosthodontic replacement needs to be carefully discussed with the patient and documented.
[4259][Para 017] After completion of the periodontal and restorative periodontal treatment, the patient is receiving ongoing 3-monthly supportive periodontal therapy to maintain the improvements made to her periodontal condition and reduce the risk of relapse.
[4260][Para 002] Medico-legally, it is important to keep detailed records of all discussions regarding diagnosis, management options and treatments carried out. It should be ensured that patients clearly understand the significance of periodontitis and the critical role they play in managing it on a regular basis, especially in relation to plaque control, smoking cessation and diabetes control. Adequate notes detailing advice given at each appointment should be kept. Patients should also be advised of likely consequences if treatment advice is ignored.

[4290][Heading 2]  How Would One Assess the Possibility of a Mandibular Fracture?
[4291][Para 001] Fracture is suggested by:
[4292][Para 004] • Pain, swelling and tenderness at the fracture site
[4293][Para 004] • Bleeding, bruising or haematoma at the fracture site
[4294][Para 004] • Displacement or step deformity
[4295][Para 004] • Change in the occlusion
[4296][Para 004] • Mobility of fragments or of teeth
[4297][Para 004] • Difficulty opening the mouth or movement in lateral excursion
[4298][Para 004] • Paraesthesia or anaesthesia in the distribution of nerves involved near the fracture.
[4299][Para 030]  How Would One Assess the Possibility of a Fracture of the Zygoma or the Facial Skeleton?
[4300][Para 001] In addition to the features noted above, a fractured zygoma may present with:
[4301][Para 004] • Facial asymmetry and flattening of facial contour (may be masked by overlying soft tissue swelling for a few days)
[4302][Para 004] • Step deformity along the relevant infraorbital margin
[4303][Para 004] • Altered sensation (anaesthesia or paraesthesia) of the cheek, nose, upper lip and teeth
[4304][Para 004] • Circumorbital ecchymosis (bruising around the eye)
[4305][Para 004] • Restricted eye movements and diplopia (double vision).
[4306][Para 017] Extraoral examination did not indicate the presence of a fractured mandible, zygoma or maxilla. There was no restricted mouth opening, no pain on opening and no obvious swelling associated with the temporomandibular joint.
[4307][Para 017] The lips were slightly swollen but not lacerated.

[4315][Para 030]  What Investigations Would You Ensure Had Been Carried Out At the Patient’s First Attendance At the A&E Department? Explain Why.
[4316][Para 001] A posterior–anterior radiograph of the chest should have been taken if the patient had difficulty breathing, to determine whether the lost tooth fragments were inhaled.
[4317][Para 002] Facial radiographs should have been taken to assess the possibility of fracture of the maxilla, zygoma or mandible. A suitable selection of films for this purpose would be a 10-degree and 30-degree occipito-mental view, a posterior–anterior view of the jaws and a panoramic view.
[4318][Para 002] A soft tissue radiograph of the lips should have been taken if a laceration had been present and tooth fragments were unaccounted for. This would exclude the possibility that small tooth fragments have been embedded in the lip. Larger fragments of tooth in the lip are usually obvious on examination, palpation and debridement of the wound. Such fragments may cause infection or exaggerate the amount of scar tissue, affecting the appearance of the lip.
[4319][Para 002] These films may have been overlooked at first examination in the A&E department if the fractured teeth were not recognized or if the hospital’s medically trained staff concentrated on excluding more serious head and neck injuries.
[4320][Para 024]  What Features of the Anterior Teeth are Important At Examination? How Would You Examine Them?
[4321][Para 020] Mobility of the Teeth
[4322][Para 001] The teeth should be tested gently for mobility in a bucco-palatal direction, using a mirror handle or, if very tender, using the operator’s fingers. A further examination of any mobility can be carried out under local anaesthesia when a more accurate assessment can be made. The degree of movement and the position of the fulcrum of movement (to help distinguish between root and coronal fractures, although this is not always easy) should be noted after assessing the upper and lower anterior teeth. In this case, the upper and lower central incisors were firm and not mobile.
[4323][Para 020] Occlusion
[4324][Para 001] The occlusion should be assessed to determine whether all teeth make contact in a stable intercuspal position and that no pain is elicited on bringing the teeth together or in excursive movements.
[4325][Para 017] The patient was able to bring his teeth into maximum interdigitation and noted no interferences when doing this.
[4326][Para 020] Fractured Teeth
[4327][Para 007] The degree of fracture of the teeth should be inspected. Although it is not visible in Fig. 39.1, the pulp of the upper right central incisor was exposed. Because of tenderness elicited when the crown was palpated, the true extent of the injury could only be assessed under local anaesthesia. The pulps of the adjacent fractured teeth were not involved.
[4328][Para 020] Percussion Sounds of Teeth
[4329][Para 001] Traumatized teeth should not be tapped to check the percussion sound because it is too distressing for patients and has very little value at the acute stage of management.
[4330][Para 020] Sensibility Testing
[4331][Para 001] These may be thermal tests (e.g. cold test using Endo-Frost at −50°C) or electric pulp testing and are useful to assess pulpal sensibility.
[4332][Para 002] These tests have been shown to give false-negative results for up to 3 months after acute trauma, and so they will not provide any useful information and can make patients more anxious.
[4333][Heading 2]  How Do You Interpret These Findings?
[4334][Para 001] Because there were no lacerations of the lip, it must be assumed that the tooth fragments have been lost. There was no mobility of the upper incisors, and the patient was able to bring his teeth into maximum intercuspation without any interferences. The extent of the upper right central incisor fracture can only be investigated further under local anaesthesia. The patient must consent to this after it is explained that the tooth may be unrestorable after this and may need to be extracted. The upper left central incisor and lower right central incisor did not have any pulpal involvement.
[4335][Para 015] Investigations
[4336][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Perform?
[4337][Para 001] Intraoral radiographs are required and should include a periapical radiograph of the injured teeth (Fig. 39.2).
[4338][Para 002] An upper standard occlusal radiograph is useful if a root fracture is suspected after clinical examination.
[4339][Heading 2]  What Do the Radiographs Show?
[4340][Para 001] The periapical radiograph shows:
[4341][Para 004] • Good alveolar bone levels
[4342][Para 004] • Upper right central incisor has loss of 50% coronal tooth tissue extending to the crestal bone level – note the radiographic appearance of an oblique, shear fracture
[4343][Para 004] • Upper left central incisor loss of mesial corner with no pulpal involvement
[4344][Para 004] • No radiolucent lines across the roots or changes in the periodontal ligament space around any of the upper incisor teeth to suggest root fracture.
[4345][Para 015] Diagnoses
[4346][Para 024]  What are the Diagnoses in This Case?
[4347][Para 016] 1. Upper right central incisor enamel–dentine–pulp fracture
[4348][Para 016] 2. Upper left central incisor enamel–dentine fracture
[4349][Para 016] 3. Lower right central incisor enamel fracture.

[4353][Heading 2]  What Emergency Treatment Would You Provide?
[4354][Para 001] The patient must consent to an examination under local anaesthesia to investigate the extent of the fractured upper right central incisor.
[4355][Para 002] Once the tooth has been anaesthetized, any loose fragments should be removed. The extent of the fracture can then be visualized and the restorability assessed. If the tooth is unrestorable, upper and lower alginate impressions should be taken to fabricate an immediate partial denture.
[4356][Para 002] If the tooth is restorable, moisture control and access to further tooth tissue for bonding can be gained through the placement of retraction cord or by removing palatal gingival tissue with electrosurgery. The original fragment can be rebonded with flowable resin composite (if available), or the tooth can be built up with resin composite, shade matched to the remaining anterior, hydrated teeth. Crown lengthening surgery can also be considered if there is insufficient tooth tissue remaining.
[4357][Para 002] The aim of management is to preserve pulp sensibility irrespective of the time elapsed since the pulp was exposed, and this is achieved by carrying out a pulpotomy.
[4358][Para 024]  How Would You Perform a Pulpotomy?
[4359][Para 016] 1. Under local anaesthesia and using a small, round diamond bur and copious water, remove the coronal 2–3 mm of the exposed pulp.
[4360][Para 016] 2. Pressure should then be applied by using a cotton wool pledget soaked in sodium hypochlorite. If bleeding does not stop, another 1–2 mm of pulp tissue should be removed and the process repeated. In an adult with closed apices, bleeding up to the level of the canal orifice indicates the need to abandon the pulpotomy and to extirpate the pulp. In children with open apices, pulpotomy should always be carried out, regardless of the level, to support continued root development and, thus, strengthening of the root.
[4361][Para 125] 
[4362][Para 008] 
[4363][Para 052] Fig. 39.3 Restoration of the upper right central incisor (UR1 or 11) after a pulpotomy and the upper left central incisor (UL1 or 21), both with resin composite. © Serpil Djemal.
[4364][Para 016] 3. The resultant healthy pulp should be dressed with nonsetting calcium hydroxide and sealed with glass-ionomer cement. The tooth can then be built back up to full contour with resin composite.
[4365][Para 030] Resin Composite Build-Up
[4366][Para 001] The upper central incisors and the lower right central incisor should be built back up to full contour with resin composite (Fig. 39.3).
[4367][Para 002] Moisture control can be achieved by using a rubber dam or cotton wool roll and gauze. The crevicular fluid can be managed with retraction cord impregnated with astringent or by electrosurgery, as needed.
[4368][Para 002] There is no indication to prescribe antibiotics, and oral hygiene measures should be resumed as soon as possible.
[4369][Heading 2]  When Should the Patient Be Reviewed?
[4370][Para 001] The patient should be seen again at 3 months after injury, at 6 months and then annually. Each follow-up visit should include:
[4371][Para 004] • A pain history from the patient
[4372][Para 004] • A clinical examination of the teeth to look for possible discolouration, mobility, tenderness to percussion and the presence of a sinus
[4373][Para 004] • A periapical radiograph to look for changes in the periodontal ligament space or apical radiolucency
[4374][Para 004] • Sensibility testing using cold test (e.g. Endo-Frost at −50°C and electric pulp testing.
[4375][Para 002] The aims of the follow-up visits are to monitor the traumatized teeth for pulp health and, in particular, for signs or symptoms of pulp necrosis.
[4376][Para 002] Root canal treatment should only be initiated if there are two of the signs or symptoms of pulp necrosis, as described above.
[4377][Para 002] Throughout this period, the need for good oral hygiene should be reinforced.
[4378][Heading 2]  What Complications of the Injury Require Follow-Up?
[4379][Para 001] The other anterior teeth should also be monitored for signs and symptoms of pulp necrosis, as detailed above. The composite resin restorations may require repair or replacement because of wear or discolouration in the future.

[4385][Para 001] It is important to fully document when, how and where the injury occurred. Remember that the account from the patient is their version and not a matter of fact. Recording the exact details given by the patient is important. You may be asked for a report at a later date, and so the more details recorded, the better.

[4398][Para 025] Case 40
[4399][Heading 1] An Anxious Patient
[4400][Para 027] EMILY Sherwin
[4401][Para 028] Summary
[4402][Para 029] A 23-year-old student is referred to you for removal of her wisdom teeth. She is very anxious at the prospect of minor oral surgery and has been told that you specialize in treatment under general anaesthesia. Assess the treatment options and their suitability for this case.
[4403][Para 014] History
[4404][Para 019] Complaint
[4405][Para 007] The patient has no presenting complaint.
[4406][Para 012] History of Complaint
[4407][Para 007] The patient has had several episodes of pain, swelling and bad taste related to both lower impacted wisdom teeth during the last year. Her general dental practitioner has diagnosed pericoronitis and prescribed local treatments, but the episodes are increasing in frequency and severity, and the last required systemic antibiotics.
[4408][Para 012] Medical History
[4409][Para 007] The patient has moderately well-controlled epilepsy and suffered her last seizure approximately 4 months ago. She is treated with phenytoin 300 mg daily. She also reports allergy to penicillin and co-trimoxazole (Septrin), both of which have caused rashes.
[4410][Para 012] Dental History
[4411][Para 007] The patient has had a few dental restorations placed since the age of 10 years. Her general dental practitioner has provided intensive preventive treatment because she is very nervous. She can tolerate regular recall consultations but has required no invasive operative treatment for many years. Her last restorative procedure had to be abandoned on two occasions because of acute anxiety and fainting.
[4412][Para 014] Investigation and Diagnosis
[4413][Para 007] The patient has had episodes of pericoronitis and requires extraction of at least her mandibular third molars. Further details of the indications for removal of lower third molars and their radiographic and clinical assessment are provided in Case 25.
[4414][Para 017] The patient has mesio-angularly impacted, but relatively superficial, third molars and you assess them as being relatively straightforward surgical extractions that will require minor bone removal but not tooth sectioning.
[4415][Para 015] Anxiety Management
[4416][Heading 2]  What Options are Available for Controlling Patients’ Anxiety? What are Their Advantages and Disadvantages?
[4417][Para 032] See Table 40.1.
[4418][Para 017] After discussing the options, risks and benefits, the patient elects to have her extractions performed under intravenous sedation.
[4419][Heading 2]  What Constraints are Placed On the Use of General Anaesthesia for Dentistry?
[4420][Para 001] General Dental Council guidance on the use of general anaesthesia is contained in the Council’s document Standards for Dental Professionals (June 2013). This document was active from 2005 to 2013; however, the standards that supersede it make no reference to the provision of general anaesthesia for dentistry, and so the previous document is used as guidance. Failure to comply would render a dentist liable to a charge of serious misconduct.
[4421][Para 002] The guidance states that:
[4422][Para 202] Dental treatment under general anaesthesia should:
[4423][Para 082] • only be carried out when it is judged to be the most clinically appropriate method of anaesthesia; and
[4424][Para 082] • only take place in a hospital setting (see the note below) that has critical-care facilities.
[4425][Para 082] • General anaesthesia may only be given by someone who is:
[4426][Para 082] • on the specialist register of the General Medical Council as an anaesthetist;
[4427][Para 082] • a trainee working under supervision as part of a Royal College of Anaesthetists’ approved training programme; or
[4428][Para 082] • a nonconsultant career-grade anaesthetist with a National Health Service (NHS) appointment under the supervision of a named consultant anaesthetist, who must be a member of the same NHS anaesthetic department where the nonconsultant career-grade anaesthetist is employed.
[4429][Para 082] • The anaesthetist should be supported by someone who is specifically trained and experienced in the necessary skills to help monitor the patient’s condition and to help in any emergency.
[4430][Para 166] • The publication A Conscious Decision defines ‘hospital setting’ as ‘any institution for the reception and treatment of persons suffering illness or any injury or disability requiring medical or dental treatment, which has critical care facilities on the same site and includes clinics and outpatient departments maintained in connection with any such institution’.
[4431][Para 030]  What Guidelines are Available Regarding Conscious Sedation and Dental Treatment?
[4432][Para 001] Recent guidelines include:
[4433][Para 038] Intercollegiate Advisory Committee for Sedation in Dentistry. (2015). conscious sedation in the provision of dental care. London: RCS.
[4434][Para 058] https://www.rcseng.ac.uk/dental-faculties/fds/publications-guidelines/standards-for-conscious-sedation-in-the-provision-of-dental-care-and-accreditation/
[4435][Para 038] Scottish Dental Clinical Effectiveness Programme. (2017). Conscious sedation in dentistry (3rd ed.). Edinburgh: NHS Education for Scotland. http://www.sdcep.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/SDCEP-Conscious-Sedation-Guidance.pdf
[4436][Para 030]  Is Epilepsy a Contraindication To the Use of Intravenous Sedation?
[4437][Para 001] No. Benzodiazepines (e.g. midazolam) are the drugs of choice and have anticonvulsant properties. In any case, this patient’s epilepsy is well controlled. An epileptic seizure under sedation is most unlikely.
[4438][Heading 2]  How Would You Assess the Patient’s Fitness for Intravenous Sedation?
[4439][Para 001] The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) classification is useful when assessing fitness for sedation or general anaesthesia (Table 40.2).
[4440][Para 018] Table 40.1
[4441][Para 021] Methods of Controlling Anxiety
[4442][Heading 2]  Which Groups Would Normally Be Considered Suitable for Treatment with Sedation in a Primary Care Setting?
[4443][Para 001] ASA groups I and II.
[4444][Heading 2]  Does This Mean That Patients in ASA Groups III and V Should Never Be Treated Under Sedation?
[4445][Para 001] No. Many patients in ASA groups III and IV may benefit from sedation because it reduces the patient’s anxiety and, as a result, their endogenous catecholamine secretion. However, such patients require careful assessment and planning and should be treated in a hospital setting with input from medical teams as necessary.
[4446][Heading 2]  What Medical Investigation Would You Perform?
[4447][Para 001] The systemic arterial blood pressure must be checked. Normal blood pressure is considered to be 120/80 mm Hg; however, small variations are common, and the systolic blood pressure is often raised in anxious subjects. Hypertension that is well controlled is not a contraindication to sedation. However, patients with a diastolic blood pressure that is consistently above 110 mm Hg should be investigated before sedation is given.
[4448][Para 017] When you take the patient’s blood pressure it is 140/90 mm Hg, consistent with her anxious demeanour.
[4449][Heading 2]  Is This Patient a Suitable Candidate for Treatment Under Local Anaesthesia with Intravenous Sedation?
[4450][Para 001] Intravenous sedation would appear to be an ideal adjunct to local anaesthesia. The patient has practically no experience of dental procedures, has a history of failed treatment under local anaesthesia alone and is anxious about the extractions.
[4451][Para 015] Treatment
[4452][Heading 2]  What is the Drug of Choice for Intravenous Sedation?
[4453][Para 001] Midazolam is a benzodiazepine, which is well suited to dental sedation. It is soluble in water and presented in a 5-ml ampoule in a concentration of 1 mg/1 ml. This presentation is ideal to titrate for conscious sedation in dentistry.
[4454][Para 018] Table 40.2
[4455][Para 021] The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Classification for Assessing Fitness for Sedation or General Anaesthesia
[4456][Heading 2]  Are There Any Contraindications To the Use of Midazolam?
[4457][Para 001] Allergy to benzodiazepines is an absolute contraindication but is extremely rare. Some drugs interact with midazolam, but careful administration of the sedative drug will minimize any difficulties.
[4458][Heading 2]  What is Meant By ‘Titration of the Dose’? Suggest a Suitable Titration Regimen for a Healthy (ASA group I) Adult Patient Being Sedated with Midazolam.
[4459][Para 001] Titration is administration of a drug in small quantities whilst observing the patient’s response. Sedation is judged to be adequate when the patient looks relaxed and displays a slight delay in response to questioning of commands (e.g. ‘raise your arm’). There is often a degree of slurring of speech.
[4460][Para 002] A suitable regimen would be 2 mg of midazolam injected intravenously over a period of 30 seconds, followed by a pause of 90 seconds, during which the patient’s response is observed. If sedation is inadequate, further increments of 1 mg should be administered every 30 seconds until sedation is sufficient. A local anaesthetic can then be administered and treatment carried out in the normal way.
[4461][Heading 2]  What are the Undesirable Side Effects of Intravenous Midazolam?
[4462][Para 001] Intravenous sedation with midazolam is an extremely safe procedure when the drug is administered according to the above guidelines. However, all drugs have side effects, and the major side effect with midazolam sedation is respiratory depression. There is a dose-related decrease in both respiratory rate and tidal volume, which is most pronounced in the first 10 minutes of sedation.
[4463][Heading 2]  How Should a Patient Be Protected From This Potentially Dangerous Side Effect?
[4464][Para 001] Clinical monitoring by observing the patient must be carried out by both the dentist and a suitably trained and experienced dental nurse. The use of a pulse oximeter to monitor arterial oxygen saturation and heart rate is mandatory for intravenous sedation.
[4465][Para 002] All suitable pulse oximeters have ‘alarm limits’. The minimum acceptable arterial oxygen saturation is 90%. If the alarm sounds, the patient should be encouraged to take deep breaths. If this is not successful, the airway must be opened by using airway manoeuvres such as head tilt, chin lift or a jaw thrust. If breathing is still inadequate as indicated by arterial oxygen saturation and clinical monitoring, supportive ventilation should be provided along with the administration of the reversal agent flumazenil, a benzodiazepine antagonist.
[4466][Heading 2]  Why Must a ‘Second Appropriate Person’ Such As a Dental Nurse Always Be Present During Sedation and Recovery?
[4467][Para 001] To help monitor the patient’s condition, assist with any emergency and act as a chaperone in case the patient experiences a benzodiazepine-induced sexual fantasy, which might result in accusations being brought against the dentist or another member of the oral healthcare team.
[4468][Heading 2]  What Postoperative Care is Required?
[4469][Para 001] At the end of the procedure, the patient is slowly returned to the upright position over a period of 3–5 minutes and helped to a supervised rest area. The patient must not be discharged until she has sufficiently recovered so as to be able to stand and walk without assistance.
[4470][Para 002] The patient should be discharged into the care of a responsible adult escort, who must also be given written and verbal postoperative instructions.
[4471][Para 024]  What Instructions Would You Give This Patient and Her Escort Following Treatment?
[4472][Para 004] • Do not travel alone: travel home with your escort, by car if possible.
[4473][Para 004] • For the next 8 hours:
[4474][Para 034] • Do not drive or ride a bicycle
[4475][Para 034] • Do not operate machinery
[4476][Para 034] • Do not drink alcohol
[4477][Para 034] • Do not return to work or sign legal documents
[4478][Para 034] • Do not use the Internet
[4479][Para 030]  Are Benzodiazepine Antagonists Used Routinely To Hasten Recovery After Dental Sedation?
[4480][Para 001] At present, antagonists such as flumazenil are recommended for emergency procedures such as benzodiazepine overdose and should not be used to hasten recovery. However, elective reversal of benzodiazepines may be helpful in some patients such as those who must travel some distance home on public transport. In such cases, it is important that the usual postoperative instructions for intravenous sedation are given and adhered to.
[4481][Para 015] Prognosis
[4482][Heading 2]  Is the Patient Likely To Require Intravenous Sedation for All Future Dental Treatments?
[4483][Para 001] Not necessarily. Sedation will have ensured that the extractions were performed as pleasantly as possible and any existing dental phobia should not have been reinforced. The amnesic effect of benzodiazepines is likely to reduce the patient’s memory of the whole procedure. During future visits for dental care, anxiety-reducing methods should be used so that eventually dental care can be provided routinely.
[4484][Heading 2]  What Documentation Should Be Completed for Intravenous Sedation?
[4485][Para 001] Along with completing the usual contemporaneous clinical notes, sedation-specific information should also be recorded. This should include the names of the dentist and the dental nurse; presedation checks; the dose, site, time, batch number and expiry date of the sedation drug given; monitoring carried out during sedation; and recovery and discharge information.
[4486][Para 025] Case 41
[4487][Heading 1] Blisters in the Mouth
[4488][Para 027] Barbara Carey, Esther Hullah, and Jane Setterfield
[4489][Para 028] Summary
[4490][Para 029] A 63-year-old female patient of your general dental practice reports severe oral discomfort with blistering. Identify the cause, and outline the appropriate management.
[4491][Para 218] 
[4492][Para 008] 
[4493][Para 011] Fig. 41.1 The appearance of the gingiva.
[4494][Para 009]  
[4495][Para 014] History
[4496][Para 019] Complaint
[4497][Para 007] The patient complains of soreness involving the cheeks, gums and palate, which started 12 months ago and has increased in severity since. She reports blisters that burst to release a clear fluid. She is able to tolerate soft foods in her diet but avoids anything hard or sharp as even minor trauma can cause a blister to bursts. When a blister bursts, it leaves a painful ulcer that is slow to heal. Brushing of teeth is painful and associated with bleeding.
[4498][Para 017] She denies any cutaneous or genital blisters. The history is negative for dysphagia and odynophagia. However, she describes recurrent nose bleeds and nasal crusting. There are no ocular symptoms.
[4499][Para 012] Medical History
[4500][Para 001] The only relevant past medical history is hypertension, for which she takes ramipril.
[4501][Para 014] Examination
[4502][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[4503][Para 001] Extraoral examination is unremarkable, with no cervical lymphadenopathy. The eyes appear normal.
[4504][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[4505][Para 001] The appearance of the gingivae, shown in Fig. 41.1, demonstrates extensive gingival erythema of the buccal and labial gingiva in all quadrants. There are ulcers on the posterior gingiva on the right side. Inflammation is generally limited to the attached gingiva but extends onto the alveolar mucosa and into the sulci in several places.
[4506][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[4507][Heading 2]  Which Diseases Cause Oral Blisters? How Do the Blisters Form?
[4508][Para 001] Causes or oral blisters are listed in Table 41.1.
[4509][Heading 2]  What Name is Given To the Gingival Appearance?
[4510][Para 001] This appearance is called desquamative gingivitis and is characterized by inflamed, peeling gingiva and separation or loss of the epithelium. The gingiva appears erythematous and oedematous. Unlike plaque-induced gingivitis, the gingival erythema can extend the full width of the attached gingiva and beyond it to the alveolar mucosa. Patients often report gingival discomfort and, sometimes, bleeding.
[4511][Para 024]  What are the Main Causes of Desquamative Gingivitis in Order of Prevalence?
[4512][Para 004] • Lichen planus
[4513][Para 004] • Mucous membrane pemphigoid
[4514][Para 004] • Pemphigus vulgaris
[4515][Para 030]  Which of These Conditions Would You Include in Your Initial Differential Diagnosis? Explain Why.
[4516][Para 001] On the basis of the answers above, only three conditions commonly cause both oral blisters and desquamative gingivitis:
[4517][Para 016] 1. Mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP). A good history of blister formation with subsequent rupture makes either pemphigoid or pemphigus the most likely diagnosis. In MMP, 90% of patients with oral lesions have desquamative gingivitis with or without additional involvement of buccal mucosa and palate. The lips and tongue are not frequently affected. MMP is slightly more common in women than in men and often presents after 55 years of age. All these features fit the current presentation, and the nasal crusting and bleeding may signify nasal involvement because nasal, oesophageal, laryngeal and genital mucosae and the eyes may be affected.
[4518][Para 018] Table 41.1
[4519][Para 021] Causes of Oral Blistering
[4520][Para 016] 2. Pemphigus vulgaris (PV). Approximately 70% of patients with PV have oral lesions on presentation, and it eventually involves the oral mucosa in greater than 90% of patients. The oral lesions are usually more extensive than in the current patient, with ragged irregular areas of ulceration derived from ruptured vesicles and blisters in all parts of the mouth. Compared with MMP, PV is less likely to present with gingival lesions alone. It is rare to find intact intraoral blisters in pemphigus, and patients often do not notice them because the epithelium of the blister roof disintegrates quickly. The long history and the absence of skin lesions in the present case also count against PV and make MMP more likely. However, investigations are necessary to completely exclude the possibility of PV.
[4521][Para 016] 3. Lichen planus (LP). LP is the commonest cause of desquamative gingivitis and gingival ulceration, but it rarely produces blisters. Most patients with LP have buccal mucosal and lateral tongue involvement and only 10% present with gingival lesions alone. Erythema and ulceration are consistent with LP, but other features such as reticular white striae or white plaques are not present in the gingiva of this patient. Occasionally, desquamative gingivitis caused by LP may be associated with genital involvement, and it is important to ask patients whether they have any genital itch or soreness. In females, the presentation of vulvovaginal–gingival LP is associated with significant morbidity and scarring of the affected sites. Although blister formation in LP is rare, when it does occur, the gingiva is a common site.
[4522][Para 030]  What Diagnoses Have You Excluded? Explain Why.
[4523][Para 001] Erythema multiforme (EM) is unlikely in this case and only merits consideration because of the presence of blisters. It most frequently occurs in young adults between the ages of 20 and 40 years and exhibits a slight male predilection. Diffuse areas of mucosal erythema, painful erosions, and bullae (large blisters) affect primarily the vermilion of the lip, buccal mucosa, labial mucosa, alveolar mucosa, and tongue. Skin lesions may also be present with a characteristic target-like appearance. EM lesions usually appear over the course of 3–5 days and resolve within approximately 2–3 weeks. EM does not cause desquamative gingivitis.
[4524][Para 018] Table 41.2
[4525][Para 021] Investigations
[4526][Para 020] Angina Bullosa Haemorrhagica (ABH)
[4527][Para 001] This term is used to describe acute recurrent subepithelial oral mucosal blisters filled with blood that are not attributable to a systemic disorder or haemostatic defect. They typically arise on the palate or oropharynx and heal rapidly. The distribution, slow healing and clear fluid–filled blisters in this patient make the diagnosis extremely unlikely. ABH does not cause desquamative gingivitis.
[4528][Para 020] Drug Reactions
[4529][Para 001] Some may cause lichenoid reactions and, very rarely, produce pemphigus and pemphigoid-like presentations. This patient is taking the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor ramipril, which has been implicated in oral lichenoid reactions. If the presentation were more typical of LP, it would be necessary to investigate the possibility of a drug reaction.
[4530][Para 020] Rare Vesiculobullous Conditions
[4531][Para 001] Those that may affect the mouth can be excluded at this stage. Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with coeliac disease and usually causes skin lesions. Oral mucosal involvement is rare and may manifest as vesicles, erosions, or erythematous macules on the palate or tongue. Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) encompasses a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of rare inherited disorders characterized by marked blistering and erosions occurring after minor trauma. There is often scarring of the affected sites.
[4532][Para 020] Other Causes of Oral Blisters
[4533][Para 001] These include viral infections, which present as acute single episodes of vesicles (small blisters), often accompanied by systemic signs and symptoms of viral infection. They may include, for example, herpes simplex (acute primary gingivostomatitis, chicken pox) or coxsackievirus infections (hand foot and mouth or herpangina). Gingival ulcers and erythema are common, but not typical desquamative gingivitis.
[4534][Para 024]  What Additional Questions Would You Ask During History Taking? Why?
[4535][Para 020] Do You Have Any Blisters On Your Skin?
[4536][Para 001] Cutaneous blistering confirms the presence of a systemic, probably autoimmune, disease; aids in the diagnosis; and provides further lesions for investigation. Cutaneous pemphigus lesions manifest as flaccid blisters that rupture quickly, resulting in painful erosions that bleed easily. In MMP, patients may present with localized blisters or erosions, which often occur on the face, scalp, arms or legs and heal with atrophic white scars. Cutaneous LP manifests as pruritic, purple, polygonal papules or plaques on the skin. Target-like lesions are a hallmark of EM, are often on the hands or feet and may be painful. A history of herpes simplex virus infection (e.g. cold sore) would also suggest a likely trigger for EM.
[4537][Para 020] Do You Have Any Problems Anywhere Else?
[4538][Para 001] The oral cavity is the most common site of involvement in MMP. Other sites of involvement include the conjunctiva, skin, pharynx, external genitalia, nasal mucosa, larynx, anus and oesophagus. Pemphigus may affect the oesophagus, upper respiratory tract, eyes and genital or perianal sites.
[4539][Para 017] In this case, the history was negative for cutaneous lesions. The history of recurrent epistaxis and nasal crusting is suggestive of involvement of the nasal mucosa.

[4552][Heading 2]  How Do You Interpret These Histological Features?
[4553][Para 001] Separation of the full thickness of the epithelium at the level of the basement membrane, without epithelial damage, is consistent with a diagnosis of MMP. PV is excluded because of the lack of acantholysis and the level of separation.
[4554][Para 002] For immunobullous disorders, direct immunofluorescence (DIF) is the ‘gold standard’ diagnostic test, revealing the presence and binding site of autoantibody in tissues. Linear binding of C3, immunoglobulin G (IgG) or IgA at the basement membrane is diagnostic of pemphigoid. There is no intercellular binding of IgG or C3 around the cells in the epithelium to suggest PV. LP is excluded because of the lack of basal cell degeneration and lymphocytic infiltration of the epithelium and positive immunofluorescence findings.
[4555][Para 014] Diagnosis
[4556][Para 001] The patient has pemphigoid, of which there are several types. There is no skin involvement, excluding bullous pemphigoid (a pemphigoid variant predominantly affecting the skin), and so the final diagnosis is mucous membrane pemphigoid.
[4557][Para 015] Treatment
[4558][Heading 2]  How Should This Patient’s Condition Be Managed?
[4559][Para 001] The primary goals of treatment of MMP are to halt the progression of disease, alleviate symptoms, and prevent complications (chronic tissue inflammation and scarring). The treatment options are:
[4560][Para 004] • Symptomatic treatment with agents such as benzydamine hydrochloride mouthwash for pain relief.
[4561][Para 004] • Topical corticosteroids may be effective alone, but only if the disease is very mild. They are more effective when combined with systemic agents in more severely affected cases. Betamethasone 500 microgram soluble tablets used as a mouthwash up to four times daily as a 3-minute rinse (taking care to spit out all remaining mouthwash after use) or clobetasol propionate 0.05% mixed with benzocaine (Orabase) applied directly to the affected areas are frequently used in secondary care.
[4562][Para 225] 
[4563][Para 092] 
[4564][Para 093] Fig. 41.3 Direct immunofluorescence appearance of the separate biopsy specimen.
[4565][Para 004] • Dapsone is frequently used in patients with oral MMP who fail to respond to local therapy or in those who present with widespread oral or multisite disease.
[4566][Para 004] • More potent immunosuppressants such as topical tacrolimus are effective in some patients, and systemic glucocorticoids may be required in refractory disease. Azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil can be used as ‘glucocorticoid-sparing’ agents to reduce the required doses of prednisolone and maintain remission after discontinuation of glucocorticoid therapy.
[4567][Para 002] This patient requires multidisciplinary treatment and should be referred to an ophthalmologist to identify and manage any ocular lesions that may be present but not yet identified. The patient may also require referral to an ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialist for management of nasal and laryngeal involvement.
[4568][Heading 2]  Can This Patient Be Managed in Primary Care?
[4569][Para 001] The investigation and treatment options require that the patient be treated in a secondary care setting, at least until a definite diagnosis is made and the condition is stabilized. After that, the general dental practitioner has an important role in maintaining adequate plaque and calculus control because poor oral hygiene worsens desquamative gingivitis. Patients using systemic or topical glucocorticoids are predisposed to oral candidosis, and this should be monitored at subsequent visits.
[4570][Heading 2]  Are There Significant Complications?
[4571][Para 001] Yes. The chronic ulceration may lead to varying degrees of scarring. In some patients, the disease may predominantly or exclusively affect the eyes, and scarring causes adhesions between the lid conjunctiva and the surface of the eye (symblepharon formation), restricting movement, infolding the lashes, inflaming the surface of the eye and ultimately causing blindness. The oral mucosa is relatively resistant to scarring, but scarring in the eye, larynx or oesophagus may be severe.
[4572][Para 002] Patients are also at risk of the adverse effects of steroids and other immunosuppressive agents, including bone marrow suppression and increased risk for infection or malignancy.

[4574][Heading 1] Will You See My Son?

[4576][Para 028] Summary
[4577][Para 029] The mother of a 6-year-old child brings him to your practice to ask for an appointment. She has been to other practices but felt that the dentists were unfamiliar with autism and that her son was not welcome.

Recently, he has been putting objects into his mouth and biting his clothes. His mother is worried that he may be in pain but is unable to tell her.
