His mother thinks that he may be allergic to wheat and dairy produce and consequently tries to exclude these from his diet. He has had no formal allergy diagnosis and no advice from a dietician.
[4589][Para 014] Examination
[4590][Para 104] Extraoral Examination
[4591][Heading 2]  The Patient is Shown in Fig. 42.1. What Do You See?
[4592][Para 001] Many children with autism look like any other child. However, you notice that this patient fails to make eye contact with you and seems to have a relatively large head, a feature seen in some young children with autism.
[4593][Para 017] While you speak to the mother in the waiting room, the child is flapping his hands and rocking backwards and forwards. He does not seem to be aware of his surroundings.
[4594][Para 017] It appears that you will not be able to perform an examination easily. The mother appears stressed and anxious.
[4595][Heading 2]  What is Autism Spectrum Disorder?
[4596][Para 001] Autism is a lifelong developmental disability that affects how people perceive the world and interact with others. Individuals with autism can have difficulties with everyday social communication, social interaction, repetitive behaviours and sensory issues.
[4597][Para 002] Autism has a wide range of presentations and so is described as a ‘spectrum’.
[4598][Para 002] Approximately 50% of people with autism have learning disabilities; however, some have normal or above normal intelligence.
[4599][Para 002] Asperger’s syndrome is a form of autism, in which there may be average or above average intelligence. Specific learning difficulties such as dyslexia or difficulty understanding or processing language may also be present.
[4600][Para 002] Dyspraxia is also common.
[4601][Para 002] There is no cure for autism. However, a range of strategies and approaches to enable learning and development may help some people.
[4602][Heading 2]  What is the Cause of Autism?
[4603][Para 001] Early suggestions that autism might result from abnormal parenting or having been abandoned. Although the exact cause of autism is still under investigation, there is overwhelming evidence that a combination of both strong genetic factors and weaker environmental factors alter the brain structure and neuron function.
[4604][Heading 2]  Who is Affected?
[4605][Para 001] Autism affects at least 1% of the UK population and affects all races and socioeconomic groups.
[4606][Para 002] Males are four times more frequently affected compared with than females. However, girls are underdiagnosed because of their better language and social skills and ability to mask their difficulties to fit in with their peers. Because girls are not diagnosed early, they may display secondary difficulties – depression, severe anxiety and eating disorders, especially anorexia.
[4607][Para 002] It is not unusual for siblings to be affected, although this may not be recognized if signs are limited to subtle lack of social skills or failure of language development.
[4608][Heading 2]  What Features of Autism Will Affect Your Management?
[4609][Para 001] Sensory processing problems are extremely common in children with autism, and sensory issues often trigger anxiety during a dental appointment. A child may be hyposensitive or hypersensitive to sights, sounds, smell, taste and touch – all of which are challenges encountered in a dental surgery.
[4610][Para 002] Oral care may be compromised because the texture of the toothbrush and the strong taste of the toothpaste may not be tolerated. Dietary control and prevention may be made more difficult by rituals around eating or strong preferences for foods with particular packaging, colour or texture. There may be idiosyncratic behaviours such as food having to be arranged on the plate in a certain way.
[4611][Para 002] Aversion to physical contact can make examination, treatment, and the usual means of physical reassurance ineffective.
[4612][Para 002] Self-stimulatory behaviours are common. These repetitive habits (‘stimming’) can take many forms, including visual or tactile stimulation or movements such as rocking and hand flapping. Stimming is thought to provide reassurance in stressful situations and helps block out other unwanted sensory input. If the child receives too much sensory information, ‘meltdown’ can occur. This is an uncontrolled emotional or behavioural reaction to overwhelming stress or sensory overload that can trigger a flight-or-flight reaction.
[4613][Para 002] Difficulty in expressing pain is a further sensory issue because these individuals’ response to pain may be different. The mother is worried and thinks that her son may be in pain and that because his communication is impaired, he would be unable to tell her. Dental professionals need to look out for alternative indicators of pain such as sleep disruption, random emotional outbursts unusual for the child or problems eating.
[4614][Para 002] Verbal communication is a major problem. Many children with autism never develop functional speech and are reliant on communication aids, often visual aids. These children may have very limited understanding of colloquial speech, jokes and sarcasm.
[4615][Para 002] Nonverbal communication is poorly understood by many children with autism, particularly the facial expressions and tone of voice that indicate emotions. This may mean that you have to adapt things you normally take for granted in managing other paediatric patients. For example, there is often absence of eye contact, which makes it difficult to gain and maintain attention. Also, physical reinforcements such as patting or stroking may not be acceptable to the child.
[4616][Para 002] The child’s behaviour might appear disruptive, challenging, frightening or bizarre and may include self-harming. Children with autism lack the ‘theory of mind’ (the ability to understand other peoples’ thoughts and emotions) and are, therefore, not aware of how their behaviour is seen by those around them. The child may dislike or be extremely frightened of new situations and people.
[4617][Para 002] Autism is associated with a strong need for routine. These individuals would like events to be predictable and new experiences may unbalance the whole day. They dislike things that are unfamiliar to them and definitely do not like surprises.
[4618][Para 002] In many cases, diets are unusual because many parents exclude wheat, dairy products or yeast in an attempt to improve the child’s condition and behaviour. This and the patient’s own dietary demands, mean that you may have to think imaginatively when offering preventive dietary advice.
[4619][Para 002] Children with autism have significantly more eating and feeding problems compared with other children. This is often linked to their sensory issues and is not necessarily associated with the severity of autism.
[4620][Para 002] Other things to consider include the strong genetic element in autism. You may need to take into account the possibility that the parents themselves may suffer from a mild form of the disorder and that their communication and social interaction may appear unusual.
[4621][Para 002] Sleep disruption is very common in children with autism, and this affects the whole family. As a result, parents’ resilience may be compromised, and they may resort to anything to influence the child’s behaviour.
[4622][Heading 2]  Are Significant Medical Conditions Associated with Autism?
[4623][Para 001] Yes, 10% of individuals may have other conditions such as fragile X syndrome, tuberous sclerosis or syndromes, including Down’s syndrome. These may compound the learning disability or behavioural problems.
[4624][Para 002] Many children with autism have mental health problems such as anxiety, obsessive compulsive disorder and depression. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is frequently present, and patients may be prescribed methylphenidate (Ritalin) to address this. Epilepsy is a common association and, if not present in childhood, often manifests in adolescence.
[4625][Heading 2]  Should This Patient Be Referred for Hospital or Specialist Care?
[4626][Para 001] Given time, you would probably be able to examine and may even be able to carry out simple treatments for the patient by adapting your approach. If you consider that there is pain, infection or other acute condition, then it would be appropriate to make immediate referral to a specialist care centre where general anaesthesia is available.
[4627][Para 002] However, you still need to examine him to establish whether there is disease present.
[4628][Para 002] There is no reason why patients at the more able end of the spectrum cannot be treated in general practice for routine preventive and even simple restorative care.
[4629][Heading 2]  What Will You Do Next?
[4630][Para 001] It appears that the patient may be in pain. You may want to examine the mouth to determine the cause quickly, but without a careful plan of action, you will probably fail. Before you can proceed, you will need some information from the mother.
[4631][Para 024]  What Information Will Help You Plan Treatment?
[4632][Para 004] • Patient’s likes and dislikes – useful in establishing a rapport with the child and avoiding any actions which might distress the child
[4633][Para 004] • Any communication aids that are used (see below)
[4634][Para 004] • Possible associated behavioural conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
[4635][Para 004] • Possible associated medical conditions such as epilepsy, and medication for them
[4636][Para 004] • Whether tooth brushing is managed and whether toothpaste is tolerated
[4637][Para 004] • Whether the child is able to give a degree of cooperation and accept physical contact (experiences such as having a haircut are often good indicators of this)
[4638][Para 004] • Any therapies being used to help the condition.
[4639][Para 002] In a planned situation, this information would be best collected through a previsit questionnaire.
[4640][Heading 2]  Might Treatment and Therapies for Autism Affect or Aid Dental Care?
[4641][Para 001] Drug treatments only address symptoms and behaviours. Those commonly used include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, antiepileptics, methylphenidate (Ritalin), and melatonin. Although these have some oral adverse effects such as dry mouth, they should not compromise treatment. Of course, any liquid medication must be sugar free.
[4642][Para 020] Early intensive behavioural therapies
[4643][Para 001] A range of communication-based, behavioural and educational approaches are used to support people with autism. These include approaches such as PECS (Picture Exchange Communication System), TEACCH (Treatment of Autistic and Communication Handicapped Children), ABA (Applied Behavioural Analysis), sensory integration and speech and language therapy. ABA can be effective therapy but is very labour intensive, costly and of limited availability. It breaks down learning into tiny chunks, using imitation and reinforcement to encourage children with autism to communicate. Positive responses are rewarded by reinforcers such as food, social interactions, games or toys. Given more time, visits to the dentist could be rehearsed with the patient’s ABA teacher and parent. If, as here, this cannot be undertaken, at least knowing the rewards used may be very helpful in reinforcing good behaviour at this and future visits.
[4644][Para 002] Complementary treatments are often sought by parents. Some parents consider that fluorides and some dental materials worsen or even cause autism. Some negotiation and compromise may be required on both sides to allow successful treatment.
[4645][Heading 2]  What is Your Plan To Examine the Child?
[4646][Para 001] Conventional behaviour management techniques rely on building a positive relationship with the child. However, because of problems with social communication, your approach will have to be adapted substantially, taking into consideration the child’s understanding, ability to communicate and sensory issues.
[4647][Para 002] You need to ensure that the visit does not become a negative experience. You will need to reinforce all positive behaviour and regard this as the first of, perhaps several, short visits. These may achieve little more than ‘saying hello’ and allowing the child to see you, your staff and the surgery and experience its sights and smells. Autistic children are highly anxious in new situations, but repeated exposure helps.
[4648][Para 002] Invite the mother and the child into the surgery. Reassure the mother that her child’s behaviour does not worry you or your staff, and try to appear confident. Make sure there is a quiet, calm atmosphere, without distractions such as music playing or telephones ringing. Observe the child’s behaviour, and keep in mind that the most likely cause of noncompliance is anxiety.
[4649][Para 002] Do not expect the child to sit in a dental chair. Try engaging him at a sink, playing with running water. Try having him use a toothbrush, if acceptable. This may allow you to view the child’s mouth.
[4650][Para 002] Some children develop the habit of repeating what is said to them (echolalia), seemingly understanding, but usually not. One positive aspect of this behaviour is that copying the sound ‘ah’ may facilitate toothbrushing and also allow you to see inside the mouth.
[4651][Heading 2]  How Can You Communicate with the Patient?
[4652][Para 001] Try to engage the child. Knowing what he likes and dislikes is most important. Try to identify an activity involving something in the surgery, perhaps moving the dental chair or playing with the light or a toy, that can be used to reinforce good behaviour.
[4653][Para 002] There are some basic rules that will keep you in good stead. Keep the language very simple, and do the following:
[4654][Para 004] • Use the child’s name at the beginning of every sentence to get his attention.
[4655][Para 004] • Always look at the child when you are talking to him.
[4656][Para 004] • Speak slowly.
[4657][Para 004] • Avoid idiomatic expressions such as ‘take a seat’ because they may be taken literally.
[4658][Para 004] • Humour has no effect and will not be understood.
[4659][Para 004] • Omit unnecessary words, especially social language – ‘please’ and ‘thank you’ will only be understood by individuals with mild autism.
[4660][Para 004] • Be patient.
[4661][Para 002] Pictorial communication aids such as Makaton or PECS may be used by some individuals. Makaton uses iconic symbols and line drawings to convey the meanings of words. The more user-friendly PECS system teaches nonspeaking children to exchange pictures of things that they want for the item, using their visual skills rather than verbal skills, as shown in Fig. 42.2.
[4662][Heading 2]  If the Patient is in Pain, What Would Be the Likely Causes?
[4663][Para 001] Without having set up the visit in the way described above, you may only achieve a glimpse of the teeth, and so you will need to know the likely causes in advance. For this patient, these are potentially:
[4664][Para 004] • Caries – especially if the diet or behavioural reinforcers are cariogenic
[4665][Para 004] • Trauma from a nonvital deciduous incisor – children with autism can be more clumsy and may have epilepsy, commonly resulting in trauma
[4666][Para 004] • Self-mutilation – some individuals with autism may pick at the gingiva, causing ulceration or inflammation
[4667][Para 004] • Mobile lower incisors – resulting from physiological loss in a child 6 years of age

[4672][Para 017] Using the strategies described earlier, you manage to get the child to let you look at his teeth while his mother brushes them. No caries is obvious, but both lower central deciduous incisors are very mobile. These appear to be the cause of the discomfort, and the mother can be reassured. No intervention is likely to be helpful or possible. This is a self-limiting problem. The parent should be instructed to show the mobile teeth to the child in a mirror to help him understand.
[4673][Para 017] If caries had been noted, there would probably have been no option but to refer the patient for treatment under general anaesthesia. [4675][Heading 2]  What is Your Strategy for Further Visits?
[4676][Para 001] Plan frequent short visits to make progress in small increments until the child accepts dental examination while seated in the dental chair. The aims are to provide an intensive preventive regimen so that treatment is unnecessary and to be able to undertake examinations to ensure the regimen is effective.
[4677][Para 002] A ‘social storyline’ may help prepare the child for the next dental visit and reduce anxiety. This is a series of pictures or photographs that tell the child what will happen and what can be expected. Different children will respond to different styles and formats of social stories.
[4678][Para 002] Offer to have your photograph taken, together with any images of the practice and staff involved. An example is shown in Fig. 42.3. You will need to investigate the child’s own communication strengths.
[4679][Para 002] Dietary analysis is critical, given the unusual diets in many cases, as noted above. Safe reinforcers and snacks may need some imaginative thought because wheat and dairy products may be unacceptable, chronic diarrhoea may have ruled out fruit, and the child may only eat food of one colour. Sugar-free confectionery may have to be considered.

[4681][Para 008] 
[4682][Para 011] Fig. 42.3 Example of social storyline preparing for a visit to the dentist.
[4683][Para 009]  
[4684][Para 002] Establishing the habit of toothbrushing is essential for children with autism. Not only does it maintain gingival health but it will also deliver fluoride through the toothpaste. As for other children with disabilities, adults’ toothpaste with a high fluoride content is appropriate, given the importance of preventing caries. If the toothbrushing habit has been established, a toothbrush is usually the best way to entice children with learning difficulty to open the mouth.
[4685][Para 002] The mother should bring the patient’s own toothbrush and paste. These form a conceptual link for the patient between visiting the dentist and his teeth and also allow you to capitalize on behaviour that is normally part of the patient’s home routine.
[4686][Para 002] The dental treatment of children with autism in a general practice can be a challenge, but if the practitioner is willing and able to adapt his or her approach, more able children with autism can be treated. Parents are often disappointed by dental staff who know too little about the condition and who feel they are ill equipped to manage a child with autism. More severely affected children usually require referral to a specialist.
[4687][Para 014] Further Guidance
[4688][Para 001] Further information for dental professionals can be found at the British Society of Paediatric Dentistry website (www.bspd.co.uk), including a questionnaire for parents and information leaflets on autism and dental care for children with autism.

[4711][Heading 2]  What Alternatives are There for Replacing the Missing Teeth, and What are Their Relative Advantages and Disadvantages?
[4712][Para 001] The options are shown in Table 43.1.
[4713][Heading 2]  What Specific Features of Importance Would You Examine? Explain Why
[4714][Para 001] The vertical height available for the ponticWhere a tooth is missing, there is potential for overeruption of teeth in the opposing arch. It is, therefore, important to assess the dimensions of the edentulous space when the teeth are in occlusion. If there has been vertical movement of opposing teeth, this can be addressed as part of an orthodontic care plan or restoration at increased vertical dimension if no conventional orthodontics is planned. In this case, the opposing premolar had been aligned as part of the orthodontic treatment.
[4715][Para 002] The degree of bone loss of the edentulous alveolar ridge is important. If this is extensively resorbed, an elongated pontic would be necessary to mask the bone loss. This might well be unacceptable if the pontic is easily seen during talking or smiling. Pink porcelain is possible at the gingival aspect of the pontic to mask lost soft tissue height, or this issue could be overcome with surgical ridge augmentation prior to placement of a bridge. This would prolong the treatment and make it considerably more complex as well as expensive. A diagnostic wax-up or computer-aided design may help the patient visualize the potential result if resorption is a problem or if the appearance is critical.
[4716][Para 002] Size and state of existing restorations in potential abutment teeth adjacent to the space. This is the most important consideration for minimal preparation bridges; that abutment teeth require no restorations, or only small restorations, so that there is sufficient enamel for bonding. A small intact restoration should be replaced, if clinically needed, or resurfaced with new resin composite. Extensively restored teeth leave little natural tooth tissue to supply retention for conventional bridges, whereas, conversely, conventional tooth preparation may be considered unnecessarily destructive where the potential abutments are minimally restored or unrestored. The quality of existing restorations must be known if they are to be used to prepare a core, as well as the amount of coronal dentine that will remain after tooth preparation. It should be remembered that an endodontically treated tooth may have little structural tissue in the core region because of the access cavity, and therefore, axial preparation may significantly further weaken the tooth removing much of the remaining coronal dentine.
[4717][Para 018] Table 43.1
[4718][Para 021] Replacement Options
[4719][Para 002] Inclination of the potential abutment teeth A degree of vertical alignment is necessary to eliminate undercuts to create a path of insertion and allow a conventional bridge to be made in the laboratory. Provided the teeth are fairly parallel, this can be achieved with adequate preparation. If the teeth are not parallel, a fixed–movable design is useful because it allows the restoration on each tooth to have a different path of withdrawal. In the case of adhesive bridges, minor preparation/finishing margins within enamel are sometimes considered, although this can risk dentine exposure in the cervical region of the tooth and may not be necessary. Because adhesive bridges will frequently be of a cantilever design, the degree of parallelism of the abutment teeth is not as significant a problem compared with conventional fixed–fixed designs, although it can affect the path of insertion and the size of embrasure spaces.
[4720][Para 002] Reduced height of clinical crown on either potential abutment tooth. Tooth wear or repeated restoration may have reduced the clinical crown height. There may be insufficient crown height for adequate retention and resistance form in the final tooth preparation. In extreme cases, additional retention such as a post may need to be considered. However, post-crowned teeth do not make predictable bridge abutments and using these teeth should be avoided, wherever possible.
[4721][Para 002] Increased height of clinical crown on either potential abutment tooth. Recession makes crown preparation more difficult because it is difficult to prevent undercuts in long preparations without extensive tooth reduction, especially where the roots are tapered. It may be necessary to place the crown margin some distance from the gingival margin, and this might compromise the appearance and adaptation of the pontic to the edentulous ridge.
[4722][Para 002] The dimensions of the alveolar ridge are important if implants are to be considered, although bone grafting may be an option if the deficiency is not too severe. For standard implants, a minimum of 7mm mesio-distal space between the adjacent teeth, sufficient bucco-lingual dimension to accommodate the selected fixture diameter, and sufficient interocclusal space is needed (this may vary, depending on the final vertical positioning of the implant and the specific implant system being used). Particular attention should be given to the buccal contour of the edentulous ridge because a concavity would make implant placement difficult and may compromise the appearance of a bridge as lost tissue cannot be replaced with a flange.
[4723][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Carry Out? Explain Why
[4724][Para 001] Radiography. In this case, radiography of the lower left and right lateral incisors, lower left first premolar and first molar teeth. If implants are being considered, radiographs are essential to assess the feasibility and for care planning. In the case of mandibular implants, a dental panoramic tomogram (DPT) is required to allow the inferior dental canal to be identified, as well as to assess root positon. If roots converge on a potential implant-bearing area, this may preclude implants even though intraoral examination revealed sufficient space between teeth. Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) may also be helpful for detailed planning, but not generally as part of an initial assessment.
[4725][Para 002] A radiographic assessment of root length is also important, especially in cases where orthodontic treatment has been undertaken, because this can cause root shortening, which may compromise the suitability of a tooth as a bridge abutment.
[4726][Para 002] Periapical radiographic imaging can also provide information regarding the disease status of teeth – including caries, periodontal bone loss or other pathology such as periradicular involvement – requiring attention before a bridge can be provided. It may also be necessary to assess the quality of pre-existing root fillings or for root treatment if either abutment tooth proves to be nonvital on examination (not applicable in this case).
[4727][Para 008] 
[4728][Para 011] Fig. 43.1 The mandibular spaces on presentation, anterior/buccal (a) and occlusal (b) views.
[4729][Para 009]  
[4730][Para 002] Sensibility tests of potential abutment teethIn this case, the teeth are unrestored and asymptomatic, and therefore, sensibility tests are not essential, but in cases where the teeth are restored, or preparations are being considered, the pulp status of the abutment teeth should be checked before any procedure is undertaken. If the teeth show signs of loss of vitality, any bridge design would need to take this into account. If required, endodontic treatment would have to be performed before bridge construction. The bridge should not be made until the definitive root filling has proven successful. A root-treated tooth is a compromised abutment because of its less certain long-term prognosis and the fact that there is reduced tooth structure for mechanical loading of the abutment. The preparation design should take this into account, aiming to preserve as much remaining dentine as possible. Also, it is desirable to root treat a tooth before cementing a bridge, avoiding damage to the retainer whilst gaining access to the pulp and root canal system after the bridge has been placed.
[4731][Para 002] Study models are useful in some cases. They can be used to make a diagnostic wax-up to show the patient the likely shape of the proposed bridge and to mould a former/stent to make a provisional restoration or create an ‘intraoral mock-up’ to allow the patient to visualize the proposed restoration in situ. The clinician can then assess aspects that cannot be seen on models, for example, lip line and occlusal plane, especially where anterior restorations are planned. Models also allow the clinician to plan treatment, including abutment preparation and pontic size. Articulated models mounted using a facebow could be used to analyze the occlusion.
[4732][Para 015] Treatment Options
[4733][Heading 2]  What Type of Replacement Appears Ideal?
[4734][Para 001] The patient has indicated a preference for a fixed prosthesis, and there seems no clinical reason to suggest any other option. A minimal preparation bridge is the most tissue-conserving option. A conventional bridge in this region would mean considerable destruction of the unrestored abutment tooth (lower left first molar and/or premolar and both lateral incisors in this case). Minimal preparation bridges are often thought to carry the risk of earlier failure compared with conventional bridges. Recent clinical research indicates this is not the case when careful case selection and appropriate design and maintenance are followed. There would be no advantage in providing a metal-based partial denture. The costs would be similar to those of a bridge, and patient satisfaction is likely to be less. An implant-retained restoration would also preserve tooth tissue and provide an aesthetic, fixed solution but is expensive and requires surgical intervention and there is insufficient bone to accommodate the fixture anteriorly.
[4735][Para 002] The possibility of leaving the gaps unfilled should also be considered. The occlusal stability of teeth should be borne in mind if this is considered. Adjacent teeth might drift into the gap or the opposing teeth might overerupt, creating occlusal interferences or complicating restoration of the spaces at a later date. These changes could be kept under review by using study casts. Examination of the overall occlusion may give an indication as to the likelihood of undesirable movements; for example, a well-interdigitated occlusion may reduce the chances of drifting or tilting. The presence of ‘holding contacts’ between teeth in opposing arches would mitigate against overeruption compared with those cases where a space leaves teeth out of interocclusal contact. However, even bearing the above factors in mind, a prosthesis remains only advisable and not essential. This is a decision based on appearance, and the final decision must rest with the patient.
[4736][Heading 2]  What Factors Might Make You Suggest a Removable Prosthesis Instead?
[4737][Para 001] The cost is probably the most common reason for choosing a removable denture rather than a bridge. However, a number of specific reasons might favour the choice of a removable prosthesis:
[4738][Para 004] • Multiple missing teeth requiring replacement on both sides of the arch
[4739][Para 004] • Mobility or significant periodontal bone loss or inflammation around abutment teeth
[4740][Para 004] • In the likelihood of the patient losing more teeth in the short term, easy addition of replacements to an acrylic-based partial denture
[4741][Para 004] • A high smile line with marked resorption of the edentulous alveolar bone in the upper arch – this is most satisfactorily hidden by an acrylic flange. In such cases, a better aesthetic result can be achieved with a removable prosthesis, where soft tissue requires replacement
[4742][Para 004] • Poor oral hygiene or a high caries rate – this would make it unwise to provide a fixed prosthesis, which is difficult to clean and may increase the likelihood of further primary disease. As a general principle, all primary disease should be controlled and evidence of oral health maintenance achieved before any complex restorative work is considered, including indirect restorations. A denture could arguably compromise a larger number of teeth, and neither replacement would be ideal in this instance. However, a carefully designed partial denture is the better option.
[4743][Para 030]  If the Patient Opted for a Removable Prosthesis, What Designs Would You Consider?
[4744][Para 001] In this ‘bounded saddle’ situation, a metal-based tooth-supported design is ideal. Abutment teeth would require small rest seat preparations, and one abutment tooth would require a clasp. A lingual connector would be required. A second clasp on the opposite side would provide sufficient retention.
[4745][Heading 2]  Should the Study Models Be Mounted On an Articulator To Make the Bridge?
[4746][Para 001] Properly articulated models mounted with the use of a facebow are essential when a bridge:
[4747][Para 004] • Involves many teeth
[4748][Para 004] • Changes the anterior guidance
[4749][Para 004] • Includes occlusal surfaces involved in guidance
[4750][Para 004] • Increases the vertical dimension.
[4751][Para 002] The choice of articulator will depend on the clinician’s preference, but in most cases with straightforward restorations, a semiadjustable articulator is satisfactory. For simple crowns and bridges, when the guidance is straightforward such as in the present case, either handheld models or a simple hinge articulator can be sufficient.
[4752][Heading 2]  What is the Ideal Design of a Minimal-Preparation Bridge?
[4753][Para 001] The ideal design of an adhesive bridge varies, depending on the site and size of the edentulous space. Various possibilities are shown in Fig. 43.2. In the upper anterior region, a simple cantilever design lasts longest. In the lower anterior region, a fixed–fixed design may be more dependable as it is easier to seat at cementation. In the present case, a cantilever design using the molar or premolar as a retainer to replace the lower left second premolar, or fixed–fixed designs are possible.
[4754][Para 002] In this case, a minimal-preparation adhesive mesial cantilever design was selected for the lower left posterior bridge. In the anterior region, a fixed–fixed design was selected. The completed bridges are shown in Figs 43.3 and 43.4.
[4755][Para 002] The following design features are worth noting:
[4756][Para 004] • Fixed–fixed versus cantilever design. Research has shown that a cantilever design can be more predictable in general terms because it negates the risk of a silent debonding of one retainer wing. However, where two adjacent lateral incisors are used as abutments, it can be difficult to ensure accurate seating where the lingual morphology of the lateral incisors do not have a defined cingulum to assist positive seating with the pontics perfectly aligned. A fixed–fixed design is generally not recommended because of the risk of a silent debonding of one wing resulting from the differential mobility of the abutment teeth. However, in this site, where the two abutments teeth have similar surface area for adhesion and comparable mobility in both magnitude and direction, the risk of this is reduced. In addition, a fixed–fixed design is more straightforward to cement and does not carry the risk of poor pontic alignment, as described above. Nevertheless, if this design is adopted, it is essential that the patient is warned of the possibility of a unilateral debonding of one of the retainer wings and advised that if he or she feels the bridge may have moved, advice should be sought as soon as possible. Additionally, the dentist should be vigilant in checking this at each review appointment. Conversely, where incisors are being replaced and one canine and one incisor are the abutment teeth, the differential mobility between the two abutment teeth is significantly different and a fixed–fixed design would not be advisable.
[4757][Para 125] 
[4758][Para 008] 
[4759][Para 052] Fig. 43.2 Possible bridge designs to fill the left second premolar region (i) and lower incisor (ii) spaces. i, Lower left second premolar space. a, The gap can be left and provided overeruption of the opposing dentition does not occur, the existing situation would be stable. In this case, the UL5 is already showing signs of over-eruption (see Fig. 43.1), and therefore, unless an orthodontic retainer is worn, the vertical position of this tooth cannot be guaranteed. b, A fixed–fixed adhesive bridge with retainer wings on the lower left first premolar and first molar teeth. c, A mesial cantilever design using the LL6 as abutment. d, A distal cantilever design using the LL4 as abutment. Distal cantilevers are generally less predictable than mesial cantilevers, and therefore, unless a distal abutment is not present or unsuitable as a bridge abutment, a mesial cantilever would usually be the design of choice. In this case, the LL6 is unrestored and, therefore, is a suitable abutment tooth. The design of the retainers is described in more detail in the text. ii, Lower incisor region. a, Two individual cantilever bridges can be constructed, cantilevering mesially from each of the adjacent lateral incisors. b, A fixed–fixed design utilizing the two lateral incisors. Note the retainer wing design over the entire lingual/occlusal surface of the proposed abutment teeth.
[4760][Para 004] • Extension of the retainer wing. To maximize the rigidity of the retainer and utilize the maximum surface area of enamel available for bonding, the retainer wings are designed to extend over the entire occlusal and lingual surfaces of the posterior abutment teeth. This also means the cement lute is loaded in compression, rather than shear, as would be the case if only the axial surfaces were incorporated in the design, reducing unfavourable forces that might cause debonding. If a restoration is present in an abutment tooth, the retainer wing must be extended to beyond the margins of the entire restoration, such that the retainer margins are in contact with enamel for bonding. A minimum of 0.5–0.7mm retainer thickness is required for rigidity, reducing flexion and thereby reducing the risk of bond failure. For the incisor bridge retainers, the wing is also extended just onto the incisal edge of the abutment teeth to aid in location and to protect the cement lute from shear forces. This design negates the need for an incisal location ‘lug’, as is sometimes described, which would need to be removed at the fit appointment before the luting cement has fully matured. Vibrations caused during this process may compromise the strength of the cement lute. A location lug may also prevent full seating of the retainer wing, rather than aiding location, and this may compromise bridge retention.
[4761][Para 004] • Preparation. No tooth preparation was undertaken in this case, as this is only required if the bulbosity of the axial surfaces of the abutment teeth would create undercuts that might limit the path of insertion or connector height. Maximizing the connector height is, nevertheless, important for ensuring the rigidity and strength of the connector and to reduce the size of the embrasure space between the pontic and the abutment tooth. Tooth preparation, including rest seats and retention grooves, is not advised because this carries the risk of exposing dentine and compromising bond strength of the adhesive cement and may slightly increase the risk of caries associated with restorations and sealants (CARS – secondary caries) developing if the cement lute fails and leaks. It also constitutes a more complicated procedure, in which the detail of these preparation features must be captured accurately at the impression stage, poured up in the laboratory and cast with a sufficient degree of accuracy so that the restoration fit is not compromised, all for little or no gain with regard to the function and survival of the restoration.
[4762][Para 125] 
[4763][Para 008] 
[4764][Para 052] Fig. 43.3 The completed bridges. Anterior/buccal view in occlusion and two views with teeth apart showing the occlusal appearance of the retainers.
[4765][Para 004] • Occlusion. A design extending the retainer wing over part or whole of the occlusal surface, as described, is likely to cause some change in the occlusion. However, if this is cemented ‘high’, it is not unreasonable to expect dento-alveolar compensation to occur following cementation, resulting in re-establishment of the interocclusal contacts in the weeks following placement (commonly known as the ‘Dahl effect’). It would be wise, of course, to monitor these contacts to ensure that this does occur during the review period.
[4766][Para 004] • Cementation. A self or dual-cure resin luting cement should be used for cementation, paying careful attention to the manufacturer’s instructions or procedural steps. A light-curing cement is not appropriate because the light would not be able to penetrate the metal retainer for a reliable cure beneath the retainer wing. It is also advisable to consider using an opaque cement that blocks the silver metal appearance, sometimes seen as greying through of the abutment teeth, especially anteriorly. It is worth noting, however, that the metal wing prevents light from passing through the abutment teeth, and this change in translucency should be taken into account when shade matching. Patients must be informed of these aesthetic changes during the planning phase before execution to manage their expectations.
[4767][Para 030]  What Would You Do if the Bridge Fails Through Debonding?
[4768][Para 001] If the bridge decements shortly after placement, it is acceptable to recement the bridge and ensure that there is no occlusal interference. If the problem persists, a conventional bridge or an implant may then be indicated. However, if the planning stages have been carried out accurately and thoroughly, this issue may be due to the cementation process, and due care would be required to ensure that all stages of luting were carried out appropriately.

[4773][Heading 2]  What are the Main Issues with Patient Communication in This Case? What Should Be Explained and Highlighted To the Patient?
[4774][Para 001] As with all cases, it is essential to communicate clearly with the patient from the beginning of treatment and throughout.
[4775][Para 002] In the first instance, it is important to understand clearly what patients’ main concerns are and what they hope to gain from treatment. The initial conversation with a patient is important because it is an opportunity to identify and discuss expectations and to ensure that treatment is focused on addressing all their concerns or discussing what is possible or advisable in a situation where their expectations cannot be met. This is also an opportunity to explain to patients what the limitations of the treatment are and what the possible complications may be, as well as the prognosis and maintenance implications. It is important to remember that no prosthetic replacement will last forever. This must be borne in mind during care planning and explained to patients so that they can make appropriate informed decisions with regard to their treatment choices. The diagnostic wax-up may form part of this discussion, with an intraoral ‘mock-up’ to assist the patient in visualizing the possible result, but it is important to bear in mind that the mock-up can be misleading with regard to what is achievable, and so a critical assessment of this is wise before relying on it too heavily during consultation and planning.
[4776][Para 002] The above discussions form an integral and essential part of the process of obtaining informed consent from a patient, and this should be appropriately documented and discussed with the patient as part of the consent process.
[4777][Para 025] Case 44
[4778][Heading 1] Anticoagulation for a Prosthetic Heart Valve
[4779][Para 027] Nicholas M. Goodger
[4780][Para 028] Summary
[4781][Para 029] A 60-year-old man presents at your general dental practice requiring a dental extraction. He is taking oral anticoagulants. How will you deal with his extraction?
[4782][Para 218] 
[4783][Para 008] 
[4784][Para 011] Fig. 44.1 Oral anticoagulation record book.
[4785][Para 009]  
[4786][Para 014] History
[4787][Para 019] Complaint
[4788][Para 007] The patient has a broken-down upper first molar that is tender on biting. The patient points directly at the tooth and requests extraction.
[4789][Para 012] History of Complaint
[4790][Para 007] The tooth has been root filled and crowned but is tender to percussion. There have been several similar episodes of pain in the past year. The crown has been lost from the tooth.
[4791][Para 012] Medical History
[4792][Para 007] The patient reports that he had rheumatic fever as a child, and, as a result of cardiac valve damage, he had received a prosthetic heart valve 7 years ago. He is taking warfarin (9 mg daily) and bendroflumethiazide (5 mg daily). The patient carries an anticoagulation book from his local clinic, showing that his international normalized ratio (INR) prothrombin time (PT) is usually between 3.5 and 4.5 ( Fig. 44.1 ). It was last checked 10 days ago, when it was 3.9.
[4793][Heading 2]  How Does Warfarin Work, and How is Anticoagulation Monitored?
[4794][Para 001] Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist. It prevents the liver from utilizing vitamin K to make clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. The patient is usually under the care of an anticoagulation clinic, although some patients are monitored by their general medical practitioner. Blood tests are performed regularly, and the results and drug doses are recorded in a yellow book that the patient should always carry.
[4795][Heading 2]  What is the Inr Test, What is Its Normal Therapeutic Range and How Should the Result Be Interpreted?
[4796][Para 001] The INR is a standardized method of presenting the results of a PT test. The result is the ratio of the patient’s PT to that of a standardized control and measures the effectiveness of the extrinsic and common pathways of blood coagulation, those most affected by warfarin. The therapeutic range for patients who have had deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE) is 2.5–3.5. For patients with a prosthetic heart valve, it is 3.5–4.5, depending on valve type, at the top of the therapeutic range.
[4797][Para 002] In theory, the INR is a standardized test using an internationally accepted standard. Unfortunately, in practice, accurate standardization of the INR is often not reproducible, and small changes in the decimal places of the result cannot be relied on to reflect small changes in anticoagulation. The test should be regarded as an estimate of anticoagulation, rather than an accurate measure.
[4798][Heading 2]  Is This Patient At Risk of Infective Endocarditis?
[4799][Para 001] Yes, all patients with the following conditions are considered at risk, and a prosthetic heart valve is a factor that carries a very high risk of fatal outcome if endocarditis develops:
[4800][Para 004] • Valve replacement
[4801][Para 004] • Acquired valvular heart disease with stenosis or regurgitation
[4802][Para 004] • Surgically corrected or altered congenital heart defects∗
[4803][Para 004] • Previous infective endocarditis
[4804][Para 004] • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
[4805][Para 014] Examination
[4806][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[4807][Para 007] No lymphadenopathy is present, and the extraoral examination reveals no abnormalities. However, a large bruise is apparent on the patient’s right forearm, consistent with the degree of anticoagulation.
[4808][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[4809][Para 007] The patient has a number of teeth with large restorations and several crowned teeth. His periodontal condition and oral hygiene are relatively good, with only small amounts of detectable interdental plaque.
[4810][Para 017] The upper first molar tooth is broken down. Root-filling material can be seen in the open pulp chamber and much of the root surface is carious. The tooth is tender to percussion. The second premolar is not tender to percussion but produces a dull percussive note. No draining sinus is present. The periodontal condition seems reasonable, and there is no significant bone loss around the tooth on probing.
[4811][Para 017] There is caries around the distal margin of a crown on the first premolar.
[4812][Para 015] Investigations
[4813][Heading 2]  What Investigations are Required, and Why?
[4814][Para 001] The premolars and molars should be checked for vitality. The first premolar is vital, but both the second premolar and the first molar do not respond to testing with an electric pulp tester. A radiograph is required to determine whether the molar is restorable, that is, to gauge the extent of caries and determine the success of the root filling. If it turns out that extraction is required, a radiograph will be necessary to assess the difficulty of the extraction. This is particularly important in a patient who may suffer prolonged bleeding. The periapical view is the ideal view.

[4818][Para 009]  
[4819][Heading 2]  The Periapical View is Shown in Fig. 44.2. What Does It Show?
[4820][Para 001] The first permanent molar is extensively carious. A root filling is present, but only one gutta percha or silver point is visible in the palatal canal. It extends beyond the apex by approximately 2 mm. The buccal roots are not clearly visible but appear to contain no root filling. The overextended root filling lies close to the antrum, and the antrum extends down between the roots of the first molar and the second premolar. There is no apical radiolucency. The second premolar is also root filled. The root filling appears to stop just short of the anatomical apex at an appropriate point, but a small apical radiolucency is present, surrounded by the lamina dura of the tooth socket. The caries below the crown on the first premolar is visible, and the second molar contains a large pinned amalgam.
[4821][Para 015] Diagnosis
[4822][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis? Explain Your Diagnosis
[4823][Para 001] The patient’s pain is caused by periapical periodontitis of the first permanent molar.
[4824][Para 002] The patient points clearly to this tooth as the source of his pain. This and the tenderness on percussion indicate inflammation of the periodontal ligament, and the overfilled root canal is a likely cause. No radiolucency is shown on the radiograph. However, it is not required for diagnosis in the presence of typical signs and symptoms. There may be either only a small apical lesion or one on the apices of the buccal roots or in the trifurcation, both of which are superimposed on the film.
[4825][Para 002] The second premolar has an unsuccessful root filling and a small periapical radiolucency, almost certainly a periapical granuloma. However, it is not tender to percussion and is not felt to be the cause of the pain by the patient. The first premolar is vital, and the caries would produce pain of the pulpitis type without tenderness on biting or percussion.
[4826][Para 015] Treatment
[4827][Heading 2]  What Treatment Would You Recommend?
[4828][Para 001] The primary consideration should be that the patient is at risk of infective endocarditis, and potential sources of infection should be eradicated. The first molar cannot be restored without another root filling and extensive preparation. The patient prefers extraction, and this is the appropriate course of action. The first premolar is more problematic. It appears to be symptom-free, and the apical granuloma has probably been present for some time. This lesion is a potential source of infection, and it must be eliminated, either by extraction or another root filling. The success of the new root filling must be monitored to ensure that it is successful, and if not, either apicectomy or extraction will need to be considered. Treatment may be complicated by the anticoagulation treatment, so there must be a comprehensive treatment plan that takes the rest of the dentition into account.
[4829][Heading 2]  Is the Extraction of the First Molar Likely To Be Straightforward?
[4830][Para 001] No. The tooth is broken down and root filled, and there is little or no bone loss from periodontitis. It will be difficult to grasp with forceps and may be brittle. The roots extend close to the antrum, and there is a risk of creating a surgical oroantral fistula.
[4831][Para 002] A simple forceps extraction may be possible, but the extraction may well require a mucoperiosteal flap and bone removal. A simple forceps extraction would be preferable in an patient on anticoagulation medication because bleeding is more easily controlled when it is limited to a socket and the surrounding gingiva. A surgical extraction would be less traumatic overall, and separating the roots and elevating them singly would reduce the risk of an oroantral fistula.
[4832][Heading 2]  The Patient is At Risk of Endocarditis. Is Antibiotic Cover Required?
[4833][Para 001] Not necessarily. Before 2008, antibiotic cover would have been routine, and the patient would have been administered oral amoxicillin or an alternative antibiotic regimen. In 2008, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommended that antibiotic cover was no longer recommended for dental procedures, even for the highest-risk patients. However, in 2016, the revised guidance stated that antibiotic cover was not routinely required for patients undergoing dental procedures, indicating that sometimes it may be provided.
[4834][Heading 2]  Why Did the Recommendations Change So Dramatically?
[4835][Para 001] In the past, antibiotic prophylaxis was based on a precautionary principle. It seemed logical because bacterial endocarditis had a high fatality rate, oral bacteria were sometimes implicated and antibiotics could prevent bacteraemia. However, much of the presumed benefit was based on animal models of the disease and the results of those studies could not be extrapolated to humans. There were cases where prophylaxis had been correctly given but had failed. More recent evidence from case control studies suggests that prophylaxis is possibly ineffective.
[4836][Para 002] Although dentistry has frequently been blamed for bacterial endocarditis, there is little or no evidence to suggest that dental procedures were to blame, nor oral bacteria. Low-grade bacteraemias caused by eating and toothbrushing are common enough to be considered normal. There is no evidence to link the level of bacteraemia with the risk of endocarditis, and these normal bacteraemias would appear to be as dangerous as those occurring after dental procedures.
[4837][Para 002] If there is little benefit from antibiotic prophylaxis, there is significant risk. Adverse effects of antibiotics range from fatal anaphylaxis to the development of resistant strains. It has been suggested that death caused by anaphylaxis is five times more likely than death caused by endocarditis. Although this is difficult to ascertain (and anaphylaxis is both avoidable and treatable), it sheds a rather different light on the value of antibiotic cover. A further factor is cost; resources spent on antibiotic prophylaxis are probably wasted and may cause harm.
[4838][Para 002] This UK guidance is not consistent with guidance from Europe and the US. There has been concern about patients who were at the highest risk of endocarditis, and some cardiologists and cardiothoracic surgeons felt that the UK guidance ignored this potentially vulnerable group. Prophylaxis, therefore, remains in use for the highest-risk patients.
[4839][Heading 2]  How Should Endocarditis Be Avoided?
[4840][Para 001] The emphasis should be on prevention, and patients at risk of endocarditis must maintain a high standard of oral and dental health. They will require effective regimens for the prevention of caries and periodontal disease and must have infections identified and treated promptly and effectively. Patients need to be aware of the signs and symptoms of endocarditis and told to return or seek other expert advice immediately if they do develop. Unnecessary medical and dental interventions should be avoided, and patients need to understand the risks of infection from nonmedical sources as well. Chlorhexidine mouthwash or other topical agents should not be offered as prophylaxis against infective endocarditis. They are not effective.
[4841][Para 002] In patients who might be at high risk of endocarditis such as those who have had previous episodes of endocarditis and those with prosthetic valves, the dentist should discuss the risks and benefits of prophylaxis with the patient’s cardiologist.
[4842][Heading 2]  If the Patient Requested Antibiotic Prophylaxis, What Would You Do?
[4843][Para 001] National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidance states that practitioners must be able to give clear and consistent information about endocarditis and explain the risks and benefits of antibiotic prophylaxis. If a patient insists on receiving antibiotic cover, support from the patient’s medical practitioner or cardiologist may assist in the decision making. A disagreement over antibiotic cover, however, cannot be allowed to delay treatment of infection in a patient at risk of endocarditis. Changes in guidance could place you in a difficult situation; you would be found liable if a patient developed an adverse reaction to antibiotics administered for no better reason than the patient’s request. If either the patient or the cardiologist considers antibiotic cover to be necessary, it would prudent to arrange for the cardiologist to determine the antibiotic regimen.
[4844][Heading 2]  Would You Expect This Patient To Suffer Prolonged Bleeding After a Dental Extraction?
[4845][Para 001] Potentially yes, and if untreated, such bleeding could necessitate hospital admission. The mouth is a highly vascular site, and saliva has fibrinolytic activity. Untreated prolonged haemorrhage could be fatal, although the risk is low.
[4846][Heading 2]  Does the Patient Require Reduction of the Inr To Enable Minor Oral Surgery?
[4847][Para 001] Until recently, it was accepted that the INR had to be reduced for procedures such as intramuscular injections, minor surgery and dental extraction. The INR was reduced to 2.5 or below for inferior dental (ID) nerve block, simple extractions and soft tissue surgery. However, it has recently been demonstrated that the incidence of bleeding after a dental extraction performed without reducing or stopping warfarin is less than has been thought and that any bleeding may be relatively easily controlled. Current UK guidance is available from the British Committee for Standards in Haematology, British Dental Association, National Patient Safety Agency and the Scottish Dental Clinical Effectiveness Programme. The guidance recommends that oral anticoagulants should not be stopped for outpatient oral surgery, including extractions, provided the degree of anticoagulation is stable, with an INR between 2 and 4. Additional procedures to reduce the risk of bleeding such as suturing sockets with an oxidized cellulose (Surgicel) dressing and use of tranexamic acid mouthwashes, are recommended.
[4848][Heading 2]  Why Did These Guidelines Change?
[4849][Para 001] For two reasons. Firstly, clinical research has shown that it is safe to extract teeth without reducing or stopping warfarin if the INR is below 4.0 and when the sockets have been packed with a haemostatic agent and sutured. Secondly, it has been realized that stopping anticoagulants places patients at risk of thrombosis, embolism or both. Clearly, these complications are of major importance and potentially fatal. The risk of thromboembolism after withdrawal of anticoagulants for a day or two is debated, but it is clear that significant complications can arise when anticoagulants are stopped for a few days. To ensure patient safety, the decision has been made to maintain the level of anticoagulation, if at all possible.
[4850][Heading 2]  Suppose More Extensive Surgery Were Planned?
[4851][Para 001] For more major surgery, the risk of haemorrhage would rise significantly. The patient would then have to be treated in a hospital setting because he or she would need to be switched from warfarin to heparin. Heparin is given as a daily dose using low-molecular-weight heparin preparations such as enoxaparin (Clexane), avoiding heparin infusion. These have a half-life of only a few hours, allowing anticoagulation to be readily reversed in an emergency with the use of antagonist drugs. Anticoagulation with heparin is monitored by the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and is usually kept at 1.5–2.5 times the normal level.
[4852][Heading 2]  Do You Still Need To Check the Inr? How Recently Should the Last Inr Test Have Been Done?
[4853][Para 001] Yes, you still need to ensure that the INR is 4.0 or less. The more recent the test, the better. In the past, it was suggested that a result less than 24 hours old was required to adjust the warfarin dose.
[4854][Para 002] Because the warfarin dose is not adjusted, a test result up to 72 hours old may be accepted. However, if the INR result on the patient’s anticoagulation record card fluctuates without change in dose, only a test performed on the day of treatment should be accepted. If there has been no recent test, one should be requested, or the appointment may be postponed until the next test result is available.
[4855][Heading 2]  The Patient Says He Tests His Own Inr. Is That Acceptable?
[4856][Para 001] Coagulation testing can now be performed by using small handheld, battery-operated devices, allowing coagulation testing to be performed by medical practitioners or the patients themselves (‘point of care’ testing or ‘near-patient’ testing). Results from a medical practice can be considered reliable because machines are checked and calibrated regularly. Some patients opt to test their own INR at home, and some evidence suggests that their anticoagulation is managed very well. Selected patients are trained to interpret their own results and are able to adjust their own doses. Provided the patient’s coagulometer is monitored under a quality assurance scheme, the results can be relied on. However, patients cannot take the responsibility for adjusting their dose for a medical procedure but can do so only for routine dosing. With approximately 1 million UK patients taking warfarin, and the total rising, this type of testing is likely to be encountered more frequently.
[4857][Heading 2]  How Can Warfarin Anticoagulation Be Reversed in an Emergency?
[4858][Para 001] Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist, and administering vitamin K intravenously can reverse its effects (oral dosing is effective but much slower in action). Vitamin K takes some time to become effective because the liver must synthesize the necessary clotting factors. For a more rapid effect, Beriplex, which is a soluble powder containing human prothrombin complex, can be given for rapid reversal in emergency situations. Alternatively, the missing clotting factors can be replaced immediately by transfusing fresh frozen plasma.
[4859][Heading 2]  What Additional Precautions Might You Take To Ensure Haemostasis?
[4860][Para 001] In general, warfarin is associated with oozing of blood from soft tissues, rather than bleeding from bone. Current guidance recommends no reduction in warfarin dose, a single interrupted or mattress suture across the mouth of the socket and an oxidized cellulose (Surgicel) pack for all extractions. Haemostasis must be achieved, usually by applying gentle pressure on the gingiva. Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic agent that inhibits conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, stabilizing clots once formed. It can be administered as a 5% mouthwash and must be used four times a day for several days after extraction.
[4861][Para 002] If there is severe periodontitis, then treating this first, even if only around a few teeth, significantly reduces postoperative bleeding.
[4862][Para 017] In this case, a further test was required, and the INR had fallen slightly to 3.7. The tooth was extracted and the socket sutured. Haemostasis was achieved after a slightly prolonged period.
[4863][Heading 2]  What Postoperative Instructions are Necessary Regarding the Patient’s Bleeding Tendency?
[4864][Para 001] No specific instructions are necessary. The patient should be warned not to eat or drink or rinse the mouth for a few hours after extraction. A little blood in saliva is to be expected but should vanish over a few hours. If there is bleeding from the socket or fresh blood in saliva, then biting on a damp gauze swab (provided for the purpose on discharge) should stop the bleeding. Pressure must be maintained for at least 5 minutes at a time to stop the bleeding. If this fails, the patient should not hesitate to contact your practice or a local hospital accident and emergency (A&E) department. The patient may rinse with hot salt mouthwashes on the following day.
[4865][Heading 2]  What Postoperative Instructions are Necessary Regarding the Risk of Endocarditis?
[4866][Para 001] All patients at risk of endocarditis must be warned to be alert for signs and symptoms of endocarditis. Unfortunately, these are relatively nonspecific in the early stages. The symptoms may be of acute onset and progress rapidly or persist for weeks or months before cardiac signs develop. Endocarditis caused by oral streptococci is usually of this latter subacute type. Patients with endocarditis of prosthetic valves progress to heart failure more rapidly. Low-grade endocarditis is often a diagnostic challenge in the early stages, and patients and dentists need to have a high index of suspicion. Patients should seek advice if they develop:
[4867][Para 004] • Influenza-like symptoms of malaise and fatigue
[4868][Para 004] • Fever or night sweats
[4869][Para 004] • Weight loss and loss of appetite
[4870][Para 004] • Rash
[4871][Para 004] • Vague and poorly localized pains
[4872][Para 004] • Splinter haemorrhages beneath the nails
[4873][Para 004] • Painful red nodules in finger tips (Osler’s nodes)
[4874][Para 004] • Haematuria
[4875][Para 004] • Joint pains
[4876][Para 004] • Signs of heart failure
[4877][Para 004] • Change in heart murmur
[4878][Para 004] • Transient ischaemic attacks and strokes.
[4879][Para 015] Postoperative
[4880][Heading 2]  The Patient Returns 3 Hours Later Reporting That Bleeding Has Continued Throughout Most of This Period. Why Did the Bleeding Restart?
[4881][Para 001] Bleeding in the immediate postoperative period is stopped by platelet plugs forming in the vessels. This mechanism is unaffected by warfarin, which inhibits only coagulation. After the initial haemostasis, coagulation fails to consolidate the platelet plugs. When the vasoconstrictor in the local anaesthetic wears off, there is a period of hyperaemia as a result of inflammation, and bleeding may start again.
[4882][Heading 2]  How Would You Manage This Postextraction Bleeding?
[4883][Para 001] Initially, check that the socket is only oozing because rapid bleeding would necessitate immediate measures. Then, take a history and assess the degree of blood loss, which, to the patient (and sometimes the dentist), always seems worse than it actually is. Examine the patient by using a good light and suction to remove the old socket dressing and poorly formed blood clots, and identify the bleeding area.
[4884][Para 002] If only soft tissue is bleeding, pressure and a new dressing will probably be all that is required. However, bleeding after packing and suturing may be arising from bone. If a bleeding point can be identified, it can be crushed with a hand instrument. Electrocautery should not be used on or near bone. Bone wax should only be used if all else fails because it delays healing in the longer term. Replace the Surgicel pack, or place a Whitehead’s varnish pack, and resuture the socket over the pack to provide pressure to the gingival margins and to keep the pack firmly in the socket. Bleeding from the surgical incision may require additional sutures and deeper sutures to compress the sides of the incision on to the underlying tissues.
[4885][Para 002] Measure blood pressure and pulse to assess whether there has been serious blood loss.
[4886][Para 002] Reassure the patient, who is often very worried and well aware of the problems of the anticoagulation treatment. Observe for 15–30 minutes, and reinforce the usual postoperative instructions. It should be emphasized that the patient not rinse until the next day. It is unlikely that these measures will fail.
[4887][Heading 2]  What Would You Do if There Were Tachycardia and Lowered Blood Pressure?
[4888][Para 001] This would indicate significant blood loss, and as mentioned above, the patient should be speedily admitted to hospital for intravenous fluid administration to prevent circulatory collapse.
[4889][Heading 2]  What Would You Do if These Steps Did Fail?
[4890][Para 001] In a practice setting, the patient should be transferred to a hospital casualty or specialist unit or to an anticoagulation clinic. This should be arranged speedily, and the patient will require an escort. There, the INR and the platelet count would be checked. Antifibrinolytics such as aprotinin and tranexamic acid can be used in conjunction with packing and suturing. If the bleeding persists or if the INR is above the therapeutic range, the patient will need to be admitted for reversal of the anticoagulation by infusion of fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrates (a more effective preparation of concentrated dried factors II, VII, IX and X) and vitamin K. The vitamin K injections will not reverse the action of the warfarin for 12 hours and so are not effective in such emergency situations, but they aid stabilization of anticoagulation after the bleeding stops. Major bleeding may necessitate a few days in the hospital.
[4891][Heading 2]  Warfarin Interacts with a Variety of Other Drugs. Which Drugs That Might Be Prescribed in Dental Practice Can Affect Warfarin Anticoagulation?
[4892][Para 001] In all drug interactions with warfarin, there is increased anticoagulation and a risk of bleeding. Aspirin and related drugs also increase the risk of bleeding, not through interaction but through their separate antiplatelet activity. Discussion with the patient’s anticoagulation clinic would be prudent if any of the following drugs are required:
[4893][Para 004] • Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
[4894][Para 004] • Antibiotics, including erythromycin, metronidazole, tetracyclines and penicillins
[4895][Para 004] • Fluconazole, ketoconazole and miconazole (including topical preparations).
[4896][Para 030]  How Can I Keep Up with All These Changes in Guidance?
[4897][Para 001] This case demonstrates how rapidly accepted practice and guidance from national bodies can change. A few years ago, the patient would have had antibiotic cover and adjustment of the warfarin dose before treatment. Guidance can, unfortunately, come from a wide variety of sources, and it is not always clear whether it is generally accepted, recommended or mandatory. Guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence apply to the National Health Service (NHS) in England and Wales, but not in Scotland, where a separate institution, the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network, plays the equivalent role. Guidance or references to it may also be provided by Royal Colleges, the British Dental Association, the General Dental Council and professional indemnity organizations. Overseas bodies such as the American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and similar bodies in Europe and in the Southern Hemisphere may also provide useful sources of guidance (see below). Guidance on medications in the British National Formulary or Dental Practitioners Formulary is regularly updated and usually considered definitive. Almost all guidelines first appear in peer-reviewed scientific or professional journals, although it may take some time for them to become accepted and be given the official seal of approval. This demonstrates the importance of continuing professional development to ensure that dentists remain up to date, one of the key principles for dentists of the UK General Dental Council.
[4898][Heading 2]  What if the Patient Had Been Taking One of the Novel Oral Anticoagulants Instead of Warfarin? How Do These Differ From Warfarin?
[4899][Para 001] Patients with prosthetic heart valves almost never take the ‘novel oral anticoagulants’ (NOACs) because these are indicated for the prevention of conditions such as stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation. Examples of NOACs are rivaroxiban, apixaban and edoxaban, which are direct inhibitors of factor Xa, and dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor.
[4900][Para 002] Because good evidence on which to make recommendations is not yet available, it is prudent to treat patients taking these drugs with caution. An inhibitor for dabigatran – idarucizumab – is available and can be used in an emergency to control bleeding, but those for the factor Xa inhibitors are still under development.
[4901][Para 002] The INR test is a poor reflection of anticoagulation with use of these drugs, and so alternative tests are required. However, routine monitoring is not required or normally undertaken, and so the dentist may not have a clear understanding of a patient’s degree of anticoagulation. Minor procedures such as scaling would not require special tests, but for extractions and procedures with significant bleeding risk, the dentist should consult the patient’s physician and current guidance. NOACs have rapid onset of action and short half-lives, and so they may be interrupted for short periods for dental treatment. If NOAC therapy is stopped, the normal procedure is to omit the morning dose prior to dental extractions if taken twice daily and then take the evening dose after treatment. If the patient is taking a morning-only dose, then that dose should be delayed until 4 hours after treatment has been completed.
