[4915][Para 025] Case 45
[4916][Heading 1] A White Patch On the Tongue
[4917][Para 027] Helen McParland, and Edward Odell
[4918][Para 028] Summary
[4919][Para 029] A 52-year-old woman has a white patch on her tongue. Make a diagnosis, and decide on appropriate treatment.
[4920][Para 218] 
[4921][Para 008] 
[4922][Para 011] Fig. 45.1 The patient’s tongue.
[4923][Para 009]  
[4924][Para 014] History
[4925][Para 019] Complaint
[4926][Para 007] The patient has no complaint.
[4927][Para 012] History of Complaint
[4928][Para 007] You have just noticed the lesion in a patient attending for the first time in several years. There is no written record of the white patch in her notes. The patient had noticed the lesion but had ignored it. She thinks it has probably been there for several years.
[4929][Para 012] Medical History
[4930][Para 007] The patient is otherwise fit and well. She smokes 4 cigarettes a day and drinks 4–8 units of alcohol each week.
[4931][Para 014] Examination
[4932][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[4933][Para 007] No lymph nodes are palpable in the neck, and there are no abnormal findings on extraoral examination.
[4934][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[4935][Para 007] Apart from this lesion, the remainder of the oral mucosa is normal.
[4936][Heading 2]  The Appearance of the Lesion is Shown in Fig. 45.1. What Do You See?
[4937][Para 001] There is a flat and homogeneous white patch on the left lateral border and ventral tongue mucosa. It is well defined and varies slightly in whiteness.
[4938][Para 017] If you were able to feel the lesion, you would find that it is soft and feels no different from the surrounding mucosa.
[4939][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[4940][Heading 2]  What are the Common or Important White Patches in the Mouth? How are They Caused?
[4941][Para 001] Almost all oral white patches are caused by increased keratinization of the epithelium. Keratin absorbs water and appears white, and it is brighter white where it is thicker. The exception is a chemical burn, where the white surface layer is caused by necrosis or ulceration. Common and important causes of oral mucosal white patches are listed in Table 45.1.
[4942][Para 018] Table 45.1
[4943][Para 021] Causes of White Patches in the Mouth
[4944][Heading 2]  Which Lesions Would You Include in the Differential Diagnosis for the Current Lesion?
[4945][Para 001] Likely diagnoses:
[4946][Para 004] • Idiopathic white patch (leukoplakia)
[4947][Para 004] • Smoker’s keratosis.
[4948][Para 002] Less likely diagnoses:
[4949][Para 004] • Chronic hyperplastic candidosis
[4950][Para 004] • Lichen planus or lichenoid reaction
[4951][Para 004] • Frictional keratosis
[4952][Para 004] • Squamous cell carcinoma.
[4953][Para 030]  What is Leukoplakia ?
[4954][Para 001] The literal meaning of leukoplakia is ‘white patch’. The term is correctly defined as a white patch that cannot be characterized as any other lesion. The use of this term is correct only after all possible known causes have been eliminated through whatever investigations are required. Unfortunately, the term leukoplakia is often used very loosely in the clinical context, either for a white patch of any cause or for the small minority of white patches with a risk of malignant transformation. This has led to great confusion. Now that the term has also been incorporated into the names of several lesions for which the cause is known (e.g. candidal leukoplakia, hairy leukoplakia and syphilitic leukoplakia), it is being used inconsistently to the point of being unhelpful.
[4955][Para 024]  Justify Your Differential Diagnosis
[4956][Para 020] Leukoplakia or Idiopathic White Patch
[4957][Para 001] Although there are many groups of well-defined white patches, the largest single group is that for which no cause can be identified. This is, therefore, a likely diagnosis for the present lesion because there are no clinical features that suggest a specific cause. The group of idiopathic white patches includes some more specific terms that might be applied to this lesion.
[4958][Para 004] • Sublingual keratosis refers to a white patch affecting the floor of the mouth or the ventral tongue, and lesions here are considered to have a high risk of malignant transformation. The typical lesion is bilateral and may be extensive in the floor of the mouth, often with a wrinkled surface of ‘ebbing tide’ parallel corrugations. However, sublingual keratosis is defined only by its site, and any white patch affecting the ventral tongue or the floor of the mouth could be termed sublingual keratosis. The present lesion only just extends to the ventral tongue mucosa.
[4959][Para 004] • Smoker’s keratosis is a white patch of no known cause and found in the mouth of a smoker. This type of lesion is a flat, homogeneous white patch, sometimes with a finely wrinkled surface, on nonkeratinized mucosa. Smoking is assumed to be the cause, although there is rarely any evidence to support this unless the lesion arises where the smoker habitually holds a pipe or a cigarette. This patient’s lesion could be smoker’s keratosis, but this is not a particularly useful label and does not imply that it should be treated any differently from an idiopathic white patch. Smoker’s palate (stomatitis nicotina) is a separate condition and is discussed below.
[4960][Para 004] • Frictional keratosis is common along the occlusal line, on edentulous alveolar ridges and on the lateral tongue. It may be associated with sharp teeth or restoration(s) and be unilateral or bilateral. Frictional keratosis usually merges gradually with the surrounding normal mucosa and is not as sharply defined as the present lesion. Tongue biting also causes keratosis, but the surface is often shredded, and there may be similar lesions on the buccal mucosa, usually just behind the commissure. Unless the lesions are associated with clear evidence of habitual biting or sharp teeth or if they resolve on removing the cause, it can be very difficult to identify them on the basis of their clinical appearance.
[4961][Para 004] • Chronic hyperplastic candidosis causes white plaques and is sometimes called candidal leukoplakia. These lesions arise most commonly on the postcommissural buccal mucosa and dorsal tongue and may be associated with red areas. These lesions are more common in smokers. Unless the site is typical, it is almost impossible to make the diagnosis clinically. Biopsy and resolution following antifungal treatment are the most useful indications to identify these lesions. The present lesion is not typical, but this cause cannot be confidently excluded on clinical grounds.
[4962][Para 004] • Lichen planus and lichenoid reactions may cause homogeneous white patches. This more unusual presentation seems to be more common in smokers, and it is not at all clear whether these so-called plaque-type lichen planus lesions are a genuine presentation of lichen planus or are induced by smoking. To be sure of the diagnosis, it is advisable to find evidence of more typical lichen planus elsewhere – on the skin, in the buccal mucosa or in the form of desquamative gingivitis. There is no evidence to suggest that the current lesion is caused by lichen planus, but the plaque type cannot be completely excluded on clinical grounds alone.
[4963][Para 004] • Squamous cell carcinoma diagnosis must be included for any white patch in the mouth without an identified cause. The chances of this particular lesion being malignant appear low. Although it is in a high-risk site, it is a flat, homogeneous lesion without ulceration, red areas, speckling or induration. The patient is a light smoker and is in the risk age group for squamous cell carcinoma. Although very unlikely, this just might be a carcinoma.
[4964][Para 080]  Which White Lesions Have You Excluded? Explain Why
[4965][Para 004] • Leukoedema and patches of Fordyce spots (sebaceous glands) are normal mucosal variants that affect primarily the buccal mucosa. Leukoedema causes a milky white appearance and is usually seen in those of African descent. Fordyce spots are sebaceous glands. They occasionally form clusters that resemble plaques but have a slightly yellow appearance, and individual glands are usually visible within the lesion. Both are present from childhood, and neither affects the lateral tongue.
[4966][Para 004] • White sponge naevus and pachyonychia congenita are examples of rare, inherited conditions that cause diffuse keratosis or multiple discrete white patches on the mucosa. These possibilities are excluded on the basis of the localized extent of the lesion, age at onset and the absence of other skin or nail abnormalities and family history.
[4967][Para 004] • An aspirin burn or other form of chemical trauma is unlikely. Such trauma results from the application of aspirin directly to the mucosa, usually in response to toothache. Lesions are mostly in the buccal sulcus and affect the mucosa on both sides of the site where the tablet was placed. This is an unlikely possibility and may be readily excluded through direct questioning.
[4968][Para 004] • Thrush affects larger areas of the mucosa, at least parts of the lesion may be wiped off and the underlying mucosa is inflamed. Chronic candidosis, rather than acute candidosis, could have caused the present lesion, as discussed above.
[4969][Para 004] • Hairy leukoplakia usually forms bilateral white lesions along the lateral border of the tongue, usually in immunosuppressed patients. Although the possibility of an undiagnosed immunosuppression, particularly resulting from human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, cannot be excluded, the appearances are not typical of hairy leukoplakia. Lesions remain limited to the lateral tongue in almost all cases.
[4970][Para 004] • Syphilitic leukoplakia may also be readily. The patient must have tertiary syphilis, and the site of the white patches is the dorsum of the tongue.
[4971][Para 004] • Smoker’s palate (stomatitis nicotina) may be excluded because it affects only the hard palate of pipe or cigar smokers and that of heavy cigarette smokers.
[4972][Para 015] Investigations
[4973][Heading 2]  Should a Biopsy Be Performed? Explain Why
[4974][Para 001] Yes. As a general rule, all white lesions in the mouth require biopsy. Completely typical keratotic lichen planus and typical frictional keratoses are considered exceptions to this rule by some authorities, but this would only be acceptable if the clinician were very experienced in the diagnosis of oral white lesions. Even those with extensive experience can be misled occasionally by a carcinomatous lesion that appears to be an innocuous white patch.
[4975][Para 002] The reasons for performing biopsy are:
[4976][Para 004] • To exclude/confirm squamous cell carcinoma
[4977][Para 004] • If not malignant, to determine whether dysplasia is present
[4978][Para 004] • To identify chronic candidal infection, if present
[4979][Para 004] • To help identify specific conditions and cause(s) for the lesion.
[4980][Para 030]  Is This Lesion Suitable for Biopsy in General Dental Practice? Explain Why
[4981][Para 001] Yes. The final decision will depend on your experience and confidence and the position of the lesion and its accessibility; however, there is no reason why this biopsy should not be performed in general dental practice. If you perform a biopsy, you are taking on yourself the responsibility of telling the patient the diagnosis, and so you may prefer to refer the patient to a hospital for opinion and biopsy.
[4982][Para 002] If there is any suspicion of malignancy, the patient should be referred to a specialist centre via an expedited referral pathway, according to local and national protocols. Any lesion that shows clinical features suggesting malignancy should be sampled by the person or team who will manage the patient’s care.
[4983][Para 024]  What Features of a White Patch Might Indicate Malignancy and Contraindicate Performing Biopsy in Dental Practice?
[4984][Para 004] • Associated red areas
[4985][Para 004] • Speckled areas
[4986][Para 004] • Ulceration, especially if chronic
[4987][Para 004] • Induration
[4988][Para 004] • Enlarged lymph nodes draining the site
[4989][Para 004] • Lesion in a high-risk site.
[4990][Para 030]  Is a Biopsy Really Necessary? Are There No Less Invasive Tests That Could Help Identify Risk Lesions?
[4991][Para 001] To those not experienced in oral white lesions, it may seem that immediate performance of biopsy is an excessive reaction. After all, benign lesions are so much commoner than potentially malignant causes. To a degree, this is true because almost 5% of the population over 50 years of age have white lesions of some type. Less invasive screening tests have, therefore, been sought to identify the lesions that require biopsy. A number of techniques have been proposed.
[4992][Para 020] Exfoliative Cytology and Brush Biopsy
[4993][Para 001] A sample of epithelial cells can be removed from the lesion by vigorous brushing with a stiff bristle brush. The smear containing cells is examined by using a variety of techniques, including computer-assisted cytopathological analysis. These techniques have improved and have become more reliable but, to date, have not replaced the need for biopsy.
[4994][Para 020] Toluidine Blue Staining
[4995][Para 001] Toluidine blue (tolonium chloride) staining was described decades ago but its use has recently been revived in the form of new commercial test kits. The dye can be applied to the lesion by dabbing or in a mouthwash, and it is claimed that lesions that retain the blue stain indicate a higher risk of dysplasia or carcinoma compared with those that do not. The predictive value of the test remains unclear, with better results shown in high-risk populations. False-positive reactions are common because the dye binds to ulcer slough, staining ulcers, lichen planus and other benign lesions.
[4996][Para 020] Optical Tests. Autofluorescence
[4997][Para 001] The oral mucosa contains a large number of autofluorescent molecules such as collagen and keratin. It is claimed that this normal fluorescence is lost in dysplasia and carcinoma. Handheld blue light illuminators with filters to detect the green florescence are available for screening, but their predictive value is low.
[4998][Para 020] Chemiluminescent light examination
[4999][Para 001] This technique illuminates the mucosa with white light, with or without an initial dilute acetic acid rinse and/or tolonium chloride staining. It is claimed that dysplastic and malignant lesions are more readily seen.
[5000][Para 002] Both these illumination techniques remain to be proven in well-controlled studies.
[5001][Para 002] All these tests are screening tests, and none is of sufficient accuracy to be used as a diagnostic test for carcinoma or dysplasia. Until such techniques are validated, biopsy remains the safest and only justifiable course of action. Studies show that patients do not find biopsy a traumatic procedure and that healing is rarely problematic. It is an investigation that any dental surgeon should be able to perform, and it should not be delayed.
[5002][Heading 2]  How Much Would You Remove and From Where?
[5003][Para 001] The ideal biopsy sample of mucosa to assess a white patch or mucosal condition is approximately 10 mm long and 4–5 mm wide. The sample should extend to muscle and provide sufficient deep tissue to support the epithelial sample for the pathologist to inspect microscopically. In the lateral tongue, this is only 2–3 mm depth because the muscle lies near the surface. In buccal mucosa, the ideal depth is slightly more – up to 5 mm. If a lesion is suspected to extend deeply, then a thicker sample will be required. This size of sample is readily removed, the wound is easily closed and healing is quick and without significant symptoms.
[5004][Para 002] The site sampled should comprise mostly the lesion but with a part of the margin and some adjacent normal mucosa. In a higher-risk lesion, any suspicious areas (see the list above) would be included. If several such areas were present, multiple samples might be required.
[5005][Heading 2]  The Biopsy Specimen is Required To Assess Dysplasia. What is Meant By ‘Dysplasia’?
[5006][Para 001] When applied to white or red oral patches, ‘dysplasia’ means the microscopic changes that indicate a risk of malignant transformation.
[5007][Heading 2]  What are the Features of Epithelial Dysplasia?
[5008][Para 001] Dysplasia is recognized by combinations of histological features listed in Table 45.2.
[5009][Heading 2]  How Do These Changes Differ From the Histological Changes Seen in Squamous Cell Carcinoma?
[5010][Para 001] Many, if not all, of these features are usually seen in squamous cell carcinomas. Carcinoma differs from dysplasia only in that it invades underlying tissues, usually as separate islands and strands of epithelium, and may metastasize to distant sites.
[5011][Para 018] Table 45.2
[5012][Para 021] Histological Features of Dysplasia
[5013][Heading 2]  How is Dysplasia Assessed?
[5014][Para 001] The scoring of dysplasia is extremely difficult, is not very reproducible and requires experience. Most pathologists categorize dysplastic lesions as mild, moderate and severe dysplasia. Severe dysplasia is sometimes called carcinoma in situ.
[5015][Para 002] With increasing severity of dysplasia, there is increasing risk of malignant transformation. Although dysplasia is the best indicator of the risk of malignancy, the relationship between the two is complex. Severe dysplasia nearly always indicates a relatively high risk, but carcinoma will occasionally develop in a white lesion that shows minimal or no dysplasia.
[5016][Heading 2]  Are There More Accurate Predictors of Transformation That Can Be Applied To the Biopsy?
[5017][Para 001] It has been shown that measuring the total DNA content of the epithelial cells (ploidy analysis) is helpful to predict malignant transformation. Aneuploidy (the presence of an abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell) has shown to be a predictor of malignant transformation.
[5018][Para 002] Loss of one allele of key tumour suppressor genes (loss of heterozygocity) in epithelial cells has also been shown to be helpful in predicting malignant transformation.
[5019][Para 218] 
[5020][Para 008] 
[5021][Para 011] Fig. 45.2 The histological appearances of the biopsy sample.
[5022][Para 009]  
[5023][Para 002] Both ploidy and loss of heterozygocity analysis are an adjunct to supplement histological evaluation but are only available in a few specialist diagnostic laboratories.
[5024][Heading 2]  Does Dysplasia Always Progress?
[5025][Para 001] No. Dysplasia does not always progress, and in some cases of mild dysplasia, it may regress. Dysplasia indicates increased potential for malignant transformation but does not necessarily mean that this may eventually occur in any particular lesion. Some dysplastic lesions never become malignant, and those that do may not transform into cancer for months or years.
[5026][Heading 2]  The Histological Features of the Lesion are Shown in Fig. 45.2. What Do You See and How Do You Interpret the Changes?
[5027][Para 001] The surface is covered by a regular orthokeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. The epithelium is abnormal for either the lateral border or the ventral tongue, neither of which shows even orthokeratosis.
[5028][Para 002] There are minimal signs of dysplasia. The epithelium shows good stratification, with well-organized basal, prickle cell, granular cell and keratin layers, each composed of cells at the same stage of maturation. The basal cell layer is slightly disorganized. Instead of a well-defined single layer of small dark cells, there is a slightly irregular layer of cells with nuclei that vary a little in size and staining intensity. Near the centre, there is one darkly staining cell in a suprabasal position (arrowed). No Candida was found in a section stained with periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stain.
[5029][Para 002] Changes such as abnormal keratinization and slight basal cell irregularity are not very marked. The epithelial cells form a well-organized epithelium; there are only occasional abnormal single cells, minimal nuclear abnormalities and no evidence of increased growth. These signs might be graded as either nondysplastic or mildly dysplastic, depending on the pathologist. The final diagnosis given in this case was keratosis with mild dysplasia.
[5030][Para 015] Diagnosis
[5031][Heading 2]  What is the Final Diagnosis? Is This a Lesion with a High Risk of Malignant Transformation?
[5032][Para 001] The diagnosis is idiopathic white patch (leukoplakia) with mild dysplasia. This is a lesion with a risk of malignant transformation.
[5033][Para 015] Treatment
[5034][Heading 2]  What Treatment is Indicated?
[5035][Para 001] The following principles of treatment apply to all idiopathic white patches. The patient should stop smoking and moderate her alcohol intake. If candidal infection had been detected, it should be treated and periodically checked for recurrence. In this case, and others in which dysplasia is mild or absent, it is appropriate to monitor the lesion closely for changes in appearance, initially at 3-monthly intervals and then extending to annual review, provided the lesion does not change significantly. The aim is to detect any change in the severity of dysplasia or malignant transformation, and this may require biopsy from time to time, depending on the changes noted. Photographic or digital images aid recognition of changes and are a valuable adjunct to the long-term review of white patches.
[5036][Para 002] Lesions with moderate or severe dysplasia may be removed through knife or laser excision. Occasionally, patches are too large to treat in these ways, and the only option is close monitoring to detect malignant transformation as early as possible.
[5037][Para 002] In addition, it is important to remember that dysplasia may affect any mucosal areas exposed to tobacco smoke and alcohol. There is a risk of carcinoma arising in the pharynx and in the respiratory tract, and symptoms arising from these areas indicate a need for endoscopy.
[5038][Para 015] Prognosis
[5039][Heading 2]  What Features Would Indicate That a White Patch Might Become Malignant Over the Coming Years?
[5040][Para 001] The features associated with increased risk of malignant transformation are listed in Table 45.3.
[5041][Para 017] In this case, the lesion remained unchanged, and the patient was reviewed at 3-monthly intervals for 1 year and at 6-monthly intervals for 2 years, and she remains under annual review. Four years after presentation, a second biopsy was performed, and the degree of dysplasia was still mild. Excision was considered because the lesion is relatively accessible and in a site that is at high risk of carcinoma, but it was not carried out because the dysplasia remains mild and the patient prefers not to have surgery. The patient is also maintaining close observation of her white patch and will return for an earlier appointment if she feels it has changed.

[5069][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[5070][Heading 2]  What are the Causes of Mixed Red and White Patches in the Mouth?
[5071][Para 001] The causes of white patches are discussed more fully in Case 45. Several may also be associated with red areas.
[5072][09 Block] 
[5073][Para 024]  Which of the Above Lesions Would You Include in the Differential Diagnosis for This Particular Lesion?
[5074][Para 016] 1. Squamous cell carcinoma
[5075][Para 016] 2. ldiopathic white patch with or without dysplasia, including speckled leucoplakia
[5076][Para 016] 3. Chronic hyperplastic candidosis
[5077][Para 016] 4. Lichenoid reaction.
[5078][Para 030]  Justify This Differential Diagnosis
[5079][Para 001] The most important consideration in the differential diagnosis of all oral white patches is that squamous cell carcinoma or an oral potentially malignant disorder may be the cause. This is especially so when lesions are red and white or speckled.
[5080][Para 002] Squamous cell carcinoma is a likely diagnosis and the most significant one. Although this patient is young for squamous cell carcinoma, cases are seen in the fourth decade of life, and the incidence in younger patients appears to be increasing in the UK and elsewhere. The patient drinks and smokes heavily, and these are the main risk factors for oral squamous cell carcinoma. She drinks 14 units of alcohol per week, which is the maximum recommended intake. The maximum intake is considered ‘safe’ in terms of liver and cardiovascular disease risks, but no safe limit is recognized for cancer. There is no safe intake for tobacco, and the combined relative risk of carcinoma for this patient is at least 5–10 times higher than that for a nonsmoker or an occasional drinker. Regardless of the patient’s age, the presence of the lesion in a high-risk site, its speckled appearance and association with smoking are very worrying. This lesion should be considered carcinoma until proven otherwise.
[5081][Para 002] A potentially malignant disorder would be the next most likely diagnosis. Option 2 in the differential diagnosis covers all white patches of unknown aetiology, some of which carry a risk of malignant transformation and show dysplasia on microscopic examination. The risk of malignant transformation is higher in those with a red component, which may be seen either in a speckled area or in a separate, usually adjacent, site. The risk factors are the same as those for carcinoma, and if this lesion is not carcinoma, it is almost certainly at risk of malignant transformation.
[5082][Heading 2]  Which Lesions are Less Likely Possibilities? Explain Why
[5083][Para 001] Candidal infection should always be considered a cause of white patches, particularly when red areas are associated. This infection is very common. The combination of red and white is most likely to signify thrush (acute hyperplastic candidosis. However, lesions of thrush are usually more widespread than in the present case, and at least some of the white plaques may be removed by rubbing. Chronic hyperplastic candidosis (candidal ‘leukoplakia’) forms a discrete white plaque that is sometimes associated with red areas. Although it is normally found on the buccal mucosa and on the dorsal surface of the tongue, it is a possible diagnosis for the current lesion. It should also be remembered that almost any white patch in the mouth may be susceptible to infection by Candida, simply because of the increased thickness of keratin on the surface of the epithelium. Thus, the presence of candidal infection does not preclude an underlying carcinoma, dysplasia, lichen planus or similar conditions.
[5084][Para 002] Lichen planus and similar conditions are relatively common causes of intraoral white lesions. Lichen planus, lichenoid reactions and lupus erythematosus are usually readily identifiable by virtue of the presence of lacy white striae, association with atrophic areas and desquamative gingivitis and their symmetrical bilateral distribution. In smokers, both lichen planus and lichenoid reactions may present as discrete white plaques, but these plaque-type lesions are not usually associated with red areas. Localized single white lesions may also result from topically induced lichenoid reactions such as those to dental restorative materials. However, these are all most unlikely to be responsible for the current lesion because their clinical appearance and distribution are distinct.
[5085][Para 024]  What Features Might Indicate That This Lesion is Already Malignant? Which are Early Signs, and Which are Late Signs?
[5086][Para 204] 
[5087][Para 015] Investigations
[5088][Heading 2]  What Investigations are Indicated?
[5089][Para 001] Biopsy is generally considered mandatory for any oral white lesion. This is especially important if no cause is apparent. When malignancy or significant dysplasia is suspected, as in the present case, the biopsy should be performed as soon as possible because early diagnosis is a major factor for the successful treatment of oral squamous cell carcinoma.
[5090][Heading 2]  Would You Perform This Biopsy in General Practice?
[5091][Para 001] No, definitely not. Although removing a sample of the tissue is well within the capability of the general dental practitioner, it would be unwise to do so. The patient will return for the result, and dental practitioners are not usually the appropriate persons to break the news of malignant disease to the patient. There is also a theoretical risk that biopsy of the wrong site or unintentional removal of a small lesion in its entirety might compromise subsequent treatment, but this is a largely theoretical problem. In a practice environment, the patient should be referred urgently, preferably the same day, to a centre where definitive treatment can be provided. This will allow the most appropriate biopsy to be performed. No other investigations are indicated at this stage.
[5092][Para 002] UK treatment centres operate an urgent cancer referral pathway for suspected malignancy. Dentists must make themselves familiar with fast-track referral processes, according to their local cancer network protocols.
[5093][10 Block] 
[5094][Heading 2]  Which Part of the Lesion Should Be Removed for Biopsy?
[5095][Para 001] The specimen should include those areas most likely to be malignant – the red and speckled parts. Some normal tissue should also be included, and the sample should be about 1 cm long, 4–5 mm wide, and of an even depth, including underlying muscle. Larger malignancies are often friable, and if the specimen is too small, it may disintegrate on removal. No attempt should be made to excise the whole lesion until a diagnosis is obtained.
[5096][Heading 2]  The Biopsy Specimen is Shown in Fig. 46.2. What are the Microscopic Features, and How Do You Interpret Them?
[5097][Para 001] The lower power view (Fig. 46.2a) shows the tongue mucosa with underlying muscle. The overlying epithelium is very irregular, and instead of being an even and well-organized layer, it forms an irregular series of rete processes that penetrate deeply into the underlying tissue. The deepest epithelium is breaking off into apparently separate islands and strands, and these extend deeply between muscle bundles. The higher power view (see Fig. 46.2b) taken from the deep surface shows the deepest epithelium invading muscle. The epithelium is disorganized, with cells demonstrating a squamous morphology in the centre of islands and an irregular darkly stained basal cell layer around the edge. This epithelium has lost its ordered maturation and stratification and is invading the underlying muscle. Invasion indicates malignancy, and the malignant epithelium shows squamous differentiation.
[5098][Para 015] Diagnosis
[5099][Heading 2]  What is the Diagnosis?
[5100][Para 001] The patient has squamous cell carcinoma. It is only superficially invasive and probably an early lesion.
[5101][Para 015] Treatment
[5102][Heading 2]  What Types of Treatment are Possible, and What is the Prognosis?
[5103][Para 001] This lesion has been diagnosed at an early stage compared with most oral carcinomas. Treatment is likely to be surgery, followed by radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy. The final treatment decision will depend on the results of investigations to stage the carcinoma (to determine its size and the extent of any metastases to lymph nodes and distant sites). The decision to provide postoperative radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy will depend on the histological features of an adequately excised tumour. If treated in the early stages, a 5-year survival rate of 85% or better can be achieved. If survival reaches 10 years, the patient is likely to be considered cured. However, 10% of patients with oral carcinoma develop a second primary lesion in the mouth or upper aerodigestive tract. The chances of developing a second lesion may be reduced by stopping smoking, and so the patient should be encouraged to do so. Smoking-associated cardiovascular disease, if severe, may also compromise treatment.

[5105][Para 008] 
[5106][Para 011] Fig. 46.2 The histological appearances of the lesion: a, lower power view; b, higher power view.
[5107][Para 009]  
[5108][Para 002] Further details of the treatment of oral carcinoma are given in Case 45.
[5109][Para 017] After the biopsy, further investigations including computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) showed no cervical lymph node metastasis in this patient.
[5110][Heading 2]  Should the Patient Have Her Cervical Lymph Nodes Treated?
[5111][Para 001] Although no metastasis has been detected in the cervical lymph nodes, a neck dissection may still be required. This is because malignant cells continually separate from the carcinoma and pass in small numbers into the lymphatics and the bloodstream. The majority of these cells die. However, some could have reached the cervical lymph nodes and be present as very small metastatic deposits not detectable by imaging or FNAC. Approximately 25% of these deposits are not detectable clinically and are termed ‘occult metastases’. If left untreated, they would continue to grow, ultimately invading beyond the lymph node and spreading to distant sites.
[5112][Para 002] The following factors are associated with an increased risk of metastasis:
[5113][Para 004] • Large primary tumour
[5114][Para 004] • Long duration
[5115][Para 004] • Poorly differentiated histological grade
[5116][Para 004] • Aggressive pattern of invasion seen histologically
[5117][Para 004] • Depth of invasion
[5118][Para 004] • Vascular invasion at primary site.
[5119][Para 002] Neck dissection performed to remove possible occult metastases is called a prophylactic or elective neck dissection.
[5120][Para 002] Whether to treat an apparently normal neck when a patient has a small carcinoma is contentious because neck dissection carries significant morbidity. However, the development of metastases later reduces the patient’s chances of survival. For this reason, an elective neck dissection is recommended. A neck dissection may also be required for surgical access and to aid reconstruction.
[5121][Para 002] Metastasis from tongue carcinoma is recognized to be unpredictable. When the carcinoma has invaded to a depth of 4 mm, there is a greater likelihood of metastasis. This patient’s risk of occult metastasis is compounded by the aggressive tumour infiltration pattern.
[5122][10 Block] 
[5123][Heading 2]  Could Neck Dissection Not Be Advised On the Basis of Better Evidence?
[5124][Para 001] Yes, the technique of sentinel node biopsy has been developed to predict lymph node metastasis accurately. In this investigation, a radioactive tracer is injected into and around the carcinomatous lesion on the day before surgery. The tracer drains along the same lymphatic routes to the lymph nodes to which carcinoma cells would travel. At surgery, a radioactivity-detecting probe is used to identify the nodes with concentrated radioactive tracer. These ‘sentinel’ lymph nodes are removed and sent to the pathology laboratory on the basis that they are the ones most likely to contain metastasis. A thorough and detailed microscopic examination is carried out to examine all the nodes in multiple sections, with the use of special stains.
[5125][Para 002] If the nodes contain no metastasis, no neck dissection is performed. If they contain metastasis, a neck dissection is indicated to remove the rest of the cervical nodes because other metastases may be present.

[5137][Para 049] History of Complaint

[5142][Para 012] Dental History
[5143][Para 007] The patient is new to your particular practice but has always attended the dentist regularly.
[5144][Para 012] Medical History
[5145][Para 007] The patient is fit and well.
[5146][Heading 2]  On the Basis of What You Know Already, What is the Likely Diagnosis?
[5147][Para 001] The pain is almost certainly caused by pulpitis. It is brought on by hot and cold and is poorly localized. It has progressed from intermittent pain, suggesting reversible pulpitis, to a severe pain that lasts hours. The severity and duration now suggest that pulpitis might be irreversible.
[5148][Heading 2]  What is Irreversible Pulpitis?
[5149][Para 001] Irreversible pulpitis is a concept rather than a well-defined clinical condition. Pulpitis is usually chronic and progresses intermittently and unpredictably with or without acute phases. At some stage, the pulp is irretrievably damaged, probably because pressure from inflammation impedes pulpal blood flow. This causes loss of vitality. The ability to predict pulp necrosis would be useful when deciding possible management options. Unfortunately, the clinical symptoms that accompany pulpitis are variable, especially in multirooted teeth, and pain is a subjective sensation. Severe pain of long duration, spontaneous pain and waking at night are usually taken to indicate the irreversible stage of pulpitis; however, predicting the future course of disease is never reliable, and making this diagnosis involves an element of uncertainty, depending on operator experience.
[5150][Para 014] Examination
[5151][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[5152][Para 007] The temporomandibular joints appear normal, and there are no palpable submental, submandibular or cervical lymph nodes.
[5153][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[5154][Para 007] On examination, you discover poor oral hygiene, with gingivitis around posterior teeth. The dentition is moderately restored.
[5155][Para 017] In the lower left quadrant, the second permanent molar tooth has an occlusal amalgam. The premolars appear sound.
[5156][Heading 2]  What Parts of the Examination Would Be Most Useful? Why?
[5157][Para 001] Teeth should be percussed to establish whether any are tender. Adjacent, apparently healthy control teeth should be percussed first for comparison. Tenderness indicates inflammation in the apical periodontal ligament, and causes would include very-late-stage irreversible pulpitis or a necrotic pulp.
[5158][Para 002] Palpation of the mucosa overlying the tooth apices with a fingertip. Tenderness indicates extension of inflammation from the periodontal ligament to the surrounding bone and the activity of any inflammation present. Affected teeth are compared with clinically sound teeth. Lower molar apices are close to the lingual mandibular cortex and must be palpated lingually as well as buccally.
[5159][Para 002] Mobility should be assessed. Mobility is increased slightly if there is inflammation of the periodontal ligament. If a periradicular abscess or acute inflammation is present, the tooth may be raised in the socket. You must exclude increased mobility caused by periodontal disease, root fracture, recent trauma or a premature occlusal contact.
[5160][Para 002] Periodontal probing should be performed to detect loss of attachment or exposed dentine. Dentine hypersensitivity would not cause such severe, long-lasting pain. However, pocketing or previous periodontal treatment could have exposed a lateral canal or canal in the furcation, allowing bacteria access to the pulp.
[5161][Para 002] Search for a sinus would indicate periradicular infection. Sinuses may heal and present as a small fibrous nodule, indicating past or intermittent infection. The search must include the lingual alveolar mucosa because the apices of lower molars lie closer to the lingual cortex than the buccal cortex.
[5162][Para 017] On examining the patient, you find that no teeth are mobile, are tender to percussion or have apical tenderness. There is no detectable sinus. Inflammation appears limited to the pulp. No periodontitis is present.
[5163][Para 015] Investigations
[5164][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Perform?
[5165][Para 001] Tests of pulp sensibility are required to increase confidence in your assessment of the status of the pulp. Electric testing and thermal (hot and cold) testing are available, and use of a stimulus that usually provokes the pain is recommended. Ensure that healthy adjacent, opposing and contralateral teeth are also examined to obtain a reference measure of the patient’s response. If tests yield equivocal responses, a test cavity without local analgesia should prove conclusive.
[5166][Para 002] A periapical radiograph of the molar teeth is required.
[5167][Heading 2]  What are the Limitations of Tests of Sensibility?
[5168][Para 001] Tests of sensibility do not measure pulp vitality (blood flow) but test for a continuous sensory nerve pathway from the pulp to the brain. For this reason, they are referred to as sensibility tests.
[5169][Para 002] It is assumed that pulp without sensory innervation is devitalized, but this is not necessarily so. Inflammation can alter sensation and sensation may be incorrectly localized (see Case 1). Conversely, a positive response does not guarantee the histological health of the pulp.
[5170][Para 002] Tests sometimes indicate a hypersensitive pulp, and this is a more useful piece of information because detection of hypersensitivity is not prone to false-positive or false-negative results.
[5171][Heading 2]  What are the Causes of Misleading Electric Pulp Test Results?
[5172][Para 001] Both false-positive and false-negative sensibility responses can occur. Causes, together with precautions that minimize the risk of a spurious result, are listed in Table 47.2.
[5173][Para 017] On performing these tests, you discover that the lower second molar gives a hypersensitive response to hot gutta percha. The pain lasted until a local anaesthetic was given.
[5174][Heading 2]  The Periapical Radiograph of Mandibular Left Second Molar is Shown in Fig. 47.1. What Do You See?
[5175][Para 001] The mandibular left second molar shows extensive radiolucency under the existing radiopaque amalgam restoration encroaching the pulp horns (most likely to be caries). There is no obvious periapical radiolucency, and an impacted mandibular third molar is visible along with the intact borders of the inferior alveolar canal.
[5176][Para 015] Diagnosis
[5177][Heading 2]  What is the Most Likely Diagnosis?
[5178][Para 001] Irreversible pulpitis in the lower left second molar tooth caused by the large carious lesion. When the pain started 8 months ago, the carious lesion would have been smaller and the pulpitis reversible. If it had been treated preventively and operatively at that stage by the oral healthcare team, it is high likely that any endodontic treatment would now be required for a necrotic pulp.
[5179][Para 015] Treatment
[5180][Heading 2]  What Emergency Treatment Would You Provide At the First Appointment?
[5181][Para 001] The carious lesion is extensive in the second molar. Assuming the tooth is to be retained and conserved, the first priority is relief of pain. Having assessed the pulpitis as irreversible, extirpation of the pulp is the only appropriate treatment, and this will require cleaning and shaping of the root canals to ensure that no remnants remain. Extirpation with barbed broach alone risks leaving fragments of inflamed vital pulp that could cause pain after treatment. A root canal dressing of nonsetting calcium hydroxide will inhibit bacterial growth. This must be sealed from rest of the mouth with a suitable provisional dressing material to prevent bacterial ingress, pending definitive treatment.

[5190][Heading 2]  What Definitive Treatment Does the Patient Require for the Second Molar?
[5191][Para 001] The patient should return for cleaning, shaping and obturation of the root canals and a definitive coronal restoration. A cuspal-coverage indirect restoration, either an onlay or a core with a full-coverage crown, should be considered for protection against occlusal forces. Post crowns in molar teeth are to be avoided because of the incidence of perforations and root fractures. Retention should be sufficient from the undercut shape of the pulp chamber and the remaining coronal tooth structure (see Case 1 and Case 9).
[5192][Para 002] After discussing the possibility of restoring or extracting the second molar, the patient opts for root canal treatment. All options, including the normal advantages and disadvantages of each, need to be discussed. These conversations need to be fully documented in the notes and time given to the patient to understand his responsibility and consequences of the care provided. By managing patient expectations at this stage, later medico-legal issues can be avoided.
[5193][Para 017] You carry out the first stage of treatment successfully. However, the patient fails to return to complete the treatment. When he returns after 6 months, you discover that the tooth has remained asymptomatic but the coronal temporary restoration has been lost and the lingual cusp has fractured off. The pulp chamber is open to the oral cavity, but the tooth is still restorable.
[5194][Heading 2]  What Effect Will This Have On the Long-Term Prognosis for This Tooth?
[5195][Para 001] Loss of the coronal seal allows microbial invasion of the root canals and dentine tubules. Bacteria and their metabolic and breakdown products are irritants and penetrate apically and along lateral canals to induce or maintain periradicular inflammation. In addition, the flora in the canal change, and a more mixed oral flora with anaerobes become established in the canal. This may be more difficult to eradicate and is more likely to penetrate through the apex and induce an acute abscess. Fracture of the lingual cusp further weakens the tooth and complicates building up a core to support the definitive coronal restoration.
[5196][Para 218] 
[5197][Para 008] 
[5198][Para 011] Fig. 47.2 The gutta percha master point try-in periapical radiograph.
[5199][Para 009]  
[5200][Heading 2]  What Should Be the Next Stage of Treatment?
[5201][Para 001] Root canal treatment must be recommenced as soon as possible. The tooth should be isolated with rubber dam and the root canals cleaned and shaped with use of appropriate files and copious irrigation with sodium hypochlorite. Sodium hypochlorite is antibacterial, but some bacteria may survive in the lateral canals and dentine tubules that are blocked by the smear layer produced by instrumentation. The smear layer must be removed by occasionally irrigating with 17% EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) solution. Hypochlorite will then be able to penetrate dentine and the lateral canals. It is important that coronal root canal preparation is carried out first to reduce the bacterial load and improve access to the apical portion of the root canal. The gutta percha master point try-in radiograph shows the multiple curvatures of the mesial canals (Figs 47.2 and 47.3).
[5202][Heading 2]  How Long Should This Tooth Be Monitored After Completion of Root Canal Treatment? What are the Criteria for Success?
[5203][Para 001] Root canal treatment should be reviewed after 1 year, as suggested in the guidance of the European society of endodontology (2006). Outcome must be evaluated clinically and radiographically. The radiographic assessment must be made by comparing the appearances with previous films, taken under conditions that are as near standardized as possible.
[5204][Para 002] Criteria for success and failure are shown in Table 47.3.

[5214][Para 027] Francesco Mannocci
[5215][Para 028] Summary
[5216][Para 029] A 60-year-old female patient has pain from a root-treated tooth. What will you do?
[5217][Para 218] 
[5218][Para 008] 
[5219][Para 011] Fig. 48.1 The preoperative periapical radiograph of the lower left quadrant.
[5220][Para 009]  
[5221][Para 014] History
[5222][Para 019] Complaint
[5223][Para 007] The patient presents complaining of discomfort from a lower left posterior tooth. The filling was lost from the tooth about 4 months ago.
[5224][Para 012] History of Complaint
[5225][Para 007] She has suffered intermittent problems since the tooth was root canal treated 2 years ago. Pain is triggered by biting on the tooth, and changes in temperature have no effect. The symptoms have remained similar in intensity ever since the root canal treatment was completed.
[5226][Para 012] Dental History
[5227][Para 007] The patient has always attended regularly for dental treatment, requiring occasional treatment for failed restorations over the last 10–15 years.
[5228][Para 017] The lower left second permanent molar was originally treated endodontically because the patient developed acute pulpitis. Two attempts at root canal treatment were carried out before the intense pain subsided, with the root canal filling being placed at a third appointment. An endodontic instrument separated in one of the root canals at the second appointment; the patient was informed of this by the dentist, and this was documented in the notes. A temporary restoration was placed to allow a period to assess resolution of symptoms, but the patient preferred not to return to the same dentist, feeling that the treatment had gone wrong.
[5229][Heading 2]  How Do You Assess the Case So Far?
[5230][Para 001] Several features of the history are significant.
[5231][Para 002] Pain on biting and well-localized pain indicate periapical periodontitis, and the cause is almost certainly failure of the previous root canal treatment.
[5232][Para 002] There was a separated instrument which probably means that an inadequate apical seal would have been achieved in that canal, reducing the chances of a successful outcome. The extraction of the tooth, which may or may not be followed by an implant-supported fixed prosthesis, needs to be mentioned as an alternative to the root canal retreatment.
[5233][Para 002] The provisional restoration was lost 4 months ago. This indicates complete loss of coronal seal to the root canal system, allowing microleakage of bacteria and their toxins along the length of the root filling. The extent to which this occurs is time dependent. As a general rule extrapolated from experimental data, if the root canal filling has been exposed to the oral cavity for 3 months or more, retreatment may be considered, even in the absence of clinical signs or symptoms.
[5234][Para 014] Examination
[5235][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[5236][Para 001] There is no facial swelling or tenderness associated with the tooth.
[5237][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[5238][Para 001] You examine the patient, following the protocol outlined in Case 47. The lower second molar has a large cavity distally with obvious caries and exposed gutta percha root filling in the pulp chamber. It has tilted mesially and is tender to percussion. The third molar has a large, poorly contoured amalgam restoration.

[5243][Para 014] Investigations
[5244][Para 001] A radiograph is necessary, and a periapical view of the teeth in the lower left quadrant is the most appropriate.
[5245][Para 024]  What Information Do You Wish To Obtain From the Radiograph?
[5246][Para 205] • What do you think of the nature and quality of the previous endodontic treatment?
[5247][Para 004] • Are any root canals detectable? Failure of treatment may have been caused by failure to detect or fill all canals. Any remaining canals in teeth that have large carious lesions, restorations or marked tooth wear or have suffered trauma may be sclerosed as a result of tertiary dentine formation.
[5248][Para 004] • Is there periradicular radiolucency? This would indicate persistence of infection or inflammation.
[5249][Para 004] • What is the estimated working length? This can only be estimated from a periapical radiograph, which is always slightly magnified even when taken using a paralleling technique.
[5250][Para 004] • What is the root morphology? The number of roots and their orientation can be identified. Root curvatures and diameters can also be observed; however, it is important to remember that radiographic images are two-dimensional representations of three-dimensional structures. Canals are often much wider bucco-lingually than can be appreciated on a conventional radiograph.
[5251][Para 030]  The Preoperative Periapical Radiograph is Shown in Fig. 48.1. What Do You See?
[5252][Para 001] The canine and premolars have been restored, and no caries is present, although there is significant tooth wear anteriorly. The tilted second molar has been root treated, and the fractured instrument is visible in one of the mesial canals.
[5253][Para 002] The film is not of adequate diagnostic quality and must be graded in the notes as such using the updated guidance. The packet or sensor has not been placed far enough posteriorly to include the third molar, and the periapical tissues are not visible. The collimator has coned off the distal part of the film because the tube head has been positioned too far anteriorly. Use of a paralleling technique with a film holder has produced a true parallel projection, but this has superimposed the mesial canals. It is not possible to determine which of the two canals contains the fractured instrument, and it will be necessary to determine exactly where the instrument is, if an attempt is to be made to remove it.
[5254][Heading 2]  How Will You Locate the Separated Instrument Fragment?
[5255][Para 001] By using the parallax technique. A second radiograph must be taken at the same vertical angulation, but at a different horizontal angle, usually from the mesial aspect.
[5256][Heading 2]  The Original and Second Parallax Views are Shown in Fig. 48.2. What Do You See, and Where is the Instrument?
[5257][Para 001] The image on the left in Fig. 48.2 is the original radiograph and that on the right is the radiograph taken from the mesial aspect. The second radiograph is better positioned and clearly shows the presence of the fractured instrument and that there is no periapical radiolucency. The poorly contoured amalgam in the third molar can now be assessed.
[5258][Para 002] Using the MBD (mesial, buccal, distal) rule, when the x-ray beam moves to the mesial, the buccal canal will appear to move to the distal. The separated instrument appears to move mesially, and so it must be in the mesio-lingual root canal.

[5261][Para 011] Fig. 48.3 Root canal instruments more prone to fracture in root canals. From left to right: a barbed broach, used to extirpate pulp tissue; stainless steel, hand and rotary nickel titanium files used to prepare and shape the root canal; and a Gates–Glidden bur, used for preparation of the coronal root canal.
[5262][Para 009]  
[5263][Heading 2]  What Endodontic Instruments are Prone To Fracture, and What Has Fractured in This Tooth?
[5264][Para 001] The broken instrument is a spiral root canal filler, recognized by its tapering helical shape and broad pitch.
[5265][Para 002] Instruments prone to fracture are shown in Fig. 48.3.
[5266][Heading 2]  How Can Instrument Separation Be Prevented?
[5267][Para 001] In the past, reuse and heat sterilization of instruments weakened them, but the current guidance recommending single-use instruments largely has overcome this problem. Instruments that jam in a root canal during use may become distorted, thus becoming weakened, and should be immediately discarded. All files should be inspected during use for signs of distortion, as shown in Fig. 48.4.
[5268][Para 002] Otherwise, the most important factors are correct use of instruments and correct access cavity design. Rotary nickel titanium files, in particular, must be used in an electric torque-controlled motor at the correct setting and with minimal apical pressure.
[5269][Para 002] Correct access cavity preparation underpins the success of root canal treatment. The cavity should allow straight-line access for instruments to the root canals. If not, the instruments will be overstressed in use and develop weak points. Fig. 48.5 outlines the ideal access cavity preparation for all tooth types.
[5270][Para 002] Use of some instruments that are prone to fracture can simply be avoided. Gates–Glidden burs can result in overpreparation, and nickel titanium orifice shapers are a better option. Spiral root fillers are mainly used to place nonsetting calcium hydroxide paste between appointments. However, this is largely unnecessary because alternative applicators are available, as shown in Fig. 48.6.
[5271][Para 218] 
[5272][Para 008] 
[5273][Para 011] Fig. 48.4 Examples of distorted files that should be disposed of to avoid fracture within the root canal.
[5274][Para 009]  
[5275][Para 015] Treatment
[5276][Heading 2]  How Will You Remove the Fractured Spiral Filler Fragment?
[5277][Para 001] Magnification is an essential aid to treatment, both to locate the canals and to identify the fragment.
[5278][Para 002] Initially, try simple techniques. Sometimes, an ultrasonic scaler tip applied to the fractured instrument can transmit sufficient energy through the instrument to break down the dentine jammed against it and loosen it. The main disadvantages are the potential for excessive root dentine removal and disintegration of the end of the fractured instrument. Where there is space alongside the instrument, it may be possible to bypass it by using a small Hedström file. On the outward stroke, the flutes may engage with the instrument and pull it out.
[5279][Para 002] Alternatively, specially designed instruments are available. Instrument Removal System (IRS, Dentsply) and Masseran kits both adopt the same principle. Fig. 48.7 shows how the IRS system is used. It consists of two components. The outer part is a colour-coded hollow tube, made in a series of internal and external diameters to accommodate different sizes of root canals and fractured instruments. Inside the tube is a rapidly tapered titanium wedge that locks to the outer tube with a screw thread. The end of the hollow tube is bevelled and has a window cut on one side. The tube is slipped over the head of the fractured instrument and the internal tapered wedge is screwed down until it grips and wedges the fractured instrument against the tube so that it can then be rotated and pulled out. A gutter of root dentine may need to be removed from around the head of the fractured instrument to allow the tube to slip over it.
[5280][Para 218] 
[5281][Para 008] 
[5282][Para 011] Fig. 48.5 Correct outline for pulp chamber access cavities.
[5283][Para 009]  
[5284][Para 008] 
[5285][Para 011] Fig. 48.6 Nonsetting calcium hydroxide paste with fine capillary tip (left) and assembled (right) for passive injection into the root canal.
[5286][Para 009]  
[5287][Heading 2]  How Easy Will Its Removal Be?
[5288][Para 001] Removal of the separated instrument fragment is always unpredictable and referral to an endodontic specialist needs to be considered. However, the following factors may indicate the likely outcome.
[5289][Para 002] Location within the root canal, coronal, middle or apical third. If the instrument is present in the coronal third and visible using magnification there is a much greater likelihood that it can be removed. Instruments that have fractured apically in curved canals present the greatest challenge. Obtaining access to them in a straight line is often impossible without removing excessive dentine, and there is a risk of perforating the root. It is usually advisable to leave such fragments in situ.
[5290][Para 218] 
[5291][Para 008] 
[5292][Para 011] Fig. 48.7 Components of the Instrument Removal System for removal of fractured instruments in root canals. a, The two components; b, assembled; c, a high-power image of the instrument tip; d, diagrammatic representation showing how the instrument is used to grip and remove the fractured instrument.
[5293][Para 009]  
[5294][Para 020] Type of instrument
[5295][Para 001] Most stainless-steel files can be removed if they are accessible. These are now commonly used to create an initial guide path prior to nickel titanium instrumentation and, if used correctly, should not have engaged the root canal dentine excessively. Instruments that are designed to cut dentine are more likely to be embedded into it if used incorrectly. For this reason, nickel titanium files and Gates–Glidden burs are usually difficult, if not impossible, to remove.
[5296][Para 020] Width and length of fragment
[5297][Para 001] Wider and more rigid instruments are more difficult to remove, as are longer segments of instruments. Both are more likely to have a large surface area in contact with dentine and bind dentine with greater friction.
[5298][Para 020] Anatomy of canal
[5299][Para 001] It is easier to bypass and remove instruments from an oval canal than from a round one.
[5300][Heading 2]  What Options are Available if a Separated Instrument Cannot Be Removed?
[5301][Para 001] This partly depends on when the instrument separated. If this happened in the early stages of canal preparation, it is likely that the canal remained infected and treatment was compromised. Fracture during the finishing stages of preparation, after adequate irrigation with sodium hypochlorite, might have reduced the numbers of bacteria sufficiently to allow obturation to the level of the instrument, leading to a successful outcome.
[5302][Para 002] Retreatment of the remaining canals and the canal up to the separated instrument may be sufficient to eliminate residual bacteria from the root canal system and create an adequate seal coronally and throughout the root canal system.
[5303][Para 002] Alternatively, or if retreatment fails on that root alone, root resection or hemisection will allow the affected root to be removed. This is only possible if the roots are not fused and so would not be possible in the present case. Periradicular surgery may also be a possibility but would be difficult in a lower molar tooth because of the density of the buccal bone and the proximity of the inferior dental nerve canal. Unfortunately, extraction may be the only possible option.
[5304][Para 017] In this case, the spiral root canal filler was removed easily because it was possible to bypass the instrument and remove it with a Hedström file. Subsequent root canal preparation with nickel titanium rotary instruments produced a more tapered root canal preparation, allowing excellent shaping, debridement, irrigation and obturation. The final retreatment periapical radiograph is shown in  Fig. 48.8 . The tooth was definitively restored with a full-coverage gold crown to ensure a good coronal seal and provide cusp reinforcement and a good contact point with the adjacent tooth.
[5305][Para 218] 
[5306][Para 008] 
[5307][Para 011] Fig. 48.8 Postoperative periapical radiograph of the completed root canal treatment, prior to final restoration.
[5308][Para 009]  
[5309][Para 002] As for all endodontic treatments, a 1-year recall, including a periapical radiograph and clinical examination, is indicated to assess healing.
[5310][Para 002] In summary, the dentist must always inform the patient if instrument separation occurs during endodontic treatment, with a full explanation of the management options and possible outcomes. This conversation must be contemporaneously recorded in the patient notes. Indeed, the risk of instrument separation should be discussed as part of the initial consent procedure for endodontic treatment – assessment of treatment complexity, curvature of root canals and so on should be taken into consideration before a decision is made as to treat or refer the patient to a specialist.
