[5313][Para 025] Case 49
[5314][Heading 1] A Swollen Face
[5315][Para 027] Tara Renton
[5316][Para 028] Summary
[5317][Para 029] A 30-year-old man is referred to your dental hospital by his general practitioner with a painful swelling of the right side of the face. What is the cause, and what treatment would you provide?
[5318][Para 218] 
[5319][Para 008] 
[5320][Para 011] Fig. 49.1 The patient on presentation.
[5321][Para 009]  
[5322][Para 014] History
[5323][Para 019] History of Complaint
[5324][Para 007] The patient has had toothache intermittently for many months. A few weeks ago, the pain became excruciating and did not respond to analgesics. Then, suddenly, it reduced in severity, and the patient thought it had resolved.
[5325][Para 017] However, about 10 days ago, a different pain developed. A tooth on the upper right has become very tender, and he has not been able to bite on it. The swelling suddenly enlarged yesterday.
[5326][Para 017] Over the last few months the patient has been prescribed several courses of antibiotics, and he finished a course of oral erythromycin 2 days ago.
[5327][Para 012] Medical History
[5328][Para 007] The patient is otherwise fit and well.
[5329][Para 014] Examination
[5330][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[5331][Para 007] The patient is shown in  Fig. 49.1 . The swelling is hot, tender and firm centrally, but peripherally, it is almost painless and softer. It extends from the nose to the anterior border of the masseter, and the lower eyelid is very oedematous and contains blood pigment, as if bruised.
[5332][Para 017] The swelling is not pointing extraorally. There are palpable tender lymph nodes in the upper deep cervical chain.
[5333][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[5334][Para 007] The patient has slight limitation of mouth opening, but this does not significantly hamper examination. The sulcus adjacent to the upper first molar and both premolars is tender and slightly reduced in depth by a firm swelling. The upper first and second premolars and the first molar have large amalgam restorations. However, the patient indicates clearly that the second premolar is the cause of the pain, and this tooth is slightly mobile and raised in its socket. It is very tender on percussion and nonvital on testing with ethyl chloride. The first molar and the first premolar appear vital.
[5335][Para 015] Investigations
[5336][Heading 2]  Which Additional Investigation is Critically Important? Why?
[5337][Para 001] Taking the patient’s temperature. This gives a good indication of the systemic effects of the infection and reflects the amount of pus in abscesses and/or the tendency of the infection to spread. The patient has a temperature of 37.2°C.
[5338][Heading 2]  Would You Take a Radiograph?
[5339][Para 001] In this case, a radiograph is not a useful investigation. Tests of vitality are much more likely to identify the causative tooth and, in any case, there appears to be no doubt about the diagnosis.
[5340][Para 218] 
[5341][Para 008] 
[5342][Para 011] Fig. 49.2 Periapical radiograph showing the causative premolar.
[5343][Para 009]  
[5344][Para 002] However, there are good reasons why taking a radiograph may not help or even be counterproductive:
[5345][Para 016] 1. It takes up to 3 weeks for radiographic changes to develop at the root apex after pulp necrosis.
[5346][Para 016] 2. The radiographic features may be misleading if you attempt to use them to diagnose loss of vitality. When root apices are radiographed with the maxillary antrum superimposed, the normal periodontal ligament appears wider. This may be confused with early apical changes of infection.
[5347][Para 002] Both these problems are appreciated in Fig. 49.2, the periapical radiograph of this patient, which is completely normal.
[5348][Para 015] Diagnosis
[5349][Heading 2]  What Do These Findings Tell You?
[5350][Para 001] The combination of inflammation, the nonvital tooth and the adjacent probable abscess indicates an odontogenic soft tissue infection. The history of severe toothache that suddenly resolved suggests pulpitis that was subsequently relieved by necrosis of the pulp. The subsequent pain of a different character with a tender tooth suggests an apical abscess. The patient points clearly to the second premolar, and this is almost certainly the cause of the pain because pain involving the periodontal ligament is well localized.
[5351][Para 002] Trismus is an important sign, indicating that infection or inflammation has spread to involve the muscles of mastication. However, trismus is not severe and probably results from inflammation and oedema of the buccinator and the anterior fibres of the masseter, which lie at the posterior border of the swelling.
[5352][Para 002] The infection has induced minimal systemic effects, and the patient is not significantly pyrexic. Luckily, the infection appears to be localized. The firm centre to the swelling and the swelling in the sulcus will contain pus.
[5353][Heading 2]  What Types of Soft Tissue Infection Arising From Teeth Cause Facial Swelling? How May They Be Distinguished, and What is the Relevance of Doing So?
[5354][Para 001] Facial swelling may be the result of oedema, abscess formation, cellulitis or a combination of these.
[5355][Para 002] It is important to determine which of these types of infection is present because the treatment and sequelae of each are different. Abscesses require drainage. Cellulitis requires aggressive treatment, usually including antibiotics, and oedema requires no direct treatment but resolves when the causative tooth is removed or the pulp treated.
[5356][Para 002] Despite the fact that the use of the terms mentioned above is convenient, in practice, most odontogenic soft tissue infections are caused by mixed microbial flora and do not fall neatly into one category or another. It is not unusual to find an abscess with a surrounding zone of cellulitis, and a degree of oedema is always present. Which type of infection develops is determined by the virulence of the pathogens (and the synergy between the species in the mixed flora), the resistance of the host and the anatomical constraints on the infection.
[5357][07 Block] 
[5358][Para 030]  If Infections are Not Easily Characterized, What are the Important Features On Which Treatment Must Be Based?
[5359][Para 001] The critical factors that must be determined are whether:
[5360][Para 004] • an abscess cavity is present (palpation, eliciting fluctuation)
[5361][Para 004] • there is evidence of systemic effects (malaise, pyrexia, a toxic-shocked appearance)
[5362][Para 004] • the infection is spreading rapidly (judged by the history and observation during treatment)
[5363][Para 004] • the patient is predisposed to infection (from the medical history).
[5364][Para 030]  Which Type of Infection is This?
[5365][Para 001] This appears to be primarily an abscess with surrounding oedema.
[5366][Para 218] 
[5367][Para 008] 
[5368][Para 011] Fig .49.3 Coronal section showing the paths of spread of infection from upper molars and premolars. Infection may pass buccally below the buccinator muscle into the sulcus or cheek intraorally (A), above the buccinator into the buccal space (B), into the sinus (C) or into the palate (D).
[5369][Para 009]  
[5370][Heading 2]  In What Tissue Space(s) is the Infection Tracking or Localizing? What are the Boundaries of This Space?
[5371][Para 001] This abscess appears to be in the upper part of the buccal space. This is a potential space between the buccinator and facial muscles and the parotid fascia, filled normally with loose connective tissue. Posteriorly, it communicates with the masseter muscle and around the front of the ramus to the pterygoid space. Oedema spreads beyond the buccal space to involve the lower eyelid and anterior cheek in the canine fossa. The abscess is not yet pointing to the skin.
[5372][Heading 2]  Why Has the Infection Localized Here? Will It Remain Localized Here?
[5373][Para 001] Abscesses arising from the canine, premolar and molar teeth and perforating the buccal plate of the alveolar bone will spill out into the soft tissues either above or below the attachment of the buccinator. The attachment of the buccinator usually runs below the apices of the upper teeth, so the infection is likely to pass superficially to the buccinator and into the cheek. If it passes below the attachment, an alveolar abscess or sinus will develop. Paths of spread of infection from an upper premolar are shown in Fig. 49.3.
[5374][Para 002] Despite being a thin muscle, the buccinator is a significant barrier to the spread of infection. It is unlikely that the infection would be able to perforate the muscle and develop a sinus into the mouth. Several sequelae are possible. Pus would be most likely to gravitate and spread through the whole buccal space down to the lower border of the mandible; it could point and then drain to the skin or spread laterally around the buccinator to involve other areas of the face, tissue around the masseter muscle or the pterygoid space. Its future course cannot be predicted.
[5375][Heading 2]  Is This a Potentially Life-Threatening Infection? If So, Why?
[5376][Para 001] Not yet. In this case, the infection appears localized, the spread is not particularly rapid and there are no significant systemic symptoms. If the infection spreads more, the situation would change.
[5377][Para 002] Involvement of the tissues around the eyelid is worrying. At present, the swelling here is caused by oedema, but if infection were to spread to the upper lid or the medial canthus of the eye, the patient would be at risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis. This is a very rare, but potentially fatal, complication.
[5378][Para 002] It would also be possible for the infection to spread posteriorly into the pterygo-mandibular space and the infratemporal fossa. From here, the infection could spread to the cavernous sinus or the middle cranial fossa through the veins.
[5379][Heading 2]  What is Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis, and What are Its Features?
[5380][Para 001] Thrombosis of the cavernous sinus results from spread of odontogenic infection along two main venous pathways. Bacteria and infected emboli travel posteriorly from the upper lip and face via the anterior facial vein. This connects via the ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus without valves, which might otherwise prevent this retrograde flow. Alternatively, infection may spread from the pterygoid space via the pterygoid plexus of veins that connect directly to the cavernous sinus via the foramen ovale.
[5381][Para 002] The local features are seen on one side at first, but the signs become bilateral as the thrombus grows. The features are listed below:
[5382][07 Block] 
[5383][Para 002] In addition to treatment for the infection, anticoagulation is required for thrombosis. The mortality rate is high.
[5384][Para 015] Treatment
[5385][Para 024]  What are the General Principles of Treatment for All Odontogenic Infections of Soft Tissues?
[5386][Para 020] Treatment Should Be Started Immediately
[5387][Para 001] Infection may spread quickly and, in some cases, progress to a life-threatening situation. Identify patients with a risk of significant complications. Those at risk of airway obstruction, cavernous sinus thrombosis or toxaemia and present malaise or a high temperature should be treated immediately, possibly even with parenteral antibiotics while awaiting definitive diagnosis, and admitted to hospital for treatment.
[5388][Para 020] Pus Must Be Drained As Soon As Possible
[5389][Para 001] With most infections causing facial swelling, the only treatment required is effective drainage of pus and removal of the cause. To ensure success, a drain may need to be placed in the incision.
[5390][Para 020] Remove the Cause As Soon As Possible
[5391][Para 001] Removal of the causative tooth both prevents continuing infection and also drains the intraosseous abscess. The exception to this rule is when the cause is pericoronitis. In this case, the soft tissue, rather than the tooth, is the cause, and extraction can be detrimental (see Case 32).
[5392][Para 020] Provide Antibiotic Treatment, if Necessary
[5393][Para 001] Antibiotics provide little benefit over drainage and removal of the cause but are often used and occasionally required. Pus should be collected on drainage and submitted to microbiology for culture and sensitivity investigation, in case a change of antibiotic is required subsequently.
[5394][Para 020] Provide Supportive Measures
[5395][Para 001] Ensure that the patient eats, maintains good fluid intake and rests. Consider admission to hospital until recovery has started, and provide appropriate analgesia.
[5396][Para 020] Review Progress Regularly
[5397][Para 001] Daily review of those patients treated on an outpatient basis is appropriate. Those whose infection is serious enough to merit admission to hospital require more frequent review, between every hour and 6 hours, depending on their status. If signs and symptoms do not improve progressively, further investigation and treatment are probably required.
[5398][Heading 2]  What are the Principles of Obtaining Drainage? How Will You Drain the Pus in This Case?
[5399][Para 001] The principles of incision for drainage are:
[5400][Para 004] • Take the anatomy into account, and avoid incising near important structures.
[5401][Para 004] • Incise only when pus has localized, unless rapidly increasing swelling is threatening the airway, in which case it should be drained as quickly as possible.
[5402][Para 004] • Incise where the abscess is pointing or at the point of maximum fluctuation.
[5403][Para 004] • Incise along the most direct route to the pus.
[5404][Para 004] • If incision does not release pus, deepen the incision by using blunt forceps, not a scalpel. Open the forceps blades to break open the abscess wall (Hilton’s method).
[5405][Para 004] • After incision, explore, identify and open all locules of pus.
[5406][Para 004] • Provide dependent drainage, if possible.
[5407][Para 004] • Place a drain if the abscess is large, is deep or if the incision might close before the abscess resolves (e.g. if the incision penetrates layers of muscle, fascia or skin that can move independently). Leave the drain in place for at least 12–24 hours, or until drainage stops.
[5408][Para 004] • If possible, drain intraorally to prevent facial scarring and skin contraction.
[5409][Para 004] • On the skin, incise along Langer’s lines or in a skin crease.
[5410][Para 004] • On the skin, try to incise healthy skin. It will scar less.
[5411][Para 002] In this case, the pus lies between the buccinator muscle and the skin. It is not pointing and is palpable in the upper buccal sulcus. Incision at this site under ethyl chloride spray anaesthesia is perfectly appropriate. However, the incision must extend through the buccinator to be effective, and some might prefer to obtain drainage, with the patient under brief general anaesthesia.
[5412][Heading 2]  Should Drainage Ever Be Delayed?
[5413][Para 001] Occasionally, drainage must be delayed until pus is properly localized into an abscess. If no pus can be identified on examination, incision will be futile. Waiting a day and providing antibiotics may result in pus localizing. Therefore, such a decision must be carefully considered.
[5414][Heading 2]  Will a Drain Be Required?
[5415][Para 001] Quite probably. The abscess is not very deep, but the incision must pass through a muscle. However, drainage will be dependent: the incision is being made below the pus, and gravity will favour drainage. It may not be possible to decide in advance. If pus drains freely on incision and a cavity in the tissues is present, it would be sensible to place a drain, preferably a strip of corrugated rubber or, as a second choice, gauze. This should be sutured to the edge of the incision to prevent displacement. In this case, a drain would be as easily placed under either local or general anaesthetic.
[5416][Heading 2]  Can the Tooth Be Conserved After Soft Tissue Infection? How Might You Remove the Tooth?
[5417][Para 001] A soft tissue infection does not mean that the tooth has to be extracted, and almost all teeth could, in theory, be preserved. However, most such cases arise as a result of neglect; the tooth is often badly broken down and is best extracted. Occasionally, when infection is spreading rapidly or if the airway is compromised, the tooth is extracted to avoid delaying treatment, but even these severe complications do not mandate that the tooth be extracted. The critical factor is that drainage is obtained.
[5418][Para 002] If the tooth is to be conserved, it must be opened and drainage effected through the pulp chamber, in addition to draining pus by incision. Ideally, the pulp chamber can be closed again fairly quickly. As soon as drainage ceases, the pulp chamber can be cleaned and a dressing placed. If pus continues to drain for some time, the chamber may be left open for up to 24 hours. After this period, there is a risk of oral flora entering tissues, reducing the chances of subsequent successful root treatment. Many clinicians prescribe antibiotics because they consider drainage to be less effective when the tooth is retained.
[5419][Para 002] Extraction is the more usual treatment. If local anaesthesia can be obtained and trismus is not severe, the tooth may be extracted at once. Infiltration anaesthesia is often difficult to achieve because of the low pH of inflamed tissues. Injection into infected tissue also carries the risk of wider dissemination of bacteria. Block anaesthesia is required.
[5420][Para 002] General anaesthesia may be necessary. If so, it will be convenient to admit the patient to hospital and complete all the surgical treatments at the same time. General anaesthesia may take some time to organize, and in the meantime, it would be appropriate to try to extract the tooth under local anaesthesia. General anaesthesia should not be used in an attempt to overcome trismus. Forcing the jaws open will spread the infection.
[5421][Para 002] If a surgical extraction is required, it may be delayed. As a general principle, surgery should be avoided if the surgical field is infected. However, this rather old rule is often not followed now because of the availability of very effective antibiotic treatment. Some operators will perform a surgical extraction immediately, and the risk of spreading infection or inducing osteomyelitis seems to be extremely small.
[5422][Para 017] In this case, anaesthesia could not be obtained, and so drainage and extraction were performed under general anaesthesia. A short, corrugated rubber drain was inserted.
[5423][Heading 2]  When Should Antibiotics Be Prescribed for Odontogenic Soft Tissue Infection?
[5424][Para 001] The attitude to antibiotic treatment varies among different centres. Antibiotics are unnecessary for the treatment of the majority of localized soft tissue abscesses, and this is particularly so when pus collects superficially in the buccal sulcus or on the palate. Drainage and removal of the cause are much more important. However, in practice, many patients who require incision and drainage tend to be prescribed antibiotics by clinicians, without a clear rationale.
[5425][Para 002] Antibiotics should be prescribed if:
[5426][Para 004] • the patient is prone to infection (e.g. because of diabetes or immunosuppression)
[5427][Para 004] • there is spreading infection (cellulitis)
[5428][Para 004] • the airway is compromised
[5429][Para 004] • there is significant malaise, pyrexia or toxaemia
[5430][Para 004] • the tooth is to be preserved rather than extracted (the cause is not immediately eliminated)
[5431][Para 004] • cavernous sinus thrombosis is possible.
[5432][Para 002] Antibiotics prescribed for spreading infection may cause pus to localize, and drainage of abscesses may only be possible a day or so later.
[5433][Para 002] Antibiotics should never be provided as an alternative to draining pus.
[5434][Heading 2]  What Microorganisms Cause Odontogenic Soft Tissue Infections?
[5435][Para 001] Odontogenic soft tissue infections are mixed infections. The microbial flora usually contains about 25 species derived from oral flora, of which about half are cultivatable. Anaerobes outnumber aerobes by 10 or 100 to 1, and the commonly isolated species are Porphyromonas sp., Prevotella sp., Peptostreptococcus sp. and Fusobacterium sp.; however, facultative anaerobes are usually present, often members of the Streptococcus milleri group. Although numerically a minor component of the flora, these organisms are important when selecting antibiotics.
[5436][Heading 2]  If You Decided To Do So, Which Antibiotic Would You Prescribe Initially? Explain Why
[5437][Para 001] Almost all the organisms in odontogenic soft tissue infections are sensitive to penicillins. There is a small, but increasing, proportion of resistant strains, but these do not seem to contraindicate the use of penicillins. It is not necessary to prescribe penicillinase-resistant drugs just because one member of the microbial flora shows resistance and they are of no proven benefit in odontogenic infection. Penicillin V or G is sufficient, provided drainage can be achieved.
[5438][Para 002] Metronidazole is effective against the anaerobic species and is often prescribed. However, metronidazole should be used as an adjunct to a penicillin and never alone. It will kill the anaerobes but leave facultative anaerobes such as the S. milleri group unscathed. These organisms are capable of causing a spreading soft tissue infection as a monoculture. Removing their anaerobic microbial competitors with metronidazole risks turning a relatively well-localized, mixed infection into a spreading streptococcal infection. In the wrong site, this could be fatal.
[5439][Para 017] In this case, the patient received a single dose of 500 mg amoxicillin and 400 mg metronidazole intravenously during administration of the anaesthetic. The same doses were prescribed for oral intake three times a day for 5 days afterwards, and this is an appropriate regimen for most odontogenic soft tissue infections. However, as noted above, it may not have contributed greatly to the patient’s recovery.
[5440][Heading 2]  Why Bother To Take a Specimen for Culture and Sensitivity Testing?
[5441][Para 001] As noted above, empirical treatment with penicillin with or without metronidazole is almost always effective. However, in some cases, the infection stabilizes but fails to resolve. This may result from inadequate drainage, but a change of antibiotic may be considered a sensible precaution. The result of sensitivity testing may be helpful in selecting another antibiotic and identifying any unusual pathogens present. As culture and sensitivity testing takes about 3 days, it must be requested as soon as a sample of pus can be obtained and before antibiotics are administered.
[5442][Para 002] To be useful, the sample for culture must be taken in such a way as to favour the growth of anaerobes and fastidious organisms. Ideally, it should be taken directly from the abscess through a needle or through a sterile skin incision and transported anaerobically to the laboratory. Samples on swabs contaminated by oral flora are unlikely to be useful and may even provide a misleading result.
[5443][Para 002] When interpreting the results of culture and sensitivity tests performed on a simple swab of pus, it must be remembered that the organisms isolated are unlikely to be representative of all oral flora. Routine culture methods in most hospitals will detect only a few species, probably not the main components of oral flora. Unless a change to a different antibiotic is clearly justified, it would be better to consider changing the dose and route of administration.
[5444][Heading 2]  How Quickly Should the Swelling Resolve?
[5445][Para 001] Patients may often feel much better within a few hours, and a noticeable reduction in swelling, trismus, pain and pyrexia should be observed within 24 hours. By this time, drains do not usually show pus and are removed and dressings placed over the site, if extraoral. If there has been no resolution, the diagnosis, antibiotic treatment and effectiveness of drainage must be reviewed. Almost complete resolution should follow in 3–6 days, as in the present case.

[5449][Para 025] Case 50
[5450][Heading 1] Missing Upper Lateral Incisors
[5451][Para 027] Sophie Watkins
[5452][Para 028] Summary
[5453][Para 029] A 17-year-old girl presents to you at your general dental practice requesting restoration of the spaces between her upper front teeth. What is the cause, and how can a better appearance be achieved?
[5454][Para 014] History
[5455][Para 019] Complaint
[5456][Para 007] The patient does not wish to have gaps between her upper front teeth.
[5457][Para 012] History of Complaint
[5458][Para 007] The patient’s permanent teeth erupted at a normal age, but with large spaces between them. The primary predecessors had all been present and were exfoliated normally. None of the permanent teeth have been extracted. She has recently completed orthodontic treatment planned to facilitate replacement of the lateral incisors.
[5459][Para 012] Medical History
[5460][Para 007] The patient is fit and well.
[5461][Para 012] Family History
[5462][Para 007] The patient’s mother had a number of teeth missing. They had been replaced with a partial denture at an early age.
[5463][Para 014] Examination
[5464][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[5465][Para 007] The patient has a skeletal class I appearance without facial asymmetry. There is a slight deviation of the mandible to the patient’s left-hand side on mouth opening, but without limitation of mouth opening, temporomandibular joint clicks or crepitus or masticatory muscle tenderness.
[5466][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[5467][Para 007] The patient’s soft tissues are healthy, and her oral hygiene is good, with no calculus deposits, gingival inflammation or bleeding on probing. The teeth appear sound, with the exception of slight mobility associated with the upper right central incisor. The spaces in the lateral incisor regions are currently filled with teeth added to her removable orthodontic retainer.
[5468][Para 002] The clinical appearance on presentation is shown in Fig. 50.1.
[5469][Heading 2]  What Features are Relevant To Treatment?
[5470][Para 001] Both
[5471][Para 002] upper lateral incisors are absent. There is a mild class III incisor relationship, with a normal overjet and a reduced but complete overbite. The teeth are well aligned and upright after orthodontic treatment with appropriate dimensions of space for the lateral incisor teeth that are missing.
[5472][Heading 2]  What are the Possible Causes for the Absence of Lateral Incisors? What is the Most Likely Cause in This Case?
[5473][Para 032] See Box 50.1.
[5474][Para 002] In this case, the most likely cause for the missing lateral incisors is developmental – hypodontia. Excluding third molars, the reported prevalence of hypodontia ranges from 1.6 to 6.9%, depending on the population group studied. The teeth most commonly missing are, in descending order of frequency, the third molars, the mandibular second premolars, the maxillary lateral incisors and the maxillary second premolars. The maxillary lateral incisors are lost in about 1–2% of the population. The fact that the patient’s mother wore a denture to replace missing teeth from an early age suggests a possible familial aetiology. Trauma or extraction and the related sequelae are readily excluded by the history (anamnesis).
[5475][Para 015] Investigations
[5476][Heading 2]  What Investigations are Required?
[5477][Para 001] The reason for each investigation is outlined in Box 50.2.
[5478][Heading 2]  The Dental Panoramic Tomograph is Displayed in Fig. 50.2b. What Does It Show?
[5479][Para 001] The dental panoramic tomograph confirms the absence of the upper lateral incisors, with no evidence of supernumerary teeth or other bone lesions in this region. All other teeth, including the unerupted third molars, are present. This confirms the diagnosis that the upper lateral incisors are developmentally absent.

[5481][Para 008] 
[5482][Para 011] Fig. 50.1 a, Extra oral view, b, anterior labial view and c, maxillary occlusal view of the patient on presentation.
[5483][Para 009]  
[5484][Para 095] Box 50.1 Possible Causes for the Absence of Lateral Incisors
[5485][05 Block] 
[5486][Para 002] The root of the upper right central incisor has significant resorption, making its prognosis poor. The other central and canine tooth roots are upright, and the root apices of the canines are distally placed. This is important in the planning of orthodontic treatment. Canines can be difficult to move bodily through the alveolar bone because of their bulky root form, and therefore, the position of the root apex prior to orthodontic treatment is important. In this case, the pre-treatment distal positon of the root apex made distalization of the canines to open spaces for the lateral incisors more predictable. This is beneficial, especially if implants are planned as a treatment option in the future, when the roots of the teeth need to be clear of the potential implant-bearing edentate area.
[5487][Heading 2]  What Might Have Caused the Root Resorption of the Upper Right Central Incisior Root?
[5488][Para 001] There are several possible causes, including:
[5489][Para 016] 1. An ectopic Upper Right Lateral Incisor. A mesially impacted lateral incisor can cause root resorption. It is, therefore, important to take radiographs as soon as it is noted that a tooth has not erupted at the expected age. Lateral incisors usually erupt at 8–9 years, and therefore, if the patient reaches 10 years with no clinical sign of a lateral incisor, radiographic investigation is essential, or earlier if the contralateral tooth has erupted successfully. 
[5490][Para 206] Box 50.2 Reasons for Investigations
[5491][01 Block] 
[5492][Para 016] 2. Trauma. A traumatic injury to a tooth such as avulsion, intrusion or subluxation, in which the injury damages the periodontal ligament.
[5493][Para 016] 3. Orthodontic forces. Excessive orthodontic force/rapid orthodontic tooth movement can cause resorption of the root apices. It is, therefore, important to monitor the tooth roots radiographically during orthodontic treatment, especially where the roots are particularly narrow/tapered. However, this is unlikely to occur at a single root. Nevertheless, if a root is severely resorbed, it is unwise to attempt orthodontic movement.
[5494][Para 016] 4. Lesion such as a cyst or a tumour. In this case, the radiographic appearance was not indicative of a pathological lesion.
[5495][Para 002] Whatever the aetiology of the resorption, it is very important to ensure that the patient is made aware of this as soon as it is identified and that the doubtful prognosis, the possible consequences and the management options are discussed. In this case, orthodontic movement was undertaken with great care, and careful clinical and radiographic monitoring was undertaken; after having made the patient and her parents/guardians aware of the doubtful prognosis of the upper right central incisor, including the risk of further root resorption during orthodontics, which could result in mobility and loss of the tooth as a consequence.
[5496][Para 002] Having been given these warnings both verbally and in written form, including all the options for treatment, the potential consequences and the options for management if the tooth was to be lost, the patient and her parents/guardians were then able to give their fully informed consent. It is very important medico-legally that informed consent is documented in cases such as this, taking the compromised tooth into account in the current treatment planning and with regard to future options. The findings and discussion with the patient must be documented contemporaneously.
[5497][Para 015] Care Plan
[5498][Heading 2]  What are the Main Treatment Options? What are Their Advantages and Disadvantages?
[5499][Para 032] See Box 50.3 and Fig. 50.3.
[5500][Heading 2]  The Patient’s Main Concern Was Her Appearance. What Other Treatment Options Might Have Been Available, and How Would You Demonstrate the Possible Results To Her?
[5501][Para 001] If the patient is considering committing herself to a long and complex (and potentially expensive) treatment, the potential result of each of the treatment options should be considered carefully. Possible outcomes can be assessed by using study models and diagnostic wax-ups. The feasibility of the orthodontic treatment options can be visualized by using Kesling set-up – cutting the teeth to be moved off duplicate study casts and fixing them in an orthodontically achievable position. The patient and the dentist can then see what might be achieved with each treatment option. There are also computer software programmes that can show on images of the patient’s face the effects of altered tooth positions.
[5502][Para 017] In this case, after discussion, the patient opted for the third treatment option outlined in  Box 50.3 , that of space opening and prosthetic replacement of the missing lateral incisor teeth.
[5503][Heading 2]  How Would You Carry Out the Orthodontic Treatment?
[5504][Para 001] The tooth movement demands fixed appliance treatment. Tooth tilting with use of a removable appliance would result in a poor appearance in the midline and may produce spaces that are difficult to fill with a prosthetic replacement. Fixed appliance therapy allows the incisors to be moved bodily, and derotation and distalization/uprighting of the canines is possible. This option, of course, would need referral to a specialist orthodontist and his or her team for multidisciplinary planning and treatment execution. It is also important to remember the risks associated with the root of the compromised upper right central incisor, and great care is required in moving this tooth with fixed orthodontics. The treatment plan should take into account a possible need to replace this tooth as well as the missing lateral incisors.

[5521][Heading 2]  If the Resorbed Root Had Been an Absolute Contraindication To Orthodontic Treatment, What Other Option Might Have Been Appropriate?
[5522][Para 001] If orthodontic space opening had not been possible without compromising the prognosis of the central incisor tooth, the canine teeth could have been built up to resemble the missing lateral incisor teeth instead of providing orthodontic treatment, accepting some anterior spacing or to assist in correct space closure. An example of this can be seen in Fig. 50.3a. The preoperative periapical view in Fig. 50.2a indicates that the tooth position at initial presentation might have lent itself to this approach, but only if the patient was happy to accept some spacing.
[5523][Heading 2]  How Would You Now Replace the Missing Lateral Incisors?
[5524][Para 001] Initially, the spaces are filled with teeth added onto the orthodontic retainer. After a period of settling, definitive restorations can be considered.
[5525][Para 002] In this case, definitive prosthodontic treatment had to be as conservative as possible because the upper anterior teeth were vital and sound and the patient was young. The doubtful long-term prognosis of the upper right central incisor was an important consideration. These teeth could be replaced with fixed or removable prostheses; however, in most circumstances, a fixed restoration would be the patient’s strong preference. The options, therefore, would include the following.
[5526][Para 020] Adhesive Bridgework
[5527][Para 001] This is a conservative option because it requires little or no tooth preparation. Adhesive bridges, when appropriately designed, can be an option with a very predictable outcome but require sufficient enamel for bonding of the retainer wings. Because the teeth in this case were unrestored, there was ample enamel for bonding, making this a viable treatment option. Conventional bridgework would be contraindicated here because it would be unnecessarily destructive of the abutment teeth.
[5528][Para 020] Implant-Supported Restorations
[5529][Para 001] Implants are now a widely used treatment option for tooth replacement and can produce predictable aesthetic and functional results. It is important to ensure that there is sufficient space between adjacent teeth and sufficient bone volume to accommodate the implants. This will, therefore, need to be planned as part of any orthodontic treatment.
[5530][Para 002] For dental implants to be an option, even if this is not the initial care plan, radiographs are necessary to ensure the tooth roots adjacent to the spaces (upper canines and central incisors in this case) are not encroaching on the potential implant-bearing area and that the mesio-distal space is sufficient to accommodate the size of an implant both at the gingival level and also between the root apices (usually approximately 7 mm). It is also worth considering that because hypodontia is frequently associated with microdontia, it is not always appropriate or, indeed, possible to open the spaces to this dimension; therefore, it is important that the patient is made aware of this before any treatment is started. In this case, the tooth movements were quite extensive; in such a situation, it is wise to warn a patient that it may not be possible to move the tooth roots sufficiently to create space for an implant before orthodontic space creation is started. Managing patient expectations regarding treatment outcome is critical in such cases.
[5531][Para 002] Implants involve one or more surgical procedures and can be costly and, therefore, are not always the most appropriate option. They are also not indicated for patients under the age of 18 years because of the continuing growth of the jaws. Indeed, some would suggest that growth continues for some time after this age and would advocate delaying implants until patients are much older, especially in single tooth sites, because this can result in infraocclusion relative to the adjacent natural teeth.
[5532][Para 002] It is advisable for the dentist who is going to undertake the restorative treatment to review the case prior to orthodontic debond to ensure that the dimensions of the spaces and the tooth/root position are optimal for the most predictable outcome of the restoration to be provided. This includes ensuring that the spaces are symmetrical and that appropriate occlusal guidance is available, as well as radiographs to assess root position, as mentioned above.
[5533][Para 002] In this case, in view of the doubtful prognosis of the upper central incisor, implants were considered a good option to avoid loading the compromised tooth. However, in view of the patient’s age and the fact that the incisors were not showing significant mobility at this stage, the recommended treatment of choice was adhesive bridges, maintaining the central incisors for as long as possible and considering an implant-supported restoration to replace them if and when problems occur in future.
[5534][Para 002] Possible bridge designs are shown in Figs 50.5 and 50.6.
[5535][Para 020] Bridge Designs
[5536][Para 001] Normally, a fixed–fixed design in a minimum-preparation bridge (as shown in Fig. 50.5) should be avoided. This is because the differential mobility of the abutment teeth can result in debonding of one retainer, creating an area of stagnation below it and, thus, an increased risk of development of a carious lesion. For this reason, a typical minimum-preparation bridge design to replace a lateral incisor would be a cantilever design retained on either the canine or the central incisor (as shown in Fig. 50.6a and b).
[5537][Para 002] It was important to consider orthodontic retention. The canines were originally mesio-labially rotated, and the orthodontic result would, therefore, be potentially unstable. Relapse would result in the pontics swinging out labially if bridge design option a were chosen in the absence of orthodontic retention. Option b does not include the canines, but because one of the central incisors had a poor prognosis, it was not appropriate to use the incisors as bridge abutments. In cases where a midline diastema has been closed, retention can be incorporated in the adhesive bridge design such as a cantilever design retained on linked central incisors (option c), but, again, because of the condition of the roots of the central incisors, this option was contraindicated in this case.
[5538][Para 002] A fixed–fixed bridge extending from canine to canine (Fig. 50.5) or canine to incisor (Fig 50.6 option d) would include fixed orthodontic retention of the positions of the canines and central incisors, but once again, this involves the questionable incisors. A potentially unstable orthodontic result may in itself favour debonding of one or more of the wings, and so if a linked or fixed–fixed design is used, regular recall will be essential to detect this early. In case of debonding, the bridge must be removed and either replaced or recemented, if considered appropriate. If this is planned, an assessment of the reason for the debonding must be made to ascertain whether this is an appropriate course of action or whether an alternative design or a different restoration is indicated. Prior to recementation, the abutment teeth and the retainer wings must be cleaned thoroughly. Intraoral air abrasion is useful for this, if available.
[5539][Para 218] 
[5540][Para 008]

[5543][Para 002] Therefore, in this case, option a was the most appropriate bridge design, and orthodontic retention was maintained by making a new retainer fitted simultaneously on the day the bridges were cemented. The patient was given clear instructions to wear the retainer every night and warned clearly, both verbally and with written instruction, that orthodontic relapse is a risk if she does not comply with this advice. It would be wise to ensure that patients read and fully understand the consequences and that they sign the form indicating they have done so. A copy of this form should be retained in the patients’ records for future reference.
[5544][Para 002] The final bridge design and appearance are shown in Fig. 50.7. Note how the metal retainer wing is extended over the entire palatal surface of the canine tooth to utilize the maximum available enamel for bonding. Box 50.4 shows a suggested wording and diagrams which can be used in a laboratory prescription for this design of bridge. The orthodontic care plan should take into account the occlusal clearance required to cover the palatal surfaces of the canines, although if there is insufficient interocclusal space, alveolar compensation (the ‘Dahl effect’) is likely to occur as part of post orthodontic vertical settling if the bridges are cemented ‘high’ in occlusion. In this instance, the occlusal contacts should be monitored at review.

[5549][Para 002] The bridges were cemented by using an opaque resin cement to obscure the colour of metal retainer wings showing through and to prevent ‘greying’ of the abutment teeth, as is sometimes described, although this is more commonly a problem where more translucent (incisor) teeth are used as abutments. Although this successfully prevents grey shine-through, the altered translucency can affect the final shade and must be taken into account during shade selection, by holding something (e.g. a gloved finger or a cotton wool roll) against the palatal aspect of the abutment tooth to mimic this change.

[5555][Para 030]  What Warnings Must Be Given To the Patient When Undertaking This Treatment and Obtaining Consent?
[5556][Para 001] The upper right central incisor has a doubtful medium- to long-term prognosis because of the short root evident on the radiograph. It is essential that the patient is aware of this and is involved in the decision regarding choice of restoration, both at this stage and in relation to what options may be available in future. In this case, because the teeth are not excessively mobile and the short root has been monitored over some years, it was decided to maintain the tooth for the time being, rather than extract and replace it as part of the current phase of prosthetic treatment. This decision was based on the acknowledgement that any restoration provided now will require replacement at some stage in the future in view of the patient’s young age and that hastening the loss of the tooth was not in the patient’s best interests. This was discussed with the patient, who was fully involved in the decision-making process, while obtaining informed consent. The decision not to include the central incisors in the bridge design was part of this discussion, as was the associated importance of removable orthodontic retention, and the patient was fully informed and involved in the care planning process. Contemporaneous notes were made throughout this process and the patient’s expectations of treatment managed carefully.

[5559][Para 011] Fig. 50.7 The final result. Note the bridge retainer wings are extended over the entire palatal surface of the abutment teeth to incorporate the maximum available enamel for adhesion. In this case, there was interocclusal space for the thickness of the metal retainer wing, but if this is lacking, then it is not unreasonable to consider cementing the bridges high in occlusion and allowing the occlusal contacts to be re-established as a result of alveolar compensation, as described earlier.
[5560][Para 009]  
[5561][Heading 2]  Planning for Failure: What Would Be the Options for Restoration if the Central Incisors Became More Mobile and Failed?
[5562][Para 001] In a case such as this, it is important to plan for failure of teeth that have a guarded prognosis because this forms part of the informed consent process during discussions of treatment planning with the patient.
[5563][Para 002] When the incisors do fail, a new adhesive bridge could be considered, replacing all four upper incisors. These long-span adhesive bridges are less predictable compared with shorter-span bridges, but where two canines are utilized as the abutment teeth, the robust nature of these teeth, coupled with the bulky crown and associated area of enamel for bonding, makes this a pragmatic option in this region. If the abutment teeth are significantly different in size, especially with differential mobility, a long-span fixed–fixed bridge is less predictable. An example of this may be where a lateral incisor and a canine are the potential abutments. The greater inherent mobility of the incisor, along with the smaller surface area of enamel for bonding compared with that of the canine, would make the restoration less predictable because it may predispose to retainer wing debonding on the more mobile abutment.
[5564][Para 002] Another option would be an implant-supported bridge. In this case, consideration could be given to providing implants in the lateral incisor regions, subject to bone availability and appropriate space between the adjacent teeth, which could then be used to provide a longer-span bridge to replace all four incisor teeth if this became necessary in future, without the need for further implant surgery or, if the prognosis of the upper left incisor tooth remained good, this could be retained and a cantilever bridge provided, replacing the upper right central and lateral incisor only, as long as a suitably wide diameter implant could be placed in the lateral incisor region to support a cantilever bridge. In this case, the patient elected to delay the treatment with implants and chose the less invasive option of adhesive bridges at this stage. However, it is essential that patients are aware of the consequences of this option so that they can make a fully informed decision.
[5565][Para 025] Case 51
[5566][Heading 1] Anterior Crossbite (Class III Malocclusion) with Displacement in the Mixed Dentition
[5567][Para 027] Dirk Bister
[5568][Para 028] Summary
[5569][Para 029] A 10-year-old male patient presents with a class III incisor relationship, he is in the mixed-dentition. There are signs of tooth wear affecting the front teeth.
[5570][Para 014] History
[5571][Para 019] Complaint
[5572][Para 007] The patient complains about an uncomfortable bite, and the front teeth are meeting ‘the wrong way around’.
[5573][Para 012] History of Complaint
[5574][Para 007] The parents report that he developed a class III malocclusion after the upper and lower permanent incisors erupted and came into contact.
[5575][Para 012] Medical History
[5576][Para 007] The patient is medically fit and well.
[5577][Para 014] Examination
[5578][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[5579][Para 007] The patient presents with a mild class III profile when his posterior teeth are in maximum intercuspation. However, his facial features are normal when biting on the incisors (before displacement).
[5580][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[5581][Para 007] The patient can achieve an ‘edge to edge’ incisor relationship. There are signs of tooth wear (attrition) affecting the upper incisors, particularly the upper central incisors ( Fig. 51.1 ).
[5582][Para 017] The patient then postures forwards (so-called ‘displacement’) into a comfortable bite to achieve good contact between the back teeth (maximum intercuspation).
[5583][Para 002] In the UK, the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN) is used to assess eligibility for treatment free of charge at the point of delivery (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/Orthodontics/).
[5584][Para 002] The IOTN of this patient is 4c, which is defined as ‘anterior or posterior crossbites with greater than 2 mm discrepancy between the retruded contact position and maximum intercuspation’. More detailed information on IOTN can be found at: https://www.bos.org.uk/Public-Patients/Orthodontics-for-Children-Teens/Fact-File-FAQ/What-Is-The-IOTN.
[5585][Para 015] Diagnosis
[5586][Heading 2]  What are the Possible Causes of Class III Malocclusion?
[5587][Para 001] Potential causes of class III malocclusion are:
[5588][Para 016] 1. Unusual eruption path of the upper incisors leading to a forward mandibular displacement
[5589][Para 016] 2. Underdevelopment of the maxilla
[5590][Para 016] 3. Overdevelopment of the mandible
[5591][Para 002] or a combination of any of the above.
[5592][Para 014] Treatment
[5593][Para 001] A dental panoramic tomogram (DPT) or an upper standard occlusal (USO) radiograph should be taken for planning orthodontic treatment. This will enable the practitioner to exclude the presence of supplemental/supernumerary teeth in the upper anterior labial segment. A lateral cephalogram may be considered if a significant skeletal discrepancy is diagnosed clinically (i.e. there is no displacement and a reverse overjet greater than 2 mm and/or a reduced overbite/open bite; this should trigger a referral to a specialist). The DPT and USO radiograph can be taken by the general dental practitioner.
[5594][Para 002] The choice of treatment depends on the underlying aetiology, as discussed below.
[5595][Para 218] 
[5596][Para 008] 
[5597][Para 011] Fig. 51.1 a, The patient achieves an edge-to-edge incisor relationship when in retruded mandibular position. The patient is asked to roll the tongue to the back of the mouth and close until the anterior teeth come into contact. Alternatively, the mandible can be manipulated manually to achieve the rearmost position. b–d, On closure, the patient postures his mandible forwards to achieve maximum intercuspation, as seen on the images on the top right lower right and lower left. There are signs of attrition affecting the upper central incisors in particular.
[5598][Para 009]  
[5599][Para 012] ‘Camouflage’ Orthodontics
[5600][Para 001] ‘Camouflage’ Orthodontics is defined as leaving the causative underlying skeletal discrepancy untreated. The teeth are moved so that a normal occlusion is established. In case of normal inclination of the maxillary teeth and a minor skeletal discrepancy, opt for tooth movement only. This can be achieved by using either sectional fixed appliances or an upper removable appliance. The latter approach was chosen as a case study here (Fig. 51.1) and does not necessarily require treatment by a specialist orthodontist.
[5601][Para 002] Partial upper fixed appliances are also known as ‘two-by-four appliances’: The upper first molars are usually banded, and the four incisors are bonded. This treatment should ideally be provided by an orthodontic specialist.
[5602][Para 002] Treatment, usually of short duration, in the mixed dentition that aims at correcting the aetiology of malocclusion is also known as interceptive treatment.
[5603][Para 012] Comprehensive ‘Early’ Treatment for Class III Malocclusion
[5604][Para 001] Correction of the skeletal discrepancy can be attempted with a facemask in the mixed dentition or by using a fixed appliance in the permanent dentition. Jaw surgery can be considered in severe cases, with multidisciplinary collaboration among the orthodontist, and the oral and maxillofacial surgeon. Correcting a mild skeletal discrepancy in the mixed dentition by using a facemask is successful in approximately 70% of cases.
[5605][Para 012] Appliance Design for the Upper Removable Appliance
[5606][Para 001] The appliance consists of an active component, a retention component and a baseplate. A large ‘Z’ spring is used to procline the upper central and lateral incisors, thereby eliminating displacement (Fig. 51.2). This is the active component. Alternatively, other types of springs can be used (e.g. T-springs).
[5607][Para 002] Adams’ cribs on deciduous molars and molars are used for retention. A posterior bite plane can be useful to open the bite and allow the incisors to move forward without interference with the lower dentition.
[5608][Para 002] When the appliance is fitted and activated, it needs to be noted that it will be ‘bouncy’: The upper spring will create a downward force. The Z-spring is activated by pulling it mainly upwards (cranial) and only slightly forwards so that it does not come to rest in front of the upper incisors on insertion.
[5609][Para 218] 
[5610][Para 008] 
[5611][Para 011] Fig. 51.2 a, Image of an upper removable appliance for proclination of the upper labial segment. Two ‘Z’ springs are placed on right-hand side and the left-hand side to procline the upper central and lateral incisors. Adams’ cribs are used for retention as well a posterior bite plane. An upper midline expansion screw has been added to address the crossbite tendency. b–d, Treatment outcome after approximately 8 weeks of treatment. The patient’s upper incisors have been proclined and the patient now occludes the anterior teeth but without displacing forwards. At this stage, the appliance is gradually withdrawn and night-time-only wear is prescribed.
[5612][Para 009]  
[5613][Para 002] The appliance is usually worn full time for a period of 6–8 weeks, followed by nighttime wear for approximately 3 months. There is a posterior open bite once the upper incisors have been proclined, as seen in the images provided (see Fig. 51.2). This settles once the appliance is worn at nighttime only. This is a good example of interceptive orthodontic treatment (Fig. 51.3).
[5614][Para 012] Consent
[5615][Para 001] Obtaining valid consent is one of the nine principles that registered dental professionals must follow at all times (https://standards.gdc-uk.org/pages/principle3/principle3.aspx).
[5616][Para 002] Consent in orthodontics is ideally a two-stage process: In the first stage, the patient and their parents/legal guardian(s) are given the relevant information (often at the stage of orthodontic records: impressions/scan, clinical photographs and radiographs). Information leaflets describing the different aspects of orthodontic treatment are available through the British Orthodontic Society at: https://www.bos.org.uk/Public-Patients/Patient-Information-Leaflets. In this case, leaflets on treatment with a removable appliance, the risks of orthodontics, diet advice, and retention are particularly important.
[5617][Para 002] In the second stage, on the return visit, the patient and parent/legal guardian sign the consent form. It is important to note that consent is an ongoing process and that adherence to treatment (i.e. wearing the removable appliance full time) is paramount to its success.
[5618][Para 012] Potential Legal Issues and Pitfalls
[5619][Para 001] As with all orthodontic treatment, careful note keeping and monitoring of treatment progress are mandatory. The clinical problem is assessing the amount of displacement. The increased displacement will make it easier to treat this patient because his upper front teeth have to move forward less to achieve a positive overjet.
[5620][Para 012] Patient Adherence
[5621][Para 001] Adherence to wearing/maintaining the removable appliance may be an issue in some cases. It is important to remember that most appliances are not worn for the time requested by the orthodontists. Microsensor technology (e.g. TheraMon(R)) can be used to monitor wear, although this technology is not infallible. Patient consent should be obtained when monitoring devices are used.
[5622][Para 218] 
[5623][Para 008] 
[5624][Para 011] Fig. 51.3 Final result after occlusal settling, approximately 2 months later. The patient has discontinued upper removable appliance wear, and the posterior buccal segments have settled.
[5625][Para 009]  
[5626][Para 012] Prognostic Factors for Treatment of the Upper Arch
[5627][Para 001] A good vertical overlap of the incisors needs to be achieved at the end of orthodontic treatment; otherwise relapse may occur. Ideally, the upper incisors should not already be proclined before commencing orthodontics. Patients need to be advised that continuation of existing growth patterns can jeopardize the orthodontic treatment outcome particularly long-term.
[5628][Para 012] Long-Term Outcome
[5629][Para 007] The bite for this patient remained stable, and no further orthodontic treatment was required.
[5630][Para 014] Summary
[5631][Para 001] Teeth in anterior crossbite can be treated in the mixed dentition by using interceptive orthodontics. This type of treatment can be simple and cost-effective. The need to comply with removable appliance wear needs to be made clear at the start of treatment, and progress needs to be monitored and documented carefully. Obtaining patient consent regarding the long-term prognosis of class III treatment is also important. Growth may not always be favourable – the mandible tends to grow for a longer period compared with the maxilla, and there is potential for the reverse overjet to relapse.
[5632][Para 025] Case 52
[5633][Heading 1] Localized Periodontitis?
[5634][Para 027] Edward Odell, and Mandeep Ghuman
[5635][Para 028] Summary
[5636][Para 029] A 30-year-old male patient is referred for periodontitis that has not responded to treatment. What is the cause, and how would you proceed?
[5637][Para 218] 
[5638][Para 008] 
[5639][Para 011] Fig. 52.1 Periapical radiographs sent on referral.
[5640][Para 009]  
[5641][Para 014] History
[5642][Para 019] Complaint
[5643][Para 007] The patient complains that he has been undergoing intensive treatment for gum disease, but with little success. His upper right first molar is slightly loose, and his dentist wishes to extract it. He would like a second opinion.
[5644][Para 012] History of Complaint
[5645][Para 007] He noticed the gum disease 9 months ago. He has never had pain or discomfort from the tooth.
[5646][Para 012] Dental History
[5647][Para 007] The patient is a regular attendee at his dentist’s clinic. He has no dental restorations, no caries and no other oral problems. The previous dental practitioner had provided intensive oral hygiene instruction, root surface debridement under local anaesthesia, and reassessment. The patient brushes twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste and uses interdental brushes of two different sizes, as well as flossing daily.
[5648][Para 012] Medical History
[5649][Para 007] The patient is fit and well. He has no allergies and takes no medication. He has never smoked.
[5650][Heading 2]  What are Your Initial Thoughts?
[5651][Para 001] Periodontitis is often difficult to treat. Many patients are not able to maintain a sufficiently effective oral hygiene regimen or have other risk factors that have not been controlled or are beyond control. It remains possible that this patient is not cleaning effectively regularly despite his efforts, and this must be assessed. Or perhaps previous treatment did not completely remove all the subgingival calculus. Assuming the previous treatment was optimal, there has been sufficient time for nonsurgical periodontal treatment to have had some effect.
[5652][Para 014] Examination
[5653][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[5654][Para 007] The results of the extraoral examination are normal. No lymph nodes are palpable.
[5655][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[5656][Para 007] One lower third molar is partially erupted; the upper third molars are unopposed and distally inclined. There is no dental caries, and no restorations are present.
[5657][Para 017] The patient’s oral hygiene is very good. Only a few flecks of interdental plaque are present. The gingivae in most areas are healthy in appearance and do not bleed on probing.
[5658][Para 017] On full clinical periodontal assessment, three areas of concern are identified:
[5659][Para 131] 1. The upper right first molar is mobile about 1 mm in the bucco-palatal direction. It is grade 2 mobile and is not depressible in the socket. A 9-mm probing depth is present disto-palatally, and the distal furcation has grade 2 furcation involvement. The gingivae appear loose, but they are not oedematous, and there is only slight bleeding on probing. Inflammation appears diffuse, rather than being related to the gingival margin or pocket. The gingiva lifts easily from the tooth.
[5660][Para 131] 2. The lower right second premolar has a 5-mm probing depth disto-lingually and a 4-mm depth mesio-lingually. The tooth is not mobile. The gingivae are dusky red, not oedematous and relatively firm, although there is slight bleeding on probing.
[5661][Para 131] 3. There is a 6-mm pocket on the mesio-lingual aspect of the lower left second molar, with no bleeding on probing.
[5662][Para 017] Root surfaces on all affected areas feel smooth on probing.
[5663][Para 015] Investigations
[5664][Heading 2]  What Do You See in the Two Periapical Views That the Patient’s General Dental Practitioner Sent?
[5665][Para 001] The upper radiograph (Fig. 52.1) shows extensive bone loss distally to the first molar. There is loss of lamina dura around the whole of the distal root, into the furcation and around the apex. No calculus is visible.
[5666][Para 002] The lower film shows a curved area of alveolar bone loss associated with the first and second premolars. The lamina dura and alveolar crest on both teeth appear intact. The bone loss is consistent with the probing depth. No calculus is visible.
[5667][Heading 2]  What Further Investigations are Required?
[5668][Para 001] The vitality of the upper first molar must be determined. Bone loss extends beyond the apex, and there is a significant risk of loss of vitality. The apical lamina dura is not clearly defined, particularly in relation to the maxillary sinus, giving rise to further suspicion.
[5669][Para 002] A radiograph is needed to appreciate the bone levels around the lower left molars and possibly those around other teeth as well. However, before selecting a suitable view, further thinking is required.
[5670][Para 017] In the meantime, you check the vitality of the upper right first molar. It is vital and not hypersensitive to cold and electric pulp testing.
[5671][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[5672][Heading 2]  What are Your Thoughts Now?
[5673][Para 001] This is odd. The patient is motivated, and his oral hygiene is good; however, there are three areas of localized attachment loss, and these cannot be accounted for by local factors such as overhanging restorations or calculus.
[5674][Para 002] Perhaps the patient has a progressed form of molar incisor pattern periodontitis, which is defined as rapid attachment and bone loss occurring mostly at an earlier age, sometimes with a familial pattern. The sites of lesions (on two first molars and one premolar), the age of the patient and failure to respond to treatment suggest this. Would further nonsurgical periodontal treatment with adjunctive antibiotics help?
[5675][Para 002] Perhaps the patient has some systemic predisposition to periodontitis. The most likely cause would be diabetes or smoking. However, diabetes would have to be undiagnosed or poorly controlled to contribute to disease of this severity. Both diabetes and smoking are associated with periodontitis in a more generalized distribution and rarely predispose to localized disease.
[5676][Para 002] Other medical predisposing conditions include neutropenia, Down’s syndrome and rare developmental neutrophil defects. These become obvious in childhood and can therefore be excluded in this case.
[5677][Para 017] You decide to take a panoramic radiograph because you are suspicious that there may be more areas affected and because the pattern of disease is unusual. The result is shown in  Fig. 52.2 .
[5678][Heading 2]  What Additional Information Do You Gain From the Panoramic Radiograph?
[5679][Para 001] The lower left third molar is missing. The lower second molars have a conical root morphology.
[5680][Para 002] There is a shallow angular bone defect mesial to the lower left second molar. This certainly reinforces the suspicion of molar incisor pattern periodontitis.
[5681][Para 002] Have you missed something? Go back and look again at the periapical and panoramic radiographs and reassess the history.
[5682][Heading 2]  What Radiographic Features are Inconsistent or Suggest Alternative Causes?
[5683][Para 001] The upper periapical shows a large area of destruction of bone, and it is poorly localized, with the furcation appearing fuzzy. Bone around the apex and the maxillary sinus is not clearly defined, but the tooth is vital. If this were periodontitis, you would expect an endodontic–periodontal lesion, with abnormal results on sensibility testing and an observable corticated sinus margin radiographically.
[5684][Para 002] The same area of the panoramic radiograph shows much more worrying features. You had been concentrating on the periodontal condition and had not noticed that the maxillary antrum above the tooth is indistinct and that the floor of the antrum is eroded over the first and second molars. Compare this area with the contralateral floor of antrum. There is a radiolucency above the molar roots on the right and a poorly defined upper border.
[5685][Para 002] The lower periapical view is also unusual. The lamina dura and the alveolar crest are visible between the premolars despite the smooth, rounded shape of the bone loss adjacent to this. Therefore the bone loss is not interdental, but limited to the lingual cortex and extending across two teeth. The lingual cortex is thicker than the buccal cortex: an infrabony pocket caused by periodontitis could cause such a defect, but more interdental bone loss would be expected because periodontitis is usually initiated interdentally.

[5689][Para 009]  
[5690][Para 002] Now that you have recognized the extent of the upper molar lesion, your suspicions are confirmed. This is not periodontitis.
[5691][Heading 2]  What Conditions, Diseases or Lesions May Mimic Plaque-Induced Gingivitis and Periodontitis?
[5692][Para 001] There are many; some mimic gingivitis and others periodontitis. Most are rare. The most significant ones and their characteristic features, as well as useful diagnostic tests, are shown in Table 52.1.
[5693][Heading 2]  What is Your Differential Diagnosis On the Basis of What You Know So Far? Justify Each Possible Cause
[5694][Para 001] The cause must explain multiple lesions, a predilection for the gingival location and a relatively destructive, poorly defined lesion in a relatively young adult. On the basis of the information presented in Table 52.1, a few causes are likely:
[5695][Para 004] • Langerhans’ cell histiocytosis is the most likely condition and meets all these criteria. It is rare, but the most common amongst rarities.
[5696][Para 004] • Squamous odontogenic tumour also meets all the criteria but is even rarer.
[5697][Para 004] • Metastatic malignant neoplasm must be considered. A primary malignancy at a remote site is possible but unlikely at this age. Multiple lesions, particularly in this pattern, would be unlikely.
[5698][Para 015] Further Investigations
[5699][Heading 2]  What Will You Do Next?
[5700][Para 001] A biopsy is required to achieve the correct diagnosis for any of these diseases. The gingiva is readily sampled under local anaesthesia, and the best site would be soft tissue from the margin of either of the larger lesions – the lower premolar or the upper right molar. A buccal interdental papilla would be ideal.
[5701][Para 002] It would probably be best to extract the affected upper molar tooth. It has lost most of its supporting bone, and obtaining the correct diagnosis is the greater priority. In any case, the prognosis for this tooth is poor, and its removal would allow good access to the deeper tissue to obtain the biopsy sample. The socket could be curetted to obtain additional material from the alveolar bone (keeping in mind the risk of accidentally forming an oro-antral communication).
[5702][Heading 2]  The Biopsy Specimen is Shown in Fig. 52.3. What Do You See?
[5703][Para 001] The left-hand panel shows the gingival margin. No epithelium is present over the pocket wall, and this ulceration is not compatible with periodontitis. There is a cellular infiltrate in the pocket wall. The second panel shows the infiltrate at higher power. This is not the dense lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltrate of periodontitis. The background cells have prominent pink cytoplasm and large pale lobulated nuclei (cells labelled ‘L’). These are typical Langerhans’ cells. Bright red eosinophils are also present (labelled ‘E’).
[5704][Para 002] The appearances are typical of Langerhans’ cell histiocytosis. Sheets of neoplastic Langerhans’ cells infiltrate the tissues and attract eosinophils, which tend to cluster together and degranulate externally. Bright red eosinophil granules can be seen lying between cells, on the right-hand side of the second panel.
[5705][Para 002] Although the diagnosis is clear, it is necessary to identify Langerhans’ cells specifically. Macrophages can also look similar. In the past, this was done by using electron microscopy to demonstrate the characteristic Birbeck’s granules in the cell cytoplasm – tennis racket–shaped vesicular organelles. Immunocytochemical staining for the cell surface molecules CD1a and langerin is easier and faster. The third panel shows a low-power view in which a brown stain indicates CD1a on Langerhans’ cells. At high power (in the fourth panel), the stain can be seen to be localized around the cell, forming a dark ring at the cell membrane.

[5715][Para 014] Diagnosis
[5716][Para 001] The diagnosis is Langerhans’ cell histiocytosis.
[5717][Heading 2]  What is a Langerhans’ Cell?
[5718][Para 001] A dendritic cell found in epithelium. These cells develop in bone marrow from the monocyte lineage, migrate to the epithelium of the skin and the mucosa and reside there to present external antigens to the immune system.
[5719][Heading 2]  What is Langerhans’ Cell Histiocytosis?
[5720][Para 001] A clonal proliferation of Langerhans’ cells presenting as a spectrum of disease severity (Table 52.2).
[5721][Para 002] All types have a predilection for the skull and the jaws. Lesions may be painful or asymptomatic and may be accompanied by soft tissue swelling. This patient has multifocal single-organ-system disease because only bone is affected.
[5722][Para 015] Treatment
[5723][Heading 2]  What Treatment Would You Recommend?
[5724][Para 001] A radiographic survey of the skull is required, together with a bone scan or skeletal survey to identify any lesions elsewhere. Medical examination and a detailed history are required in case of soft tissue involvement.
[5725][Para 018] Table 52.2
[5726][Para 021] Langerhans’ Cell Histiocytosis
[5727][Para 002] Lesions in chronic multifocal disease and solitary eosinophilic granulomas usually respond to curettage. This will require removal of the upper right first and second molars to gain access and to ensure complete removal. All involved soft tissue must be excised. There is, however, a risk of oro-antral communication.
[5728][Para 002] The lower right premolar lesion may be curetted without tooth loss, but the surrounding presumed affected soft tissue must be removed and may result in tooth loss. A more conservative approach may be possible if the patient accepts the risk of recurrence. Any recurrence could be recuretted.
[5729][Para 002] The lower left molar lesion could have been caused by periodontitis and requires biopsy for treatment planning.
[5730][Para 002] Long-term follow-up is required. Lesions may recur, and new lesions may develop over a period of many years.
[5731][Para 002] From the medico-legal perspective, this case highlights the particular importance of thorough and systematic radiographic reporting to observe any unusual abnormalities, which should prompt referral for specialist investigation and further management. Fortunately, these types of conditions are rare, but delayed referral may have severe consequences, resulting in significant morbidity or mortality, especially in the case of neoplastic lesions.

[5781][Para 021] Terminology for Extra Teeth
[5782][Heading 2]  What is the Cause of Supernumerary Teeth?
[5783][Para 001] The cause is unknown, but some clues are available. Supernumerary teeth may be caused by mutations in single genes, for instance, the CBFA-1 gene. Mutations of this gene cause cleido-cranial dysplasia, in which the presence of multiple supernumerary teeth is a prominent feature. More is known about congenitally missing teeth, and only a single gene mutation is sufficient to cause teeth to be absent. For instance, mutations in the skeletal patterning gene MSX-1 are associated with missing second premolars and third molars, and mutations in PAX-9 are associated with missing molars and lower incisors. It seems likely that supernumerary teeth in otherwise healthy patients have similar relatively simple genetic causes.
