[5792][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[5793][Heading 2]  What is the Cause of the Patient’s Pain?
[5794][Para 001] Pulpitis. As noted above, the symptoms fit pulpitis. The first permanent molar is the most likely source; it is vital and has extensive caries. Periapical periodontitis can be eliminated as a cause because the pain would be well localized and because there are no nonvital teeth in the quadrant.
[5795][Heading 2]  Give a Differential Diagnosis for the Lesion in the Left Maxilla. Explain Which Cause is Most Likely and Why
[5796][Para 001] The unilocular, dome-shaped lesion with a thin bony margin of expanded periosteal new bone and the overall round shape are highly suggestive of a cyst. The most common cysts in the alveolus and maxilla are odontogenic cysts. There are no radiological features of malignancy.
[5797][Para 020] Dentigerous Cyst
[5798][Para 001] Relatively common and found in children. Dentigerous cysts arise around the crown of an unerupted tooth, and the cyst lining is attached to the tooth at the amelo-cemental junction. This cyst is certainly closely associated with the crown of the unerupted, inverted second premolar, but the radiographic views are not clear enough to see whether the edge of the cyst joins the tooth at the amelo-cemental junction. This information would have led to an almost conclusive diagnosis, but even without this information, a dentigerous cyst is the most likely diagnosis.
[5799][Para 020] Odontogenic Tumour
[5800][Para 001] A less likely possibility. The lesion is not multilocular to suggest ameloblastoma, but in theory, an odontogenic tumour is possible. The odontogenic tumours to consider in children are usually ameloblastic fibroma and ameloblastoma. However, these are solid, are less radiolucent and cause more expansion.
[5801][Para 002] The adenomatoid odontogenic tumour can present as a dentigerous cyst and might be considered if mineralization was detected in the cyst on radiographs. This lesion usually arises on the upper lateral incisors in females but, although unlikely, is a possibility.
[5802][Para 020] Radicular Cyst
[5803][Para 001] The most common odontogenic cyst. However, it would have to arise at the apex of a nonvital tooth. The first molar tooth with caries and all other teeth in the quadrant are vital, excluding this diagnosis. This will only turn out to be the diagnosis if the vitality test result is incorrect.
[5804][Para 218] 
[5805][Para 008] 
[5806][Para 011] Fig. 53.4 The panoramic radiograph with the features outlined.
[5807][Para 009]  
[5808][Para 020] Antral Cyst
[5809][Para 001] These cysts arise in the antral mucous glands (antral inclusion or retention cysts) but would be unlikely to cause such marked expansion. Also, they would not have a bony margin because they arise within the antral mucosa rather than in bone and so do not expand the alveolus as they enlarge.
[5810][Heading 2]  Do You Need To Make a Definitive Diagnosis Before Treatment?
[5811][Para 001] No, a dentigerous cyst is almost certainly the cause. Dentigerous cysts and the alternatives can be treated in the same way. Therefore treatment can be planned on the basis of this provisional diagnosis and the final diagnosis confirmed later.
[5812][Para 015] Treatment
[5813][Heading 2]  What Treatment Would You Recommend for the Pain?
[5814][Para 001] The caries in the first molar should be removed and a temporary sedative dressing placed. The details of the final restoration will depend on the findings after excavation of the caries and the effectiveness of the dressing in reducing pain.
[5815][Heading 2]  What Types of Treatment are Available for Cysts?
[5816][Para 001] Cysts are usually enucleated; that is, the bony cavity is opened, the cyst lining separated from its inner bony surface and removed and the cavity allowed to fill with blood clot and reorganize.
[5817][Para 002] Alternatively, the cyst may be decompressed and marsupialized. Decompression involves opening the cyst to the exterior to relieve the internal pressure. Radicular, dentigerous and many other cyst types enlarge through hydrostatic pressure, and so decompression prevents further enlargement. Marsupialization is the method by which permanent decompression is ensured. The cyst is opened and the lining is sutured to the overlying mucosa to convert the cyst into a pouch communicating with the mouth (or sometimes the nose or the antrum). Without the internal pressure that causes enlargement, the cavity slowly shrinks and reorganizes from its periphery.
[5818][Para 002] Procedures are slightly different for odontogenic keratocysts because of their risk of recurrence. The lining is thin and easily torn on removal, making enucleation difficult. Access to the cavity needs to be good to ensure that all the lining is removed, and the lining is sometimes treated with a fixative – Carnoy’s solution. This can be dabbed onto the lining to make it tougher and also to kill the epithelium so that any small fragments left behind cannot seed recurrences.
[5819][Heading 2]  What are the Advantages and Disadvantages of Decompression and Marsupialization in the Treatment of Cysts?
[5820][Para 032] See Table 53.2.
[5821][Para 002] Because marsupialization has several disadvantages, it is usually used only for a short period for specific reasons. The cyst can be enucleated when it has shrunk to a more manageable size or away from important structures.
[5822][Heading 2]  What Treatment Would You Recommend for This Particular Cyst?
[5823][Para 001] The inverted second premolar cannot erupt and needs to be removed. The cyst extends around the apices of the adjacent teeth, and marsupialization would offer the advantage of preserving their vitality. However, after marsupialization, washing out the cavity regularly would be difficult; therefore in a child, it would be better to perform enucleation and complete the treatment in one episode. If the adjacent teeth were devitalized, they would require root treatment unless orthodontic assessment for the crowding suggests gaining space with extraction. In practice, it may be possible to enucleate without devitalizing the adjacent teeth.
[5824][Para 018] Table 53.2
[5825][Para 021] Advantages and Disadvantages of Surgical Procedures
[5826][Para 002] A further possibility when enucleating a cyst is to break down the bony wall that separates the cyst from the antrum, remove the cyst lining and extract the unerupted tooth. This effectively re-forms the antrum immediately and marsupializes the cyst into the antrum. A nasal antrostomy (opening from the sinus through the lower part of the lateral wall of the nose) would be required to ensure drainage from the sinus until the antral healing is complete.
[5827][Para 002] Whichever procedure is carried out, a sample, preferably all, of the cyst lining should be taken for histological examination to confirm the diagnosis.
[5828][Para 015] Further Investigations
[5829][Heading 2]   Fig. 53.5 Shows the Histological Appearances of the Cyst After Enucleation. What Do You See, and How Do You Interpret the Appearances?
[5830][Para 002] The left figure shows a length of the fibrous cyst wall (W) that is lined on its inner aspect by epithelium of regular thickness (E). In the bottom right corner, there is a focus of inflammation, seen as dark nuclei of inflammatory cells (I) and, above it, a large pink mural nodule of cholesterol clefts in loose tissue (C) protruding into the lumen. The cholesterol elicits a foreign body giant cell reaction, and although they are not clear at this magnification, the very dark angulate areas among the cholesterol crystals are foreign body giant cells. Haemorrhage (H) is present in and around the mural nodule, visible most easily as red cells on the left of the nodule between it and the epithelial lining. The cholesterol is derived from breakdown of cell membranes of erythrocytes and inflammatory cells that die in the cyst. Two less inflamed areas are shown on the right. The rest of the cyst is lined by similar nonkeratinizing epithelium, often very thin and without rete processes.
[5831][Para 218] 
[5832][Para 008] 
[5833][Para 011] Fig. 53.5 Appearances of the cyst lining after removal, sections stained with haematoxylin and eosin. The width of the cyst wall is 1–1.5 mm.
[5834][Para 009]  
[5835][Para 002] Taken together with the radiological features, the appearances indicate a dentigerous cyst. Dentigerous cysts are lined by nonkeratinizing stratified epithelium, although this is not, in itself, a diagnostic feature. In the early stages, the epithelium is characteristically only two cells thick because it is reduced enamel epithelium that has separated from the tooth crown. As the cyst enlarges and impinges on the mucosa or the antrum, it becomes inflamed. The inflammation causes the epithelium to undergo hyperplasia, thicken and develop rete processes. Inflammation causes haemorrhage and release of cholesterol to form crystals in the wall, which ulcerate into the lumen to form the mural nodules. The appearances can then be very like a radicular cyst and the histopathology is not diagnostic. Therefore the main reason for submitting the surgical specimen for examination is to exclude an unexpected diagnosis such as odontogenic keratocyst or ameloblastoma. These alternatives have characteristic histological appearances that are not present here.
[5836][Para 002] The definitive diagnostic criterion is that the epithelial lining and the cyst wall join the unerupted tooth at the amelo-cemental junction. This might be seen only by the surgeon during the surgery.

[5897][Para 015] Treatment
[5898][Heading 2]  Is This Patient Suitable for Treatment in General Practice?
[5899][Para 001] The severity of the complaint and the age of the patient indicate that there is a predisposition to periodontitis, which may progress despite treatment. The initial phases of treatment could be carried out in general dental practice, but some teeth already have a poor prognosis. This is a complex case, and unless you have a special interest or are a specialist in periodontology, the case may be best referred for treatment by a periodontologist.

[5909][Para 030]  What Care Plan Would Be Appropriate?
[5910][Para 001] The prognosis for the three worst affected upper anterior teeth is hopeless because of loss of bony support, drifting and poor appearance. Additionally, if the teeth were to be saved, they would require new crowns. The upper right first molar has furcation involvement and bone loss to the apex and is likely to require either unpredictable complex treatment or extraction. The anterior teeth are symptomless and do not require immediate extraction but should be extracted in the near future to minimize the risk of attachment loss of adjacent teeth and infections/abscesses and to improve appearance. An immediate replacement denture is the treatment of choice because no definitive restorations can be planned until the periodontitis is brought under control and the longer-term prognosis for the other teeth is clear.
[5911][Para 002] In the mandibular arch, the left lateral incisor has bone loss to the apex and probably requires extraction. The long-term prognosis for the lower right canine remains to be determined, but at least initially, it is worth taking a conservative approach and assessing the response to initial nonsurgical periodontal treatment.
[5912][Para 002] The care plan would include:
[5913][Para 004] • patient information and education of the presenting clinical issues and appropriate and achievable goal setting, planning and self-reflection to help the patient manage the situation in the medium to long term
[5914][Para 004] • oral hygiene advice to include instruction in plaque control – tooth brushing and interdental cleaning
[5915][Para 004] • extraction of both upper central incisors, the upper right and lower left lateral incisors and the upper right first molar
[5916][Para 004] • immediate replacement prosthesis
[5917][Para 004] • root surface debridement of all pockets greater than 4 mm under local analgesia, particularly the lower right canine
[5918][Para 004] • periodontal reassessment after 3 months
[5919][Para 004] • regular periodontal maintenance therapy initially on a 3-monthly basis
[5920][Para 004] • continued care of the remaining dentition, including caries prevention
[5921][Para 004] • extraction of further teeth, as required
[5922][Para 004] • assessment for permanent prosthetic replacement.
[5923][Para 002] The details, including the time commitment and cost of treatment, must be discussed with the patient. The patient must be given a written personalized care plan to consider and agree to.
[5924][Para 002] The patient indicates that he would rather attempt to preserve the lower right canine than have it extracted, even though there is no guarantee of success.
[5925][Heading 2]  What are the Options for an Immediate Replacement Prosthesis in the Upper Arch?
[5926][Para 001] Immediate removable acrylic denture using wrought stainless steel clasps for direct retention. The denture must be kept clear of the gingival margins as much as possible so as to not compromise periodontal health. The patient already has inadequate oral hygiene and has never had a denture before. Once the anterior ridge remoulds, the denture will not fit well in this region and chairside relining will be necessary. Acrylic offers the advantage of ability to add further teeth should periodontitis progress.
[5927][Para 002] Immediate minimum-preparation bridge is much more complex, and success is less predictable. The span is long and the occlusion unfavourable.
[5928][Para 002] Implant solutions With ongoing, unstable periodontitis, there is a significant risk of long-term complications such as peri-implantitis resulting in failure. Again, success would be unpredictable with the complex techniques required. There is little residual bone, and implants would require autogenous bone grafts or guided regeneration techniques with membrane placement. Immediate loading implant techniques have a higher risk of aesthetic complications, including recession, and are not recommended.
[5929][Para 024]  What are the Options for an Immediate Replacement Prosthesis in the Lower Arch?
[5930][Para 020] Immediate Removable Acrylic Denture
[5931][Para 001] In the lower arch, this is a less advantageous option. A simple partial denture will be relatively bulky and cannot be designed to avoid the gingival margins. Compared with an upper denture, it would therefore be much more likely to compromise plaque control, and carries the risk of being poorly tolerated.
[5932][Para 020] Immediate Minimum-Preparation Bridge
[5933][Para 001] This could comprise a cantilever pontic retained on the central incisor or the canine. The canine is the obvious choice because of its more favourable crown-to-root ratio, but you will need the maximum wrap-around to maximize retention. The quality of laboratory work will be critical because the restoration cannot be temporized if the fit is not satisfactory; if the immediate replacement does not fit after the extraction, the patient will be left with an unsightly gap. In this immediate option, haemostasis and moisture control will be of critical importance if the adhesion of the immediately placed bridge is to be sufficiently strong. The design of the pontic must be optimized to favour plaque control in view of the patient’s susceptibility to periodontitis. It may, however, be the best option if a replacement is required.
[5934][Para 020] No Replacement
[5935][Para 001] In the short term, it is quite possible that the patient would accept the appearance of the gap. This would be the best option for periodontal treatment, and the situation could be reassessed when the prognosis of the lower teeth becomes clearer.
[5936][Para 002] The patient opts for an upper immediate removable acrylic denture, extraction of the lower left lateral incisor and conservative periodontal treatment for the lower canine. He completes the first eight items of your care plan, and no further extractions are necessary. After 6 months, the patient has responded very well to nonsurgical periodontal treatment. There has been marked gingival shrinkage around the lower canine, there is no bleeding on probing, and the pocket depth is 4 mm. The excellent response to treatment is, of course, largely the result of the effort of your hygienist/hygiene therapist, who has motivated and educated the patient and performed the treatment.

[5943][Para 024]  What are the Options for Definitive Treatment?
[5944][Para 020] A Bridge.
[5945][Para 001] This would be possible, but there are some difficulties. The extensive bone loss from periodontitis has resulted in marked shrinkage of the ridge after extraction. This would require the pontic to be placed more palatally than is ideal; this, in combination with the high lip line and the reduced lip support, could make the appearance of a bridge less than ideal. This problem could be overcome by a removable prosthesis with a labial flange.
[5946][Para 002] The span is long, and one of the abutment teeth is a lateral incisor. It is unrestored, but lateral incisors are never abutments of choice because of their small root, thin coronal dentine and angulation. In addition, as Fig. 54.4 shows, there is bone loss of half the root length. Although this tooth is currently stable, doubts about long-term maintenance persist, and this tooth is not suitable to take the load required of a bridge abutment, even if the adjacent canine were prepared as well. If a bridge were to be provided, it might be wiser to extract the compromised upper left lateral incisor and construct a fixed–fixed bridge by using both canines as abutments. This would allow better control of the appearance. Had the tooth been less compromised, it might have been included in a double abutment with the canine. A bridge would also involve considerable expense, and if a double abutment is used, there is significant risk of failure of the cement lute on the lateral incisor. This would be difficult to diagnose because the bridge would remain stable and would lead to caries. The double abutment bridge design is no longer recommended.

[5956][Para 001] This is probably the best option. It is less expensive than a bridge or implants, much simpler and can be designed to favour oral hygiene procedures and addition of further teeth in the future.
[5957][Para 002] The patient was very happy with the appearance of the acrylic partial denture and found it well retained until recently. However, after discussing the other options, the patient opts for a new cobalt–chromium–based removable prosthesis. An additional factor not visible in the figures is that the lower incisors had overerupted as a result of the drifting of the upper teeth. The occlusion makes the option of a bridge untenable without adjustment of the lower incisors.
[5958][Heading 2]  Who Should Design the Prosthesis – You or the Laboratory? Why?
[5959][Para 001] The design of any denture has to be a team effort between you and the laboratory, with you, as the dentist, taking the final responsibility for the restoration. In an ideal environment, the dentist should have access to a model surveyor and use the skills learnt in dental school to regularly survey and design. However, with increasing emphasis on a team approach, it should be possible to devolve the detailed design to your laboratory technician. At a minimum, you will need to discuss which teeth need to be replaced and identify any teeth with doubtful prognosis.
[5960][Heading 2]  Could You Refer the Patient?
[5961][Para 001] Yes, you could refer the patient to a colleague who is a specialist or to one with specialist interest. Since 2007, the General Dental Council has registered an additional group of dental professionals – clinical dental technicians (CDTs). These professionals, under their scope of practice, can provide partial dentures on prescription from you, the dentist.
[5962][Heading 2]  What are the General Principles To Consider When Designing Any Partial Denture?
[5963][Para 001] See box below.
[5964][Para 211] Determine which teeth are to be replaced, and outline the saddles.
[5965][Para 087] Plan support for the denture. Is the denture going to be tooth supported, tooth and mucosa supported or just mucosa supported?
[5966][Para 087] Plan the path of insertion on a model surveyor, identify guide planes and consider their preparation. Because this patient has lost the anterior teeth and has a high lip line, the anterior acrylic flange has to conform closely with soft tissues, so the model will have a tilt to the posterior teeth on the surveyor table.
[5967][Para 087] Plan direct retention normally provided with clasps. Consider engaging 0.25-mm undercuts with cast cobalt–chromium occlusal approaching clasps and 0.5 mm with gingival approaching clasps.
[5968][Para 087] Is there adequate direct retention or will you have to provide indirect retention?
[5969][Para 087] Consider major and minor connectors. These together with proper base extension will help provide stability against lateral and anteroposterior displacing forces. Advantages of different connectors are given in Table 54.1.
[5970][Para 087] Review design for three aspects: simplicity, biological acceptability and appearance. Is as much gingival tissue as possible left uncovered? Are there unsightly anterior clasps or prominent occlusal rests that are really unnecessary?
[5971][Para 087] What tooth preparation is required? This may include rest seat preparation, ideally modifying the profile of existing restorations on the teeth, adding composite resin, preparing guide planes and altering the height of survey lines to allow correctly constructed clasps.
[5972][Para 080]  The Final Design is Shown in Figs 54.6 and 54.7. What are the Design Features in this Particular Case?
[5973][Para 004] • The path of insertion was determined by the soft tissue profile of the anterior edentulous saddle. When a large labial undercut is present, the model must be tilted down posteriorly during surveying to ensure that the flange fits well and has the best possible appearance.
[5974][Para 004] • Support was derived from rests placed on the upper right canine, second premolar, first molar, left lateral incisor, canine and first molar. This is probably more than necessary, but the design has not become overcomplicated. The rest on the left canine is necessary in case the compromised lateral incisor is extracted in future. Without it, the denture would have no left anterior support after the extraction. This demonstrates the importance of planning for possible failure and also the need for good communication with the laboratory technician. This rest on the canine might not have been included otherwise.
[5975][Para 004] • Direct retention was provided by cast cobalt–chromium occlusally approaching clasps placed on the posterior teeth because of the patient’s high smile line. The clasps face into the main saddle. However, the recurved clasp on the upper right premolar is still visible (see Fig. 54.7). The clasp tips are placed in undercuts relative to the planned path of insertion. There is sufficient direct retention, and so indirect retention is unnecessary.

[5982][Para 004] • The major connector of anterior and posterior palatal bar connectors has at least 5 mm clearance from the gingival margin (Table 54.1). This type of connector does not provide soft tissue support, and so a fully tooth-supported design is necessary. [5984][Para 004] • The pontic design chosen for the upper right molar was a metal sanitary pontic. The tilting of the second molar had reduced the space. Use of a sanitary pontic has avoided placing metal tagging and an acrylic tooth in this periodontally vulnerable interdental area.
[5985][Para 030]  What is Indirect Retention, and Why is None Required for This Denture?
[5986][Para 001] If a partial denture has two clasps, the denture will tend to rotate away from soft tissues about an axis between the two clasps. Indirect retention is provided by a rigid component placed on the teeth opposite the saddle such that the saddle cannot rotate away from the ridge. Indirect retention is usually required for free end saddles (distal extension) and in Kennedy class IV situations, where direct retention from anterior clasps at each end of the saddle would be unsightly. In a single free end saddle situation, the denture will rotate around the distal clasps, and a rest must be placed on a tooth opposite the saddle and as far away from the axis of rotation as possible. In the present case, direct retention from clasps is sufficient.
[5987][Para 014] Medico-Legal Issues
[5988][Para 001] Fortunately, no medico-legal issues were raised in this case. However, what could the patient have been concerned about? The patient could well have questioned why the periodontal disease was not diagnosed more fully and discussed with the previous dentist about better management, not just treated at 6-monthly hygienist visits. Also, although the patient may have been happy at the time of luting of the upper anterior crowns, he might have just accepted the slightly light shade or felt he had to accept that. Issues regarding management of a patient unhappy with care provided by his or her previous dentist is always difficult and often best handled with advice from your defence organization.
[5989][Para 002] The final result in this case was a restoration that the patient was delighted with and one that you should be pleased with. One posterior clasp is visible, but the overall result is excellent. This case effectively illustrates how a relatively simple care plan produces the most predictable result.

[6031][Para 080]  Which of These Possibilities are the Most Likely? Explain Why
[6032][Para 020] Benign salivary gland neoplasm
[6033][Para 001] The site of the swelling is compatible with a palatal salivary gland origin, although it is slightly more anterior than is typical. Salivary glands are more numerous in the posterior hard palate or soft palate, and a swelling level with or behind the molars would be more characteristic of a salivary gland origin. If the lesion is arising in a gland, then a neoplasm is the most likely cause of long-standing painless swelling. About 50% of minor gland neoplasms are benign, and 50% are malignant. The most common single benign tumour, by far, is pleomorphic adenoma, and this is a very likely cause in this case. Pleomorphic adenomas are most common in middle age and old age but have a wide age distribution; however, the young age of the patient need not exclude this possibility.
[6034][Para 002] Malignant salivary gland neoplasms are equally common in minor glands, as noted above. If the tumour is malignant, then mucoepidermoid carcinoma or polymorphous adenocarcinoma would be the most likely causes because they are the most prevalent. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is rarer, but clinically significant possibility because it requires more extensive surgery and carries a poorer prognosis. The lack of ulceration and the patient’s young age point to a benign neoplasm over a malignant one, but a malignant tumour is a definite possibility because most salivary gland malignant neoplasms are of low grade and can have a benign presentation.
[6035][Para 002] Dental causes must be considered because they are very common. The site would be highly typical for an abscess arising from a nonvital lateral incisor or the palatal root of an upper first molar, but there are no symptoms or signs of acute infection. The slow and painless growth might suggest a cyst as a likely cause. However, the swelling appears to arise in the palate rather than the alveolus, which is not expanded. Dental causes seem less likely than salivary gland causes, but because they are common, it would be prudent to exclude them.
[6036][Heading 2]  Which of These Possibilities are Unlikely? Explain Why
[6037][Para 001] A mucous retention cyst is the most likely nonneoplastic, salivary gland–related cause, and the bluish tinge to the lesion suggests a cyst. However, this lump is firm and appears to be of long duration. A mucous retention cyst would be expected to burst or fluctuate in size if present over a long period. This lesion is rather large for a mucocoele on the palate.
[6038][Para 002] Antral or nasal causes must be borne in mind but are also unlikely. Any lesion that had eroded through the palate or sinus wall would be expected to be ulcerated or inflamed.
[6039][Para 015] Investigations
[6040][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Perform?
[6041][Para 001] Tests of vitality of all the teeth in the upper right quadrant are required to exclude the possibility that a nonvital tooth is present and is the cause of an abscess or cyst. Radiographs are required for these and other reasons.

[6054][Heading 2]  Fine-Needle Aspiration of the Lesion Was Performed, and the Appearances of the Aspirate are Shown in Fig. 55.2. What Do You See?
[6055][Para 001] The cells are stained with Papanicolaou stain, which stains nuclei blue and cytoplasm blue-green, or orange if keratinized. Fig. 55.2a shows a sheet of uniform cells with moderate amounts of cytoplasm. Their cytoplasm, polygonal shape and cohesive growth indicate that these are epithelial cells and their uniform nuclei suggest they are benign. The second field, shown in Fig. 55.2b, shows smaller numbers of spindle cells without significant cytoplasm in a myxoid matrix. Taken together, these appearances are characteristic of pleomorphic adenoma.
[6056][Para 014] Diagnosis
[6057][Para 001] The diagnosis is pleomorphic adenoma.
[6058][Para 015] Treatment
[6059][Heading 2]  How Should This Lesion Be Treated?
[6060][Para 001] The appropriate treatment is excision with a small margin, at least a few millimetres. Pleomorphic adenoma is benign, but it is often incompletely encapsulated, and simple enucleation would result in recurrence. The defect could be closed with either a temporary acrylic plate or local surgical flaps, depending on the surgeon’s preference. Radiotherapy is ineffective as a primary treatment and would not be indicated for a benign neoplasm (although it is sometimes used for widespread recurrences of parotid pleomorphic adenomas).
[6061][Heading 2]  Would You Like Further Investigations Before Carrying Out Treatment?
[6062][Para 001] Although the pleomorphic adenoma is benign, it can resorb bone by pressure. Before excising the lesion, it is important to know whether the palate has been perforated because any postsurgical oronasal or oroantral fistula would have to be repaired. This lesion is relatively small, and this step might be omitted, but with a larger tumour, it would be an appropriate reason for carrying out computed tomography (CT) or cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scan.
[6063][Heading 2]  The Histological Appearances of the Excision Specimen are Shown in Fig. 55.3. What Do You See?
[6064][Para 001] Very different appearances are seen in different areas of the tumour (it is pleomorphic). Fig. 55.3a shows sheets of epithelial cells in which there are small ducts containing eosinophilic material (E). At the edges of the sheets, cells separate and progressively merge with more dispersed cells in a myxoid stroma (M). These sheets and dispersed cells are the same cell types as those seen in the smear made from the fine-needle aspirate shown in Fig. 55.2. Here, they are seen in section, in their correct relationship to each other, whereas the smear is of whole cells spread onto a glass slide, hence their different morphology.
[6065][Para 002] Fig. 55.3b shows numerous small duct-like clusters of cells (D) separated by a hyaline fibrous stroma (F). Many of the ducts have a bilayered structure with a partial outer layer of cells with clear cytoplasm.
[6066][Para 002] Other fields show incomplete encapsulation but a well-demarcated periphery. These features are typical and diagnostic of pleomorphic adenoma. If the lesion appears excised histologically, cure can be expected.
[6067][Para 015] Prognosis
[6068][Heading 2]  Are There Any Significant Complications of Pleomorphic Adenoma? Are You Concerned for This Patient?
[6069][Para 001] Yes, carcinoma may arise in a long-standing pleomorphic adenoma, and carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma carries a very poor prognosis. However, this process takes many years, usually 10 or more, and is therefore seen mostly in older patients. This is an unlikely risk in this young patient with a short history, and complete removal will prevent this complication. There was nothing in the history or the clinical examination to suggest malignancy, and fine-needle aspiration or biopsy followed by examination of the excised specimen has excluded it.

[6075][Heading 1] Rapid Breakdown of First Permanent Molars (Molar–Incisor Hypomineralization)
[6076][Para 027] Mike Harrison
[6077][Para 028] Summary
[6078][Para 029] A 7-year-old boy presents with his first permanent molar teeth which, according to his parents, have decayed rapidly, starting immediately on eruption. Identify the cause, and discuss the treatment options.
[6079][Para 218]

[6085][Para 007] The child complains of pain from his back teeth on both sides. The pain is worse with sweet foods and cold liquids and persists for several minutes after the stimuli are applied. Toothbrushing with cold water is also painful, but the teeth do not cause pain on biting.

[6087][Para 007] The pain has been present for a few months and has increased in severity over the last month. The child now reports that one of his back teeth feels broken. The first permanent molars erupted on time, and the child’s mother noticed that some of them appeared to crumble as soon as they emerged through the gum. She has read in magazines that fluoride can damage teeth and has switched to a toothpaste without fluoride on the assumption that this is the cause.

Toothbrushing has been performed with adult-formula fluoride-containing toothpaste, starting at approximately 1 year and continuing until 7 years of age.

[6093][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[6094][Para 007] The child has no facial swelling or asymmetry, and no lymph nodes are palpable.
[6095][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[6096][Para 007] The child is in the early mixed dentition stage. All four first permanent molars have areas of brown, rough, irregular enamel. Severity varies among teeth, and the worst affected are the maxillary molars, with enamel appearing to be completely absent in some areas. These teeth have soft dentine exposed occlusally. The lower right first permanent molar is the least affected, with only a small localized brown enamel defect on the buccal aspect. This is hard on probing. In addition, there are areas of white enamel opacity in the incisal third of the labial surface of all permanent central and lateral incisors, and the white enamel opacity is most pronounced in the maxillary central incisors. The remaining primary dentition is caries-free and appears normal in structure and morphology. Oral hygiene appears to be good. The clinical appearance of the dentition at presentation is shown in Figs 56.1 and 56.2.
[6097][Heading 2]  On the Basis of What You Know Already, What Do You Suspect?
[6098][Para 001] The enamel defects appear to be hypomineralization of the incisors and hypoplasia of the molars. The discrete areas of white enamel opacity on the central incisors are characteristic of enamel hypomineralization, where the contour of the surface is intact and the enamel is of normal thickness. The molars are so severely affected that diagnosis is difficult, and this is consistent with either hypoplasia – where contour is abnormal, leaving it vulnerable to extrinsic staining and caries – or hypomineralization, which has undergone posteruptive breakdown.
[6099][Para 218] 
[6100][Para 008] 
[6101][Para 011] Fig. 56.2 Labial view of the central incisors in occlusion, on presentation.
[6102][Para 009]  
[6103][Heading 2]  Do the Enamel Defects Follow a Chronological Pattern, and if So, At What Time Was the Affected Enamel Formed?
[6104][Para 001] The incisal and occlusal parts of the permanent central incisors and first molars form almost at the same time, starting to mineralize just before birth. The affected enamel would have been formed after birth and during the first 1–2 years of life. This can be seen in Fig. 56.3.
[6105][Para 002] This distribution of enamel defects is often referred to as molar-incisor hypomineralisation (MIH). There is some evidence that the occurrence of MIH is not completely chronological. The occlusal and buccal surfaces tend to be the worst affected. Canines and premolars are unaffected despite mineralizing at the same time. Defects may be asymmetrical, and enamel loss by post-eruptive breakdown occurs most commonly on affected molars.
[6106][Heading 2]  What Additional Questions Would You Ask, and Why?
[6107][Para 001] A chronological pattern suggests systemic illness, which may be identifiable in the history. Defining a possible cause may allow other causes, such as fluorosis, to be excluded. You need to ask for further details about the prenatal and perinatal medical history.
[6108][Para 002] The following conditions may be relevant, and information on them should be specifically sought:
[6109][Para 004] • Significant maternal illness
[6110][Para 004] • Preterm birth
[6111][Para 004] • Frequent febrile illness in infancy
[6112][Para 002] These disturbances may manifest as enamel defects distributed along the enamel formed around birth. You should also enquire about all severe systemic disturbances in the first 2 years of life, for example, meningitis, encephalitis, severe measles or pneumonia. Even relatively minor fevers or infections such as ear infections are known to be associated with similar enamel defects if frequent during infancy. There is very little evidence to support medicines being the cause. Fluoride can only cause enamel defects if consumption in infancy is known to be excessive and prolonged.
[6113][Para 218] 
[6114][Para 008] 
[6115][Para 011] Fig. 56.3 Time of mineralization of the permanent dentition.
[6116][Para 009]  
[6117][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[6118][Heading 2]  What is the Likely Cause of the Child’s Pain?
[6119][Para 001] Sensitivity to hot and cold is characteristic of pain mediated by a vital pulp. It could be a result of exposed or more porous dentine or of caries deep in the defects. MIH is frequently associated with pain and sensitivity, and the pulp tissues in severely affected teeth may have chronic low-grade inflammation.
[6120][Heading 2]  What is Your Initial Differential Diagnosis for the Enamel Defects?
[6121][Para 001] Dental caries is the most common cause of destruction of first permanent molars and should be considered, even though the appearances would be very unusual. The combination of enamel defects on the permanent molars and incisors suggests a working diagnosis of MIH, presuming that the molars had a normal surface contour before eruption but underwent significant posteruptive breakdown (PEB) in the parts where the enamel was very hypomineralized.
[6122][Para 002] Enamel hypoplasia is less likely but should be considered. Developmental, acquired, generalized and localized forms are recognized. Other causes that might be considered are amelogenesis imperfecta, cytotoxic chemotherapy for malignant disease, significant renal disease in infancy or, rarely, fluorosis. In many cases, no cause is found, and the term idiopathic enamel hypoplasia is used.
[6123][Heading 2]  Justify This Differential Diagnosis
[6124][Para 001] Dental caries is the most common cause of destruction of the dental hard tissues. Newly erupted teeth are particularly prone to dental caries until their enamel maturation is completed in the oral environment. The permanent first molars are also prone to early caries because of their deep fissures. However, the possibility of caries seems unlikely. Although there is no guarantee that the diet history elicited is truly representative of the child’s actual diet, there are no restorations or caries in the deciduous dentition. The molars have discoloured or absent enamel over a wide area. This is not typical of dental caries unless carbohydrate intake is excessive or the patient’s teeth have some other predisposing factor such as enamel hypoplasia. The soft dentine indicates that some caries is present, but the pattern of destruction suggests that the caries is secondary. The zones of opacity on the incisors look like early ‘white spot’ demineralization but are present at a site that is almost never affected by caries.
[6125][Para 002] Neonatal jaundice is a very common condition and, in almost all cases, can be excluded as a cause of enamel hypoplasia. In this child, the position of the enamel defects is inconsistent with a short period of jaundice at birth.
[6126][Para 002] Fluorosis is a common cause of enamel opacities and enamel hypoplasia in areas where it is endemic. The deciduous dentition is usually only mildly affected. The level of fluoride required to cause enamel defects depends on concentration, period and age at ingestion.
[6127][Para 002] Fluorosis is almost certainly not the cause of the current problem. The defects in the molars would result from only very high fluoride concentrations, in excess of 25 parts per million (ppm). Such levels do not occur in the UK. In addition, fluorosis of this severity is found only in endemic areas and should not follow a chronological pattern.
[6128][Para 002] Mild fluorosis may be seen as a result of supplementation, and this is presumably what the parent has read. In such cases, there are usually fine opaque white lines following the perikymata and small irregular enamel opacities or flecks with or without staining. Such mild defects are also common in normal teeth and increase in frequency when the fluoride level is lower than 0.7 ppm. Although the severity of the defects and the distribution are incompatible with the diagnosis of fluorosis, it needs to be considered because the child has been using adult-formula fluoride-containing toothpaste from an early age. Ingestion of adult-formula fluoride toothpaste would be the most likely cause of mild fluorosis in those living in the UK.
[6129][Para 002] Amelogenesis imperfecta must be considered, even though it is rare. Amelogenesis imperfecta can cause enamel hypoplasia, hypocalcification or hypomaturation and either of the first two conditions could lead to the appearances seen in the molar teeth in this case. However, several factors indicate that this is not amelogenesis imperfecta. There appears to be no family history, the pattern appears chronological rather than affecting all surfaces of all teeth equally and the deciduous dentition is unaffected. Although these features are not conclusive because of the wide range of clinical presentations seen in the many different types of this disease, they do make the diagnosis most unlikely.
[6130][Para 002] Idiopathic molar–incisor hypomineralization is a convenient term used to describe cases of enamel defects with this distribution for which no cause can be ascertained.
[6131][Para 015] Investigations
[6132][Heading 2]  What Investigations are Indicated, and Why?
[6133][Para 001] Intraoral radiographs are indicated to assess the proximity of the coronal defects to the dental pulp. A dental panoramic tomograph (DPT) is indicated to ascertain the presence and stage of development of the remaining permanent dentition in view of the possibly poor long-term prognosis of some of the first permanent molars. This patient’s DPT is shown in Fig. 56.4.
[6134][Para 002] If there were extensive softening of the occlusal dentine of the molars or if radiographs indicated deep caries, pulp sensibility tests would be required.
[6135][Heading 2]  What Does the Dental Panoramic Tomograph Show?
[6136][Para 001] All permanent teeth, with the exception of the third permanent molars, are present, and the patient’s dental age is consistent with his chronological age. The gross structural defect in the first permanent molars is reflected in their radiographic appearance. The worst affected teeth – the maxillary molars – have irregular enamel outlines, and there is reactionary dentine in the distal pulp horns. The view is unsuitable for detailed examination of the teeth, but no large carious lesions are evident, and the unerupted permanent second molars appear to be of normal shape and to have a normal enamel structure.

[6141][Para 015] Diagnosis
[6142][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[6143][Para 001] The patient has enamel defects that do not follow a perfect chronological pattern. In the absence of a known insult to account for the defects, idiopathic MIH is the most appropriate working diagnosis. The diagnosis may need to be reviewed if more teeth erupt with similar defects. The diagnosis is sufficiently accurate to help determine the management options.
[6144][Para 015] Treatment
[6145][Heading 2]  What Treatment Options are Available for the Molars?
[6146][Para 001] Extraction is considered an appropriate treatment for the permanent first molar with a poor long-term prognosis, particularly when, as here, caries is also present. Preservation of these molars through adulthood would require provision of full-coverage crowns. These have a finite lifespan, and their intermittent replacement; the risks of undetected leakage, caries and pulpal involvement; localized periodontitis; and the expense and inconvenience would all cause significant difficulties during the lifetime of the patient.
[6147][Heading 2]  When Should the Molar Teeth Be Extracted?
[6148][Para 001] Timing of the extractions is important, and several factors must be taken into consideration, as shown in Table 56.1.
[6149][Heading 2]  How Can the Molars Be Preserved Until the Patient is At the Optimal Age for Their Extraction?
[6150][Para 001] Preformed stainless steel crowns offer durable, cheap and relatively simple restoration. Laboratory made nickel–chrome onlays have been advocated as a less destructive option, should it be decided that the teeth are to be retained for full coronal coverage restorations later in life. A preventive resin restoration can be provided for the less severely affected molar in the lower right quadrant.

[6158][Heading 2]  What Advice Would You Give the Mother With Regard To Fluoride Use?
[6159][Para 001] The misconception about fluorosis should be dispelled: fluorosis can only develop while teeth are forming. Provided the child can rinse and spit out effectively, it would be appropriate for him to use an adult-formula fluoride toothpaste. This would provide a significant benefit in preventing caries (and the mother would also gain from using it). No fluoride supplement is indicated for this child, who, at least on the basis of a preliminary analysis, eats little sugar and has no caries. There might be a particular advantage in using a fluoride mouthwash during adolescence and early adulthood when a person’s diet often changes markedly.
[6160][Para 015] Prognosis
[6161][Heading 2]  What is the Long-Term Prognosis of Molars with Enamel Hypomineralization Defects?
[6162][Para 001] You need to form an opinion on the likely natural history of each tooth with enamel mineralization defects. Can the affected molars be successfully restored with simple direct resin composite restorations? This is determined by the extent and location of the defect and by the degree of hypomineralization and PEB. Occlusal surfaces with defects surrounded by normally mineralized cusps can usually be restored successfully with resin composite restorations. Defects that involve cusps or that extend over to the vertical walls of the crown can be very difficult to treat with adhesive materials.
[6163][Para 002] If extraction has been considered as an option but maintaining the tooth is still desired, some aspects of future restorative care need to be discussed with the child’s parents:
[6164][Para 004] • At what age could a definitive full-coronal restoration be provided? Age greater than 18 years, at skeletal and gingival maturity.
[6165][Para 004] • What material should be used? Gold or porcelain.
[6166][Para 004] • How long would you expect this restoration to last before it needs replacement? A predicted replacement cycle of 15–20 years is reasonable for a full-coronal-coverage restoration if good patient maintenance is achieved
[6167][Para 004] • How would it be most likely to fail, and what would be the clinical consequences? Failure by cement leakage may lead to pulp pathology, requiring endodontic treatment.
[6168][Para 002] It is advisable to document these discussions so that you can demonstrate that the decision to keep a molar of dubious long-term prognosis was a shared one and that the patient and his carers were fully informed.

[6175][Para 029] A 72-year-old man with squamous cell carcinoma is referred to your cancer treatment centre. How should he be managed?

[6183][Para 012] History of Complaint
[6184][Para 007] The patient first noticed his symptoms 6 weeks ago and has sought treatment because of the earache. He had noticed a ‘crack’ in his tongue that has not healed for some time, but this has always been painless.
[6185][Para 012] Medical History
[6186][Para 007] He had a small myocardial infarction 7 years ago and has mild hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine and aspirin. He has smoked 20 or more cigarettes a day for the last 55 years and drinks a quarter bottle of whisky per day.

[6188][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[6189][Para 007] The examination of the neck is normal, apart from a possible mass just below the right angle of the jaw. It is difficult to ascertain whether or not the mass is hard. It is deeply situated and approximately 15 mm in diameter.
[6190][Para 049] Intraoral Examination
[6191][Heading 2]  The Appearance of the Tongue is Shown in Fig. 57.1. What Do You See?
[6192][Para 001] There is a large fungating ulcer arising on the right lateral border of the tongue. It is approximately 30 mm in size and has raised everted borders. Towards the dorsal surface, the mucosa bulges, as if there is a mass beneath the intact epithelium, and there is a white patch affecting the mucosa just dorsal to the ulcer margin.
[6193][Para 017] If you could palpate this ulcer, you would find that it is indurated (firm or hard on palpation) and extends down towards the floor of the mouth and up beneath the dorsal mucosa towards the midline. The lesion is clearly much larger than it looks. The patient has reduced tongue mobility.
[6194][Para 014] Diagnosis
[6195][Para 001] In this case, the diagnosis has already been made at the referring hospital. The patient has squamous cell carcinoma, and the appearance and presentation are typical. The patient knows the diagnosis.
[6196][Heading 2]  Why Might the Patient Have Earache?
[6197][Para 001] Ear pain is thought to result from malignant infiltration (or other damage) of nerves that pass through or supply the ear on their way to the periphery. Thus in the tongue or pharynx, pain may be generated as a result of involvement of the lingual nerve, which contains fibres from the chorda tympani from the ear, and of the auriculo-temporal nerve (branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve), which also supplies the external auditory meatus. Similar referred pain may result from involvement of the glossopharyngeal nerve.
[6198][Para 018] Table 57.1
[6199][Para 040] TNM (Tumour–Node–Metastasis) Classification of Oral Cancer
[6200][Para 044] 
[6201][Para 015] Principles of Treatment
[6202][Heading 2]  What are the Principles of Treatment for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma?
[6203][Para 001] Patients with oral carcinoma often present too late for cure, and some may not benefit from treatment. Three treatment options are possible:
[6204][Para 016] 1. Attempted cure
[6205][Para 016] 2. Active palliative care
[6206][Para 016] 3. Supportive care only, until death occurs.
[6207][Para 002] If cure is attempted, the highest chances of success are given by multimodality treatment – a combination of surgery, radiotherapy and, more rarely, chemotherapy. In oral squamous cell carcinoma, chemotherapy is always given in combination with radiotherapy. The most aggressive treatment that the patient is able to withstand will be recommended because, if the first round of treatment fails, the chances of survival are much reduced.
[6208][Para 015] Further Investigations
[6209][Heading 2]  How Might You Predict the Chances of Successful Treatment?
[6210][Para 001] By using staging and grading. The chances of successful treatment depend on how large the carcinoma has grown and whether it has already spread to other sites in the body. Staging is a standardized method for assessing these parameters and is used to predict survival and also to plan treatment. Accurate staging is therefore essential.
[6211][Para 002] Oral cancers are staged by determining the tumour size and depth of invasion (T), the lymph node status (N) and the presence of distant metastasis (M) (Table 57.1). These parameters are then combined to determine the stage (Table 57.2). Survival decreases with increasing stage. In determining stage and therefore survival, the tumour size and depth of invasion, whether there is spread of the cancer beyond the lymph node in cervical metastasis, and whether there is distant metastasis are important factors to consider.
[6212][Para 018] Table 57.2
[6213][Para 021] Staging of Oral Cancer
[6214][Para 002] Staging depends on the fact that carcinomas tend to progress in a predictable way. First, tumours enlarge by invading the surrounding tissues and then the cells break away and travel via the lymphatics to seed metastases in lymph nodes. Blood-borne metastases to distant sites develop last. Although the sequence is usually predictable, the speed at which any individual carcinoma progresses through these stages varies widely.
[6215][Para 218] 
[6216][Para 008] 
[6217][Para 011] Fig. 57.2 Survival curves for oral carcinoma. The left graph shows survival for oral carcinoma of all sites by TNM (tumour–node–metastasis) stage. The right hand graph shows survival for patients with and without metastasis to cervical lymph nodes.
[6218][Para 009]  
[6219][Para 002] Grading is a histological method to determine how aggressive the carcinoma is and how quickly it is likely to progress (or may already have progressed) from stage to stage. It is a measure of how differentiated the carcinomatous epithelium is – that is, how much it resembles its tissue of origin. Well-differentiated carcinomas grow in tissues as large islands and form keratin. They usually grow slowly and metastasize late. Poorly differentiated carcinomas have more cytological pleomorphism, no keratin and invade more aggressively as small clusters of cells or even as single cells. They are more likely to produce metastases early in their course.
[6220][Para 002] Staging is more important than grading because the size and extent of the tumour determine whether surgery is possible. Grading is useful in deciding which treatments are appropriate and how radical they should be.
[6221][Heading 2]  How Will You Determine the Disease Stage?
[6222][Para 001] Size (T) can be determined through clinical examination. This is not very accurate and, if the carcinoma is posteriorly placed, may require examination under general anaesthesia. Radiographs must be taken to assess the involvement of bone, because bone invasion automatically indicates a T4 size. Imaging provides a more accurate estimate of size and extent compared with clinical examination.
[6223][Para 002] Presence of lymph node metastasis (N) can be determined through clinical examination. Large, hard, fixed nodes will be obvious, but lymph nodes nonspecifically enlarged as a result of ulceration or infection may also be present. Enlarged lymph nodes may require fine-needle aspiration under ultrasound guidance to confirm whether or not carcinoma is present. Imaging is very useful to detect small lymph node metastases and those in deeply sited nodes. The patient should undergo computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or positron emission tomography with computed tomography (PET/CT) to detect the involved lymph nodes. Which is used will depend on local circumstances.
[6224][Para 002] Distant metastases (M) should be determined through clinical examination and imaging. The imaging modalities noted above may all be used.
[6225][Para 017] After staging investigations, this patient’s carcinoma is staged as T3, N1, M0, making it a stage III lesion. Fine-needle aspiration of the palpable submandibular lymph nodes shows metastatic carcinoma cells. Imaging shows no obvious metastatic spread beyond the submandibular lymph node, and there are no other enlarged lymph nodes. CT scans of the chest and abdomen rule out distant metastasis, and liver function test results are consistent with the patient’s alcohol intake. An anaesthetist declares the patient fit for the long general anaesthesia that would be required for surgery. The patient could opt for any of the treatments recommended.
[6226][Heading 2]  What are the Chances of Cure?
[6227][Para 001] In general, the 5-year survival rate for oral carcinoma is poor. The reason is the late presentation, leading to large carcinomas on presentation, often with extensive lymph node involvement and distant metastases. In addition, many patients are medically compromised by a lifetime of heavy smoking and excessive alcohol intake or are too old or infirm to be able to tolerate aggressive treatment.
[6228][Para 002] The survival rates for oral carcinoma of all sites are shown in Fig. 57.2. These are Kaplan–Meier survival curves; each step in the line represents one or more members of the study population dying of carcinoma at the time indicated on the x axis. The graphs show the disease-specific survival, on the left broken down by stage and on the right broken down by presence of lymph node metastases. Note how important metastasis is in determining survival.
[6229][Para 002] In practice, some patients die sooner than this, but of other illnesses that are often smoking induced. The proportion of patients predicted to survive 5 years after diagnosis of tongue carcinoma is 75% for stage 1, 60% for stage 2, 45% for stage 3 and only 25% for stage 4. Thus this patient has only a 55% chance of surviving 5 years.
[6230][Para 015] Treatment Planning
[6231][Heading 2]  What Factors Determine the Appropriate Treatment?
[6232][Para 001] Choosing the appropriate treatment is sometimes difficult, and many factors need to be taken into consideration.
[6233][Para 018] Table 57.3
[6234][Para 021] Advantages and Disadvantages of Treatment Modalities
[6235][Para 004] • The patient’s wishes. The patient must decide whether he or she wishes to undergo treatment and which treatment modality is preferred.
[6236][Para 004] • Medical history. Major head-and-neck surgery carries a risk of perioperative death of approximately 2–3%. Many patients have coexisting diseases secondary to smoking and drinking alcohol – emphysema, chronic bronchitis, angina, cirrhosis of the liver and a history of myocardial infarction are not unusual. However, untreated oral carcinoma will be fatal, and many patients are prepared to accept the risks associated with general anaesthesia and surgery.
[6237][Para 004] • Extent of carcinoma. The primary lesion may be unresectable because of extension to the base of skull, infratemporal fossa, cavernous sinus or across the midline in the pharynx. Metastatic disease in the neck may be unresectable if the carcinoma has invaded beyond the lymph node to involve vital structures such as the carotid arteries. Even if the cancer is theoretically resectable, it may be difficult or impossible to reconstruct the resulting defect.
[6238][Para 004] • Surgery causes cosmetic and functional defects that may not be acceptable to the patient. Resection of the tongue base causes complete loss of ability to swallow and predisposes the patient to aspiration of food. Carcinoma in the maxilla may require removal of the eye, and speech is lost after laryngectomy.
[6239][Para 004] • Home circumstances. After surgery and during radiotherapy, patients need good support at home. Family, nursing, or social services may provide this. Alternatively, some patients may need to be admitted for a longer period or move to a nursing home.
[6240][Para 004] • Availability of treatment. May also need to be considered. In the UK, expertise in surgery and radiotherapy is available throughout the country, but brachytherapy is not offered in all centres. In some developing countries, radiotherapy is the primary treatment modality.
[6241][Para 030]  How is the Ideal Treatment Determined?
[6242][Para 001] In the UK, the patient should be under the care of a multidisciplinary team, which usually includes a surgeon, a radiotherapist, a medical oncologist, a pathologist, specialist nurses, a speech therapist, a dietitian, a dentist and a hygienist. Each patient should have an individual treatment plan formulated at a multidisciplinary team meeting, during which all the relevant information is presented. Treatment options are recommended on the basis of evidence-based protocols, but the final choice rests with the patient.
[6243][Heading 2]  What are the Roles of Surgery and Radiotherapy?
[6244][Para 001] The aim of surgery is to excise the carcinoma, with the largest possible margin. At other body sites, it is usual to attempt to excise a malignant neoplasm by about 3 cm. This is rarely possible in the head and neck region, and margins of only a few millimetres are usual if the lesion is large. Larger margins may be possible, but only at the cost of reduced function and deformity. The head and neck region contains many important structures, and although many can be sacrificed and/or reconstructed, the resulting quality of life may be unacceptable. In some cases, surgery is palliative, designed to remove the bulk of the lesion to reduce the symptoms arising from it.
[6245][Para 002] Radiotherapy may be undertaken as the primary treatment, as an adjunct to surgery or as a palliative measure. Radiation causes cell death through deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) damage, to which malignant cells are more susceptible compared with normal cells. Cells are most susceptible when they are dividing, and so carcinomas with high rates of cell division, usually the poorly differentiated ones, are most susceptible. The radiation dose is measured in Grays (Gy), and the maximum dose is usually 60–70 Gy given over a 6-week period. Radiotherapy has adverse effects. It causes significantly unpleasant symptoms and therefore should not be seen as a soft option in comparison with surgery.
[6246][Para 002] Chemotherapy may be offered in conjunction with radiotherapy to patients who are relatively fit and have large or late-stage disease. In suitable cases, this may improve 5-year survival by about 10%.
[6247][Para 002] The advantages and disadvantages of surgery and radiotherapy have been described in Table 57.3. However, it must be kept in mind that many patients will undergo both treatments.
[6248][Para 018] Table 57.4
[6249][Para 021] Choice of Surgery and Radiotherapy
[6250][Para 002] Factors affecting the choice of surgery and radiotherapy are shown in Table 57.4.
[6251][Para 014] Treatment
[6252][Para 007] The recommended treatment for this case was excision of the carcinoma at the primary site and a prophylactic neck dissection en bloc (in one continuous specimen). Postoperative (adjuvant) radiotherapy is planned. The defect in the mouth will be reconstructed with a radial forearm flap. The patient opted for this treatment strategy and made a good recovery after surgery.
[6253][10 Block] 
[6254][Heading 2]  What Tissues are Removed in a Block Dissection of the Neck? Why?
[6255][Para 001] In the classic radical neck dissection, the following are removed: the entire sternomastoid muscle, internal and external jugular veins and the contents of the submandibular and submental triangles, including the submandibular gland and all the lymph nodes along the internal jugular vein from the base of the skull to the clavicle. Removing all these tissues in one block ensures complete removal of the carcinoma because the lymph nodes are removed with the surrounding fat or other tissues.
[6256][Para 218] 
[6257][Para 008] 
[6258][Para 011] Fig. 57.3 The pathology specimen, macroscopic views.
[6259][Para 009]  
[6260][Para 008] 
[6261][Para 011] Fig. 57.4 The pathology specimen, microscopic views.
[6262][Para 009]  
[6263][Para 002] Excision of the sternomastoid muscle sacrifices the spinal accessory nerve, which passes through it. This causes postoperative drooping of the shoulder because it supplies the trapezius as well as the sternomastoid muscles. Therefore in most cases where there is no extensive or bulky disease in the neck, either a part or all of the sternomastoid muscle and the internal jugular vein may be left in situ.

At the top is the hemiglossectomy (HG) section, and below it are the contents of the submandibular triangle (SMT) and submental tissue (SM). The sternomastoid muscle has been preserved, and the fat surrounding the jugular vein and cervical lymph nodes is on the left (F). The omohyoid muscle extends across the back of the specimen (O). Luckily, in this case, carcinoma extends upwards and medially rather than down into the floor of the mouth, where excision would have been more difficult.
[6267][Heading 2]  The Microscopic Appearances are Shown in Fig. 57.4. What Do You See?
[6268][Para 001] On the left, at medium power, is typical squamous cell carcinoma, comprising islands of epithelium invading around and between muscle fibres. The carcinoma is forming keratin and, in this area, is well or moderately well differentiated. The next panel shows a more poorly differentiated area at high power. Pleomorphic cells with irregular nuclei (anisonucleosis) and darkly staining nuclei (hyperchromatism) are infiltrating along a pink muscle fibre running from top left to bottom right (MF). There is invasion as single cells (S). The third panel, at high power, shows a small vein (V) filled by carcinoma, and the inset shows a cluster of carcinoma cells in a lymphatic vessel. Invasion as single cells and lymphatic and vascular permeation are poor prognostic factors and indicate a high risk of metastasis. Two of the lymph nodes from the neck dissection are shown on the right with a scale in millimetres. Metastases (MT) are seen as round pink areas because of the keratin in them. There is a compressed rim of residual blue lymph node tissue at the periphery (L).
[6269][Para 017] The surgical result was reviewed at a meeting of the multidisciplinary team. The closest margin of excision was 5 mm. Metastatic carcinoma was present in two of the 28 lymph nodes found in the neck dissection, but there was no extranodal extension. The patient is doing well postoperatively.
[6270][Heading 2]  Are These Excision Margins Adequate?
[6271][Para 001] A margin of 10 mm of normal tissue would be ideal, but in many cases, the excision margins are only a few millimetres. If no radiotherapy had been planned, a margin less than 5 mm would be an indication for postoperative radiotherapy, and the treatment plan would be changed. This patient has poorly differentiated carcinoma, intravascular spread and metastases. Postoperative radiotherapy can compensate for close or incomplete excision, and so a full course of postoperative radiotherapy to the primary site and neck is recommended.
[6272][Heading 2]  What is the Procedure for Radiotherapy?
[6273][Para 001] Radiotherapy must start within 6 weeks of surgery for the best results. Once the patient has recovered from surgery and the swelling has settled, the preparation for radiotherapy can begin. The radiation will be given in many small doses or fractions to reduce side effects. To ensure that the patient is positioned reproducibly in the x-ray beams, a close fitting acrylic mask, including alignment markers, is made for the patient’s face, on a model cast from an impression.
[6274][Para 002] The radiotherapy treatment plan is made on a computer, with calculation of the doses absorbed by the tissues in and around the tumour site. Radiation is delivered by one or more beams of radiation, and metal wedges shield sensitive tissues such as the eyes. In the UK, radiation is usually given at a rate of one fraction per weekday. Recently, hyperfractionation protocols (two fractions per day) have been shown to be equally effective and have fewer side effects. This patient will receive 66 Gy over 6.5 weeks.
[6275][Heading 2]  After Completing Treatment, What Follow-Up is Required, and Why?
[6276][Para 001] The patient must be monitored regularly for many years. The greatest risk of recurrence is in the first 3 years, and initially, he will be seen every few weeks for a year, gradually extending the review periods to a few months. It must be remembered that in all patients with oral carcinoma, in addition to the risk for recurrence and metastasis, there is a 1-in-10 risk of development of a second primary carcinoma somewhere in the upper aerodigestive tract.
[6277][Heading 2]  What is the Role of the Dentist in the Care of These Patients?
[6278][Para 001] The dentist in the hospital cancer team will have examined the patient at diagnosis and arranged for extraction of teeth of poor prognosis and for treatment of caries. Teeth in the radiotherapy field used to be routinely extracted. They are now often conserved because advances in radiotherapy have reduced the risk of osteoradionecrosis and because teeth are often restorable with the use of modern techniques. There may also be a need for an obturator or facial prosthesis postoperatively. Ideally, the dentist in the cancer team would continue to care for the patient for a period after treatment.
[6279][Para 002] General dental practitioners will care for patients in the longer term; they need to provide advice on intensive preventive measures, ensure oral health, and prevent infection, particularly around teeth in irradiated bone. There is a need for continued surveillance of the mucosa for recurrence and new lesions and also a need to provide reassurance and support for patients and carers. Support for smoking cessation is important. See also Case 67.
[6280][Heading 2]  After 21 Months, a Recurrence Develops in the Mouth. What Can Be Done?
[6281][Para 001] If the recurrence is small and accessible, it can be resected. It may be possible to provide radiotherapy, but only if the site has not already been given a full course of radiation.
[6282][Para 002] If no curative treatment can be provided, the patient will require palliative care. Palliative care is the control of symptoms, allowing the patient to end his or her life with dignity. The patient may be cared for at home by family, and community specialist nurses and the local hospice may coordinate treatment and organize short admissions to give some respite to carers. Pain is controlled with strong analgesics, such as morphine, and if the carcinoma fungates and starts to smell, it may be dressed with topical metronidazole. Low-dose palliative radiotherapy or chemotherapy may be possible. The hospice and community palliative care services help the patient with spiritual and physical needs, as well as providing advice on putting affairs in order.
[6283][Heading 2]  Why is There Such an Emphasis On Early Detection of Oral Cancer?
[6284][Para 001] Oral cancer, like many cancers, is potentially curable if diagnosed early. However, a missed or delayed diagnosis potentially condemns the patient to death. It is therefore imperative that at every dental examination, the mouth is examined thoroughly to ensure there are no lesions of concern. Should such lesions be identified, early and rapid referral should be made by using rapid access schemes, according to local and national protocols. It is also important that general dental practitioners keep themselves up to date regarding knowledge of potentially malignant lesions, which are much more common. Delayed diagnosis is bad for the patient and also for the dentist. Litigation is increasingly becoming a feature of dental practice, and a late or delayed diagnosis could trigger a report to the General Dental Council as well as a legal challenge.
[6285][Para 025] Case 58
[6286][Heading 1] A Complicated Extraction
[6287][Para 027] Chris Dickinson
[6288][Para 028] Summary
[6289][Para 029] A 35-year-old man attends your general dental practice surgery requesting extraction of a tooth.
[6290][Para 218]

[6307][Para 024]  What Do You See in the Patient’s Mouth?
[6308][Para 004] • The palate appears bruised with two purple-coloured lesions, one on each side of the palate extending from the gingival margin up the sides of the vault. Neither lesion appears to be raised above the surface.
[6309][Para 004] • There is a discrete, sharply defined, slightly red (erythematous) patch in the anterior palate, just to the left of the midline.
[6310][Para 004] • There are a few scattered red spots on the soft palate.
[6311][Para 030]  What Do These Changes Tell You?
[6312][Para 001] Individually, none of these lesions can be diagnosed on the basis of the appearance alone. However, in combination, the appearance is almost diagnostic. The purple lesions appear vascular and could be haemangiomas or another blood vessel lesion, including Kaposi’s sarcoma. The red patch has the characteristic appearance of erythematous/chronic atrophic candidosis. Both lesions are associated with immunosuppression, and you should immediately suspect human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection because Kaposi’s sarcoma is extremely rare with other causes of immunosuppression. In this clinical setting, the palpable lymph nodes also support this diagnosis. It is almost certain that the patient is HIV-positive.
[6313][Heading 2]  What Do You Need To Know? What Would You Say To the Patient?
[6314][Para 001] You need to identify whether the patient is aware of his HIV infection but has chosen not to reveal his full medical history or whether he is completely unaware of it. Almost all patients who know that they are HIV-positive will inform their dentist about it, provided they are asked in an appropriate manner. Patients sometimes withhold this information because of previous insensitive management, refusal to provide treatment or worry that practice confidentiality cannot be relied on. However, your questions need to be carefully phrased, taking into account the fact that the patient may be unaware of his HIV infection. It is very important that you approach this matter with sensitivity. You could adopt the following line of questioning:
[6315][Para 004] • Tell the patient that he has some unusual signs in his mouth and that you cannot easily explain it. Ask whether he has noticed them.
[6316][Para 004] • These changes may be infections. Enquire whether he knows of any reason why he might be particularly prone to infection.
[6317][Para 004] • Point out that there are several possible reasons for being prone to infection and that it would be worthwhile investigating further to find the cause. Provide examples such as anaemia, immunosuppression as a result of steroid therapy or viral infection. Patients who know that they are at risk of HIV infection may often use the mention of a viral infection as a prompt to discuss the possibility.
[6318][Para 004] • If the patient indicates that he or she is HIV-positive, ask whether you might have the address of the patient’s clinic so that, if necessary, you may contact the physician for medical advice relating to dental treatment.
[6319][Para 004] • If the patient gives no indication about being HIV-positive, then he or she should be referred to a general medical practitioner or to a specialist in oral medicine or oral surgery unit for further investigation.
[6320][Para 002] It is inappropriate to ask questions about lifestyle or sexuality. Even pointing out that HIV infection is one potential cause of the oral signs may not be well received in a dental setting. It would be reasonable to check the medical history questionnaire, including whether the patient has recorded coming into contact with someone with HIV infection or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
[6321][Para 002] If the patient discloses having HIV infection, you should respond in a positive manner and acknowledge that you will respect the confidentiality of this sensitive information.

[6326][Para 001] None. All may be seen in other types of immunosuppression and many can be found, albeit rarely, in patients with normal health.

[6352][Heading 2]  Is It Appropriate To Extract the Tooth in General Dental Practice?
[6353][Para 001] The General Dental Council (GDC) advocates treating patients with HIV in general practice. Denying this patient treatment on the grounds of his HIV infection alone would put you in breach of the GDC and British Dental Association (BDA) guidance, and might lay you open to a legal case under the Equality Act 2010, UK.
[6354][Para 002] However, when a patient has late or symptomatic HIV infection, his or her medical history may be so complex that a referral to a specialist centre is appropriate. Referral may not be possible in an emergency situation, and treatment, including extraction, may need to be carried out in a general practice setting.
[6355][Heading 2]  You Will Need Medical Advice. How Will You Obtain It?
[6356][Para 001] People with HIV usually attend outpatient hospital clinics. The patient’s general medical practitioner may not have the most up-to-date test results, but clinics are usually very helpful if contacted for information. However, the patient’s right to confidentiality must be respected at all times. First, the patient’s permission must be obtained to make contact, and second, it is enough to explain to the clinic what you propose to do and to request the results of any tests without mentioning the patient’s disease status or irrelevant information.

[6364][Heading 2]  Would Any Special Infection Control Precautions Be Required for the Extraction?
[6365][Para 001] No, the patient should be treated normally. It is assumed that all patients have the potential to carry an infectious disease, and dental practices should follow the standard level of infection control (‘universal precautions’) for all patients. Additional precautions are required for surgical procedures, but not for routine dentistry.

[6368][Para 002] There are three main classes of antiretroviral drugs: nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) and protease inhibitors (PIs). Recently, there have been developments in entry, integration and maturation inhibitors. These are mainly confined to those patients who have a high degree of resistance to the mainstream antiretroviral drugs.
