[6381][Para 002] Antiretroviral combination therapy is usually effective, and this patient’s oral signs are likely to disappear with time and as platelets rise in number. Antiretroviral drugs and HIV-associated salivary gland disease may cause dry mouth, and this is a risk factor for caries. People with HIV are also more prone to periodontal attachment loss and gingival recession. The preventive aspects of dental treatment will need to be emphasized, and if there were evidence of continuing attachment loss or excessively high levels of caries, then a referral to a specialist centre would be appropriate. Otherwise, it would be appropriate to reduce the interval between recalls if there are risk factors for dental disease.

[6396][Para 019] Complaint
[6397][Para 007] The patient complains of difficulty eating. He cannot open his mouth widely enough to place as much food inside as he could before and also has difficulty chewing.
[6398][Para 012] History of Complaint
[6399][Para 007] He has noticed the reduction in mouth opening over a period of several years but has never sought advice. It has not been overly painful, although during the same period, he has felt an uncomfortable burning sensation in the buccal mucosa on eating.
[6400][Para 012] Medical History
[6401][Para 007] The patient is otherwise fit and well.
[6402][Heading 2]  What are the Causes of Limitation of Mouth Opening, and How May They Be Classified?
[6403][Para 001] Limitation of mouth opening is most frequently caused by trismus. Trismus is best defined as the clinical sign of limited mouth opening less than 35 mm, which can result from a wide variety of causes. Historically, the definition of trismus was ‘spasm of the muscles of mastication’, but the broader description of limited opening is more relevant clinically. Trismus is usually reversible and most often results from treatable causes such as trauma or infection. It can be associated with other clinical symptoms such as pain in the jaw and difficulty performing activities that involve opening the mouth, such as toothbrushing or eating. The irreversible causes of trismus, such as oral submucous fibrosis or ankylosis after trauma, may be progressive in their early stages and do not respond to currently available treatment strategies. The causes of trismus are listed in Table 59.1 below. See also Case 8.
[6404][Heading 2]  What Questions Would You Ask?
[6405][Para 001] The patient should be asked whether there has been trauma or irradiation to the skull, temporomandibular joint (TMJ) or face and whether there have been any episodes of swelling of the face or around the joint. He should also be asked whether he uses betel quid (areca nut or ‘paan’).
[6406][Para 017] The patient gives no history of trauma, irradiation, inflammation or infection. However, he has been a betel quid chewer for more than 20 years.
[6407][Para 014] Examination
[6408][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[6409][Para 007] The patient looks mildly anaemic. There is no facial asymmetry or evidence of scars or inflammation around the joint. No tenderness can be elicited from the muscles of mastication. There are no clicks, crepitus or tenderness associated with the TMJ and no mandibular deviation on opening the mouth.
[6410][Heading 2]  What Measurement Would You Take?
[6411][Para 001] The maximum voluntary mouth opening. The normal interincisal opening in an adult is approximately 35 mm. Measurement will provide a baseline reading against which to judge treatment efficacy or trismus progression. It will also indicate the feasibility of dental and other intraoral treatment.

[6421][Para 015] Diagnosis
[6422][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[6423][Para 001] The presentation and features are characteristic of oral submucous fibrosis. Gradual limitation of mouth opening and restriction of tongue movements are seen in a betel quid user who shows typical mucosal blanching and fibrosis presenting as bands in the buccal mucosa.
[6424][Para 218] 
[6425][Para 008] 
[6426][Para 011] Fig. 59.2 The lower lip mucosa.
[6427][Para 009]  
[6428][Heading 2]  What Other Features of Oral Submucous Fibrosis Might Be Seen?
[6429][Para 001] In the early stages, some patients complain of vesiculation of the mucosa. In severe cases with extensive tongue involvement, the filiform papillae are lost.
[6430][Heading 2]  What is Betel Quid Chewing?
[6431][Para 001] A habit practised by many people in the Indian subcontinent, much of south-east Asia and some parts of Africa. The basic quid comprises pieces or paste of areca nut and slaked lime, wrapped and tied into a packet in a vine leaf. A variety of other components is usually added; the combination varies between regions, but tobacco is almost always included, together with flavouring agents such as cinnamon, cloves and ginger. The areca nut contains alkaloids, which have a psychoactive effect and make the habit addictive. The quid is only chewed intermittently and lies in the buccal sulcus for long periods. Many users keep a quid in their mouth all day, and some even sleep with a quid in the mouth. It has been estimated that 10% of the world’s population use betel quid, and chewing is a major health problem in many countries, including western societies with significant immigrant populations from endemic areas.
[6432][Para 024]  What are the Possible Effects of Betel Quid Chewing?
[6433][Para 004] • Oral submucous fibrosis
[6434][Para 004] • Oral and pharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
[6435][Para 004] • Periodontitis, recession and root erosion at the site of use
[6436][Para 004] • Tooth staining
[6437][Para 004] • Decreased taste sensation
[6438][Para 004] • Possible worsening of asthma
[6439][Para 004] • Possible association with diabetes and malignancy.
[6440][Para 030]  What is the Significance of the Diagnosis? What Else Would You Look For?
[6441][Para 001] Oral submucous fibrosis is a potentially malignant disorder. Tobacco and other carcinogenic agents in the quid make this habit one of the highest known risk factors for oral carcinoma.
[6442][Para 002] The patient’s oral mucosa must be carefully examined for carcinoma and potentially malignant lesions. The features of early carcinoma and potentially malignant lesions are discussed in Case 45 and Case 46. Approximately one-third of patients with submucous fibrosis have oral white patches, and dysplasia is present in the mucosa of up to 16%. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma occurs in 5–8% of cases.
[6443][Para 002] The second significant feature is restricted mouth opening. This is often progressive and responds poorly to treatment. In the late stages of disease, the patient may be unable to open the mouth at all, and incisor extractions may be required to allow feeding. Limited opening is a major handicap in the diagnosis and treatment of malignancy and premalignant lesions. It makes examination, detection and treatment extremely difficult, and the prognosis for oral carcinoma in a patient with submucous fibrosis is very poor, mostly as a result of late diagnosis.
[6444][Para 015] Investigations
[6445][Heading 2]  What Investigations are Required? Explain Why.
[6446][Para 001] Biopsy is required to assess the dysplasia. If there are lesions that raise suspicions of malignancy, red or white patches or areas of otherwise abnormal mucosa, they should be sampled for microscopy. More than one biopsy may be required. If no particular part of the mucosa is suspect, a sample should be taken from the area where the quid is held in the mouth.
[6447][Para 002] The biopsy will probably also provide evidence to support the diagnosis of oral submucous fibrosis. However, in such a typical case, biopsy for this purpose alone would not be justified. It might be considered in an early case where the diagnosis is in doubt.
[6448][Heading 2]  Would You Perform This Patient’s Biopsy in a General Practice Setting?
[6449][Para 001] No. This patient is at high risk of oral carcinoma, and so biopsy and further recall should be carried out in a specialist centre. Further discussion about when to perform biopsy of potentially dysplastic mucosa can be found in Case 45.
[6450][Heading 2]  A Biopsy Specimen From the Quid Site is Shown in Fig. 59.3. What Do You See, and How Do You Interpret the Findings?
[6451][Para 001] The mucosa is covered by epithelium that is atrophic, and the thickness of the normal buccal mucosa is about twice the normal thickness from the surface to the dermal papillae in this specimen. It is normally nonkeratinized, except for a thin layer near the occlusal line. The epithelium is largely well organized, and stratification and maturation are not particularly disordered; the epithelial layers are easily differentiated. There is an expanded basal cell layer comprising rather disorganized small and darkly staining cells, which show anisonucleosis (nuclei of different sizes) and irregularly shaped, often angular, nuclei. Towards the centre of the epithelium, there is a cluster of prickle cells between two dermal papillae, showing early and single cell keratinization. These features point to mild dysplasia. Below the epithelium, there is even fibrosis of the connective tissue and scattered lymphocytes.
[6452][Para 002] The deeper tissue shows the fibrosis of the connective tissue more prominently. All the tissue between the epithelium and the underlying muscle is replaced by relatively acellular dense fibrous tissue. The superficial muscle is atrophic and is being replaced by fibrous tissue. Occasional residual muscle fibres lie in the fibrosis. This deeper tissue is uninflamed.
[6453][Para 002] The fibrosis involving deep muscle is consistent with the diagnosis of oral submucous fibrosis, and the overlying epithelium shows mild dysplasia.
[6454][Para 015] Treatment
[6455][Heading 2]  What Questions Would You Ask the Patient About His Betel Quid Chewing Habit?
[6456][Para 001] You need to know whether the patient includes tobacco in his quid, how many quids he uses each day and whether he sleeps with one in the mouth. In addition, you should check other tobacco-related habits, because many quid users smoke cigarettes as well, and some in India smoke a traditional coarse unfiltered tobacco product, ‘bidi’ or ‘beedi’, a rolled uncut tobacco leaf. Some users also practise a form of snuff dipping, placing ground quid constituents (‘pan masala’) loose in the sulcus.
[6457][Heading 2]  What are the Available Treatments or Treatment Options? What is the Potential Value of Each?
[6458][Para 032] See Table 59.2.
[6459][Para 002] No treatment regimen yields satisfactory results, and the aim is maintenance of oral health and prevention of complications. If patients are committed to mouth opening exercises, they may be spared the worst effects of extreme trismus. However, if disease is advanced at diagnosis, progressive limitation is likely. The best results are seen in those who have relatively localized disease at diagnosis, perhaps limited to the site of quid placement.

[6461][Para 008]

[6463][Para 009]  
[6464][Para 018] Table 59.2
[6465][Para 021] Treatment Options
[6466][Para 002] The aims are best achieved by helping the patient with cessation of the habit and by detecting malignancy or dysplasia as early as possible. If suspicious lesions develop, they may be treated by using the same modalities of treatment as in other patients (e.g. surgery and chemotherapy or radiotherapy), as allowed by the degree of trismus. All abnormal mucosa must be regarded with the utmost suspicion and a biopsy performed.
[6467][Heading 2]  What is the Role of the General Dental Practitioner in Such a Case?
[6468][Para 001] Dental practitioners have an important role in the prevention of betel quid chewing just as in the prevention of smoking. As noted above, most chewers are also smokers, and health workers need to address both tobacco habits.
[6469][Para 002] The majority of those who regularly chew betel quid are from low socioeconomic groups and, at least in the UK, are often poorly informed about the health risks. Health education for chewers is most important and may need to be extended to other family members. The difficulty in convincing patients to give up their habit should not be underestimated. The habit is addictive and is embedded in the cultural, social and religious customs of many ethnic groups. Many justify chewing on the basis of its supposed health benefits that are accepted in their culture. The general dental practitioner can help the specialist centre to modify the patient’s high-risk behaviour, reinforcing the message to remove tobacco from the quid and encouraging patients to reduce the areca content and the frequency of chewing. The importance of prompt referral and regular mucosal examination for dysplastic lesions and carcinoma has already been stressed.
[6470][Para 002] In the small number of patients who develop oral submucous fibrosis, dental treatment involves difficult choices and would be best carried out in a specialist centre. Initially, with limited trismus, treatment is not a problem and could be readily performed in a general dental practice. However, some restorative treatment will be rendered impossible as restriction of mouth opening progresses, and a thorough and effective regimen of preventive treatment must be instituted as soon as possible. Extraction of teeth with even small carious lesions or moderate periodontitis may become necessary, although it should be left until the last possible moment. It is still possible to restore and clean some teeth in late disease, although both activities are compromised. Every effort should be made to retain a stable occlusion to prevent progression to permanent overclosure.
[6471][Heading 2]  This Patient Has a Typical But Late Presentation. What are the Earliest Features?
[6472][Para 001] The earliest features are relatively subtle and nonspecific. There is typically burning of the mucosa and roughness, sometimes described as ‘tiny vesicles’. All or part of the lining mucosa may be affected, and these symptoms associated with betel quid chewing should be regarded with the highest suspicion.

[6497][Heading 2]  What Aetiology of Tooth Wear Would Be Consistent with These Findings From the History and Examination Thus Far?
[6498][Para 001] The tooth wear is consistent in appearance with an aetiology of erosive tooth wear, which is the loss of dental hard tissues through the processes of erosion, attrition and abrasion in combination. Although each process may manifest via separate dynamics, significant clinical tooth wear is usually the result of a combination of these processes, and erosion is often the dominant factor. Therefore the condition is commonly referred to as erosive tooth wear.
[6499][Para 002] The history of a previous eating disorder and current symptoms of heartburn and indigestion (most likely from gastro-oesophageal reflux disease [GORD]), suggests that erosion is the predominant factor in this case. Moreover, the distribution of enamel loss further reinforces the suspicion that regurgitation of gastric acid from the stomach may be the primary source of the acid. Erosion from dietary acids is usually associated with more enamel loss on the buccal or labial surfaces of the upper anterior teeth. However, if the patient rinses or swills acidic drinks in the palatal vault prior to swallowing, the pattern of erosion is very similar to that seen when gastric acid is regurgitated. Abrasion and attrition are also likely to be contributing to tooth wear, especially if persistent acid exposure leads to a relative softening of the surface few microns of enamel.
[6500][Para 024]  Define Erosion, Abrasion and Attrition.
[6501][Para 038] Erosion is the chemical dissolution of dental hard tissues and is caused by acids.
[6502][Para 038] Attrition is the loss of dental hard tissues and is caused by the physical action of tooth grinding against tooth.
[6503][Para 038] Abrasion is the wear of dental hard tissues and is caused by physical means other than teeth grinding together.
[6504][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis for Erosive Tooth Wear
[6505][Para 024]  What are Your Differential Diagnoses for the Cause of the Tooth Wear in This Patient?
[6506][Para 016] 1. Tooth wear caused primarily by dietary erosion and secondary abrasion and attrition
[6507][Para 016] 2. Tooth wear caused primarily by gastric erosion with secondary abrasion and attrition
[6508][Para 016] 3. A combination of tooth wear primarily caused by dietary and gastric erosion, with secondary abrasion and attrition.
[6509][Para 030]  What Specific Questions Would You Ask Regarding the Tooth Wear? Explain Why
[6510][Para 001] Tooth wear is often multifactorial, and the patient must be questioned about all causes.
[6511][Para 020] Does the Patient Have a High Consumption of Acidic or Cariogenic Foods or Drinks?
[6512][Para 001] Frequent acid intake is a common cause of dental erosion, and the presence of caries, in addition, requires further investigation. The intake of both acid and cariogenic foods and drinks must be ascertained together with the way in which they are consumed.
[6513][Para 020] What is the Patient’s Current Oral Hygiene Regimen?
[6514][Para 001] There is evidence of poor oral hygiene, which may be complicated by the patient’s working patterns. The timings, frequency and effectiveness of toothbrushing, interdental cleaning and choice of oral care products will impact on both periodontal conditions, caries and erosive tooth wear. This is especially the case in terms of the use of fluoride-containing products, such as high-fluoride toothpastes, mouthrinses and gels. Furthermore, agents such as those containing bioavailable calcium and phosphate may be useful for promoting remineralization of white spots, caries and erosion lesions.
[6515][Para 020] How Did the Eating Disorder Manifest Itself Previously, and is It Well Controlled?
[6516][Para 001] The history of an eating disorder and the presence of caries suggests that the patient has struggled to achieve a healthy balanced diet in the past. Eating disorders have complex and extensive ramifications on general and oral health. Anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa increase the risk of erosive tooth wear for two reasons. First, abnormal dietary patterns can involve either restricted food consumption (anorexia) or excessive binging (bulimia), which can cause dietary erosion, followed by purging (forced vomiting) in both conditions, which causes regurgitation-related gastric erosion. Such eating disorders are lesscommon in males than females, but their incidence is increasing, with current estimates of prevalence rates around 25% among males. Psychological conditions such as these must be handled carefully with the patient and his or her relatives; however, it is important that dental professionals discuss the impact of these conditions on oral health and liaise with appropriate medical professionals.
[6517][Para 020] Does the Patient Suffer Acid Reflux From theStomach?
[6518][Para 001] Regurgitation of stomach acid may be noticed by the patient because of the taste. However, it may go unnoticed if it happens at night and may or may not be associated with symptoms of gastric disease. Occasional mild reflux into the oesophagus or the pharynx is relatively common, for example, during exercise; however, persistent reflux requires medical management. Be aware that patients may have become accustomed to regular, low-level reflux, and so careful questioning during history taking (anamnesis) may be required to elicit this information from the patient.
[6519][Para 020] What is the Patient’s Alcohol Intake and Pattern of Consumption?
[6520][Para 001] The patient has indicated an intake of 10–20 units of alcohol each week. Patients often underreport their alcohol intake, and it would be worth checking this with the patient. Many alcoholic drinks are acidic, contributing to dietary acid (below), and binge patterns of drinking are often associated with vomiting. The possibility of a history of chronic alcoholism should be considered but dealt with respectfully and with dignity among the patient and their relatives.
[6521][Para 020] Does the Patient Grind or Clench His Teeth Duringthe Day or At Night?
[6522][Para 001] Bruxism or other parafunctional habits are common causes of increased wear. Of course, patients may not be aware of grinding habits because they become accustomed to the habit. If nocturnal bruxism occurs, often a partner can help confirm its occurrence and frequency and whether it is associated with a sleep disorder, such as sleep apnoea, or not.
[6523][Para 017] In response to your questioning, the patient denies frequent intake of acidic substances, current vomiting or bruxism. However, he indicates that he does suffer some acid regurgitation associated with his dyspepsia (heartburn) and that alcohol and stress are associated with the attacks. He has had heartburn and regurgitation for 20 years but is not taking any regular medication to relieve the symptoms. He has not visited his medical practitioner regarding these symptoms. His eating disorder is well controlled and has been for at least a decade.
[6524][Para 015] Investigations
[6525][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Perform?
[6526][Para 001] A thorough dietary record should be logged by the patient to determine the true consumption of cariogenic and acidic foods and drinks. Diet analysis sheets need to be filled in for 4 or more days, including a weekend, and it is emphasized that the patient should write down all the foods and drinks taken during that time, including between-meal snacks (essentially, anything that passes between his lips during that period). Both frequency and amount need to be noted, and the patient should be told specifically to note suspect foods such as carbonated drinks, citrus fruits and drinks, vinegar and other acidic condiments, and white wine to ensure that none is missed. It may be wise not to divulge the ‘high risk’ items prior to asking the patient to complete the diet diary, in case this biases the data recorded.
[6527][Para 002] Impressions or study casts or digital intraoral scans of the patient’s teeth should be taken. These will provide a baseline record against which progression of future erosion can be determined. The basic erosive wear examination (BEWE) can also provide a useful, simple scoring system for classifying the risk of tooth wear in more borderline cases; however, this is clearly a high risk case. Tests of tooth sensibility and intraoral bitewing and selected periapical radiographs will be needed to diagnose the extent, location and severity of caries and whether any teeth have compromised pulp sensibility.
[6528][Para 002] Diet analysis confirms the patient’s statement that he has a low consumption of acidic foods and beverages. This therefore excludes dietary acid as a cause, leaving gastric acid as the only other erosive source. Regurgitation erosion occurs when the stomach juice passes from the stomach into the mouth. The pH of stomach juice is around 1 or 2, and if regurgitation occurs frequently, the damage to teeth can be catastrophic and rapid.
[6529][Para 015] Further Erosive Tooth Wear Differential Diagnosis
[6530][Para 024]  How Might Gastric Acid Enter the Mouth?
[6531][Para 016] 1. GORD
[6532][Para 016] 2. Eating disorders
[6533][Para 016] 3. Chronic alcoholism
[6534][Para 016] 4. Rumination.
[6535][Para 030]  What Features of These Conditions Might Aid Your Definitive Diagnosis?
[6536][Para 001] GORD is usually associated with heartburn (intermittent retrosternal pain radiating along the oesophagus, worsened by lying down or a recent large meal), or epigastric pain (centred on the xiphisternum). When symptoms are related to meals, the term dyspepsia is sometimes used. In most patients, symptoms of GORD are self-limiting, and little or no acid enters the mouth. In others, complete regurgitation into the mouth is frequent and pain becomes persistent, causing patients to seek medical advice. A small proportion of patients treat their pain with over-the-counter antacids and are unaware of the potential of damage to their teeth or oesophagus. A history of taking antacid preparations is a useful indicator for the activity of GORD, and this patient has already indicated that he has noticed some regurgitation. This is the most likely cause.
[6537][Para 002] Eating disorders are a cause of erosion, as discussed above. In 2013, it was estimated that 725,000 people in the UK had an eating disorder. Thus less than 1 in 100 patients in general dental practice are likely to be affected by an eating disorder. Both anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa tend to affect adolescent females. Sufferers lose body weight by starving themselves and/or vomiting to lose weight in an attempt to improve their body self-image. A small proportion of patients with severe anorexia die as a result of the disorder. Unlike patients with anorexia, those with bulimia usually have a stable body weight. They eat and drink in binges and self-induce vomiting to control their body weight. There may be an accompanying history of drug and/or alcohol abuse.
[6538][Para 020] Alcoholism
[6539][Para 001] is associated with dental erosion, either through vomiting or due to the low pH of some alcoholic drinks.
[6540][Para 002] Rumination is an unusual practice involving habitual chewing of food, swallowing and then regurgitating the food mixed with stomach acid to be chewed and swallowed again. It is considered rare, but there is no accurate information on its prevalence, and it is thought to affect young, healthy and, mainly, professional people. If the habit is continued, it can cause significant damage to teeth.
[6541][Para 017] The patient gives a clear history of regular heartburn and symptomatic regurgitation. He denies rumination and alcoholism.
[6542][Para 015] Diagnosis
[6543][Para 024]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[6544][Para 016] 1. Generalized plaque-induced gingivitis
[6545][Para 016] 2. Generalized severe erosive tooth wear consistent in appearance with multi-factorial erosion, abrasion and attrition
[6546][Para 016] 3. Multiple carious lesions bucco-cervically and proximally.
[6547][Para 015] Treatment
[6548][Heading 2]  How Will You Manage the Patient’s Condition?
[6549][Para 001] The patient should be referred to a gastroenterologist or his general medical practitioner for further investigation of his symptoms. Reflux may be caused by a reduction in pressure around the lower oesophageal sphincter (e.g., in hiatus hernia) or abnormal oesophageal motility. Referral is necessary to detect such associated conditions and, if symptoms merit, to consider treatment with drugs that block acid secretion. It is important to ensure the patient’s consent to liaising with the medical practitioner, especially if the patient is less than 18 years of age and an eating disorder is suspected; then, careful and sensitive questioning, with involvement of the family, may be required, along with contemporaneous record keeping. Some patients may be reluctant to have dental practitioners raise such concerns with medical practitioners. However, eating disorders are one of the leading causes of mental health–related deaths – whether as a result of the systemic effects of malnutrition or of suicide – and oral healthcare professionals have a clear role to play because they may be the first to spot the early signs, such as poor oral health related to abnormal eating behaviours. If in doubt, medico-legal advice should be sought if a young patient with a suspected eating disorder does not consent to the dental practitioner liaising with parents or general medical practitioners.
[6550][Para 002] A minimally invasive approach to restorative dental treatment of erosion should be taken. No immediate treatment is required if the erosion is relatively minor and the patient is happy with the appearance of his or her teeth. If the cause is identified and treated, erosion will cease or progression will be slowed down. Study models taken at yearly intervals may be compared with those taken at the initial visit to assess progression, and if the tooth wear progresses, restoration may be considered.
[6551][Para 002] In the early stages of erosion, direct resin composite restorations will protect the palatal surfaces from further damage. An example in another patient is shown in Figs 60.2–60.4.
[6552][Para 002] However, the finite lifespan of such restorations requires the patient’s commitment to further treatment, with a median time of 6–7 years before revision becomes necessary). This can often be performed with simple minimally invasive revisions, including polishing, surface refurbishment and repair, as opposed to complete replacement of the restoration. Therefore from a consent perspective, it is important that patients are aware, at the outset, of the likely maintenance requirements associated with direct resin composite placement. More complex alternatives for restoring worn teeth, including indirect restorations designed to change the occlusal vertical dimension, are discussed in Chapter 61.

[6564][Heading 1] Worn Front Teeth
[6565][Para 027] Rupert Austin, and Deborah Bomfim
[6566][Para 028] Summary
[6567][Para 029] A 60-year-old man presents at your general dental practice saying that his teeth have worn down. What is the cause, and how should his condition be managed?
[6568][Para 014] History
[6569][Para 019] Complaint
[6570][Para 007] The patient is concerned about his short and discoloured upper front teeth. He is also finding that he has difficulty eating. The appearance of his teeth has recently become more important to him because he has taken a job where he has to deal with the public. He wishes primarily to improve his appearance and seems to be sufficiently motivated to complete a course of complex dental treatment.
[6571][Para 012] History of Complaint
[6572][Para 007] The patient has only recently started to attend his dentist regularly, after a 10-year period without treatment.
[6573][Para 014] Examination
[6574][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[6575][Para 007] No submandibular or cervical lymph nodes are palpable, the temporomandibular joints appear normal, and there is no tenderness around the muscles of mastication. Despite the anterior tooth wear, there is no clinical evidence of a major loss of occlusal vertical dimension, such as an overclosed facial appearance and increased freeway space.
[6576][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[6577][Para 007] The oral soft tissues are healthy. All teeth are present. There are deposits of plaque and staining around the cervical margins of his teeth. Despite the plaque, only a few sites display bleeding on periodontal probing, and there are no clinical signs of loss of attachment, with pocket probing depths of 2–4 mm. The appearance of the dentition can be seen in Fig. 61.1.

[6580][Para 001] The patient is suffering from localized severe erosive tooth wear (tooth surface loss). Erosive tooth wear is caused usually by a combination of three dynamic processes: erosion, attrition and abrasion. In this case, the tooth wear is consistent in appearance with both attrition and erosion as the main factors. See Box 61.1.

[6589][Para 001] Diet analysis is required to determine whether there is excessively frequent intake of dietary acids because the frequency of intake of dietary acids increases the risk of erosive tooth wear.
[6590][Para 020] Referral To the General Medical Practitioner
[6591][Para 001] To Investigate the Gastric Causes of Erosion
[6592][Para 002] Radiographs to assess bone levels, root morphology and possible periapical pathology. Radiographic assessment, by means of either a dental panoramic tomograph (DPT) or full-mouth long cone periapical radiographs, is necessary. Because the patient has not attended a dentist for a decade, the DPT would provide a useful survey of all maxillary and mandibular teeth. Periapical radiographs of all teeth are a reasonable alternative in this case, especially because of the better quality of images of the anterior region, in comparison with a DPT. Periapical radiographs taken with the paralleling technique, as opposed to the bisecting angle technique, would allow a more accurate assessment of bone levels.
[6593][Para 002] Maxillary and mandibular study casts (Fig. 61.2) are required to determine the ideal restorative treatment option, in terms of choosing the best materials and techniques for restoring the teeth. To plan restorations for extensively worn teeth, the casts should be articulated in the retruded contact position on either a fully adjustable or semiadjustable articulator, using a facebow. Obtaining an accurate occlusal record is particularly important in this case because the patient has a habitual forward mandibular posture. The retruded contact position is a reproducible jaw relationship; therefore, study casts mounted to this occlusal record can be used to analyze this patient’s occlusion and to help determine the appropriate occlusal vertical dimension at which the definitive restorations could be provided. The articulated study casts can then also be used to produce a diagnostic wax-up at an increased vertical dimension to provide the proposed shape of the restorations. The diagnostic wax-up can be duplicated in stone and a soft vacuum-formed splint (or silicone matrix) formed around it; this is useful both as a surgical stent for crown lengthening and for constructing provisional chairside crowns suitable for a reorganized occlusion.

[6601][Para 095] Box 61.2 Advantages and Disadvantages of Options for Managing the Occlusal Relationship
[6602][05 Block] 
[6603][Para 015] Care Planning
[6604][Heading 2]  What is the Main Problem in Providing Restorations for These Teeth?
[6605][Para 001] The short height of the crowns is the main clinical problem. The lack of enamel surface area is likely to result in poor bond strength for resin composite restorations. If conventional crowns were used, reduction of crown length would be required to create space for the crowns, and this would leave short, unretentive preparations, with an insufficient mechanical ferrule effect to retain the crowns (i.e. less than 2 mm of dentine height).
[6606][Heading 2]  What are the Two Potential Treatment Philosophies That Can Be Used To Manage the Occlusion During Provision of New Restorations in Cases Such As This? What are Their Advantages and Disadvantages, and Which Approach Should Be Chosen in This Specific Case?
[6607][Para 001] One option for an extensively worn dentition is to place restorations at an increased occlusal vertical dimension. This is known as the reorganized approach to managing the occlusion. Alternatively, the existing jaw relationship could be maintained (i.e. the habitual occlusion) and short anterior crowns conforming to the existing intercuspal position and vertical dimension could be provided. This is known as the conformative approach to occlusal management. See Box 61.2.
[6608][Heading 2]  Which Approach is Necessary in This Case, and How Would You Manage the Vertical Dimension?
[6609][Para 001] In this case, the reorganized approach should be adopted. This is because the crowns of the worn anterior teeth are very short. If direct resin composite restorations were used, there would insufficient surface area for bonding; in addition, the teeth would have an incorrect height-to-width ratio. If crowns were used, the natural crown would need to be reduced in height to provide occlusal clearance, and this would result in even shorter unretentive preparations and crowns with an incorrect height-to-width ratio.
[6610][Heading 2]  How Might This Problem Be Overcome?
[6611][Para 001] Therefore, both an increase in the vertical dimension and surgical crown lengthening are necessary to gain space for the new tooth height. Surgical crown lengthening with alveolar bone remodelling is beneficial for increasing the available tooth tissue for retention of restorations. The gingival margin is repositioned apically to create a longer tooth, which provides greater surface area for composite bonding or an increased ferrule for retention of a crown in the conventional manner. Crown lengthening does not alter the occlusal vertical dimension because the additional crown length needed for preparation is obtained by exposing the root surfaces. Surgical crown lengthening is preferable to electrosurgery, which merely alters the gingival contour and is prone to causing a relapse. In this case, the teeth are so short that a combination of both techniques –increasing the vertical dimension of the occlusion and lengthening of the surgical crown – are required. See Fig. 61.3.
[6612][Heading 2]  How is Surgical Crown Lengthening Achieved?
[6613][Para 001] The diagnostic wax-up is converted to a clear, vacuum-formed stent for guiding the surgical removal of excess gingival soft tissue and bone around the teeth (Fig. 61.4).
[6614][Para 218] 
[6615][Para 008] 
[6616][Para 011] Fig. 61.3 The maxillary anterior teeth after surgical crown lengthening. Note the apical repositioning of the gingival margin. This will provide increased surface area for bonding of restorations or an improved axial wall height for subsequent indirect crown preparations.
[6617][Para 009]  
[6618][Para 008] 
[6619][Para 011] Fig. 61.4 The vacuum-formed stent in situ, indicating the level of gingival tissue removal required.
[6620][Para 009]  
[6621][Para 002] After site preparation and establishment of local anaesthesia, incisions are traced along the stent, and soft tissue is excised to recontour the gingival architecture. Muco-periosteal tissue flaps are then raised buccally and palatally, and crestal bone is removed with a bur. Both the height of the bone and its width must be adapted, remodelling the alveolar contour so that the soft tissue will return to its new apical position but be able to retain the normal shape of the gingival margin. Bone is removed palatally and buccally. The amount to be removed must be determined to ensure that sufficient crown length is produced to allow a retentive preparation but support from the root is not compromised. The optimal distance from the crest of the alveolar bone to the gingival margin is 3–4 mm, which is also known as the biological width. Sufficient bone must be removed to preserve this distance, or the gingival tissues will regrow to their original position.
[6622][Para 024]  What are the Disadvantages of Crown Lengthening?
[6623][Para 004] • Crown lengthening results in the crown margins lying on the root surfaces of teeth. The cross-sectional area of the root is smaller than the crown so that the preparation is rather tall and narrow (and, therefore, weaker), and the final restoration is more triangular in shape, with a potentially altered emergence profile of the crown at the new gingival margin.
[6624][Para 004] • Crown lengthening can result in loss of the interdental papilla, which results in poor soft tissue aesthetics, known as ‘black triangles’.
[6625][Para 004] • Some patients develop significant sensitivity because of the exposed dentine.
[6626][Para 004] • Part of the periodontium is removed. The support of teeth with short roots may be compromised as a result.
[6627][Para 004] • The procedure is uncomfortable for the patient, and up to 6–12 months may be needed for the new gingival contour to stabilize.
[6628][Para 030]  Are There Any Alternatives To Crown Lengthening?
[6629][Para 001] An alternative approach to surgical crown lengthening would be to accept the clinical crown height but gain additional retention by placing a post in the root canal. However, elective root treatment should be avoided whenever possible in cases of tooth wear. This is especially so when there is significant attrition, for instance, that resulting from a parafunctional habit. The additional occlusal loading may result in decementation of the post or fracture of the root.
[6630][Para 002] Secondary dentine formation below the wear may also complicate root treatment by causing sclerosis of the pulp chamber and the root canal system.
[6631][Para 014] Treatment
[6632][Para 007] In this case, the decision was to provide a localized anterior reconstruction at an increased vertical dimension of occlusion by using direct resin composite restorations in combination with crown lengthening of the maxillary anterior dentition.
[6633][Heading 2]  How Should the Stages of Treatment Be Organized Into a Care Plan Culminating in Definitive Restoration? Why is Each Stage Required?
[6634][Para 032] See Table 61.1.
[6635][Heading 2]  What Does Relative Axial Movement Mean in Relation To the ‘Dahl’ Technique?
[6636][Para 001] In patients with localized anterior tooth wear, when there are adequate sound or restored posterior teeth to predictably maintain the existing occlusal relationship, the extra vertical space needed to provide sufficient thickness for the new restorations can be created by using relative axial movement of teeth (i.e. the relative intrusion of the anterior teeth and extrusion of the posterior teeth), which is known as the Dahl approach to creating interdental occlusal space for restorations. This is a more minimally invasive option compared to the creation of space by preparing teeth for crowns. The original Dahl appliance was described as an anterior bite plane constructed from cobalt–chrome, similar to a palatal plate major connector, which was cemented to the palatal aspects of the teeth with a relatively weak cement such as a glass–ionomer (Fig. 61.5). This approach allowed the posterior teeth to overerupt and also intruded the anterior teeth so that tooth movement, rather than tooth reduction, provided the additional interocclusal space necessary for direct or indirect restorations. The appliance was worn for approximately 3–6 months, depending on the rate of relative axial movement, with regular recalls to assess axial movement. Once the anterior teeth intruded and the posterior teeth extruded, thus re-establishing the intercuspal position, the cobalt–chrome appliance was removed, leaving a space between the front teeth, which was then used to provide interocclusal space for the new restorations.

[6641][Para 011] Fig. 61.5 A different patient with a conventional Dahl appliance that was used to allow relative axial movement, after which the cobalt–chromium appliance was removed and restorations placed on the anterior teeth.
[6642][Para 009]  
[6643][Para 002] More recently, direct resin composite restorations are being prescribed as the first restoration of choice for localized anterior tooth wear cases, in order to provide the new definitive restorations at the increased vertical dimension of occlusion and allow the posterior occlusion to re-establish in due course. This avoids the need for a lengthy provisional phase of treatment. However, if the definitive restorations are to be conventional full-coverage crowns, then the direct resin composite restorations are often seen as a provisional treatment to be used whilst the occlusion is being reorganized, and then the definitive crowns can be provided in a conformative approach to the new intercuspal position.
[6644][Para 014] Medico-Legal Issues
[6645][Para 001] As with all cases where potentially lengthy and complex prosthodontic treatment is required, such as those increasing the occlusal vertical dimension to replace missing tooth tissue from erosive tooth wear, it is medico-legally advisable for general dental practitioners to liaise with specialist colleagues to formulate an optimal care plan and to ensure that patients understand all the risks and benefits of the potential options for their oral rehabilitation. A general dental practitioner has a key role to play in case selection and communicating to patients the benefits of either local anterior reconstruction or full-mouth rehabilitations at a reorganized occlusal scheme. The treatment can then be carried out in general dental practice, with frequent liaising with a prosthodontist or restorative specialist and some guidance during the initial phases. Once the provisional restorations have allowed the occlusion to establish a new intercuspal position that is stable and maintainable, provision of definitive restorations conforming to this new occlusal scheme is then straightforward and can be carried out in general dental practice. However, on occasion, patients do not respond in a predicable manner when the occlusal vertical dimension is changed. As can be seen in Fig. 61.6, although the patient was comfortable with the new restorations and had satisfactory function and aesthetics, with just the anterior teeth in occlusion, relative axial movement had not occurred at 12 months after treatment and a hard occlusal splint had to be provided for nighttime wear to prevent excessive wear of the restorations. The plans and discussions must be recorded contemporaneously, and keeping clinical photographic records of the different stages is desirable. The patient must be made fully aware of his or her responsibility towards maintaining optimal oral hygiene to prolong the functional life of the definitive restorations placed, as well as attending 6-month recall consultations to ensure that avoidable problems are prevented. This level of care also involves use of a complete oral healthcare team, including hygienists or therapists who can deliver the preventive care required.
[6646][Para 218] 
[6647][Para 008] 
[6648][Para 011] Fig. 61.6 Photograph of the dentition at 12 months after treatment, showing a 2-mm space between the maxillary and mandibular teeth that had not been closed by relative axial movement.
[6649][Para 009]  
[6650][Para 002] Therefore, when multiple restorations, especially indirect conventional restorations, are being used to provide a local or full-arch oral reconstruction at an increased vertical dimension, it is advisable to seek specialist opinion from a prosthodontist or a restorative dentistry specialist. This helps ensure good communication with patients so that they can understand the nature of the treatment and provide fully informed consent after being educated about the maintenance measures required, should the treatment proceed optimally, and about the potential benefits and risks, including the requirement for replacement or further remedial work that may be needed.

[6672][Heading 2]  How Do You Interpret the History and Examination Results So Far?
[6673][Para 001] The clear history of toothache (which is normally correctly identified by patients) and the large restorations suggest that one or more teeth may be the cause of the pain, probably as a result of caries or complications of restoration. The pain is poorly localized, severe, feels like toothache and has been exacerbated by hot and cold stimuli, almost certainly indicating pulpitis. The recent onset of pain unrelated to hot and cold suggests late or irreversible pulpitis but that the causative pulp remains partially vital. The history does not suggest spread of infection or inflammation to the periodontal ligament, which is normally associated with pain on biting and accurate localization of the causative tooth by the patient.

[6676][Para 017] When this was done, it is found that no teeth were particularly tender to percussion. The first molar is slightly hypersensitive, both by electric pulp testing and application of a cold stimulus (ethyl chloride), neither test causing acute pain.

[6678][Heading 2]  What Investigation Would You Now Undertake, and Why?
[6679][Para 001] An intraoral periapical radiograph of the lower left premolars and the first molar should be taken. So far, the examination indicates that the first molar is the most likely cause of the pain. However, the patient is vague as to whether the second premolar is tender to percussion, and it contains a large restoration. There may be two causes for the pain.
[6680][Para 002] A radiograph cannot provide direct evidence of vitality. However, it will provide information on the possible causes of loss of vitality, the presence of caries and inadequate restorations, as well as revealing previous attempted root canal treatment and periapical granuloma or infection (provided there has been sufficient time for apical bone loss to develop). A radiograph will also be required in the event that either extraction or root canal treatment is necessary.

[6690][Para 030]  What Would You Do Next, and Why?
[6691][Para 001] Further radiographic views are required. The radiograph has not aided diagnosis of the dental pain because no unsuspected cause for the pulpitis has been identified. However, it has revealed an apical radiolucency on the second premolar and the first molar, and this is not compatible with an uncomplicated periapical granuloma, infection or cyst. The presence of an apical radiolucency on the second premolar is also incompatible with the history and examination results, which indicate that this tooth is vital.
[6692][Para 002] The presence of both radiopacity and radiolucency requires consideration of a wider differential diagnosis, which would include fibro-cemento-osseous lesions, odontogenic tumours and a variety of bone disorders. The margins of the radiolucent lesion are not visible on the radiograph and need to be defined before a more accurate differential diagnosis can be proposed. Because some fibro-cemento-osseous lesions may be bilateral, appropriate views would be a dental panoramic radiograph or right and left oblique laterals. These will also allow all teeth and their supporting structures to be assessed because the patient is being seen in the practice for the first time. Bitewing radiographs to assess caries would also be appropriate in a new patient with several heavily restored teeth if there is clinical suspicion of caries.

[6698][Heading 2]  Part of the Dental Panoramic Radiograph is Shown in Fig. 62.2. What Do You See?

[6706][Para 015] Diagnosis
[6707][Para 024]  What are the Causes of a Mixed Radiolucency Such As This in the Jaws?
[6708][Para 004] • Cemento-osseous dysplasias
[6709][Para 136] — Periapical
[6710][Para 136] — Focal
[6711][Para 136] — Florid
[6712][Para 004] • Chronic osteomyelitis
[6713][Para 004] • Paget’s disease of bone
[6714][Para 004] • Fibrous dysplasia
[6715][Para 004] • Metastatic malignancy.
[6716][Para 030]  What is the Most Likely Diagnosis? Explain Why
[6717][Para 001] One of the cemento-osseous dysplasias is the most likely cause of the patient’s jaw lesions. The diagnosis may be made on the radiographic appearances alone. No other condition produces multiple lesions centred on the apices of the teeth, each with a central radiopacity and a variable and poorly defined radiolucent rim. As disease progresses, this pattern may become less distinct, but it is clearly visible in several of this patient’s lesions. This patient has the florid form of the disease, with one or more quadrants affected. The periapical form affects a few teeth, usually the lower incisors, and the focal form gives rise to one large lesion, but all are part of a spectrum of disease severity. The diagnosis is supported by the patient’s race, these conditions being more prevalent in those of African and Mongoloid races. The lesion(s) are normally asymptomatic.
[6718][Heading 2]  What Diagnoses Have You Excluded? Explain Why
[6719][Para 001] Chronic osteomyelitis produces a patchy mixed radiolucency but would show symptoms of dull, boring, central bone pain that is quite distinct from those reported. Sinuses or other signs of infection would probably be present. However, this diagnosis should not be completely excluded without further consideration because the sclerotic bone of fibro-cemento-osseous lesions, such as florid cemento-osseous dysplasia, is prone to infection, particularly dental infection, and in the past, the condition was thought to be a form of osteomyelitis. A biopsy to confirm the diagnosis is contraindicated because of the risk of initiating osteomyelitis.
[6720][Para 002] Paget’s disease of bone may be confidently excluded because it almost never affects the mandible without producing obvious lesions, signs and symptoms in other bones. If this were Paget’s disease, the maxilla would usually be more severely affected. Paget’s disease affects predominantly older Caucasians.
[6721][Para 002] Fibrous dysplasia might be considered a cause of patchy and poorly defined radiolucency, but it presents with expansion of the jaw, usually the maxilla, during the first or second decade of life.
[6722][Para 002] Metastatic malignancy might also be considered a further cause. Most cancers cause purely radiolucent lesions, but some, notably prostate and breast cancers, may cause bony sclerosis and ‘sun ray’ radiopacity. However, the site is usually near the angle of the mandible, and the radiological appearances are sufficiently characteristic of florid cemento-osseous dysplasia to exclude this sinister diagnosis.
[6723][Heading 2]  How Might You Confirm the Diagnosis Without Biopsy?
[6724][Para 001] Any previous radiographs should be reviewed to determine whether the lesion has been present and slowly progressing for several years. This would confirm the diagnosis.
[6725][Para 218] 
[6726][Para 008] 
[6727][Para 011] Fig. 62.3 Section from the dental panoramic tomograph taken 11 years previously.
[6728][Para 009]  
[6729][Para 017] A previous dental practitioner was contacted and provided the radiograph seen in Fig. 62.3 , which had been taken 11 years previously.
[6730][Para 002] The radiograph shows the lower left quadrant. The lower left second premolar and first molar contain smaller restorations than at present, and there is probable caries in the second premolar. However, the first premolar appears to contain the same restoration as at present, and at its apex, there is a lesion typical of early cemento-osseous dysplasia comprising radiolucency with central opacity at the root apex. This early stage of the lesion provides conclusive evidence for the proposed diagnosis.
[6731][Heading 2]  What Would You Do About the Patient’s Pain?
[6732][Para 001] The causative tooth must be properly identified, and in this patient, the electric pulp test suggested that the first molar is to blame. The increased sensitivity on electric and cold pulp testing may be explained by the presence of pulpitis or small vital pulp remnants in an otherwise nonvital pulp.
[6733][Para 002] When pulp tests fail to identify a definite cause, the most effective method is to perform a test cavity without local analgesia in the most likely tooth. This is not possible (or usually required) in a tooth with acute pulpitis but works well in cases of chronic low-grade pain if a pulp is completely or partially viable or when the patient’s response to testing cannot be relied on.
[6734][Para 002] Alternatively, a diagnostic local analgesic injection may be given to abolish the pain, but this is not usually useful for first molars, where a block is required for effective analgesia. Once the anaesthetic is given, no further pulp tests are possible at that visit.
[6735][Para 002] When a test cavity was performed, the first molar was found to be nonvital, with vital pulp in one canal only. Either root canal treatment or extraction was required.
[6736][Heading 2]  What About the Apical Radiolucency On the Second Premolar?
[6737][Para 007] This was another early lesion of cemento-osseous dysplasia. Some years later, radiographs revealed that the lesion had developed a zone of radiopacity centrally.
[6738][Heading 2]  Does Florid Cemento-Osseous Dysplasia Have Any Significant Complications?
[6739][Para 001] Yes. Precautions must be taken to ensure that the patient does not develop osteomyelitis in the sclerotic bone of the mandible. A regimen for prevention of caries and periodontal disease must be instituted to reduce the risk of future dental infection. In this patient, the periodontal condition of the first molar was poor, so extraction was the preferred option. Other nonvital teeth should also be extracted if there are reasons to suspect that root canal treatment may not be successful. Antibiotics should be prescribed during the healing period for all extractions involving the affected bone. Any surgery in the mandible should be similarly covered and is best performed in hospital rather than in a general practice, unless the practitioner has the appropriate experience.

[6782][Para 024]  What Further Questions Might Help Confirm Your Diagnosis?
[6783][Para 020] Did Either Parent Have a Similar Problem?
[6784][Para 001] Cherubism is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Radiographs of both parents may reveal unsuspected healed lesions, and this would aid in making a definitive diagnosis.

[6789][Heading 2]  Would Any Further Radiographs Help Confirm the Diagnosis?
[6790][Para 001] More detailed radiographic examination with intraoral images would be helpful for the following reasons:
[6791][Para 004] • To demonstrate involvement of the maxilla. More severely affected patients usually have lesions in the maxilla, usually centred on the tuberosity, but sometimes extending to distort the orbit. These can easily be missed on extraoral images but, if present, confirm the diagnosis.
[6792][Para 004] • To identify displacement or destruction of teeth. As noted above, cherubism often destroys tooth germs and displaces teeth.
[6793][Para 030]  Is Biopsy Required?
[6794][Para 001] In a classic case of cherubism, the diagnosis may be made with certainty on the basis of family history and clinical and radiographic features. [6795][Heading 2]  A Biopsy Specimen Was Removed From the Expanded Alveolar Ridge. The Histological Appearances are Shown in Fig. 63.3. What Do You See?
[6796][Para 001] The lesion is composed of cellular fibrous tissue, which appears loose and oedematous, with spaces, rather than dense collagen, between the cells. Scattered in the fibrous tissue are multinucleate giant cells. These are relatively small giant cells and have only 4–8 nuclei each.
[6797][Para 218] 
[6798][Para 008] 
[6799][Para 011] Fig. 63.3 The histological appearance of the biopsy specimen.
[6800][Para 009]  
[6801][Heading 2]  How Do You Interpret These Appearances? Are They Consistent with Cherubism?
[6802][Para 001] Lesions with many giant cells fall into two broad categories – (1) those with granulomas such as tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and foreign body reactions and (2) giant cell lesions. No granulomas are present, and these appearances indicate a giant cell lesion, the causes of which are:
[6803][Para 004] • Central giant cell granuloma
[6804][Para 004] • Brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism
[6805][Para 004] • Aneurysmal bone cyst
[6806][Para 004] • Cherubism.
[6807][Para 002] These conditions cannot be distinguished from one another on histological grounds alone. However, the only one that matches the clinical and radiographic findings in this case is cherubism.
[6808][Para 014] Diagnosis
[6809][Para 001] Taken together, the evidence supports a diagnosis of cherubism, and this is a typical case.
[6810][Para 015] Aetiology
[6811][Heading 2]  What is the Cause of Cherubism?
[6812][Para 001] Cherubism is caused by any one of several mutations in the SH3BP2 gene, a regulator of the C-Abl oncogene, a poorly understood signalling molecule involved in the regulation of cell division and many other cell functions.
[6813][Para 002] The condition is usually inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. It would be expected that one parent would be similarly affected. Females are often less severely affected, and cases may appear to be sporadic.
[6814][Para 015] Treatment
[6815][Heading 2]  What Treatment Would You Recommend? What Other Advice Would You Give To the Parents?
[6816][Para 001] No treatment is required, although the parents and the child may need reassurance. The parents can be told that lesions of cherubism usually grow fastest before the age of 5 years. Although there will be further growth during the next few years, the lesions will stop growing spontaneously and start to regress around the age of puberty. The swelling should have completely resolved by the age of 25 years, and only radiographic changes will remain into the fourth decade.
[6817][Para 002] Surgical intervention is not usually necessary but may be performed for cosmetic reasons if the lesions are resolving slowly. Some teeth will be lost through the disease process. The parents should also be warned that future children and siblings are likely to be affected. Genetic counselling would be appropriate.

[6819][Heading 1] Recurrent Neck Swelling
[6820][Para 027] Bethan Thomas, Niall O’Neill, and Michael Escudier
[6821][Para 028] Summary
[6822][Para 029] A 35-year-old man presents complaining of an intermittent swelling in his neck at mealtimes. What are the possible causes, appropriate investigations and treatment options?
[6823][Para 218] 
[6824][Para 008] 
[6825][Para 011] Fig. 64.1 The patient on presentation.
[6826][Para 009]  
[6827][Para 014] History
[6828][Para 019] Complaint
[6829][Para 007] The patient complains of a swelling of the left neck below the angle of the jaw. It appears suddenly on eating and is painful, lasts 30–60 minutes and then subsides slowly. He reports that the swelling is worse when eating certain foods, such as citrus fruit.
[6830][Para 012] History of Complaint
[6831][Para 007] The swelling first appeared suddenly during a meal 3 years ago. It resolved within 15 minutes. In the following month, the patient experienced the same swelling three times and since then has experienced occasional swelling, always associated with food intake. The swelling always resolves quickly and does not cause pain. However, over the last 4 months, the swelling has recurred more frequently and the area has become tender. In the last 2 weeks, the swelling has occurred at almost every meal and takes at least 1 hour to resolve.
[6832][Para 012] Medical History
[6833][Para 007] The patient is otherwise fit and healthy. He is not currently on any medication.
[6834][Heading 2]  How Do You Interpret the Information You Have So Far?
[6835][Para 001] The patient is describing the symptom known as ‘mealtime syndrome’, which refers to swelling of a salivary gland associated with eating, the thought of eating or the smell of food. The location of the swelling is important, indicating that the site correlates with a salivary gland. The recurrent nature of the swelling indicates that mealtime syndrome is the most likely underlying process. The cause of mealtime syndrome is obstruction of a salivary gland duct. Between meals, the low flow of saliva can leak around a partial obstruction. When flow is stimulated, the increased volume of saliva is prevented from passing down the duct causing the gland to swell. This can induce pain because the gland is restricted within a capsule. The increase in severity of the symptoms indicates that the degree of obstruction has increased.
[6836][Heading 2]  Are There Any Specific Questions You Would Ask? Why?
[6837][Para 001] The patient should be asked if he has noticed any abnormality such as a sudden resolution of the swelling following a discharge of saliva or salty fluid into the mouth because this would confirm intermittent obstruction. A report of foul-tasting saliva could indicate infection of the gland.

[6839][Para 104] Extraoral Examination

[6852][Heading 2]  Are There Any Other Causes of Intermittent Swelling That Need To Be Considered?
[6853][Para 001] Yes. Intermittent swelling may be seen in wind instrument players who force air or liquids back into the gland. This may present as unilateral or bilateral swelling. Several other chronic conditions can cause persistent swelling. These include sialadenitis (usually the result of obstruction), primary Sjögren’s syndrome, sialosis, drug-induced salivary gland swelling (caused by iodine-containing compounds, phenylbutazone, chlorhexidine and other drugs). This last group does not generally cause such obvious and short-lived swelling as is seen with obstruction.

[6860][Heading 2]  The Ultrasound Scan is Shown in Fig. 64.2. What Do You See?
[6861][Para 001] Ultrasonography is a dynamic investigation, and the ultrasound operator may observe the screen for several minutes, altering the angle of the ultrasound transducer (transmitter/detector) to provide views at different angles. Representative images are captured to demonstrate key findings and support the scan report but interpretation of a single image can be challenging for the less experienced clinician. Ultrasound scans are conventionally orientated with the skin surface of the patient (ultrasound transducer) at the top of the image. Objects that reflect ultrasound, such as stones, appear white and cast a dark acoustic shadow because of the inability of the ultrasound waves to penetrate the calcified stone. Dilated ducts, proximal to the stone, appear as dark spaces.
[6862][Para 002] The unlabelled ultrasound scan is shown on the left, and the annotated landmarks are highlighted in the image on the right. There is a calculus in the left submandibular gland. The gland is slightly heterogeneous/mottled in appearance because of sialadenitis. The calculus appears as a hyperechoic (white) body (white arrow), with a postacoustic shadow (double-headed white arrow). The stone measures approximately 5 mm in length, lying within the left submandibular gland, posterior to the posterior limit of the mylohyoid muscle. The exact location of a stone is assessed by the ultrasound operator with reference to the angle of the ultrasound transducer; however, this information, which is stated in the report, cannot be accurately determined from a single still image.

In Fig. 64.3b, following infusion of the contrast, the outline of the main duct is clearly visualized, demonstrating a normal calibre within the section lying in the sublingual space. The stone is lying at the genu of the duct and is wider than the duct anterior to it, indicating that simple basket retrieval along the duct would not be an option in this case. The hilar region of the duct is opacified by the contrast, and the secondary and tertiary ducts are demonstrated (arrows). In Fig. 64.3c, 1 minute after removal of the sialography catheter, the contrast has been lost from the main duct distal to the stone within the sublingual space. However, in the region of the stone, and proximal to this, that is, deeper into the ductal system, some contrast is retained (arrows), indicating that the duct is partially obstructed by the stone, preventing outflow.
[6876][Para 015] Treatment
[6877][Heading 2]  What is the Most Common Technique for Treating Sialolithiasis?
[6878][Para 001] Surgery has been the traditional method to manage salivary gland obstruction. Stones located in the distal-most parts of the submandibular and parotid ducts may sometimes be removed via an intraoral incision. If the stone is within the gland, surgery to remove the whole submandibular or superficial parotid gland has been the traditional way to remove the stone.
[6879][Heading 2]  What are the Complications of Surgery?
[6880][Para 001] Complications are rare but may be significant, causing distress to the patient. Submandibular gland removal is relatively simple and free of complications, but parotid gland surgery is difficult. The complications are described below.
[6881][Para 002] Frey’s syndrome, or gustatory sweating, results when parasympathetic nerves supplying the parotid or submandibular gland are cut to remove the gland. During healing, the nerves regrow and may innervate the sweat glands of the overlying skin. The affected skin then sweats, sometimes profusely, on eating or thinking of food. This is an unpleasant and distressing complication and is difficult to control with anticholinergic drugs. Administration of Botox injections into the affected skin is one means of managing this complication.
[6882][Para 002] Nerve palsy The facial nerve is at risk during superficial parotidectomy because it passes through the gland. Its mandibular branch, the marginal mandibular nerve, runs along the lower border of the mandible and is at risk if the incision for submandibular gland removal is placed too high. The hypoglossal nerve may be damaged during submandibular gland removal.
[6883][Para 002] Fistula formationIf part or all of the gland is left in situ, saliva may track along the incision, prevent healing and drain permanently to the exterior, facial skin in the case of a parotid fistula. In time, the tract will epithelialize and become chronically infected, resulting in a scar.
[6884][Heading 2]  Is a More Conservative Approach Possible?
[6885][Para 001] Yes, minimally invasive techniques for the management of salivary obstructive disease are available. These mostly aim to disrupt the stone so that the fragments are washed out by the flow of saliva. It is also possible to remove the stones as a whole and dilate the ductal stenoses. These techniques require careful selection of patients to ensure success, and there is always a possibility that they will fail and surgery will ultimately be required. Methods include those shown in Table 64.4.

[6897][Para 015] Another Possibility
[6898][Heading 2]  If the Obstruction Had Been Caused By a Stricture, How Would Your Management Have Differed?
[6899][Para 001] Strictures are caused by inflammatory fibrosis, usually around stones, although the stones may be passed spontaneously, leaving only the stricture. The duct proximal to a stricture often dilates because of back pressure, and a series of strictures and dilatations gives rise to the ‘string of sausages’ or ‘string of beads’ appearance on a sialogram. This appearance indicates inflammation around the duct or sialodochitis.
[6900][Para 002] Strictures located at or near a duct orifice may be dilated by introduction of graded lacrimal duct dilators or serial dilators. More proximally located strictures are less accessible and present a more difficult management problem, which has traditionally been treated with surgical resection of the gland. More recently, for the dilatation of strictures with the use of a balloon catheter, an adaptation of the techniques used in angioplasty has been developed (see Fig. 64.5). Although this is often successful, some strictures may relapse repeatedly, requiring alternative treatments such as surgery or medical management to ease symptoms by reducing salivary flow.

[6929][Para 001] Periodontal examination, including recording of probing depths and gingival bleeding. A wide pocket that can be probed to the apex would indicate a probable endodontic–periodontal lesion. A localized deep pocket would raise the suspicion of a vertical root fracture.
[6930][Para 002] Check the marginal integrity of the resin composite restoration by gently ‘drawing’ a straight ball-ended probe along and across the filling–tooth interface without pressure (pressure might cavitate any early carious lesions present).

[6936][Para 004] • Aid identification of the source of the sinus
[6937][Para 004] • Detect or exclude caries
[6938][Para 004] • Help eliminate root fracture as a cause. This is difficult as the fracture line would have to be in the line of the x-ray beam (bucco-palatally) to be visible and even then might be superimposed on the root canal or root filling
[6939][Para 004] • Confirm the alveolar bone levels.

[6957][Para 137] Treatment
[6958][Para 070]  How Would You Manage This Case?
[6959][Para 001] This retreatment case does not present particularly difficult challenges. Both on the periapical radiograph and on the CBCT image, the lumen of the canals is clearly visible beyond the root filling, suggesting that the canal has not been blocked with dentine. Also, the CBCT image clearly shows that the distance between the pulp floor and the furcation is at least 5–6 mm, ensuring ‘safe’ removal of the resin composite restorative material, which clearly reaches the pulpal floor, minimizing the risk of perforation at the furcation area.
[6960][Para 002] The resin composite material can be removed coronally by using high-speed burs and in the deeper part of the pulp chamber by using dedicated ultrasonic tips, which will aid in selective, minimally invasive removal of the material.
[6961][Para 002] Once a provisional working length is established by using the posteroanterior radiograph or the CBCT image, the gutta percha is removed by gently softening it with a drop of chloroform or other solvent and by using Hedström files size 25 or 30 ISO. Superflexible Ni-Ti files in reciprocation or in continuous rotation can also be used for this purpose. It is essential not to engage the Hedström files in the curves of the canals because such files are easily separated. The provisional working length is essential to prevent extrusion of gutta percha into the periapical tissues while attempting to remove it. This is a risk that is relevant clinically, particularly when the obturation is close to large apices.
[6962][Para 002] Once the existing root canal obturation material has been removed, it is essential to identify the orifice of the second mesio-buccal canal.
