[6992][Heading 2]  How Do You Assess the History So Far?
[6993][Para 001] Severe headaches with nausea and visual disturbance on an occasional basis would suggest migraine as a cause.
[6994][Para 002] However, migraine usually has onset in young or middle adulthood and would be unusual as a new diagnosis in a postmenopausal patient. The headache is not described as unilateral, as most migraines are, and there is no typical description of an aura. Dizziness, nausea and blurred vision, however, can be associated with migraine.
[6995][Para 002] Bruxism is irrelevant. It may be associated with masticatory muscle tenderness but is usually asymptomatic.
[6996][Heading 2]  What is the Role of the Dentist in Headache Diagnosis and Treatment?
[6997][Para 001] It would be wise to consider this question before dismissing the complaint, referring the patient to a medical practitioner or taking on analysis of the problem. A dentist would be expected to have a fairly broad knowledge of the signs, symptoms and causes of craniofacial pain, but mainly for diagnostic and patient referral purposes.
[6998][Para 002] The primary role of the dentist in headache is to exclude pain of dental or local origin. This is most important but not always easy.
[6999][Para 002] The key causes of pain of dental origin that might present as headache are:
[7000][Para 004] • Pulpitis and referred pain of dental origin
[7001][Para 004] • Sinusitis
[7002][Para 004] • Temporomandibular joint/myofascial pain disorders.
[7003][Para 002] In addition, some causes of head and neck pain can be misinterpreted by the patient as pain of dental origin, causing the patient to present to the dentist. The key causes to consider are:
[7004][Para 004] • Trigeminal and other neuralgias
[7005][Para 004] • Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (cluster headache-type conditions, including sudden-onset unilateral neuralgiform headache, with conjunctival irritation and tearing [SUNCT]).
[7006][Para 127] Table 66.1
[7007][Para 021] Questioning the Patient
[7008][Para 004] • Giant cell arteritis
[7009][Para 004] • Persistent idiopathic (atypical) facial pain.
[7010][Para 002] The dentist should be very familiar with these causes of pain and should also be able to diagnose many others. However, it is not the role of the dentist to undertake the primary diagnostic responsibility for other causes of headache or chronic orofacial pain. Orofacial pain is usually managed by a multidisciplinary team, which may well include a dentist, and in such a setting, the dentist may take on considerably more responsibility. In other settings, the dentist will not have the necessary neurological knowledge or access to investigations.
[7011][Para 002] Some dentists extend their care to treatment of headache, migraine and a range of musculoskeletal pains. There is danger of extending beyond one’s competence or to nonorthodox treatments without a good evidence base.
[7012][Para 002] Your role in the management of true headache, whether in primary or secondary care, should be limited to:
[7013][Para 004] • Identifying and treating dental causes, or
[7014][Para 004] • Making a provisional diagnosis
[7015][Para 004] • Ensuring appropriate referral
[7016][Para 004] • Informing the patient about possible causes and treatments.
[7017][Para 002] One of the most important factors is to be able to identify any sinister signs that might indicate significant underlying disease.
[7018][Heading 2]  What Further Information Do You Need?
[7019][Para 001] You will need to question the patient for further details about the features that are listed in the left column of Table 66.1. When you do this, the patient gives the answers shown in the right column.
[7020][Heading 2]  How Can Pulpitis Be Excluded As a Cause of Craniofacial Pain?
[7021][Para 001] Toothache is the commonest cause of pain sensed by the trigeminal system. Diagnosis of toothache is discussed under several other cases in this book. The key features of pulpitis are that it may be intermittent or constant, sometimes with a dental trigger; exacerbated by hot, cold and osmotic stimuli; and may be poorly localized. Periapical periodontitis, sensed in the periodontal ligament, is well localized and sensitive only to pressure. Pain from multirooted teeth may have both a pulpal and periodontal components.
[7022][Para 002] The main problems in excluding pulpal pain are caused by teeth with cracks or low-grade chronic pulpitis, such as in teeth with leaking restorations or small amounts of caries below restorations. When a cause is not evident, it may be necessary to investigate a number of teeth by performing tests of vitality, replace restorations and place orthodontic bands or copper rings to exclude cracks; this may be quite time consuming and require several visits. Short, stabbing neuralgia-type pain from a pulpitic or cracked tooth can often be detected with cold stimulation or by applying biting pressure on to individual cusps.
[7023][Para 002] One of the most useful diagnostic features of toothache is the patient’s interpretation of the pain. In past decades, when dental disease was prevalent, most patients would have sufficient experience to make a clear diagnosis themselves. Now that caries is less prevalent and less extensive, patients may have no experience of either the severity or the poor localization of toothache and so attribute the pain to other causes.
[7024][Para 002] Pain from the pulp is classically poorly localized and may radiate to other teeth, the opposite jaw, the temporal region or any area supplied by the trigeminal nerve. More rarely, pain can be referred to trigeminal nerves from areas innervated by other cranial nerves and even cervical spinal nerves. Referred pain may be as severe as nonreferred pain, but there is usually a component of pain felt locally to aid diagnosis. Dental pain misinterpreted as headache is usually felt on the front and sides of the head. Referred pain will not radiate across the midline.
[7025][Para 002] Referred pain can be a major diagnostic problem. When a dental cause is suspected, a long-lasting Marcain local analgesic may be applied to suspected sources in an attempt to find out whether it blocks the pain. However, response to diagnostic blocks is not necessarily definitive because there is a strong placebo effect.
[7026][Para 002] The character and distribution of the pain in this patient exclude all dental causes.
[7027][Heading 2]  How May Pain of Temporomandibular Disorders Be Excluded?
[7028][Para 001] This pain originates in the muscles of mastication, is felt there and is referred to the superficial tissues in and around the joint and the ear. It may be identified by its distribution and accompanying signs of abnormal mandibular movement. Because the symptoms can be very variable, a diagnostic appliance may be helpful.
[7029][Para 002] Pain may be unilateral or bilateral and tends to be a dull, constant pain that is worsened on mouth opening, on biting hard foods or on palpation of the joints. There may be wear facets indicating bruxism or another mandibular parafunction.
[7030][Para 002] This pain is often misinterpreted as headache by patients, but it is superficial and should not be confused with intracranial pain.
[7031][Para 002] The character and distribution of the pain in this case immediately exclude this cause.
[7032][Heading 2]  How Can Sinusitis Be Excluded As a Cause of Headache?
[7033][Para 001] Sinusitis usually follows an upper respiratory tract infection and is accompanied by nasal obstruction or stuffiness. The pain is usually well localized and is more likely to be confused with toothache than with headache. Maxillary sinusitis causes tenderness of the teeth adjacent to the sinus. If the sinus is fluid filled, the pain may alter with posture. Only sinusitis in the sphenoid, ethmoid and frontal sinuses is likely to be confused with headache, but even there, sinusitis is considered a very rare cause of headache.
[7034][Para 002] A high proportion of self-reported and physician-reported chronic sinusitis may be caused by migraine. Sinusitis may be of dental origin if inflammation spreads from the roots of the upper molar teeth. There may then be additional pain of dental origin.
[7035][Para 002] The pain in this patient is predominantly posterior, acute and severe. Sinusitis cannot be the cause.
[7036][Heading 2]  Are There Other Headache-Like Pains That May Be Mistaken for Dental Pain?
[7037][Para 001] Yes, and the most important is probably temporal arteritis (giant cell arteritis). The pain of temporal arteritis is felt in and around the temporal artery and muscle but is frequently referred to the jaws or teeth and mistaken for toothache. The temporal artery wall is inflamed and gradually destroyed by inflammatory cells, including multinucleate giant cells, and the lumen is occluded. Ischaemia of the temporal muscle is felt as pain on mastication.
[7038][Para 002] The same process affects other branches of the carotid artery, including the ophthalmic artery, and so blindness may result. This can happen very quickly, and a suspected diagnosis of temporal arteritis should be investigated as an emergency. The tender enlarged artery may be palpable. Diagnosis is supported by a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate; biopsy of the artery is diagnostic, although corticosteroids are often started immediately because of the risk of blindness.
[7039][Para 002] Other causes of referred pain include obstructive salivary disease, earache and joint pain from degenerative disease of the cervical spine.
[7040][Heading 2]  Could This Patient Have Neuralgia?
[7041][Para 001] Neuralgia is pain felt in the distribution of a nerve and that is not triggered by a normal pain stimulus. It may result from nerve hypersensitivity or central causes and be acute or chronic but is not felt by the patient to be a headache. Trigeminal neuralgia is more likely to be misconstrued as severe pulpitis, and teeth may be unnecessarily extracted or filled before the diagnosis is made. It particularly mimics the pain of a cracked tooth. Atypical trigeminal neuralgia, with its constant pain and wider distribution, is often misconstrued as migraine, dental pain, temporomandibular joint pain dysfunction or atypical facial pain.
[7042][Para 002] The features of cranial nerve neuralgias are shown in Table 66.2.
[7043][Para 002] When a pain of trigeminal or glossopharyngeal neuralgia-type is diagnosed in a patient younger than 50 years of age, there is a possibility that it has a central origin such as a neoplasm or multiple sclerosis and must be investigated. Similar acute or chronic, often chronic burning, nerve pain is also experienced by those suffering from peripheral neuropathy, which may accompany diabetes, chemotherapy, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and other conditions. Neuralgic pain may also follow nerve damage caused by trauma or surgery. Greater than 70% of patients with lingual or inferior alveolar nerve damage present with neuralgia.
[7044][Para 002] This patient’s pain does not follow the sensory distribution of the cranial nerves. The character and distribution are different; this is not neuralgia.

[7046][Para 001] The common causes of recurrent headache are shown in Table 66.3. An occasional headache is so common that it is often regarded as normal. In all, 80% of the population have had at least one tension-type headache in the previous year. Only intermittent, but relatively frequent, headaches that meet the criteria listed in Table 66.3 are amenable to diagnosis without specialist knowledge and investigations.

[7055][Heading 2]  Could This Be a Pain of Idiopathic Origin?
[7056][Para 001] In the current classification of headache and craniofacial and oral pain, there are several categories of idiopathic facial pain with defined diagnostic criteria. These include the entities of persistent idiopathic facial pain (atypical facial pain and atypical odontalgia). Useful features are unusual descriptions of pain and distributions that appear anatomically impossible, crossing dermatomes or the midline. Burning mouth syndrome is another type of idiopathic facial pain and is now recognized as neuropathy. All these conditions are characterized by constant pain that may regress spontaneously. These diagnoses should not be applied until all possible causes have been excluded; they are best supported by the results of investigation in a specialized pain centre.
[7057][Para 002] There are no features to suggest that this patient has an idiopathic pain. All other causes must be excluded before this diagnosis can be entertained.
[7058][Para 015] Differential Diagnosis
[7059][Heading 2]  What is Your Differential Diagnosis? What Would You Do Next?
[7060][Para 001] This is a true headache. Of the other potential causes, only migraine remains a possibility, but as noted above, this is unlikely. No definitive diagnosis is possible, but there are several features that suggest that this is a sinister headache.
[7061][Para 004] • Sudden onset
[7062][Para 004] • Acute, extreme pain
[7063][Para 004] • Few discrete headaches, all severe
[7064][Para 004] • Associated with nausea and visual disturbance.
[7065][Para 002] The patient is overweight, is a smoker, and is likely to have peripheral vascular disease; there must be concern that these unusual headaches might be caused by minor strokes or leakage from a subarachnoid vessel or an aneurysm. There is no muscle weakness and loss of consciousness to confirm the diagnosis of stroke, and these symptoms are usually present when stroke is the cause. However, headache is the commonest preceding symptom of subarachnoid haemorrhage and is seen in about half the cases with a ruptured aneurysm.

[7102][Heading 2]  What Features of the Intraoral Examination are Particularly Important in This Patient?
[7103][Para 001] Examine the whole mouth and the visible oropharynx for carcinoma and potentially malignant changes.
[7104][Para 002] People who have had oral cancer will be under review in their cancer centre, usually for 5 years. They will be checked regularly for recurrence. Although recurrence of oropharyngeal carcinoma may be difficult to see in a routine dental examination, every opportunity to examine for recurrence must be taken.
[7105][Para 002] In addition, the patient is a former smoker and is at risk of a second primary carcinoma. Approximately 10% of patients with oral carcinoma develop a second primary, and so, with this in mind, the mouth must be examined carefully. Second primary cancers are less likely to occur after tonsil and oropharynx carcinomas caused by human papillomavirus, but not all carcinomas at these sites are caused by the virus. A careful examination of the mouth and the visible pharynx is required.
[7106][Para 015] Diagnosis
[7107][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[7108][Para 001] The patient has radiation caries. This name is given to aggressive caries that occurs frequently after radiation to the head and neck region. Here, it shows the classic distribution of lesions at the incisal edges, the tips of cusps and the cervical margin.
[7109][Heading 2]  What is the Significance of This Diagnosis?
[7110][Para 001] The whole dentine may be affected, but the enamel shell remains largely intact and pain is not generally reported. Caries may become very extensive and go unnoticed until teeth fracture.
[7111][Heading 2]  What are the Factors Contributing To Radiation Caries?
[7112][Para 001] Reduced quantity and buffering capacity saliva caused by radiation effects on the salivary gland. Other contributory factors are high-sugar diet; reduced oral clearance of sugars; poor oral hygiene, often compounded by limited mouth opening; and a sore mouth. Changes in the oral flora may be a factor.

[7116][Para 009]  
[7117][Heading 2]  Why Can the Salivary Glands Not Be Protected During Radiotherapy?
[7118][Para 001] Radiotherapy (use of ionizing radiation to treat disease, usually x-rays to treat cancer) also damages normal tissue. Because so many important and radiosensitive tissues lie in the head and neck region (particularly salivary glands, eye, spinal cord and thyroid gland), protecting them is difficult, and some compromise often has to be made between effective cancer treatment and its adverse effects.
[7119][Para 002] The full curative dose for most head and neck cancers is 60–65 grays (Gy; 1 Gy is the absorption of 1 joule of radiation energy per kilogram), but mild salivary gland damage can be detected after only 4 Gy, and severe permanent damage occurs with doses above 30 Gy to the glands. Some protection is provided by fractionation, delivering the total dose in small daily amounts or fractions, usually 2 Gy each weekday for 6 weeks. Fractionation allows some recovery time between treatments, thus reducing toxicity to normal tissues. However, if the salivary glands lie in the path of the beam as it passes from skin to cancer, fractionation offers insufficient protection, and complete dry mouth will occur during treatment, with partial and slow recovery afterwards.
[7120][Para 002] Additional protection is provided by using intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT). This method uses multiple smaller ‘beamlets’ to converge on the cancer from different directions. The intensity and shape of the beams change at each fraction and are calculated to match the size of the tumour from each direction. These features guarantee the necessary high dose to the tumour while greatly reducing the dose to the sensitive normal surrounding tissues. An example of a radiotherapy planning scan is provided in Fig. 67.4, which shows the areas of different radiation intensities colour coded, with the highest dose in red and lowest in blue. You can see two features of importance. The first is that the salivary glands will get irradiated. The second is how closely the effective dose is applied to the carcinoma. If the patient were not correctly aligned in the beams, even by only a few millimetres, part of the tumour might receive an insufficient dose. To ensure accurate beam delivery, the patient must be held immobile under a hard plastic mesh mask (Fig. 67.4), making radiotherapy a very claustrophobic experience. With the use of IMRT, the dose to the salivary gland and the mucosa can be substantially reduced, but not abolished; and a degree of dry mouth always follows radiation to the mouth, nose, nasopharynx and oropharynx.
[7121][Para 218] 
[7122][Para 008] 
[7123][Para 011] Fig. 67.4 Radiotherapy planning scan (left) showing the effective radiation dose to the target volume in red, around the left tonsil and lymph nodes lying posteriorly. The dose is achieved by multiple intersecting beams of x-rays. Note how the right parotid gland, outlined in orange (arrow) has been spared by bringing the beam in from behind its posterior margin. However, the left parotid gland, although not receiving a full dose, will absorb a significant radiation dose, as will much of the oral and nasal mucosae and the left submandibular gland (not in the plane of this computed tomography [CT] slice). Note how the red zone of full effective dose is tightly defined, and only a few millimetres misplacement of the patient’s head would allow part of the carcinoma to receive only a partial ineffective dose. [7126][Para 021] Adverse Effects of Radiotherapy To the Mouth and Adjacent Areas
[7127][Para 002] The minor glands in the mucosa, although only producing 10% of the total volume of saliva, produce the majority of mucins, which serve as lubricants and aid hydration of the mucosa.
[7128][Para 002] Although there may be recovery of salivary function for up to 2 years after radiotherapy, xerostomia is a distressing long-term effect. Generally, patients use sips of water for symptomatic relief; salivary substitutes could also be tried.
[7129][Heading 2]  What are the Other Adverse Effects of Radiation To the Mouth and Adjacent Areas? Has This Patient Developed Others?
[7130][Para 001] Radiotherapy effects are divided into early, longer-term, and general effects and are listed in Table 67.1.
[7131][Para 002] Oral mucositis – inflammation of the mouth – affects all patients initially. Its features include erythema, ulceration, swelling and atrophy. It causes extreme soreness and can prevent eating, necessitating nasogastric or percutaneous feeding during and for quite a while after cancer treatment.
[7132][Para 002] This patient has limited mouth opening, most likely as a consequence of fibrosis in the masticatory muscles. Similar changes may also result from scarring after surgery. If trismus were of recent onset and progressive, there would be a suspicion that it may be caused by tumour infiltrating the muscles and thus indicate recurrence; otherwise, radiation is the likely cause.
[7133][Para 015] Investigations
[7134][Heading 2]  What Investigations and Additional History are Required? Explain Why
[7135][Para 001] Clinical and radiological examinations. These are performed to assess the extent of caries, periodontal condition, any periapical disease, alveolar bone levels and restorability of teeth.
[7136][Para 002] Oral care habits. Ask patients whether they are brushing their teeth and about their toothpaste use. Patients may stop brushing during the painful period of mucositis because this condition renders the mouth too sensitive to toothpaste.
[7137][Para 002] Ask about food intake. Many patients have difficulty eating during and after radiotherapy because of painful mucositis, taste disturbance, dryness and muscle fibrosis affecting chewing and swallowing. They may be prescribed high-calorie food supplements to maintain their weight, but these have high sugar content. Some patients with cancer may consume up to 10 sugary supplements a day and continue to use supplements long after active treatment because swallowing continues to be difficult, and preparation of special foods can be time consuming.
[7138][Para 015] Treatment
[7139][Heading 2]  What are the Treatment Options?
[7140][Para 001] The ideal treatment would maintain the teeth with restorations and periodontal treatment, thus avoiding extractions or periodontal surgery. Treatments, including restorations, root surface debridement and use of local anaesthetic, can be carried out without special precautions. Dentures can be constructed but should be reviewed regularly to check for mucosal trauma, which could precipitate osteoradionecrosis (ORN). For this reason, it is best that the patient manages without replacement of missing teeth, for example, with a shortened dental arch. Dentures are more difficult to manage with xerostomia, and there is greater risk of Candida infection and increased caries risk in an already vulnerable mouth. Implant construction after cancer treatment should be done by a specialist. It may be the only option if jaw resection was carried out. Implants in areas of bone that have been subjected to high-dose radiotherapy should be avoided.
[7141][Heading 2]  What is Osteoradionecrosis?
[7142][Para 001] ORN is osteomyelitis affecting bone after radiotherapy. Most cases of osteomyelitis of the jaws have a local or systemic predisposing factor, and irradiation acts by reducing the vascularity of the bone.
[7143][Para 002] ORN, by definition, is present when there is exposed devitalised bone for greater than 3 months in an area that has been irradiated. It may present with pain, redness, swelling, altered sensation, discharge, skin fistula or a pathological fracture. ORN may arise spontaneously but develops most often after an extraction. Risk factors for ORN are shown in Table 67.2.
[7144][Para 018] Table 67.2
[7145][Para 021] Risk Factors for Osteoradionecrosis
[7146][Para 002] ORN is very resistant to treatment. Antibiotics do not penetrate well to the site of infection, and healing is compromised by the reduced vascularity. Patients with suspected ORN should be referred to a specialist oral surgeon. Management may be conservative, but sometimes surgery and bone grafting may be needed.
[7147][Heading 2]  How Could You Manage Very Broken Down Teeth in the Radiation Field?
[7148][Para 001] Find out from the patient’s oncologist the dose of radiation the patient received to the area concerned. If a tooth is on the same side as the cancer and the patient had a full course of curative radiotherapy, extraction would carry a high risk for ORN. Ideally, extractions should be avoided and teeth managed conservatively. Root treatment and decoronation of teeth are preferable if the risk is high.
[7149][Para 002] The risk of ORN is lifelong. Patients should be referred to an oral surgeon if an extraction is required.
[7150][Heading 2]  Why Has This Patient Suffered Such Severe Complications?
[7151][Para 001] This patient never had a dental assessment prior to radiotherapy. Such an assessment with treatment of pre-existing disease dramatically reduces the risks of oral complications later. The patient should have been given information about the oral complications of radiotherapy and preventive advice. Oral disease would have been treated and necessary extractions performed prior to treatment. Such assessments are usually arranged with specialist dentists attached to the head and neck cancer team.
[7152][Heading 2]  Which Teeth Should Be Extracted Prior To Radiotherapy?
[7153][Para 001] Teeth that are infected, unrestorable or have pockets of greater than 5 mm depth should be extracted. Extraction of partially erupted third molars, as well as any teeth that are likely to become inaccessible after cancer treatment, is recommended, bearing in mind that there is a high risk of caries needing treatment in the future and of reduced mouth opening.
[7154][Para 002] Other teeth must be assessed, taking several factors into account: the position of the tooth, volume of radiation to the area, strategic importance of the tooth and patient choice and compliance. Extraction of the second and third molars may often be recommended in cases of tonsillar or tongue base cancer, where a high radiation dose is given to the tooth-bearing area.
[7155][Para 002] Any necessary extractions should be done as soon as possible to allow time (minimum 10 days) for healing before radiotherapy is started.
[7156][Para 002] Patients should be given information about the risks of radiotherapy and instructed to always inform their dentist about the treatment they have had. An alert card is useful for this.
[7157][Heading 2]  What Preventive Advice Would You Give the Patients?
[7158][Para 001] After radiotherapy, the mouth becomes very sore, and brushing is difficult, and so a very soft brush may be necessary. Once the soreness reduces, a medium manual or electric toothbrush should be used twice a day. High-fluoride toothpaste (e.g. Duraphat 5000) should be prescribed and continued lifelong; excess toothpaste should be spat out without rinsing. Sugary dietary supplements should be discontinued as soon as possible in consultation with the patient’s dietitian. Taking supplements through a straw will reduce adhesion to teeth, and rinsing with alcohol-free fluoride mouthwash after each supplement may be helpful in reducing caries.
[7159][Para 024]  What is the Role of the General Dental Practitioner?
[7160][Para 004] • Do not assume that patients with cancer will receive routine dental care in the hospital.
[7161][Para 004] • Recommend regular recalls at least every 6 months to ensure that any dental disease is identified and treated early.
[7162][Para 004] • Reinforce advice on smoking cessation and moderating alcohol intake.
[7163][Para 004] • Reinforce preventive care, with instructions on oral hygiene, application of fluoride varnish at least twice a year and use of high-fluoride toothpaste.
[7164][Para 004] • Carry out restorative treatment, if required, or refer to a specialist.
[7165][Para 004] • Refer to oral surgery if extraction is considered the only option for a tooth.
[7166][Para 004] • Treat candidosis.
[7167][Para 004] • Be observant for ORN, which may occur after slight trauma, for example, from a denture or spontaneously.
[7168][Para 004] • Be aware of the risk of recurrence or a new primary, and carefully examine the mouth, visible oropharynx and neck.
[7169][Para 004] • Make prompt referral in case of suspicious lesions.
[7170][Para 025] Case 68
[7171][Heading 1] Should I Repair or Replace These Restorations? – the ‘5 Rs’
[7172][Para 027] Louis Mackenzie, and Avijit Banerjee
[7173][Para 028] Summary
[7174][Para 029] A 40-year-old woman presents as a new patient at your general dental practice complaining of two fractured teeth and requesting advice on treatment options. Assess and diagnose the condition of the restorations, and identify the management options that can be presented to the patient.
[7175][Para 014] History
[7176][Para 019] Complaint
[7177][Para 007] The patient recently fractured two teeth whilst eating – the mandibular right first permanent molar, which is uncomfortable on biting and is sensitive to thermal stimuli, and the maxillary left first permanent premolar. The patient also has aesthetic concerns regarding staining around the direct resin composite restorations on her maxillary left central incisor and mandibular left first permanent molar and is also concerned about the appearance of a porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crown restoring her maxillary right first premolar.
[7178][Para 012] Dental History
[7179][Para 007] The patient has not visited a dentist for 7 years. Previously, she was a regular attender and underwent a range of restorative procedures between the ages of 20 and 30 years. She has a healthy diet, good oral hygiene and no medical conditions that would complicate dental treatment.
[7180][Para 014] Examination
[7181][Para 007] Extraoral and soft tissue examinations detected no pathology, but intraoral examination revealed the following positive findings, which are illustrated in  Fig. 68.1 .
[7182][Para 016] 1. Fractured, mobile, disto-lingual cusp on the mandibular right first molar adjacent to an occlusal amalgam restoration
[7183][Para 016] 2. Fractured buccal cusp of the maxillary left first premolar adjacent to a mesio-occlusal-distal amalgam
[7184][Para 016] 3. Marginal staining of a class IV resin composite restoring the maxillary left central incisor
[7185][Para 016] 4. Marginal staining of the occlusal resin composite restoring the mandibular left first molar
[7186][Para 016] 5. Open buccal margin on the PFM crown restoring the maxillary right first premolar.
[7187][Para 014] Assessment of Failing Restorations
[7188][Para 001] Failing dental restorations exhibiting minor defects are a common clinical occurrence in everyday dental practice, representing the major part of contemporary general dental practice, with greater than 50% of all operative procedures being carried out for this reason. Caries associated with restorations and sealants (CARS – secondary caries) is the most prevalent reason given for restoration replacements, regardless of the restorative material used. The subjective nature of diagnosing restorative failure presents challenges, and it is widely acknowledged that the unnecessary replacement of ‘sound’ restorations is common, resulting in a range of negative consequences, including those listed below:
[7189][Para 004] • Every time a restoration is removed cavities become significantly larger regardless of material because of cavity overpreparation.
[7190][Para 004] • Further preparation weakens residual tooth tissue.
[7191][Para 004] • Operative intervention may initiate or precipitate cracks/fractures.
[7192][Para 004] • Operative treatment may cause further damage to the dentine–pulp complex.
[7193][Para 004] • Operative interventions involving proximal surfaces carry a very high risk of iatrogenic damage to the adjacent structures.
[7194][Para 004] • Deepening proximal preparations increases the risk of damaging the periodontal attachment (biological width violation).
[7195][Para 004] • As restorations become larger, there is increased risk of future failure.
[7196][Para 004] • Increased length of restorative margins may increase risk of microleakage and CARS.
[7197][Para 221] 
[7198][Para 092] 
[7199][Para 093] Fig. 68.1 Clinical views of the teeth the patient has concerns over.
[7200][Para 004] • Complete removal of restorations increases restorative difficulty and may result in unrestorable clinical conditions.
[7201][Para 004] • The interval to the next restorative intervention may be progressively shortened.
[7202][Para 004] • Unnecessary restorations waste clinical time and resources.
[7203][Para 114] Assessment Training
[7204][Para 001] It is widely reported that when assessing failing restorations, individual clinicians are inconsistent in their decision making and that wide variation exists among dentists in deciding whether or not to replace a restoration. This has a major negative impact on the validity of clinical studies designed to measure restoration longevity.
[7205][Para 002] With regard to the number of existing restorations examined, accuracy of assessment is an important clinical skill. Training in the assessment of existing restorations has been demonstrated to result in significant improvement in clinical performance by offering the following benefits:
[7206][Para 004] • Measuring and describing failure results through clearer thought processes
[7207][Para 004] • Removal of subjective decision making, thus increasing reliability and reproducibility
[7208][Para 004] • Internalization of objective assessment skills, resulting in faster, more accurate diagnoses.
[7209][Para 114] Evaluating the Clinical Quality of Restorations
[7210][Para 001] When assessing existing restorations, the operator’s vision is the most important tool, and it may be significantly improved by the use of magnification and good lighting. Clinical photography is an essential skill in contemporary dental practice; in addition to improving diagnostic accuracy and patient communication, high-quality clinical images of the patient’s preoperative condition form an important dento-legal record.
[7211][Para 002] After visual examination, further investigations such as the use of measuring probes, articulating paper, pulp testing, shade measurements and radiographs (where justified) may be used to obtain additional information.
[7212][Para 002] Use of high-quality, standardized radiographic images is an important diagnostic and monitoring tool, but training is also recommended for the radiographic assessment of existing restorations to overcome the challenges of diagnosing radiolucencies, superimposition and masking by radiopaque materials.
[7213][Para 012] Classifying Restorative Failure
[7214][Para 001] The Ryge standardized method of classifying tooth–restoration complex (TRC) failures has been available since the 1970s. This well-respected system was designed to help improve the accuracy and consistency of decision making and to enhance the reliability and relevance of clinical studies.
[7215][Para 008] 
[7216][Para 011] Fig. 68.2 Radiographic appearance of the lower left first permanent molar restored with an occlusal resin composite.
[7217][Para 009]  
[7218][Para 002] More recently, a clinical evaluation system – Hickel classification system – has been introduced, and it aims to provide a more sensitive scale that enables the early detection of restorative deterioration and the accurate monitoring of subtle differences over time. This system defines the clinical criteria for the evaluation of direct and indirect restorations and is designed to provide a benchmark to assist practitioners in making accurate decisions, thereby reducing the risk of unnecessary treatment and overtreatment. The classification is divided into three separate indices:
[7219][Para 004] • Aesthetics (four subcriteria)
[7220][Para 004] • Function (six subcriteria)
[7221][Para 004] • Biology (six subcriteria).
[7222][Para 002] Each of the 16 restorative assessment criteria is given a score on a five-point scale. Scores 1, 2 and 3 divide acceptable restorations into three distinct categories, and there are two further categories defining unsatisfactory restorations. See Table 68.1.
[7223][Para 002] The Hickel system provides a standardized classification of the common types of restorative failure and provides guidelines that describe the timing of failure. See Table 68.2.

[7227][Para 016] 2. Use Table 68.4 to assess the functional condition of the restoration.
[7228][Para 016] 3. Use Table 68.5 to assess the biological condition of the restoration.

[7250][Para 002] Clinical photographs are useful for documenting aesthetic assessment findings and may be supported by using colour measurements with an appropriate shade guide. Formal written consent is required for clinical photography, and all photographs should be documented and reported, as part of the patient’s confidential clinical record.
[7251][Para 002] Although fractures, open contacts and abnormal wear are relatively easy to diagnose, marginal adaptation is much more challenging, and its inaccurate diagnosis probably results in more unnecessary restoration replacements than any other assessment parameter. When assessing restorative margins, it is vital to remember that:
[7252][Para 004] • A discoloured margin is not indicative of CARS
[7253][Para 004] • The majority of restorations present with overfilled (43%) and underfilled (25%) margins
[7254][Para 004] • Gap width, depth and continuity of margins are important considerations when assessing marginal defects
[7255][Para 004] • In easily accessible areas gap widths in excess of 400 μm are necessary for secondary caries to develop.
[7256][Para 002] CARS is identical to primary caries, but it occurs adjacent to the margin of existing restorations. There is general agreement that epidemic levels of overdiagnosis of CARS exists and that many restorations are unnecessarily replaced as a result. Marginal discolouration and localized restoration defects are commonly misdiagnosed as secondary caries. When assessing restorative margins, it is essential to carefully consider that:
[7257][Para 004] • There is poor correlation between marginal appearance and histological findings
[7258][Para 004] • CARS is an infrequent occurrence with resin composite restorations when placed under ideal conditions
[7259][Para 004] • CARS is diagnosed most commonly at proximal cervical margins, but the clinically relevant gap dimensions required for its development are not clear
[7260][Para 004] • Use of the International Caries Detection and Assessment System (ICDAS) is recommended when assessing, monitoring and diagnosing defects at the margins of existing restorations
[7261][Para 004] • Like primary caries, CARS is multifactorial
[7262][Para 004] • Accurate diagnosis of CARS is difficult
[7263][Para 004] • The differentiation between inactive and active caries is fundamental to successful management.
[7264][Para 014] Minimum-Intervention Treatment Options
[7265][Para 001] Prevention is the cornerstone of minimum-intervention management of existing restorations.
[7266][Para 004] • Modifying patient behaviour with regard to maintenance increases restoration longevity by reducing the risk of failure
[7267][Para 004] • Failure to educate and monitor patient adherence to recommended dietary and plaque control protocols will increase the likelihood of premature restoration failure
[7268][Para 004] • In many clinical situations, restorations with minor defects may be maintained successfully for many years through good oral hygiene practices alone
[7269][Para 002] Once preventive patient factors have been optimized, minimally invasive management strategies should be prioritized because improvement in clinical conditions has been demonstrated to result in a significant increase in the functional longevity of restorations. Minimally invasive management options may be classified using the ‘5 Rs’ system (Table 68.6).

[7272][Para 049] Review
[7273][Para 020] Diagnosis
[7274][Para 001] This occlusal resin composite restoration on the mandibular left first permanent molar has a number of small (< 150 μm), interrupted, marginal gaps affecting approximately 50% of the restorative margin (functional assessment: grade 2) (Fig. 68.3).
[7275][Para 002] The suspected aetiology is that an occlusal bevel may have been placed around the outline form of the cavity during preparation. Thin extensions of marginal resin composite may then have fractured under occlusal loads and resulted in shallow defects susceptible to extrinsic marginal staining.
[7276][Para 020] Management
[7277][Para 001] It is reported that dentists are more likely to resort to surgical interventions when existing restorations are made of resin composite compared with amalgam. As the clinical images in Fig. 68.4 (taken 8 years apart) demonstrate, it is usually unnecessary to replace restorations solely on the basis of a diagnosis of marginal staining. No treatment was carried out for this tooth. The restoration will be monitored at routine examination appointments, and the patient is reassured that there is no CARS present and that removal and replacement aimed at aesthetic improvement would result in unnecessary cavity enlargement.

[7281][Para 020] Management
[7282][Para 001] The presence of marginal excess beyond the outline form of cavities restored with direct composite is a common clinical finding. Where excess is in accessible locations, it can very easily be removed by using appropriate rotary instruments at negligible biological cost, as was carried out in this clinical example. Recontouring and repolishing surfaces have also been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of unnecessary restoration replacement for amalgam restorations.

[7288][Para 020] Diagnosis
[7289][Para 001] Direct and indirect restorations with defects are common clinical presentations. For example, most crowns are reported to have poor resemblance to adjacent residual dentition, and these differences are obvious to both patients and clinicians.
[7290][Para 002] In this clinical example, the shade and translucency of the PFM crown on the maxillary right first premolar do not match those of the adjacent teeth (Fig. 68.5) (aesthetic assessment – grade 3: clear deviation, but acceptable to patient in this case), and a gap (> 250 μm) is present on the buccal margin, with dentine exposure after the dissolution of luting cement (functional assessment: grade 4). [7291][Para 002] Special investigations revealed that the abutment tooth responded positively to thermal pulp sensibility tests, and no radiographic pathology, other than the radiolucent appearance of the open margin, was detected.
[7292][Para 020] Management
[7293][Para 001] As the patient was willing to accept the aesthetic defects and was keen to minimize the expense of restoration replacement, the open buccal margin was cleaned with hand and small rotary instruments, revealing minimal carious demineralization and no extension into inaccessible proximal areas. The margin was sealed with resin-modified glass–ionomer cement (RMGIC) to reduce the risk of CARS (see Fig. 68.5). The patient has been happy with this minimally invasive resealing procedure, the result of which has now been successful for 3 years. The restoration is being monitored at routine assessment appointments, and radiographic examinations are repeated at appropriate intervals based on the patient’s current caries susceptibility.
[7294][Para 049] Repair
[7295][Para 020] Diagnosis
[7296][Para 001] Tooth tissue fractures adjacent to intracoronal restorations are a common finding because tooth preparation weakens the residual tooth structure. In this case, the disto-lingual cusp of the mandibular right first permanent molar has fractured and is retained only by weak attachment to the periodontal ligament (Fig. 68.6) (biological assessment: grade 5).
[7297][Para 218] 
[7298][Para 008] 
[7299][Para 011] Fig. 68.4 Upper left incisor (UL1 or 9) before and after the resin composite restoration surface was polished/refurbished, removing the aesthetically displeasing stained margin.
[7300][Para 009]  
[7301][Para 008] 
[7302][Para 011] Fig. 68.5 Upper right premolar showing defective crown margin that has been resealed with resin-modified glass–ionomer cement (RMGIC) to aid aesthetics and cleansability.
[7303][Para 009]  
[7304][Para 008] 
[7305][Para 011] Fig. 68.6 Fracture disto-lingual cusp of lower right molar (LR6 or 30), which has been repaired using dental amalgam and finally polished to reduce biofilm accretion.
[7306][Para 009]  
[7307][Para 020] Management
[7308][Para 001] Although it is reported to be dentists’ least favoured option, repair should be considered as the first option in contemporary minimally invasive operative practice because repairs have been demonstrated to be successful, with high bond strengths reported for both amalgam and resin composite repairs. Repairs also reduce the risk of further tooth tissue fracture, which is a common complication of total removal of restorations.
[7309][Para 002] As in this example, repairs may require removal of the localized defective part of the tooth–restoration complex. Cavity shapes may also require modification to increase resistance and retention form by preparation with burs and/or particle air abrasion, and the use of adhesives for resin composite repair. The dovetail preparation used in this amalgam repair technique does not require the use of adhesives because the new amalgam develops high bond strengths with the residual amalgam.
[7310][Para 049] Replace
[7311][Para 020] Diagnosis
[7312][Para 130] When fractures occur in the aesthetic zone, patients will usually request a tooth-coloured restoration, as in this example of the UL4 (Fig. 68.7) (aesthetic assessment – grade 5: desire for improvement; functional assessment – grade 5: filling loose in-situ; biological assessment – grade 5: cusp fracture).
[7313][Para 020] Management
[7314][Para 001] Although total restoration replacement may be associated with a range of complications (listed previously), minimally invasive strategies may still be employed, as in this example.
[7315][Para 002] As the retention of the residual amalgam restoration was uncertain, it was removed completely. The colour contrast of amalgam allows this to be done conservatively and the resultant mesio-occlusal-disto-buccal cavity was restored with a direct resin composite restoration, which will be reviewed at routine examination appointments.
[7316][Para 014] Medico-Legal Issues
[7317][Para 001] As in all cases, the patient must been taken along the decision-making journey with the dentists and the oral healthcare team. Managing the failing TRC forms a large part of the clinical work carried out by oral healthcare practitioners. Replacing restorations must only be carried out in those clinical situations where no other alternative exists. The consequences of the ‘5 Rs management’ strategy should be fully discussed with the patient and clearly documented in the patient’s records, along with the results of all investigations and the clinical photographs taken, with date stamps and annotations, where necessary. Consent must be obtained from the patient, and no operative intervention should be commenced without careful diagnosis of the cause of failure and the successful application of nonoperative preventive regimens by the patient.

[7341][Para 028] Summary
[7342][Para 029] A 30-year-old man presents to you with missing central and lateral incisors. What are the treatment options and their likely chances of success?

[7351][Para 007] The patient fell 6 months ago and knocked out his two front teeth. He has been wearing an immediate replacement denture since.

[7355][Para 007] The patient is otherwise fit and well.

[7357][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[7358][Para 007] The temporomandibular joints appear normal, and no submental, submandibular or cervical lymph nodes are palpable.
[7359][Heading 2]  What Can You Deduce From the Clinical Appearances Seen in Figs 69.1 and 69.2?

[7361][Para 004] • Extraoral examination of the lips and the amount of tooth and gingiva visible when the patient is in a resting lip position and smiling
[7362][Para 004] • The case becoming more challenging as more gingiva and tooth are visible

[7375][Para 004] • Asking the patient to smile and then to give a maximum extension smile is also helpful.
[7376][Para 114] Intraoral Examination
[7377][Para 001] A thorough intraoral clinical examination should be carried out to ensure that no primary disease is present. Any existing periodontal disease, caries or endodontic problems should be identified and treated prior to any implant treatment. Preventive protocols should be instituted and checked for adherence before any further complex prosthodontic treatment is advised. Once soft and hard tissues have been examined, focus should be on the edentulous space.
[7378][Para 012] Evaluation of the Edentulous Space
[7379][Para 001] Figs 69.3 and 69.4 show that the upper right central and lateral incisors are missing. The ridge height in this region is irregular. Approximately 3 mm of keratinized tissue band is visible. This is the pale pink soft gingival tissue near the tooth. When smiling, the patient does not show the gingival zeniths (highest point) of the contralateral natural teeth (see Figs 69.1 and 69.2).
[7380][Para 002] The upper left central incisor is restored with resin composite involving the mesio-incisal surfaces. Healthy, sharply defined papillae are visible around the remaining teeth. No gingival recession or loss of papilla is noted.
[7381][Para 002] The patient is wearing a removable, acrylic, mucosa-borne partial denture with no clasps. The palate appears to have healthy mucosa, and no inflammation is present over the denture-bearing region. There is minimal gingival inflammation around the premolars, and oral hygiene seems to be satisfactory.
[7382][Para 002] It is important to keep in mind that susceptibility to periodontitis is associated with increased implant failure and risk of peri-implantitis.
[7383][Para 002] No signs of parafunctional activity can be observed. Any signs of parafunctional activity such as occlusal facets, or worn/fractured cups as a result of clenching or grinding will also factor in the decision regarding treatment option. Narrow diameter implants are contraindicated in patients showing signs and symptoms of bruxism.
[7384][Para 002] The edentulous ridge height and width are assessed by careful digital palpation. Large concavities are usually readily detectable.
[7385][Para 002] An important measurement is that of the available tooth space/dimensions of the edentulous ridge. It is best to measure at the narrowest point between adjacent natural teeth at the level of the crown. A commonly quoted minimum span is 6 mm, allowing a narrow 4 mm implant diameter, with 1 mm of bone surrounding it.
[7386][Para 002] However, it is also important to remember that the selection of the most appropriate diameter of implant has a bearing on the final aesthetics to allow the correct emergence profile of the definitive restoration. As a guide, aim for a head diameter of an implant being similar to the root diameter of the tooth being replaced, provided space allows.
[7387][Para 002] Also, assess if too much space exists between adjacent teeth. If this is the case, you will need to decide whether wider prosthetic teeth or spaces/midline diastema between them will be acceptable. Asses the distance between the edentulous ridge and the opposing dentition to determine if there is sufficient interocclusal space. This can be carried out by using a Williams periodontal probe, with the patient occluding in the intercuspal position.
[7388][Para 002] In examining the edentulous ridge, the assessment of overlying soft tissue is important, specifically the amount of keratinized tissue available. Keratinized tissues will provide a better peri-implant soft tissue architecture compared with nonkeratinized mobile mucosa. As has already been mentioned, there is an adequate 3 mm band of keratinized mucosa available.
[7389][Para 012] Assessment of Prosthesis
[7390][Para 001] If the patient happy with the current denture, aim to copy it. It can, however, be difficult to transfer the aesthetics of a removable prosthesis to that of a fixed prosthesis. Examination of the current prosthesis is also a good indicator of the interocclusal space being sufficient or not. Care should be taken to ensure that the prosthetic teeth are not ridge lapped or set up labial to the alveolar ridge because this will give a false record of the actual space available. In Fig. 69.2, the prosthetic teeth appear longer than the contralateral natural teeth, and there is no papilla between the central and lateral prosthetic incisors.
[7391][Para 002] Any fixed restoration will not have a labial flange, and that may result in poor upper lip support. Is a flange needed for labial support? It is possible to position teeth more labially in a removable prosthesis. It is, however, not possible to allow normal-sized teeth to exist in a smaller span or to have a fixed implant prosthesis placed anterior to alveolar bone. It is possible to create interproximal papillae in a removable denture, but natural papillae are not guaranteed in individual implant crown restorations.
[7392][Para 015] Investigations
[7393][Heading 2]  What Investigations Would You Carry Out, and Why?
[7394][Para 001] Periodontal examination, including a basic periodontal examination (BPE), probing depths and gingival bleeding. It is necessary to identify if active periodontal disease is present in the remaining dentition.
[7395][Para 012] Examination of the Occlusion
[7396][Para 001] Record occlusal contacts in the patient’s retruded contact position, in the intercuspal position and protrusive and lateral excursions. For single implant-retained restorations, it is important that the initial contact occurs on adjacent natural teeth. In this case, there are no signs of wear facets or worn occlusal surfaces, and the teeth interdigitate closely in the intercuspal position, suggesting a stable intercuspal position.
[7397][Para 012] Radiographic Examination
[7398][Para 001] Periapical radiographs, shown in Fig. 69.5, obtained with use of a paralleling technique, offer the clinician information about:
[7399][Para 004] • The overall anatomy of the maxilla in the edentulous space
[7400][Para 004] • Adjacent teeth, root length, shape, angulation and proximity
[7401][Para 004] • Vertical height of available bone
[7402][Para 004] • Normal anatomical features, as well as any anomalies or pathological features.
[7403][Para 002] Avoid placing implants near teeth that are associated with periapical radiolucent areas.
[7404][Para 024]  The Periapical Radiographs are Shown in Fig. 69.5. What Do You See?
[7405][Para 004] • Adjacent roots of the upper right canine and upper left incisor are parallel
[7406][Para 004] • Presence of a retained root in the upper right incisor region
[7407][Para 004] • Adequate bone support of upper right canine and upper left incisor

[7416][Para 012] Cone Beam Computed Tomography
[7417][Para 001] In some complex cases, plane film images may need to be supplemented with three-dimensional (3D) imaging with computed tomography (CT). Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) allows small volume scans, which are ideal for dental practice, an example is shown in Fig. 69.7. The advantages are that the volume of bone available is known, and accurate measurements can be made. With the use of planning programs, implant length and diameters can be selected. It can also be used in the planning to construct a 3D surgical guide to aid surgical implant placement.

[7425][Para 012] Diagnostic Set-Up
[7426][Para 002] To help decide the size and shape of the replacement teeth, a diagnostic wax-up can be created. On a study cast, the teeth are waxed up as a guide, as shown in Fig. 69.8. The set-up should establish the height and width of the crowns and their emergence profile and provide an estimate of the level of soft tissue coverage. The set-up could be made in wax or as digitally generated images, both of which can be difficult for the patient to visualize, appreciate and comment on. It is preferable to try something in the patient’s mouth. If a screw-retained implant restoration is planned, it is important that this is replicated in the wax-up because the palatal aspect will be more bulky compared with that of a natural tooth. A putty index of the wax-up is then taken and filled with a temporary crown material and positioned in the mouth. Once set, this can be trimmed to allow the patient to visualize what could be achieved in the definitive restoration. It is important here to ensure that the patient realizes the lack of soft tissue papillae and colour match. The potential gingival discrepancy at the apex and the amount of lip support may not be depicted accurately. This stage is of paramount importance in terms of managing the patient’s expectations about the outcome of the final treatment. Conversations must be recorded accurately in the patient’s notes.

[7444][Para 014] Medico-Legal Considerations
[7445][Para 001] Good record keeping of the clinical findings and discussions with the patient are essential. An implant option should be discussed with the patient even if you are not the clinician providing the treatment. When discussing implant options, it is important to clarify that this option is not a lifelong solution and that the restoration has a limited life expectancy, as in other treatment options. The basic treatment sequence should be discussed, as follows.
[7446][Para 049] Examination
[7447][Para 004] • Completion of any necessary ongoing disease control/prevention, dental treatment, extractions, periodontal treatment, restoration of teeth and preventive maintenance
[7448][Para 004] • Diagnostic set-up with specialized radiographs, if needed
[7449][Para 004] • Discussion/documentation of treatment options
[7450][Para 004] • Construction of any provisional or transitional restorations, as required
[7451][Para 004] • Construction of a surgical stent for implant placement
[7452][Para 004] • Surgical placement of implants
[7453][Para 004] • Adequate time to be allowed for healing and osseointegration
[7454][Para 004] • Prosthodontic phase, which may include provisional restoration prior to definitive restoration
[7455][Para 004] • Maintenance
[7456][Para 002] This discussion should emphasize the complicated nature of treatment and also the time frame.
[7457][Para 002] If a referral is to be made, it is important that you refer your patient to someone with suitable skills in implant treatment and that the patient keeps you updated of ongoing treatment. A discussion should be had about who will provide ongoing maintenance and management of complications that may occur during and after treatment. The patient must be fully engaged throughout these discussions and the procedures.
[7458][Para 025] Case 70
[7459][Heading 1] Domiciliary Care
[7460][Para 027] Ellie Heidari
[7461][Para 028] Summary
[7462][Para 029] A 60-year-old female patient has called your practice with regard to a possible broken complete upper acrylic denture. She mentions that she dropped the denture and can now see a fracture line in the middle of it but that it is still intact. She is afraid that the denture, fitted 3 years ago, will shortly break in half. Your patient started attending the practice a few years ago but has been an irregular attender. In the last several weeks, she has been living in a care home because of complications associated with her hip replacement operation. As a result, she is now unable to travel to your practice and, thus, requires a domiciliary visit to a care home. She is otherwise fit and healthy with well-controlled blood pressure.
[7463][Para 014] History
[7464][Para 019] Complaint
[7465][Para 007] The patient dropped her maxillary denture 3 weeks ago and has noted a line in the middle of the denture base. She is anxious that it might break in two. She also has noticed that her mouth is comparatively dry since she started her medication. She takes numerous sips of water during the day.
[7466][Para 012] Medical History
[7467][Para 007] She has a history of osteoporosis, and she had a recent surgery for her fractured hip. She is currently having a course of physiotherapy. The pain is controlled with fast-acting opioids (tramadol tablets) that she usually takes three to four times a day. Her American Society of Anaesthesiologists (ASA) score varies from II to III and depends on her current medical condition and how well controlled it is. Her hypertension had previously been controlled with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) medication (lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor) and now has stopped. Her most recent blood pressure reading was 155/85 mm Hg.
[7468][Para 012] Dental History

[7470][Para 012] Social History

[7472][Para 015] Problem
[7473][Heading 2]  How Can You Provide Dental Treatment for This Patient?
[7474][Para 001] You and your oral healthcare team can assess this patient’s dental needs by visiting her in the care home and provide domiciliary care while she is recovering from her operation. Prior to your visit, it is important to contact the care home and involve the care manager, who might wish to involve the patient’s daughter. The care (support) workers will advise you about a suitable time for all parties involved (the care home staff, the patient and the patient’s daughter). Try to avoid busy times (e.g. lunch and visiting times) if you wish to get full support from the care home staff.
[7475][10 Block] 
[7476][Para 049] Part 1: The Processes and Procedures of Domiciliary Care Provision
[7477][Heading 2]  What is the Definition of Domiciliary Oral Healthcare?
[7478][Para 001] The British Society for Disability and Oral Health guidance for the Domiciliary Oral Healthcare Service (2009) describes domiciliary oral healthcare ‘as a service that reaches out to care for those who cannot reach a service themselves. Domiciliary care is intended to include oral health care and dental treatment carried out in an environment where a patient is resident either permanently or temporarily, as opposed to that care which is delivered in dental clinics or mobile units’.
[7479][Heading 2]  Who Can Provide Domiciliary Oral Healthcare?
[7480][Para 001] Domiciliary care may be provided via the general dental service (GDS), salaried primary dental care service (SPDCS) or, occasionally, the hospital dental service (HDS).
[7481][Heading 2]  Why is It Important That You Provide Domiciliary Oral Healthcare for Your Patient?
[7482][Para 001] Although this patient’s mobility might be limited temporarily, she has equal rights to the same high-quality oral health care as when she was able bodied and fully mobile. You need to provide unbiased dental care, considering the individual’s needs, demands and expectations. You can always contact your local specialist services for advice/support with her individualized care plan, when necessary. You should be aware of available local specialist dental services (including the local community dental services [CDS]) and how to contact them.
[7483][Para 018] Table 70.1
[7484][Para 021] A Range of Guidance or Relevant Documents for Provision of Domiciliary Care in the UK
[7485][Heading 2]  What Information Does the General Dental Council ‘Standards for the Dental Team’ Provide With Regard To a Patient’s Health and Wellbeing?
[7486][Para 001] The General Dental Council (GDC) 1.6.3 standard mentions that ‘you must consider patients’ disabilities and make reasonable adjustments to allow them to receive care which meets their needs. If you cannot make reasonable adjustments to treat a patient safely, you should consider referring them to a colleague’. The GDC standard 1 (includes patient expectations and put patient’s best interest first) states that ‘all aspects of their health and well-being will be considered and they will receive dental care that is appropriate for them’.
[7487][Heading 2]  What Other Laws, Standards and Guidance are Relevant for Provision of Domiciliary Oral Healthcare?
[7488][Para 001] Table 70.1 Outlines the current guidance and references. These are few of many that you need to be aware of.
[7489][Para 002] The information contained in the tabulated documents is useful. You should visit the relevant websites regularly to ensure that you have access to the latest and updated versions of guidance.
[7490][Heading 2]  What Would Be Your Next Steps Now That You are Aware of Your Responsibilities?
[7491][Para 001] You need to follow your local domiciliary protocol (Fig. 70.1). The protocol will contain vital information about your acceptance criteria, patient care pathway, data security and patient confidentiality.

[7495][Para 009]  
[7496][Heading 2]  How Can You Ensure Patient Confidentiality and Avoid a Medico-Legal Allegation?
[7497][Para 001] The GDC standards set out in ‘Standards for the Dental Team’ important principles that you need to be aware of and to practise accordingly. A review of standards 3 (Obtain valid consent), 4 (Maintain and protect patients’ information), 6 (Work with colleagues in a way that serves the interests of patients), 7 (Maintain, develop and work within your professional knowledge and skills) and 8 (Raise concerns if patients are at risk) is recommended prior to your visit. Note that the medical/dental defence organisations also can provide useful documents for your information.
[7498][Para 002] An example of how you can protect patient data (when you provide domiciliary care) is having an encrypted and password-protected laptop that will be stored in a secure location during the domiciliary visit and afterwards. For more information about data protection, see the Information Commissioner’s office (ICO) (Table 70.2) and the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, 2018) websites.
[7499][Heading 2]  What Questions Will You Ask When You Contact Your Patient?
[7500][Para 001] In general, you can explore issues regarding the patient’s ability to attend the surgery, and once there, the ability to be transferred to the surgery’s dental chair. If possible, arrange transport for the patient to attend the surgery (see Fig. 70.1). You can enquire about transport arrangement by liaising and seeking advice from your local CDS. However, in this case, because it is impractical for the patient to attend your dental surgery, you need to know if/when she can return to the surgery. You may want to assess the likelihood of the patient’s ability (e.g. recover fully from her operation) to return to the surgery for her future dental appointments. The information gained during this encounter (from the patient’s medical history, her capacity assessment, support, etc.) will enable you to decide whether you should refer the patient to a specialist dental service (e.g. CDS) or make reasonable adjustments to provide the needed care yourself. You need to prioritize the patient’s care (urgent or on a waiting list) once you have accepted the responsibility to provide care for your patient.
[7501][Para 002] This is also the time to gather information about the patient’s request. Is she requesting a new denture? In some cases, the patient’s family members are keen on getting her a new denture, and you need to discuss different treatment options with the patient and the carer(s) before your visit. In this case, the patient wishes to keep her denture and repair it, if necessary.

[7522][Heading 2]  How Would You Perform Risk Assessment for Provision of Domiciliary Healthcare?
[7523][Para 001] The Scottish National Dental Advisory Committee (NDAC) document entitled: Emergency Drugs and Equipment in Primary Dental Care (2015) considered three risk areas:
[7524][Para 016] 1. The nature of the dental care. Some dental procedures such as examinations and the construction of dentures are essentially noninvasive and will carry a much lower risk. This current case and your first visit to the care home would fall into this category.
[7525][Para 016] 2. The patient’s medical history and any possible/likely causes of collapse or reaction to treatment. Your patient’s medical history indicates ASA levels II and III, and the patient presents with low levels of dental anxiety.
[7526][Para 016] 3. The physical environment and any possible risks related to this (Fig. 70.2).

A table where you can set up for an examination is recommended. [7577][Para 001] The patient is edentulous. You need to assess dryness of mucosa (see Table 70.6) and the denture’s stability and retention caused by xerostomia because of the opioid’s side effect. [7582][Para 004] • Check if a lower denture is present. Also, assess retention, support and stability. Then, if possible, assess the dentures as functional units, and check occlusion and freeway space.

[7588][Heading 2]  What Would Your Provisional Care Plan Be?
[7589][Para 001] The GDC standards describe a holistic approach as when clinicians ‘take account of patients’ overall health, their psychological and social needs, their long-term oral health needs and their desired outcomes’.
[7590][Para 002] You have the following care options:

[7594][Para 030]  What Advice Will You Give the Patient and Her Carers Before Leaving?
[7595][Para 001] At your next visit, the denture will be fitted. Advise the patient to clean her dentures over a water-filled sink in the future. Inform the patient that once you have fitted the repaired denture and assessed it (extraorally and intraorally), there is a risk of another fracture if the denture has been repaired in cold-cure acrylic. She can then decide if and when she wishes to have a new complete denture in the future. She will also be reviewed after some time to ensure that she is coping with her denture(s).
[7596][Para 002] After completion of your treatment, you need to ensure that your working area is clean and that you have left your contact details with the care home. You might wish to enquire about the care home’s visiting dentist. Fig. 70.1 (see Part 1) outlines steps to be taken on your return to the surgery.
[7597][Heading 2]  What Information Can Be Included in an Oral Health Care Plan for Patients in Care Homes?
[7598][Para 001] It would be useful to write an oral health care plan for this patient, outlining oral hygiene procedures, denture care routines (e.g. advice on cleaning and use of a denture brush) and when the next dental visit is recommended. The patient will need periodic (annual) assessment of denture quality, health of the supporting tissues, oral lesions and bone loss, and oral health status. The role of carers in assisting and supporting this patient with her oral health (e.g. need for supervision for denture removal/cleaning) can be outlined after obtaining the patient’s permission. Discussions about denture adhesives may be required. You can visit the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE) website for more information about oral health assessment tools and a daily mouth care plan.
[7599][Heading 2] Final Thoughts
[7600][Para 001] You must present a rational approach to commissioner about a need for domiciliary services. This can entail identifying health needs of your specific community (e.g. highlighting the findings of an oral health needs assessment), service gaps, potential for redesigning services and the level of resources required.
[7601][Para 002] Domiciliary services can improve access to care especially for older people in residential and nursing care homes. It causes minimal interruption to the patient’s day and can addresses issues such as transportation problems and missed appointments.
[7602][Para 002] Consider carefully available options for arranging to see the patient in a dental surgery as you might not be able to offer a more comprehensive dental treatment on a domiciliary visit.
[7603][Para 002] Ensure that you have updated risk assessments and standard operating procedures.
[7604][Para 002] Please bear in mind that a denture set can get lost in residential and nursing care homes, therefore consider copy dentures and ask the lab to add your patient’s name.
[7605][Para 002] Consider involving the care home staff in oral health care training.
[7606][Para 002] It is important to record your oral health advice and the care you have provided in the residential and nursing care homes’ patient’s records.

[7608][Heading 1] Managing Complaints
[7609][Para 027] Len D’Cruz
[7610][Para 028] Summary
[7611][Para 029] A 29-year-old patient attends your clinic with pain from his lower left quadrant.
