[7616][Para 014] History
[7617][Para 019] Complaint
[7618][Para 007] He points to the lower left second and third molar area, saying he has had a bad taste from the tooth.
[7619][Para 012] History of Complaint
[7620][Para 007] The tooth has been hurting on and off for the past month or so but has got worse over the last few days. The tooth is sensitive to hot and cold, and it has started to ache spontaneously. It is occasionally tender on biting. He is also getting food caught there. Previously, he had been advised that a wisdom tooth was erupting there, but he has had no previous problems. He is going on a cruise with his fiancée in a few weeks’ time and wants to get this sorted out before that.
[7621][Para 012] Medical History
[7622][Para 007] The patient is medically fit and healthy.
[7623][Para 014] Examination
[7624][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[7625][Para 007] Nothing abnormal is noted.
[7626][Para 012] Intraoral Examination
[7627][Para 007] The patient is fully dentate, with a small number of existing clinically sound restorations. The lower left third molar is mesio-angularly impacted against the lower left second molar. There is some food packing and plaque debris between these two teeth. There is a periodontal probing depth of 5 mm associated with this area, distal to the lower left second molar. The tooth does not respond to thermal or electric sensibility tests.
[7628][Heading 2]  What Radiographs Would You Take?
[7629][Para 001] The periapical radiograph in Fig. 71.1 shows the following:
[7630][Para 004] • An extensive distal radiolucency is associated with the lower second molar tooth, most likely caused by caries.
[7631][Para 004] • The third molar is mesio-angularly impacted, and there is vertical bone loss up to two-thirds of the distal root of the second molar.
[7632][Para 004] • The third molar is not close to the inferior dental (ID) canal, and it has a conical root.
[7633][Para 004] • There are radiopaque restorations present coronally in the lower left first molar and lower left second molar, probably amalgam.
[7634][Para 004] • There is distal calculus associated with the lower left first molar and some alveolar crestal bone loss.
[7635][Para 015] Diagnosis
[7636][Para 004] • Irreversible pulpitis in lower left second molar
[7637][Para 004] • Vertical localized bone loss distally to the lower left second molar caused by impaction of third molar
[7638][Para 004] • Mesio-angular impaction of the third molar
[7639][Para 004] • Calculus in lower left first molar with concomitant bone loss.
[7640][Para 014] Treatment Options
[7641][Para 001] A number of options are available, and all will need to be discussed to obtain valid consent from the patient. It will depend on operator skills in oral surgery and endodontics as well as the patient’s preferences and expectations. It will depend on access to both these specialist services if the operator does not feel confident, competent or trained to definitively manage the lower left second and third molars.
[7642][Para 049] Lower Left Second Molar
[7643][Heading 2]  Is This Tooth Restorable?
[7644][Para 001] Access to the distal aspect of the tooth to reach the carious tissue to remove it and allow the patient to maintain the restored tooth afterwards is hindered severely by the presence of the mesio-angularly impacted third molar.
[7645][Para 002] The lower left second molar may, however, be restorable after root canal treatment if the lower left third molar is removed.
[7646][Para 002] There is still significant loss of tooth structure, and a protective indirect coronal restoration will be required in the form of a full-coverage crown.
[7647][Para 002] There is bone loss distally, but any pocketing may resolve after the extraction of lower left third molar.
[7648][Heading 2]  How Complex is the Endodontic Procedure?
[7649][Para 001] This would be considered a Tier 1 endodontic procedure in the National Health Service (NHS) if there are no other complicating factors such as limited mouth opening or local difficulty in placing a rubber dam.
[7650][Para 002] An alternative option would be to extract the lower left second molar and allow the third molar to erupt. It would remain in its near horizontal position but could be uprighted with orthodontic treatment and brought into reasonable approximation to the lower left first molar. This would need a potential orthodontic opinion, and tooth movement after extraction is not guaranteed.
[7651][Para 012] Lower Left Third Molar
[7652][Para 001] This currently nonfunctional tooth could be extracted to allow access to and treatment of the lower left second molar.
[7653][Para 002] The third molar is impacted against the second molar, and its removal may require a surgical approach. However, the favourable conical-shaped roots and the potential buccal inclination of the impaction may allow careful nonsurgical elevation/rotation displacement of the tooth in trained hands. If the operator lacks the confidence, training or competence (GDC Standards for the Dental Team 7.2.1) to extract this tooth, this will need to be discussed with the patient and a suitable oral surgery referral made.
[7654][Para 038] Standard 7.2 You must work within your knowledge, skills, professional competence and abilities (Standards for the Dental Team General Dental Council https://www.gdc-uk.org/professionals/standards)
[7655][Para 038] Standard 7.2.1 You must only carry out a task or a type of treatment if you are appropriately trained, competent, confident and indemnified. Training can take many different forms. You must be sure that you have undertaken training which is appropriate for you and equips you with the appropriate knowledge and skills to perform a task safely.
[7656][Para 223] 
[7657][Para 008] 
[7658][Para 052] Fig. 71.2 A periapical radiograph of the lower left second molar, with a filling in one of the mesial canals.
[7659][Para 038] Standard 7.2.2 You should only deliver treatment and care if you are confident that you have had the necessary training and are competent to do so. If you are not confident to provide treatment, you must refer the patient to an appropriately trained colleague.
[7660][Para 002] The availability of NHS or private services will influence how soon the treatment could be carried out and whether or not this would delay the treatment of the lower left second molar. The patient is in pain, and so even if this tooth is scheduled for extraction, the pain should be addressed, and this means pulp extirpation of the second molar and a suitable provisional dressing.
[7661][Para 002] Alternatively, both lower left second and third molars could be removed. Even though this might be the endpoint of care if the restorative treatment to both teeth fails, it is not necessarily an advisable first option because the patient will be left with little posterior support in the lower left quadrant. If patients are in pain, they sometimes may wish for immediate extraction to alleviate their symptoms, but consideration must be given to the final irreversible consequences of such a care plan.
[7662][Para 014] Treatment Provided
[7663][Para 001] In this case, the third molar was extracted uneventfully by a colleague of the operator in the same practice.
[7664][Para 002] Molar endodontics was commenced on lower left second molar subsequently. A rubber dam was not used, as can be seen in the radiograph ( Fig. 71.2 ). This is an ill-advised approach because there are obvious risks of the operator dropping the instrument and the patient swallowing or inhaling the handheld instruments. This would be considered negligent and indefensible medico-legally. There may be merit in preparing the access cavity without the rubber dam in place to help with its orientation when the tooth is rotated or tilted. Once the access cavity is cut and the canal orifices located, a rubber dam must be applied before handheld instruments such as files are used. Saliva contamination should be avoided. In this case, because the tooth was in good alignment with the rest of the dental arch, rubber dam placement was indicated from the outset.
[7665][Para 218] 
[7666][Para 008] 
[7667][Para 011] Fig. 71.3 A periapical radiograph after obturation of lower left second molar showing unfilled canals and perforation through the furcation area. There also appears to be a poorly condensed coronal restoration with a distal marginal discrepancy.
[7668][Para 009]  
[7669][Para 017] A rubber dam was then placed and the root canal treatment completed.Unfortunately, it was only on completion of the root canal procedure that the operator realized that the distal canal had not been filled and that a perforation was evident. This was noted on viewing the postobturation radiograph ( Fig. 71.3 ).
[7670][Para 017] The patient was informed immediately and the options of reviewing the tooth discussed, referring the patient for a specialist endodontic opinion or extraction of the tooth. With the patient’s consent, the lower left second molar was extracted ( Fig. 71.4 ).The operator apologized and accepted responsibility for the perforation and the less-than-ideal treatment provided.
[7671][Para 002] When something goes wrong, it is always important to analyse why it happened to learn from the event and reduce the chances of the error occurring again. Such events can be analysed in a number of ways, one of which is a root cause analysis (RCA – Table 71.1). This can be accomplished by adopting a clinical perspective in looking at the technical and clinical aspects of the incident as well as the dento-legal and contextual aspects, and this brings into play other human factors concerning all those involved.
[7672][Para 014] Complaint
[7673][Para 007] Not surprisingly, the patient was upset about losing two teeth within a very short time when he had had no other dental problems previously.
[7674][Para 017] He wrote in a letter of complaint demanding to know why this had happened and why he had not been given the option of a referral for an endodontic procedure, if the operator felt it was difficult or beyond his or her capabilities.

[7679][Heading 2]  How Do You Deal with a Written Complaint?
[7680][Para 001] No one ever likes receiving a complaint and particularly not in these circumstances when the care provided has led to the loss of a tooth. The first thing to do is to contact your indemnity organization for assistance. This will almost certainly be considered a case that the organization would want to settle on your behalf if the patient makes a claim for compensation against you.
[7681][Para 002] Your vulnerabilities will be assessed by using a three-stage approach. To establish clinical negligence, the following three things must be established:
[7682][Para 016] 1. There is a duty of care between you and the patient.
[7683][Para 016] 2. The duty of care was breached.
[7684][Para 016] 3. The breach of duty directly resulted in losses (causation).
[7685][Para 002] As soon as you have agreed to treat the patient, duty of care comes into existence. Breach of duty refers to doing something a reasonable dentist would not have done or not doing something a reasonable dentist would have done. In this case, a reasonably skilled dentist would not have perforated the tooth. Losses, that is, extraction of the tooth, have resulted from the perforation.
[7686][Para 012] Manging the Complaint
[7687][Para 001] The GDC expects patient complaints to be dealt with quickly and professionally and every practice to have a written complaint process.
[7688][Para 002] A number of templates are available from organizations such as the British Dental Association. The process will depend on the part of the UK in which you are practising because the response times to the complaint will vary. The essential components of a complaint process are outlined in Table 71.2.
[7689][Para 002] The GDC standards Section 5 say that you must:
[7690][Para 016] 5.1 Make sure that there is an effective complaints procedure readily available for patients to use and follow at all times
[7691][Para 016] 5.2 Respect a patient’s right to complain
[7692][Para 016] 5.3 Give patients who complain a prompt and constructive response.
[7693][Para 018] Table 71.1
[7694][Para 021] An Example of a Root Cause Analysis of This Case
[7695][Para 018] Table 71.2
[7696][Para 021] The Steps in the Process of Handling a Patient Complaint
[7697][Para 002] It is worth reading the detailed guidance in Section 5 of GDC standards on this aspect. The GDC advises that if a complaint is justified, then you should offer a fair solution. This may include offering to put things right at your own expense if you have made a mistake (GDC Standard 5.3.9).
[7698][Para 002] If the individual is an NHS patient, he or she has the right to complain through the NHS system. In England, this is operated by NHS England. The patient has the right to complain to the practice, but if he or she does not want the practice to deal with it, then NHS England can investigate the matter. The practice will be expected to direct a letter to the patient but send it first to NHS England to ensure that all the points raised by the complainant are addressed, an apology and, where appropriate, a practical solutions are offered, an explanation of the events is given, and an action plan is prepared to prevent it from happening again.
[7699][Para 002] If the patient remains unhappy, then he or she should be directed to other avenues such as the relevant ombudsman for health services complaints or the dental complaints service for complaints about private treatment.

[7709][Para 139]  What is Going To Be Your Strategy for the Appointment?
[7710][Para 016] 1. You will look through the patient’s records (before your nurse invites the patient into the surgery) to see what the previous dentist has assessed and tried to achieve with the dentures made.
[7711][Para 016] 2. You check the medical history and note that the patient is on antidepressants, but you will update this when you see the patient. The previous dentist does not appear to have undertaken or recorded a comprehensive history, simply getting on with the technical aspects of making new dentures because the previous ones had ‘failed’.
[7712][Para 002] You decide, correctly, to perform a more comprehensive history taking and examination. If this is straightforward, it would be appropriate to record some primary impressions at this visit. However, if not, you will need to spend the time to properly assess the clinical situation (Tables 72.1 and 72.2). This is important because you need to try to determine if your new dentures can really improve the situation and what changes you would need to make to ensure any resolution of the cause of the problems. It is imperative not to be tempted to ‘dive in’ and start treatment when you have not ascertained the cause of the problem(s) and thought about how to resolve these, with discussions involving the patient throughout this process. In this way, the patient is taken along the decision-making process and can be involved in his overall care. This will increase the patient’s perception of the value of the care he is receiving and his responsibilities as part of his care delivery pathway. This approach also helps reduce the risk of miscommunication between the dentist and the patient and ensure that all expectations from both sides are managed appropriately. In this way, the risk of medico-legal issues arising later is significantly diminished. All the conversations and decision-making processes must be documented contemporaneously.
[7713][Para 139]  What are You Going To Check in Your History Taking?
[7714][Para 016] 1. The current problems experienced by the patient and previous denture-wearing history
[7715][Para 016] 2. Is the patient having problems only with the upper or lower denture, or both?
[7716][Para 016] 3. Is the patient experiencing looseness of the denture because of lack of stability/retention of the lower denture?
[7717][Para 016] 4. Is the static or functional retention of the upper complete denture poor?

[7726][Para 070]  What is a Possible Reason for the Inadequacy of the New Post-Dam?
[7727][Para 001] If your previous colleague had overbuilt the post-dam in acrylic, it would prevent the denture from seating properly, thus reducing overall mucosal contact. Close mucosal contact and an adequate saliva flow are vital for retention. This is why noting from the medical history that the patient is on antidepressants may affect your management because the use of many types can lead to hyposalivation as a side effect.
[7728][Para 002] You can see some papillary hyperplasia on the posterior aspect of the palate and possible enlargement of the tuberosities. This is always difficult to tell unless sequential study models of the upper arch are available because it might just appear exaggerated as a result of the resorption of the anterior maxillary ridge. The above factors (tuberosity enlargement, hyperplasia and fibrous change), together with the overerupted anterior teeth and resorption of the mandibular ridge, are sometimes referred to as ‘combination syndrome’. Use of this classification is not particularly helpful, however, because these factors are rarely all present simultaneously, and even if they are, it is not actually a ‘syndrome’. Combined with a dry mouth, as a consequence of the use of antidepressants, the above factors will lead to difficulty with denture retention.
[7729][Para 002] Other features that you should have observed are the angular cheilitis and the denture-induced hyperplasia in the labial sulcus of the 43/34 upper left and upper right canine and first premolar region. There is plaque and calculus associated with the lower incisors, and so it would be appropriate to undertake a basic periodontal examination (BPE) score and, if indicated, a probing chart for these teeth.

[7731][Para 016] 1. These teeth tend not to offer a useful undercut below the survey line for direct retention with clasps.

[7741][Para 014] Prosthetic Management of the Upper Fibrous Ridge
[7742][Para 001] Mucostatic impressions for upper fibrous ridges have to be recorded with great care as to not cause displacement of the ridge. Special trays with an anterior open window have been advocated (Figs 72.2 and 72.3) or an impression with greater relief over the ridge anteriorly, used with alginate, might be satisfactory. The aim of the impression is to avoid displacing the fibrous, mobile section of the maxillary ridge during the recording of the impression, or this will lead to both soreness and reduced stability of the final denture.

[7793][Para 014] Conclusions
[7794][Para 001] Not all complete-over-partial dentures placed over natural teeth are overwhelmingly challenging. However, with this series of cases, you have learnt the importance of performing a thorough assessment prior to committing yourself to a particular treatment and of recording the primary impressions. Also, you have become aware that management of patient expectations, by carefully communicating what you can realistically achieve, is crucial to successful clinical and medico-legal outcomes. Perhaps you got away with your errors in the last case of the morning because of your skill and judgment applied subsequently – or was it just good luck?

[7796][Heading 1] ’Invisible Custom-Made Braces’
[7797][Para 027] Dirk Bister
[7798][Para 028] Summary
[7799][Para 029] Here, two orthodontic treatment modalities using customized orthodontic appliances – lingual fixed appliances and aligners – are compared side by side. Both options provide treatment with minimal aesthetic impact on the patient during treatment, and both can be custom-made for the patient. For the lingual fixed appliances, a class II division 2 malocclusion with an asymmetrical buccal segment relationship is shown. The orthodontic treatment was complex and included a unilateral change of the buccal segment relationship. DW LingualSystems was used in this case. This is compared with a mild class II malocclusion treated with aligners (Align Technology), and in this case, no change in the occlusion was planned.
[7800][Para 054] Summary (Case 1)
[7801][Para 007] A 22-year-old patient presented with bimaxillary retroclination, an increased traumatic overbite, and crowding affecting both the upper and lower arches. The buccal segment relationship on the right was over half unit post-normal but was normal on the left. There was a subsequent lower centre line shift to the right-hand side. The upper lateral incisors were mesio-labially rotated. In the UK, the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN) is used to assess eligibility for treatment free of charge at the point of delivery (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/Orthodontics/). The IOTN for this patient was 4f, which means that there was traumatic overbite, which provided the health component for qualification. Information on IOTN can be found at https://www.bos.org.uk/Public-Patients/Orthodontics-for-Children-Teens/Fact-File-FAQ/What-Is-The-IOTN.

[7846][Para 014] Care Planning
[7847][Para 001] Nonextraction management was planned for both cases. Both patients requested treatment with an orthodontic brace that has the least visible impact during treatment. The decision was made to use custom-made lingual fixed appliances for one and aligners for the other.
[7848][Para 002] ‘Invisible’ braces are widely publicized to patients and to dentists, and this is appealing to both general dentists and specialists; there are several reasons for this (Table 73.1).
[7849][Para 002] The two examples of ‘invisible braces’ chosen are transparent aligner-type appliances and lingual appliances. The latter are fixed appliances that are attached to the inner surface of teeth.
[7850][Para 002] The former (aligners) are transparent and removable and must be worn nearly full time to be effective. Some manufacturers use fixed attachments in combination with the aligners, as shown in case 2.
[7851][Para 002] The appeal, for the nonspecialist practitioner in particular, is that both types of appliances appear to require little specialist knowledge to provide patient care. Both types of orthodontic braces usually require either a three-dimensional intraoral scan or polyvinyl siloxane impressions, including a record of the occlusal relationship; photographic records; and initial radiographic records. These are sent to the respective company to manufacture the orthodontic appliance.

[7862][Para 021] Features of Lingual and Aligner ‘Invisible’ Orthodontic Appliances
[7863][Para 002] At the company, trained personnel will produce the individualized appliance. Some manufacturers provide the dentists with ‘virtual set-ups’ that are designed to help visualize the desired treatment outcome. The virtual set-up can also be used as a tool for obtaining consent from patients. The patient, the dentist and the company jointly agree to the proposed care plan.
[7864][Para 002] Dentists can determine/modify the care plan before the appliances are made, and this makes them responsible for the care provided. However, depending on the dentist’s preferences, the manufacturer may suggest an orthodontic care plan. It is important to note that the dentist should be in a position to assess the care plan critically before committing to treating the patient. In other words, the responsibility for patient care ultimately lies with the dentist/practitioner and not with the company or other third party (e.g. advisor provided by the company). This clearly has medico-legal implications.
[7865][Para 002] Another consideration is the time it takes to submit the records and to evaluate and potentially modify the proposed care plan; all these factors need to be considered in the overall cost of the orthodontic treatment.
[7866][Para 002] Once the care plan has been finalized, the dentist agrees to pay the fees for the appliance. This may require a significant upfront payment. Currently, both types of ‘invisible’ appliances are mailed to dentists, who will then deliver them to patients to commence treatment, either by indirectly bonding the appliance to the teeth or by delivering the aligners and fitting the necessary attachments, where required.
[7867][Para 014] Consent
[7868][Para 001] Obtaining valid consent is one of the nine principles dental professionals must follow at all times. This should include a detailed description of what to expect during treatment (e.g. discomfort, initial speech impediment, compliance) and diet advice.
[7869][Para 002] In case 1, the patient was required to wear intermaxillary elastics for a prolonged period to correct the class II buccal segment relationship and the increased overbite. It requires expertise to judge whether correction of the class II buccal segment relationship on the right and the overbite correction can be achieved through wearing of elastics or whether other treatment approaches should be considered. It is likely that an increased overjet with incomplete overbite would ensue if the upper and lower labial segments are aligned without correcting the buccal segment relationship. The alignment and the overbite reduction are not likely to be stable over the long term unless normal overjet and overbite are achieved.
[7870][Para 002] In case 2, nearly full-time wear of the aligners was necessary to achieve the desired treatment outcome. Interproximal enamel reduction and attachments were required.
[7871][Para 014] Potential Legal Issues and Pitfalls
[7872][Para 001] Custom-made appliances (e.g. labial or lingual fixed appliances as well as removable appliances [aligners]) usually require payment to the manufacturer before treatment commences. The upfront costs for the dentist can approach £2000, depending on the appliance.
[7873][Para 002] In an ideal set-up, which is usually undertaken, the dentist is required to assess and, if necessary, modify the care plan before the appliances are manufactured. It is important that the operator is aware of the relative strength and weaknesses of the different appliance systems; biomechanics can vary considerably. It is also important to note that patient consent should be obtained for long-term retention of the orthodontic outcome, particularly if the aesthetic concerns were the initiator for treatment.
[7874][Para 002] Practitioners may be more easily persuaded to commence orthodontic treatment if custom-made appliances are used; the implication is that specialist training and knowledge may not be required to the same extent as for fixed labial appliances to achieve the desired treatment outcomes. Inadequate training may lead to discrepancies between patient expectations and treatment outcomes.
[7875][Para 014] Treatment and Outcomes
[7876][Para 001] For patient 1, the treatment time was 18 months. Intermaxillary elastic wear started early in treatment, and correction of the centre lines and buccal segment relationships were achieved. The overjet and overbite were normalized, and the upper and lower labial segments were well aligned. The retention regimen encompassed vacuum-formed retainers on a full-time basis for 3 months. This allows the gingival tissues to recover from orthodontic treatment and the occlusion to settle. Fixed retention can also be considered but is not usually provided or maintained by general dental practitioners because this knowledge is not part of the undergraduate curriculum for orthodontics. Treatment of patient 1 was expected to take longer than that of patient 2 because the treatment aims were more complex.
[7877][Para 002] For patient 2, the overall treatment time was 12 months. Initially, 14 aligners were provided. After 7 months, impressions for orthodontic ‘refinement’ were taken, and seven more aligners were provided. The teeth were aligned successfully, and, as planned, occlusion had not changed significantly.
[7878][Para 002] Retention needs to be planed for the long term, particularly for alignment of the labial segments. In case 1, we would not expect relapse of the buccal segment relationship, but alignment and overbite are likely to require maintenance over the long term. The need for commitment to maintenance and knowledge of the costs associated with it must be made clear to the patient, particularly when orthodontics is undertaken for aesthetic purposes. These costs can be significant. It is also worth remembering that fixed retainers are not infallible and re-treatment may become necessary at some stage, depending on the patients’ requirements.
[7879][Para 025] Case 74
[7880][Heading 1] Swollen Lips
[7881][Para 027] Martyn Ormond, Esther Hullah, and Michael Escudier
[7882][Para 028] Summary
[7883][Para 029] A 29-year-old man presents with swollen lips and generalized oral soreness. What is your diagnosis?
[7884][Para 218] 
[7885][Para 008] 
[7886][Para 011] Fig. 74.1 The appearance of the patient’s lips.
[7887][Para 009]  
[7888][Para 014] History
[7889][Para 019] Complaint
[7890][Para 007] The patient reports intermittent lip swelling and a sore mouth for the last 6 months.
[7891][Para 012] History of Complaint
[7892][Para 007] The lip swelling developed slowly, with no obvious precipitating event, around 6 months ago at a time when he was otherwise well. The swelling fluctuates in size, and he is unable to identify any specific triggers. In addition to the lip swelling, he also reports persistent oral soreness and mouth ulcers. There is no previous history of lip swelling, oral soreness or mouth ulcers.
[7893][Para 012] Medical History
[7894][Para 007] The patient has asthma, for which he uses a salbutamol inhaler. He also has hay fever, which he manages with daily oral antihistamine drugs during the spring months.
[7895][Para 014] Examination
[7896][Para 019] Extraoral Examination
[7897][Para 001] The extraoral appearance of the lips are shown in Fig. 74.1.
[7898][Heading 2]  Describe What You See
[7899][Para 001] The lower lip is enlarged and rounded, with the vermilion rolled outwards. The vermilion shows patchy erythema and cracking, with a fissure close to the midline. There is an area of erythema spreading outwards and downwards on the right cheek. The vermilion border has lost its definition. The upper lip appears largely normal in size, but there is a small midline fissure.
[7900][Para 017] The lower lip is not tender but feels soft and rubbery. You undertake examination of the neck and conclude that there is no cervical lymphadenopathy.
[7901][Para 049] Intraoral Examination
[7902][Heading 2]  The Intraoral Appearance is Shown in Fig. 74.2. Describe What You See
[7903][Para 002] The buccal mucosa is swollen bilaterally. It looks soft and oedematous. On the patient’s right (Fig. 74.2a), the surface has formed slightly projecting, rounded nodules separated by fissures, which can be described as having a cobblestone appearance. On the left buccal mucosa (Fig. 74.2b), there is more generalized swelling with two folds.
[7904][Para 017] If you could examine the patient, you would find that there is also gingival swelling around the posterior teeth and deep fissures along the lower buccal sulci, with linear ulcers in their depths.
[7905][Heading 2]  What is the Most Likely Diagnosis, and Why?
[7906][Para 001] Given the patient’s age, history and clinical findings, the most likely diagnosis is orofacial granulomatosis (OFG). This condition typically develops before the third decade of life and is thought to affect both genders equally. Lip swelling affects the majority of patients, with each episode lasting days to weeks. Over time, the lips may become firm and persistently swollen. The perioral skin may become red, dry, itchy or cracked, with some patients developing angular cheilitis.
[7907][Para 218] 
[7908][Para 008] 
[7909][Para 011] Fig. 74.2 The right (a) and left (b) intraoral appearance.
[7910][Para 009]  
[7911][Para 002] The intraoral findings vary among patients but include generalized swelling of the labial and buccal mucosae, often with a cobblestone pattern, or more localized tags. Linear ulcers with raised margins may be found in the buccal sulcus. Less commonly, patients may experience aphthous-like ulcers. The gingivae often show localised or generalised swelling and ertythema.
[7912][Para 002] This clinical picture is so typical that few other diagnoses need to be considered unless investigations confirm an alternative diagnosis.
[7913][Heading 2]  What Other Causes of Recurrent Generalized Lip Swelling Might You Consider? Explain Why
[7914][Para 001] Other possible causes of recurrent generalized lip swelling, together with features relevant to diagnosis, are listed in Table 74.1.
[7915][Para 024]  What Further Questions Would You Ask the Patient To Reach a Working Diagnosis?
[7916][Para 020] What is the Duration of the Episodes of Swelling?
[7917][Para 001] The lip swelling of OFG would be expected to last days to weeks before resolving. Acute inflammatory causes such as angioedema resolve in 48 hours.
[7918][Para 020] Is There Complete Resolution Between Episodes?
[7919][Para 001] OFG, Crohn’s disease and Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome may initially resolve between episodes, although the swelling may become permanent after months or years.
[7920][Para 020] Are There Bowel Symptoms?
[7921][Para 001] If Crohn’s disease is present, there would be abdominal pain, diarrhoea and frequency of bowel movements, possibly weight loss and perianal discomfort. However, mild disease may be asymptomatic.
[7922][Para 020] Is There Shortness of Breath or a Chronic Cough?
[7923][Para 001] These might indicate lung involvement in sarcoidosis.
[7924][Para 020] Is There an Associated Rash?
[7925][Para 001] Episodes of angioedema are usually associated with urticarial rashes (‘hives’) elsewhere on the body. Erythema nodosum, producing painful subcutaneous nodules, is seen in both Crohn’s disease and sarcoidosis.
[7926][Para 020] Is There a History of Allergy?
[7927][Para 001] About 80% of patients with OFG have a history of atopy (hay fever, asthma or eczema). Angioedema is also usually allergic in nature.
[7928][Para 017] On further questioning, the patient confirms that the swelling develops over a number of hours. He also suggests that his symptoms may occasionally be triggered by certain foods. The swelling lasts for days before resolving slowly. He does not report any gastrointestinal disturbance, and there is no family history of inflammatory bowel disease. All other family members are well. His asthma is well controlled, and there is no history of hospital admissiosn. He has been assessed in an allergy clinic, where his hay fever was found to be caused by tree pollen.
[7929][Para 015] Investigations
[7930][Heading 2]  What Investigations Might You Consider? Why?
[7931][Para 001] Possible further investigations are listed in Table 74.2.
[7932][Para 017] In this case, a swab was taken from the commissure and surrounding skin. Culture revealed Staphylococcus aureus, which was sensitive to fusidic acid. Full blood count and haematinic screen, complement and C1-esterase inhibitor levels, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) were all within normal limits. A decision was made to perform a biopsy.
[7933][Heading 2]  Where Should the Biopsy Be Taken From?
[7934][Para 001] The pathogenesis of orofacial granulomatosis and oral Crohn’s disease is granulomatous inflammation in tissues. To prove this, a deep biopsy is required because granulomas may be few and widely scattered, sometimes deep in tissues. The best tissues to sample are mucosal tags and linear ulcers, or a deep biopsy of the buccal mucosa may be performed. Unless it is the only site involved, biopsy of the lip is best avoided because any scarring on the labial mucosa will be visible, and thus unacceptable to the patient.

[7939][Heading 2]  The Biopsy Specimen is Shown in Fig. 74.3. What Do You See?
[7940][Para 002] At low power, left, the mucosa looks largely normal because the swelling is caused by oedema, and the tissue fluid present cannot be seen. The main feature is the presence of numerous clusters of inflammatory cells. There are up to 11 clusters of inflammatory cells at all levels in the mucosa, and three are shown by arrows.
[7941][Para 002] On the right, a high-power view from the top right of the left-hand-side image shows the clusters to be granulomas. Granulomas comprise epithelioid macrophages, seen as a sheet of pale pink cells (M) surrounded by a cuff of lymphocytes (L). Multinucleate giant cells are also present in some granulomas (arrowed).
[7942][Para 218] 
[7943][Para 008] 
[7944][Para 011] Fig. 74.3 Biopsy specimen of the buccal mucosa.
[7945][Para 009]  
[7946][Heading 2]  How Do You Interpret the Findings? How Does It Aid in the Diagnosis?
[7947][Para 001] There is granulomatous inflammation in the mucosa, consistent with orofacial granulomatosis, Crohn’s disease or sarcoidosis. These cannot be differentiated through biopsy.
[7948][Heading 2]  Does the Presence of Granulomatous Inflammation Raise the Possibility of Other Diseases?
[7949][Para 001] In theory yes, but these other diseases do not cause this clinical presentation. For example, tuberculosis, deep mycoses, and foreign body reactions are all characterized by granulomatous inflammation. Additional histological features are usually present in these other diseases: caseation in tuberculosis, fungi in mycoses and foreign material in foreign body reactions. Therefore these diseases do not need to be considered in this case.
[7950][Para 015] Diagnosis
[7951][Heading 2]  What is Your Diagnosis?
[7952][Para 001] Because there are several similar conditions compatible with the clinical presentation and results of investigations in this case, a working, rather than a definitive, diagnosis of orofacial granulomatosis is appropriate.
[7953][Para 002] The patient needs to be kept under review to see whether he develops bowel symptoms or signs that would lead to a diagnosis of Crohn’s disease, or facial paralysis for a diagnosis of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome.
[7954][Para 015] Treatment
[7955][Heading 2]  What are the Management Options?
[7956][Para 001] This patient requires treatment in a specialist centre.
[7957][Para 002] Fusidic acid cream should be prescribed for the angular cheilitis.
[7958][Para 002] All patients need to be informed about the nature of the disease and that its progression is unpredictable. Lip swelling is disfiguring, and it is important to ask the patient about social interactions and his mood in case psychological support is needed.
[7959][Para 002] No one treatment is ideal for every patient with orofacial granulomatosis, and so this patient may need to try several treatment approaches. A significant number of patients respond to dietary manipulation on the basis that the disease may be a hypersensitivity reaction to dietary components, particularly cinnamon and benzoate compounds. Avoidance of these is reported to induce a response in up to 70% of patients. The diet can be difficult to adhere to and should be managed through a dietician.
[7960][Para 002] Topical corticosteroids, such as prednisolone or fluticasone mouthwashes, can be useful, particularly in patients with oral ulcers. Occasionally, treatment may include intralesional corticosteroids injection into the swollen lips or systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressive drugs for more severe disease.
[7961][Para 014] Further Advice
[7962][Para 001] An example of a patient information leaflet from the British Society of Oral Medicine can be found at http://www.bsom.org.uk/ under patient information.
[7963][Para 110] Case 75
[7964][Para 111] Failing Implant Restoration
[7965][Para 112] Kalpesh A. Bavisha
[7966][Para 113] Summary
[7967][Para 013] A 40-year-old woman presents with recession around an implant-retained crown and feels the implant tooth is loose. What are the treatment options and their likely chances of success?
[7968][Para 009]  
[7969][Para 074] Fig. 75.1 Intraoral clinical photograph – anterior view in the intercuspal occlusal position.
[7970][Para 057] History
[7971][Para 045] Complaint
[7972][Para 013] The patient feels that the gum between her upper front teeth is disappearing and that the teeth feel loose. She has no pain.
[7973][Para 045] History of Complaint
[7974][Para 013] The patient has noticed the gum shrinking for the past several months.
[7975][Para 045] Dental History
[7976][Para 013] The patient had single implant crowns to replace the maxillary central anterior teeth 7 years ago. She attends her dentist every 6 months for regular review consultations.
[7977][Para 045] Medical History
[7978][Para 013] The patient is otherwise fit and well.
[7979][Para 057] Examination
[7980][Para 045] Extraoral Examination
[7981][Para 013] The temporomandibular joints appear normal, and no submental, submandibular or cervical lymph nodes are palpable.
[7982][Para 045] Intraoral Examination
[7983][Para 013] The patient lifts up her lip and shows you her upper front teeth.
[7984][Para 033]  The Appearance of the Dentition with the Implant-Retained Crowns is Shown in Fig. 75.1. What Can You Deduce From the Clinical Appearance?
[7985][Para 013] The upper right and upper left central incisors are implant-retained crowns; the upper left lateral incisor tooth is also crowned.
[7986][Para 013] The gingival papilla between the maxillary central incisors is missing. The teeth appear generally stained and discoloured. Calculus deposits are noted on the teeth surfaces, especially the gingival margins of the mandibular anterior incisors, upper right canine and lower left canine.
[7987][Para 013] There is slight erythema of the entire attached gingiva, as well as gingival recession associated with the natural dentition. The gingiva appears swollen and inflamed. This is most probably caused by a combination of poor oral hygiene and plaque accumulation. Gingival recession is present around the canines and premolars and may be a consequence of not only a plaque-associated inflammation but also an unfavourable tooth-to-bone volume ratio. This ratio can result in thin buccal bone overlying the teeth, increasing the risk of gingival recession in some patients.
[7988][Para 013] The soft tissue architecture around the maxillary implant restorations is not ideal anatomically, but it does not look inflamed clinically. There is marginal gingival inflammation around the maxillary lateral incisors, with a broad rounded gingival margin and little stippling.
[7989][Para 013] It is important to establish whether a full-sized interdental papilla was present when the implant crowns were fitted. This can be done by measuring the space between the tip of the papilla and the corresponding contact point of the crown. Photographs after crown placement are also an invaluable aid.
[7990][Para 102] Investigations
[7991][Para 013]  What Investigations Would You Carry Out, and Why?
[7992][Para 045] Periodontal Examination.
[7993][Para 013] Before picking up a periodontal probe, it is advisable to place gentle finger pressure on the buccal soft tissue overlying the implants. There should be no bleeding or exudate, and this procedure should not cause any discomfort to the patient. This procedure will also offer an insight into the level and origin of any mobility of either isolated teeth or a dento-alveolar segment.
[7994][Para 013] It is important to recognize the different types of peri-implant inflammation. Inflammation of the peri-implant mucosae has been termed peri-implant mucositis because no anatomical periodontal ligament is present adjacent to the implant surface. This is different from peri-implantitis, which is a more tissue-destructive disease that results in the loss of bone around an implant.
[7995][Para 013] The examination should include accurate recording of probing depths and gingival bleeding. Probing around implants is similar to probing around teeth. The junctional epithelium is delicate and can be breached by the periodontal probe. The underlying connective tissue offers less resistance than the fibre bundles found associated with the natural dentition. In general, the probe will stop short of the bone margin by approximately 1 mm.
[7996][Para 013] Standard periodontal probes can be used. Around healthy implant tissues, the probing depth should be less than 4 mm, with no or minimal bleeding.
[7997][Para 013] Probing around implant restorations can be difficult to perform clinically. The bulbosity/emergence profile of the restoration may not allow accurate recording of probing depths. Removal of a screw-retained restoration is not recommended for routine probing around implants and is not feasible with cement-retained restorations.
[7998][Para 013] If there is an increase in probing depth, gingival hyperplasia, purulent exudate and/or copious bleeding, it may be best to make an early referral for further investigation. This referral would be to your local specialist prosthodontist, implantologist or, ideally, the clinician who originally placed the implants. A more detailed examination will require removal of a screw-retained restoration.
[7999][Para 013] For cemented implant restorations, excess cement left on the implant or abutment surfaces will allow plaque to accumulate and result in inflammation of the peri-implant tissues, just as in indirect restorations cemented onto the natural dentition. It is important to ensure that excess cement is not the cause of the inflammation. It would be unlikely in this case because the restorations have been in place for several years and because inflamed tissues are a recent finding.
[8000][Para 013] Check the mobility of the implant-supported restorations. It is rare for an implant to feel loose. Even with significant bone loss, an implant restoration can still feel firm. It is important to distinguish a loose crown, which is a more common occurrence. A loose crown may be caused by a loose abutment screw, a screw fracture or debonding of a cemented crown.
[8001][Para 013] On performing these investigations, you discover a 7mm probing depth associated with the upper left central incisor and a probing depth of 4 mm with the upper right central incisor, generalized marginal gingivitis with bleeding on probing and plaque accumulation around the crown margins. No mobility is noted because the crowns appear firm.
[8002][Para 013] If there is any concern about an implant-supported restoration, it is advisable to obtain plain film radiographs (see later).
[8003][Para 045] Occlusal Examination.
[8004][Para 013] It is important in single implant-supported restorations that the natural teeth are the first teeth in contact. An easy way to determine this is with the use of Shimstock foil, which has a thickness of 8 μm. In the intercuspal position, the natural teeth should hold the Shimstock foil. Between the implant restoration and the opposing contact, it should be possible to drag the Shimstock foil through without tearing it. Asking the patient to clench hard will result in the Shimstock foil being held firmly between the implant restoration and the opposing contact.
[8005][Para 045] Radiographic Examination of the Upper Incisors.
[8006][Para 013] Periapical radiographs, taken using a paralleling technique and beam-aiming device, are required to:
[8007][Para 013] • Evaluate marginal bone levels. With implant restorations it is important to establish baseline radiographs. Whether this should be done at the time of implant placement or during fitting of the final restoration is still being debated. The frequency and timing of taking radiographs is also controversial. Usually, a radiograph is taken after 1 year of implant function and can be repeated 2 years later. Subsequent timing can be of decreasing frequency and related more to clinical need. Where there is evidence of a change in bone levels, the frequency of taking radiographs may need to be increased. In describing bone loss, it may be useful to describe the extent of bone in relation to the radiographically visible implant threads. Depending on the system, the implant may have micro-threads, macro-threads or both. If possible, stating the number of threads exposed may allow for a better comparison of radiographs because these are a fixed reference point.
[8008][Para 013] • Abutment fit and crown margin fit. If unsure about the fit of an abutment or screw-retained crown, a radiograph can confirm whether it is fully seated. For an abutment, there should be no space between the abutment and the wall of the implant when utilizing an internal connection, as seen in Fig. 75.2.
[8009][Para 013] • Presence of subgingival deposits calculus and/or cement. Cement, if radiolucent, may not be seen on the radiograph.
[8010][Para 013] • Absence of continuous radiolucency around the implant. Because there is no lamina dura around an implant, there should be no radiolucency around the implant. Radiolucency around an implant is likely to be a result of failure of osseointegration of the implant and the surrounding alveolar bone.
[8011][Para 033]  The Periapical Radiographs are Shown in Fig. 75.2. What Do You See?
[8012][Para 013] The detailed radiographic report is explained in Table 75.1.

[8015][Para 057] Diagnosis
[8016][Para 033]  What are Your Provisional Diagnoses?
[8017][Para 161] See Table 75.2.
[8018][Para 013] • Peri-implantitis associated with poor plaque control
[8019][Para 013] • A previous history of periodontitis
[8020][Para 013] • Chronic gingivitis
[8021][Para 013] • Inadequate root canal filling of the upper left lateral incisor.
[8022][Para 102] Treatment
[8023][Para 013]  How Would You Manage These Conditions?
[8024][Para 045] Nonsurgical Management.
[8025][Para 013] The management of peri-implantitis involves oral hygiene instruction as well as supra- and subgingival debridement.
[8026][Para 175]  Is Special Equipment Required for Cleaning Around Implant Restorations?
[8027][Para 013] No. Conventional instruments can be used with care to remove biofilm without causing damage. Aim to improve the patient’s level of plaque control with careful oral hygiene instruction/advice.
[8028][Para 013] Check for any potential occlusal causes and take measures to make it easier for the patient to clean the restoration; also, aim to improve access, embrasure contour, and emergence profile.
[8029][Para 013] Titanium instruments can be used to prevent scratching of the implant surface. Some advocate the use of plastic instruments to prevent damage, but these instruments can be difficult to use, and it is more important to ensure that the biofilm and any more tenacious deposits have been removed.
[8030][Para 013] Surfaces that are difficult to clean include the implant surface because of the naturally rough surface and the presence of threads. If needed, greater access and the use of specialized titanium brushes and burs, with direct access and a surgical approach, may be required.
[8031][Para 051] Table 75.1
[8032][Para 061] Radiographic Findings of the Periapical Radiograph Shown in Fig. 75.2
[8033][Para 051] Table 75.2
[8034][Para 061] Radiological Diagnosis
[8035][Para 175] Surgical Management (Carried Out by a Specialist).
[8036][Para 013] Aim to have direct access to all of the implant exposed surfaces. A soft tissue flap is raised under local anaesthesia, with the aim of allowing removal of the biofilm. Several techniques are available to do this, including the use of ultrasonic instrumentation, specialized titanium micro-brushes, drilling of the implant surface to remove the threads, chemical debridement or even bone grafting. This surgical intervention may result in the implant threads becoming visible, compromising the final aesthetics.
[8037][Para 013] The importance of an early diagnosis of peri-implantitis is important, and early specialist referral is recommended to prevent further bone loss and any subsequent implant loss. As shown in this case, the clinical signs are not always accurate indicators of the extent of the disease.
[8038][Para 013] Most implant-supported restorations with perimucositis can be managed in a straightforward manner with routine oral hygiene measures. The patient should be instructed on how best to clean around the implant restoration by using routine brushing and interproximal cleaning techniques. Assess whether the patient is physically able to clean the restorations or whether cleaning procedures need to be modified to allow the patient to clean with ease. This should have been considered at the planning stage before treatment execution.
[8039][Para 013] Implant restorations require additional maintenance. Implants are designed to allow maximum osseointegration. Their surfaces, however, are not easy to clean once they become contaminated. Early intervention when disease is suspected, and with specialist referral when necessary, is key. A failing implant may not result in any significant clinical signs or symptoms. These changes may be only detectable with probing the tissues around the implant and taking and interpreting appropriate radiographs. A late diagnosis of a failing implant is likely to result in further surgery for the patient, a compromise in aesthetics and, at worst, removal of the implant, all of which may result in medico-legal action. Patients should be aware of the need for regular maintenance at home and at the clinic.
[8040][Para 045] Medico-Legal Issues
[8041][Para 013] Accurate recording of clinical findings and patient discussions is essential. In this case, documentation, including previous probing depths and periapical radiographs, are indispensable to demonstrate the progressive disease process. The patient should be encouraged to maintain a meticulous oral hygiene regimen, and appropriate referral to a suitably qualified clinician for the management of peri-implantitis is recommended.
[8042][Para 013] In summary, the General Dental Council, UK recommends:
[8043][Para 013] • Maintaining detailed and extensive clinical records
[8044][Para 013] • Completing the initial phases of history, examination and investigations robustly
[8045][Para 013] • Recording a diagnosis
[8046][Para 013] • Providing an individualized written treatment plan that includes details of the need for treatment, the treatment options (the risks and benefits), the phases of treatment, the costs of treatment and the expected normal sequelae of surgery
[8047][Para 013] • Considering referral at an early stage, particularly if reparative surgery is required.
